Seems like a lot people hated the game because they expected it to be like Civ. It is a shame for the game is actually an RTS, closer to Starcraft but with so much more diversity and depth. Unlike starcraft, the strategy is centered around grabbing ressources and messing up with your opponents using black market powers.
The game is just always evolving, with 4 different factions who define your playstyle entirely. There are vastly different maps, pushing you to adapt to the new conditions and resources available every time. Finally, the black market adds another layer of complexity entirely as different powers are available every game. A game where you can uncover new ressources will be drastically different from one where you can claim more lands or one where you can steal ressources from each others.
Finally, the developers are constantly updating the game with new add-ons that offer new sets of rules and challenges to adapt to.
If you want a fun deep RTS with a max duration of 30 minutes, that will challenge you constantly to adapt and judge where the market will go, this is the game for you!

I have not yet played the previous iterations (Amnesia) but I have to say this game has some truly terrifying and heart pounding moments that I have not experienced since Dead Space 1. The graphics are superb, the in game sound is amazing from heart beats to accidentally knocking over buckets
I will say that the enemy (?) encounters are a very small portion of the game proper and the rest is piecing together what is happening or completing whatever the current objective is. I find it perfectly suitable for this game.
What I truly enjoyed most of all was the philosophical questions posed by the games creators with regards to copies of human personalities and minds. Especially with regards to what is me?
Last point, though choices need to be made through the progression of the game that challenge the moral framework of the player, attempting to decide the best fate in truly unique occurrences and each decision I found tugged at raw emotional strings. A game like this one truly challenge what kind of person you are in a way that real life most likely never will.

You're a Tier One operator, you're on active duty in Afghanistan and your name is... Rabbit?
This Medal of Honor game reeks of Call of Duty influence, except sadly the gameplay isn't as fluid as Call of Duty's and the campaign isn't as interesting either. Down to the stupid player character names (Rabbit = Soap anyone?), it's clear EA tried to revive a classic series and bring it back to life to compete with the big boys. Unfortunately, they failed and we're left with a generic FPS game set in the brown 'n' bloom desert. With an unengaging plot which tries too hard with it's cutscenes, there's little to push you to press forward in the campaign.
Enemy AI is garbage too, leading to mostly dull fights in the streets, rooftops and warehouses of Afghanistan. The guns look nice, and feel good to shoot. They even
nice. It's just a shame they're stuck in this game. Graphics can be appealing at times but mostly the dull uninspired enviroments leave a lot to be desired, and the lack of graphics options in the main menu was a let down as I had no way to reduce the jaggies which soured my experience a little.
In conclusion, EA tried to create a Call of Duty killer yet only managed to spawn a generic, drab, uninspired FPS set in the desert which spells boring enviroments -a-palooza and tries to pull you in with a cliché and boring story. Avoid.

This game is a decent game. It has pretty grafix and it runs decently. It's worth picking it up on a sale to experience the mediocre but enjoyable story. This is the perfect Call of Duty clone. It wants to be Modern Warfare so bad it's not even funny. Down to the smallest detail. If I have one complaint about the Singleplayer is that it's sensitivity option is PURE♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ It doesn't go low enough. I've lowered the DPI on my mouse and it still goes WAY faster than I would like to. It's such a basic option, yet they didn't fiddle enough with it so it makes the game kinda unplayable for me, I had to pull every trick in the hat, lower Windows sensitivity and so on so forth, to make it playable. Every game's sensitivity option should go from 0 to 100. 0 being DEAD STOP, not moving at all, 100 being crazy fast. Not this game. This game is special.... This is even more curios because the MULTIPLAYER's sensitivity option is very good. It does what it's supposed to do, it goes as low as you want it to, until it stops moving completely. Weird. So this nice segway brings us to multiplayer. If you're buying it for the MP, DON'T. Get the latest COD, it'll be the same. At the time of writing there are only about 100 players playing the MP at any given time! Only a couple of the 4-5 MP modes are played, and those are not the best kind of modes. Not to mention that those 100 players, given their dedication, are MAX level and have every little♥♥♥♥♥♥unlocked, so they're like 5 times more powerful than you, due to the better upgrades they have. If you want a compelling MP experience similar to this go play COD, or try your luck with Medal Of Honor Warfighter, but even with Warfighter I don't think the MP community is what it was at launch, not that this game even EVER had a decent MP community, not even at launch. So bottom line is, buy this game at a sale to experience the decent Singleplayer campaign. That is all.

So, Nether. I initially picked this up and played it during the beta and would not have recommended it then (as seems to be the general opinion, judging by the Early Access reviews).
My two major complaints were simple. First, the movement felt wonky and made gunplay in PvP feel incredibly odd. Secondly, it was hard to be immersed in the atmosphere when most things were decorated with nothing but trash bags. If you've looked at whether or not I've recommended this game, then you might surmise that these issues were rectified.
The game does have its issues, no doubt. However, what's really doing it for me is the atmosphere. There is a lot of detail, a lot of tall grass to hide in and plenty of places to hide from enemies. As far as post-apocalyptic survival goes, this does it for me.
Let's go over some of the main points!
There are zones in the game that are totally safe. You cannot kill people in these zones, you cannot even bring up your ironsights. This very well might put some people off of the game, especially those wanting an experience similar to DayZ or perhaps Rust, where you want PvP all the time, anywhere. However, I appreciate the difference. It's nice to come back after a courier mission and take some time to relax and plot your next action.
This is made a little more interesting by the fact that these safe zones periodically... well... become unsafe. You can kill people, you can kill invading monsters. Watch your trigger finger... or keep an eye out for someone that looked at you funny early on.
This game is not detailed when it comes to survival. You need to eat, you need to drink, you need to keep your health up. You won't bleed out, you won't get poisoned. It keeps this aspect of the game simple. If you've eaten enough food, you regenerate health slowly. Very slowly. But it is a nice reason to stay well-fed.
You'll find yourself scavenging for foodstuffs, weapons, ammo, cash. You'll kill monsters and get their skin, claws and skulls. Honestly, if you're after something super-detailed here, probably not for you. But if you don't mind the simplicity and just want some reason to eat food while hunting for people/monsters/etc., then it does the trick.
Right, so there are monsters in this game. They're called 'Nether', but that always makes me try to come up with some inappropriate innuendo. Either way, what is the AI like? Not great, but surprisingly... not bad. They'll run at you, they'll call for nearby monsters to help and... they'll teleport and try to get behind you -- yes, teleport. It's a thing they're meant to do, not a buggy weirdness. They can chase you fairly effectively, handling the inside of buildings well enough to pose a threat and even able to climb stairs after you.
On their own, they're really nothing to worry about. If you have a knife, you can likely kill one no issue. It's when they're in groups that they're a danger. But there's more than just the AI to worry about once the shots start ringing out as you desperately try to cling to life...
Outside of safezones, it's free reign. Kill whomever you want. The game has a mechanic where you can join a 'Tribe'; pick one out of several colourful, but standard, apocalyptic factions and fight for them to take territory and earn rewards. Don't worry -- you can still kill fellow tribemates! There is a reputation system that discourages you from doing so and wanton fratricide will see you kicked out from your tribe.
There is an interesting mode of gameplay I'm fond of. Playing AS one of the monsters. You can buy a potion for relatively cheap (with in-game money), drink it and get the option to become one of the creatures. Some clunkiness to be had here, you have to log out and log back into the server, then choose your character as a monster. Monster mode, however, is fun. You don't lose anything on death, you're fast, you're nimble and you're practically blind. It changes up the experience in a way I quite enjoyed. What I like most about this is that you're always left wondering if the monster over yonder happens to be a player... and if they have a pack of friends.
Oh and you can group with friends pretty easily, if that's something you like to do.
Overall, PvP is perhaps limited when compared to other titles. You won't be kidnapping anyone and sacrificing them to volcano gods, you won't be forcefeeding them bleach. But you will be feverishly glancing up at windows and wondering if someone is watching you.
One thing that puts people off is that you can gain levels, build your character... then you die and lose all the hard work. The developers have mitigated this with an 'Account Level' system. You get perks that persist... nothing huge, but nice perks that give you some overall accomplishment. The game keeps track of your overall PvP and PvE kills, which is a nice touch. Thankfully, rebuilding a character is not a massive undertaking and you can get the primary perks you want in an incredibly short amount of time. Does this maybe kinda cheapen it for the more-hardcore crowd? Maybe. I don't mind it and I have other games to get my hardcore gaming cravings satiated.
So, there are some problems. I don't feel it's gamebreaking, but it's worth noting. Technically speaking, the graphics are nothing special and perhaps a bit dated. I feel that they make up with this with a great deal of atmosphere -- this is something you'll have to decide on your own after checking out some videos or screenshots. It might be a little hardware intensive for what you get.
Sounds can be a touch funky. Especially underground. You're never sure if the gunshots you hear are just around the metro tunnel bend or... actually just above you on the street level.
Terrain can be odd. There are cases where you're moving over some ruined rubble and you suddenly start levitating in the air. Like, way up. You continue on and you find yourself sinking into the rubble. Odd stuff like that -- thankfully, it's not the norm.
The UI is... mreh. Kinda funky. Backpacks don't 'equip', you have to just have them in your inventory. And sometimes you have to drop them and pick them back up. The skill menu doesn't tell you exactly what stuff does, so you end up having to look up what the mysterious %+ boosts are actually doing as you level up your Survival skill. Similarly, crafting suffers from odd menu stuff as well... functional, but not pretty.
All in all, I just wanted an atmospheric survival game in a post-apocalyptic setting. And yeah, this does that pretty well. Honestly, the atmosphere is just fantastic by my reckoning. I would compare it to a bit of Metro 2033 mixed with DayZ's openworld PvP. It has issues... but it has a lot of fun, if you're a fan of the setting and the genre. Will it last you in the long run? I'm planning on playing it for a fair bit more, at least. I think it's worth a shot and can keep you entertained for a good amount of time... and that's something I definitely would not have said for it in Early Access.
If you've tried it out before, it might be worth taking a second look.

NOTE: This review is a redux of my original review.
Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II: The Sith Lords is made by Obisidian Entertainment and serves as a sequel to Bioware's Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic. I've played through this game twice. My first playthrough was on the Jedi path and without the Restored Content and M4-78 mods. Honestly, I didn't like it and I wrote a negative review on it. However, after some time had passed, I tried the game again, but I went down the path of a Dark Jedi and had the previously stated mods installed. This review is based on my second playthrough:
Pros:
+Slightly better graphics than KOTOR I
+Story is decent and more clear thanks to the RCM and M4-78 but does have some minor issues.
+Details of the environments surpasses KOTOR I
+Like the idea of influence and converting your party to be a Jedi or Dark Jedi
+Well designed characters, but I felt their backstories weren't as fleshed out as in KOTOR I (however there are some exceptions to this criticism)
+Maintained alot of elements that made KOTOR I great (choice / morale system, path of Jedi or Sith, etc)
+Mods like the Restored Content Modification and M4-78 fix most of the problems found in the "Vanilla version" of the game. (Hats off to the people who developed the mods)
Cons:
-The turn-based combat (like in my KOTOR I review, this is something I don't like in RPGs in general)
-The ending (those of you who've played the game know what I'm talking about)
-The influence and Jedi conversion can be VERY tedious as some characters aren't as easy to convert / influence
-I was a bit disappointed that the story didn't really relate much to KOTOR I as I thought it would be. The story is connected to KOTOR I by characters from the previous game but kinda are like side characters and refernces to events and other characters from the previous game.
Overall, (8/10) Star Wars KOTOR II: The Sith Lords is a solid game but (in my opinion) not as good as the original. However, its still worth a try if your a die hard Star Wars fan or an RPG fan. NOTE: If you want the best version of this game get: 1. The Restored Content Mod, 2. M4-78, 3. Visas HD Re-Skin from the Steam Workshop.

With first impressions in mind, it may be hard to decide if buying the game would be worth it. Certainly I was not the only one that felt the same way after reading some of the reviews on this game. After choosing to buy it, there was no regrets to be felt as the game progressed.
The beginning can throw off gamers from seeing the true colors of this game. It almost felt like watching a cartoon with the 'odd' opening cutscene, full of characters you won't be introduced fully to until later, playing right after the setting is introduced. It is unskippable so prepare to watch it and its entirety. Afterwards, feeling skeptical about the game is totally natural. Eventually, this notion is more than compensated with the game's solid gameplay and attention to detail, specifically how the main character, Parin, reacts to people and the environment. As this game is a port from the PSP well over a decade ago, the developers certainly took the time to add in small details that made the game more enjoyable.
The game ramps up difficulty fairly quickly and is proven to be a challenge, especially those who are unprepared. The combat seems to be on point with the game being somewhat forgiving when being damaged, also adding in how invincibility frames plays a role in survivability. However, bare in mind that the controls for some moves are quite sensitive and may activate undesired attacks. Overall, it isn't a terribly difficult game unless you are trying to attempt triple S rank on every stage or playing on Crazy mode, the highest difficulty possible, or perhaps both.
The story is very lighthearted and in many cases child-friendly, but that alone is a big part of the reason why this hidden gem of a game stands out. It is rare to find a good game in the market that isn't even remotely close to having any adultlike values. The voice acting, as amazing as the cast is, can be slightly better though as sometimes there are scenes where the voices of some characters do not match their body language or the current mood of the cutscene.
I recommend playing through this ARPG at least once if you are a fan of RPG-like genres. I would also recommend using a controller if possible as the style of control with keyboard or mouse can be confusing to use. There is simply a ton of replay value and charming RPG elements that is well worth the $9.99 (Guaranteed worth it if bought on sale).
EDIT (Author's Note): This is my first review on a game and did this as this game seems to not be getting enough attention.
-----------------------------------------------
TL;DR - A cute style ARPG that has a few blemishes that shouldn't hinder gamers from enjoying Parin's adventure. This hidden gem game is often very, very overlooked as good.

Medal of Honor can be compared mostly to the recent episodes of the Call of Duty franchise. You get a military shooter with very linear and short campaign and a multiplayer mode which was designed for the masses. In both parts MoH fails to compete against the successful series. However, there are some parts which are more valuable than in the case of the other. I played through the game twice, so it can be considered as one of my favorite military shooters to date.
I would start with the graphics and overall design. Unlike Warfighter, MoH uses the Unreal Engine which is a good choice for any shooters. The utilization however is not the best. The game has the usual "previous generation console issues" like blurry textures, worthless anti-aliasing and optimization problems. Also I need to mention that the level design is pretty varied. The night scenes mostly look good with all the lightning, but sometimes I encounter areas which are so poorly detailed. There are almost completely empty rooms, small flames coming from nowhere and a other annoying things. It is maybe not fair to judge a game's graphics four years after release, but I was not amazed at the time when it came out. In 2010 I have seen much better visuals already and the cut-scenes in the game are so disappointing, they are just ruining the atmosphere.
One of the better parts of the game is the gameplay. The gunplay is fun, however the behaviour of the weapons sometimes clumsy and weird. Overall it is still acceptable. There are multiple weapons to use from both sides during missions. The short campaign includes the usual sections, like sneaking, sniping, shooting with mg, etc. There are some good ideas either, which seems pretty experimental and brave at times. Some of the areas are nicely done, allowing some freedom and variation, though most of them are pretty linear and strict. At one point on day 2 we crossed under a bridge while troops were marching above us. The game gave me the control, but I was told to let them pass. Once I tried to shoot the separated soldier, all the others started to shoot. Actually, after a few shots they fled, and my partner just desperately wanted to climb the bank of the river bed and chase them. So, sometimes you got more freedom, but in these cases you would never know what happens if you do not stick to the plan, you can even fail the mission because of a bug. And, if I speak about bugs, I encountered a few during my gameplay. Sometimes these breaks the game, like when one of your teammate stuck into a wall, so you need to reload a previous checkpoint. Fortunately, the game saves pretty often, so you do not lose much progress if something bad happens. These linear sequences sometimes nicely choreographed, so I do not complain about it all the time.
I have mixed opinions about the writing and storytelling too. You have to control various soldiers during the campaign. These are from different classes, allowing you to explore the full arsenal of the division. However, this may prevent the connection to one certain soldier, making characters less memorable. As I mentioned before, the cutscenes are not managed to give me a good impression, but some of them are exceptions. I really liked the ending. The tense was pretty high in those last minutes, which elevated the game quite a bit. It was really sad and touching. The whole storytelling tries a different approach to the genre and sometimes it is what moves the player forward. I recently watched the Lone Survivor movie and I had similar feeling during the playtime. The game gives back the feel of the war zone in the middle east well.
Now comes my favourite part of the game, the audio part. Ramin Djawadi wrote an amazing soundtrack for this title, which earns the game a playthrough on its own. I played the game with lowered effects volume, so that the music can be more enjoyable. The album is also one of my favourite military soundtrack album. The sounds are also pretty much in place. You do not hear anything awkward. The weapon sounds are good, the impacts makes you feel the pressure during combat. The overall feedback is great. Last part in the audio section is the dialogues. This is a shooter, so the most frequent lines you will hear are orders for movement, shoot and others. The lines during cut-scenes and between fights are mostly passable. They do not worsen the experience.
Overall, this game feels like an early release. It would needed more polish and work on details. I do not say, that multiplayer could compete against any of the CoD's, but the singleplayer part could be much more enjoyable. That way this could be a must have. However, I still recommend this game, because it is still closer to my heart than many other shooters out there.

Do you like baseball?
I didn't. I really didn't. I liked a lot of different sports but I always thought baseball was boring, archaic and more an excuse to sit outside, drink beer and gawk at the occasional on-field event.
But then, for whatever reason -- I didn't have much else going on -- I started to watch baseball, because it was always on, pretty much every day, and it started to wrap itself around my brain in a pleasing way. Baseball is low-intensity matched with extreme peaks and valleys of emotion.
More importantly -- Baseball is a long continuous set of calculations based on the manipulation of variables in series after series of problems. Every at-bat, every pitch, every inning, every game is a test of odds and outcomes based on the pitcher, the batter, the fielders, the field, the weather, past results obscuring present values... Baseball is a worthwhile flux.
So - OOTP 17. This is the most advanced and ridiculously satisfying way to run your own personal baseball simulations. So maybe I should rephrase - Do you like Baseball as a concept? Because you will love OOTP.
(Also this year they added little moving pawns to the broadcast view, so it's starting to get satisfyingly similar to half-watching an actual baseball game.)
For those already owning OOTP 16 and mulling an upgrade I would say - the engine runs much faster this year on x64, some under the hood stuff has been nicely tweaked, bells and whistles (the pawns) aren't nothing, and of course, I feel pretty good about supporting this developer, given their track record.

If ever there was a game that deserved to be judged fairly by history, this is probably it.
Everyone interested in this game at all knows the story. KoToR 1 is undisputably one of the greatest games of a generation. The follow up had immense hype, development was going well, and then the publishers pushed it out the door unreasonably early.
The result, and reaction, was predictible. A game that for all it did right could never quite measure up. I often referred to it as "the best public beta ever". That's something I stand by playing it now. Some people enjoyed it as a flawed masterpiece. Others derided the obvious lack of debugging. We all agreed the final chapter was obviously rushed and simply wasn't done. It was a shame, and it fell squarely on the publsher.
Luckily, the game's community was kind. As was this re-release, with some mild enhancements, and Steam Workshop integration. That means there is literally no reason to have this on Steam and not be using the (fabled) Restored Content Mod, that undoes so many wrongs. One single press of a green subscribe button in the workshop undoes a foolish, greedy mistake. A truly great piece of work loaded with bugfixes, and finally seeing the game as it should have been from the beginning in 2005.
And what a game it finally is. So many bugs gone, so many plot holes filled with the dialogue that was recorded but never programmed to trigger in the final release, a so much more complete experience. It's a massive, almost overwhelming game. Unlike most Star Wars, it isn't overly sugary sweet, the line between good and evil is rarely clear at points. It's got real depth. And it's an epic adventure for the ages.
I love the KoToR games. I always did. Nobody in their right mind disliked the first game. And it really warms my heart to see that, even if it took me 10 years to see the final result, the second game turned out alright after all.

While I have not played as much of this game as many of the other player I still believe that this is a game worth a lot to people who want a simulation of military tactics and decisions. To call it a sandbox is an understatement due to the fact that one has endless options for mission making not only from the adequate assets provided but also from the steam workshop, where there are hundreds of thousands of mods including a lot of extra objects.
Once you have a mission, either made for you or by you, you can play using your knowledge and common-sense any one of the many different roles. With a wide range of weapons and their variations you could end with different results every time you play.
There are two things most people complain about with this game one is the steep learning curve as most of the buttons on your keyboard will perform a certain action (a keyboard with a numpad is helpful) and the other is your fps. The majority of gamers will get around 30fps or less but a powerful computer can achieve 60fps. One should feel it necessary to fiddle with the graphic settings as just a few tweaks may bring you out of the red. Keep in mind I play with an average of 15-30fps on normal settings but still have a lot of enjoyment.
In the end this game is one that I enjoyed and anyone that isn’t life dependent on non-stop action and doesn’t mind using their brain from time to time will enjoy too.

Probably Archery does support gamepads, so maybe I would have had more luck there, but the game is fun nonetheless.

TL;DR Gurumin tries hard. It tries very hard but feels like it lacked a good quality assurance cycle or clear leadership from the creative team and the result is a haphazard mix of good and terrible gameplay. But unfortunately it is more of the latter which makes it not worth purchasing.
And now the full review:
Gurumin wants to be Legend of Zelda so badly that it hurts, but fails to engage the player in all the ways that Nintendo understands. Would it be fair to call it a bad game? Unfortunately since you have to front cash for it, yes it really isn't worth the money and here is why.
The developers have really done a great job on the art-style of the game although the background music varies from great to ear-bleeding, however I will admit that initially it started off very strong. But after about 4 hours of gameplay you suddenly realize how you start to lack any motivation to keep playing. The game is extremely linear although you can choose in which order you want to tackle batches of levels that are unlocked. There is a progression system of a kind with various headgear you unlock and upgrade but in all honesty the only two which you will ever use are the Vampire Disguise hat and the Nightcap since these have the most practical bonuses and overshadow all of the others. You gain new moves but they are just more powerful versions of the same early abilities and there was an attempt to introduce elemental weaknesses with fire/elec/ice but it really causes the combat to become anything but fluid as you pause the game, select the different drillbit and then unpause again. The devs could have simply added hotkeys and it would have really made the game feel much better. There is an unforgivable attempt to extend how long the game is by mirroring levels with some different enemies thrown in. But this also adds to the tedium as you retread the same areas you just completed but in reverse. The 'keep the beat' method of getting critical hits is original but totally unworkable as your attention is focussed on the phantom blob creatures themselves so I don't know why they kept it in the game.
The game quickly runs out of steam and you can tell the developers noticed this as they try to mix things up with platforming sections. Now... 3D platformers are fine but they require some great camera work to ensure that players are able to judge distances and the main character needs to have decent air-control or jumping distance - Gurumin doesn't do any of this and therefore you will often miss landings or plummet to insta-death. Gurumin also does the unforgivable mistake of giving you an ice/snow themed level with precision jumps, sloping edge platforms that Marin will skid off if you don't stay in the middle and slippery surfaces. The level is an exercise in patience as you creep around everywhere and spend much of your time finding the perfect angle for the camera to make that critical jump over insta-death canyons.
There is a plot here.. somewhere... but it really would only appeal to young children (5-7yr olds). However the difficulty of some parts of the game would make the game inaccessible to them. What should be a central driving force to keep the player pushing forwards becomes yet another missing ingredient for a good game. Characters are also 1-dimensional and the developers idea of creating a 'mystery' means they just don't explain why anything is happening or they drizzle out trivial details. That isn't mystery, that's compensating for a shallow story.
Sorry folks but when I reach the point where I want to turn the game off to go do housework because the game is so tedious, you know that there is a problem with it's design.

There's not a lot that anyone can divulge about this game without revealing a ton of magnificent plot points, so I'll try to summarize without spoiling this incredible title.
This game is intense, and as always, the team that brought the famously popular AMNESIA: The Dark Descent as well as several other horror titles before have mercilessly painted the game in a grim palette that's border-line decadent. The cold, lonely, dripping halls of the under water stations you will tromp about trying to get your bearrings are claustrophobic, horrifyingly lit and look like you've walked into everything right around the time Cthulu decided to get his lazy♥♥♥♥♥out of the bottom of the ocean and wreck the entirety of existence. The silence is deafening, forced to listen old transmissions of a hopeless world that is dead, and where you might honestly be the only sane man left.
As the game progresses, you will be presented with many, many moral choices. Though the dialogue is by no means tedious between the protagonist, and his pretty 'assistant' as we'll call her, they discuss a great deal on their concepts of what is life, what is death and what that means to the world around them. You set out in hopes of restoring this assistant's project dubbed the 'ARK', a artifical world where humanity's last dying hope may be to leave behind everything that is human, and take off as nothing but mere data on a little sattellite, roaming the cosmos for thousands of years.
As of the time I'm writing this review, I have not yet completed the game. The monsters are masterfully crafted, and every little groan, scream, or perturbed murmuring they make induces nothing but sheer panic. Their appearances are sheer terror, and thanks to the claustrophobia of the dimly lit halls of this station, you will be forced to make some very daring escapes, or cry in a corner while the monster howls at you. The moral choices I discussed are something I can't really reveal without being entirely heavy handed, but suffice to say, if you enjoy thinking and recieving inputs other than your own on the possibilities of 'what is life', you're sure to find yourself staring forlorn and frustrated as you're presented with someone else's life, in a 'what would I want if this was fair'. But none of it is fair.
The only negative comments I can make? Well, I'm not sure this engine has been properly stream-lined. It really lieks to eat up resources, and there are parts where I putter along with choppy graphics. The chatter between the protagonist, and 'assistant' are somewhat common place, and if you're looking at this title for the hopes of being utterly alone, I'm afraid you'll be disappointed. She likes to talk when there's no monsters around, and will be in your ear buzzing like a busy bee. But don't worry, if you don't mind the break from screaming and crying she never chirps up when there's real danger present. That, you get to face alone.
A absolute classic for the horror genre. And thank God they hit the mark again, it seems the AMNESIA team quickly come to save the day before this genre becomes all hallway shooters with spooky scary zombie mutations.

There's no deeper baseball simulation out there today unless you manage to get a job in a MLB front office. I've been mildly addicted to the franchise for years and this is another great outing but where it really excels is how the customization options allow for the creation of fantastic stories.  The forum on the OOTP website is awash with stories of baseball leagues incorporating the fiction of Fallout(complete with occasional deaths from radiation, drug addiction, and deathclaws), Tolkien(orcs make surprisingly good catchers), Star Wars(Wookie umpires, don't argue with them), or spurring users to create totally new(though probably derivative) fictional universes.
If that appeals to you check it out, I can almost guarantee it'll be money well spent for a baseball fan.
What follows is a brief story from my first OOTP 17 game. Relatively brief anyway.
The universe is mostly ours but the major pro baseball league is the United Nations Baseball League featuring 32 teams, 16 in the Americas(North American Pro League-DH), 16 in the Pacific Rim(Pan-Asian Super League-No DH) each league features four divisions of four teams each, division winners make the playoffs. No interleague play because well the travel would be sort of ridiculous.
I started with an opening draft where I'll be guiding my Perth Koalas as GM so I'm relying on the AI to handle the gameday management under manager Shugo Endo. Notable players include local boy Adrian Wall(1B), power hitting Jordan Najera(C), the 22 million dollar man Jesus Suarez(CF), the all-around excellent Alex Ozeguera(RF), and team leader Andy Varner(OF). Despite all those position players the real power is on the mound, where I spent our first three picks on starters Rickey O'Dowd, Mike Davis, and the great Canadian hope Willard Hayward, we also have one of the best closers in the league in Jose Reyes a 21 year old fireballer out of Cuba and a top notch setup guy in Ryan Nance. So that team sounds pretty good, what's the problem? Glad you asked.
For starters this GM does not like his manager and most of these players have their own fatal flaws, such as defense Wall, Suarez and Najera would all be better suited to DH work, the guys I have to play defense to shore up these niggling issues like Varner cannot hit period. One of the great things about OOTP(sorry this probably belonged up top) is that you'll see two sets of players ratings, one regarding the view of the league at large and one for your scout's opinion, those two will start to converge, but with that opening draft I'll find myself wondering how much to trust my scout and how much his opinion differs from that of the league in general and I'll be repeating the process in amateur drafts. This is a problem for my Perth Koalas because Varner, our shortstop Davon Jones, and outfield prospect Freddie Kozak are among many players where my scout thinks they are way better than the league does.
Luckily pitching cures a lot of ills and with 4 of our top 6 draft picks in the rotation O'Dowd, Davis, Hayward, and Darren Fyfe are cleaning up while fifth starter Frank Rosales is performing above expectations, it helps that Reyes is mostly unhittable and Suarez is playing like the best outfielder on our side of the Pacific. There are injuries to deal with but the first two months of the season sees us pulling away from our division rivals the Melbourne Emus, Brisbane Dragoons, and Taipei Liberty, competing with the Beijing Reds(amusingly because of the name the Reds initially were setup to play in the Great American Ballpark) for the best record in the PASL. Injuries popped up from time to time, but mostly involved our mediocre left field situation(starter Nick Bailey has a .302 OBP and his backup Kenichi Takeuchi hits .217) until the chaos started.
A few relievers started to get hurt, annoying but something I can work around as long as the rest of the staff is healthy. The biggest issue was losing talented middle reliever Soetsu Tanaka for the season, but hey at least he isn't Nance or Reyes. Then Reyes blows out his arm, he'll need Tommy John surgery and the man had a 0.99 ERA at the time.
Okay, going into June without 2 of our top 3 relievers, As long as Nance is still around and the rotation's intact. We keep on plowing through the PASL, seven all-stars O'Dowd, Davis, Hayward Suarez, Najera, Wall and our third baseman Johnathan Lugo. Our lead in the division is from 15-20 games for months, we are dominant. How dominant, well aside from the massive divisional lead for almost a month Najera and Suarez were in the top five in the league in homers. What I'm saying is that things are good Nance is filling in admirably for Reyes, my biggest problem is that my potential free agents want to be paid and for some reason they want to be paid in American dollars not Australian ones.
Najera, leading the league in homers- 20 mil(currently making 10)
Aaron Biles(2B) leading the team in average and OBP- 10 mil(currently making 1.4)
Suarez(CF) best all around player and fastest man around- not interested doesn't like manager Shugo Endo
Then actual problems started. In late July we lose O'Dowd, down for the O'Season. Which means I need more starters and Frank Rosales the initial 5 starter has been traded away because his personality description is literally 'Clubhouse cancer. The kind that gets managers fired' I'm not a fan of Endo, but with Suarez wanting out of Australia I need this clubhouse functional, this may very well be our best shot for a championship for years. The only counter to Rosales' disruptive influence is Varner and he's hovering around or below .200, so I shipped out Rosales for reliever Hideki Sato in early June.
Now O'Dowd's gone and I could really have used Rosales right about now instead of an expendable middle reliever. Luckily the lead we've built up is so massive that it won't matter in the division, but in the postseason I wanted to be able to line up O'Dowd, Davis, Hayward, and Fyfe, now it's Davis, Hayward, Fyfe, and some random dude. That's an issue and it's late July so I have five days to look into a replacement. Nobody's available for a reasonable price, so I figure you can win with two and a half dominant pitchers, especially as long as Nance's healthy.
In mid-September(after we clinched) Nance goes down for the season. Sato, that guy I got for Rosales in early June is our new closer and he has about a week to settle into it before the playoffs.
We win the division with 93 wins, ending the season on a 7 game losing streak and in the process lose Nick Bailey the good left fielder and Ozeguera(RF hitting .298) picks up a nagging back injury that'll last a couple of weeks. Ozeguera can play but he'll be hampered.
So we start the playoffs against the 92 win Yokohama Anglers without our best left fielder, best starter, 3 of our top 4 relievers, and with our right fielder constantly complaining about tightness in his back. This isn't ideal. To digress a little this is one of the things that makes OOTP great, in a game like XCOM if you lost that many major soldiers going into the endgame you might reload an earlier save or just start a new game, in OOTP you keep going because there's always another season and maybe just maybe our leadership crew of Varner(hitting .188), Sato(new to closing), and Endo(despised by our star CF) can hold it together and pull off a Grand Championship Series win.
Davis starts game one and we immediately hand him a three-run lead, then the offense stops. Yokohama scores one in the seventh, eighth and ninth to tie. Sato's first save chance is also his first blown save. Unfortunately Endo has pulled Suarez, Wall, Ozeguera, and Najera so we don't have any offense left. In the eleventh both teams score two. It goes to the fifteenth before we win on a walkoff slam from Lugo(3B). Only 11 wins to go.
If you read through all of this, sorry it's longer than I thought it would be, but I think you get what I'm saying.

LiF:YO is a very great and unique game, but it has its faults.
The Grind:
One of the biggest turn-offs to this game is the grind, although how punishing the grind is, really depends on server settings. Im especially someone who gets tired very quickly from grinding, however I just keep coming back to this game, because the grind feels rewarding. You get a lot of satisfaction after you complete each big project youve set out on.
Community based gameplay:
This is not a solo game. While you can of course play it solo, you wont get very far. You need a couple friends to really make it deep in the game. You need a few people so you can specialize in different jobs. Each type of job produces goods for another, which makes you really depend on one another to keep the flow of growth for your claim.
RP potential:
This game is an IDEAL sandbox for RP gameplay, it can be hard to find a good RP server and community, but some of the best true medieval RP experiences can be had.
Gameplay and Mechanical complaints:
Animals AI is really weak, but it makes for easy exploits in the early game for getting materials from animals, which can easily kill you when your not heavily equipped. In later game you can kill animals quickly enough that you dont notice them getting stuck as often.
Hauling Logs, and pulling carts are a real pain. I really wish you could put logs onto carts to transport more then one at a time. Pulling carts is a slow process too, and I would like to see the ability to have horse drawn carts. Because without the ability to pull a cart with a horse, they are really only good as stationary storage.
Gameplay/Mechanic praises:
Hunting animals can be frustrating but its also rewarding. I feel like the hunting/tracking system deserves some praise - It just adds a really cool element to track and animal, and see where it has wondered through the world.
Building/crafting is also praise worthy. There is so much depth to this, using basic resources to create basic components, which can be used in the final product of something, or combined to create a more advanced component. the process of creation feels realistic as well, and I think thats what plays into making everything feel so rewarding.
Quality, every item/resource/component all of it has a quality. In the early game quality doesnt matter so much, but once you get going, you have to find high quality everything, as it plays a big role in durability.
Skill tree is pretty unique, with prerequisites for more advanced skills of certain types. You can not be a master of everything, rather you must focus your profession. You want to be a smith? be a smith, learn basic smithing of tools, then weapons, and eventually armor and jewelry. But your gonna need a friend to be a farmer, and another friend to be your animal expert, maybe even another to be your master mason.  (depends on skill cap of each server, but you always have to specialize to some degree)
Updates:
Even though the devs for this title are working on the MMO version, and a RTS/city builder version now. This version of the game still recieves frequent updates and fixes. The devs will also work closely with server admins in the presense of unique server-side problems.
Graphics:
For the kind of game this is, with a changable voxel-like map, the graphics are really great. Texture details are really nice(especially after the update they had a couple weeks ago). and some of the landscapes are just beautiful with great draw distances. My biggest complaint would be on the animals, They all seem so stiff, their animations are rigged and not very flavorful. I feel like each animal probably only has a set of 5 animations: Idle, sleep, run, aggro, attack.
Audio:
Nothing special, audio quality is good and even immersive at times. on the down side, their doesnt seem to be a whole lot of ambient/ world sounds variations. The lack of variation puts a damper on the ambient sounds produced by certain farm buildings. that same chicken cluck or cow complaining every 30 seconds, at first you dont notice it, then it becomes annoying, and eventually you just block it out and pay no attention to it.
Overall, this game has captured my attention for a good long while, I find the gameplay very unique and rewarding.
however, I know that this game is definitely not for everyone, and it has its fallbacks, and still feels lacking in some areas.
So I give it a 8/10.
If your into community based build/survive genre of games, I'd definitely reccomend this game. It might not be worth the $40 price tag to most people, so perhaps wait for a sale if your unsure.

If I'm honest, I expected this to be sort of a lazy indie game clone: Bastion had narration, Limbo had bleak environments and silouhettes, Tag had paint that covers surfaces and alters their attributes, but there's still something unique and special about Nihilumbra, and that's the story. Even though the story centers around (generously speaking) only one character, and even despite the cliched appearance, I was left satisfied nonetheless.

Greetings!
I want to start out by stating that this game is so much different then its predecessor.
This game is dark and brooding; Knights of the Old Republic was a much more friendly feeling game to me.
I have played both games multiple times through. My dad played these games when I was a toddler, and he introduced me to hem when I was around eight or nine. I played both games on my dad's old XBox, and I recently bought The Sith Lords on Steam. I have already logged over 90 hours on Steam and am still not satisfied.
Now for my impressions-
KOTOR 2 is a game that allows you to delve into the deepest mysteries of the Force. I will try not to leave any spoilers, but you have a mentor you can approach at any time and learn of the Force, and learn from her wisdom; her mistakes. I loved this element, someone to speak to on your journey, someone to learn from.
The available party members in this game are extremely varied in personality and background. The characters are so fleshed out through  extensive dialogue and action. They react to your choices postively or negatively. KOTOR 2 introduced an influence system. It was a great addition, although didnt really change your party members opinion of you. Great system, but a few flaws. My favorite characters were Hanharr and Mira, Visas Marr, Hk-47, Darth Sion and Darth Traya.
The plot has a few holes (very minor, barely noticable), but that is a result of Obsidian cutting certain content to get the game complete on time.
If you have not yet, I highly suggest getting The Sith Lords Restored Content Modification, which fills many of these holes. It added new levels, new dialogue, quest fixes, and deeper character developement. I wouldnt play the game without it anymore.
The games has a sense of moral ambiguity. You do one thing, and a party member who will react positively, and another who will react negatively. Also, the mentor(whom I referenced earlier), has a skewed sense of ethical standards. She discourages giving aid, but she dissaproves of common bullying. She is neither a Jedi nor a Sith, and she is likely the most interesting character in the game.
I thouroughly enjoy this game after each playthrough; I always find something new I hadn't before.
If you haven't yet, I highly suggest you play this game. I sincerely hope it lives on, along with the first one, through the fans. It is one of my favorite games, if not my all time favorites, and believe me, I've played many games.

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II - The Sith Lords is my all time favourite game to date.
It is one of those rare games that gives you a strong sense of adventure and enjoyment like no other, even to the point where the dialogue can be very satisfying at times.
Whilst it was rushed slightly into production due to tight time constraints, the Restored Content Mod is currently available for all on the Steam Workshop if the player desires to play through the game including cut content, for a more full experience.
I also highly reccommend playing through the first game beforehand, if you have not already, as there are several awesome links to that game. However, it is not vital to understand the story.
The start of this sequel is quite similar to that of the previous game, however you play as a new character- the Exile.
You a adrift in space in the Ebon Hawk - the infamous smuggler's starship from the previous game- unconcious, unaware of what has happened. With the help of your trusty droid, T3-M4, who you can play as in the optional prologue, you dock at a nearby station- the Peragus Mining Facility.
You awake on the station, trapped, and much like in the previous game you must escape, meeting interesting characters on your journey who all have an important role in the storyline.
You escape the station, after encounters with the Sith, who you realise are hunting you as they are led to belive you are the last surviving Jedi.
The following system, Telos, is where you start discovering that this may not be the case. In an attempt to start a resistance, you travel around the galaxy gathering support and uniting heroes for the final stand against the Sith. You are the last hope for the Republic.
The tale is extremely gripping and enticing, and whilst the format remains almost the same as KOTOR, there are surprises around every corner, with things not always going to plan- adding to the adventurous feel.
There is little noticable graphical improvement from the last game, and so the graphics still feel slightly aged. This, however, does not create an impact on the enjoyability of the game as they are still appealing- and as any half decent gamer knows, graphics is not the most important thing.
The control given to the player is better than before, with more character influence, dialogue options, light/dark side paths, whereas there remains to be 2 optional endings.
However, though, this game is slightly buggier than it's predecessor due to the rushed release, but the game has recieved a fairly recent patch, which will solve most issues.
The HUD, combat and controls remains virtually identical to KOTOR, so it is turn-based, which may appeal to some, and full controller support has been added for the gamers that prefer them to a mouse and keyboard, or want an alternative way to play this title.
Pros:
-Excellent story, with great adventure
-EPIC finale
-Brilliant atmosphere
-New characters each with their own extensive background
-Further control over your destiny, and other characters
-As always, great replayability
Cons:
-A few more game bugs, nothing major- but still annoying
-Little graphical improvement
-Another 10/10
KOTOR II should take a similar time to complete as the previous game, with plenty of sidequests.
This game will always be at the top of my favourites. I have never played any games quite like the KOTOR series, set aside by their unparalleled stories.
P.S. I personally reccommend installing the Sith Lords: Restored Content Mod to enjoy any lost cut content to give the game a fuller feel- and the widescreen game stretch fix from the Steam Workshop. However, I would not reccommend installing 'M4-78' to the game, the droid planet that was cut from the game before release, as I believe it is confusing, and not half as enjoyable as the other worlds.

While I have not played as much of this game as many of the other player I still believe that this is a game worth a lot to people who want a simulation of military tactics and decisions. To call it a sandbox is an understatement due to the fact that one has endless options for mission making not only from the adequate assets provided but also from the steam workshop, where there are hundreds of thousands of mods including a lot of extra objects.

I've played this game since the 7DFPS version and trialed the demo when it was on Greenlight. The concept of the game is unique and interesting, but the execution of the full release leaves a bit to be desired and seems to be a stray shot.
Getting the hang of the controls is half the fun. However, once you understand how the bow and the arms work (as a veteran of Probably Archery, and probably a real-life archer), the challenge is significantly diminished since repetition of the correct technique is not at all difficult. Unless you're going for pinpoint accuracy and high scores, you can beat all the minigames within 20 minutes.
The minigames need much more depth. There are several shooting gallery-like levels, with the more interesting ones including the charging Berserker and the Warband, and the need Eggsterminator one is a chuckle and the most fun. The problem is that these minigames are single-level experiences, with the exception of the Berserker, which only has four very quick levels. I don't imagine it's difficult to code in different levels for each minigame (different target layout, more challenges, etc.). Unfortunately, you'll get the feeling of "Wait, that's it?" when you complete a minigame.
I can't get into any multiplayer games. I don't know whether it's because not many people are playing it, or not many people around me are playing it. Nonetheless, that seems to be where the most replay is, with Team Deathmatch and Horde Mode with multiple waves. But it'd be nice to have single-player versions of those too.
I have no idea why Zombie Soccer is part of this game. It feels like a side-project tacked onto the game to add value. I haven't been able to actually play an online match, but it otherwise doesn't look or feel good.
Basically, the game has good mechanics but poor replay value. There's simply no depth to the minigame experience. Most of the time spent in the game is figuring out how the controls work, but once you've mastered that, it's not something you'd probably go back to. In some ways, the free Greenlight Demo was more enjoyable -- and free. To pay ~$10 for this game, I'd expect more replay value.

I usually don't bother with free games on steam, because lets face it, most of the are poorly made or don't have much effort put into them, 1982 however is the EXACT OPPOSITE of that and is a retro throwback/tribute game/passion project done right with good execution, and I am honestly supprised this game is free, I would gladly pay at least 5 dollars for this game
For any retro enthusiasts (like me) or for anyone that is looking for a fun but simple time killer, let me break it down for ya
1982 is literally a cluster♥♥♥♥ of many arcade games from the 80's mashed into one in the forms of gameplay elements and references
From things like 2084 and Defender popping up as rainbow pixel text (references to Robotron 2084 and Defender respectively) to fighting foes that drop white laser looking things and turn into mushrooms when shot (Centipede) fighting ghosts that dodge your shots (Pac Man) and even powerups that you can shoot to use differently (common in many scrolling schmups) as well  as some formations of ships kamikazing or moving towards you (Galaga, note that this is not all the quote on quote "stolen" gameplay elements, and I use that term LIGHTLY because this game is far from a rip off, but this is some of the gameplay elements)
The refences aren't there just for chuckles or smiles, they actually drive the gameplay in fun and suprisingly creative ways
To top it off the colorful backgrounds reminicscent of the Atari/Intelevision days is a nice touch and the cheesy 80's techno voice and catchy beat is a nice touch
But the best part is its supprisingly varied modes, you can play modes such as normal (obviously you just try to get the highest score you can) or you can try surival (you die in one hit, the game normally has a health bar which can get refilled via a power up) or time attack, where you have unlimited lives , these varried modes coupled with adjustable diffculty give this game even more replay value than you would expect
Hey, even if this review doesn't convince you, download and try it anyway, it's free, so you have no money to spend, however I feel as though this is one of those rare moments when a free game on steam was awesome and worth the time to take downloading (very quickly while on topic) and to be honest, with how suprisingly fun the game is, I feel bad it was free, keep supporting good free games like this and maybe some of these small indie game makers will make an even bigger and better game that deserves your $, not saying that this game is bad, what I'm getting at is these are the kinds of free games that need to be looked at not only froma  game standpoint, but to give small companies like this the positive attention they need
Check out this game if you like retro arcade schmups or if your looking for something basic and fun yet just a bit in-depth (ie modes and gameplay elements)

Being a cheapskate, and after seeing that the Gurumin was going to be released for the 3DS but at a heftier price, I found out that Gurumin was also available on Steam for less so I made one of the bigger mistakes of 2016 and purchased the game. How was I to know right? After all, a game being remade for the 3DS and gaining quite the amount of attention should be good right? RIGHT? RIGHT? RIGHT?
WRONG.
Choppy graphics, repetitive gameplay, dreadful dialogue and very generic backgrounds. Not to mention the sparse enemy types, wonky hitboxes, poor controls and the dreadful 'BOING' (you all will know what I mean). Just take my word for it when I say that this game is  super generic, and even the different stages are basically reskins of the ones before with changed room placements.
Equipping the drill with different elements to nothing besides providing a bit more damage against specific enemy kinds without modifying stats or providing skills or abilities. That's quite sad given that the main catch of the game is the drill, and the methods you are supposed to 'improve' your drill basically does not do anything different. Yes, you can buy drill skills, but most of the time you will still end up spamming your normal attack.
Controls are slippery, swimming is horrendous (you have to be at the surface of the water in order to jump out from it and sometimes I was just literally a few pixels away from the surface and wondering why my jump button didn't work) while the fact that the act of swimming itself drains your hitpoints adds to the frustration. Certain areas that requires precision platforming was simply terrible. Add to the fact that there are so many invisible walls and sometimes you're wondering whether the game developers completed programming to a certain point, saw that the game was 'playable' and released the game without programming the remaining parts of the game that were required.
In short, unless there's a Steam sale that puts this below $5, don't get it. And once the game goes for below $5, still don't get it.

This game surprised me a lot the moment i decided to play it, mainly because I had no expectations when I played it.
Gameplay
The gameplay is very solid, to the level of normal hack n slash, although the trick/gimmick here is that if you time your attacks to the "beat" you'll deal critical hits, which deal more damage.
The puzzles are extremely easy but it is to be expected of a game that does have childish features. The platforming is average but it does have interesting ways to reach certain targets (like the homming attack that you do when you jump).
Controls
The controls offer different ways to play the game, either only mouse, keyboard and mouse or controller. But I recommend using the controller since it's the intended way of playing it and because you won't get used to the other 2 ways for a while.
The buttons are very responsibe and there's no delay.
Story
The story is extremely simple and easy to follow, you discover a village of monsters and decide to spend some time playing with them, but one day the bad guys from another place start to spread fog in the world and destroy the village, thus your objective is to recontruct the village by getting the objects back to their respective monsters.
Characters
They're childish, but they're enjoyable and there's a good amount of friendly humor in the game.
Soundtrack
As expected from falcom, they deliver in that department and the songs are ones that I would listen from time to time. Not all of them are memorable, but they do offer a good ambientation to the stage.
Overrall
It's a solid game that you'll probably play once (or more if you're a completionist). But it's one that I definetly recommend.

It’s time for a new review of a sports casual title. But I’m almost inclined to consider that an understatement since there’s nothing truly casual about Air Hockey. Before the recent implementation of some truly savage AI opponents, you had to contend with human players of various skill and determination. Perhaps it was still casual back then. Air Hockey is the creation of a small team that goes by the Standby moniker. The name seems befitting since the feedback I offered so far, has been more than just taken into account. Positive changes took place and I’m pleased to notice that the developer continues to expand his project in order to cater to as many players as he can. It goes without saying that as far as Steam debuts are concerned, Air Hockey ticks all the right boxes.
The term and physical game of Air Hockey are products of the 1970s in the same manner in which home consoles and arcade cabinets also sprung up during this crucial era for the evolution of new entertainment mediums. Gaming would never be the same again. A fortunate thing and I do see the benefits of having actual games, in their many forms of boards to tables and not just digital versions. Onto the subject at hand, the Steam version of Air Hockey is more than just an adaptation of the classic game. The fast-paced action has been spiced up by the addition of a bonus/malus system that can quickly misfire and offer truly unpredictable outcomes. As for the story, surely you didn’t expect a campaign mode to this particular genre and topic? There’s no need for a storyline in order to enjoy Air Hockey. Not at all.
You don’t see many sports games powered by Unreal Engine 4. Well, Air Hockey is one such title and unsurprisingly, it uses the graphics engine to its advantage. From neon lighting and particle effects to motion blur and and other visual distortions, players are treated to a full spectrum of power-ups that leave little room for boredom to set in. Performance-wise, I encountered no frame rate drops, crashes or glitches. It was all so buttery smooth and in tune to the gameplay that requires quick relflexes and thinking ahead. You may wish to fiddle with the mouse sensitivity from the in-game options, since the default setting seems a bit off or delayed, when compared to the AI opponents even on their lowest difficulty setting. Further customization of the tables and pucks is being planned in future updates of Air Hockey.
The soundtrack could use more variety and yet the sounds effects themselves are adequately represented. We can’t stress the need of any voice acting though. A robotic voice shouting the now infamous “You’re winner!” phrase would not be out of place regardless if Big Rigs might object or not.
One thing which Air Hockey has managed to simulate so well in its digital form, is the increased chance of winning (or losing) matches very fast thanks to inadvertently marking own goals. Both the AI and the players are susceptible to this, since the puck reaches a velocity that makes it hard to anticipate where it shall hit or more precisely, the effect itself is enhanced by the player’s handle (also known as a “striker”) and its sensitivity setting. The already fast-paced matches benefit from this extra element of surprise that can see score boards tip in favor to players in less time than it takes to set up an online session for Air Hockey. Speaking of which, the MP component was the only mode available at launch yet the developer has wisely added singleplayer as well. Calling it challenging would still not convey the full picture.
And it’s perfect that way. You’ll have to spend quite a lot of time until you can find an online match to play with, so the Artificial Intelligence steps quite admirably in the shoes of an opponent worthy of your efforts. Separated by clearly defined difficulty settings, the AI can offer anything from a friendly spar to an infernal race for scoring at least once against the CPU foe. The aforementioned power-ups also trigger in SP matches, but if you’ll wish to witness the full experience of all those visual glitches and bonues, you’ll need to play with a friend. The relatively small community is basically, the biggest obstacle for Air Hockey right now. Singleplayer was only added as a step forward from a more conventional tutorial and I agree that it’s entertaining and difficult at the same time. But it can never replace the fun of outwitting another human mind, trained or not in this particular game.
Do yourself a favor and give this game a try if you’ve had fond memories of its physical version. Better yet, offer it as a gift to someone else and play with them, in order to unlock Air Hockey’s full potential. It’s more than decently priced for what it offers. I can only hope that in time, its community may grow along with the list of available modes and effects.

A unique game which invovles resource gathering and quick decisions about numbers. I enjoy economic simulators, so this was pretty high on my list of games to get. I don't like how formulaic it can be though. It's similar to RTS games like Starcraft in that there is a certain build at the beginning of the game, as well as midgame and endgame strategies. (which is kind of a turnoff for me). But a round is relatively short, which is a plus in my eyes, because nothing is worse than playing an hour into a game just to lose. I was hoping more along the lines of a space-themed Capitalism II, but it's much more like Starcraft minus the fighting. (Sorry, I haven't played multi-player; this review is strictly for the single-player experience).
+ Not many number crunching games, so this was a welcome entry.
+ Plays very quickly, if you're spending more than a few seconds looking at the screen without clicking, you're probably going to lose.
+ Good replay value.
+ Good production value.
- AI can be pretty difficult.
- Even if you're well positioned, you can lose instantly if you don't pay attention to your stocks.
- At the time of writing, the game is still going for about $40 which is a pretty steep price.
8/10 Won't appeal to everybody, but a much needed entry in economic gaming~

Disclaimer -- I buy OOTP directly from OOTP Developments. Although I get a Steam key, I don't install or play through Steam, hence my 0 hours logged. I assure you, starting with OOTP 14, I have logged countless hours playing OOTP: the greatest sports simulation known to man.
If you love baseball but don't own OOTP, all I can say is, man, you are missing out. I knew of OOTP for years before I finally decided to give it a try with version 14. Once I got the hang of things, I could not believe I had put off playing this game for so long. This is literally the sports game of my dreams, and of any baseball fan's dreams. It is absolutely on my Top 5 Games I'd Take to A Desert Island list (...everyone should have one of those lists...)
How anyone could give OOTP a Negative review is utterly beyond me. This is the deepest, most flexible and immersive sports simulation on the market, hands down. Deeper than Football Manager. The only thing I can think of is, perhaps the negative reviews think all sports games need to look like MLB The Show or NBA 2K. Those are great games in their own right, but OOTP is every inch a baseball game as "The Show" and then some. Since version 16, OOTP has been officially licensed by MLB, so anyone who avoided OOTP because it couldn't give you the "official MLB" experience offered by The Show, well, that problem has been put to rest.
There is almost nothing you can't do in OOTP. Feel like GMing the Tokyo Yakult Swallows in the Nippon Professional Baseball League? Be my guest. Want to manage the Red Sox' AAA Pawsox affiliate? Go to it. Feel like skippering the 1925 New York Yankees and the likes of Babe Ruth, Lou Gehrig, Bob Meusel? Have at. Feel like setting up a completely fictional league tailored exactly to your specifications? Why not. The depth and flexibility of OOTP are simply breathtaking. You won't believe it until you experience it for yourself.
All that said -- yes, get ready for a learning curve. The game is DEEP. I've heard it described as the 'Dwarf Fortress' of sports games. (I've also heard Dwarf Fortress described as the OOTP of roguelike/simulations...)  The complexity and depth can be intimidating. But what amazes me is, OOTP is not just played by die-hard baseball fans. Plenty of players with little interest in baseball have given OOTP a try and gotten hooked. (The fact that OOTP is developed by a team of Germans tells you all you need to know about its broad international appeal!)  And there is no question you may have that you cannot get an answer to in the OOTP Developments forums -- there is an extremely knowledgable and dedicated fanbase there who are very happy to answer even the most basic questions about baseball and OOTP -- they are more than happy to welcome new players!
TL:DR --  If you (A) love baseball, (B) love sports, and / or (C) love in depth immersive management games, don't overthink it:  BUY OOTP 17 NOW  !!!  Easiest no-regrets decision you will ever make.

There's not a lot that anyone can divulge about this game without revealing a ton of magnificent plot points, so I'll try to summarize without spoiling this incredible title.
This game is intense, and as always, the team that brought the famously popular AMNESIA: The Dark Descent as well as several other horror titles before have mercilessly painted the game in a grim palette that's border-line decadent. The cold, lonely, dripping halls of the under water stations you will tromp about trying to get your bearrings are claustrophobic, horrifyingly lit and look like you've walked into everything right around the time Cthulu decided to get his lazy♥♥♥♥♥out of the bottom of the ocean and wreck the entirety of existence. The silence is deafening, forced to listen old transmissions of a hopeless world that is dead, and where you might honestly be the only sane man left.
As the game progresses, you will be presented with many, many moral choices. Though the dialogue is by no means tedious between the protagonist, and his pretty 'assistant' as we'll call her, they discuss a great deal on their concepts of what is life, what is death and what that means to the world around them. You set out in hopes of restoring this assistant's project dubbed the 'ARK', a artifical world where humanity's last dying hope may be to leave behind everything that is human, and take off as nothing but mere data on a little sattellite, roaming the cosmos for thousands of years.
As of the time I'm writing this review, I have not yet completed the game. The monsters are masterfully crafted, and every little groan, scream, or perturbed murmuring they make induces nothing but sheer panic. Their appearances are sheer terror, and thanks to the claustrophobia of the dimly lit halls of this station, you will be forced to make some very daring escapes, or cry in a corner while the monster howls at you. The moral choices I discussed are something I can't really reveal without being entirely heavy handed, but suffice to say, if you enjoy thinking and recieving inputs other than your own on the possibilities of 'what is life', you're sure to find yourself staring forlorn and frustrated as you're presented with someone else's life, in a 'what would I want if this was fair'. But none of it is fair.
The only negative comments I can make? Well, I'm not sure this engine has been properly stream-lined. It really lieks to eat up resources, and there are parts where I putter along with choppy graphics. The chatter between the protagonist, and 'assistant' are somewhat common place, and if you're looking at this title for the hopes of being utterly alone, I'm afraid you'll be disappointed. She likes to talk when there's no monsters around, and will be in your ear buzzing like a busy bee. But don't worry, if you don't mind the break from screaming and crying she never chirps up when there's real danger present. That, you get to face alone.
A absolute classic for the horror genre. And thank God they hit the mark again, it seems the AMNESIA team quickly come to save the day before this genre becomes all hallway shooters with spooky scary zombie mutations.
Great game, highly recommended!
What a ride! It is one of those games that you'll remember for your lifetime.

Is it scary? Sure.
Does it make you feel vulnerable? Yes.
Does it have a good atmosphere? I suppose so.
Is it fun to play? Not at all.
This game sure is rather popular and has been a steady recommendation for those seeking a good horror game the past few years. I think this is erroneous. I found that when I stripped away the "Oooh, so spooky" layers and actually looked at this game from a mechanical standpoint, I realised it was rubbish and instantly understood why I had next to no fun with it. The game is dreadfully boring and chore-like in that you complete extremely mundane objectives (usually A to B stuff) and perform the most bog standard tasks conceivable; such as opening doors, pulling levers, solving puzzles designed for mentally handicapped infants, maintaining your lantern oil and ensuring you don't lose your sanity because you dared to hide in the dark for the space of 20 seconds... the last one isn't a joke.
Additionally, there was something about the castle itself I didn't really like, either. I'm not quite sure what it was but the castle felt very basic and not very interesting in it's layout and architecture. It kind of felt like a less severe version of Wolfenstein 3D where most of the rooms were just too square shaped most of the time. Either that or I was just so bored that I started noticing stuff that doesn't matter. The only cool, memorable moment I experienced with my time with the game was when you go through a flooded area and there are invisible footprints splashing around in the water, chasing you, forcing you take higher ground on whatever you can find for safety. I thought that part was creative.
If a game being scary is enough for you, then you'll probably enjoy it. However if you're at all interested in polished, refined and FUN game design then you'll probably loathe this game. It's just incredibly dull despite it's horror.
For a game of this type that is actually done well, try out Alien Isolation.
