Weirdly comical survival game that is based on the famous 1980's, Friday The 13th movies with killer named Jason in the lead role.
You need a lot of teamwork and/or luck to escape Jason's playground of death. Knowing the map layout, your characters advantages and flaws of Jason is only one piece of the bloody pie. Game has luck element, meaning items can be found in various locations on the map and some moves against Jason may backfire quick if RNG is not on your side.
At this stage there are three maps available, all of them are in forest like environment with lakes and rivers, countless cottages around the map with key objective locations. Depending on how you plan your escape, you will not only have to find all the required objective pieces for repairs but also navigate to the designated area for save extraction.
At the moment you can escape by water vehicle (if you replace rotor and refuel the 2 seater boat), by land vehicles (yellow 2 seater and blue 4 seater, by installing new battery, refueling and finding the car keys), and by foot (if you manage to repair the fusebox and call police). You can also simply evade Jason until the timer runs out, and you will win but that is not that easy, and rather dull because you pretty much make dead people wait longer.
That said if you play Jason, it's very rewarding in terms of experience and the actual killing. Jason has insane amount of kill moves available either through the skill system, where you spend CP "character points" I assume, to purchase different kill moves or simply grabbing survivor and using countless number of environmental kills.
Survivors however can buy perks using the same CP's, you get those with random positive and negative effects or if you're lucky depending on rarity you can get one without any negative suffixes. Survivors also get cosmetic items, like clothing which is level gated and unlock when you reach certain level.
You can also play not only with different types of survivors but with different types of Jason's, influenced by the movies themselves. Every Jason has something unique about him and also some positive or negative attributes. Pretty much all of them use same set of skills, but some get higher or lower cooldowns, quicker or slower movement and different special kills depending on their weapon.
I played over 10 hours and honestly apart from the server issues I was having a blast. Game rewards you similarly if you did good or died quickly in the match, just make sure you wait out till either everyone escape or dies. Otherwise you won't get much experience points. Playing as Jason is a treat in itself as you have your way with survivors and let me tell you it's a bloody mess. Pretty much all of the kill moves are of the disturbing sort, so make sure you don't let 10 year old play this, or maybe if you are similar to Jason's mother... who am I to say what you should do. You've been warned! ;D
P.S. It is advised to use a microphone for some sort of communication, because game doesn't have chat support while in the match. Which I found strange and I feel like it should be a thing, well anyways.
Enjoy the bloody mess!

I have never played final fantasy VI before, but have always wanted to  since i was a kid. I only had access to a PS1 at the time my final fantasy interested began and the only final fantasy games available for it began at FF7.
To begin with, this game is a port of a remake, with modified graphics and user interface. Other reviews have been quite negative about the graphics of this game, but their complaints are mostly comparing it to previous renditions of the game. Taking a look at the artistic style of the game on its own, I would commend it. The sprites for the characters look goregous, and the portraits of each characters are based on the original concept art by Yoshitako Amano himself.
The graphics of the world map are just as you would expect of an early final fantasy game.
The controls and user interface are perhaps the biggest critisism of this game. There is next to no remapping of controls and the control scheme  on keyboard are very awkward for a modern game (ENTER as the primary interact button, ESC to open menu, backspace, arrow key movement, and L/R-shift buttons are what you'll be using most). That, combined with a strange user interface make the game feel clunkier than more modern games (This is especially noticeable during missions where precise movement is pretty important).
In terms of the story, if you don't know it already, FFVI features a large cast with no set main character. The story begins with Terra, who has represented FFVI in other games such as Dissidia, and follows her story a very slight amount more than the other characters you'll come across. It is a very different approach to common RPG games with a set main character, but I feel FFVI greatly benefits from this approach, which gives the characters more opportunity to develop. Each character may appear to follow a cliche for the first part of the story, but they are immensely developed the further along the story you get. Despite its praise, I definitely felt remorse that Terra wasn't focused more on during the story, but thats not to say what the story does show of Terra is uninteresting in any way (might just be personal bias on that one. Terra is my favourite character).
The villain is the iconic Kefka, who is definitely in the running for best final fantasy villain of all time, and the Empire; both of which serve to drive the story forward in dramatic ways.
Overall, the story is definitely worth buying this game if you haven't already obtained another version. The content within this game seems to be definitive of final fantasy VI, so all the content is here from what I understand (secret bosses, playable characters, unique dungeons and items). I would probably recommend it less to someone who already has one of those other versions mentioend earlier as there are likely problems you'll have with this version compared to the others.

The developers either need to change this game from a 'stealth' game into a shooter and remove the Guards and Thieves game mode and the different team advantages such as health and night vision OR cut down on the game modes and get rid of some of them. In the end I still highly recomend this game, especially if you have a goup of friends to play with, there will be rage when you get killed, but when you reck some noobs you will feel like a god.

Medal Of Honor (2010) a corridor shooter. You follow your squadmates through linear environments, and click on taliban to kill them.
It's a pretty game, but there's just no substance. It tries to stress the importance of keeping each other alive, but your teammates are invincible, friendly fire has no effect, and your fellow soldiers frankly don't give a damn about you outside of scripted sequences. They can have a perfect shot directly behind someone who is blasting AK rounds at you, and they will often not bother taking it. To be honest, they're more or less entirely useless outside of cutscenes and scripted sequences, only serving as voices telling you what and what not to do, or time wasters you need to wait for before you can progress into the next area. Seldom does the game even allow you to move ahead of them - one of the few times it allowed me to, doing so triggered a glitch that prevented the game from progressing until I reset to the last checkpoint.
About the only helpful thing your teammates do for you is give you ammo when you stand next to them and press "F", or whatever the action is bound to. They only give you ammo when you're running low, but often what they do give you are hundreds (in one case up to a thousand) of rounds at a time. As long as you're using weapons they have the right sort of ammo for in their pocket munitions factory, you will never run dry. This sort of undercuts the tension when you're supposed to be completely isolated and on your own in hostile territory.
The game tries to mix things up with sections where you must SOFLAM target something to call in airstrikes, or operate a helicopter's guns/missiles yourself, but really the only thing that changes in those is loss of independent movement and embiggening of the special effects upon successfully pointing and clicking on a "bad guy". There are also stationary sniper sequences that are more "Where's Waldo?" then the standard shooting range stroll.
Everything is unrelentingly guided. This is evident from the very first scene, in which you're in the passenger seat of a car that you can't get out of, and the game doesn't even trust you enough to give you camera control. It wants to suck you in to an epic story of badass sacrifice in the line of duty, and it wants everything to happen just so. The problem is that it all rings hollow, and by the time the game pleads with you to feel some emotion over the death of an american soldier (wrenching camera control from your grasp again, naturally), you've already mowed down hundreds of other people without consequence.
Any interest (emotional, intellectual, even visceral eventually) they were trying to instill in the game is just completely undercut by how rote the whole experience is. Its a shame that such beautiful visual design, with sometimes surprising variation and attention to detail is wasted on an experience that allows for no sense of agency, and plays one note over and over beneath all those new coats of paint.
In any case, while the game overstayed its welcome fairly rapidly for me, it IS only around four hours long.
Follow orders and you'll get through this, all right? You'll just never get those four hours back.

Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic II is a very special game to me. It has a well written storyline with plenty of side quests. It has really solid gameplay especially for its age. Being able to take the turn based combat into real time freely while preparing the next few actions you want to take in combat is a brilliant mechanic. The story aside from towards the end where it just felt rushed, was actually better compared to Knights of the Old Republic I.
Gameplay was heavily improved over the original game and the companions you have felt just as well developed. The tag story rich is no understatement. This in my opinion is one of the best RPG's of all time. A lot of people find you towards the end of the game are a bit strong at least within my circle of friends who have played the game. Which I find in certain parts is true but Kotor II really does bring a moderate challenge in its gameplay. I felt many of the boss battles were a pretty entertaining.
Towards the end i'm not ashamed to say I abused Force Lightning Storm and some kiting strategies to deal with a lot the enemies that i'd be fighting in groups of 5 or more. The game's lightside darkside system as always is just so well designed. My favorite part of my playthrough was me trying to perspective how i'd interact with these characters thrown into the scenario of the Jedi Exile and acting on my opinion and not a light side or dark side choice.
The crafting system is really well done I loved the lightsaber crafting options and skill system requirements for crafting. The skill tree for combat was amazing a lot of diversity and freedom. Getting to the force skill tree it's in my opinion one of the best skill tree's i've ever had in a game really one of my favorite parts of the whole game is the amazing force abilities and the progression they make. I only wish there was more because it was so much fun achieving these force powers.
Kotor II is the dream sequel to Kotor I honestly all it makes me want is for another one. We all pray for Kotor III because of how amazing these gems of the past are. There are still a few flaws obviously in the game glitches mostly. The biggest issue the game has is its age. Not because of graphics but more because of modern optimization.
To start with the issues is how often it crashes. If it crashes at the loading screen for you or something i'm sorry never seen that issue happen to me once fix its resolution in its files. I found the game crashes from being full screen in very specific cutscenes often in world transitions. Hitting alt enter in the loading screen windowed modes the game. This fixed all of my crash issues i'd often just save before a cutscene since in most games they're obviously coming and alt enter if it crashed so I could enjoy my full screen glory. (When it didn't crash happened like 5 times throughout the game no mods installed)
The inventory system itself is very poorly sorted wish I had a search bar to find items or certain stat types not even a big issue though. Abusable medpack tricks like activating one during your healing round inside your inventory while casting heal. Albeit I like this trick since it helped me in a situations where I failed to pay attention to gameplay and got chunked down. The AI for companions is pretty bad they like to run into fights repeatedly forcing my to loop between characters to continuously get them away from enemies as they'd run back in on 10% health and no force points. Good times with that I can say that much.
Lightsaber on lightsaber combat damage is a little bit too high. For boss battles and even regular lightsaber combat I could say even having half damage on lightsaber damage. Maybe by having a special melee defense perk to reduce the damage would be nice since my Master Flurry Shreds boss HP. While bosses shred my HP way to quick kind of reducing the excitement of drawn out boss battle. This is the biggest fault of the combat system in the entire game and it's still not even that bad. I don't know if there is a mod for this but my final complaint is these older games often have no map markers which helps exploration but is more irritating when you have no idea where to go and the journal isn't helping much. I found this an occasional issue that can be extremely annoying. My last real issue besides the rushed ending is the slow start definitely wish I could skip that start.
Also not enough Sith using force lightning abilities that ♥♥♥♥♥ top tier. (Fighting the Sith was really cool in all seriousness)
Summing up review in a Tldr;
Pro's:
-Good RPG gameplay
-Amazing Real time turn combat
-One of the best written Star Wars stories ever made
-Pretty Lightsabers
-Strongly developed characters including the player character
-Brilliant Force Powers
-Decently Challenging
-Awesome light and dark side choices
-Amazing level up skill tree
-Diverse gameplay options even though most of us go with jedi for the sake of our childhood
-(Apathy is death)
-Great Crafting system
Cons:
-(Forgot to add this) Getting a lightsaber takes a bit which kind of sucks but some might find this to be a good thing
-Slow start (First 4 Hours)
-Rushed ending (Last 2 Hours)
-Inventory system is in need of a search bar you get a lot of garbage and have a lot of inventory space I think infinite
-Cutscenes crash issues which for me were cured by windowed mode in certain cutscenes (Biggest issue in the whole game)
-Lightsaber combat damage is really quick the damage to saber users have is too fast I personally just wanted longer fights because how epic they were.
-Small abusable glitches nothing special
-Not the brightest AI but not even near broken
(Sorry if this isn't written that well i'm far from an English major)
Overall Kotor II is the best Star Wars game I have ever played hands down and one of the best RPG games I have ever played it's one of my top 5 favorite games and if you get into it you'll understand why.

Obsidian no surprises here has taken the Knights of the Old Republic franchise and actually improved it gameplay wise by implementing new features like a more advanced crafting system, the lightsaber forms and a wider range of abilities in general. I was particularly overjoyed by the lightsaber forms as I felt Obsidian had paid close attention to the Star Wars lore and each form brought something new to the table and promoted a more strategic approach to fights.
Story wise, I felt Obsidian made an impressive story but it did feel a little too cryptic and convoluted at times and I have to admit that the first game set the bar very high with the amazing twist which this game lacked. However, the characters were astounding and I loved the Handmaiden's backstory in particular and I could tell that Obsidian had invested a lot of thought and time to make these characters relatable and likeable.
I felt that this game was less bug ridden than it's predecessor and it ran smoother altogether which is always nice even though it wasn't free of bugs entirely as at times some cutscenes skipped for whatever reason. Once again, the choices you make in the game heavily influence what kind of character you become and the interactions you have with your crew and Obsidian proves that KOTOR is one of the best titles when it comes to decision making.
Another triumph by Obsidian here and a more than worthy sequel and I expect more greatness from them in the future.

When I returned to play this game there were only 5 dedicated servers with more than 6 online players. All of them were heavy RP or restrictive rules servers. The drama of bad admins and restrictive rules really diminishes how fun this game can be.
The graphics are good enough to lose yourself in the world. I enjoyed a few of the professions; even if it seemed like bit of a cell game grind.
Tunneling underground is awful; same goes for getting stuck on elevation inclines, or horses getting stuck on inches of water.
The combat is very enjoyable though I've yet to play on a server where lag was minimal enough where it could ever seem competitive. The lag makes it really hit and miss, though skill does make a big difference.
Building and construction were enjoyable. The only complaint might be that it takes leather to repair stone walls? I don't really get the logic behind that.
The lack of integration with steam community-mods is off-putting for players who have never entered a console command in their life. Joining a server with a custom map means re-validating your steam files every time you switch.
I was surprised how well the game ran with how the elevation works. Minecraft being 1:1 and LiF being 1:10. That said horse animations and lag were pretty bad at high speeds; horses falling "floating" down cliffs and the like. That and the combat mentioned earlier. I think the saving grace is that lag does not prevent you from grinding which takes up the majority of the game.
Almost forgot to mention NPC's. The animals are immersion breaking. Bears have "invisible armor" where it takes 30 crossbow bolts to the face to die? Meanwhile with no armor they hit you for 130 (which is all of your life for most). Wolves glitch and circle you while  hitting you while you can’t hit them (sometimes). The AI for animals is the most minimalist I've seen for a game; run straight, turn, run straight, turn. No sense of danger; they only run on close proximity or damage. Due to the forced high hit points of mobs most people resort to luring the dumb animals to the water where they glitch out and you murder them. Animals (when you are in the water) seems to get "stuck" when not even in the water. Definitely a large amount of pathfinding issues with the AI as well as their intelligence as well.
I had fun but I can’t recommend it. Perhaps with some bugs fixed; the MMO bringing a standardized ruleset and omission of bad admins that might change.

Attempt at doing a revised Harpoon suffers from implementation problems, no longer supported by devs
- No save/load system in the middle of battles
- When there are more than a few combat units and missile swarms, the game slows like molasses (even with an fairly advanced gaming rig)
- Unrealistic bits that go beyond simplification. For example, altitude has no effect on top speed/fuel consumption, so F35's can fly mach 2 at wavetop level across the Atlantic...on afterburners.
The source code was released a few years ago, so there's some hope that the modders might tweak this. There is a big naval warfare niche to fill for something between an arcade game and a mega-simulation like Command: Northern Inferno. But this game is not it.

As a Final Fantasy VI veteran I was turned off from this game when I first purchased it a year ago. I am so glad I gave it another chance recently.
Most people's (including mine) first observation when they turn the game on is the graphics, reminding me of something out of RPG Maker. They really took a lot of the immediate feeling out of the game for me at first, it just didn't feel nostalgic enough. But playing through for a little bit you will completely overlook this.  I actually got to the point that I enjoyed the newer graphics, which I'm still dumbfounded by.
The sound was amazing, it sounded much more crisp and vibrant than my SNES cart. Like seriously, I didn't realize how much better the Opera song could get, but this versions rendition was superb!
Controls were okay, probably my only mediocre score I'd give to this version. Noticeably when controlling the character on a map, for example, if you're facing one way and want to go the opposite you actually have to go through a buffer of sorts where your character has to face the direction before it can move. Not that big of a deal, but a little annoying. Controls in the battle screen were okay too, just took a bit to get comfortable with the command screen.
The game content was amazing, the same game I've been playing for 20+ years now with a few bugs patched here and there. PLUS the extra dungeons that made their first appearance in the Gameboy Advance version showed up in this one, which made me super excited. I loved the challenge of both (keeping that part vague to be spoiler free).
Oh, I didn't mention achievements yet! Yeah, I know they're a gimmick, but after over 2 decades of playing this game it actually gave me a reward for doing 100%, which the original didn't. I had around 80 hours of playtime on my file when I got the Final Fantasy VI Master achievement.
Overall, it really is a great game when you step away from that feeling of how the original looked. Give it an honest try and don't be so quick to judge based on the updated graphics. Also, I see other people complaining about not being able to change the resolution, I'm kind of confused by this because when I load my game up there's an options menu to change your resolution. 9.5/10

I would call NWAC a good game. That's a good choice, when you're  looking for the way to get to know basics of naval warfare. The main rival, Command Modern Air naval Operations (CMANO), is a truly hardcore game and Jane's Fleet Command (JFC) may look annoyingly outdated. The interface is clear and player-friendly. The missions are interesting. The graphic is good for a wargame: ship models are nice, but transient conditions (missile starts, hits, aircraft launches etc.) are made roughly. So I highly recommend it for beginners.
The drawback is that after having played it for some time, or looking through the literature, you'll find out how unrealistic it is. Mostly it's connected with simplified radio-electronic warfare & aspects issues. You'll literally feel you're bound to these limitations. That's why I prefer CMANO now.
The game has some performance issues, though I had not experienced any bugs during the gameplay, that are worth to be mentioned. The fact is that when lots of aircraft, anti-ships and anti-air missiles are in the air (I'm talking about 100-200+ object), the time compression lost it's effect, and the game tends to slow down and run close to the real-time. However, there's a video-guide on performance optimization (haven't used it) and you may meet similar  difficulties in CMANO too.

Great combat mechanics, great benefits given if you do 1v1 on 4v4 matches, gives you a good reward if you do that rather than ganging up on someone, great gear customization, and of course, actually a good campaign throughout these years, especially for multiplayer-driven game.
Although, considering this game completely new to everyone, there are flaws to point out that made me not recommend this game for today's full-time entertainment to avoid all frustration you should probably not bother with.
It uses P2P rather than dedicated servers, means interruptions will happen 80% of the time no matter what would happen to the host, and you probably won't know who got picked as a main peer. 90% of the time the game will disconnect you in a middle of a match to get your precious rewards, progress for orders and such, and will just send you to the main menu without resstoring the connection.
That explains everything, the P2P format, as mentioned above, also doesn't have any kind of ping control. In my experience, solo-queueing for games, I would get red bar people with really bad connection, and every action I would do to them would be delayed. On my screen I parried them, 3 miliseconds later, I get hit from that parry and get staggered; when he blocks the hit, there is a chance he will get hit if he changed his stance during that time and it is not fun to play with. Ubisoft has to launch the functionality to check for high latency people and do something about it.
People say the game is pay to win; you can buy feats (so called abilities) for all characters that
. Saves you time, you get access to those feats, but they don't matter much (unlike Thick Blood feat that prevents Warden from getting a "Damage overtime" damage), you just get to use them early. You can buy them for around ~30 dollars which is a massive moneygrab.
The matchmaking balance would matter not at this point, you think gear at certain reputation levels would make people stronger, but only in one degree, there is always a downside on gears so try to see what they actually have as weakness to abuse them, I like how it works. I mostly play warden with just an upgraded blade for a sword and nothing else equipped, its just up to a user to dodge/parry etc.
Speaking of orders. Majority of them give you very little to achieve on Player vs AI matches, yet they give you a big grind most of a time on PvP that is the most challenging; rewards are almost as equal.
Not recommended for today's play due to network issues on ubisoft's side.

Hi, everybody!
OK, So I have just come out of a 30h stint of Dishonoured, so I'm going to make a couple of comparisons to that here.
OK So the good/normal stuff.
It's a Rail Shooter = There is only one way to progress one possible direction of events can unfold. This is good in that it directs the story in the direction that the writers want it to go. I like rail shooters, Half Life is a rail shooter, by definition.
The Shooting controls.
YAY SOMEONE GOT IT RIGHT! The way it is set up, by default, is how I, and other pro FPS players, have our controls (mostly).
Crouch and sprint whilst the button is depressed, not on toggle. Rifle Zoom on Rcklick, also on toggle. WOOT WOOT! Really this is only a little thing as it can usually be changed in the keyboard settings, but I didn't have to change it, for once. Would have been nice if melee was mapped to F, tho. (usually I would have it on E, but that was needed for peeking, which didn't feel as good as the Dishonoured's version)
The Stealth/Knifing - there were about 6 opportunites to employ this, if you wanted to. Which is reasonable for a gun-focussed campaign. The stealth itself was only OK... you had to kill in the prescribed order, if you went off the script, everyone is alerted and it devolves into a gun fight. I also feel that the enemies hit harder during the stealth sections if you stuffed it up and started a gun fight, as an incentive to do it the way the writers wanted you to. You could run behind someone and they would not hear you. But stealth the wrong guy (or the right guy in the wrong order) and he'd alert the whole base.
Health bar - was a fast-regenerating red mist that surrounds the vision, similar to CoD, I believe, but better in that it only took a couple of hits (3?) before I was restarting at the checkpoint. Good and bad.The mechanic suited the game andt he fast-paced storyline.
Enemies - these would flank and attack, and dive for cover, the AI seemed fine, their accuracy was acceptable. Exept the snipers.
Sniping (Barret sections)
These were pretty good. You had wind, bullet travel time, and an IR camera to deal with.everything was there except the recoil. Oh there is one bit where you are sniping and your spotter is calling shots. He does a fairly hopeless job of it. and their snipers are useless shots. Then they had Dragonov's VS our Barret.
Run-And-Gun (the story proper)
Mostly fine, sections of running to find cover, picking your shots, and not getting shot or grenaded in the process. You can always ask your allies for more ammo if you're out, too - which is kinda nice. There are some points (you will realise them when it happens) where eventually you realise the enemies have infinite respawn, and the nex event is actually triggered by you moving up closer to the enemy stronghold.  I didn't really like that mechanic. Nor did I like the absolute reliance on Air support to take out dug-in targets such as AA turrets and mortar fire. What would the Rangers do without the Airfoce, I wonder? Hmmm... drop a grenage instead of a signal flare, I imagine.
Story Telling:
I didn't like how you were constantly being told parts of the story through different Character's eyes. At least, I didn't like how it was done in this game. Usually when this is done, it creates some extra layer of depth to the game, due to the new character having a different mechanic, such as Raven in MSG2  Where you swithced from gun play to sword play. In this, when you change guys, you swap your M4 for (I dunno, some other full auto assault rifle. I plead ignorance). There wasn't really enough difference in each character to truely make each one feel unique. It really was just more of the same as the other guy buy now they are calling me something different when they talk to me.
The story: (no spoilers)
Was a nod to the boys on the ground, their trials, and their hardships. This was done in the outworking of the story, quite well. not really a spoiler, but if you don't want any clues about the game story at all...
would be my favourite line in the movie/game. Their desperation felt sincere, That's a rare thing in gaming story lines. I feel like it was a pity the game was only 5h long, but it told the story they wanted it to, without drawing it out - which maight actually leave you feeling cheated if it went on 'forever' and that ending was the one that you got. it was a good length for the story that was told. Just the game itself was well done and felt a bit short, if only because I wanted a bit more of the exellent game play,
There are more things I could comment on, I guess, like the part where you play the Apache Gunner, which served well if only to break the gameplay up and provide some variety. but really, everything about this game was good to OK, and worth a play through. I think I got this either for $4 on special, or in a bundle, So i can't complain about the price. If your idea of fun is trying to figure out whether paying a couple of thousand dollars to increase the price of a resource by five dollars for 20 seconds is the optimal strategy, OTC may be the game for you. So many choices to make but none of them are particularly interesting.
If you want to get a feel for the level of mind numbing detail in OTC, read the free Almanac before buying the game. This poorly written document is chock full of formulas - this game must have been designed by a programmer. I'm a programmer myself, but I don't want to tinker with formulas for fun.
I've heard of other Stardock games being referred to as spreadsheet games. I thought OTC might be different but it seems that Stardock lacks the creative energy that is essential for creating compelling games.

With the Anime Weekend Sale currently going on, I figured I would write up a review of this game.
I acquired this game through a humble bundle and put it in my library, where it was promptly forgotten about. Fast forward a few months when I'm starting up my LP channel on Youtube, and this game's title stuck out to me like a sore thumb. I had no idea what it was going in.
The main character of this game is Parin, a young girl sent to live with her grandfather after her parents go out on an expedition. Tiese Town has no children to speak of and Parin has no one to be friends with.
A few days later, Parin hears a scream and sees a weird little girl cornered by her neighbor's dog. Parin kicks the dog (poor puppy!) and saves the girl. Parin finds out that the girl, Pino, is a monster, and can only be seen by children. Parin is taken to Monster Village by Pino and quickly makes friends with all its inhabitants. The game then goes into a jazzy intro sequence with some awesome music!
GAMEPLAY is very similar in style to the Legend of Zelda: the protagonist moves through dungeons filled with monsters to reach a prize at the end.  I would say it's most similar in style to Ocarina of Time, except all the "waiting" to fight enemies is taken out. The game has a ranking system based on how many monsters you killed in the dungeon, how many treasure chests you opened/how many pots you broke, and how long it took you to complete the dungeon. You unlock new areas by getting furniture from the ends of dungeon and giving it to the inhabitants of Monster Village.
The STORY is also very intriguing; things don't really come to a head until Eggplant Caverns is reached. A lot of things mentioned in passing come together, tying up loose strings that you thought didn't matter.
The GRAPHICS are kind of cartoony, which gives it a unique and charming look; this game was originally released in 2004, and brought to Steam in 2015. The graphics held up really well!
The MUSIC for this game is super jazzy, in a good way! All of the tracks are pleasant to listen to, and very memorable. I would say that it's almost on the same level of Jet Set Radio's soundtrack. (here's a link to my favorite song from the Gurumin OST:)
All in all, Gurumin is a very charming game and definitely one that should be part of your library. If you want to get an idea of what gameplay is like, I've linked the first episode of my LP at the top of this review. :)

I got this game for free on steam when they used the game as promotion for their other games.
I'm not into horror games.
But being a stealth-fan, enjoying for example the thief-series, I can appreciate the stealth, superb sound design, dynamic play and and well developed story in this game. It also is very physical experience. Walking, jumping, opening doors, lifting things feel very organic and authentic, and is actually part of the enjoyment of the game. Hats off to the physic engine in this game.
It is probably still the better horror experience out there, if you get scared by horror games, that is. And that is the rub. This game is an experience, and it is supposed to be a tense one. But if you don't get scared easily by games, it actually quite soon becomes a little tedious. Because even though the physics are good, and the puzzles are ok (but nothing to write home about), they whole point is still to get scared. The puzzles are not the point.
Now, there is nothing wrong with that, but I mean that the game mechanincs and puzzles are secondary and not awesome, not the meat of the game. It can actually become a little boring, because while you are trying to finish some puzzle or get some story-plot you have to avoid some monster, or collect "resources" so that you can see at all. And some levels are rather large and dark. So, running around forever in a dark cave, stopping and waiting for the monster...  It can take a while to finish a simple objective if you don't know where you are.
Now, light. An ok mechanic in this game, but also extremely contrived. I understand the point is to create tention: "do I have enought light?", "can I hide?" "Am I going insane?". But when you "get the game-style" it just becomes tedious. Your character is weak, and deteriorates quickly in the dark. You cannot fight. So while you are trying to progress you just have to waith for the moster, find enough light and not go insane. Again, if you get scared, you might like it. Personally I don't enjoy playing while being tense all the time.
I do see the great work going into this title though, and pretty much everything it has to offer is well thought of and well made. Voice acting is really good, and again, the physics engine really shines - you "sense and feel" your character. The game is very suspenseful and even though a little older, the graphics still conveys the atmosphere really well, and should run well on most machines.
Interesting point: I like being stealthy and sneak around, but in this game I kept wishing I had a weapon, and I did not want to sneak that much in the end, and started running not caring about the monsters.
I did not finish the game though, but did about 75%
Recommended if you like scary games. Probably one of the better game of this kind.

Out of the Park Baseball (OOTP for short) 17 is a text based baseball simulation.  It contains features for historical gameplay, single player gameplay, custom universe/leagues gameplay and online multiplayer gameplay.  The game allows you to take an active role in developing rosters and teams, or managing them.  This is done through being a General manager, a manager and even play as the commissioner(you are able to play all three at once, or any combination of the two).
OOTP 17 offers new features over previous editions.  They now have full support from MLB and MLBPA(obtained through licensing), so you will have accurate rosters, faces(done through facegen models) and with no worries that they will disappear.  Simulation speed has been increased as the new code is allowing the use of multicore processors, which is a huge benefit.  The AI also has been enhanced to be smarter in how they draft players, manage players, and develop teams.  They will also make decisions depending on your goals and strategy.  These are just some of the major changes that OOTP has offered over previous editions.
OOTP has one of the strongest modding communities around for sport simulation games.  The community greatly enhances the vanilla gameplay.  For instance, historical gameplay has accurate rosters, player attributes, statistics and settings for the era you choose to play(you can play from the grass roots of baseball, negro leagues, or any specific season).  You can choose to play it as a single season campaign or start a franchise and build your league from the 1880’s to whenever you choose to end(the starting point is up to you!).  The community also offers tools to develop uniforms and baseball caps, and there’s literally thousands already pre-made for you to use if you want to choose from them.
The gaming modes available(and some of this is a repeat of above, I apologize), are single player, and multiplayer.  Single player modes allow you to play out single exhibition games with modern and historical teams.  You can play as MLB teams, which will have player accurate rosters and attributes.  You are also able to create your own fictional leagues, which is a massively popular feature for many players in the OOTP community.  You can start from any time frame, and you can customize the league to fit your needs or gameplay style(there are many sliders to adjust to your likings, and needs).  Regardless of the league, the game will track and keep a massive history of your statistics as your world/league develops.
The game also features multiplayer gameplay where you can compete in leagues against others, which will put you against the most difficult of opponents(or easy, if they don’t know what they’re doing ;) ).  The league will track statistics as if you were in a single player franchise.  Many leagues out there have dedicated websites where you can follow the action of the league as it unfolds.  It is really a neat feature.
The development team is very active and proactive in fixing bugs and glitches within their games.  You don’t have to worry about issues going unnoticed or fixed, and they are very open minded to additional features they may have fixed(as long as they are deemed reasonable of course).  The best way to suggest and fill out bug notifications is to use the main forums on their websites, which is
.  The community is also very helpful in helping new players learn and teach players about the game(I myself have helped a few players learn the game of baseball and the workings of OOTP).
In conclusion, after 2000+ hours of OOTP 16 gameplay, and 1200+ hours of OOTP15 gameplay, I can honestly say this is the best addition to the series to date.  I have never had a game give back so much in value then what OOTP has.  It is simply the best baseball simulation on the market(possibly the best sports simulation as well).  The game is very polished, and if you are a baseball fan, or a sports fan, I highly recommend that you take a chance on OOTP17.  You will NOT be disappointed.
This game is a 10/10 for me.  I hope to see you on the field! Feel free to add me if you need any help with this game, or series!  I am always willing to help out new players get established in this great sports simulation!

Nihilumbra is, overall, a great experience. A platformer somewhere along the lines of Limbo, it's less atmoshperic, but its thought-provoking premisis, coupled with some intelligently designed platforming and puzzles, make it a real gem of the genre.
The game's short but thoughtful philosophical interludes are perfectly fitted within the environments that the game has you explore, and it succesfully conveys the feeling of a journey toward maturity, gradually finding out more about the world as it is and what you can (or can't) have an impact on. The narrator's remarks are frequent but never too revealing, thus leaving you the liberty to link and interprete the metaphors for yourself.
Nihilumbra also gradually opens up its gameplay through the aquisition of colours, with which you can change the environment. One lets you create ice, which helps you traverse certain sections more quickly, or enables you to make certain objects or enemies slide and fall, given that there is an initial momentum to begin with. Another is mud, which acts both as a means of slowing down - yourself and others -, stealthily traversing a section, as well as a sticky surface, allowing you to stick to walls or ceilings. Each of the six colours has its unique multiple purposes. The great thing about this is that most puzzles or obstacles you encounter along the way have multiple solutions, so you can do it your own way.
The aesthetics are very well designed - the diverse environments look beautiful, yet not majestic. The music used is very suitable as well, and nicely adapted to each of the worlds you explore. However, I think it's used in excess. Sure, since it's not trying to convey an atmosphere as tense and empty as Limbo's , I wouldn't have pleaded for complete silence, but there are some sections of the game which would have benefitted from less rather than more background noise.
While the main story mode is rather easy, and can be completed in around 3 hours, the real challenge here is represented by Void mode. It's a redesign of the original maps, but made much much much harder. So hard that I think the contrast between the main game, where I was never stuck for more than 2-3 minutes, and Void mode, where simply the first level of the first chapter took me around 20 minutes to complete, is a bit sharp.
Overall, I can only tell you to buy this game. It's fairly priced for the content it offers, it will delight you with its beautiful visuals and smart story analogies.

An intensely philosophical and brooding rumination on war and morality,
is a masterfully written sequel to the original BioWare classic.
As brightly as the narrative and writing may shine however, (a worthy successor to the quality of the first), the game often falters in other aspects.
borders on what could be considered broken; featuring an overall design that lacks polish, quality and ultimately feels unfinished and sorely lacking of QA testing. Granted, this was due to time constraints and pressure from LucasArts, but it is only thanks to the efforts of the community in recent years, (namely the team behind the Restored Content Mod that I'll be trying out next), and the rare update that this can be played and enjoyed as much as it is.
Dialogue is frequently skipped over at unreadable speeds, there are significant issues with clipping, camera movement, loading and most animations, and achievement unlocks are all over the place - I got the "Dancing Queen" achievement randomly on Peragus Station.
also doesn't feel like much of a departure from the first. Combat is almost identical but yet no longer satisfying or a challenge to play; the developers appear to have compensated for the now♥♥♥♥♥♥weak enemies by simply adding more of them, with the rare boss fight often amounting to a self-healing tank, bullet sponge or absolute pushover.
As a result, you'll die very little and this leaves you feeling as if you're playing on rails; as if combat hardly matters. But for a series that is so reliant and with so much potential depth in its combat and stat management, this was disappointing.
As already alluded to though, the quality shown through the writing and branching dialogue saves
from what could have been a disaster. For those who have played the original, the game picks up a short time after the events of the first
and builds upon a lot of the lore surrounding it. A feature for importing your save file isn't available, but there are plenty of options through dialogue to link the choices made in the first. Though admittedly seen as more of a part of the overarching narrative than unique themselves, the companions and major NPCs are, for the most part, fascinating.
HK-47 is back, (by popular demand, no doubt), and Kreia personifies the complexities that
deals with and, along with Visas, delivers the excellent writing in an equally stellar performance.
Remember Malachor V.
Very few modern titles use the capabilities that gaming - as a medium - presents anymore, but like the first, Obsidian manipulates both the character and the player with a narrative and means of perspective which is fascinating to watch and all the more immersive to experience. Questions of responsibility and complicity are frequently raised, often leaving it open for you to ponder your choices and the nature of the Force itself. The interwoven plots and rich storytelling of
and the like could not be possible in film or television; and it is this that makes video games such an art form.
Play
for the story. Though still worth a purchase, just be aware of what you’re getting into.
It is a flawed gem, but a great one at that, and its achievements exceed the faults that could've held it back. A worthy follow up to the original, pick this up along with the Restored Content Mod and make it into the best it can be.
A war-torn, Nihilistic thumbs-up.

Its a modern naval strategy war game. Its a quite good game - you get to control subs, ships, helicopters and a variety of planes in modern day scenarios via a tactical interface but you can see whats going on via a sort of tv picture which does get you in on the action. The game is fairly complex its got fairly deep gameplay with a few differnet systems to learn, but its still fun for light gamers like myself.
The downsides are the lack of a save facility during the missions themselves, which can been quite long at times, and because of the complexity of the calcs this game runs slowly if a lot is going on which restricts the engagements to small skirmishes (also required due to the lack of a save facility). If it wasnt for the above I am sure this game would have been expanded by various moders dramatically into an all out war game with massive campaigns made available.
This game is a strategy game where you launch various assets to react to threats, you see them pop up on the radar and most of the game is played on a map. Graphics are fairly spartan and it is surprising that it slows down so much but I guess its lack of programming efficiency more than anything because this game is by a small dev.
Overall its enjoyable playing out the skirmishes, there arent that many modern naval games around like this - really just this and Dangerous Waters and this game is more immediate and better looking (just) than DW but not as deep. However its also not going to develop any more, the devs have forgotten about it, and the lack of graphics, saving and speed makes it of limited commodity so bear that in mind.
Other possibilities are Dangerous Waters, 688i, Silent Hunter 3, Atlantic Fleet, Cold Waters.

Great game.  Do not listen to the haters who played this in the past.  It has now been fixed.
Pros:  I have played the tutorials which make the game very easy to play.  I have not found any bugs so far.  This game is very like Jane's Fleet Command, but a little more modern.  I am now playing one of the campaigns and have also played one of the single missions.  There are loads of missions/campaigns on Steam and elsewhere.  The AI is very good and the game can be quite tense, though a bit slow for any younger gamers who love lots of action and shooting, etc.  This is a sedate game for older players like me who are middle-aged and no longer have the reactions of the younger generation (no problem, as most Admirals are middle aged!?).  The Steam version has obviously been heavily patched and seems to work a dream.  I have no problem with gameplay/framerates, but I must admit I have a fairly high-end machine and can run it on full graphics without any problem so far.  Far from being quirky, the interface is a doddle to use, despite reports from other reviewers.
Cons: The graphics are rubbish!  They are better than Fleet Command (which I own, so they should be now after all these years) and a bit better than Dangerous Waters (which I also own).  However, unlike Dangerous Waters, though the models look much better, the ships do not even have wakes behind them!?  The use of towed array sonar and dipping sonar is not animated!!!  I have yet to see a ship moving up and down with the waves.  The music is mind-bendingly monotonous as well as being completely inappropriate - it is gentle guitar music during a battle which involves Billions of Dollars/Pounds and countless lives!!!!!
Conclusion:  I bought the game for less than £4.00/$7.00.  Well worth it during the 'Lunar' sale.  It is now £15.00/$19.00.  Worth it, probably not.  However, for Naval Strategy fans, this is still a gem and a bit more updated than Dangerous Waters/Fleet Command whose graphics are atrocious.  I will definetely be buying the DLC and downloading the many workshop missions/campaigns

After playing this game for a few hours I think a better name for OTC would be "Mars - the spreadsheet".
Lots of numbers, lots of tweaking numbers. I love playing strategy games but I don't OTC to be much fun. The references to the classic Dan/Dani Bunten game MULE had me fooled. I was hoping for an elegantly designed game with deep strategy, a modern take on MULE. There is nothing elegant about the design of OTC.
If your idea of fun is trying to figure out whether paying a couple of thousand dollars to increase the price of a resource by five dollars for 20 seconds is the optimal strategy, OTC may be the game for you. So many choices to make but none of them are particularly interesting.
If you want to get a feel for the level of mind numbing detail in OTC, read the free Almanac before buying the game. This poorly written document is chock full of formulas - this game must have been designed by a programmer. I'm a programmer myself, but I don't want to tinker with formulas for fun.
I've heard of other Stardock games being referred to as spreadsheet games. I thought OTC might be different but it seems that Stardock lacks the creative energy that is essential for creating compelling games.

This game is fun, especially if you're a horror fan. They absolutely nailed the atmosphere and music and the intensity of the gameplay is great.
On launch day there are a few issues, as is with 99% of multiplayer games these days, but i've been able to play the  majority of games with no lag and very few issues. That said, there will be dozens of reviews of people complaining about something temporary like server stablity at launch. If you're like me, you basically ignore every review that complains about launch day stuff (not just here, but in any game really) because they are problems that won't be there in a week.
That said, getting to play as Jason is awesome and you really are unstoppable once you get the hang of the abilities. He's probably a little too strong in the hands of a good player against a handful of people, but a big group of good councillors can give you a hard time for sure, especially once they learn that sneaking and evasion are huge.
There is some progression in the form of traits and abilities and unlocks, which are all pretty cool, the various characters are kinda meh, but the extra unlockable Jason's are really awesome and probably where a lot of time will be spent grinding. There are also secrets and hidden achievements for people into that, though I doubt most will have the presence of mind to think about stuff like that initially anyways.
There will be people complaining about a lack of depth to the game, because it really is as simple as Jason kills and survivors survive, but that's a really silly complaint because while the concept is simple, it's still very random and unpredictable and takes some skill to be "good" at it.
The game isn't perfect and there are a few bugs, but it's really impressive what a small team was able to accomplish here and the passion they have for the source material is evident.
If you're a horror fan, a fan of the series or just enjoy survival type games in general, you will probably have a good time with this game, especially if you bring friends!
I for one am positive i'll get my money's worth out of this game, but I did kickstart it in Oct 2015, so it's been a long time coming,

To simply put this game is fun and great. If you're a Friday the 13th fan then this is a must buy or if your a survival horror fan then I highly recommend the game to you as well. If you don't fit any of those, well take a look at some vids, see for yourself, the game is pretty enjoyable and provides a lot of laughs. It does have a lot of replayablility from what it currently has, anyone complaining about replayability, look at shooters or sports games? Whether you get bored fast or not differs entirely on the person. As for balance, well the game is nicely unbalanced, there is always room for tweaks in the future of course as the game might evolve but Jason is meant to be super strong, I mean he is Jason! So don't be frightened by the fact of how powerful he is if your new to the game. Naturally in inexperienced play Jason has the upper hand, but once your become accustom to how to play as the Counselors and their different play styles and grow experienced with how things work, you will notice a much even playing field. It is a 1v7 so teamwork is kinda key, might be an issue for you if your playing with randoms but its a fantastic game to play with friends. I usually find that 7 great counselors do a fantastic job of escaping, and put Jason to shame. As for people complaining about the price of content. Friday the 13th has more than double the amount of content than Dead By Daylight had when it was first released. Not to mention the quality of the game is far superior(Graphics, Map Size/Map Beauty,Animations,Mechanics, Items, etc), and the fact that there will be more content in the future that will be free for the base game(aside from whatever DLC might be planned in the future), example: soloplay/storymodes. So overall the price is pretty fair, if they had story mode for release I wouldn't be surprised if the price was 50$. By no means is it a perfect game or the best game in the world, but its a pretty well crafted survival horror and one of the best ones at that, it does the legacy of the films justice.

The premise is simple enough - you have to build a Mars-based resource exploitation and trading company, grow it faster than your competitors, and eventually buy them out in a hostile takeover via the stock market. Anyone who has ever played Civ and tried to go for non-military victories is going to appreciate what this game has to offer.
I would say that the only downside is that the game is quite cognitively straining because it requires the player to to juggle a lot of numbers and economic variables, so this is not something you want to play if your goal is to blow off some steam after a hard day at work.
Caveat emptor: the game is very addictive!

This review is for the game ''Medal of Honor'',a first-person military shooter video game,developed by the video game company Danger Close Games(Single-player) and EA Digital Illusions CE(multiplayer).It was published by Electronic Arts and released in October 12,2010 for NA and October 15,2010 for Europe.The game uses the Unreal Engine 3 for the single player campaign and the Frostbit 1.5 for the multiplayer mod.The game is available for Microsoft Windows,Playstation 3 and Xbox 360.
Single player-campaign plot
The campaign,of the thirteenth installment of the Medal of Honor series,takes place during the first days of the invasion of Afghanistan,in 2002.The story might be based on on the events that took place during Operation Anaconda that occured in March 2002,approximately six months after 9/11.In the game you will get to experience warfare that happened in reality like the seizing of Bagram Airfield,the Battle of Takur Ghar and the Battle of Shah-i-Kot.
Throughout the game you will be exchanging roles between the Navy SEAL DEVGRU ''Rabbit'',a Delta Force sniper code-named ''Deuce'',Ranger Dante Adams and the Apache helicopter gunner Brad Hawkins.Apart they will face great battles and will have to overcome great obstacles in order to protect their country,their freedom and their well-being.
Multiplayer
Multiplayer is really rich in weapon customization,perk unlockables,achievements,statistics and ribbons giving the sense of fulfillment to the player while playing multiplayer.Sadly the multiplayer is quite dead already.Unfortunately no more that 100-200 gamers play daily.
Recap
Medal of Honor series used to be Electronic Arts' flagship.Unfortunately interest got lost since EA focused more on the development was focused on creating and expanding the Dragon Age series,the Dead Space series,the Crysis series and especially the Battlefield series,whom today are EA's flagship.
Pros
+Beautiful graphics
+Interesting fast paced storyline,sometimes heartbreaking
+Exciting and easy to use shooting mechanisms
Cons
-Deceased multiplayer
-Linear mission based storyline(too linear for my taste)
Q:Do i recommend this game?
A:Depends.If you want to explore the single player campaign and progress through the Medal of Honor universe absolutely yes.If you buy it for the Multiplayer mod do not bother you'll be playing alone or with a bunch of 12 year olds.
P.S I didn't refer much on the Plot section because i didn't want to spoil the game to you.Buy it and play it thoroughly.
Support the developers.Electronic Arts thank you for this game.

I picked up this game because of the setting. It takes influences from bioshock and puts its setting at the bottom of the ocean and is set 100 years in the future. One day you go in for a brain scan to see if doctors can fix you up after a horrible car crash, however, you wake up in the future and have to figure out how you got there. Without going into spoilers the way they explained it was a very fresh concept, but also terrifing in its own right. This game gets two things right, its world and the story. On the surface this a medicore "survival horror game" with basic stealth and monstors that sure are scary at first, but i wasn't changing my underwear when they showed up. Actually the can pretty much just run past all the monsters like in a haunted house. Also none of the monsters pose any real threat. They are kinda like high school bullies in that sense. They corner you and beat you up, but then just leave you in the corner to cry. I only died once during my 7 hour playthorugh. What kept me going was the story. It reminded me of a really good episode of doctor who in the tennant era. Before I go into minor spoilers I'm just going to say go out and buy it. It is a fantastic experience that you will not forget.
*******WARNING MINOR SPOLIERS*********
The basic setup of the game is that you wake up 100 years in the future at the bottom of the Atlantic ocean at a giant base only to find out that a meteor has crashed into the earth and killed everyone on the surface. You quickly find a character that explains she was tasked with trying to launch a satellite into space that contains a simulation of earth filled with brain scans of people on the base to try and preserve the human race. The game is filled with many twist and turns and the real horror of the game comes from the atmosphere and the reality of what you are doing not the monsters that occasionally try to take your lunch money. The problem I had with the monsters is that they didn't give a good reason to why they where there. If they had just taken the monsters out i think it would have been an even better game.
*************OVERALL***************
If you go into this game thinking its going to be the next blare witch project your going to be very dissapointed. What you get is a fantastic world to explore and an engaging story that will keep you comping back to see how it ends and when it does it will make you take a look on how you view the world. Just walking around the ocean floor looking at the base is just breath taking. I cant recommend this game enough and can't wait to see what this studio develops next!

I really dislike games that make me feel like an idiot, and sadly SOMA is one of those games.
While some people enjoy wandering around the ocean floor looking for whatever switch or ladder you're supposed to find, I am not one of them. Sure, I don't want the game to hold my hand all the time but it always feels like I've missed some instruction in SOMA and I have no idea what I'm even supposed to be looking for, not to mention what I'm actually doing there in the first place. Not only do I feel like an idiot when I finally find the switch, computer, ladder or [insert random object] I'm looking for, I also understand LESS of why I was even looking for it in the first place.
That is not a gratifying experience.
I might have played it the wrong way by sneaking around and generally avoiding areas with monsters, but I doubt that you’d be running around like some Yolo Swaggins if your main goal is to survive. It’s a survival horror game for crying out loud.
Also, I don't understand what's supposed to be scary about SOMA. Is it the supposed ideas you should be getting about existentialism, or the more annoying than scary monsters? After finishing the game, I don't know. Apart from a few jump scares and a pretty cool ocean floor sequence (among many uncool sequences) towards the end, the game simply isn't scary. There is nothing in the story to make up for this lack of tension either. While the voice acting is superb and I liked the idea of the data buffers left behind by the people who lived there, I don't really feel anything for the people who are talking to me from a century ago. There is no real explanation of what ACTUALLY happened (other than a few fragments in files and references from NPCs) that I've been able to find and they don't even let you play through any of the events leading up to the main part game (apart from the prologue/tutorial). The only thing I got is a dream sequence for about a minute that makes even less sense than the rest of the game. Still, it could be that I’ve missed vital clues that are supposed to reveal more stuff. Or maybe I’m just an idiot. Either way I don’t get it. At all.
Why are the monsters not scary? Well, because they are mostly roadblocks rather than monsters. They make enough noise to phone in exactly where they are and their behaviour is ridiculously predictable for all but a few of them. And why are they annoying? Well because they tend to alternate between super monsters with night vision to completely deaf, dumb and blind walking roadblocks. I’ve had the same monster see me in the shadows and knock me down, only to stand right next to me moments later without noticing me. I don’t know if that’s a feature, but moments like that kills the mood and immersion immediately. After that point I just laughed, or sighed, in the face of every moaning roadblock throughout the rest of the game. It’s also extremely easy to avoid most of them (bar one with x-ray vision and motion sensors) by running into a corner and leaning out. At one point I managed to trigger the same sequence three times and avoided the monster by doing the exact same thing. Out of spite I did it a few more times only to have the same thing happen each and every time.
Now, things are not all bad. The environments are really cool and well made (especially the interior designs) and the game sounds really good with some really good sound effects and voice acting. I enjoyed rummaging through computers, living chambers etc. in monsterless areas and just looking at the fish the first time I ventured out into the ocean. Still, the ocean walks become just as tedious and laborsome as the rest of the game once you’ve done them for the umpteenth time.
Mechanically the game uses similar controls to the ones found in Amnesia, and they mostly work well. It does create a bit of stress and tension when you have to assemble a component by actually putting the pieces together using the mouse and keyboard (or controller), but it can also be extremely frustrating due to some inaccurate triggers where you are close, but not close enough, to initiate or complete an action. Besides that I did enjoy the interactive controls and the different puzzles. It was surprisingly fun to plug in cables and pull down pipes in order to progress in the game
One thing I do like is the fact that you don’t die the first time you get caught by a monster, instead you get knocked down, the monster moves away and you have the chance to move on or find one of the brain-like things that work as health packs. It’s a nice feature for a game where you can’t fight back. But just like everything else in this game, nothing good without bad. I don’t know why, but sometimes you die the second time you get caught and sometimes you don’t. This COULD be based on how many times you’ve died (for example dying repeatedly to the same monster) but at one point I got caught in a sequence of getting knocked down, waking up, getting knocked down, waking up for a good 2 to 3 minutes before I actually died and I respawned at the checkpoint which just ruined the experience even more for me.
Also, the fish towards the end of the game are some of the most annoying “enemies” I’ve ever encountered, in any game.
While the game has a kind of nice idea of having the main character talk and “think” for himself, he’s not a very likeable person and I found him annoying, whiny and even more clueless than myself. When faced with moral choices he sometimes displays multiple personalities where he at first supports one course of action (or at least that’s what it feels like), only to whine and get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off about it after going through with it while at another point he just seems to not give a ♥♥♥♥ at all. He also seems to be suffering from either senility or just being extremely thick, considering he either forgets or refuses to understand something that’s been explained to him on multiple occasions. I suppose that it’s done on purpose for some reason, probably to further question your “humanity” or existence, but I merely found it confusing and somewhat annoying.
To be completely honest, I was expecting a lot more horror from the story itself through audio logs and flashbacks to the past where you got to experience the events that led to the situation you find yourself in as well as feeling more “hunted” by the monsters. I was also expecting much more of a reveal of who, or what, you actually are in the game. Instead I was “forced” to just sneak around dodging roadblocks while finding the next switch to pull, all the while thinking to myself “when will this end?” and the big reveal wasn’t very big or much of a reveal at all. While I did get scared a few times, it just wasn’t enough and I never found myself being truly engaged by the story or afraid of what might happen to me.
I did enjoy the ending, not only because the game was over, but because it was pretty clever so if you make it through the game the ending is kind of worth it.
To conclude: I feel the game could’ve worked better as a pure exploration game with the horror story told through sound, writing and flashbacks that lets your mind come up with even scarier scenarios. Pretty much the way a lot of the stuff is done in Amnesia, or in a good book for that matter. Sure, your mileage may wary depending on how you play the game and what you find and I likely missed things that others found but all in all I was very disappointed.
While I at first wanted to call it a bad game I now feel (mainly because of the ending) that all in all it’s a decent game with a nice idea that works in a few areas, but falls short in most and I give it a 4/10 and I don't recommend it unless you're a fan or just want to play it anyway.

Basically, it's low rent Ys: Oath in Felghana/origin with a more lighthearted story.  There's a lot of love put into this game and there's much to like, but conversely this was likely a B-team or frugal project.
The soundtrack as expected of a falcom game from the era is great (with the exception of one minigame track).  Visuals and story are pretty basic but serviceable.
Although combat and the main mechanics/item management are additive and fun, in general the loose design, mediocre platforming control/camera and recycled levels are the game's main weakness.  You won't see much of it if you simply race to the end, but if you shoot to do all the levels pretty much everything's used twice- there's really more music than there are unique stages.  Still, the game's got decent replay value given how tricky it is to get everything.  It also has some nice little puzzles and minigames thrown into the mix to vary things up a smidge.
In summation, the game's value is decent for its cost, but unless the setting really appeals to you or you want something a little easier I'd play the Ys games that are on Steam first.

SOMA brings up some heavy moral and psychological topics during it's playthrough, which adds to the psychological horror theme a lot. You need to care what's happening in the story, or this game will be unenjoyable. The plot is pretty simple, but gets more complex as you progress. The atmosphere adds to the experience, you're at the bottom of the ocean, isolated from everything you know. You need to make tough decisions based on your personal morals and none of your choices are good or bad, they are complicated, and that's why it makes you think about life. Involving topics such as what kind of life is worth living on with, euthanasia/suicide and afterlife.

Exzeal is a shmup that's built entirely around its scoring systems.  If you like thinking about what you are doing and how you can do it better, this is a great game.  If you just want to shoot stuff and dodge bullets though, this game is hard to recommend.
Many of the attack waves don't really do much, or have hard to reach hit boxes that don't make sense just shooting at normally.  Instead, look at your ships attack type and how it gets bonuses, and how you can maximize each wave.  There's a way to kill even the trickiest of enemies, and there's likely a different way to do it "well".
Exzeal has five ships to try out and they all play differently and have different solutions to the game's many puzzles.  The XII Stag ship in particular is a nice addition for those who are familiar with it, and burning up enemies with your exhaust never gets old.  Note: to play the hidden fifth ship, select type 3 with exactly 13 seconds left on the timer.
The biggest downside to this game is, oddly enough, hand fatigue.  Two of the ships have a charge up mechanic, which can be sped up by rapidly rotating your joystick / thumb pad / keyboard fingers.  The XII Stag ship has an auto-rotate button, however the others do not (this would have been a great addition).  It's not as bad as Psyvariar games, but I definitely feel the burn after longer play sessions.  I can just envision an arcade owner getting frustrated as players wear out the joysticks every week from spinning circles non-stop, hehe.

Exzeal was initially launched in 2007 to Arcade (Sega Naomi board) and in 2009 for Xbox 360 as part of the "Shooting Love 200X" collection, which brought together beyond this game other three: "Shmups Skill Test", "Minus Zero" and "Trizeal Remix", all of them developed by Triangle Service (japanese developer founded by a former employee of Konami) and now in 2016 this game finally comes to Steam at the hands of Degica, publisher that has been noted for bring to the Steam (and thus to the whole world) many shmups (acronym for shoot' em up aka STG) previously restricted only to Japan. Exzeal is a vertical shmup and a beautiful direct sequel of the classic Trizeal. However, Exzeal differs from Trizeal in essence, because while Trizeal had 3 different transformations of the ship at any time during the game (at the touch of a button), Exzeal doesn't allow this, however there are 4 different types of ships settings that can be selected before the start of the game, they are: [Type 1] with a normal shot and also a much more powerful shot which is charged holding down the appropriate button (R-Type style) so, when fired, this charged shot eliminates many enemies at once and is important to say that you can  charge the charged shot faster making a  360-degree rotation movement with the analog stick; [Type 2] similar to type 1, but the charged shot travels beyond the ship's front and back as well on the upper and lower diagonals; [Type 3] allows only front normal shots, but causes more damage than regular shots of the other types and finally [Type 4] has normal front shot and also a kind  of short-range generated by the movement of the ship in the directions rear, left and right. These 4 different types of configurations bring good variety to gameplay  The game's graphics were very good for the 2007 standards and remain good even today. The songs are great, contributing directly to the immersion of the game. The controls respond well to commands  (I used the official wireless Xbox 360 controller through the analog stick). The player can save replays of matches and the game also has an online leaderboard very good where you can watch the replay of other players  inside the leaderboard, something always useful for those who want to know and learn the patterns and techniques used by the best players. An intensely philosophical and brooding rumination on war and morality,
is a masterfully written sequel to the original BioWare classic.
As brightly as the narrative and writing may shine however, (a worthy successor to the quality of the first), the game often falters in other aspects.
borders on what could be considered broken; featuring an overall design that lacks polish, quality and ultimately feels unfinished and sorely lacking of QA testing. Granted, this was due to time constraints and pressure from LucasArts, but it is only thanks to the efforts of the community in recent years, (namely the team behind the Restored Content Mod that I'll be trying out next), and the rare update that this can be played and enjoyed as much as it is.
Dialogue is frequently skipped over at unreadable speeds, there are significant issues with clipping, camera movement, loading and most animations, and achievement unlocks are all over the place - I got the "Dancing Queen" achievement randomly on Peragus Station.
also doesn't feel like much of a departure from the first. Combat is almost identical but yet no longer satisfying or a challenge to play; the developers appear to have compensated for the now♥♥♥♥♥♥weak enemies by simply adding more of them, with the rare boss fight often amounting to a self-healing tank, bullet sponge or absolute pushover.
As a result, you'll die very little and this leaves you feeling as if you're playing on rails; as if combat hardly matters. But for a series that is so reliant and with so much potential depth in its combat and stat management, this was disappointing.
As already alluded to though, the quality shown through the writing and branching dialogue saves
from what could have been a disaster. For those who have played the original, the game picks up a short time after the events of the first
and builds upon a lot of the lore surrounding it. A feature for importing your save file isn't available, but there are plenty of options through dialogue to link the choices made in the first. Though admittedly seen as more of a part of the overarching narrative than unique themselves, the companions and major NPCs are, for the most part, fascinating.
HK-47 is back, (by popular demand, no doubt), and Kreia personifies the complexities that
deals with and, along with Visas, delivers the excellent writing in an equally stellar performance.
Remember Malachor V.
Very few modern titles use the capabilities that gaming - as a medium - presents anymore, but like the first, Obsidian manipulates both the character and the player with a narrative and means of perspective which is fascinating to watch and all the more immersive to experience. Questions of responsibility and complicity are frequently raised, often leaving it open for you to ponder your choices and the nature of the Force itself. The interwoven plots and rich storytelling of
and the like could not be possible in film or television; and it is this that makes video games such an art form.
Play
for the story. Though still worth a purchase, just be aware of what you’re getting into.
It is a flawed gem, but a great one at that, and its achievements exceed the faults that could've held it back. A worthy follow up to the original, pick this up along with the Restored Content Mod and make it into the best it can be.
A war-torn, Nihilistic thumbs-up.
A pleasent surprise.
