First and foremost is the clarification: this is a very long yet well-made game that is absolutely a successor to the first Knights of the Old Republic. I have only done one playthrough and it took me more than 65 hours to complete. It has all of the features of the original game and has added many new ones that seamlessly integrate with this second entry in the series. The story is rich and in-depth and the characters are memorable for the most part but feel a little flatter in this game than they did in the first. It also cleverly uses mechanics so that you can compete missions and fights in a variety of fashions and lots of your choices have very visible effects, but not all of them. Overall, this is a good game.
HOWEVER, I played the first KOTOR on my smartphone and I must say I prefer that one easily over this one, though for mostly personal reasons. The story of the first one felt tighter and more polished whereas with this game it feels like they tried to stretch it out for no good reason. I felt plagued by unnecessarily long fights as a result of too many enemies and zones that are large but I couldn't see the reason why they had to be so large. I also am a completionist so I try to do every sidequest possible and so quickly became annoyed with the constant trecking and back-tracking all over every map. There is also the fact that the characters are there but feel flatter and less developed than they did in the first game; they also don't feel like they are crucial part of stroy like they did in the first game. Finally is the fact that this story just doesn't feel as good as the one from the first KOTOR. I felt like it left too many loose ends, the plot twists fell flat, and it just plain left me feeling unsatisfied as compared to the first entry there just isn't a sense of closure.
Now, a lot of this has to do with personal taste and so someone else might completely disagree. As for bugginess I didn't encounter any bugs, glitches, etc. during my playthrough.
In conclusion: I would recommend the game, but I'm worried you'll feel less satisfied if you've already played the first KOTOR.

Keep in mind that I got this when it was free, so I might be less harsh on the game than I would be if I bought it at full price.
The main attraction of this game is without a doubt the ballistics and the "bullet cam" featured in it, and both of those things are neat. The difficulty decided how realistic things get, where on the lowest difficulty your rifle is basically hitscan and on the highest you get very limited help AND bullet drop + wind is a factor. You can even customize your own difficulty if you want help (there's a feature where you hold your breath and you get an indicator of where your bullet will go, for example) but also want wind to be featured, for example. Hell, there's even sections where you can mask your shots with the sounds of the battlefield.
I did get a bit tired and lowered the frequency of the bullet cam towards the end of the game, because as much as it's a neat feature you'll get a bit tired of it - you'll go for headshots 95% of the time as any other shot is somewhat unreliable as a one-shot-kill unless you hit a vital organ, and seeing the same animation of a skull crack 500 times isn't the most exciting thing in the world. Outside of sniper rifles the gunplay is relatively unimpressive as well, and the most exciting thing is probably the fact that ammo is somewhat scarce. There's also fully regenerative health which lowers the tension of having your cover blown. This game would benefit from a system where you either have partially regenerative health and had to rely on healing items, which seems to be what they have in Sniper Elite 3 from what I've seen.
The stealth system is functional at best. If you get found, you're probably better off simply fighting your way through the remaining enemies rather than try to relocate, as the normally abysmal sight of the enemies get boosted to incredible levels when they are aware of your presence. You do have a silenced pistol as your default sidearm, and you'll be relying on it as there's no canned "stealth kill" animations for unaware enemies, and you'll have to scavenge for ammo for that particular weapon - which is good. There are NO silenced sniper rifles, which is a plus in this case.
The game does.. not have the best replay value. There's collectibles, actually a ridiculous amount (especially the bottles you are supposed to shoot), but there's not really an incentive to go for them besides achievements. There's one level that seems out of place where you get to choose your loadout, and it's the only time in the game where you get to do so.
The game shines when you are picking of enemies and taking your time, or you're masking your shots and picking off stragglers. When it allows you to do this, it is truly a pretty neat sniper fantasy provider from one end to another. But once open combat ensues, the secondary weapons handle in a far less satisfying way - they are inaccurate and feel weak unless you are literally 2 meters away from your target, and once you get a semi-automatic rifle you're probably better off "quickscoping" enemies with that as opposed to using your submachine gun in open combat.
I have not tried the multiplayer aspect of the game. The "Team Distance" game mode sounds fun as it highlights the sniping aspect of the game, and it sounds like it would remind me of awp_ maps from CS:S - where you're at a distance and looking out for movement on the other side.
If you can get this game free or on a good sale it's worth it for a single playthrough, but don't expect too much more than that from it. I am also biased since I play sniper classes in most games where they are available, and the free promo of this game did make me pre-order Sniper Elite 3, so I guess it did its job!

This game is fun, especially if you're a horror fan. They absolutely nailed the atmosphere and music and the intensity of the gameplay is great.
On launch day there are a few issues, as is with 99% of multiplayer games these days, but i've been able to play the  majority of games with no lag and very few issues. That said, there will be dozens of reviews of people complaining about something temporary like server stablity at launch. If you're like me, you basically ignore every review that complains about launch day stuff (not just here, but in any game really) because they are problems that won't be there in a week.
That said, getting to play as Jason is awesome and you really are unstoppable once you get the hang of the abilities. He's probably a little too strong in the hands of a good player against a handful of people, but a big group of good councillors can give you a hard time for sure, especially once they learn that sneaking and evasion are huge.
There is some progression in the form of traits and abilities and unlocks, which are all pretty cool, the various characters are kinda meh, but the extra unlockable Jason's are really awesome and probably where a lot of time will be spent grinding. There are also secrets and hidden achievements for people into that, though I doubt most will have the presence of mind to think about stuff like that initially anyways.
There will be people complaining about a lack of depth to the game, because it really is as simple as Jason kills and survivors survive, but that's a really silly complaint because while the concept is simple, it's still very random and unpredictable and takes some skill to be "good" at it.
The game isn't perfect and there are a few bugs, but it's really impressive what a small team was able to accomplish here and the passion they have for the source material is evident.
If you're a horror fan, a fan of the series or just enjoy survival type games in general, you will probably have a good time with this game, especially if you bring friends!
I for one am positive i'll get my money's worth out of this game, but I did kickstart it in Oct 2015, so it's been a long time coming,
I'd say so far, it's fun enough to say it was worth the wait.

This is seriously one of the best games you can buy on Steam if you can manage to look past the awful remastered sprites and changes to the battle system ported from the Android version of this on the Google play store. This game is so incredible that I don't even know why I'm even bothering to review this, probably because I'm bored at work and have nothing better to do while I'm typing this right now.
*As a side note, I've never played much of this version specifically but have beaten both the version on the PSN store which is originally from the Final Fantasy Anthology collection for the PS1 several times along with the SNES original and have put plenty of hours into the original Japanese version of this game which was re-translated into English by fans on this great and wonderful phenomenon which we call the internet.
Story - Do I even need to explain this!? C'mon steam user, if you don't already know that FFVI has not only has one of the best stories in the Final Fantasy series but one of the best stories in a JRPG of all time then my work is done here. It would be a crime against all of gaming to post a bunch of spoilers in this section for some random dude who's never played this game before to have it spoiled before he's even touched this game yet. Sure there's plenty of ***holes on the internet who are more than happy to spoil everything about this game for you but definitely not in this review! The only thing I will mention with the story is that there is a twist half-way through the game which you'll probably never see coming and pretty much breaks one of the biggest norms of a story from JRPGs of this era which is one of the biggest reasons why it is remembered to this day.
P.S. - I am only willing to spoil the story of terrible games because it saves you money so that you won't waste your time playing a ****** game when you could be playing something much better like this.
Gameplay - If you have played any of the older, turn-based Final Fantasy games then there isn't much new here. This pretty much plays like your standard 2D JRPG game but with a few unique differences. The battle system in this game is about what you would expect from your standard 2D JRPG from this era but with a few twists. See, the way using magic works in this game is a few hours in you unlock summons which are called Espers in this game which you can equip to your characters although you can only equip one Esper per character at a time if I remember correctly. To find Espers, you have to find a shard of magicite within the game which each one is for a different Esper. By equipping an Esper and fighting battles with it equipped, you earn ability points or AP which goes toward learning spells from the magicite you have equipped with each Esper teaching a certain set of magic spells. As you may be able to tell by reading this far into this section of my review, you can pretty much break the game by gathering as many Espers as possible and grinding so that all of your characters learns every magic spell in the entire game although some characters are better at using magic than others. For example, Terra is going to be much better at using magic than someone like Edgar or Sabin who normally rely on physical attacks or tools such as a chainsaw (whatever you do in this game, GET THE CHAINSAW!!! seriously this thing can take out most bosses in the game in just 2-3 attacks). Along with magicite, you can equip your characters with weapons and armor that you find or buy throughout the game with certain weapons or armor having a special effect on your characters in battles. The battles in this version specifically have menus for each character in your party and your character is ready when their menu in particular rises partway up the screen with options such as attack, magic, item, equipping a weapon or armor, using an esper, using a character's special ability such as Blitz with Sabin or a Tool with Edgar, or to escape from a fight. A better example of what I'm trying to explain here can be better understood by looking at some of the pictures on the store page of this game. Also a few hours into the game, you will be able to use several methods of transport around the world map such as an airship, a boat in the ports of some towns which travel to pre-designated towns or citites, and of course a chocobo which will be the first you will come across after starting the game. The chocobo is going to be one of the most useful at first since when using it on the world map you are immune to random battles but note that chocobos can't travel over mountains or in bodies of water such as an ocean or lake. The dungeons in this game also play as you would expect from a JRPG of this era with chests to find, some with puzzles and a boss battle at the end before reaching the next part of the game. I will also mention that near the end of the game you can go on sidequests to find special weapons, pieces of armor or even hidden characters which will make the final dungeon and battle much easier for you than it normally would be along with using the battle Coliseum at the end of the game where you bet on one of your characters to win but take note that they will be controlled by a programmed AI so you won't have any control over what they do or how they fight.
Sound - The soundtrack to this game is arguably among the best that gaming has to offer. Not only does the music have a variety of influences but also is one of the most memorable in gaming. I guarantee that by the time you play through and finish this game that you'll fall so deeply in love with the soundtrack of this game that it will be stuck in your head for the rest of your life. This is one of those games where if for some strange reason you don't fall in love with the soundtrack then I would seriously have to ask what the actual **** is wrong with you.
Graphics - In FFVI, traveling in the world map actually isn't like in your standard JRPG of this era with an overhead view but actually uses a rendering technique called Mode 7. See, Mode 7 was a technique used in JRPGs for the Super Nintendo back in the early 1990s where since the console couldn't actually render 3D polygons with a decent framerate it instead used Mode 7 to give the illusion of 3D when traveling on the world map. However, when in towns or dungeons it is presented as you would expect from a 2D JRPG but has a unique feel and design all its own. The way the towns and dungeons in this game are designed perfectly give the vibe and feel that the developers intended which is part of the reason why this game is as beloved and timeless as it is. Some towns and dungeons will give you this feeling of being joyful and at home while others actually have some horror elements such as the Tower of Fanatics and an ancient and ruined castle found underground. As something to put out there, as I mentioned before the sprite redesigns of the characters in this version are awful but there is a mod you can download for free which actually uses the original sprites from the SNES/PS1/GBA versions of this game which are much better in my opinion and didn't really need to be changed anyway.
Overall - This is a game I have played through and beaten numerous times over the past 20 years and never gets old or boring. If you love JRPGs or even like JRPGs at all then this is a must-have and must-finish game for you. I could sit here for hours making this review longer than it already is but theres nothing I can do to give you the experience of this game for you. Theres a good reason why this is one of those games which is considered one of the best games ever made and I may get some hate for what I'm about to say but I'll just put on my fire-retardant suit, gas mask and body armor before I write this next sentence.

To simply put this game is fun and great. If you're a Friday the 13th fan then this is a must buy or if your a survival horror fan then I highly recommend the game to you as well. If you don't fit any of those, well take a look at some vids, see for yourself, the game is pretty enjoyable and provides a lot of laughs. It does have a lot of replayablility from what it currently has, anyone complaining about replayability, look at shooters or sports games? Whether you get bored fast or not differs entirely on the person. As for balance, well the game is nicely unbalanced, there is always room for tweaks in the future of course as the game might evolve but Jason is meant to be super strong, I mean he is Jason! So don't be frightened by the fact of how powerful he is if your new to the game. Naturally in inexperienced play Jason has the upper hand, but once your become accustom to how to play as the Counselors and their different play styles and grow experienced with how things work, you will notice a much even playing field. It is a 1v7 so teamwork is kinda key, might be an issue for you if your playing with randoms but its a fantastic game to play with friends. I usually find that 7 great counselors do a fantastic job of escaping, and put Jason to shame. As for people complaining about the price of content. Friday the 13th has more than double the amount of content than Dead By Daylight had when it was first released. Not to mention the quality of the game is far superior(Graphics, Map Size/Map Beauty,Animations,Mechanics, Items, etc), and the fact that there will be more content in the future that will be free for the base game(aside from whatever DLC might be planned in the future), example: soloplay/storymodes. So overall the price is pretty fair, if they had story mode for release I wouldn't be surprised if the price was 50$. By no means is it a perfect game or the best game in the world, but its a pretty well crafted survival horror and one of the best ones at that, it does the legacy of the films justice.

I have probably had to close and re-open the game like 20 times because I accidentally hit new game, because every other FF title ever started on continue. Also, the controls in the menus do not feel fluid or nice AT ALL. Just like in the original there is 3 columns in the menu screen. But if the spot below your cursor is blank, and you want to go down one and right one, you have to spam right until you get there because pressing down makes it jump clear to the next item in that column. Overall I enjoy this game very much, but it fells like the programmers must never have even played through this, leave all the testing to QA so they never realized how awful the menu control is. If you were hoping for M.U.L.E. or any other game about forming a business in the crucible of the wonder that is offworld colonization, then this is not that game.  However, if you like to win at games about number accumulation in real time, then you are in luck.  Offworld Trading Company is the epitome of real time number accumulation games!
The gameplay is basically day trading as a manic depressive.  Place buildings to make some commodity related numbers go up and others go down over time.  Some tiles are worth more numbers than others, but you have a very limited number of claim numbers to place.  Perform acts of sabotage to lower your opponents' numbers, but be careful: it costs cash numbers!  Whenever you buy something, the cost number of that commodity goes up.  Whenever you sell something, the cost number goes down.  Can you consistantly sell the most commodity numbers when they have the highest value numbers?  Usually you have no idea who is shifting what numbers.  When you play this game, this is your life now.
To win the game, you need to earn the biggest amount of numbers to buy your opponents' stocks so your numbers eat them in a "hostile takeover."  Lets say both you and your opponent have enough money to buy the other out: first click wins, because numbers!
Mercifully, games of Offworld Trading Company are usually over within a half-hour, but win or lose you will have literally nothing to show for it.  In a story-based game you may have heard a story.  In a building game, you might have built something cool.  In a 4X game, enough might have happened that you ended up building a story.  But there's nothing at all memorable about a match of Offworld Trading Company, just a sense of relief that the frantic shifting of numbers is over.
I tried to salvage this by getting good at Offworld Trading Company, but now I don't think it's possible.  I tried playing Skirmish on "manager" difficulty (a level playing field) and the AI wins every time.  I tried prioritizing upgrading my base.   I tried prioritizing having the most of the highest value commodity.  I tried cornering the market via tackling a scarce resource.  None of this works, the AI first out-upgrades my base and then buys me out before I catch up.  Maybe the AI is programmed to know something about the game I don't, maybe a computer is just naturally better at shifting numbers than a human player, or maybe it just flat out cheats.  At this point, I honestly don't care anymore, I'm just sad.
In summary, Offworld Trading Company is a saddening game that makes me hate numbers.

TLDR: a must-try for people interested in strategy games, unless they absolutely hate rts
A very ingenious RTS design. Instead of watching and micro units and  unit-production , you watch prices and resource flows, trying to stay ahead of the competition  in building your economic engine. You spend your time racing for patents (usually a gamechanger in one of the supply chains), prime resource nodes, managing  stock purchases and of course sabotaging your enemy with different black market actions. This may sound boring to non-economically minded people, but it exceeds the usual rock-paper-scissors complexity many strategy games feature and does get hectic. There are four "factions" with different strengths, the puzzle is finding a good setup for a given map/resource distribution and anticipate price/supply shifts to profit from them before conditions change. Or maybe you find a way to force them to change in a beneficial manner? 96 hours in i dont have the sense of having mastered the mechanics  yet.
There is a good variety of gamemodes: skirmish with different rules and maps, a daily challenge with a leaderboard, a campaign mode with lots of different options and factions and of course multiplayer. The later was clearly the design focus and i think works best. I think the campaign mode is weakest part of the game. After a  series of different scenarios and chances to build up your economic faction, you arrive at a climatic skirmishbattle to buy out your competition. In practice you often end up with  an overwhelming advantage or occasionally as if theres no chance to keep up.
Overall: people who enjoy strategy games, should check this out for many interesting and different ideas. Dont be put off by the economic theme!

FFVI is, main franchise and spin-offs in, the best Final Fantasy ever made. This could not be the most original opinion about this game, but it's my own truth. Among all the Square/SquareEnix masterpieces, from the 7th instalment to the latest ones - and most of all the first ones, IV, V and so on, VI stands out for almost everything. An awesome story, featuring all the best FF trademark locations and such: castles, ships, airships, different worlds, chocobos, cities; an impressive array of characters, each one BOTH unique in their history and in their moveset AND customizable due to the Esper system, which allows you to teach to every party member every kind of magic linked to a particular summon. So, you'll have pure mages but also warriors and rogues able to cure party members and so on. Sometimes you'll also be obliged to choose two or three different parties in order to complete a dungeon, and also you'll often find yourself playing with only some of the characters due to the elaborated, awesome story. And don't say anything about the graphics - you'll become used to them in 30 minutes even if, like me, you come from a 15 years of FF playing. Of course this is not SNES, this isn't even a GBA port - it's a smartphone port - but it features all the old and the new (end-game dungeons etc.) things. It's simply great. Play FFVI everywhere, play it on Steam too!

I haven't spent that much time in the game yet, but I've been pleasantly surprised so far. I decided to buy the game after joining the open beta weekend in February 2017. It might be interesting to note here that I have played Mount & Blade Warband for almost 1000h, most of which in multiplayer.
I haven't tried the single player yet, and I'm not sure if I ever will. I jumped straight into multiplayer, being sceptic at first. The blatant historic incorrectness, and a combat system that seems lifted from M&B Warband didn't appeal to me at all. But I was wrong.
There are 12 characters divided into 3 factions, and you can play any character from any faction at all times, once you've unlocked them. Each character comes with a distinct moveset, strengths/expertise, and weaknesses. You can pick up any character and jump into the game, but (for me) the real fun starts when you really learn the character's strategies and tactics.
Sometimes you meet an opponent that is just too skilled, other times you encounter one that spams a certain mechanic that his character possesses. But the game offers sufficient ways for you to beat that player; you just need to look a bit more into the options that your character has. This keeps it fair and fun (at least, until now).
The multiplayer reminds me a lot of that of Assassin's Creed, in terms of character and ability loadout selection, map styles and overall menu feel. You can customize a lot about the classes you've unlocked, and this too feels like I'm playing an AC multiplayer. After leveling up, you gain access to new cosmetic options; while you can unlock others by spending the currency you accumulate by playing.
I know there have been many complaints about the matchmaking/network issues. I admit that I sometimes get an error that causes me to crash to the main screen. But these are rare, and my strong internet connection prevents me from having any serious problems.
I hardly ever buy or recommend games at full price. But I took a gamble here, and I think I made the right decision. For Honor's combat system is surprisingly deep and has me looking forward to the next match.

SOMA brings up some heavy moral and psychological topics during it's playthrough, which adds to the psychological horror theme a lot. You need to care what's happening in the story, or this game will be unenjoyable. The plot is pretty simple, but gets more complex as you progress. The atmosphere adds to the experience, you're at the bottom of the ocean, isolated from everything you know. You need to make tough decisions based on your personal morals and none of your choices are good or bad, they are complicated, and that's why it makes you think about life. Involving topics such as what kind of life is worth living on with, euthanasia/suicide and afterlife.
The game however as an actual game isn't that interactive as Amnesia, there are puzzles, sneaking around for objects and running for your life, but overall it's more about the psychological aspect, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, it's just worth considering before you try out the game.
In my opinion it's the greatest psychological horror that was released in the last few years, but as a video game it would fall short without the story behind it. It's more of a psychological experience rather than a game you play, but for that, it's top ♥♥♥♥ing notch.

I want to start off saying this isn't a bad game. The reason why I leave this game a negative review is because the description on the game's page is misleading. The game advertises itself as have 35+ hours of gameplay; however, this is incorrect. On average, it takes maybe 11 hours to beat the game. I looked up the game on the HowLongtoBeat website and it is listed as 9-11 hours and 17 hours for completionists, meaning that even for people who want to experience all of the content in the game, it only takes them 17 hours on average, which is half the amount of time that the game makers advertise. One of the reasons I originally purchased this game was because I believed I'd be getting a decent game length out of it, and I didn't. I don't have anything against shorter games, but it was a game I had been expecting to put more time into because of this advertisement.
I will go over the game's pros and cons now.
Pros:
-Decent platforming game with unique levels
-Good for people who like to collect items or beat their own high scores/times
-Cute character designs
-Catchy music
-Wearing items changes the costume on the character
-Runs well even on non-gaming pcs and laptops
Cons:
-Game can be beaten in 9-17 hours on average (not as advertised 35+)
-Characters are not fleshed out enough
-Unlocking areas or progressing the story is sometimes extremely obscure without a guide
-There is an adult character that tries to go on dates with the little girls in the game and it is passed off like a silly joke. This part particularly irked me because the game is otherwise appropriate for kids to play and yet it normalizes a grown adult trying to pursue romantic relationships with prepubescent girls. This is another reason why I choose not to recommend the game, but the main reason is the false advertisement.

Nihilumbra was a..odd game for me, Think as if you went to a fine diner, The people who work there are nice, The place is neat and tidy with a touch of low priced food, The same low priced food that looks wonderful but ends with a rather sour taste.
Story: Not quite a masterpiece but far from being a best seller.
The story is you are born as a piece of void who escapes the emptiness of it all, You move from place to place picking up new colors and learning more about the world around you, Sadly you do not have much time to learn about these places as the void not only sends monsters to destory you but also comes after you itself. In your luck, A voice assists you on the way, Telling you of the void and it's creatures. Who this voice is exactly, We never know, It can't be a voice in our head because our character does not know these things until the voice tells so.
Graphics: Fits for it's lore and stays in a nice place.
I'm not much as a graphics freak so most of the time it doesn't matter, But the graphics are quite nice since they are hand drawn. Since this was a mobile port moved to PC, I feel they did a good job. One thing I do love is how much detail is given to your character. When you push a item, Your "feet" will actually push against the ground to push said object, Pay attention to your character, You might see something new.
Puzzles: Oh wow Look at all the pretty colors..
Ack, Most likely the worst part of the game. As someone who's thinking is not quite fast as others, This game can be very unfair as fast reflexes and thinking is needed. Most of the puzzles are very bland and easy to figure out, Some did take many tries for me, But I feel that was more on my part. The color mechanic could have been used much better but the depth of the puzzle do not drop far from the flower. Most of them are pushing boxes to leave on a button or getting past an enemy, Which would have been fine if they had a bit more variety would have made it where it wasn't so tedious.
Music: Wait? You can only unlock old timey mode AFTER you beat the game?
The music fits the game very well, but since I was raging more over the puzzles, It was too hard to pay attention. Old timey mode sounds great but I really wish you could have had it for the whole game because I actually ended up prefering it.
Final feelings: I wish I could play void mode.

puzzles, But I do feel the game holds a good spot on my top 50 favorite games, It's empty yes but it's good while it lasts but the end just left such a bitter taste in my mouth that I really can't say I would recommend this game, I mean it's a good indie piece, And the translation wasn't broken up or off-putting but, The puzzles are the core of this game and if the core is bitter, You might not want to take another bite.

Mission: Escape from Island is a grammatically incorrect FPS that sees your character crash on an island and attempt to find a way out.
You start out by crash landing in a helicopter in the worst cut-scene known to man and then must find a health pack in order to walk like a regular person again. The health pack by the way is right in front of the helicopter but it's super easy to miss, so I ended up walking and head-bobbing for half a kilometer before reaching another health pack. Upon getting that second health pack the entire game upped the saturation to 15/10 and blinded me.
On the head-bobbing note, why is that still a thing in video games? The human eye naturally adjusts for head-bobbing and nearly eliminates it entirely. I don't walk around like a damn rooster, video game.
The remaining objectives in the game involve exploding three objects, in which the object just magically dissappear into the heavens and simply activating a few switches.
The combat in the game barely works. Enemies don't shoot at you until they are 15 feet away and your character has perfect accuracy, making the one enemy-type in the game completely worthless. Enemies will often not see you or just slowly walk towards you and die with what sounds like a Microsoft Sam scream.
The last level in the game sees you call a helicopter to pick you up, except the helicopter just falls through the ground during the cutscene but you win anyways. Also the game ends on a "to be continued" screen but you can't exit that screen without opening your task manager.
Everything in this game is an asset from somewhere else, including the stuff that the developer seems to have just found on the internet. The mountain texture is likely a rock texture from a russian website, I know this because on parts of the mountains you can literally see the website watermark from the texture image they used.
This game also uses music from Kliment, a Russian artist and most likely did not get proper permission to use his song, which is on loop throughout the entire game. I have contacted Kliment about this in case he feels the need to deal with it.
There have also been reports that the game may be using assets from the Fallout series or other titles. At this time I cannot confirm that.
Overall, Mission: Escape from Island is a fake game, plain and simple. Do not purchase this if you want to play an actual video game.

I have to admit having played pretty much every Sea Wargame under the sun from the paper version of Harpoon through to Command : Modern Air and Naval I have a bit of a soft spot for this. It is not the prettiest under the sun but its good enough. The interface is a little sluggish and aircraft have the tendency not to do what they are meant to but it seems to balance out well the desire for an accurate simulation and the desire for fun. If I want an all singing all dancing simulation where I can set up any scenario under the sun and run it to see what happens then C:MAN is the clear winner but you don't get the feel from that of blazing ships and harpoons slamming into tankers. For a quick fix then NW:AC meets that.
No one has yet come up with the perfect game. C:MAN would come close if it had more 3D models and had an AI capable of handling itself from a cold start with just named resources. The best for years was Harpoon Classic with Jutland being the state of the art for 3D but some of the other games by people like NWS showed what could be done with minimal graphics. What is needed is someone to join everything up.
Anyway, I digress. As a naval warfare nut I like this as a gentle way to spend the odd few hours.

So almost got 2 hours into it so far, I can say for $40 it is lacking in content, but if you are a fan of the Friday the 13th franchise then you will likely be able to look past that and enjoy the game, it really taps into that classic Friday the 13th feeling and puts you in the shoes of the idiot's that you scream at saying don't go in there and yet you end up doing the exact same things.
I played a good 6 matches straight and the community is pleasant so far from what I've seen it is an enjoyable experience. I even survived and escaped one of the matches because we all worked together as a team, either that or the Jason player just wasn't that good at being Jason yet. Many people are complaining that you have to wait till the match is over to get your XP but to be honest I've had more laughs and enjoyed being dead because when you do die you can only chat with other people who are dead all while watching the remaining survivors try so hard to stay alive, it really is a good time. With only 3 classic Friday the 13th maps it is lacking but the maps are really big. The biggest complaint I see is people saying Jason is too overpowered but that's how it's meant to be, this isn't Dead by Daylight, Jason is not a pushover killing teens is what he does best, once you get out of the mindset of you can beat Jason with brute force you start to have a lot more fun as you look for more complex and creative ways to outsmart the Jason player.
Long story short, if you are a fan of the Friday the 13th franchise I really don't think you'll be disappointed with this game. If you have played Dead by Daylight and like the way that game plays you should stick to Dead by Daylight because this game plays nothing like it. If you have a group of of 7 friends you can get together for this by all means you are in for a really good time with some friends, but even with complete total strangers I still had a really good time. Can't wait to play some more with some friends down the road.
UPDATE: So for sure the game is fun, play a few matches weed through some people make a few friends along the way, once you have 6 people you can make a private lobby with the fun factor just simply skyrockets for this game. Go out there and make some friends.

I am going to explain this with a board game analogy. If Starcraft is RISK then Offworld Trading is the Settlers of Catan of RTS.

If you are looking for a 20 hr story driven campaign then this is not the game for you. The base game is mostly just a tutorial and a campaign of scenarios to play the RTS game they made. I played about 20 hrs of the campaign mode before jumping into the multiplayer queue.  4 player FFA has no real ladder anxiety that many RTS have. I am even playing in the community tournaments on the weekends after a solid month of playing.
If anything I said made sense to you I would highly recommend to pick up if it goes on sale.

Look, it can seem discouraging reading all the negative reviews, so allow me to provide a positive one.
I LOVE this game, and you know what?  I love this version of the game too.  Yes, it's a port of the iOS version.  BIG FREAKIN' DEAL.  A lot of people gripe about the crappy sprites.  I couldn't care less about the sprites, in fact I think they look good.  Are they a little washed out and "pastel-y"?  Yes, but I like them.
HOWEVER, what made me decide this was an INSTANT BUY was the fact that they FIXED THE BLOODY BUGS THAT PLAGUED THE FIRST GAME (Yes the GBA version fixed a lot of these, but see #7 below).  Specifically, they fixed:
1) The Evade bug
2) The Psycho Cyan glitch
3) The Relm's sketch bug that could crash your game (and some reported that this bug could corrupt their save game also)
4) The Rippler bug that could permanently remove Interceptor from Shadow if he's targetted with it.
5) A handful of bugs involving Gau's rages
6) The Vanish-Doom bug
7) *BONUS* The Imp-immunity bug introduced in the GBA version.
This version also includes the extra content introduced in the GBA version.  Specifically the 4 new espers, 2 new dungeons, and SUPERIOR translations and dialogue (although, no pithy "son of a submariner" quips).
Yes, the battle layout is a little awkward, but I honestly got over it VERY quickly (and on keyboard no less!).  If you don't like the layout, go into the setup menu that you can get into when you first start the game, and make the controls whatever you want.
FINAL THOUGHT: Look, I don't deny this version might not be what everyone wants.  Many people REALLY like the original pixel-version sprites.  They like the darker look (this version ups the natural brightness).  Other people REALLY appreciate the PSX port that added CG scenes to the beginning and end.  Others Really prefer the GBA version for its many bug fixes, original sprites, and new content (and the fact that its exclusive bug means a White Cape pretty much makes you immune to anything a Malboro can throw at you aside from physical violence, but also makes the Bad Breath lore mostly worthless).  I'm saying to me, this game was worth every penny.

I just need to start off by saying I have been waiting for what seems like forever to finally get to play this game. I am a major Friday the 13th fan (you should see my memorabilia collection) so this game has had my attention since it was first announced.
Now to the game: The game does have a lot of promise if the devs stick with it and build on what they have. The graphics, when noit glitching, look very good and feel very realistic. Jason is overpowered, but if you ever watched any of the movies then you would realize why that is.
Unfortunately there is still a long way to go for this game. Some issues should have been dealt with long before its release. Some glitches shouldn't exist but yet they do. There's a major issue with counselor on counselor killing and then there's the kids that think it's fun to have their bussy be Jason while they point ut where everyone else is on the map to that buddy. Big oversight. I've been launched across the map too many times to count while polaying Jason after getting hit by a counselor. Both Jason's and the counselor's hit boxes are way off, attacks that should hit don't and those that shouldn't do.
I'm still playing and loving the game but would love to see those problems go away. Here's to looking forward to many more years of this game and seeing to what great places it goes.

is a post-apocalyptic survival game that has you facing both other humans and mutants alike. It's a great concept and it works for most of the part, but there's one thing that completely kills the experience.
The Pros:
· A fun crafting system that'll allow you to craft weapons from weaponparts you've collected.
· The Nether mutants look disgustingly good, which gives them an additional sense of threat.
· Knowing that both other players and Nether mutants could constantly be watching you will keep you alert and immersed. Nether mutants will teleport behind you and challenge your skills in combat, whereas other players can gun you down at any given second (except when you're in a Safe Zone). I found that this shift of threats kept me adjusting and finding new tactics.
The Cons:
· The open world is linear and rather dull. The detail of overgrowing vegetation and crumbling buildings is gorgeous, but there's so little loot that there's no real purpose to search for it. Just kill some Nether mutants and sell their spines and blood to buy things you need, or kill other players and make good use of what they dropped. Dozens of old stores and abandoned cars, but rarely is there any loot nearby. The world is like a delicious cake, but it's filling is pure mud. Everything feels like a useless prop rather than being part of the world.
· The community kills the game... literally and figuratively. If you spawn, you have the option to spawn in a Safe Haven or just in the world. If you choose a Safe Haven, chances are you won't be able to leave it. Other players are constantly covering the exits and entrances of Safe Havens, leaving everyone who comes out look like a sitting duck. Plus, nine out of ten times, the loot dropped by killed players won't even be picked up. If someone's running over to grab it, he too gets shot, and so on. This literally wastes a ton of what the game has to offer. The objectives will have you delivering packages in a Safe Haven, but it's pure suicide.
The Visuals:
· Gorgeous lighting, stunning detail and disgusting Nether mutants.
is a visual beauty.
Final Verdict:
·
could be one of the top survival MMO games currently out there, but its community and poor delevoping choices make it merely a dumbed-down shell of what it could have been. Fun is to be had though, as long as you're on the good side of the gun barrel. 6.5/10

Modelled after the game format used in Heroes of Might and Magic, and improved upon hugely, Disciples is an engrossing game to play once you've mastered the rather steep learning curve involved.  There are two different types of magic, one for use in the battle arenas, and one for use whilst travelling across the world map, and if you don't have your wits about you, neither will make sense.  Apart from that the game unfolds nicely (play the main release first, as this is the expansion, even though it plays without the original) and has an involving, if very complicated, storyline.
Watch out for crashes and other curruptions even in the updated version.  Always save before going to battle or visiting shops as these tend to create crash points.
They've made changes to the combat system in this exapnsion, and personally I don't think they're for the better.  Certain character types (mellee in particulart) now have two slots per battle round, rather than just one, and reinsert themselves high up the turn table when their first turn has been used.  This may have been done to balance the difficulty that mellee types normally missed their first round attack as they couldn't cover enough arena squares to reach an enemy.  However, mellee types have always had the extra advantage of delivering much more damage than a ranged attack, so this change really wasn't necessary.  It actually becomes confusing.  That, coupled with a revised "cover shot" system, whereby you get locked into covering yourself, not just other characters under your control, means the balance of arena battles has been seriouslly jarred and takes a while to figure things out.  You can also trap oppsition units into self-cover, so perhasps there is a small up side to this.  Like a lot of games, once you'be worked out the system you can play it to your advantage, but it's a tricky system and misjudgements are usually fatal.
On the plus side, Lambert has been brought back from what we thought was the dead,,,,

I'm not a fan of horror games, and Amnesia: The Dark Descent is all types of wrong for me.  But at the same time, I recommend it because if you like being anxious, if you like being scared, if you like a horror game, this is for you.
Amnesia does away with jump scares and instead mucks with visuals, and gameplay.  The player is (at least as far as I saw) not given a weapon, instead he has a lantern to brighten up dark places and see.  This is good because if it's too dark, the players sanity will go and can only be recovered by "progressing" in the game or solving puzzles.
The entire game though understands horror and works towards it.  There's happy shiny moments (at least in the first two hours).  There's no gardens or happy sunlight.  Everything in this game is atmospheric and created to make you uneasy.   From a slight camera tilt, to a blurry view, to evil sounding "memories" to writing that's just... unnerving.  Nothing jumps out as "SCARY" but everything adds to that feeling.
This is pure atmospheric horror and brilliantly dome. I'm not someone who has anxiety problems normally but holy hell, this game had me freaking out after only the first hour this time.  I turned off the game and I won't be back.
However that's more a personal issue, if you want TRUE horror, if you want to be scared and to be filled with dread, Amnesia The Dark Descent is for you.   Just don't play it around me, please.

This game was definitely terrifying, even horrifying at times, I would say mostly due to sound effects and music. The creators really worked a wonder with the sound and mixing it with the environment. The graphics aren't groundbreaking but they are absolutely good enough to give you a scare. I found Amnesia's story to be quite confusing at first, a lot of information is thrown at you that you won't yet have a grasp on. Upon a second playthrough though, the story would most likely all make sense as you went along. The game does save every journal entry so that you can re-read it if you want to.
Bottom line: you can trust that Amnesia will be scary. There are puzzles but they aren't too hard. There is a fairly simple item screen. Besides health, you have a sanity meter. You have a lantern. It's first person. You have the options [usually] to run or hide. Are there monsters, ghosts, zombies? Maybe. Gore? Maybe. Ways to defend yourself? Maybe. I highly recommend steering clear of any other information about the game-- it's more fun not knowing.
A bonus short game called Justine comes with Amnesia. To access it, start the Amnesia Settings Launcher instead of Amnesia: The Dark Descent. There will be a button labeled Justine. It is played exactly like Amnesia but if you die, you start over; there is no saving. I don't recommend Justine unless you have already played the main game. Plus, there are many typos and other errors in it. Nothing is hugely wrong with Justine but it has this overall feeling like you're playing an unfinished game. On the other hand, Amnesia had no noticeable errors and felt like a very finished product. Lastly, I played through both Amnesia and Justine with a friend, taking turns. Don't let that make you hesitate to play alone, or the opposite, believe that playing with someone somehow affects my review. My friend and I took it very seriously, playing only at night, with all of the lights off, using a great soundsystem, and while eating soft hot pretzels. I can only hope that you all play Amnesia: The Dark Descent in this exact way.

Play this for the story, not the combat. While it's one of the best games I've ever played, and definitely the best for immersion and roleplaying/characterisation, you occasionally have to trick the party AI into not running into a large group of enemies that aren't even in the same room. There are two occasions I remember where this was *very* frustrating. Additionally, you don't need much strategy in any of your battles (at least on normal difficulty, which is all I have experience with). This didn't bother me - it was quite the power trip frying entire groups with a few applications of Force Storm and felt pretty true to the films' universe of superpowered Jedi. I highly recommend KOTOR 2, but keep these caveats in mind before deciding to purchase it.
I played this without the Restored Content mod by mistake, although it's easily obtainable through the Steam Workshop and seems to be overwhelmingly recommended as a superior version of the game. One of the main complaints people seem to have about the vanilla version is that the ending seems rushed and too open-ended; while some of the additions from the mod would have been interesting, I personally loved the open-endedness because it gave me room to form my own interpretation of things around my player character's motivations. And what a player character I made!
Lots has already been said on the game's emphasis on questioning your morality and dark/lightsided actions. There were, personally, sufficient dialogue options to let me do whatever my character would actually do in almost any situation, and if I hadn't decided that her story was now my personal canon and that I couldn't replay the game as anyone else, I think exploring different versions of the Jedi Exile would be super fun, even just going pure Light or Dark instead of taking the greyer approach to things. There were no major breaks in immersion that I can remember (save a rather amusing graphical glitch where a couple of characters' bodies disappeared as they were walking away) and I actually had a moment where I felt guilty about breaking into someone's room and stealing all their stuff and stopped doing it XD I also did some things I, as the player, felt terrible about doing but which made sense in-character... a good test of immersion!
There's a nice range of party characters and their dialogue is well written, so you'll probably find at least one you like and want to have by your side permanently (Atton's story aaahhhhhhh). Lots of room to play around with different combat builds. I'd have loved to have even more interaction with my party, although there seem to be sufficient opportunities for influence gain based on how they react to you doing things. I definitely felt that I was in the Star Wars universe throughout the game, but with an added... sinister? edge to it; something I thought was very fitting (and totally awesome since I'm all about things being As Depressing As Possible). The prologue, with the 'murder mystery' thing it had going on, was one of the best examples of this for me.
The game ran totally fine on my ridiculously old MacBook Pro, with no crashing or gamebreaking glitches at any point during the 50 hours I played for. It looks like this is unusual though, at least for Windows users. Your Mileage May Vary.

Make sure you have DirectX and Visual C++ runtimes already installed, because this game depends on them but does not seem to include their redistributeable files like most games for some reason. If you're getting missing .dll errors, that's why.
That said, I've enjoyed the game thus far. It is different enough from Dead by Daylight that it doesn't feel like they were trying to rip off the concept or game play, though they did take a few cues. Namely, terror radius....Like Dead by Daylight, there's obvious audio cues to indicate Jason's proximity and wether or not he's actively after you. There's also visible indications of noise that give away your position when running and stuff.
Counselors obviously have to try and escape, but the process of doing so is a bit more involved. The easiest way would be to fix the phone box and call the cops....then five minutes later you can leave. Otherwise you have to seek out and collect parts to fix an escape vehicle, and then hope Jason doesn't stop the vehicle once you do get it running....or try to kill Jason, but come on...that ain't happening. There's only one way to do it, and it's so crazy specific you won't be pulling it off unless Jason is helping you. But you can actually hit Jason to stun him.
Jason is so much more of a bad *** compared to the killers of Dead by Daylight. He can kill within seconds. Unless you have a pocket knife to stick him with (Or a friend to smack him), you're pretty much dead if he grabs you. At least his executions are fun to watch.
Unlike Dead by Daylight though, you don't get to choose to be Jason. The game decides who plays as Jason. And with 8 players in a match, that's like a measly 12% chance to be chosen every match. Assuming everyone in the game has Jason set as their preference, but come on, who actually prefers to be the machete fodder?
Playing as counselors is really, really difficult. Jason can literally appear anywhere. Just like in the films, he has an inexplicable ability to teleport, but unlike the films, he can do it with you looking dead at him (in the movies he only does it when the camera cuts or pans away from him.) This gives him pretty much total map control. Even if you are gaining good distance on him, he can just teleport to the area you're heading toward....or do a blink sort of teleport where he vanishes and gains massive movement speed buff (the dreaded wooshy camera filter effect from old school horror movies)
All that said, this game wasn't exactly made to be fair. It was made to be massively one sided. Every encounter with Jason is potentially your last, and there's no telling where or when he'll pop up which actually does a good job of translating the tension and fear that they were going for. While playing counselor is much harder than survivor in Dead by Daylight, I kind of enjoy it more. Surviving feels like a real victory, and you have to rely on more than map knowledge to survive. (running in circles and constantly jumping through windows won't save you here...not for long at least.) You have to know when to run, when to hide, and most importantly, when to cripple your friend and leave them for distraction as you make your get away. :P
Definately could use a bit of balancing, but still does what it set out to do pretty well I think. Definately not a game for everyone, but if you enjoy slaughtering horny teenagers, or having your crotch chopped with an axe, this game is right up your alley.

So Final Fantasy VI... The Game: There are a lot of fanboys/girls of this game who claim that this is the pinnacle of the series, even beating its successor VII. Do I agree? Well, no. Some people mistakenly believe that this game was somehow the first to introduce the industrial/futuristic elements that VII and VIII became known for. However, this is simply not the case. Anyone who knows Final Fantasy knows that the first game to introduce those elements was IV. Yes, VI makes much more use of them than IV, but so did V, which comes somewhere in the middle. So I would say stylistically, this game was evolution rather than revolution. There are definitely some good characters on this game, such as the womanizing Edgar and his mobile castle, as well as the wonderfully brave and gorgeous Celes (although honestly, what kind of an army GENERAL would wear a one-piece swimming costume with a cape as a uniform!??), but overall, they all seem a bit one-dimensional and stale. This is no more true than the game's villain Kefka, who absolutely lacks any of the substance or backstory of Sephiroth. But I don't want to sound too negative: this is a really enjoyable game and a worthy part of the series, but don't believe the hype when some hipsters try to say it's better than VII.
So what's the good stuff about this game? Well for a start, it was the first game in the series that actually has a reasonable amount of sidequests and mini-games to speak of, which is of course considered to be the bread and butter of any JRPG these days. Before this game, there was very little to do apart from the main story itself and EXP/Job level grinding. On that last note, this game was originally advertised in North America (back when it was Final Fantasy III) as being much easier and less time consuming to do just that. And well, I would certainly agree with that. What's good is that there are plenty of testing enemies with lots of EXP/AP to pick up in the open parts of the game's second world, so you DON'T have to wait until the game's final dungeon to get the really big EXP payoffs. Even before that point, you will find that characters do level up very quickly, to the point where you might find that actually you run the risk of making the boss fights *too* easy. That's not even to speak of some of the relics, of which you can equip two in this game to create truly monstrous abilities, turning your characters into little chibi gods and goddesses. So yeah, in terms of the game, it is certainly a very playable game that set the tone for what was to come, even if it doesn't quite reach the dizzying heights of the PS1-era games.
So yeah, great game he says, but anyone from the last 20 years could have told you that. What about the PORT? After all, that's been the big controversy surrounding the Steam version of this game. Well personally, as much hate as it got, I actually think it works. Before you throw tomatoes at me, let me just explain my reasoning. Yes, the bilinear filtering is a minor inconvenience, but quite frankly, you get used to that very quickly. I mean honestly, if you actually said to someone "I didn't play on this game because the character sprites had BILINEAR FILTERING!!!" Well I dunno what people would think of you, but it probably wouldn't be very good. The other complaint is the fact that it has mobile-like graphics. Well I get what you're saying, but it's not as if you actually HAVE to play it like a mobile phone game. I've found it to work perfectly well with my game controller. The menus are nice and tell you all you need to know (although I would have preferred different methods of sorting items but that's just me being picky.) But what I really like is the battle system. Yes, while it might not be like the original with its ATB gauges and stuff, I find it really makes it a lot easier to switch between characters, so you can make tactical decisions, rather than simply having to go with whichever character whose turn it is or hit defend or whatever. I also think the compass on the airship is a nice little touch even though it's obviously a bit obsolete on the steam version. One thing I'm not massively keen on is what they did with the music. Although it's the original SNES score, which is nice, the problem is that it has been prerecorded and compressed into some format and thus does not preserve the goodness of the original Super Nintendo Synth engine. The bright side to this though is that you don't get the polyphony limitations of the SNES either, so you don't have to worry about one of the instruments going bye-bye whenever you hit a menu button or open a door or whatever. Some might call it a cute idiosyncrasy of the SNES; I thought it was a bit annoying. So there you have it: a great game, reccomended for RPG fans and FF fans.

TL;DR - I like the game for attempting a different and solid approach to the stategy genre and I recommend it for the slower-paced buy highly chaotic nature of matches themselves, but it certainly isn't everybody's cup of tea so if you're not into those things, or expect the traditional RTS experience, give this game a pass.
There's certainly a divide among the people who've tried this game, I think it stems from a clashing between a misunderstanding of the game's main concept, the expectations from watching a couple of gameplay videos and playing the game itself, which is understandable because this isn't a game that's easily put in a few words.
It seems that people are now associating RTS with APM and fast reflexes exclusively, which is another reason why this game is such a departure for most of the users who try it. Out of the gate, this game is nothing like the traditional RTS: you aren't microing units, you aren't building an army, you aren't going for the high APM, you aren't scouting bases or out-blobbing the opponent's blob army. Instead you are making decisions for the most part, decisions that impact the course of the game over time instead of immediately, leading to a slower paced game based around matches of wits and constantly monitoring a wide variety of indicators that are further influenced by the chaos theory that stems from the many other choices that other players are making during a match.
This is a game that demands close observation of numbers and the things that affect those numbers so that you make informed decisions that lead to you out-witting the competition over matches that are certainly longer when compared to other multiplayer games, especially those that belong to more recent launches. It's also a game that assumes that you can properly learn its rules, which is why the training wheels come off sooner and there's huge rifts in the handholding in between difficulty settings. The computer doesn't cheat the higher you go (at least, if you don't go higher than manager which is the standard difficulty), it just reacts sooner and expects you to keep up the pace through, again, decisions based on proper vigilance of information and indicators.
I admit to having a bias for this kind of game, since I really like strategy games, especially those driven by economic aspects and this one is certainly all about the incredibly unpredictable nature of economics and a caricaturization of the cutthroat corporate environment which all serves to keep me engaged and entertained, making for a good game in my book considering both the beautiful audiovisual design and the solid mechanics. At the same time, I find it easy to empathize with the people who get put off by this game, its rules are certainly different, it demands different things from the player, and matches themselves never tend to play out the same way twice, even on the exact same conditions because there's always something else that you, and the remaining players, can choose to do.
I thoroughly recommend the game but only if you like slower paced games with lots of stuff happening at the same time, along with learning new things and experiencing a different kind of strategy games. If you aren't one for patience, expecting the standard fast-paced, high APM, insane reflexes gameplay, I suggest you go for something else.

So this game has quite a few mixed reviews and I'm seeing both sides of the story at this point. The game itself is fun in general. It's more of a fighting game than anything else and the gameplay itself brings a new feeling to the table. However, it isn't exactly smooth sailing. The combat has a few rough edges and the game currently runs on a Peer to Peer online system.. which means if the host leaves, well I guess that's it for that match. Why they don't have a host migration system, I don't know. There's a few other issues here and there, but that's probably the biggest one. Suddenly dropping games because someone left, is a bit annoying.
There's a few bugs here and there, poison/bleed not working right for peacekeeper and a few bits of balancing that needs to be done, but overall the combat is fun and I have fun playing it.
The multiplayer seems to have 2 whole different worlds when it comes to players. The 4v4, and1v1 (or 2v2).
The 1v1 is about the honorable fights. 1 on 1, no environment killing (mostly) and see who's the best fighter. While the 4v4 is "all's fair in love and war". Some people hate it, but if you're going to play 4v4, expect to be outnumbered, pushed off ledges, and set on fire. It's just how it is, but that means you can do it too.
The campeign is "meh". It's not bad, but it's not really good. It's just there. Can play co-op, so there's that.
Yes, there's microtransactions. No, they don't matter. You can literally get every bit of steel (the paid for currency) just by playing the game and it doesn't truely feel like a grind. They get you a booster, some cosmetics, characters, or random loot boxes. None of these have an impact on the game other than some minor stats that lower other stats. Is it dumb? Yes, very dumb. $60 game, and that wasn't enough money, so lets have DLC season passsssssssssss and then microtransactionsssssssssss. It's scummy and unecessary. However, it doesn't restrict any part of the game itself.
Overall I really like the game, and am having fun playing it. However, there are a few issues that needs to be addressed such as bugs and the whole peer to peer without any sort of host migration nonsense. Buy it on sale

I originally gave Beam a thumbs down, but that really wasnt fair so I decided to change it. The game is by no means "bad", it's just not really a game. Not yet anyway. To the developers credit they fully disclose this, as do the many people who have provided reviews on their store page. I had wanted this game for a pretty long time, but when I finally purchased it I was a little disappointed. Is BeamNG cool? Definitely. Are the soft body physics impressive? Without a doubt. Are the graphics good? Yeah, they're actually really good if you ask me. Many components that make up a good game are present here. It's everything the store page tells you it is. It's just not a full game yet. It's still really early, and can be glitchy. Vehicles get hung up, the camera can swing below ground level revealing an empty abyss. Sound is very early and somewhat generic, with a few basic noises and no menu music. Load times, from what I've experienced, are a little slow and the interface, to me, is a bit clunky and confusing. With all that said, these are all things that can be expected from an early access alpha build of a game, which is exactly what Beam is at this point. I knew that when I purchased it, so for me to be frustrated that what I got wasn't a finished, polished product doesn't warrant me leaving a negative review. I wish, as I'm sure a lot of players do, that there was something in between "thumbs up" and "thumbs down". To be honest, I felt guilty when I initially gave it a thumbs down, and then I recieved a comment the very next morning from one of the developers, which I'm not going to delete. The messge is short, polite, and genuinely concerned. They appologized and asked me to provide more detail so that they may improve my experience. Reading that really made me think about my negative feedback, and if they had delivered on what they claimed to be offering. I had read about how these guys were very involed with the community and how they are constanty updating, improving, and taking fan feedback into consideration. I think that's really cool, and I believe that it proves that what they claim is their ultimate goal for their vision and how they're going about creating it is true. Rather than doing what a lot of devs do and deleting negative comments, not taking player ideas into account, not utilizing constructive critisism, or just plain abandoning the whole thing, they instead take accountability and reach out to individuals personally in a courteous and professional manner for input. When they describe their project they specifically point out that BeamNG is a work in progress and that they are constantly tweaking, improving and adding to their title, and they do this hand in hand with their customers. This isn't big business, and I'm glad it's not. Hearing directly from a developer reguarding my spefic feelings toward their game really helps to humanize an industry that is becomming more and more faceless over time, and was personally a bit of an honor. When you buy into "early access" you are supporting something that you want to see fully realized, and BeamNG is a game that I want out there.

I played in the closed alpha, TT2, closed beta, and open beta. As much as I want to like this game, there's just too much wrong with it right now. I bought the game because I was gambling on the hope that Ubisoft would fix all the issues over the coming months and in time for ranked play to come out, and because Bannerlord probably won't be out until 2018 at this rate and there's no other place to get my directional combat fix (and for what it's worth, the base directional combat and the mechanics really are fun). I highly recommend waiting to see how active Ubisoft is in patching before buying this game.
More details, for those who want a bit more than the tl;dr above:
1v1 and 2v2 are slowly turning into a turtle meta. This is because the risk/reward balance for being on the offense in this game is completely lopsided in favor of the defender. Most characters have fancy chains and combo attacks. There's no point in them using these chains because of the parry mechanic. Parrying is very easy, and allows pretty much any character in the game to confirm a guard break and deal a lot more damage off of the guard break than they could with those chains and combos.
In addition, the ease of parrying makes attacking very dangerous, especially chain attacks. If you go in with a heavy attack, you're bound to be parried by any halfway competent player. If you go in with a light attack, you're more likely to avoid the parry, but you'll probably deal about 5%-10% of a healthbar at most. Getting parried will result in somewhere around 30% of your health gone or an instant kill from the many environmental hazards. There are currently two classes who can really safely initiate, the other ten have little choice but to play mostly as counter attackers. This defensive meta might be enjoyable for some, but I've found it increasingly boring. In my opinion, the easiest fix for this would be to remove the guaranteed guard break after parry.
Dominion, the one game mode which avoids the turtle meta because it offers objectives and time pressure to initiate on your opponent, is broken in a completely different way. In 4v4s like Dominion, gear stats are in effect. You get gear for time and money (mostly time, mind you, For Honor isn't p2w) spent as a sort of progression mechanic. You also have to regear for every character, and you don't start getting truly good gear until around level 63, which is likely to take a casual "hour a day" player a week or two to achieve per character. This gear can lead to doubled damage, highly reduced stamina costs and increased stamina recovery, and the ability to gain revenge -- a sort of super mode which makes a character ludicrously strong with super armor, infinite stamina, increased damage, defense, temporary health pool, and knockdown on staggers -- in 3-4 blocks and allows it to last for double its normal length.
You are completely at a disadvantage if you're on a character without gear up against a character with gear. For Honor's matchmaking doesn't take into account the prospect that you might want to level a character with little or no gear, and will throw your undergeared self into a game against players with gear level 100+. Again, this kind of progression mechanic and stomping on people with lower gear levels might be fun for some. I, personally, can barely stomach dominion now that high item levels are becoming more prevalent. This is unlikely to be changed, but I'm really hoping that they include a no-gear/no-feats queue for Dominion.
The networking for this game is dysfunctional as well. Matchmaking breaks probably 2/5 times for me, and I get dropped from matches at a rate of probably 1/5. At least one resync happens in a match probably 3/5 times. This is despite my NAT being open and all ports being properly forwarded (these issues even happened when I briefly DMZ'ed myself, just to make sure I wasn't missing any ports that needed to be opened). In addition, there are concerns about drophacking due to p2p. According to some, with the current netcode you can pick up a person's public IP via network analyzers such as wireshark. I haven't tested this myself, and don't believe it's been done to me, but as of writing this there's a thread on reddit about it with a good number of people claiming it's happened to them. If it's true, it means that each match puts you at the risk of getting hit with a denial of service attack or port scanning to set up for something more malicious. This is something generally avoided on the player to server model. Security concerns are probably the best reason to avoid the game, unrelated to subjective opinions on what mechanics are fun.
In addition to these major issues, there are a bunch of little issues which just indicate a lack of polish:
The painful part is that most of these issues were raised before the closed alpha ended. Most haven't even been discussed by the devs, no matter the outcry they received on the testing forums.
Despite everything I've said, the base combat is fun enough that this could be a good game if they fixed some of the major issues above. At lower levels of play, before everybody started learning how to parry and turtle up, it felt polished and satisfying to have a frantic melee fight with someone, whether it was in 1v1/2v2 or in Dominion when everybody still had low gear level. Now that everybody is learning about parrying and turtling up in the duel modes and Dominion is full of people with 100+ gear with stats that straight up break the game, it's losing its fun and I'm regretting that I can't refund this. I can't recommend this game, at least not in the current direction Ubisoft is taking it. I'll happily edit this review if they make me eat my words and start actively patching balance and other issues.

An entertaining RTS from the lead designer of Civ 4, Soren Johnson. It is about the subjugating your opponents economically, and the best way to describe it would probably be M.U.L.E. for the 21st century. There is no outright combat, though you can sabotage your opponents. Your goal is to buy out the stock of all of your opponents. There are different resources that you can harvest, and you can in turn produce different goods that are in demand. It is not a high apm game, but it can still feel intense while playing. The game includes an interesting single player campaign system, where you play a series of games, the first few rounds don't depend on you defeating your opponents outright, but being the person who provides the colony the most of what they want. The person/ai in last place overall gets eliminated each round, until there finally is a regular skirmish type game between (I think) the last 4 standing. You are limited in the games with what structures you can build, and have a choice of maps to play on each of which will give you some bonus or reward as you move forward in the campaign. They also run a daily challenge, where you do a single player map and compete on score/time with other players to see who does the best.
Mohawk has continued to support the title over that past year with a lot of dlc, and I think it is probably one of the best rts titles to come out in a long time.

Elementary offers up some interesting 3-D aspects and good graphics which makes it stand out from the other HOG’s I’ve played. This game has the usual things you’d expect: objects to collect, multiple scenes and a cliché small story. However, the implementation of a rotating 3-D scene is unique and creates a different challenge. Some objects might not be visible from your current view, so you must swivel around the scene to get a good look at everything. You can also zoom in a little to get a better look at things. The control scheme for this is rather clunky and the devs could have at least used the keyboard for part of the controls.
The graphics are surprisingly good and stylized well. Even at 1440p everything is crisp and plays at 60fps.
The actual scenes themselves are nice and offer up quite a challenge at some points. I played on Expert and admit I had to use the hint button more than once as I was absolutely stuck.
The dialog is not spoken but can elicit a smile here and there.
The game has numerous puzzles that also need to be solved along the way. Some can be a little tricky but nothing too challenging.
One thing that could help would be to add a small picture next to the item you need to collect. Sometimes I had no idea what the object would look like in the game. It did this for some objects, but really needs it for all of them.
You are also ranked after each scene for how quickly you completed it and how many hints you used. This is a pointless rating system as it doesn’t affect the game and there are no achievements.
+60fps
+Crisp visuals and nice graphics even at 1440p
+Mildly funny dialog
+3-D scenes require rotating to find items
+Expert mode can be challenging
+Initial item recognition (small picture should be added next to item name)
+Clunky controls for zooming and rotating
+Dialog not spoken
+Level ranking system serves no purpose
