In this game, you are being that escapes "The Void" - a place that eats it's way into anything and everything and, inside it, there's nothing. Much like black holes, really. Somehow, your escape alerts The Void and it starts chasing you. You go from being nothing, having no purpose in life, to grow intelectually through the learning of colors, an interesting mechanism that, by painting them on the game's surface, each one will provoke a different effect on it, ranging from slippery surfaces to making them burn, etc.
In essence, this game is really philosophical. I thought the message embeded throughout the story was something from the likes of "You are insignificant, yes. But if you stand out, explore, make something different, you will become significant. You will become something." The narrator basically helps to tell the story, as through every section of the game, he says something. The art, background-wise, is very pretty. The models and tiles are nothing suprising, but that's not negative. There's an art gallery that will slowly unlock after the completion of each level.
As for length, the game is relatively short. But, after you do complete the main story, there's a void mode to be completed, which can take more than the actually storyline, and it is freakishly hard! Also, the game's controls are smooth and easily maneuverable.

I haven't yet played Void Mode, but after completing the main story here are my impressions. The levels are short but sweet with frequent checkpoints - even if you have trouble adjusting to the controls you never get sent back too far. The music is wonderful and does an excellent job at setting the mood of each area. Although I've never been a fan of auto-scrolling, especially while being chased by an invincible hazard, I found myself looking forward to the void segments the most. They're easy enough that I didn't find them frustrating at all.
One problem I had is that at times I found myself overthinking the puzzles and making them harder for myself than they really are. The solutions are always fairly simple, and the frequent checkpoints mean that even if you have trouble and die several times you're able to try again almost immediately. That being said, this game is suitable for any skill level and isn't hard to learn to play. Highly recommended.

If you're coming from cs:go or any reputable competitve fps game please avoid for the time being. Their match making system will pair you up with people from all over the world and there is NOTHING you can do about it. The average ping is between 130-300 which is beyond unnacceptable and there is no good technical reason for it or an official statement about it. You'd think this would be an issue that they would have sorted in a single day, but this has been going on since the start. I'd happily wait 5 mins to be matched if it meant I wasn't playing with people on the itnernational space station. There is no way to filter out regions, or select to play with low pingers. So you have a game with an incredibly low time to kill paired with high pingers, which makes the game broken in my eyes. So if you're into serious competitive play like I am, avoid for now. I'll switch my review out to positive once this is sorted out. The other thing is people leave comeptitve games often, there needs to be a better penalty system. Otherwise it's a good game, pretty much a different flavour of cs and I really enjoy it. If you do buy it, I reccomend playing it for at least 20 hours and it will start to make sense.

Moody and philosophical, brilliantly written and filled with multi-layered characters, immersive and emotionally involving, Knights of the Old Republic 2 is a fantastic game and one of the best stories in the Star Wars universe.
It has its share of flaws - the gameplay is rather dull, level design repetitive, graphics outdated even at the time of release. It was also originally released in an incomplete form, but this has since been fixed by a group of dedicated fan who created the The Sith Lords Restored Content Modification. Despite all the flaws, the game succeeds in what matters - sending the player on a memorable journey and leaving such an impact that all these years after its release I still can't get enough of it.
Hopefully, one day it will get a sequel it deserves.

General  7/10 because of some weak points for the PC adaptation.  (Amazing base game, but problems with the porting which can provokes Blue screen of the death and corrupting save slots)
If you only played FF VI in the SNES, then this game is a must (when it's with discounts). If you discovered the world of Final Fantasy with the seventh or twelfth games, then it is a must do, as this game is a pinnacle of an era of this franchise which also marked all the other CRPG franchises.
This adaptation is the adaptation of the mobile version which was the adaptation of the Game Boy Advance, which was the adaptation of the original SNES. All the sprites are redone to adapt to the 1080p resolution (though the aspect ratio is preserved) and the original interface for the battles are thrown away with a new one (this comes from mobile adaptation).
Also, coming from the Game Boy age, four new Espers are added (although not unique as they made their first appearances in later games of the saga), two special areas with hard encounters and two super bosses are also added. And a new game + option is added, where once you finish the game, you can load a special save slot and continuing with the game (even defeating Kefka once more time).
Something worth to state about this game. You don’t need to reach max levels for defeating the final boss or the super bosses. You can beat the game (without super bosses) around level 40, and I was able to defeat the extra content with less than level 70. But, for the new dungeon and super bosses, the mechanics of the battles will be different because you are forced to abuse of the new spell “Quick”. Although, you could still be playing as before, but probably you will be beaten too fast due the enemies react to your attack and can attack more than one character by turn.
So… why not 10/10? Because the porting is dangerous and the experience benefits from additional hardware. First, the game sucks if you don't have a controller (Ok, not that much if you use a Turn-based instead of the original one, but is killing its essence!)  BUT this brings the first danger: If you are playing in battery mode with a controller, there are certain points where the game can be frozen due changing in the power cycling of the computer (yes, this is tie to laptops) and Square-Enix was able to give me something I didn't saw for seven years: A blue screen of the death due this problem.  I can't remember if those frozen times also occurred while I was with power supply, but at least were noticeable and dangerous when it was in battery mode.
Second danger: Sometimes the game starts to get corrupt. You can notice this because the sprites of the game becomes strange (rivers disappear, your character becomes invisible, etc.). Once you notice this, you must uninstall/install the game. Otherwise, you risk to escalate to the point where a debug screen appears with all the sprites of your leader. The worst thing, this state broke the game and if you save (like the quick save slot) that slot got corrupted without any means of recovering it (even uninstalling and re-installing the game).
Can't even get to the main menu, been this way since launch.

I got this game when steam was giving out it for free. This game isn't that bad as meta-critic says it is, that said game isn't anything wowish either.
Game runs on unreal engine 3 and has some of it's signature problems, like random texture pop in's. Game looks OK for it's time, animations are great, sound works pretty well, but i had this weird problem, when you max out settings game runs good, but cut-scenes are starting to lag.
Story is mediocre, nothing really original , but nothing bizarre like COD would have, though its interesting enough to keep you playing and to have some interest about it. It mostly takes place in ruins of Berlin in last days of WW2, so most of the levels are just brown and gray rubble's of city. That said levels design is quite good, only at times it felt just too linear. Campaign took me about 10 hours on normal difficulty without searching all the collectibles.
Sniping mechanics are done really well, also with really cool x-ray cams and they give you some feeling of reward after fighting with some enemy snipers for a couple of minutes, but that couldn't be said about other weapons, they are quite inaccurate and you are alway low on ammo, i guess that was made to enforce you to use mainly the sniper rifle.
One more complain i had with cover mechanic, it didn't work well quite often, like when you are crouching behind curved wall, in some point you must go out of cover and than back in to continue walking behind the cover.
Game Has solid game-play, enemy AI isn't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and on normal difficulty game felt quite challenging. You can complete mission in stealthy way or fully guns blazing, but some levels will swamp you with enemies if you do so.
So to sum sum it up, game has some interesting idea and mechanics, but it lacks some polishing. From what i heard a lot of problems are fixed in 3rd entry so thats a good thing. And last thing, MP isn't worth your time, theres nothing really interesting, but since game's campaign is good, you should try it for a discount or if you got it also for free.

Adjusting the volume, boosting graphics to the max, you know the drill. Then I wanted to change the key bindings, to have a voice chat on the same button I always use.
. Well that was bad. Really bad as most of the keys were standardised for your average PC... I don't like using standard controls in most games. People are creatures of habit, so I was talking to myself, thinking I'm using the voice chat for my first two games.
Graphical glitches and missing prompts don't help much. As well as a bit wonky camera, bit too close to the character. But the game is fun, a bit repetitive, but a huge chunk is locked away with progression system, you know, unlocks, levels... so for now, there's real clone syndrome going on. One game we all looked the same. Most games at the start end with everyone dead, except one or two people who played longer, they know the maps, they know where things are and they're accustomed to the controls.
The first Jason I've met wouldn't shut up. Broke the immersion in the first seconds of the game, so I let myself get killed. That is an issue, you might think it's not, but it is. Cooperation and communication is vital in this game, yet
. The first one I've met talked so much you couldn't hear others well. I was in a screaming contest with him to tell the others I had the car keys... Last game I played, a Jason and a random dude made a pact, car was fixed, three people inside and the driver takes everyone to Jason to get killed. Why? Because they can communicate on the voice chat, same one everyone else is supposed to use!
With quick game you're being connected with random people from the internet. Makes sense, doesn't it? Well yes and no. The game feels like a P2P multiplayer, and it's probably what it is (EDIT: nope, the game has dedicated servers that must be set up in weird places, because getting a good, fast connection is near impossible for all players and with my internet speed, when even I have latency issues, the servers have to be way too far). Or I had the
of being connected with people whose ping was in three digits, most of the time starting with a number 5. You can't have a good game with players lagging all over the place! At one point I grabbed a dude as Jason, killed him. But he survived that, because he escaped, at least on his screen he did. After smashing down the doors it takes them up to 2 seconds to let me go in, plenty of time to use the window... and so on. Latency is a big problem for a multiplayer only game.
Really fun, but not yet done. There appears to be a character customisation menu, but you need to unlock things I think, and with all the issues the game has, that's a slow and painful grind.

The roguelite trend of the last few years has brought us a ton of games which are punishing or difficult without actually being complex or interesting, often using some kind of metagame progression as an escape valve for the player’s frustrations. Meanwhile, the strategy space is increasingly filled with bloated epics that take eons to complete and require relatively little player input. Offworld Trading Company is the perfect counterpoint to both trends, providing endless varied games of meaningful complexity in a timeframe that makes losing palatable; it's compact enough to make you want to challenge yourself, and complex enough to actually let you.
Offworld Trading Company is not a 4X game, but it manages to capture the consequence-driven excitement of the first 50-100 or so turns of something like a good game of Civ while chopping out everything that has the potential to become tedious or irrelevant. You have to determine priorities and bootstrap your way up the growth curve by pulling resources from a very limited number of tiles; payback horizons are short, and everything you do every matters immediately in obvious ways. Your ability to recognize and exploit marginal effects will dramatically affect your ability to put your grand strategy into effect.
OTC not only gets create this sense into a completely different format but actually manages to expand on the number of critical decisions without muddying or obscuring their consequence; choice of faction and choice of where to settle now feed back into decisions about when to settle and what to exploit. These decisions are in turn directly affected by opponent decisions via the game's stock market; even a sound strategy fitted to the map is not certain to succeed because awareness of opponent play has become part of its execution. The brilliance of, say, a Sid Meier design is generally the feedback between a number of subsystems and a larger game that incorporates them; this is as true of the fencing mini-game in Pirates!™ as it is of worker placement and city management in the Civ series: your degree of success in one area feeds into your performance in others, directly or otherwise. OTC features feedback of this kind not only between a variety of systems, but  between those systems and opponent decisions. To succeed you must play the map, play your faction, and play your opponent. The implementation of the market and its interplay with the supply chain gameplay results in an absolutely brilliant explosion of the strategic space without introducing obscurity, without needless complexity, without even direct control of units, and it all plays out over about a half hour.
It also has a campaign mode that's both distinct from the skirmish mode and mechanically satisfying. I'm reminded most of the campaign in Rise of Nations; no gimmicks, just a series of games whose persistent rewards can push your strategy in surprising directions. Like everything else in OTC, it's concise and satisfying.
I will say that while all of this stuff is going on in the game, the game is not screaming at you about it. It doesn’t call attention to everything that’s going on; you need to be able to find it, and if what you want out of a competitive game is a lot of onscreen flash reflecting your decisions you basically won’t find it; you have to be satisfied by your own ability to recognize and participate in what’s going on.
There are just two things I would warn potential buyers about. My primary caveat is that this game is so well-designed that it will ruin your patience and tolerance for many of the kludges that are grafted onto purportedly strategy-driven games in order to maintain a relative uniformity of user experience. So many games basically involve waiting for different kinds of buckets to fill up so that you can do X or Y; you can affect the pace, but you’re basically on a treadmill. Offworld Trading Company has made this impossible not to see and difficult to tolerate. The second is that this game is taxing; you are coping with a lot of variables and consequential decisions over a short span of time. It’s extremely satisfying, but it’s definitely not the kind of thing I can settle in to for like a whole weekend afternoon. I can sit and play something like Civ IV for four or six hours; I can play maybe two or three consecutive games of OTC.

Nether. It's a decent game with as many positive as negative sides...
Nether shows off a large open world very fast. It's easy to get lost in and creates an amazing atmosphere. This is where I want to loot things. Sadly, Nether doesn't have a very noteworthy looting system. It's a simple "Hold E" and random loot appears kind of system. While I can live with this simple system, it becomes a handicap when the only things you can loot must glow a golden color and are extremely scarce. This is sad, as I personally would have loved to dig under every tiny digitalized rock I could find in Nether, such as shelves, containers, boxes, beds, bunks, crates, bodies, skeletons, cars and every other apocalyptic container you can imagine looting.
Alongside this, I would have loved to see less "pay-2-win" aspects and a larger attempt at balancing the game as well as making weapons, the crafting process, rewards system and courier missions more exciting. I would have preferred something along the lines of a non-linear storyline to follow whenever I felt like it, but sadly that is not the case and the player is left to figure out his own ways of entertaining himself and steering clear of over-geared players who dump money into the game.
The game gives the player a great atmosphere, shows off neat concepts and ideas, creates an amazing feeling of sub-urban survival. It gets even better if you play with friends! For my own taste, the game needs more content. However, this is only my opinion, if you don't agree then it's perfectly fine.
I highly suggest you play the game yourself and make your own opinions on it!
Overall, Nether is a decent game and most certainly worth a play!

It's similar to many of the PS2 era platforming games like Crash Bandicoot, Spyro, Jak and Dexter, etc.
But there are some things to take not of. First of all, the first 20 minutes or so are confusing. The intro is pretty horrendous, in that it feels as if it cut out a large part of the story (you'll see what I mean). Speaking of story, it's definitely no tell tale games. The voice acting is... extremely underwhelming. The character (Parin) will often be seen flailing her arms, yet the voice actor is merely mumbling. Also, the game is capped at 30 fps for some reason. Not a game breaker by any means, but it's something to note.

This game is as immersive as the server and the players make it. You will find PVE, PVP, and RP environments. I have played with people from across the world, and the new maps have made it even more interesting. The MMO is certainly larger and harder to play, but the visuals and game play have improved significantly since i started playing (years). As far as the negative comments, It takes time to dev a well written product, and the updates happen regularly for a game app. Those that say otherwise probably don't write game code, if any code at all.... (Android apps don't count) If they did they would not be so critical. I also find their dev updates timely, and their committment continuous.
As for the game itself, it looks alot like Skyrim, but don't expect a complex storyline, only some annoying messages that pop up that you have ants in your pants or something like it. That being said, you make your own story as you go and interact with real people (not just groups to compelete a daily mission). There are roleplay servers, PVE servers, and PVP servers. The MMO is a vast expansive version of the YO game, and much more challenging. You can play alone, or with a group, it's your choice, and theirs. Most roles are chosen as to what you wish to do in the game (builders, crafters, hunters soldiers, or a combo) the only limitation is the skill set you develop. And to do anything interesting you have to develop the skill. You don't start the game knowing how to use a longbow or wield a sword, you have to acquire those skills, and your sword is not a magical sword, perhps a well made one though. No lightning bolts or flaming balls.
The environment is fully destructable, so you can build a clay hut or a stone castle, flatten the top of a mountain or build an island, it  is only limited by how much time and help you have.
Then there are the players, some like RP, others not so much, there are politics in the RP servers and some people get their knickers in a twist. But what you won't get are NPCs that repeatedly comment about that time they got an arrow to the knee (lord that is so old after hearing it 200 times), or that they would sell their relative (ha ha) or "Do come Back".
Then there are noobs, plenty of them (bless their hearts) and you can help them or ignore tham as to your preference. They actually will become your friends and if you help them, alot better at the game and perhaps the next supreme blacksmith or herbalist. Oh, usually they don't follow you around saying "Hi Ya"... well none so far.
This game is fun, if you can get it to work. Don't be surprised if the game fails to launch. You will likely need to tweek the configuration file and perhaps use an older monitor.
It's the most beautiful game I've ever seen by far. It seriously blows my mind with how amazing the art is. It's challenging and frustrating at times, but totally beatable.

One of the creepiest and most atmospheric horror games ever made, and surprisingly, it lives up to all the hype. There were moments that had me paralyzed with fear and too scared to continue on, but eventually, with great determination, I conquered it, and the payoff was huge. The game has a unique way of storytelling compared to most other games of its kind and respects the player's intelligence to put all the pieces together. It's a great story at that, and even though there are only about two creatures in the game, the way the game handles them makes them feel much bigger and deadlier than they actually are, especially given you aren't supposed to look at them and are often punished for doing so. Not being able to look at the monsters makes them more mysterious and frightening, as you're always anxious about whether or not one lies around the next corner, and after an amazing atmospheric filled beginning, you get more and more paranoid about how grotesque they look.
The music is intense and suits every moment perfectly, ramping up during chases and quieting down during exploration. The monster themes in particular are extremely memorable, and the music is useful for figuring out how close the monsters are to you, but it doesn't take away from the tension in anyway and enhances the quality of the experience. I played SOMA before this game, so I was familiar with this style of gameplay already and how you have to avoid and hide rather than fight back against the threats hunting you, as you can't fight back, and both games are simply masterpieces of the survival horror genre. Amnesia in particular was insanely groundbreaking and lead to loads of imitators, for better or worse, and SOMA had the best story in a horror game since the beloved Silent Hill 2. I may have preferred the storyline of SOMA overall, but Amnesia still stands tall as arguably the scariest first person horror game ever made, and right now during Halloween month is absolutely the perfect time to play through it for the first time, preferably in the dark with headphones on.
The free Justine dlc that can be found in the settings launcher is also a neat little bonus and definitely worth a playthrough despite how short it is, clocking in at less than an hour depending on skill level, and introducing a brand new monster that is blind but has impeccable hearing.
Fun enough, I would not pay money for it. But then again, I got it for free.

Arma III is one of my all-time favourite games.
If you like messing around with military hardware, doing special-ops missions with snipers and helicopters and magic earthquake machines, working with friends to capture a village or perhaps in a 60-strong platoon to capture a country then you should buy this game.
There are also a huge amount of awesome mods, from ones that add vehicles, tanks and planes from all the world's militaries to ones that add customisable beards or tactical bananas.
However, there are a few issues:
The physics engine is highly unpredictable. KSP-level. This will never be fixed. However, if you are carful and take care to avoid any obstacles (especially campfires) then it shouldn't be an issue. Jets also fly like spaceships, but that is kind of necessarry due to the map sizes.
You will need a fairly beefy PC if you want to put the view distance past 3 Km. If you're on a server with 60 other players you should also not expect above 30 fps.
Bohemia Interactive continues the tradition of desync, the effect whereby a vehicle or player suddenly stops or zooms forward wlist moving. It sucks, and it's not going to be fixed. But with staggered vehicle formations and communication it can usually be worked around, however it is very unlikely that you will ever see a jet fly smoothly across the sky.
The learning curve is pretty steep, the controls can be clunky at times and you will continue to discover new controls until your hours played get into the hundreds, but with patience and persistance it won't be much of an issue.

I can proudly (?) say I've purchased every iteration of this game since the beginning. My first foray was with the SNES when the game was released back in 94, not any of the remakes. I've revisited FF6 over the years to wax nostalgic for a bygone era of gaming. This version, unfortunately, is actually a port of the app, not of the original game. Square took the lazy way out and supersized what was already available on your phone. The various graphical changes used to make this playable on the phone were acceptable for that format but not here. It's very obvious the goal with this version was to capitalize on the game's popularity, not deliver something that keeps it alive for another 20 years. I've spent more time playing with the settings on my TV in a vain attempt to correct Square's failed efforts than I've spent playing the game, but to no avail.
My suggestion, for those wanting to play the original in its glory, is to grab the PS version via Sony's store. It's as close to the SNES as you're going to get, for better or worse. I say that because it was never meant to be played on 60" UHD displays. Let me tell you, it's ugly. As luck would have it, however, I have an old 30" that is now serving as my FF6 machine for my latest replay. This Steam version at least doesn't look atrocious as the resolution goes up. Small victory, I suppose, for the team behind it. The ultimate failing with this game isn't simply larger, brighter sprites; it's the lost pallor of gloom that was always present in the original. Whether intended or not, the muted tones and darker palette of the original enhanced the story of war against Emperor Gestahl and Kefka. You were the hero bringing light unto this bleak world!
This PC port is too sunny, too defined, too...hopeful. It lacks the pall of FF"3" and will never compete with it.

Two common things I see that people complain about from this game are the launcher issues and the amount of effort placed in making this game. To solve the launcher issues you simply need to open the local files of the game and locate the game.exe. To run the game.exe you are going to need the Run Time Packages (RTP) found here: on the RPG Maker site:
Obviously the game feels like it was made in haste and the developer utilized the original stock tilesets and images from RPG Maker VX Ace. He seemed to glaze the avatars and battlepacks to give it a slightly tinted look. If you can get past these feelings, you’ll find that the game doesn’t really have that bad of a storyline. It’s original and it has several twists and is full of a lot of cheesy jokes and metagame concepts that really isn’t common.
The only aspect of the game I criticize it for is the lack of attention paid to certain animations (most notably a dog running through village houses), and avatars missing for almost half of the villagers. A controversial move made by the developer was having the protagonist almost invincible but I liked this even more so because this game isn’t so much about leveling up but more about emphasizing the fact that you are the greatest fighter of all time. If you do manage to fight all your battles leading up to Ivan, you’re bound to unlock the thousand blows special move which is practically a safeproof move to killing even the greatest of bosses *cough* . Yes, the game is extremely easy, as I found the first boss fight against the Demon King to be the hardest, but the game’s plot and interesting setting makes up for it.
For a dollar it’s almost worth it but best to buy during a sale.

As stated by the other reviews that are several months older than this one, the game doesn't install correctly. Pretty unbelievable.
The game is short (about an hour long), but I don't count that against it. I actually rather like short games. The content within is what I take issue with. I also don't mind the use of stock RPG Maker assets. The game is a mere dollar at full price, so that's fine.
But it's clear everything was done in a slapdash manner. That Photoshop filter used to give the game a more unique look? Clearly done via some kind of batch processing without individually inspecting each asset to make sure they crop and animate cleanly. Every ability and monster in the game has received seemingly zero touch-ups to make any kind of unique encounters or combat. I mean, I get the point that the main character is super OP, but why have him still gain levels and acquire skills? Why leave all those abilities left in the game? All I needed was Cleave and basic attack. And why can I remove the limiter multiple times and get a temporary buff for doing so? It makes no narrative sense. The obvious explanation as that all these things unchanged once they were found to be basically functional.
Another problem with the shortness is that it still feels the need to pad out its time with a ridiculously high encounter rate throughout the whole game. It only seems to get higher with each new area!
Really, though. Regardless of all these issues, there just isn't enough of a story. I get that people really like bad puns/humor and pop culture references, but those should be like easter eggs and not the meat of the interactions. Unless it was meant as a way to discourage me from talking to random NPC's and interacting with things. If so, mission accomplished. Aside from that, the story has little to offer. A confusing moral (don't ever move away from your hometown?) is shoved in your face while the premise of "what happens after you beat the big bad" is told via summary. And then there's a slight twist at the end. But none of the execution actually bothers to explore the idea. I guess I expected something like Rocky II, which is about what happens to that smalltown hero when given massive success and fame (which happens in Rocky I). Not that I expected this game to be as good as an Oscar-winning movie franchise, just that I wanted there to be a STORY not a summary.
So my conclusion is that this game is kind of a scam. It doesn't run unless you fix it yourself and the effort is so low that I have to believe the dev doesn't care. He's got his money so he's good to go.

Having been a fan of Frictional Games since their horrifying Penumbra series, I was expecting an amazing game, in storytelling, graphical quality and detail, level detail, music and audio...
Let me put it plainly: I was not let down.
Frictional Games has come a very long way since Penumbra, and even since the original Amnesia: The Dark Descent. The studio has managed to create something so deep and immersive that it boggles my mind. I can't really think of another video game, let alone a horror game, that has stopped and made me think about so many issues and ethical questions. Frictional has driven home a myriad of thought-provoking story elements that would keep my mind running even when I needed a break from the game's horrors.
And boy did Frictional bring the horrors. The environments were very well designed, and in some cases, I would jump at things that weren't even threats, I tended to pick up on little things in the environments, like bodies I had seen at one time, missing when I passed by again, or doors creeping open after multiple passes. The attention to detail was not lost on Frictional, and each area seemed to be almost perfect in it's layout and item placement. Nothing felt out of place, each environment felt like it should have; abandoned, overgrown, worn out.
I don't even have the most impressive system; I was only running the game on Medium textures, with full SSAO and Bloom. There was some choppiness, but the game still looked beautiful on a lower setting. I will be replaying this once I get a new rig that can handle the highest settings.
The monsters were equally frightening. Instead of Amnesia's 2 monster system, SOMA introduced new enemies in nearly every area, causing me to learn about the enemy and how to avoid it. I also pretty much crapped my pants at each new one. These monsters were well designed and coded, and the challenge of getting by the remained even after death. This was a huge improvement over Amnesia: TDD and MFP. Hell, sometimes the enemy would appear in a totally different part than I was expecting (I'm looking at you, Tau.)
Sound design and music were amazing as well. The soundtrack was deep and chilling, and it added so much to the atmosphere. The ambient sounds and environment sounds that accompanied the game also increased the immersion, from panels and computers to the creaking of pipes and walls under pressure. The underwater sections were also done very nicely as well.
My only gripe with this game was some of the loading times. It seemed that when I saved and exited the game in an underwater area, I would need to wait around 2-3 minutes for it to load. I do not know if Frictional released a patch sometime after release that helped this, as I did notice load times decreased as time progressed from launch.
If you have never played a psychological horror/survival game in your life, this is one I would absolutely recommend starting with. It will not let you down.

This is a surprisingly fun game. The characters seem well developed, and are voiced, combat is fun... a nicely designed game. And I expect nothing else from Falcom.
Combat seems fairly simplistic so far, I expect more complicated moves to pull off will be added later on. Simplistic is not a bad thing though. The combat is enjoyable, easy to pick up, and has a couple interesting mechanics; like the critical hit timing bar. The enemies also seem balanced and combat is not drawn out to the point that I don't want to play. *cough X-Blades cough*
All the characters are voiced, although not all the text is voiced. I... am of mixed opinions on the voice acting. Some of it is good, but a good chunk of it seems like the voice does not fit the character (main character for example has the voice that does not match the little kid she is supposed to be) or has no emotion (one character talking about how his village got destroyed but is said in the exact same tone as when he's asking you to come to his village). The big thing is that all the characters have their own personality and none are just cut and paste throw away characters. Bonus points for the main characters grandpa as he actually does seem senile.
Music is not bad, it matches what you are doing, and the critical hit timing bar being tied to the music is an interesting, and unique touch. I honestly can not remember any that I've heard off the top of my head, but that just means it was neither cringe worthy bad or super memoriable.
The controls feel clunky if you use the default ones. I manually inverted the horizontal camera movement and moved around all the controls to my liking. But it DOES allow you to change them! Far too many games make it so you can't remap the controls, so if they suck you are out of luck. It took me all of 5 minutes to get them to my liking and didn't have a single issue with them afterwards. My only complaint is the spot to remap them is on the config screen before the game actually starts up and not in game itself, so you have to exit, change, then restart to see if they're to your liking. But... you can change them, so I'll let that slide.
Oh, game does not auto-save. But you can save whenever you want. So save fairly often.
Overall, this is a run and enjoyable game that I am looking forward to playing more of. And this review will be updated with any changes of opinion I have towards it.

Alright. First up, the game didn't install correctly. The "Play" button only launched an installer for the game and created a sub-folder that I had to run the executable within in order to play the game, so if you're thinking of buying this do be aware of that. Due to the "Play" button only launching the installer, the five minutes registered for my playtime is actually just the time spent installing and waiting for the review window to open up. A better estimate of my playtime is somewhere on the order of an hour (probably somewhat less), in which time I played the game to completion.
Regardless, the game itself was quite nice for a $0.99 impulse buy. The story did exactly what it set out to do - provide the sort of denouement that RPGs so often lack, addressing the question of what, exactly, a band of heroes strong enough to save the world where armies couldn't would do once they were done.
Which isn't to say it doesn't have its problems, of course. Graphical glitches abound, with tiles often being outlined in black for no discernible reason, especially when animating. The random encounter system is also somewhat underdeveloped - perhaps half a dozen times I found myself finishing an encounter only to get another literally the next step I took, and a more typical fight every five to ten steps isn't much better. Most grievously, however, the game is locked to a very tiny resolution and immediately halts in every way but musically while unfocused. The former is slightly understandable with fixed-width graphical elements, but the latter is really quite irksome.
Also unfortunate is how the "limiter" mechanic (wherein the hero purposefully limits himself in order to "challenge himself" but also to drive home story elements) is implemented - you can choose to take it off right after you put it on and become the strongest thing in the game by far. Yet even if you do this, those aforementioned story elements still act as if you had the thing on, which is rather jarring. I'd advise leaving the thing on the whole game, especially since you don't really need it too much in the first place - the game's definitely on the easy side of the spectrum. And if the developer's reading this, I'd advise just taking out the ability to remove it outside of cutscenes.

I picked this up during a Humble Bundle sale having never heard of it. I didn't know what to expect and really wasn't expecting much. To my surprise, Nihilumbra delivered and turned out to be one of the best and most underrated indie games I've ever played.
You are Born. Born was created from The Void but has somehow separated from it and is now in the world. However, The Void will not allow this and is now chasing Born in an attempt to suck him back into the darkness. In order for Born to escape The Void, he must allow everything else in his path be destroyed.
Nihilumbra is a puzzle-platformer. As you progress through the game, Born will be granted new colors, which the player can use to paint the terrain in order to solve puzzles and aid him in his platforming. In total there are five different colors. Each have a different use and create a different effect. Throughout the game, Born will be accompanied by a narrator that will talk to him. It is uknown exactly who this narrator is whether he be Born, The Void or something else. The narrator really gives this game it's charm and gives insight to the world and what is going on. Sometimes he says some really philosophical things and it really adds to the atmosphere. Speaking of that, the atmosphere is amazing. The combination of colors, textures, music and narration sets a very solemn, yet relaxing mood. The main part of the game is very short. It only took me about 4 hours to complete. However, once you complete it, you'll unlock “Void Mode” which is essentially hard mode. Void Mode offers the same levels but with different and much harder puzzles.
Overall, I'd recommend this to anyone that's a fan of platformers or puzzle-platformers. It's really unique and highly underrated. Nihilumbra is a very insightful, relaxing and fun experience. That's what this game is. It's more than just a game. It's an experience to be had.

You gain more abilities, weapon elements and upgrades as you go, all of which are up to you, so there's a decent feeling of agency here. There's even a special "Beginner Mode" which in addition to reduced damage and penalities, also stops ice from being slippery, which is just a really thoughtful feature! Gurumin could be great for all ages and player skills as a result, though younger kids might still need some help with the puzzles.
There's also keyboard and mouse support which can be remapped before playing, and adding that to the high resolution capability makes this an example of a port done right!
Despite initial apprehension and a couple of hours of admitted "hrm...", something kept calling me back to the game and I actually had a lot of fun! Maybe it's just that it reminds me of games from the Nintendo 64 or original Playstion, like Croc or Mario 64 or even Ocarina of Time, but I just HAD to play this game sitting on my couch in front of my TV. And... that's all I've done pretty much for 2 days straight now! And hopefully many more to come! This is a stupidly cute, amazingly solid, retro-console styled game through-and-through. Nihilumbra is an interesting puzzle game that is short and relatively simple. It tells a story through narration, which I quite enjoyed. You will die many times to off screen enemies and obstacles you had no way of knowing about until you died to them. I've played LiF:YO for a decent amount of time and gone trough all the stages of from nothing to a big castle, one thing i can tell you right away is that this isn't a game for everyone, its grindy and NOT a game to play alone if you wish to accomplish something great.

I feel like LiF:YO is good for learning the basics since this game has the biggest learning curve i've seen in a game so far.
So what makes LiF so great?
- Crafting system: There is so much to craft and its so complex, so you will feel good after learning something new.
- Building system: The objects you can make are amazing and all of it matter even when you've reached endgame
- Advanced combat: So many different weapons with unique playstyle and abilities, commands and unit formations!
- Skill trees: This is what matters in the long run and the reason why you can't play solo, due to the fact you can only do something while your friends can do other things.
- Gathering: Mining is one of my favorites and chopping down trees, it'll feel boring after a while but try to make the best out of it.
I have nothing bad to say about the game other than it forces you to play with more people than some are comfortable with, i personally like to play with 2-3 players when its more than that it feels unsocial and a bit like going to work.

I did finish the game. Some of it was very fun. I love to figure out puzzles. But once into the Void levels, it became so frustrating that I considered abandoning the game. Instead I referred to a walkthrough to help out. It was never that the puzzles were hard to figure out. It was the timing that was so critical in some cases. A second or less could make the difference in not getting through an obstacle.
There were times you needed to bounce so high that the figure you were controlling would go off the top of the screen. This made it very tough to "stick" a landing or bounce just right. There was no way to avoid death repeatedly because you could not see the next screen of obstacles/enemies until you were in the line of fire or off the edge of a cliff.  I could not find any way to change the key mappings/bindings. So, I was stuck using WASD. That means my fingers were in the wrong position to quickly tap on numbers to change colors, I had to rely on the mouse wheel which means cycling through colors which takes more time than desired.  There were times I just left the game up in paused mode because I did not want to replay a prior part of a level (no save nearby). So the number of hours it took me to play is highly inflated with 8 hours while I slept or worked.
For me, these frustration points were just too many. Yet, as always, I feel good having completed the game. I even played all of the extra levels that get unlocked once the void levels are completed. I actually enjoyed those extra levels and their pithy monologues more than the void levels. Those were hilarious and informative about the game's development.
However, I can not see any replay value. So if you choose to play the game, consider waiting for a sale.

There are some glitches. The view controls are counter-inuituve. I lost count of how many times I moved the wrong way as the controls seem reversed to me. Grab it on sale if you need something simple to while away a few hours or for the kids to play. For under a quid, you can't go wrong.  6/10.

Wow, what a great "good game-bad port" example. After playing Final Fantasy V on Steam (and enjoying it), i guessed that Final Fantasy VI would be an equal or greater port. But i hate to say that i was wrong. This port is terrible. Sure, it's completely playable to 100%, but it's ugly to look at the entire time. The sprites and backgrounds are pixelated and incohesive. The interface sucks. The diagonal movement here is terrible, even with a controller. Likewise, inputing Sabin Blitz commands is terrible because of the diagonals poor sensitivity. I recommend you playing it in windowed mode with a controller, it helps a little bit.
But make no mistake, the game itself is great, one of the best JRPG's that i played in my life. There's a great story with a great twist in the middle, great characters, NPC's and villains, the combat is good, exploration in a airship is fun as always, and the music brilliant, especially the opera compositions. It's the best classic, 2D Final Fantasy hands down and i recommend every fan of the genre to play it, even it you choose another version. This version has achievements, but that's little compensation. Over time, i managed to get somewhat used to this version, even if it doesn't have the same feeling as the other classical versions. If you really want it, grab it on sale. Despite the crappy port, it's compeltely playable, even if it's frustrating at times.

Medal of Honor is, without any exaggeration, the most bland game I have ever seen in my entire life. It is repetitive, there is no story, gameplay is extremely basic and no feeling of progression as you go through the extremely short (5 hours in my case) game.
The game is set entirely in Afghan tundra, with the exception of one urban level and another one set in an airbase and although  tundra is not a common environment in videogames, it is extremely overused here. Gameplay consists of simple first-person shooter action broken up by vechile sections. There was nothing in that respect that I haven't seen before.
The story was so extremely uninteresting that I forgot it in it's entirety inbetween playing it and writing this review and although that was some time, I can say with certainity that there was no thing going on for the entire duration of the game. I was simply doing stuff without any form of greater context, so my memory of it all is now a miasma of brown deserts with equally brown-uniformed men trodding around while firing the same boring guns at other brown men. The only thing I remembered was one nice moment where you were given the impression that you would be overwhelmed by the enemy in a lengthy standoff, but the opportunity for the game to do something interesting is wasted when you are saved by a helicopter at the last moment. But without doubt the worst moment in the entire story aspect is when I didn't realise the game was over untill the end credits appeared. I seriously was just playing a mission as difficult or interesting as all the other ones untill all of a sudden a cutscene came up where I found some guy dead who I had to rescue since the moment the game had reached 50% of it's runtime. Then the game just stopped. In other words, a story thread that only spanned part of the game was resolved and for some reason the game took the moment to run off in it's entirety. Nothing I did in the first half of the game changed anything meaningful about the rest of the game.
Then I tried the multiplayer. Although I have to admit that my brief experience was satisfying, that was mostly because of that I found that I was better at it than most playing. That is not a weird thing, considering that all you do in the multiplayer is run around and shoot eachother in microscopic environments. Therefore noone who plays first person shooters regularly is still playing that, which explains my experience. After 20 minutes I was done, I quit and never returned.
If you ask me, this game is just boring. I would not recommend that you pay money for it at all to play it.

So this is a typical Stardock Game.  and for those that love stardock, you may enjoy picking this up.  I got it on boxing day for about $15. (even the ones I win)  I am more into the long game simlations, which is why I opened with "typical star dock game"  your neighbours will be on your doorstep within minutes of starting the game, and if you don't take an eary lead, you are toast as you only have about 10 minutes to make up the lead or the game will end.

TL;DR I got the game for free and I feel robbed, it's buggy and Mastiff should be ashamed.
Thoughts:
Great game, I love Falcom and their games, but Mastiff's effort in the publishing of Gurumin is non-existent.
The game does have a few faults by default, one being the overly sensitive input for performing special moves (You'll sometimes do spin attacks by turning only a half circle before attacking). People who use controllers (myself included) may also find the analogue input to be overly sensitive as well, which just comes down to needing to adjust the deadzone of your controller.
Now for the things that Mastiff did wrong:
As you get past the halfway point you'll soon notice several lines of dialogue being unacceptably incomplete.
A couple of steam achievements do not unlock properly and requires you to beat the final boss and watch the whole ending TWICE per difficulty to unlock both, that is if you actually made a save before a certain point in the game, otherwise you'll have to replay the whole game to unlock the other achievement.
The unlockable Item List does not update properly and is showing a majority of blanks despite having beaten the game to 100% twice.
The PSP version (Also published by Mastiff) has content which this version does not, including:
At least 5 extra costumes.
Original Japanese voice line option (Available on the PC version through manually downloading and overwriting audio files with original Jap audio, search Steam threads if you're interested)
Skippable cutscenes.
Conclusion:
I would've recommended this game outright simply because it's another great Falcom game, but this version is an example of publishing done wrong, Mastiff has put in minimal effort to properly bring a good product to Steam.
If this had been published by XSEED we would've had a version of the game with full uncensored content for sure and without any bugs.

REALLY enjoyed this on the PSP (although I never made it past Happy mode as I wanted to fully complete the game), if you are deciding whether or not you want to own this, then here is a simplified checklist that may make this game more appealing to you.
-A game with a cute, anime artstyle and animation, with a charming and captivating cast of characters!
-That kind of game where you'd think the English dub would be atrocious, when it isn't! It features an all-star voice cast featuring the voice talents of actors you may have heard from before! (ex. Pierre and Doug are voiced by Robin Atkin Downes, aka The Medic and Dee Bradley Baker, most known for voicing many Spongebob characters is in this too!)
-A storyline that at times can be serious, but most of the time doesn't take itself seriously and has many light-hearted elements.
-An absolutely awesome and always upbeat and rocking soundtrack!
-Simple and intuitive controls (not to mention fluid)
-Has RPG elements but for those who are new to games with RPG elements, this game simplifies them, saving you the stress of understanding them.
-A ultra-simple equip mechanic, just put on a different piece of headgear on the fly to use its attributes to turn the tide in battle! (PLUS headgear can be further upgraded, gaining new perks and even strengthening its current attributes!)
-LOTS of collectibles and extras, perfect for the gamers who like to collect everything and for completionists!
-This game may have linear progression, but 100% of the time it encourages players to explore the areas (hidden areas, breakable walls) and are rewarded for their curiosity for going out of the beaten path.
-A unique lineup of enemies that have the players think of which strategies and/or weaknesses to use on them.
-Formidable boss battles that have patterns players must adapt to (it's more fun to experiment methods of defeating the bosses everytime in newer, faster, and more efficient ways!)
-5 Difficulty levels to challenge the player (it's okay for newcomers to choose the Beginner difficulty, but once they get the hang of the game, they are free to tackle the higher difficulties and are awarded new items for clearing them, there's even a hidden playable character when special conditions are met!)
And that should cover all the details about this game and if you should get it (I mean need I say more?). This game gets my highest recommendation and I cannot recommend this game enough.

This is a beautiful game with a stirring atmosphere and mood. A puzzle-platformer at it's core, it is immersive enough to make you forget that you're solving puzzles or dodging strange other-wordly creatures but feels more like a story that you're enjoying and experiencing.
I don't play many puzzle games and I still loved it so don't overlook this game because of the puzzle factor! The platforming is pretty straight forward and enhanced by some of the unique abilities the protagonist acquires (eg: being able to shoot a sticky-mud thing onto walls to cling onto or shooting bouncy grass or ice to reach sections otherwise inaccessible. There's some nice creativity at the core of this game.
Once you complete the main story (arguably not quite a 'story' in the traditional sense but still immensely enjoyable...) you unlock a harder version of the game - same areas with more complex puzzles. These, I safely avoided due to my aforetold indifference to hardcore puzzle games but that does add good replay value and may strike a chord with the puzzler in you.
In all - this is an excellent Indie title. You can even try the demo from the developer's website I believe if you're on the fence.
PS: IIRC I spent more than the 3.5 hours reported by Steam on this game (probably spent offline) but in any case this is a short game without any doubt, so bear that in mind.

SOMA is the latest in Frictional Games' horror set, following Penumbra and the Amnesia games.  Let me get it out of the way that SOMA is simply not as scary as Amnesia: The Dark Descent.  I feel its scary "enough" and should not be missed by fans.
The main character is Simon Jarett, and ordinary Canadian nerd undergoing theapy for a traumatic brain injury.  Upon getting a medical scan in Torono, he wakes up somewhere very, VERY far away.  The story is obviously inspired from I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream (the short story, not the game), as well as H.R. Geiger's art.  It is complex and tragic, and worth the price of admission alone.  There are a few problems with the story, but those are my opinions and I will keep them to myself.
Gameplay is very much similar to Amnesia - A Machine for Pigs. Simon is armed with only a flashlight and his wits, interacting with a handful of characters, solving simple puzzles, reading documents for clues and weaving around dangerous monsters without being seen.  This is simply not as scary as Amnesia: The Dark Descent, but is still sufficiently scary.
The problem is that in The Dark Descent, some monster events were scripted for cheap shots, while the more effective scares were from the fact that you were in an open field of corridors and room, in which you had to solve puzzles while simultaneously avoiding one active monster in that area with you, leaving you at the mercy of RNG and the monster's AI.  SOMA has one, and ONLY one sequence that does the latter, and its excellent, almost in line with Alien Isolation, a game I am too terrified to complete.  The rest of the time, monster appearances are fixed, along with their behavior.  By the end of the game, you will have most of the monsters wrapped around your finger for the next playthrough, except "that one awesome part."  In this sense, SOMA is somewhere in between Dark Descent and AMfP, but leans toward the latter.
I'm delighted to have played this, and I would recommend it to anyone.  Just don't expect Dark Descent, because you won't get it.  Consider SOMA on its own and you should be glad you played it too.

This game was a wonderful concordance of all of my favorite things: horror, the dreadful strangeness of our consciouness, walking-through-an-abandoned-station-listening-to-the-audio-logs-of-former-inhabitants, hard science fiction, artificial intelligence, zombies, post-apocalypse, robots, the bottom of the sea, the loneliness of space... and so much more.
I'm a fan of the genre, and a fan of Frictional Games, in particular. SOMA is not genre-defying innovation: monster mechanics will be reminiscent to anyone familiar with Frictional's previous titles, and wandering about an abandoned place finding clues is ubiquitious to the genre (though I love it!).  It is, however, a masterful execution of all of those horror/scifi game notes, clearly learned from practiced iteration through their previous titles -- the wonderful writing and all its great dreary, existential themes are combined with Frictional's eye for suspense and storytelling -- it's excellent and truly captivating.

I rarely play a long game from start to finish more than twice, for me to do so it'd require fun gameplay and a story I felt invested in and wanted to relive. I've played Half-Life 2 (and its episodes) three times over because of how in love I fell with the story. While figuring out how to get this game to work with TSLRCM, I started playing Knights of the Old Republic again, as the opposite sex and alignment but found myself somewhat bored after Dantooine. So far, I have played Knights of the Old Republic II - The Sith Lords two full times in rapid succession and I'm roughly a third of the way through my third playthrough. To say I love this game is an understatement.
The gameplay is a step up from KOTOR 1 and though I find it very enjoyable, battles can be rather bland and a bit too easy at times. The real reason to play this game is the story. However, that itself is very divisive. The Sith Lords' story is a meticulous exploration of the very basis of the Star Wars mythos: the Force. It portrays the Jedi as flawed, the Sith as broken but ultimately human (or whatever species they are) and the very concept of morality as far more complex than any of the current Star Wars canon does (admittedly I'm rather unfamiliar with the old Expanded Universe outside of these two games). This can turn off Star Wars fans just looking for a Star Wars game like KOTOR 1 that captures what makes Star Wars great. On the other hand, the mouthpiece for all these criticisms and alternative points of view is a character called Kreia who, without delving into spoilers, is... rather questionable to say the least. Though you can't convince her to change her mind, you can declare yourself in disagreement and you can defy her as you wish, or agree with her as you wish. As a Star Wars fan, I found this deconstruction of the Force to be highly enjoyable and cast the movies in a different light for me.
The other characters in the game are hardly one dimensional, the weakest ones are two dimensional at worst. It's difficult to talk about what makes these characters great without delving into spoilers so I won't, but I will especially praise Atton as an example of everything a good anti-hero should be. There are a couple that return from KOTOR 1 and their presence is very welcome. Some, such as HK-47, are enjoyable as ever and developed further while others, like T3-M4, are an improvement over their KOTOR 1 incarnations.
The mechanics are integrated much better with differet aspects of the game this time around. Your attributes and skills play a role in conversations and the creation of items at workbenches, the latter being itself a huge improvement over its handling in KOTOR 1. Playing as different classes and alignments creates very different experiences outside of combat. As a male Jedi Guardian/Jedi Master I played very differently than as a female Jedi Consular/Sith Weapon Master and as a female Jedi Sentinel/Jedi Watchman, for example. Where in KOTOR 1 you can play Dark Side or Light Side but really only make meaningful decisions towards the end, you're put in a spot where you have to take decisions from the start. As a Light Side player, early in Telos do I refuse this monetary reward to earn Light Side points but risk having to sell my wares to not gain Dark Side points a bit down the line? As a Dark Side player, do I challenge the Jedi Masters early on and engage in difficult fights or save all but one of them for later when I'm more powerful but make the survivors gang up on me?
In conclusion, I tend to compare Episodes IV and V to KOTOR 1 and KOTOR 2. Episode IV and KOTOR 1 are the more basic Star Wars adventure. The dichotomy between good and evil is clear and doesn't really try anything new but is more easily digestible and is incredibly fun regardless. Episode V and KOTOR 2 are the more creative one but takes risks that might not be to everyone's liking. While this really isn't a good analogy as both Episode IV and V are rather easily digestible whereas KOTOR 2 is a lot harder to swallow, especially if you just come in for a sequel to KOTOR 1 in body and soul, I think it works as a comparison because one is the safer one while the other is the more daring one. Both are great on their own merits, though I personally consider the latter to be better. With this game you should come in with an open mind. If you do, I highly recommend giving it a whirl and seeing if you can get something out of it. Just please install TSLRCM and possibly M4-78EP from the Workshop, the game is incomplete without at least the former.

This game tries to be both and off course is in this way quite unique.
First, it is a humorous fairy tale with rendered 3D graphics. Instead of using pictures teeming with objects you have to look for "quest" relevant objects. Of course this "Fairy Tale" runs a bit out of course and is trying to be far to funny for it's own good.
Still this "Hidden Object Adventure" has some merits that sets it apart to other games. The Minigames are a bit, well too easy though - so you can't count them in for a full bonus. And the hidden object part too is, too easy.
Sound is a bit on the bad side, no voice acting, the dialogues are just subtitles... most of them can be quite the mood killers.
This game has a lot of good potential wasted on trying to be funny. Sadly the jokes and the puns are so artificial, that a lot of good potential got drained away. The developer had a good idea with this alternative aproach to the hidden object genre. But he has wasted it on a story that is only a superficial fairy tale, a lot of shallow puns and punchlines. And of course he has also wasted the possibility to put some of the jokes through via voiceacting. I know, some developers have a tight budget. I also know that you can lose yourself in planing tape, and the story can work out quite different for an audience. The game would - with a slightly different aproach to some issues I pointed out - have had the potential to be a memorable gaming experience, even the core of definition for a new genre type within the hidden object games. But with all the things that were just done half-heartedly and only with the effort to appear "Funny and Punny" this potential was lost. The game is nothing more than just a interesting novelty, that doesn't keep it's promissing start.

Significantly more serious review:
I honestly don't have many negative things to say about this game. Perhaps I'm still coming off the post-completion high, but I think my opinion still holds some validity. Frankly, the entire game is worth playing just for the ending. I'm not going to say anything more than that on said subject.
Graphics: 9/10
Really great. Very clearly convey where you are in the environment. There is a rather lengthy period of texture pop-in upon loading up your game, but that's the only instance I've found of particularly low-res textures. The structure gel drips on walls don't look so great either, but these are minor gripes. The overall atmosphere and feel of the game is excellent.
Sound Design: 10/10
Not a whole lot to say here. The sounds are nice and atmospheric. They do a great job of immersing the player.
Story: 10/10
At risk of spoiling any plot points, major or minor, I'm not going to say a whole lot about the story. All you need to know is that it's excellent. For the earlier parts of the game, the story will keep you intrigued enough to ignore some of the fear you may have. Later in the game, the intrigue will remain, giving you a very clear sense of motive to reach your goal. Fantastic story. Great job, Frictional Games.
Gameplay: 10/10
I can't think of any instances in which I felt disconnected with the game at all. I was fully immersed at every given moment. I cannot think of any instances in which the game's controls actively fought with me either, unless they were supposed to, (environmental or atmospheric reasons). I don't believe there were any situations in which I was frustrated by the game, outside of tension brought about by the game's scares. On top of that, the moral choices which you are faced with repeatedly throughout the story will rip you apart. Just keep in mind, there isn't usually a right answer.
Scares: 9/10
Overall, I think this game is better than Amnesia: The Dark Descent. I don't know how they managed to top such a masterpiece, but they did. SOMA is terrifying, do not be fooled by the early chapters of the game. Jumpscares are relatively uncommon, unless you bring one upon yourself by turning around to look at whatever may be chasing you. Great tension, and well executed scares.
Overall Score: 9.6/10
A truly fulfilling experience, that I will not forget. Not for a long, long time. The story is interesting and satisfying, the graphics are great, the sound is excellent, the gameplay is fluid, and the scares are top-notch. I would highly recommend you purchase this game. I have nothing but good things to say about it.

Frictional Games continues to prove it's exceptional storytelling abilities in this underwater sci fi horror whilst providing a beautifully eerie game world filled with suspense and lore (providing you're brave enough to go go off the beaten path a bit). Piecing together the story line feels greatly rewarding as you come up with various ideas and theories as to what's happened until it hopefully all comes together for you in the end. The choices you will have to make may leave you thinking twice about your descisions adding replayability to the game.
While I understand the horror genre isn't for everyone, I'd go so far as to suggest people brave the horror aspect and try this game for the story alone, it's that strong.  One critiscm the game has is that it has bad gameplay, to which I would say it's a matter of perspective, you may not have a massive arsenal that you would have in other horror games, the gameplay focuses on hiding, relying on your wits and paying attention to sounds and as a last resort, fleeing to survive, which to me is the epitomy of survival-horror.
SOMA is an experience, where the old cliche "your choices matter" isn't hand fed to you but implied by it's affect on you as a player, something not many games with choices pull off. Overall a great intense horror game, go try it out if you're brave enough. 10/10

Graphics: For an 05 game, it looks pretty damn good (if you have a good graphics card, that is). Keep in mind though that it 'is' a 2005 game, so don't expect anything incredible. 8/10
Story: Here is where TSL shines. I have quite honestly never played a Star wars game with such in depth writing. From the deep and well thought out exploration of the moral grey areas between the Light and Dark sides of the Force to the deviously intricate, and VERY well written main quest, KOTOR II's writing is nothing short of incredible. 10/10
Characterization: This of course ties in with the aforementioned excellent writing. The characters in this game feel more like living, breathing people, and less like the one dimensional caricatures of KOTOR 1. The addition of a good influence character influence system (you can't just give characters gifts to 'make' them like you ala Dragon age: Origins) that prevents you from pleasing everyone increses my score from what would have been a 9.5/10 to an outright 10/10
Combat: Combat is greatly improved over KOTOR I's rather basic system. As you improve your combat feats, they don't just become more effective: they change visably as well, becoming more graceful, powerful, and masterful-looking all the time. 9.5/10
General overview: I probably should rate the game's overall sound quality, but i'm not very good at distinguishing good game audio from bad due to hearing issues. Sorry about that. Overall, i would rate this game a 9.5/10. Besides Battlefronts 1 and 2 and Star Wars Galaxies, KOTOR II is one of the best Star Wars experiences you will ever have (BE SURE to download the Restored Content mod, as it will unlock much of the content that Obsidian was forced to cut out due to LucasArts' unreasonably short Christmas Deadline).

Simply put, this is another game that tries to make 3D work in a new genre and fails: the 3D aspects add very few benefits and too many frustrations.
The visuals are colourful and fun, and the story is kinda wacky in an entertaining way that would maybe appeal to a 5-9 year old. But there is no voice acting for the younger children, and the puzzles are all over the place in terms of difficulty. There is just a lack of focus and thoughtfulness here that together with the bad 3D implementation contributes in making this an unpolished product.
So if you buy this for a child, expect to be the one using the mouse most of the time, and expect to be skipping many of the puzzles that will fly straight above their head. Also expect to be bored by its short loop of uninspired music that repeats ad nauseam. Personally, after screening this I'm putting it on the discard pile, there are many much better games for children out there.

This is a difficult game to review. On one hand, there's no doubt in my mind Final Fantasy VI is one of the best JRPG's ever made. On the other hand, this particular version of Final Fantasy VI is... divisive.
Pros:
- Fantastic JRPG. Great story line, game mechanics, fantastic soundtrack, etc.
- All the extra bonus content and bug fixes from the GBA version, which makes the game mechanics far better than the old (SNES/PS1) versions
- While the battle interface is very different from the SNES/PS1/GBA versions, once you get used to it it's actually very smooth, and is arguably even better than the traditional interface.
- Runs at a smooth 60fps most of the time, which is not common inPC Final Fantasy games.
- Redesigned Cyan Swdtech/Bushido so he's not completely worthless now
Cons:
- Visuals are... divisive, to say the least. I preferred the original visuals, and so do most people. It's not all bad, (the battle backgrounds are quite nice) but its mostly bad.
- Significant input latency when walking around on the overworld, towns, and dungeons. Weirdly enough, the battle interface is not affected, everything is very responsive there, with the exception of inputs for Sabin's blitzes.
- 3D sections (on chocobos and airships) run at 30fps, but most importantly, at half speed, which is kind of annoying.
Unfortunately, there is no definitive version of Final Fantasy 6. The SNES version looks and runs great, but has tons of bugs and a terrible translation. It's also stupidly expensive. The PS1 version fixes a few of these things, but has a pretty bad problem with load times. The GBA version features a ton of improvements: no load times, new content, several bug fixes and a new translation, but it has weak music, a bad color palette and performance issues in battles. This Steam version is effectively the GBA version with ugly redrawn graphics and input lag, but it fixes the other problems the GBA version had.
So it's all just a series of tradeoffs. I like this version the best, but I can't deny that it could be a lot better. Maybe someday Square Enix will release a definitive version of Final Fantasy VI that everyone can unanimously agree is the best. For the time being, this will do. You could do a lot worse with your 16$.

Arma III is one of my all-time favourite games.
If you like messing around with military hardware, doing special-ops missions with snipers and helicopters and magic earthquake machines, working with friends to capture a village or perhaps in a 60-strong platoon to capture a country then you should buy this game.
There are also a huge amount of awesome mods, from ones that add vehicles, tanks and planes from all the world's militaries to ones that add customisable beards or tactical bananas.
However, there are a few issues:
The physics engine is highly unpredictable. KSP-level. This will never be fixed. However, if you are carful and take care to avoid any obstacles (especially campfires) then it shouldn't be an issue. Jets also fly like spaceships, but that is kind of necessarry due to the map sizes.
You will need a fairly beefy PC if you want to put the view distance past 3 Km. If you're on a server with 60 other players you should also not expect above 30 fps.
Bohemia Interactive continues the tradition of desync, the effect whereby a vehicle or player suddenly stops or zooms forward wlist moving. It sucks, and it's not going to be fixed. But with staggered vehicle formations and communication it can usually be worked around, however it is very unlikely that you will ever see a jet fly smoothly across the sky.
The learning curve is pretty steep, the controls can be clunky at times and you will continue to discover new controls until your hours played get into the hundreds, but with patience and persistance it won't be much of an issue.

Ummm okay... so, first Steam review...
This game, uh, it's okay. I'm not gonna lie... I spent at least thirty minutes trying to figure out how to get out of the first room. And I'm not at all past that. By the time I figured out what to, 30 minutes had gone by.

In a way, it brought me back to a time when games just had no instruction, and expected you get instructions from the manual. But at the same time, it was a little uncool having to figure out how a major gameplay element works (I still haven't figured it out, but I only just got the game). To relate this to other games that this game tries to relate to, it would be similar to learning how to open portals in Portal 1/2 but not being taught how to fling yourself. I only figured out shooting at the floor because I tried to quit the game.
I'm recommending this game because I like everything about it so far, but want to warn other players that it will be confusing.

Small Spoiler Warning!:
The Good: The concept of the game is really fun. It's similar to games like Portal, yet still unique. The game didn't hold your hand. You were told the basic controls and nothing else. Figuring out that you had to shoot a beam at the floor to create a "time portal" in order to beat the puzzles was very rewarding. I got really excited when I found that out the first time. The puzzles were quirky and fun to figure out as well. I particularly liked one where I had to rewind time to shoot a switch long enough for me to make a jump and one where I found out there was a time limit to being behind a certain door. Also, the Dubstep music was a perfect fit and pumped me up.
The Bad: The lag made this game unplayable. (I'd like to add that I have a computer that should easily be able to handle this game.) Whenever you placed a portal, it would lag the entire game for a few seconds. It also lagged when shooting, jumping, and doing anything whatsoever. I finally gave up on the game on the first, time-slowing, level I wasn't able to beat it because the game kept lagging when I shot the switches, meaning i fell down because it didn't keep the platform up. If that wasn't bad enough, there were some visual glitches as well. I was on the self-same level, standing on a platform and waiting for my "alternate-time me" to start shooting the next switch. The platform I was on then switched to it's "off" graphic despite it being on, making me jump too early. It also did the opposite where the other platform was on, yet didn't give me the graphic so I didn't know to jump.
My Rating: [2 out of 5] I would sit on this game until the developer decides to fix these issues. If they were fixed, this would be a solid game that I would love to play. I had a lot of fun, despite the lag, until it made the game unplayable. Hopefully I'll be able to come back to it.
