This is a surprisingly fun game, I say surprising as my initial reaction was a little lukewarm but the more I played the more the overall charm of the game won me over.
You play Parin a spunky young girl who has come to stay with her grandfather while her parents are away. It quickly becomes apparent that there isn't much to do in the mining town where he lives, but Parin is soon sucked into an adventure to rescue a group of friendly monsters. The game is fairly light plotwise but its enough to drive things forward and the dialogue is often funny.
The games real draw is the action packed game play that requires good use of your drill and special moves to beat the crap out of a variety of foes. It features an interesting critical hit system that is linked to the games music, get the timing right and you will do extra damage. There are also some light platforming and puzzle solving elements. This is an update of an older game and it shows in the textures which are sometimes muddy and lack detail, overall though the art design is very good and Parin herself is well animated with a variety of expressions and idle animations that bring her to life.
Bear with the slightly rough start and you will be rewarded with a game that is deeper than it first appears.

OTC has very interesting gameplay, not just in the respect that hey, you're makin' money, but that you are actively participating in the offworld markets. These offworld markets being Earth's satellites like asteroid colonies and Mars colonies. You must set down your company's HQ in a spot close to useful resources, and even those will change based on what company you are playing as. Robots don't require life support, but humans obviously do.
In the world of competitive marketing, you must produce and maintain enough resources to play the economy. Various resources will become highly demanded for, you in turn must produce more of these in order to satisfy that market. But be careful. Don't produce resources that no one needs.
On top of selling these resources, you must produce some for your own good. Upgrades and new buildings require resources as well. Expanding can't be done without it. Mine silicone, carbon, pump water, electrolize hydrogen and air, and the list goes on.
Gameplay of OTC can change based on who you are playing as. Previously I noted life support, robotic companies don't require and humans do, well, if you're a robot, save operating costs and don't build electrolizers. Other companies can build things differently than others. New Meridians are very science based people and have developed technology that can manufacture resources directly on top of a resource deposit versus having a mine yank it out and send it to the HQ.
Overall, the game whether on a public stage or offline with the AI can be very competitive.
There are multiple systems in OTC. The most important one being the resource market. Selling resources like O2 and Food usually turn a large profit for manufacturing companies. But also, there is debt. Should you worry about it? In my experience, not exactly, as when you start makin' the offworld shipments you can make so much profit that the debt will literally eviscerate.
The black market is also very important. Corporations may seem very up tight and concerned about making a profit and caring for their customers, but when it comes down to corporation versus corporation, dirty deeds will be done. EMPs and electrical storms can take out production rates, goon squads will protect your stuff from thieving corporations, and worker strikes can turn manufacturing plants to your favor. But be careful, you aren't the only one that can use the black market.
Shares. The game winner. Without shares, you don't win...well, you don't lose either but more importantly you don't win. Shares in your own company will protect you, along with how much one of your shares is worth. invest in your company and increase production and your worth will rise. Buy competitor shares and keep them on their toes. Then, once you buy enough shares, buy out the company, buy out the company and you have one less competitor.

This is a beautiful game with a stirring atmosphere and mood. A puzzle-platformer at it's core, it is immersive enough to make you forget that you're solving puzzles or dodging strange other-wordly creatures but feels more like a story that you're enjoying and experiencing.
I don't play many puzzle games and I still loved it so don't overlook this game because of the puzzle factor! I found the puzzles to be just right - they were sufficiently rewarding and never too frustrating to solve. The platforming is pretty straight forward and enhanced by some of the unique abilities the protagonist acquires (eg: being able to shoot a sticky-mud thing onto walls to cling onto or shooting bouncy grass or ice to reach sections otherwise inaccessible. There's some nice creativity at the core of this game.
Once you complete the main story (arguably not quite a 'story' in the traditional sense but still immensely enjoyable...) you unlock a harder version of the game - same areas with more complex puzzles. These, I safely avoided due to my aforetold indifference to hardcore puzzle games but that does add good replay value and may strike a chord with the puzzler in you.
In all - this is an excellent Indie title. You can even try the demo from the developer's website I believe if you're on the fence.
PS: IIRC I spent more than the 3.5 hours reported by Steam on this game (probably spent offline) but in any case this is a short game without any doubt, so bear that in mind.

A good game of stealth, fun and simple.
(or OGAT as its commonly referred) is a multiplayer 3rd person shooter stealth game developed and published by Subvert Games in which high-powered guards face off against fast and elusive thieves in a contest of wits.
This game seems as inspired by saga
infiltration mechanics as it is
camera view and
character classes and art design.
The gameplay seems very fluid and responsive. Ofc, it may depend on the server, but overall it's very good.
- you can choose which side to play, Guards, Thieves, Zombies, Survivors, National Army, Terrorist and more. Each with its own equipment and gameplay peculiarity.
- you can choose your class between 8 available for each faction, discover the different abilities, weapons, statistics and useful gadgets.
You can customize your equipment, and play with different weapons and gadgets combinations. There are different arsenals available for each class and faction.
The game features the following modes:
Thieves have to steal an object on the map by using discretion (hiding in the shadows), a knife that kills with one blow (they have infrared vision) and Guards must prevent that from happening by using guns.
Zombies have to eat a “Big Brain” hidden on the map, Survivors must prevent that from happening by using guns, too.
There’s a couple of variances from those, like defusing bombs, but the structure remains the same.
The matches usually last 5 minutes max, and it’s incredibly fun. One of the strongest sides is how you develop tactics with your team without the need to chat – just by moving to certain places or performing specific actions. There’s also a RPG component though it’s unclear yet what are the benefits from it, because I leveled up my character to L4 but there was no actual impact on gameplay.
The only down-side so far is the limited amount of maps, but that’s completely normal considering they’re still developing the game.

SOMA is a pleasant surprise for the survival horror genre.  This game has excellent atmosphere, constructed with well-placed musical ensembles, sound effects, visual artifacts, and immersive voice acting.  However, what helps drive a first person survival horror like this is plot.  SOMA's plot is a psychological roller coaster ride.  From the very beginning, the game offers you choices.  The consequences of your actions are unknown but the game forces you to choose.  The true consequence comes when you find yourself wondering if what you did was the right thing.  Did you just shut off a machine or did you commit murder?  The plot is expanded upon as you discover sound bites of those who were here before you and e-mails (in the same way Doom 3 worked).
In Summary, this is an excellent game with about 10 to 15 hours of game time.  You constantly have an eerie feeling alongside the perplexing motif of questioning your own reality.  9/10

A detailed review to put aside the confusion and misinformation you may see in other reviews, including many of the negative ones.
Firstly, this game gives the impression it is a game not yet truly completed. They appear to be frequently updating the game and patching issues. The reason this is a good thing however, is this is a game already in a state workable enough to be a proper game, and as of yet I have only experienced minor connectivity issues for being on ♥♥♥♥♥♥ DSL internet. I'll be fixing that problem soon enough by getting broadband.
Secondly, this game is full release, not some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ 2-bit indie game on early access with a dead community and shady devs.
Now, let's get into the real meat of the game, the gameplay. It's worth saying up front this game may have a medieval setting but it's intended to be a sandbox RPG more akin to rust or minecraft rather than a survival combat game like DayZ, or a medieval combat game like mount and blade or chivalry. Most at least basically knowledged people understand this game is a life simulator and while there is a great deal of things you can do in the game it also means you need alot of time to do it. This is a hardcore game for hardcore, dedicated gamers to sink many hours of gameplay into.
The crafting system is complex, realistic, and in depth. Not limiting you to just crafting items and buildings, you can change the very shape of the earth itself in the game with the terraforming system. A bit awkward at times, especially when trying to flatten out ground, but the overall mechanics are very easy to use once you know where to get them. RIGHT CLICKING IN THIS GAME IS YOUR FRIEND TRUST ME
Survival is done by two things, health and eating. Your health comes back over time, and you can heal with medical equipment later on. Eating is easy, you can find apple trees, pick and eat apples. It's easy enough for the first several hours of gameplay I survived off apples until I could cook myself meat instead.
I have only played on RP servers, rather than dedicated PvP servers, but I can safely say that most of the community is smart as long as you play this realistically. Think realistically, RP as a man or woman in the middle ages, play smart, and you'll usually survive. You'll have a better time if you make or play with friends. This game was clearly meant to be played by groups of people working together. You can solo this, but it's putting yourself on hard mode for no reason if you do.
Now it's time for the Pros and Cons in my experience.
Pros
- Expansive and in depth crafting system, simple skill system to go with it.
- Hardcore survival with some servers being PK for characters you make.
- 64 player servers.
- Can run on ultra settings with 60fps relatively smoothly with minimal framerate drop, ultra settings do not kill the game's framerate, and I'm only running an i5 alienware basic.
- most of the community is friendly.
- Definitely meant to be a social experience, teamwork, and friends make the experience much better.
Cons.
- High learning curve.
- Not intended for "casuals" to be capable of remaining on the top.
- Can't be done very well without dedication.
- Not optimized to be played by solo players.
- AI animals in the game are horribly awful, completely dysfunctional, stupidly OP, and glitch into objects (running in place)

I... don't get it. This is supposed to be one of the greatest horror games of all time? Did I go into it with too high expectations? Did playing Frictional's other games first desensitize me?
My problems with Amnesia can be easily explained when you look at the second sentence on it's Steam page:
"A game about immersion, discovery and living through a nightmare."
Immersion. I had no issues immersing myself in Penumbra's universe. SOMA, despite having a very talkative protagonist, was still a relatable character, and I had no issues seeing myself in his shoes. Amnesia, however, is based around a very gimmicky sanity mechanic. It sounds like a good idea in theory, especially considering the Lovecraftian themes the game is touching on, but in practice it only served to break immersion. How am I supposed to find this world scary, or even take it seriously when the POV character is waaaaay more scared of the wind blowing open a door than I am? Not just scared, cowering in fear. Crawling and spasming on the ground over nothing and I'm just sitting here going... what the ♥♥♥♥, dude?
Discovery. SOMA had no lighting issues. Penumbra was very dark at places, but I never ran out of glowsticks or flashlight batteries. Amnesia, on the other hand? Not only is it much worse lit than Penumbra, but light sources are extremely scarce. How am I supposed to know anything about my environment, or discover anything, when I can't see a ♥♥♥♥ing thing? Not only that, but the game discourages you from spending time in the darkness. It increases your insanity. So here I am bumping between walls, trying to find my way out of a room while my character is having a panic attack because he is literally afraid of the dark?
Living through a nightmare. I'll give the game that. Playing this thing was a nightmare. Not a fun nightmare either. Not even a scary one. Just an underwhelming and thoroughly boring one.
No, I do not reccomend this game. Penumbra: Overture had a few problems but I loved every minute of it, Penumbra: Black Plague is a goddamned masterpiece. Penumbra: Requiem exists. SOMA is very, very good, as I mentioned in my review of it. Amnesia... is an extremely overhyped pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's got nothing on Frictional's other work.

It's a good, but flawed, horror game. I give it an 8/10.
Minor Game Mechanic Spoilers and Rant ahead:
Overall it's a good game but, like so many other things, a victim of its own hype. Its frequent attempts to scare me in the beginning actually kept me from becoming fully immersed in the atmosphere. Too many times early on I'd pick up a puzzle item and hear a spooky noise, or go down a corridor and hear a spooky noise, it felt like I was on the receiving end of Dr. Langeskov, The Tiger, and The Terribly Cursed Emerald: A Whirlwind Heist. Of course all this spookiness affects your sanity meter, so before I knew it I've gone from crystal clear sanity to "..." What happens when you run out of sanity? Game over right? Nah you just go to fetal position for ten seconds and recover some sanity. There will be some creepy effects with low sanity (as seen in other games) but since sanity swings so wildly it is hard to get a good gauge on it. The monsters, while undeniably creepy, just feel like roadblocks that, with a few exceptions, dismiss themselves after a minute letting you hunker down in a place and go fetch a drink.

Original Review:
It's.... really good!
As someone who seriously disliked Dead By Daylight, I was expecting another PG-13 L4D ripoff.  There are no "knocked down pick me up" states here.  If Jason catches you, you're ♥♥♥♥ing dead.  He's gonna bury his axe in your skull and twist.
The best you can hope for is to temporarily stun him and make a break for it, but that only buys you a scant few seconds.  Honestly one of the best strategies here seems to be to use your teammates as bait and make your move when Jason goes to pick them off.  This is a brilliant feeling as it conflicts with your innate desire to band together with other humans to survive.
There are bugs, and connection issues, and I'm not exactly sure whether the price tag is based on the amount of content available (hint : it doesn't seem like much)  or the Friday the 13th brand ( seems more likely!)  but overalll ...  if you are willing to excuse that stuff...... you'll have fun.
It's better than Dead by Daylight, anyway.   The killer actually kills people.

The controls: You walk smoothly and quickly as in Portal, though shooting the laser is a little jaggy (if that makes sense) as compared to Portal. Do you see that I refer a lot to portal in this section? That is because this game reminds me quiet a lot of that game, it wouldn't surprise me if this one was inspired by it. But don't be mistaken, Paradox Paradigm is completely different from that game and in a good way. Neutral:

Cons:

War movies should not be fun, they should be dramatic, even painful, as to respect the gravity of the situation/people invoved. Whereas action movies/games can be fun, because they generally focus around a caricatured protagonist who is the embodiment of some particular virtue.
This distinction would be what separates Medal of Honor from Call of Duty Modern Warfare 1-3.
If this game is a war game then yes. If this game is an action game then no. But that distinction can really only be made in the mind of the player.

I love Offworld Trading Company (OTC), it's the deep and modern non-military, economic strategy game we have all been waiting for!
Back in high school we had these business simulation games where you would take charge of a company producing good X, in competition with similar companies.
You'd decide how to spend the funds available to you - how much you'd produce, advertise, research and invest in more production capacity.
Each round of the game would represent 3 months of doing business and you would make one decision per round.
After everyone submitted their decisions, the round would end, the simulation would calculate everyone's performance and luck, and quarterly reports would come in.
It was a peculiar sort of high to see that my company had done well and beaten others to market share and/or profits.
If you can relate to this, you will like OTC.
In OTC you take charge of one of four types of companies on Mars in competition with one to seven (depending on what kind of matchup you prefer) other companies.
In a single match that lasts roughly 30 minutes you decide on the location of you HQ (to where all your resources are shipped), which land hexes you claim and what you mine or produce to make more money than your competitors.
The company to seize control of all others (via buying more than 50% of their shares) wins.
While the overall goal of each game is clear and simple, the game's mechanics are many and varied, providing ever-shifting sub-goals, making each match a unique experience.

Considering these elements defines the initial minutes of a match.
As time progresses, companies upgrade their HQs to gain access to more land claims as well as bonuses like patents, Black Market goodies or extra claims.
Eventually companies consume and can produce so much as to completely dominate the market and influence profits and business strategies of others.
Sometimes denying profits for a competitor is better than making a profit for yourself.

This game is quite simply an incredible experience. SOMA brings to life an incredible, completely surreal world in which you play as the broken mind of Simon Jarrett; don't worry I won't spoil any of the story for you.
SOMA combines the awesome horror features that we've seen previously from Frictional Games in their highly successful horror game Amnesia, as well as a terrific storyline to keep the player thoroughly engaged throughout - I found myself itching to keep playing as the story unfolded. Rest assured, this game has plenty of scary and creepy moments and like most horrors, for best immersion it's best played alone and in the dark.
It's been in development since 2010 and uses the H.P. LoveCraft Engine 3, so the stunning visuals and complex narrative is no surprise - and I mean stunning visuals, it looks gorgeous. As far as the story is concerned, I won't spoil anything, but Frictional Games does a brilliant job in creating characters that you become emotionally attached to, and (possible minor spoiler):
but, moving on..
What differs this horror from the rest is that this game asks deep, moral and ethical questions about many things, mainly the perception of life, which is why I stress that this game is an entirely solo experience; you're forced to think about these things, and I think that it has the potential to really change a person's perspective on their own lives.
10/10 would recommend to anyone; incredible

Gurumin is an action RPG by Falcom featuring a young girl named Parin who must go on an adventure to save the monster world.  As Parin you will make many monster friends while being tasked with helping them fix their world by tracking down items in all sorts of interesting environments.  The story is heartwarming in a childlike way as both your monster friends and bad guys all have interesting personalities and the well written script and professional voice acting really helps bring them to life.  Along the way you will bash evil monsters with an array of combat moves that you can unlock with money you find in each level area.  The combat is a combination of joystick twirling and timed button pressing, nothing revolutionary but it works well.  There are also platforming elements that you will use to navigate the terrain and search for hidden treasure, healing items and head pieces (hats, ribbons, etc) that you can equip to power Parin up in different ways.    Graphically Gurumin is somewhat blocky and basic, but it’s very colorful and each area you explore is filled with interesting inhabitants that evolve as you explore further, helping to reduce the repetition that often accompanies action RPG’s.  Playing thru Gurumin is like exploring a new park as a child who has a vivid  imagination; discovering monsters, avoiding the lava and having a grand old time in an adventure that is light and fun with enough of a gaming challenge to feel satisfying.  Recommended for the young at heart, plays well with a game pad too.

When I remember kotor1, there are plenty of grey situations, such as the kolto planet where you need to investigate the jedi on trial, who isn't as innocent as he seems.
The problem here for me really boils down to the story, it feels so scattered and sparse. While I see the ambition, and potential this game had, it just really needed more time in development by its own developers.
The first mission opens up, and almost feels like a survival horror game -- everything very empty, a sense of loneliness. And I question whether or not this is intentional, as the level drags on forever.
This game seems to follow the main points of kotor1. Opening level -> main planet -> find ship -> go to some jedi council place to rediscover force -> 4 planets -> etc. But like I said, everything feels unfinished. While I applaud the game for trying to take the story in a different direction, they needed more time. Each of the planets feel empty by comparison, and the amount of "things" you can do at each location where there is something meaningful to do is lacking.
For example, you go to korriban in this game too. However here, you are dropped into the valley of the sith first. Except, all of the temples are blockd off. You just fight some enemies. Then you can go into the sith academy. Deserted, with some guys to fight. Very few story elements, then you do 1-2 things for the main story to progress the plot, and leave the planet.
While everything feels unpolished, it all came down to this for me: Was the story good and compelling?
Which is why you would want to play a kotor game this far after development, as KOTOR1 does hold up and I would recommend it.
I really do appreciate the various things they had in mind: good cast of characters, some good ideas with the story ... just nothing came out as finished, and as a result, the game feels empty, and unpolished... even with the restoration mod.
I would only recommend this if you have a lot of spare time, and recently finished kotor1 and really want more -- otherwise, just play kotor1 again.

FFVI otherwise known as Final Fantasy 3 for those in the west is certainly one of the better Final Fantasy games & lays claim to being one of the best classic JRPG's of all time. If you're already a fan of the series or the JRPG genre and haven't played this yet, it's almost required history at this point to understand a crucial turning point in gaming's evolution.
The game is mostly praised for it's scale, meaningful character narrative & pushing the envelope of what people thought was technically possible on a 16 bit machine.
However, we're not using 16 bit machines anymore and it's 22 years since it was originally released. So I feel it's fair to through some criticsm against the endless tirade of nostalgic, rose-tinted fanservice this title still receives to this day.
It is true that all the main playable characters have a story arc, though some are definitely more fleshed out (Cyan) than others (Gau). Compared to more modern games, even outside the JRPG genre, the story as a whole also feels incredibly rushed.
Core gameplay deviations introduced later on in the FF series are also notably absent.
True, some people hate them with a passion (blitzball & snowboarding come to mind), but the problem with this is that the extremely basic, menu based battle system very quickly feels stale, old & very dated by the end of the game.  It's a very obvious reasoning to why Square have deviated the remake of Final Fantasy 7 so drastically from how these games used to be & why every new JRPG has a gimmick of sorts to its own combat mechanic
Though it's unlikely that anyone who isn't already a fan of Final Fantasy is going to buy this game on a whim or so forth. As with most retro gaming, while still a fantastic title of the genre, it might not be all you remember it to be back the first time you played.

Bottom Line:
While this port of one of gaming's most beloved classics can be described as polarizing at best, what is presented here will cater well to younger fans new to classic JRPGs or old fans who enjoy subtle changes to formula to enhance an already engaging and well-engineered experience.
Disclaimer: This review focuses on changes to this edition. For a comprehensive review of FF6, you can find thousands on Google. :)
Justification for Opinion:
Final Fantasy VI is one of my top 5 favorite games, and I have played through the original SNES version and GBA port dozens of times over since their respective releases in 1994 and 2007 (the 1999 PS1 port is garbage). Being 13 when the game originally came out in 1994, I have many nostalgic memories tied to this game. The story, characters, music, and world in Final Fantasy VI helped me cope through a very rough adolescence when I needed an escape.
The Whoopla:
Final Fantasy VI is well remembered as the pinnacle of the classic 16-bit RPG, right alongside Chrono Trigger. The story, music, depth of gameplay, and amazing open world that presents itself after you think you've reached the end game still enthrall gamers to this day. It's no surprise that Final Fantasy VI is often ranked as the #1 best game in the franchise. And many, like myself, consistently place it in top 20 lists of the best games ever made. Like any classic piece of interactive entertainment that is remade, revised, or updated, fans new and old have their opinions on what should be left out, kept in, or remain unchanged.
From GBA to iPhone to Steam:
The Steam/Smartphone ports of Final Fantasy VI are based on the updated Gameboy Advance port from 2007. Along with a host of added features to even out some rough edges and unbalanced spots, Tose (who ported the game to GBA) added 4 new summons, new dungeons & bosses, retranslated the script, added some additonal dialogue to flesh out a few scenes, and added some goodies to cater to longtime fans. Having the original GBA port embedded in the source code for the Steam/Smartphone releases ensures that the experience that the user plays in the new engine is as close to its original source material as possible. Although, some changes were made in order to cater to a more modern crowd.
Visual Changes:
All sprites and maps have been updated with higher resolution assets and added color. However, the developer chose to apply a muddy soft filter that dithers the sharpness of the visuals. The highlights in the color and overall saturation are also noticeably washed out. While both of these blemishes can be fixed with two very simple mods (found in the Steam Discussion board), it is still disconcerting that the mod community had to step in (as usual) to fix what should have been caught in R&D. That being said, the overall presentation, post mod, is a rather pleasing update to the base sprite set.
All reused assets are about 1.5x larger than they were in the original SNES version. While some fans find this stylistic change off-putting, I find it enduring and am very much enjoying the richness in detail that went into the original sprite work I had never noticed before. The only completely redrawn assets I’ve noticed are the character sprites, the towns/castles in the world map (which are now made of polygons), and the battle backgrounds are now comprised of much higher detail and color depth. The overworld scrolls nicely while traveling on foot in the new engine. However, while riding a chocobo or flying the airships there is a noticeable amount of slowdown for some reason. While not game breaking by any means, it does disrupt the smooth presentation of the rest of the game. Other "Mode 7" sequences work very well and have FAR less pixelization than the SNES and GBA editions: example, traveling through Serpent Trench in Sabin's senario and the escape from the Magitek Facility.
Battle System Changes:
Perhaps the most polarizing change to this edition; the User Interface was left unchanged from the transition from Smartphone to Steam. This has deterred many fans from revisiting this masterpiece on PC. Here's the low-down: Instead of having a single, large window split between enemy names and a list of character names, hp/mp, and the active time bar for each character, each party member has their own individualized window indicated by an avatar of that character (this set up somewhat reminds me of the classic Genesis RPG series Phantasy Star). The character action window will slowly creep up and reveal more of the window/available actions the closer it gets to that character's turn. This simple mechanic works really well, eliminates some screen clutter by cleverly hiding the Active Time Bar without taking the mechanic away, and has some other bonus results.
Example: In order to access Cyan's Bushido skills In the original game, you had to wait until a progress bar filled up and reached the number of the particular Bushido attack you wished to use.  While the Bushido bar was filling up you were unable to control other characters, and the enemy could attack you during this time. With this new system you choose upfront which Bushido skill you want to use. Then, while the move charges just like it used to, you are now freed up to control the other party members. Cyan will then activate his Bushido technique when his charge is complete. This works just like magic spells that take longer to cast, and it seriously speeds up the flow of battle when Cyan is in your party.
Another welcome change is the magic menu. It is now separated by tabs that represent the 4 types of magic in the game for easy sorting: black, white, status, summon. Sabin's Blitz attack now has arrows for all directions that surround Sabin when he activates his skill. This is to ensure that you got the motions correct before you commit and end your turn. This is especailly helpful for people who are either using a keyboard or are unfamiliar with fighting game motions.
To all naysayers of the battle UI, I say just try it out. With Steam returns there is no reason not to give it a shot. It quickly won over this old jaded gamer, and hours into the game I'm still REALLY enjoying the new battle UI.
Sound Design Changes:
Final Fantasy VI's stunning soundtrack has never sounded better. These are the original SNES tunes, and from what I can tell they are running at a higher bit rate. This is compared to playing the game on SNES and over 5 SNES emulators on the same sound system. All sound effects seem to be in place and I have come across no differences in my recent play tests. As this port is pulling all source material, including sound cues, from the GBA rom embedded in the game's code, I doubt there is much missing. I have yet to complete the game on Steam so if I notice anything missing/off cue I will update this review.
Overall:
Does this port replace the SNES original? Of course not! However, these few updates make the game a bit more approachable to a new audience that may have missed the game the first time around, or have never played a classic Final Fantasy. Many younger gamers who were weened during the PS2 era and beyond often find it hard to revisit retro classics. It's impossible for younger generations to feel the same sense of wonder and amazement as those of us who got to experience these classics when they were cutting edge. Nostalgia can be a fickle thing, and the wonderful memories older gamers have tied to a particular experience are as individual as the games themselves. If older gamers approach this port with an open mind, I think they’ll find this edition an absolute joy to play. For those new to Final Fantasy VI, I say play this version first and then revisit the SNES original for reference.
No matter what edition you choose to play, Final Fantasy VI is a masterclass in game design and is an experience all should enjoy!

I've owned this game since Early Access and honestly my first impression of the game was that it had potential, despite the fact that to me you couldn't get an enjoyable experience out of it yet, I truly believed that  it would be amazing once it had gotten out of Early Access. What are my thoughts regarding the game now ? Well let me give you a hint and a bit of advice: AVOID THIS GAME AT ALL COST.
It has somewhat not changed at all since the last time I played it which was several months ago, my impression back then was that it still had a few years of development to go before it could be considered ''Finished'', I was shocked to see that it had exited early Access to the point the devs considered it completed so I gave it a go, and I was very disappointed. Let's start with the screenshots shown on the page which relates to the visual appeal to the game. Really, don't get fooled by the ''screenshots'' sure, they are very pretty and surely you must expect the same kind of visuals in the game, right ? Well, the game is pathetically ugly, please go watch an actual gameplay video rather than believe the dishonest screenshots. The environment can be way too bright, there is too much bloom, the models are disgusting, the textures are blurry, the effects are weird, the only appeal in terms of visuals in this game is the water, but the credit for that goes to the guys who built the engine and not the devs. The game hurts to look, it really does, not to mention that it does not allow you to change the FOV which is horrible in the game. One last note, the city is not as interesting as it appears in the screenshots, literally everything has been copy and pasted over and over, so you really can't tell if you're in a new part of the city unless you use your map.
Let's move on to mechanics... They're also as pathetic as how the game looks itself. The looting system is basic and lack luster, the animations are awkward, as awkward as the combat in fact which is also awfully slow unless someone gets involved with a gun, the enemies are annoying and are not fun to kill as you could expect they are, and the in-game store system is sad. I'm jut going to go into detail with the looting system and the in game store system because it's rather clear that they are tired together. It's very hard to fine good loot out of containers, at best you will find one of many, many gun parts, sometimes you will find other items such as pans or bandages which are both not significant, i still haven't figured out what to the with the pan or the salt i found but I presume that they're junk items to sell, also, the bandages are weak, they only restore 1/10 of your health. The reason why I think the weak looting system is tied in with the in game store is because I am convinced that the devs made the looting so pathetic just in order to push you to sink your money into the game so you get the actual decent loot through microtransactions. So in short, this game has adopted the same business model as the War Z or also known as Infection: Survivor Stories, which is depressing considered how the game already pushes you to initially spend 15$ on it, which is not at all worth it, the game is only worth getting if it goes F2P, and that's really just for you to see how pathetic it really is, you can't get any enjoyment out of it anyway. Also, there is NO way to communicate with players in the game, if there is, then i missed it and the game gave no indication whatsoever to what it is; What does this mean ? Well it means that most players will resort to KOS if they encounter each other because there is really no way of telling someone that you don't want to kill them but also there is barely any other way to interact with them, KOS is literally the only interesting thing you can do with other players, it's utterly pointless trying to do a friendly scavenger hunt with them because resources are SO scarce that you'd end up fighting over the loot anyway, to the death.
There is also little to no story at all in this ''game'' (it's as much of a game as those slot machines, it's just there to take your money and think you have a chance to get anything good out of it), the game desperatly attempts to give scarce information over what happened or experiences your character has had (by analysing scenery your character gives dialogue), instead it just has the generic backstory of '♥♥♥♥♥♥went down, monsters appeared, people died and now city is dead'', none of it is interesting enough to get you to care.
So let's all sum this up: The game is ugly, the screenshots are deceiving; Combat is slow and awkward as are the animations; Loot is scarce, lackluster, and bland just so you are pushed to spending more money for microtransactions; no way to interact with players besides for mindless killing; There is little to no story at all, there is nothing to keep you interested in the world. Please dear god don't even consider buying this, I so badly hoped that this would become both good and big, but it just ended up being a disgusting cash grab on the side of the devs.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent has earned it's spot as the gold standard for horror games. It masturfully creates tension and suspense like no other game can. For those who don't know, Amnesia: The Dark Descent is set in a Victorian-era castle. You wake up having, of course, amnesia. The story unfolds through letters you wrote to yourself and letters you find scattered throughout the castle. I won't spoil the story or the backstory that got you there but it is incredibly well written and acted. The suspense of the story only hightens the real danger in the castle too. The monsters are terrifying and the hightened suspense at times made me truly horrified. The soundtrack kept me on edge too and is very well made. In addition to running away from monsters, there is also a good deal of puzzle solving. It's the kind of puzzles that make you think and make you feel good when you figure them out, but not the impossibly hard ones that usually need a walkthrough to solve, which is a good balance. Overall, this game is near flawless, and a must-have for any fan of horror. However, there is one thing I realized that did hinder the expierience a little bit. It is immersion breaking, so only read this after you beat the game.

I remember reading a review of SOMA, blabbering on about its philosophical genius and how it downplays the horror of gameplay for the horror of an existential crisis. I don't remember being impressed. "Great, it's a damn walking simulator," I thought to myself, with a sneer and a judgmental eye roll. "Well, Amnesia was great, and I've been following this stupid thing from that first trailer and loved the environment design they were going for, so screw it, some horror is better than no horror."
Look, you didn't give me a choice, game. I need to progress through your damned story, I needed to do it to get to the next section, and besides, she was a robot anyway.
"Oh great, start me off in a real life setting and then flip the switch, huh game?" I thought, mere minutes after clicking New Game. "Might as well just tell me it's all a fever dream, real insightful, namedrop that girl who died in the car crash every five minutes throughout the game, tell me about how it was all my fault, really cute. Truly a masterpiece of philosophical insight."
He was a robot, you read the schematics, it clearly stated his build was just a helper drone, designed to assist humans in their needs, so if I needed the chip from him, he's just filling a need, right? I didn't kill him... it, it was never alive.
First monster encounter: Meh, Mr. Stompy talks a big game, but stealthing around him is eas...♥♥♥♥♥♥ forgot to turn off the steam from downstairs... and he's on his way upstairs... ♥♥♥♥.
The words, they keep coming back. They feel etched into the depths of my brain.
Here's the thing, the metaphysical "universe as a simulation" narrative has been done plenty of times in plenty of mediums... but having it in the form of a video game (an incredibly immersive video game, mind you) makes this something truly special. At some point, your eyes will drift from the game to the edge of the screen, trace their way around a dimly lit room, and you will look back at the game... it doesn't have to ask the questions, the way a science fiction novel or movie would, never bold facedly proclaims "What's the difference between man and machine?" or "Is the world you live in truly real?" It just sticks you in the world, and you ask the questions, and they echo back at you from the howling abyss that is existence.
"He's just a robot."

This is a single player review only ( for what should be only a multi-player game)
Have you ever wondered what it would be like to start a life in the middle ages from scratch as a normal person? The answer to this question is.......it's a grind. An unbelievable, mind numbingly slow, boring, repetitive grind. This is though probably what life was like for Joe Bloggs average peasant 1000 years ago - you work hard, got nowhere then you died (of boredom).
The problem for LIF:YO is it's not realistic enough to be a true medieval simulation (thank the gods) but it is realistic enough to be an abhorrent experience as a game.
So a few good points:
1. Stable, smooth, good FPS even on high settings, no stutters, no CTDs (I have an intel i7 quad core, 8GB RAM and a GTX860M)
2. The character generation, while somewhat limited with your options provides a SUPER looking (and sometimes grotesque) character to play that also looks quite good in the game world.
3. The building models - all of them - everything I built looks top notch, building material textures are well represented, your first house is a hovel and it really looks the part - it almost smells rotten to look at, wooden fences are rough rickety constructions that look like they will fall over in a strong wind just as you would expect as they were built by an untrained pleb using the most base of tools. I found this part of the game faultless.
4. Placement system for the things you build is simple, efficient and intuitively easy to use.
5. Skill and stat development is based on doing related stuff rather than just gaining exerience points then allocating skills. Want to improve your strength and become a good miner - shovel dirt around, LOTS of dirt and your strength goes up. Your intellect does nothing, but you get stronger.
6. The number of 'workbenches' you have is enormous compared to many other games - LIF has furnaces, kilns, fires, drying racks, carpenter's benches, mortar & pestle, quern stones, beehives etc etc etc....dozens and dozens of things that each has a specialised use.
7. The skill list and learnable 'technologies' is extensive and VERY rewarding when you actually gain access to some key workbench or process . The problem is the suicidal thoughts you are having from all the grinding you did to acquire that access and the knowledge you must grind a lot more to get access to the resource to put in that new bench.
Now for the bad, and these are just a few typical issues:
1.  Grind, grind, grind and then GRIND some more. It is truly unbelievable how bad the grinding is. I played with my development and speed settings at absolute max and after 25 hrs I have just learned how to operate a kiln and furnace...but I am still a ways off from producing my first iron nail ( I can't even identify iron ore yet) of which I need 45 to build a beehive. I haven't discovered bees yet though so  not sure what to do with an empty beehive!? I also still have no storage containers as they are far to technically advanced for me (it's the nails again you see...). An example of the grind is branches, a common resource available from every tree. After 20 hours or so you will have an idea of how to build a wicker fence of branches...you need 10...to get those 10 branches will take you about 1 minute of doing the repetivite 'harvest' action in front of a tree. You can tell your character to 'mass produce' so he/she will harvest branches from this tree until there are none left to take...super.....but you, the human, must sit in your chair and wait for 1 minute because your character cannot multi-task. Rinse repeat for everything. Some things are worse than others - searching for seeds to farm may require 5-6 minutes of rummaging in grassy map tiles to produce ... nothing ... while you the player just sit and wait. If I 'mass produce' plant fibers from a tile (the character will gather fibers until he/she runs out of stamina) I literally have time to go to the kitchen, make a coffee and come back with a few seconds to spare before my character finishes with an underwhelming 15-20 fibers.
GRIND-this is the game's dominant feature.
2. The interface is somewhat clunky requiring endless button pushing to access benches and regain control of the camera. The worst of the UI has to be the inventory though which doesn't use a slot system (pleasantly refreshing) however it means your big bag of stuff actually looks like a big bag of stuff full of different things - a confusing mess with things overlapping and sitting on top of other thing so you can't actually see what you've got, add to this the fact that things often don't auto stack(because quality differs) means it is a grind to manage it. You have to manually stack things together, manually move them around your bag so you can see what it is and trying to move a tiny item icon often results in you moving the inventroy pop-up window rather than the item you are trying to click on. Realistic but not fun.
3. Building anything requires the proper tool and starts with 5-10 second building animation that lays the 'foundation frame' of whatever you want to build. Super. This animation plays even if you don't have the right tool equipped, after which you are told you don't have the right tool, must equip the tool and then sit through the animation again. Do this several hundred times and your will to live fades.
4. The general learning curve is steep and requires great detailed information (eg . what temperature does your kiln need to be to fire clay roof tiles?) - you will spend an inordinate amount of time in the Wiki or searching for answers in Steam discussion threads for info that should be included in a pop-up for produced items.
5. The game world is not great. It's a small (3kmx3km) map - that's ok in SP, you will spend all your time grinding in your immediate vicinity anyway. The map only has a couple of biomes - shorelines of beaches and lakes, flat sandy places, fine. There is a mountain, unremarkable, but again fine. Then there is forest - 90% of the map is forest with a few clearings and lots of rolling hills. It's a nice enough forest but certainly doesn't have a wow factor when you see it or walk through it. It is incredibly uniform to walk through - some parts are dominated by oak trees, some by elm, some has apple trees mixed in or pines or mulberries - a reasonable variety of trees that somehow all blur together to give you the feeling that this part of the map looks, sounds and feels exactly the same as that other part of the map I walked through 5 minutes ago which was the same as the forest on the other side of the island.
6. Enviromental danger is pretty much zero unless you tread on a wild boar. There are no hostile NPC's anywhere aside from extremely rare boars, wolves and bears which don't move around much. You don't need water to live, food is abundant (you can just eat apples forever as far as I know without health issues), the weather and temperature are inconsequential. There is no sense of threat, danger or urgency, just the ever present call of the grind.
7. It does some quirky frustrating things. I rage quit yesterday after spending 2 real world hours firing clay tiles in a kiln. I suddenly had a 'remove item' button appear on the kiln as one group of tiles looked like it was almost done - it was hard to see as the progress bar is miniscule - but they were still labelled as unfired clay tiles....take them out and have a look I thought. Nope, still unfired clay tiles in my inventory. Oh well, nearly finished...back in the kiln they go. Progress bar resets to zero meaning they have to be fired again for another 2+ real world hours.
The negative list is longer, perhaps much of it can and will be addressed as EA progresses -but at the end of the day it's the grind. The game centres on and is built around grind. The kind of grind you come to mind because it forces you, the human, to sit and wait and wait and wait to accomplish.......squat.

I was really worried after playing A Machine For Pigs, but Frictional delivered with SOMA.
It isn't quite the same; it isn't Amnesia in Space. It's a little more story focused, and there's definitely lighter gameplay mechanics (no inventory management or lamp fuel / flashlight batteries), but I wasn't annoyed because there was still enough stuff for me to DO in the game.
You'll trek from one end of a facility to the other in search of some sci-fi macguffin all the while sneaking around a monster that will do unspeakable things to you. Every monster was great in its own way, mostly due to Frictional's best sound design to date. They all have a certain caveat to them that makes each encounter fun. I've heard some complaints about the monster AI being bad,  but I guess I played in a way that didn't reveal their flaws as much.
SOMA paces itself a little more than The Dark Descent, with peaks of horror and valleys of exploration and story exposition. The story and setting is ridiculously 70s/80s sci-fi, it's great. One of the things about the story... you know "meaningful choices"? That buzzword that companies like BioWare and Telltale like to use? SOMA is the only game that I've played that actually has them.
You are put in situations where you must make choices through actual gameplay, not conversation options. The game never judges you for them, it doesn't really care what you do. It only asks "how do you feel about yourself?" There are very few "correct" choices and there was never a choice that I made that I didn't feel conflicted about.
SOMA is really good. And, I would recommend it to any fan of science fiction.

Frictional Games' formula for its games has gotten a bit stale. I realized this when I was gifted SOMA by a very good friend of mine from work, and I was excited because I was going into it completely blind, knowing absolutely nothing about it! Oooh, what kind of fun, dark♥♥♥♥♥♥are we going to get into today? Space monsters? Computer monsters? Space computer monsters ON THE MOON? But then I immediately thought the space computer monsters on the moon and I thought "Oh, God dammit, I'm gonna have to do the thing where I hide in shadows and wait for the space computer monsters to shuffle by, aren't I?"
Don't get me wrong, SOMA is pretty damn cool and I enjoyed it in SPITE of the tired monster sections and the not-ready-for-prime-time game engine. I like all the little tricks it does to add flavor to the story and underline its themes of consciousness and existence and whether the computer you or the flesh and blood you is actually the real you. I like that it's going out there to do some hard sci-fi (the kind of sci-fi that idiot nerds hold over the heads of liberal arts majors and scream OUR GUYS CAN WRITE TOO YOU'RE NOT RELEVANT GET A JOB HIPPIE LALALALALALALA) and is not afraid to create a hell of a downer where it's most needed. It partially tells its story in ways I'm not a fan of (audio logs bolted to one spot on the wall is a practice I would like developers to stop using, thanks), but I think it does a fine job telling its story overall!
That being said, I had to actually work to finish SOMA, and that was because of the constant problems with the game engine itself. The game itself is 20 gigs large, and if you don't have a solid state drive, prepare for two minute load times! But even with an SSD, the game takes a little longer than I'd like. I also had problems where the game would crash to desktop - a menace even more terrifying than the monsters themselves, because while I can just throw a heavy object in one direction of a hallway and run the ♥♥♥♥ in the other direction, the crash-to-desktop monster is a one-hit kill invisible monster that pops up whenever the game needs to load a new section, and that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ kept breathing down my neck! So a partial amount of my time with SOMA was performing rituals and doing raindances just to pray that the thing wouldn't crash and take my progress in the scary stealthy sections away from me.
But the thing that concerned me most of all is Frictional Games' insistence on sticking to what they know, even if it doesn't really quite mesh with what was going on. I felt that the hard sci-fi stuff was really strong material, and that it didn't really need the horror stuff. I mean, yeah, corrupt AI making weird reanimated soldiers is always cool, but what Frictional Games was working with was already some next level stuff. It didn't need an ur-SHODAN to liven things up! Just stick to the Philip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥inspired nightmares, there's plenty to mine from that! But I guess if we don't want to hear the throngs of people whining about how THIS IS JUST A WALKING SIMULATOR BUT UNDER THE SEA, we've got to have the same old stealth elements and the same old monster elements just to shut those people up.
So while Frictional's latest really does have its flaws this time around, it's still a solid storytelling experience. And if you are good at distracting idiot monsters, the stealth sections become something else. Like Hotline Miami, but instead of killing the monsters, you run past them to the exit, yelling "YOU GOT JUST MINDFREAKED, YOU STUPID REANIMATED CORPSE."

This is probably the most counterintuitive, addicting game I've ever had the chance to play. It's probably due to the amazing community I've found in the server I play in, because without the Wikia this game is nearly impossible.
It's basically a life simulator. You spawn with nothing but your clothes and a piece of bread in your inventory and you climb the ladder from there. You learn as you go, gaining new skills as you work to build your refuge that could, with some effort, turn into a walled city. The PVE is fun and gratifying, frustrating at times but when you finally cut that last three and saw that last building log and see your house or warehouse or blacksmith workshop rise, it's great. The PVP is tough to master but it can be done.
One good thing is that it runs smoothly even on older computers. It's a light-weight game, but it gets the job done very well, it's quite pleasing to the eye, expecially in spring and summer.

Nihilumbra is a pretty game devoid of any actual substance, which is quite ironic when you think about the message this game is trying to convey. If you're looking for a deeply meaningful and complex puzzle game, look elsewhere. The puzzles in the main game are mindless and unfulfilling, barely branching out from their basic mechanics. In "void" mode (Nihil's version of New Game +), the difficulty of the puzzles aren't scaled; the game simply becomes a platformer-hybrid contingent on split-second timing and quick reflexes. Even with the challenges this mode presents, completing stages offer no satisfaction aside from what little can be had with the absence of the narrator.
What's left after the gameplay has been stripped away is a watered-down philosophy 101 lesson told by some guy who sounds like he hates his life. The writing is awful; throughout the game, the narrator beats you over the head with how your poor little guy is feeling (spoilers: not good), but instead of creating an emotional rapport with the character, it's just meaningless drivel.
Tl;dr: pretty graphics alone don't make a game, and the sophmoric narrator ruins the game.

The game is a very cute Action RPG. It starts off with a girl (you) moving into her grandfathers house in a new city. Whilst exploring you find out there are no other kids in town which is conveniany cause you meet some new friends which call themselves monsters and they can only be seen by children. You get invited to check out their little monster town which soon afterwards gets attacked and you must now stop the dark mist from engulfing the world. You do this by getting their ancient drill weapon which no one has ever been able to pull out of the stone until now.
All in all it's an unoriginal story, but it makes up for it with fun gameplay mechanics and a cute art style.
The only issue however is the camera. You don't control it directly instead it "tries" to circle around you when it needs to. Which can cause some trouble, but you quickly get used to it and figure out how it works.
If you enjoyed classic PS2/Xbox era Cute Action RPG's you will probably find some fun with this game as well. Though I would recommend checking out some gameplay videos before hand to see what I meant by the camera to see if it's something you can handle.

Admit it: the RPG genre had a formula. Start weak. Grow strong. Grow godly strong for some reason, as if it made sense. Did the world-building and story-telling always back up this formula? In my opinion, no.
But then there's Star Wars, and its conveniently mysterious "force." What an opportunity for an RPG! The first KOTOR was a standard RPG with a classic plot twist. It was a phenomenal game in the traditional sense.
KOTOR II takes the RPG formula and turns it into an ethical dilemma on its own. The majority of the game dances around this theme. It paints no one who grows in power as much of a hero, but exposes them as a threat. Personally, I applaud this direction, despite the game's tone overall suffering from a depressing feeling.
Be warned, KOTOR II isn't much of a happy game. It's a mature, thought-provoking game. It's a rare game that tells the real story of its own mechanics. You're getting stronger. But at what cost?

Ahead: I personally do not find this game to my taste. It's just not the genre i like.
On the surface it looks like a base building sim. However, as the legendary Diablo review by ActionButton showed eloquently, sometimes what looks like a game of chess can actually be a round of Street Fighter.
OTC is like that. It may look like a base building sim, but it only looks like that insomuch Street Fighter looks like a Jump'n Run.
Important things that differentiate it from classical base building sims: The amount of buildings you can build is highly limited. I think somewhere around 20 total. You're not expected to build a huge base and never remove any of it, in fact, you're supposed to keep changing and modifying your base to meet the market's needs for the 13 resources. Just like in combat, standing still means death. There's also very little to do on the base level other than building/bulldozing producers and upgrading your HQ. All the interaction between the bits of your base are automated.
In short: The base is only your gamepad with which you engage on the actual battleground, which is one that is extremely high speed.
The actual battleground consists of selling resources when prices are high, producing or buying when they are low, managing whatever debt you have, in order to make enough money to use super abilities to disrupt enemy activities to drive them into ruin, or straight-up buy them out on the stock market.
The speed of all of the above is increased by prices (resources/stock) reacting immediately to any action taken by any player in a match. If you react a split second too late, your huge pile of electronic chips may be worthless because your opponent dumped theirs first.
This is not a game of base building.
This is a game of high frequency trading simplified to human scales.

Friday the 13th is a great take on the asymmetrical horror game experience but it definitely has its issues.
If you're looking for a game that's competitive, turn away now. Jason is made to be overpowered and you (if you're a survivor) are meant to die. If you can get past that- you're looking at a really fun game to play with your friends, or randoms online. The issues don't lie with the aesthetics, the theme or anything like that. The issues are 100% the gameplay, which unfortunately is its most important component. Luckily the issues don't ruin the game, in my opinion.
Unfortunately, the game feels clunky. Animations don't flow well together, yet look great on their own; not a huge issue but you'll be seeing these animations a lot. Combat is awful at times. Your weapons will either miss Jason when you're point blank in front of him swinging, or instantly stun him. Jason also has his issues, while he is supposed to be overpowered, he currently has a shift + grab combo that can instantly kill you unless you have a specific item in your inventory; it's fun to be chased by a killer, it isn't to be murdered and forced to spectate or leave the game. Aside from that there are also bugs dealing with the rag doll bodies, causing them to fly into the sky after being killed by Jason.
If you can get over the clunkiness and the weird bugs, go ahead and grab this game. It's great with friends, and with a good group online it's pretty damn fun too.

Once you finish picking out and characterizing your character, you’re thrown into the story in the Sengoku period. It turns out, you died before the game started and have been tasked to take care of other souls so they can move on from purgatory, or Arcanus Cella. At the same time, other souls are unable to reincarnate even though their business was taken care of. The only way to solve this is to run through dungeons to hopefully get closer to what is preventing souls from passing.
Before you go into the dungeons, there are preparations to attend to. This is exceedingly important as it can not be changed on the fly while you’re in dungeons. What’s unique about Cladun is the magic circle. The character you take control of, or the lord, will be able to change their weapons, armor, equipped magic/abilities, and the type of magic circle they will have. The one thing I do wish you could do in the dungeon, was change weapons as there are areas that require a specific weapon type. Such as in the beginning there are blocked areas that you need a hammer type weapon to get through. Magic/abilities dependant on what job the lord has, make sure you really want to change their job as it will reset you back to lvl 1 no matter what level you were (going from lvl 22 ninja to a lvl 12 samurai that you were before, you will revert back to a lvl 1 samurai) so be careful there. Not only are the type of abilities you unlock is based on your job, the magic circles you unlock is as well. As these magic circles will be based more around that job and what you might use rather than you might not. So if you find yourself wanting to use magic a lot, consider a job that is more inclined to having more mana.
Magic circles is basically the equivalent to having a party but at the same time not. There will be spaces around the lord that you can put other characters, or vassals, that will in turn have slots that will affect them and you. You can put artifacts in black slots the vassals have that can give you a boost of defense or attack, but it can take away 20% of their health. Or you can have a magic circle that will bind at least two vassals, so you have to somehow not have a low health vassal linked to a high health one as they will both die at the same time. Why is the health penalty important to the vassals? Well they are used as shields as you will not be hurt unless all vassals are dead. The magic circles are complicated, but if you know how to build strategies around them and their disadvantages, they can be a great advantage.
Once you’re ready, you’ll have 50 story dungeons to go through. All bite sized that does not take a lot of time to get through. Each dungeon contain an array of enemies and gates to unlock. Each gate will either require you to defeat the enemy (or enemies), flip switches, or press buttons to open them. A decent amount of the dungeons can actually be run through without attacking, but in the long run this will not help at all. The name of the game here is learn attack patterns, try to dodge or block if you can, and try to keep damage high. As there will be points where strong enemies will be a gatekeeper and that gate will be where the exit is. Though weirdly enough, you might actually have more trouble with regular enemies than the bosses. As the bosses are either so easy they’re weak, somehow kill themselves like what happened to me, or just be a group of regular enemies.
What I found that was really frustrating was the enemy sight. Early on you’re told that enemies will not start fighting you till you get into their line of sight, however they can see you through walls. If you’re on a particular tricky dungeon that requires you to virtually fight every enemy you come across, either because they deal a lot of damage to you or they need to be defeated to open a gate, enemies that you’re not ready for will suddenly attack. Chapter 6 was the worst, as the majority of the first dungeon enemies are ones that can do strong attacks from a distance. Traps that you can only see up close also litter the dungeons, which can either help or kill you. As it is a high chance you didn’t pick a job that lets you heal yourself, you will have to rely on heal traps. If you’re not paying attention, you can be hit with traps that can send arrows to you or light a small area with its effect. These traps can be a little frustrating since sometimes you don’t see them and die to them. Which will end you with half exp you earned and no loot to bring back. So either try and try again, change your magic circle, or grind it out till the monsters are trival based on your damage or your defense.
Once you finish the first chapter, you may see the start of after story content. In fact, a lot of after story content. If you want to get all of the achievements, there are a few that will take a long time such as leveling up to the max several times. From what the game itself gives you, once you finish a chapter an extra chapter is unlocked. These “EX” chapters serve as an extra challenge to players as well as giving you the challenge of saving a lord soul. There is also side quests, which you can do while the main story is going on, but there are quests that have to wait before you’re able to. Each quest has a specific chapter they have to be completed in, which can either be completed in any dungeon in that chapter or a specific dungeon, and can involve either killing a set amount of enemies, getting an item they drop, use a specific magic circle, or speedrun the dungeon. On top of this, there are three different types of Ran-geons, which are randomly generated dungeons that have 99 floors. Online play is also available if you have friends that also bought Cladun Returns, but I did not have a chance to try it out.
I found myself not caring for the story throughout my playthrough. It’s painfully obvious the story was not the focus of Cladun Returns, which is weird for a RPG. As long as you don’t care for a game that does not put focus on the story, this aspect will not bother you, but if you wanted a more story-centric game it will. Though, Cladun Returns does seem to focus on retaining the player longer. Giving a reason for players to level and re-level again as well as giving a lot of strategies players can try out. As long as you don’t care for grinding, this game would be good for you as well.
While I was playing Cladun Returns: This is Sengoku, I was in the constant state of liking it and not liking it. There were moments that I liked it but at the same time there were areas where it became frustrating. Cladun does bring in some interesting and unique aspects that I did overall enjoy and I do appreciate all the content they added to compensate for the story, though I do wish the story was able to hold its own. While it may be because I never played the previous Cladun games, is unknown, but this is an overall average rpg once you learn everything. If you find what Cladun offers interesting or you are a fan of previous Cladun games pick this installment up. Though I would personally wait for a discount.

This is *the* game for fans of the ClaDun series. If you liked x2 and the original, you will love this one.
The title is not just for show; many of the assets carried over from x2 have been redrawn or modified to fit the theme.
Edit: Notable New Features
Deathgeon - Ten floor dungeon where enemies start at high levels and difficult types/traps are common. Loss only occurs when you run out of time, not when you become KO'd. Supposedly you fight bosses from previous ClaDun installments on the final floor.
Mu-Geon - Technically not new, but it was not in ClaDun x2 and reappears in Returns with a caveat: Mu-Geons negate the effects of titles on equipment, artifacts, etc.
The Arena - A dungeon that consists solely of a circular arena. Kill a wave of mobs to access two chests, the exit, and a portal to the next floor. Each floor forces you through a random gate. Great for using classes or builds that would normally be bad at sustaining themselves in a standard Rangeon. Great source of titles, but really poor exp farm.
Ex Dungeons - Rearranged versions of the dungeons you played during the story. Generally more difficult but more rewarding. One unique recruitable character lives in each stage, so this is a great source of characters if you are feeling unimaginative and want some stock characters to round out your roster.
The Castle - Basically a universal, secondary Magic Circle. Each space requires a somewhat expensive stone piece. The rarer the piece, the more stats it gives and the less likely it is to recieve a disenchantment. You can pay a decent sum of gold to remove these debuffs and keep the stone or just remove a stone entirely.
Weapon Refinement - Weapons will get kill points the more you use them in dungeons. You can redeem these at the Blacksmith to attach weak titles in all four slots. You can use this system to quickly farm weak titles for your Armor and Shield.
Quests - Yes quests! These can range from visiting old story dungeons to kill new enemies that have spawned in them or clearing certain stages in a certain amount of time. They are repeatable with diminishing returns and give gold, items, and even fame.
I love the graphics style and the gameplay is pretty challenging too.

For those unfamiliar with NIS games, Cladun Returns fits their usual profile: it's a RPG second, grindathon and minmaxer's paradise first. The combat system and overall gameplay is deceptively simple. it's an action RPG vaguely similar to the Legend of Zelda series, where you control a character with a limited selection of abilities in a gridless battlefield filled with enemies and traps - most of the mind-numbing complexity comes from the insane amount of customization options and the Magic Circle system, which bolsters your main character's stats and abilities by using your other characters as something like equipment pieces. It's the same basic setup as previous entries in the Cladun series, but Cladun Returns packs in a lot of new extra features, such as additional randomly-generated dungeons, new weapon types, and new enemies. It's also a far more competent port than Cladun x2, its predecessor.
NIS games can typically be played by those not interested in endless grinds, because those features usually start up after you've already finished the game. Cladun Returns is no different, and the main campaign can be finished with only minimal detours and grinding. Unfortunately, the additions from Cladun x2 aren't very noticeable in the main campaign, and the storyline in x2 is far more complete and interesting than the plot in Returns, for those who aren't well-versed in the Sengoku era of Japan (not that the plot is the main draw of either game, of course). Due to that, it's difficult to recommend Cladun Returns above Cladun x2 to casual fans of the series.
Unfortunately, I can't recommend this above Cladun x2 to diehard fans of NIS games, numbercrunchers, or people looking for an endless grind either. The draw of the Cladun series is that the postgames transition to being intense roguelites all about slogging through randomly-generated 99-floor dungeons for loot and profit. Theoretically, the added dungeons, enemies, and customization features should make this a superior product to x2 in spite of its slightly weaker storyline - the main problem is the added content and especially the new customization features, which are often poorly playtested and sometimes downright gamebreaking.
(For example: one of the new enemy types, a giant multi-headed serpent based on Yamata no Orochi, appears in the third chapter of the main storyline - due to its wonky stat scaling you can barely scratch it, so the "best" way to fight it is to stand directly behind it so it whiffs with all of its attacks and plink it to death over the course of 4 minutes. A lot of the other new content is equally tedious, with many of the new enemies relying on lengthy invulnerability phases - the only new content that seemed to be worthwhile and fun were the new weapon types, and to some extent the new dungeon varieties.)
As far as the actual gamebreaking components go, the main culprits are the additions to the title system (which allows you to add prefixes to equipment to give yourself passive benefits). While titles in x2 typically gave useful bonuses but were almost never downright essential, some of the new titles introduced in Returns allow you to never trigger traps while walking on them (removing one of the biggest difficulties of the game), bring back all equipment earned from a dungeon run even if you get a Game Over (nullifying any real consequence for defeat), and increase all of your damage resistances to the point that you become completely immune to all attacks (nullifying every other challenge remaining).
Due to the fact that Cladun Returns allows you to add these titles to sufficiently powerful weapons through a new feature at the blacksmith shop, it's very easy to achieve effective immortality very early into the postgame if you know what you're doing, making any further grinding completely pointless. Given the entire premise of NIS games is endlessly grinding in the postgame to grow stronger, the title additions undercut the game's entire premise - why take 300 hours to boost your stats to absurd levels, when you can be handed total immortality in 30?
I love the Cladun series and I definitely enjoyed my time in Cladun Returns, so it's painful to give this game a review of Not Recommended. But as it stands, there's little reason to purchase this game over its (significantly cheaper) predecessor. Sometimes less is more.

Over and all, it's a really fun survival game that I can't stop playing.
