Cladun is a pretty hidden gem of a series, starting in the PSP made by Nippon Ichi (you may know them from their most popular games the Disgaea series) Cladun is an Action RPG with a pretty nice 8-bit pixel art, a combat system with tight controls and a HUMONGOUS depth that can make the more hardcore players feel interested. And Cladun Returns: This is Sengoku! is, at least on a technical level, the ultimate Cladun experience:

Like mentioned before, the game's aesthetic is that of 8-bit pixel art, i know what are you thinking, ANOTHER retro looking game, just stick with me, because Cladun uses the 8-bit's simplicity on it's advantage to allow the players to customize their characters literally from head to toes. You can create your own faces pixel-by-pixel with the editor, and also create your own weapons and armor to have your characters entirely like you want (you can even make hair with motion animations, also there's a ton of pre-made stuff you can base yourself on), also even without this aspect, the pixel  art of this game is rather pretty, with a nice vibrant color palette and many details.
Gameplay, like is said before, this is basically the ultimate Cladun experience, on a first look, the game looks pretty simple simple and straightforward, but eventually you realize there's so much to it: the way your characters level up makes you constantly swap between them and making you experience multiple playstyles, the magic circle is an awesome mechanic that can make you spend HOURS making amazing setups that will make you really powerful and in the game also presents two new weapon types: Shurikens which are basically a weaker, faster version of the bow, and the Sickles, wich are a longer range version of the spear (and a lot stronger IMO). The enemy variety is pretty large with approximately 60 different enemies, and each having 6 different colored version which defines their properties ( Yellow = unremarkable; Green = High ATK; White = High DEF; Blue = Inmune to Ice; Red = Inmune to Fire; Black = powerful in every aspect). Dungeons are also filled to the brim with traps, this can range from simple arrow traps to quake traps or even summoning invincible enemies, but all traps are neutral so you can exploit them and use them to your advantage to defeat enemies.
Overall Cladun has an amazing gameplay with fun mechanics and a ton of depth, heck, it even makes grinding fun!
Music: Another remarkable aspect of the series, the music! Cladun is in my opinion the best sounding series in all Nippon Ichi, with great tracks that can range from fast-paced rock to catchy Tango. Sengoku, being themed on feudal Japan, it has a clear traditional japanese focus on the music, but it still manages to make some real cool remixes out of this music style and some tracks out of the traditional japanese that sound just great (like the Arena theme), i personally think that Cladun 1 still has the best overall soundtrack, but Sengoku did an amazing job on it's own.
Story: To be honest, the story has been my biggest dissapointment with the game by far, it is a really poorly done and forgetable story. Now im not saying Cladun 1 and X2 had amazing stories, but at least they were enjoyable and interesting, and had a couple of memorable characters, here in Sengoku there is none of that, story cutsenes only happen at the start and the end of a chapter, so it barely feels like a story is going on. It does get a little bit better in the later chapters with some cutscenes during before and after bossfights, but still the story expects you to care about the characters when they are so forgetable and have so little screentime that i'ts really underwhelming. If you play games mostly for the plot, then for now i tell you to avoid this game like the plague.
Veredict: Well, i love Cladun as a whole personally but i understand 40 dollars can be quite the amount for a game that has such an indie vibe, even more if you are expecting an interesting story. But if you liked Cladun 1 and/or X2 or even you want an ARPG with a lot of customization freedom and deep, satisfying gameplay, the Cladun Returns: This is Sengoku is without a doubt a great purchase.

Frictional lends its physics-based, hide-from-the-monster formula to one hell of a story that still has me pondering. One of the most memorable game experiences I've had in the last several years.
GAMEPLAY: If you've played Amnesia: The Dark Descent or Penumbra: Black Plague, you know what to expect - first person controls, click on objects to pick them up and throw them around, and sneaking around monsters with no combat option, so you'd best get used to hiding. Strangely, most puzzles in the game don't make use of the physics engine as they did in Frictional's previous titles, typically taking the form of using a computer in some form - for example, using hints provided to select the right settings to run a simulation. It's a bit of a disappointment, as it feels like the physics engine is only there because it's a Frictional game - there are only a handful of occasions in which it's used to progress the game. Otherwise, your time will be spent exploring the environment looking for key items to progress the story. It's straightforward and functional.
GRAPHICS: The game looks nice, the underwater effects being particularly noteworthy - murky water is mildly illuminated by blurry lights on the ocean floor, as fish swim around you. The human character models are a bit awkward, having a bit of a robotic quality (which jars a bit against the REAL robots in the game), but there aren't many of them to be seen, so it isn't much of an issue. The environments are richly detailed, full of books, small statues, and other miscellaneous objects that make it all feel much more genuine. It feels like real people inhabited these areas - especially when you find the notes and pictures (which can be picked up and closely examined). My only real issues were a few frame rate drops, and that the facilities suffer from the usual problem of looking somewhat bland. I'm not quite sure who decided that all research facilities have to be completely sterile looking, but I don't blame people for going insane in these places.
AUDIO: A huge variety of sound effects, used effectively - some of my most memorable moments come from screeching radio static and the noises of some of the robots. There was great care put into the sound design, and it shows, adding a more realistic feeling to the game. Music isn't a critical factor, with most of the audio coming in-game - footsteps, rushing water, bumps and bangs, etc.
The voice acting is generally quite good, being emotive and natural sounding, though coming off as a bit stinted in places. Catherine in particular was acted very well, and one robot in particular early in the game gave me my first real shock with its mechanical and distorted, yet human voice.
ENEMIES: Varied and creepy, they do their job and they do it well. Though two I would say are a bit unoriginal, they still provide scares as needed. As noted, you will be sneaking around them rather than fighting, and it works just as well as in previous entries. The biggest problem is that they aren't given a very satisfactory explanation - though it's mentioned how they came to be, a little background story into what made these creatures the way they are individually (each one encountered is very different) would have added a bit to it - even just a memo or a piece of dialogue now and again. As it stands, they feel like a bit of an afterthought, and clash with the tone of the game a bit.
ENVIRONMENTS: The bottom of the ocean is a good setting for a horror (themed) game, and it was a nice change of pace compared to the usual hosptial, old castle, abandoned town, etc. of horror fare. You will be in one of two areas, typically: a laboratory/living quarters, or on the ocean floor, with some extras at the beginning and end of the game. As mentioined, they're very nicely detailed, and give off more of a mystery vibe than outright horror. There isn't a lot of decay and darkness here - they feel alive, or places that hosted life not so long ago. The segments between ocean and laboratory are spaced out pretty nicely, so they don't become tedious, which is important - it keeps the player on their toes, and prevents tediousness (I'm looking squarely at you, Alien: Isolation).
HORROR: This isn't an outright horror game as were the Amnesia and Penumbra titles. It's more horror-THEMED, with emphasis on more sci-fi elements, and there isn't much of the slow, lonely, tension-building oppression of the great horror titles. Which is fine - this game knows what it's doing. In fact, I think that type of horror would have clashed with this game's narrative, which necessitated having a compaion for Simon to work out the mysteries of the game. The horror elements that ARE present, however, are very effective due to their being spaced apart. The player is given time to become comfortable and let down their guard, only to be preyed upon again, a concept which some horror games have somehow failed to grasp (hang your heads in shame, Alien and Evil Within). It won't terrify you like Amnesia, but it's good for some tense scares along the way.
STORY: This is where the game shines. Its story asks tough questions of the player, and asks them to make tough decisions. The narrative has Simon go for a brain scan in relation to an injury, only to re-emerge in a lab on the ocean floor with no clue as to how he got there. As he traverses the facility, he - and the player - will have to (attempt to) discern what it means to be human, among other smaller, related questions. It made me think, and the ending had me sitting and looking at my floor as the credits rolled. It's been quite some time since a game has touched me as SOMA has, and that's what makes it so worthwhile. It's not perfect - there are a few changes I would have made to the pacing, and there's a character that's introduced fairly late in the game that feels like an afterthought - but overall, it's well worth the journey.
Overall, SOMA isn't hugely innovative in terms of gameplay, graphics, etc. But its story is what makes it so worthwhile. It's nice to see Frictional create such a thoughtful and emotional narrative after becoming known for games primarily focused on raw horror. I could recommend this game to just about anyone other than those who are easily scared.

I haven't had this much fun playing a game in years! Gurumin really holds true to some older traditions in games.
My favorite things about this game are the very easy learning curve, the replay value, the light-hearted atmosphere, and the characters. Anyone, regardless of age, can pick up and learn how to play very easily. There are still parts that challenge you to master, such as the critical hit system going with the beat of the music. Even without beating the game, there are areas and secrets you constantly find by replaying older stages with new equipment, such as being immune to water damage and being able to find a tunnel underwater. Then on top of that, the game has a bunch of endings and difficulties to unlock, all the while your stats per level are recorded, giving you the chance to compete with yourself. From the main character to the supporting ones, every character adds to this easy-going world. Even though there's this bad person running around and things look grim in the land, you don't feel that sense of urgency. It's just nice and calm, letting you take it on at your own pace.
If I had to summon up any negative things to say about this game, I might say that the beginning cutscenes can be a little lengthy. You can't skip them, but they are important in understanding the story. Sometimes, you'll notice that the lip-sync is not correct, and the characters often move their mouths longer than they actually talk. Then again, that goes to show you how hard I have to look to find things to complain about in this game.
Overall, my only regret about this game is not playing it sooner. I hope to see more great things from this publisher!

Moody and philosophical, brilliantly written and filled with multi-layered characters, immersive and emotionally involving, Knights of the Old Republic 2 is a fantastic game and one of the best stories in the Star Wars universe.
It has its share of flaws - the gameplay is rather dull, level design repetitive, graphics outdated even at the time of release. It was also originally released in an incomplete form, but this has since been fixed by a group of dedicated fan who created the The Sith Lords Restored Content Modification. Despite all the flaws, the game succeeds in what matters - sending the player on a memorable journey and leaving such an impact that all these years after its release I still can't get enough of it.
Hopefully, one day it will get a sequel it deserves.

Now for the narrating. I really adore the deep voice, but sometimes the narrator is only pointing out the obvious. For example, when you first ecounter the Kilmeth, he tells you that it can "erase colors" after you've most likely figured that out [if] you'd tried to burn it. Final Fantasy 6, one of my favorite RPGs to date. This game is amazing in every way. The baddie is actually truly bad and has even destroyed the world. Terra, one of the main protagonists has been under control by a slave crown made by Kefka to do his bidding. She's one of the few people capable of using Magic, this caught the Empire and Kefka's interest in her. She eventually gets sent to Narshe to retrieve an Esper, but instead of being able to retrieve it, she gets knocked out and eventually saved by a resident of Narshe. Suffering from amnesia, she manages to escape the town with a little help from a thief ('treasure hunter'), Locke. This marks the beginning of an epic adventure with tons of things to do.
The game has a feature where you can view different characters' view of the story. One moment you'll be controlling Terra, but eventually the group splits off and you get to experience what they're involved in as well.
Definitely worth picking up, the characters are great, plot is amazing, and even the bad guys are amazing for once.

You are a (not) evil blob thing born of the void, and decide (I think) you want to live and blossom into a healthy, young and bright upstanding adult.
I'll be frank, the story is really bare bones and overly convoluted and just outright idiotic in it's narrative.  You'll be hearing some guy almost talk to himself and keep switching his opinions of what YOU should be feeling about the situation instead of coming to that conclusion yourself and is incredibly contradictory about 90% of the situation.  He also loves stating the obvious, assuming you have the intelligence of single celled organisms.
Probably the only decent aspect of the game.  The sprites have a decent amount of variation, but the environments and overall aesthetic feels like some old mobile phone game to be perfectly honest.  As there's only 4 zones (5 if you include the unlockable Void zone) the variation in art and enemy type is extremely limited.
So as you progress, you'll acquire different colors which adds a few abilities to your arsenal (such as blue being the "ice" color, increasing speed and having enemies slip over themselves).  Unfortunately the puzzles themselves are either extremely straight forward, requiring little to no thinking, or so stupidly broken that you end up dying due to bad enemy placement and level design before figuring out how to avoid the scenerio (and even then it still is a bit RNG if you end up falling on an enemy off screen).  Even the narrator will neglect to tell you of a new enemy until AFTER straight up dying to it, and then restate the obvious of what you figured out after passing it, like the game assumed you somehow cheated to get past or something.  Supposedly after beating the storyline, you unlock Void Mode which is supposedly harder, but after getting a taste of the base game's puzzle and level design I can tell you with 100% certainty you will just end up dying 50 times before memorizing a pattern and avoiding it.  That isn't skill or a measure of difficulty folks.
The controls are honestly either okay or genuinely confusing.  You can use WASD or the arrow keys to move while your mouse is your paint brush of sorts, which seems logical.  Even using the scroll button to cycle through your colors seems okay.  Then you want to get to your color remover, and for whatever reason the game won't let you scroll to it, you need to click the icon on the top right bit of your screen which whips out a large tree branch with all the colors on it, then click the one you want. After having played the everloving crap out of Cladun/Cladun x2, I was surprised when I saw the sequel actually coming to steam.
I had no intentions of buying a PSVita so the 40 dollar (33ish because I already owned Cladun x2) was worth it for me.
If you don't love the series, or think that 40 is way too much for this kind of game (Retro graphics, etc) then wait for it to go on sale for 20~25 dollars, it's worth it. I personally think 40 is a fine price, because I know I'll be getting hundreds if not thousands of hours out of this game.
When I give ratings to a game, I don't score based on personal tastes (Did I like the game? Did I hate it?) But rather on the potential used in the game itself. (Could they have done this better? Was the core-design good?) So I'll be scoring this game using that, rather than a straight up 1~10 system.
To explain what I mean, we all have a game, somewhere in our childhood or something, that is a really bad game. We know it's bad. But we love the crap out of it. Rather than giving the clearly bad game a perfect 10/10, I would give it a 2.5/10 or something, because while I personally enjoy it, I know it could be a lot better.
The reverse side of this is something like Cookie Clicker, I hate that "Game" if you can even call it that, but as far as that kind of game goes? You can't really add anything else to it. So as far as "Potential" goes, I'd have to give it a 10/10. I hope this makes sense.
Cladun isn't the most breathtaking game, don't get me wrong I think it looks good, but it isn't something you've never seen before. I think the graphics work for the game. Could they be better? Sure. Would I want them to be? Maybe, maybe not. I don't really mind the graphics, they're decent enough for me. After all, gameplay is more important here.
I like some of the new monster sprites, but not all of them stick well with me.
(The new spiders are great, but I prefer the old totems.)
If I could get an option to use the old sprites over the new (Or even better, a toggle for each enemy) I would use it.
Graphics:
(
, but not
)
Cladun has always had amazing music. Recieving the free OST with the game is great. However, I feel like the new music isn't on par with the old. You can still play the old music in Ran-geons (Which is the only dungeon that matters, let's be honest.) But I feel that I'll be disabling most of the newer music as time goes on. Not much to say here, music is a bit too subjective for potential ratings.
Audio
(I think it's good, but not
like 1 and x2)
(The quality of the music itself is fine. Nothing that sounds bad or clips as far as I can tell.)
I can't say much here, as I haven't beaten the game yet. But the story thus far is pretty standard.
I don't want to give too much of an impression on this, as I haven't beaten it yet.
Story:
(Good thus far)
Ah gameplay, this is what you've been waiting for. What transforms Cladun from being an okay looking game with good music, into a Fantastic game you can waste your life away on.
Cladun's gameplay has been great since game one. x2 was a huge leap, so how did
fair? Well let's see...
Starting with the bread and the butter of the game, The
is improved pretty well. No longer is the game limited to 2 characters on each side. The merchant circle "Only One." is a great example of this. With 3 characters on each side, one in the front and one in the back, This is something that hasn't been seen yet. So they're still mixing it up here. It could possibly get confusing on which side is taking damage though, as they're not locked to the same x/y as the Character (Lord) For example, the circle "Master Craftsman" has a sub-character (Vassel) in a 8 point circle around the character, with 4 being aligned with the player horizontally/vertically, and the other 4 being alligned diagonally.
Fame is much easier to get this time around with the introduction of quests. Quests can be done to obtain fame, items, gold, etc. Each quest has you go into a dungeon and do a specific thing. Once you finish, you return to the quest board and claim your prize. This means you don't have to re-run dungeons over and over again looking to improve your time by 1 second.
There are two new weapon types introduced in Returns, I haven't messed with them too much, but they appear to be an alternate bow/spear. The shuriken is much faster than the bow. It can't be charged but you can equip a shield with it. The sickle is a spear with maybe twice the range, and it hits twice by default. This weapon can actually reach through 2 block thick walls. Good for sniping enemies from a safe distance.
I may add more here later.
Gameplay:
(A nice little improvement, but not much changed since x2)
Normally you don't see people rate for this, but this is a huge part of what makes a game playable.
Cladun Returns has a big town map. Bigger than Cladun and Cladun x2 Combined. But don't worry, they included a fast travel system that will let you jump around to everywhere you need to go.
Smooth Text was pretty bad looking in Cladun x2, imo, but they've made it actually readable in Returns, meaning you can just pop that on if you don't like the retro text or it messes with your eyes.
Dark Gates (Doom gates) can be set to always display. So no more accidently stepping on one and ruining your run. (You can leave them to appear as traps, like they used to, if you're into that.)
New features make raising a new character up from creation much easier. You'll still want to use your best weapons on them, but they won't be completely gimped without access to the better magic circles.
Quality of Life:
(There's a pretty good overall feel to the game.)
This is a good game, well worth the money. If you're not into the cladun series already, wait for a 40~50% sale.

Medal of Honor 2010 is not a bad game, but it's not really a game that i would recommend.
The game consists of a singleplayer campaign that was made by Danger Close and multiplayer that was made by DICE.
Campaign is about the war in Afghanistan.
Unlike most shooters now a days, they decided to focus solely on one place. You don't have this "travel round the world" that most shooters do these days, everything happens in one location.
I also liked how they hand over missions to you.
Unfortunately, the bad outweighs the good here.
This game has your typical linear designed levels. Altogether the game isn't very long - only 4 hours. Also, a lot of features that were part of MOH Airborne are not present - like choosing your loadout, big open levels, choosing you starting point, upgrading your weapons.
It was made by DICE. It kind of resembles a mix between COD and Battlefield.
Unlike the singleplayer, it uses Frostbite 1.5 (while the singleplayer uses Unreal Engine 3). Despite all that, the destruction is very insignificant though.
It features 12 maps and 6 modes. Allows a max of 24 players. Also, it has a server browser.
Combat Mission is probably the main mode of the game. It's pretty much Rush, except that you have 5 objectives, and you defend one at a time. Unlike BF's Rush it doesn't have 2 objectives at any one time. For more traditional Rush, play Objective Raid. Unfortunately in that one, the game ends after one of the objectives blows up - no extra objectives.
Defenders win if the time limit runs out. Attackers win if they destroy every objective.
Taliban are always the defenders and US are always the attackers.
US also gets an APC (unfortunately, it's only available on 2 maps).
The game features 3 classes: Rifleman, Special Ops, Sniper.
The leveling up is very similar to battlefield, that means, if you play as say Rifleman, you level up only the Rifleman class. Each class has 15 levels.
Also, just like in Battlefield, you are stuck with respective weapons to your faction, and to use your enemy's weapons, you must reach the max level.
There are a total of 15 weapons in the game, and you have 3 attachment slots for each of them.
Now what it copied from COD are the killstreaks. They named them as pointstreaks. You can get them just by playing the objective or by getting kills. Once you die you lose your streak.
Now, the other unique thing is that you are given a choice between a defensive or offensive killstreak.
I feel that the multiplayer is just too low on content.
Single player wise i think that this is a step backwards. Medal of Honor Airborne was a good example on how to make singleplayer games.
Multiplayer is alright, but i doubt you will find anyone playing it these days. Considering the amount of content given, i wouldn't blame them.

This game had promise. Something like a more console-based version of Uplink.
But that didn't really pan out with all the inconsistencies that were introduced in that vision. (e.g. tab-completion actually being useful is rather random if there are more than a couple possibilities.)
What really killed this game for me, was the need to constantly re-trace your footsteps from previous levels. (e.g. rescanning to find valid hosts that were just discovered, cracked, and were required in both the previous and current levels.)
Compunding the problem further were the ridiculous in-game file sizes that contain clues, and that none of these are retained between levels. (e.g. it's often impossible to store two different logfiles, and of course, there's no way to crop/trim them to relevant sizes.)
Both of these problems were immediately highlighted in the game, starting with the 2nd mission after the tutorial. (One could even argue that the progress from the tutorial mission is reset, but that's a common situation.)
I wanted to like this game, and have put in several different attempts to really get into it and overlook the flaws, but I just couldn't manage it.
For those looking for their next "hacking simulator" fix, I would heavily recommend replaying Uplink, and/or going with a different game, like Hacknet, which is at least internally consistent, rather than picking this one up.

1982 is an old school arcade shooter, and is a shining example of how the genre can still be amazing. It pays homage to the 80s both in its creative blend of Space Invaders (1978) and Centipede (1980), as well as in its references to other great arcade games such as Galaxian (1979), Pacman (1980), and Galaga (1981). Although it starts off like a Space Invaders clone, fans of arcade shooters and SHMUPS will notice it integrating elements of other games, most notably Centipede, Asteroids, and Missile Command.
One of my favorite things about this game is that it actually allows for some real strategizing rather than just shooting everything. The idea is that there will often be pickups that you can shoot to allow them to break and fall towards you. If you shoot them while they're falling, they'll turn into one of several different kinds of area of effect attacks (blue will shoot missiles in different directions, green causes a sizeable blast where it gets destroyed, red shoots lasers horizontally, etc.). However, if you don't shoot them and instead collect them as they fall to the bottom, you get one of several kinds of pickups (pink gives you extra firepower, green gives you energy, blue gives you a shield, red gives you rockets, etc.). So you'll be in certain situations where you have to think very quickly if the best course of action is to make an area of effect attack or get the power-up. I think this is a very nice addition to what could have been an otherwise generic, by-the-numbers arcade shooter.
In terms of aesthetics, 1982 has a very captivating art style. The color scheme is bright and vibrant, and all the sounds belong in the world of 80s arcade games. Many of the enemy shapes look like their 1980s counter-parts (for instance, the Pacman ghosts make an appearance). The controls handle extremely well and the game runs flawlessly. It allows control by mouse, keyboard, and gamepad. As usual, there are a few things that I feel could be better. One issue is that the sound of your ship firing is significantly louder than it should be, and if you die when a certain enemy is exploding (it takes a while to explode), the sound will just repeat itself over and over very loudly until you go to the main menu. I am also still a little confused as to the point of certain things. For instance, what is the point of collecting the falling people, and why do hearts come out of pickups since they obviously don't restore your health? The only other thing that felt weird is the point system, which is surprisingly low for an arcade shooter; I mean, getting something like 4 points per enemy in the beginning? I remember Asteroids and other games of that generation awarded something like 100 points per unit. It's an extremely minor nitpick but I think that boosting the score rate would make it feel more retro.
Anyway, 1982 is a great game that doesn't just play its retro card, but rather improves upon a supposedly dead genre that to my knowledge has never been explored much in a creative way since the death of arcades. It's free and it's only 18 MB, so if you're a fan of arcade games, there's no excuse to not pick this up. I will be looking out for other games by this developer. Definitely recommended.

Gurumin: A Monstrous Adventure, developed by Nihon Falcom, is a HD re-release of the 2004 Japan-only PC game, with Gurumin last seeing English storefronts on the PSP in 2007.
As a result, as well as running on just about anything, Gurumin serves as a time-capsule of videogames before contemporary design trends. Aesthetically, it's an adorable adventure game that resembles games like Blinx the Time Sweeper, 40 Winks, Ape Escape or just about any simple platformer with action elements from the fifth generation that you can think of.
Layout-wise, it's exactly what you'd think. There's about 25 levels, each 5-15 minutes long, several different minigames, a secret boss and more than enough regular bosses to keep you satiated. The plot is simple, charming, and ends on as sickening a saccharine note as you could possibly want, though not before a satisfying one-on-one beatdown to decide the world's fate. The game goes out of its way to avoid surprising you - it's a comforting, easing experience first and foremost, with enough enthusiasm and charisma for its own existence to keep you playing and wanting more.
There are other benefits from refusing to evolve into a world of DLC and microtransactions. From the secret unlockables (which I won't spoil, else they wouldn't be secrets) to the plethora of regular unlockables, to the surprising (and punishing!) extra difficulty modes - this is a game from before the era of DLC nickel and diming you on extra content that used to be a joy to unlock.
Combat was designed by the creators behind the legendary Ys series (pronounced "Ees"). It's relatively simple compared to hack n slash giants like DMC or Ninja Gaiden, and the moveset discourages playing stylishly so much as playing efficiently, but it's far from boring - which doesn't do a great job of selling it, but there's enough possibilities, from specials to being able to launch an enemy and juggle them until they explode, to keep you interested indefinitely given the burst nature of the level design. And on higher difficulty modes you'll be finding yourself playing with it in ways you wouldn't have thought to.
Gurumin is a game that lives up to its legacy, a legacy of games that existed to entertain you, not to pillage your pockets. It's a static pocket of quality and quantity content to be content with you.
It's not perfect. There are some odd glitches - notably, that you need to avoid S-Ranking every single level in order to get the "S-Rank every single level" achievement. Which is odd. For a PC-original game, the control scheme is alien, and frightening. Not to say it's unplayable with the defaults, but I do heavily recommend using a gamepad.
And then there's Hoccer. Hoccer is a minigame I needn't say much about. Hoccer is a minigame you will discover for yourself. Hoccer will destroy you, as it destroyed me, and legions of other players before us. Accept your defeat and move on. Let Motoro have his win, it's not worth it. The Horror of Hoccer.
There's also some content missing that the PSP version has - some costume unlockables and such. Keep that in mind. It's nothing major.
Gurumin is well worth your time and money, and doesn't pray on your nostalgia. It shows you why you had nostalgia for what it represented in the first place.

Fun, easy to learn/difficult to master, and rather short, Nihilumbra's story mode can probably be finished in a single sitting. Controls are easy and intuitive, and powers are doled out at regular intervals. Many of the puzzles are quite clever, though to be blunt the most fun ones are extremely front-loaded. The art style and music are absolutely gorgeous, and though simple, the clear aesthetic unity and crispness puts many other games in its price range to shame.
The game only suffers from two problems, but they are irksome:
1) Even in story ("easy") mode, there are moments that are just plain unforgiving. Many puzzles are more accurately described as "die so you see the mechanic, respawn, use knowledge get through mechanic, then die to next mechanic, repeat." Essentially savescumming as progression. This isn't Planescape: Torment where death was used to solve puzzles, it's just a way to pad out the game's length. There's a very noticeable drop-off in players who have the level 1 and 2 completed achievements; a fact that coincides noticeably with the first die-through-it puzzle.
2) The script seems like something written by a teenager going through a goth phase. and is narrated by someone extremely doped up on sleep meds. If you enjoy the slow, monotonous, repetitive naming of emotions rather than any actual content that would invoke those feelings, this may be up your alley. For most people, though, it's most likely simply to bring back repressed memories of terrible college creative-writing papers. You remember the one guy who always told everyone how deep and underappreciated he was despite not having done anything memorable? That's this game's script.
That said, the actual gameplay is generally fantastic. At least until you unlock Void ("hard") mode by beating the story. There's a reason that roughly 1/6th the people who beat the game have even a single Void level clear achievement. Void Mode is die-through-it on steroids, and will literally kill you within seconds of spawning on the very first stage of the first level. Up until you get to Void, however, it's a fun, mostly casual game that anyone with a fondness for platformers will enjoy.

“Take the greatest Jedi Knight, strip away the Force, and what remains? They rely on it, depend on it, more than they know. Watch as one tries to hold a blaster, as they try to hold a lightsaber, and you will see nothing more than a woman – or a man. A child.” - Kreia
Five years after the events of KOTOR, the galaxy is recovering from the events from the Jedi Civil War. Both the Jedi and Sith have now fallen silent. You have been exiled from the Jedi Order as punishment for following Revan into war against the Mandolorians. You have also been completely cut off from the Force, but was this a part of your punishment, or the result of something much worse?
This review is written from a huge Star Wars fan and a fan of story driven RPGs in general.
GAMEPLAY AND DESIGN
In terms of general gameplay and structure, KOTOR 2 is designed very similarly to the first game. It features the same turn-based D20 based combat system and character building as the first game and other old-school RPGs. This can be a quite daunting system to learn for those unfamiliar with these types of games, but fortunately the lower difficulty settings are forgiving enough for those without the patience or time to learn it. Combat is important, but arguably not as much as the stat and skill point distribution. Making sure you have characters with the appropriate skills determines being able to deal with obstacles in the world, conversation checks and crafting. The game does feature an automatic leveling up system which will do the leveling for you, which is fine in the late game after you have all the skills you need, but it may be worth doing some research in the early game for leveling up. The companions are all reasonably balanced and they level up with you, meaning that you can take anyone anywhere (at least from a gameplay perspective).
The game isn’t entirely open world by any means. It’s similar to KOTOR and Dragon Age: Origins, in the sense that you travel between several fairly small focused areas rather than one continuous land mass. The areas are either mostly linear action packed levels or slower paced story driven quest hub areas. Crafting is important system to pay attention to as you can craft item modifications to create weapons more powerful than the ones you find. This is a fairly simple system that involves breaking down items you don’t need for materials, but it’s just a case of knowing what the stats actually mean. Of course, on lower difficulties you can get away with not paying much attention to gear and stats and still just about get by spamming the same attacks. You won’t find it very challenging, but more than adequate for just seeing the story (which in my opinion, is the main draw of the game).
STORY AND NARRATIVE
It’s never easy to develop a follow up on such a beloved game from a different developer, but Obsidian certainly delivered on delivering a sequel that is true to the original and yet unique in its own way. KOTORs story felt very much like a grand space adventure and it captured everything that the classic Star Wars story should be. KOTOR 2 differs from this slightly. It tells a more subtle story with a focus on different themes. In stark contrast to KOTORs overt villains, KOTOR 2s threat is a lot more sinister. The battles with the Sith are fought in the shadows and the themes are a lot darker. An example of the darker tone is a reoccurring idea in the game that to the galaxy’s Average Joe, Jedi and Sith are indistinguishable. They just people with too much power fighting over religion and getting everyone else caught in the middle. This is a really unique and interesting idea and caught me completely off guard. Another good theme was the idea of the absence of the Force and the advantages it has aside from the obvious disadvantages.
The conversation system is identical to KOTOR, with the standard light and dark alignment options and the opportunities to use skills (if you have the stats) in certain special situations. In my opinion, morality is much more interesting in KOTOR 2 than in the first one. Picking light or dark and sticking to it not only changes the ending, but the entire game. It shifts your characters goals for the whole game and also effects the gameplay. Dark and light side powers become easier/harder (but not impossible) to do if you are the opposite morality and it can result in some rather large deviations on the story line during some quests. It also affects your companions and over time you can even begin to influence their morality (e.g. enlightenment vs corruption). Overall, I’d say the game changes enough to warrant multiple playthroughs with different morality choices.
On the topic of companions, you can expect yet another colourful crew of heroes, villains, droids and miscreants. They are very varied from the original games selection, but just as interesting and unique. Gameplay wise, they still have classes that need to have their stats properly assigned and equipped with the right gear. However, pretty much any configuration of companions is viable to take anywhere, which is good for the story. It makes it feel like you travel with ALL of your companions rather than just bringing your favourites and leaving everyone else on the ship. Your actions also influence your companions, resulting in them liking or disliking you more depending on how you act. Having them like you opens up more story and has gameplay benefits I can’t elaborate on without light spoilers.
A quick note on voice acting: personally I found a particular companions voice actor laughably bad (look out for the one-armed Iridonian), but he’s really the only one that stands out. The rest of the game is mostly either passable or excellent.
GAMEPLAY AND PERFORMANCE
As is customary with Obsidian games, they are often not given enough time for playtesting and optimisation leaving them somewhat lacking in the performance department. I expect you won’t encounter many problems these days however, as unsurprisingly an 11 year old game runs at 60fps 100% of time and doesn’t look half bad for its age. I did get a crash or two here and there and more than a fair share of bugs, but fortunately nothing game breaking or huge. I didn’t run into any compatibility problems either (running Windows 7).
Funnily enough, the game actually got a patch recently that fixed a lot of problems, added controller support, support for higher resolutions and some other fixes. The biggest change was the addition was the addition of Steam Workshop for the game, which allows the seamless installation of some mods that restores a whole bunch of content that was cut from the game. Look up The Sith Lords Restored Content mod if you get the game, but it should be the highest rated anyway.
TSLRCM REVIEW
TSLRCM fixes many bugs, quests and all round genral nuisances that affect the game. It adds (restores) lost cutscenes that give better reasons and fixes endings to give a more full conclusion.
It completes the game. I personally would reccomend palying the without the mod (or any mods infact) to fully taste the (lacking) game but then when re-playing it would change your experiance greatly.

Overall, not bad. But it seems like the creators saw these beautiful, story-rich art games catching on and wanted to make one so. very. desperately. The only thing the over-prevalent story can claim as its own is a narrator that won't shut up, telling you what you should feel on just about every screen, ultimately resulting in you feeling nothing. It doesn't help that the writing is poorly translated, and that the lone voice actor dutifully reads through typos as if they make as much sense to him as anything else in the script. (Honestly, given the fact that the guy had to say things like: "Red possesses the power of fire" that seems likely.) Someone missed the memo that games like this should omit text and voice acting entirely, unless it's borderline poetry.
Now that that's out of the way, other artistic elements flourish. Honestly, I bought the game because of how gorgeous the screenshots looked, and it didn't disappoint visually all the way through. The animation, in particular, is extremely detailed, and it seems like every time you watch your character move, you see something you didn't notice before. All the backgrounds are equally pretty. The orchestral soundtrack is utterly fantastic, and the most surprising thing about the game (yes, it has an orchestral soundtrack). I just wish the developer had had the wisdom to let these elements speak for themselves.
I know I'm mentioning the gameplay last, but personally, while it may have been easy, I thought the powers were a lot of fun to play with, and the mechanics for how they worked together were pretty well thought out. I haven't started Void mode yet, but I've heard it's when the game actually gets difficult, and that the 3 hour campaign is really just an extended tutorial. Honestly, I think it's a good format for a game with memorable mechanics, and this one has them. I'd love to see the game take advantage of the green and brown powers to make some insane platforming sequences. We'll have to see whether I'm disappointed or not later on.

Puzzle platformer, slow-paced, not very difficult. Main mechanic (besides moving your character) is altering game physics by "painting" 5 different colours (with different abilities, which are unlocked during main campaign) on almost any platform.

In this mode, you'll need to employ platforming skills and brain cells a bit more. Good thing is, almost any level can be finished with different approach (using different colours which adds to replayability). Beating the hard mode will unlock a change which will give you the reason to put few more hours into the main campaign from the beginning (this feature completely change the mood of the game, which is dark/depressing by its setting).
Steam achievements are not very difficult, most of them will be unlocked naturally by going through both playthroughs. Some requires higher platforming skill and exploration, but nothing impossible for 100%.
Fair price, decent length, good game. I was pleasantly surprised. Totally recommended!

Final Fantasy VI was Squaresoft's swan song to the Final Fantasy series on the SNES and, for a time, Nintendo in general. It used all the innovation of the past titles to amount to a very satisfying experience of storytelling and smooth gameplay through its Active Time Battle (ATB) system.
This PC version of the game is based on the GameBoy Advance release which fixed a few glitches and problems that the SNES version had along with having the additionnal GBA dungeon included as well as a few additionnal Espers to collect.
As such, I won't linger talking about the game's story or mechanics since they remain the same as before (and any past review of the GBA version applies there) but instead focus on the changes that came with this version.
One criticism that can be brought forward early on is that the game still uses a mobile game like interface that, while takes a bit of time to get used to, sometimes feels a bit overwhelming or out of place for a PC title.
The game supports the XBox One controller to navigate the menus and play the game in its whole. One major change has to be how navigation during battle is handled.
Unlike the original version where you either had a regular battle menu or a cross menu, this version uses individual menus that doubles as your ATB gauges. Once you get a handle of it however, it plays similarly to Chrono Trigger as you can simply move left and right to choose another ready character. I do not, however, suggest using the left or right justified tab options simply because it is difficult to navigate without an actual touch screen.
The redesigned sprites might look a bit weird for those who originally played the game on SNES or GBA but, much like with FFV, you grow to get used to it and appreciated the higher level of detail they offer. However, unlike FFV PC, spell effects are merely upscaled versions of the original ones.
The game uses the original SNES soundtrack which still sounds very good by today's standard and sound effects remain as crisp and impactful as they were. Kefka's laugh, thankfully, remains unaltered.
For anyone who wishes to experience an old console title that is slightly upgraded for the PC platform, this version is solid enough to be recommended. Either if you never had the pleasure to play FFVI before or wish to go for another playthrough, you'll feel right at home.

Frictional Games' formula for its games has gotten a bit stale. I realized this when I was gifted SOMA by a very good friend of mine from work, and I was excited because I was going into it completely blind, knowing absolutely nothing about it! Oooh, what kind of fun, dark♥♥♥♥♥♥are we going to get into today? Space monsters? Computer monsters? Space computer monsters ON THE MOON? But then I immediately thought the space computer monsters on the moon and I thought "Oh, God dammit, I'm gonna have to do the thing where I hide in shadows and wait for the space computer monsters to shuffle by, aren't I?"
Don't get me wrong, SOMA is pretty damn cool and I enjoyed it in SPITE of the tired monster sections and the not-ready-for-prime-time game engine. I like all the little tricks it does to add flavor to the story and underline its themes of consciousness and existence and whether the computer you or the flesh and blood you is actually the real you. I like that it's going out there to do some hard sci-fi (the kind of sci-fi that idiot nerds hold over the heads of liberal arts majors and scream OUR GUYS CAN WRITE TOO YOU'RE NOT RELEVANT GET A JOB HIPPIE LALALALALALALA) and is not afraid to create a hell of a downer where it's most needed. It partially tells its story in ways I'm not a fan of (audio logs bolted to one spot on the wall is a practice I would like developers to stop using, thanks), but I think it does a fine job telling its story overall!
That being said, I had to actually work to finish SOMA, and that was because of the constant problems with the game engine itself. The game itself is 20 gigs large, and if you don't have a solid state drive, prepare for two minute load times! But even with an SSD, the game takes a little longer than I'd like. I also had problems where the game would crash to desktop - a menace even more terrifying than the monsters themselves, because while I can just throw a heavy object in one direction of a hallway and run the ♥♥♥♥ in the other direction, the crash-to-desktop monster is a one-hit kill invisible monster that pops up whenever the game needs to load a new section, and that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ kept breathing down my neck! So a partial amount of my time with SOMA was performing rituals and doing raindances just to pray that the thing wouldn't crash and take my progress in the scary stealthy sections away from me.
But the thing that concerned me most of all is Frictional Games' insistence on sticking to what they know, even if it doesn't really quite mesh with what was going on. I felt that the hard sci-fi stuff was really strong material, and that it didn't really need the horror stuff. I mean, yeah, corrupt AI making weird reanimated soldiers is always cool, but what Frictional Games was working with was already some next level stuff. It didn't need an ur-SHODAN to liven things up! Just stick to the Philip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥inspired nightmares, there's plenty to mine from that! But I guess if we don't want to hear the throngs of people whining about how THIS IS JUST A WALKING SIMULATOR BUT UNDER THE SEA, we've got to have the same old stealth elements and the same old monster elements just to shut those people up.
So while Frictional's latest really does have its flaws this time around, it's still a solid storytelling experience. And if you are good at distracting idiot monsters, the stealth sections become something else. Like Hotline Miami, but instead of killing the monsters, you run past them to the exit, yelling "YOU GOT JUST MINDFREAKED, YOU STUPID REANIMATED CORPSE."

Frictional lends its physics-based, hide-from-the-monster formula to one hell of a story that still has me pondering. One of the most memorable game experiences I've had in the last several years.
GAMEPLAY: If you've played Amnesia: The Dark Descent or Penumbra: Black Plague, you know what to expect - first person controls, click on objects to pick them up and throw them around, and sneaking around monsters with no combat option, so you'd best get used to hiding. Strangely, most puzzles in the game don't make use of the physics engine as they did in Frictional's previous titles, typically taking the form of using a computer in some form - for example, using hints provided to select the right settings to run a simulation. It's a bit of a disappointment, as it feels like the physics engine is only there because it's a Frictional game - there are only a handful of occasions in which it's used to progress the game. Otherwise, your time will be spent exploring the environment looking for key items to progress the story. It's straightforward and functional.
GRAPHICS: The game looks nice, the underwater effects being particularly noteworthy - murky water is mildly illuminated by blurry lights on the ocean floor, as fish swim around you. The human character models are a bit awkward, having a bit of a robotic quality (which jars a bit against the REAL robots in the game), but there aren't many of them to be seen, so it isn't much of an issue. The environments are richly detailed, full of books, small statues, and other miscellaneous objects that make it all feel much more genuine. It feels like real people inhabited these areas - especially when you find the notes and pictures (which can be picked up and closely examined). My only real issues were a few frame rate drops, and that the facilities suffer from the usual problem of looking somewhat bland. I'm not quite sure who decided that all research facilities have to be completely sterile looking, but I don't blame people for going insane in these places.
AUDIO: A huge variety of sound effects, used effectively - some of my most memorable moments come from screeching radio static and the noises of some of the robots. There was great care put into the sound design, and it shows, adding a more realistic feeling to the game. Music isn't a critical factor, with most of the audio coming in-game - footsteps, rushing water, bumps and bangs, etc.
The voice acting is generally quite good, being emotive and natural sounding, though coming off as a bit stinted in places. Catherine in particular was acted very well, and one robot in particular early in the game gave me my first real shock with its mechanical and distorted, yet human voice.
ENEMIES: Varied and creepy, they do their job and they do it well. Though two I would say are a bit unoriginal, they still provide scares as needed. As noted, you will be sneaking around them rather than fighting, and it works just as well as in previous entries. The biggest problem is that they aren't given a very satisfactory explanation - though it's mentioned how they came to be, a little background story into what made these creatures the way they are individually (each one encountered is very different) would have added a bit to it - even just a memo or a piece of dialogue now and again. As it stands, they feel like a bit of an afterthought, and clash with the tone of the game a bit.
ENVIRONMENTS: The bottom of the ocean is a good setting for a horror (themed) game, and it was a nice change of pace compared to the usual hosptial, old castle, abandoned town, etc. of horror fare. You will be in one of two areas, typically: a laboratory/living quarters, or on the ocean floor, with some extras at the beginning and end of the game. As mentioined, they're very nicely detailed, and give off more of a mystery vibe than outright horror. There isn't a lot of decay and darkness here - they feel alive, or places that hosted life not so long ago. The segments between ocean and laboratory are spaced out pretty nicely, so they don't become tedious, which is important - it keeps the player on their toes, and prevents tediousness (I'm looking squarely at you, Alien: Isolation).
HORROR: This isn't an outright horror game as were the Amnesia and Penumbra titles. It's more horror-THEMED, with emphasis on more sci-fi elements, and there isn't much of the slow, lonely, tension-building oppression of the great horror titles. Which is fine - this game knows what it's doing. In fact, I think that type of horror would have clashed with this game's narrative, which necessitated having a compaion for Simon to work out the mysteries of the game. The horror elements that ARE present, however, are very effective due to their being spaced apart. The player is given time to become comfortable and let down their guard, only to be preyed upon again, a concept which some horror games have somehow failed to grasp (hang your heads in shame, Alien and Evil Within). It won't terrify you like Amnesia, but it's good for some tense scares along the way.
STORY: This is where the game shines. Its story asks tough questions of the player, and asks them to make tough decisions. The narrative has Simon go for a brain scan in relation to an injury, only to re-emerge in a lab on the ocean floor with no clue as to how he got there. As he traverses the facility, he - and the player - will have to (attempt to) discern what it means to be human, among other smaller, related questions. It made me think, and the ending had me sitting and looking at my floor as the credits rolled. It's been quite some time since a game has touched me as SOMA has, and that's what makes it so worthwhile. It's not perfect - there are a few changes I would have made to the pacing, and there's a character that's introduced fairly late in the game that feels like an afterthought - but overall, it's well worth the journey.
Overall, SOMA isn't hugely innovative in terms of gameplay, graphics, etc. But its story is what makes it so worthwhile. It's nice to see Frictional create such a thoughtful and emotional narrative after becoming known for games primarily focused on raw horror. I could recommend this game to just about anyone other than those who are easily scared.

OK, I'm proper scared. I've just been stalked through a sewer by something I can't see, let alone fight.
The only thing that gave it away was the languid ker-splosh of its footsteps as it ranged around after me. Every time I lost my footing on the narrow path of tottering crates and other detritus and landed in the drink, a flurry of intense sploshing rose sharply in volume as it made for my meat. It was utterly, panicinducingly horrible. I made errors in judgement, I missed jumps, I clenched. When it was all over, I nearly had a little cry.
Amnesia does Lovecraft in the purest sense: it understands that the imagined far outweighs the known in its psychological punch, and it gives you enough audio and visual cues to imagine a very carnival of horrors. From the twisted brainpipes of Frictional games, the guys behind the Penumbra series, this is every part the worthy successor, with considerably higher production values, bags more atmosphere, and a deeper exploration of the parallel themes of horror and insanity. While these screenshots shout FPS, it shares more with point-and-click adventures than shooters. There's not a weapon in sight: it's all about the puzzles, exploiting the neat physics engine, combining items to apply to the environment, and hiding when the nasties come.
The story unfolds from a locus of zero knowledge, aside from one fact: your name is Daniel. You wake in a medieval castle, and finding a note you'd previously written for yourself, you discover you're here for a reason. In fact, you've been here for some time, and as the plot expands through further diary-notes and flashbacks, the unsavoury purpose behind your presence becomes apparent. You're also just a bit afraid of the dark. The whole place is graveyard-dim, but you collect tinder-boxes to light torches and candles, and oil for your lamp. Keeping the shadows at bay is a constant – and necessary – struggle. (
)
Spend too long in the gloaming, and madness beckons. As Daniel's sanity starts to stutter, imagination plays merry hell. Insects skitter across your vision, the input-lag between mouse-gesture and action goes to hell, the ground lurches sickeningly, and you'll hear things – whispers, cries and horrid noises, one of which can only be described as someone pulling crabs apart.
Against this background, you learn of the unspeakable experiments that happened here, and your involvement with them, as something hideous dogs your steps. It's hard to talk about certain specifics without spoilers, but suffice it to say, there are scenes you'll recoil at. One area of the game is devoted to revealing the psychological and physical specifics of medieval torture methods; fascinating in a horribly suggestive way, and all, somehow, tied to your past. When it's not breathing down your neck, lurching after you or trying to eat your face, Amnesia shows you bad things and makes you feel dirty!
And that's its triumph: one of grisly atmosphere over genre convention, with tension and release in keen balance. It seems rude to pick holes – some of the vocal delivery, for example, lacks the credible touch, and occasionally, you'll have no idea what the puzzle you're working on is meant to achieve; you just have to keep trying things out. But it's well worth it, and a snip at £12.95. Despite its title, Amnesia remembers what the blockbusters of survival horror seem to have forgotten: how to horrify. (
)

Come for the multiplayer, stay for the multiplayer. Prior to release the developers said they would have a campaign that people who weren't into online gaming would enjoy just as much. If you have payed any attention to the game industry over the last decade you know that this was just a lie to get more people to buy the game. The single player campaign is terrible. The plot is just a hollow shell meant to give you a reason you're fighting but it never develops into anything more than an intro to each class. The mental voiceovers of your characters are trite and meaningless, usually amounting to "I am so tortured inside but I love to kill people merrrr".
Online play is where the game shines. It's not going to be the next CSGO or anything (and will probably only be around for a year or two before everybody abandons it for something equal or better) but it is a lot of fun with friends. There is a lot of skill involved and when you face someone who is vastly superior to you in technique you can really tell. That, in a way, makes the game more intimate. Sure you have the kids who just pick the spear samurai and spam the same attack over and over (which is annoying until you get a couple hours under your belt and realize this is a really easy move to counter) but for the most part players take the time to learn the ins and outs of their preferred class (I don't have one yet).
For those of you who still think that shaders, modelling, and textures make a game, the game is beautiful. As such it takes a fairly powerful PC to run smoothly. I do okay at a lower resolution but if too much is happening on the screen at once I'll get bogged down so much I can't even block a simple attack (happens rarely but it happens). So be wary of that if your PC is more than a couple of years old.

I'll get straight to the point: this game will definitely drill its way into your heart. *pause for laughter or groans*
*ahem* now that I have you either groaning from the pun or laughing your♥♥♥♥♥off, I'll start the real review.
This game comes to steam years later from the initial release in japan back in 2004, which got ported to PSP in June of 2006, made a north american appearance in 2007, and got an original PC release worldwide on steam.  From my point of view, everything about this game is great, with just a few minor complaints I have, which I will get to in this review.
Graphics: 9/10 - The graphics remind me of early playstation games such as Brave Fencer Musashi.  They get the job done, vibrant, and great use of color.  You can also tell it makes great use of cell-shading, but the characters do tend to look a little too simplistic.  Overall, however, this game looks great.
Gameplay: 9.5/10 - The game plays very well, and that's as much as I can say about it right now as I've only just started playing this game.  I will definitely update when the time comes, but one minor complaint: so far, I haven't really run into any boss fights. EDIT: Just ran into my first boss fight, and lemmie tell ya, they can really drill it to ya -pause again for laughs or groans-.  They're challenging, but fair.  It at least gives you time to use healing items and not have them clobber you as you do so.  Overall, the boss fights are great and vibrant.
Controls: 8/10 - Here's where I have to make a few complaints about controls here.  Some of the moves aren't very clear on what to do, especially if you're using a gamepad (or xbox 360/XBOne controller) for control.  The instructions are strictly PC oriented with no mention of what to do with the gamepad.  I would complain about it more, if it weren't for the fact that you learn pretty quickly what buttons do what move, so it's no big issue and the controls can be customized*.
However, the controls do the job well, either way.  The jump controls are interesting, but can get a little frustrating, especially having to make platform jumps.  Fortunately, the shadow effects will help you, and you can angle the camera any way you please (right stick for xbox 360 controllers).  The inclusion of timed hits to the beat of the music with the beat bar displayed on screen is a wonderful addition.  If you've mastered Crypt of the Necrodancer, you'll definitely find that getting critical hits via the beat of the music to be very easy and fun.
Sound: 9/10 - The music, even though you can tell it's synthesizer, is VERY well done.  The english voice acting is a bit cheesy, but works anyways.  The music is upbeat and well composed, in my opinion.  You'll need to get that tempo down if you want to do critical hit damage, but the timing of each beat is precise and works very well.
Overall: 9.25/10 - This game is definitely a title for platform gamers to really dig into -pause for groans or laughter-.  Hopefully, we'll see some patches released to fix some of the issues, but overall, I recommend this game for anyone who loves a good platform game.
*At least the options to do that are up, but I've seen some forum posts about the game not running because options got changed.  Hopefully, this gets patched soon, as I did suffer the same thing when I tried to change around a few options.  Should you find your game not starting up, just hit the restore defaults button on the windows menu screen that comes up and it'll start normally again. There’s a specific scene you revisit a few times throughout Nihilumbra. It begins with you falling, the world having been twisted into something surreal, yet oddly soothing. You don’t stay here long, but it was within these brief moments that I was able to collect the scattered thoughts swirling around in my head that I had previously been unable to make sense of.
These scenes represented to me what Nihilumbra was on a conceptual level. They’re beautiful, empty, and meaningless. The reason I was finding it so hard to take something away from Nihilumbra was because there was nothing there. It’s a gorgeous experience filled with expression, but its aesthetics are simply a mask with nothing underneath.
Nihilumbra tries relentlessly to carve out a philosophical core within its narrative, but it comes across as venting the poorly formed ideas of someone who has given up on the world rather than something profound. The writing feels forced and lacks any impact, obnoxiously attempting to make you feel something - anything - by simply stating those feelings as if that is somehow enough to bring them into existence. Ultimately the constant reminders that I was supposed to feel guilty or scared only caused me to become despondent and annoyed.
The detached way in which Nihilumbra handles morality makes it feel as if it doesn’t really care. It wants to come across as deep without having anything to actually say, filling its world with empty words that bounced off me as quickly as they reappeared.
Eventually I simply tuned the writing out and attempted to focus on the puzzle designs instead, yet doing this only brought out how similarly hollow and disinteresting those elements were too. Controlling various elemental powers which can be painted on the environment should provide endless interesting applications, but Nihilumbra never even scratches that surface. It provides you new tools at a steady pace but never a creative way to use them.
Puzzle designs repeat the same basic ideas the entire way through, often requiring no forethought as the answer is simply a slightly altered version of the tutorial. Nihilumbra isn’t just easy, it’s numbingly repetitive and unstimulating. The only time I felt challenged was in navigating the interface, which while not terrible tended to feel awkward and more suited to its touch-based origins than a mouse and keyboard. But then as if to mock me, completing the game unlocks “void mode”, which far from the simplistic main game radically raises the difficulty with cheap trial and error level designs. This doesn’t in turn make them any more engaging however, as the only thing being tested is your patience and how quickly you can move your fingers, rather than your puzzle solving skills.
Nihilumbra is such an exquisite game to look at, that it’s disheartening to see such lovely artwork was wasted on an experience that only manages to dull the senses. It functions, but provides no incentive to spend even a few hours to complete it. Playing it felt almost like it was actively pushing me out, unintentionally but forcefully, as if despite having outrun the void pursuing me it had already devoured the game itself.

Overall I would recommend this game. At $10 it's really hard not to; there are many games released nowadays without half the charm and without much of the same level content for a far higher price. Gurumin is not without its flaws, but I don't think the flaws are significant enough to outweigh the positives.
While the game is classified here as an Action RPG, I would argue against the RPG part of that. Is an RPG a game where your choices as your character define the world and set you on different story paths? This game doesn't do that (there are two endings available, but it's based on percentage of completion and not any choices made throughout the story, because there are none). Is it being able to assign points to various attributes like Strength, Charisma, etc.? This game doesn't do that; in fact, the only direct statistical upgrades for your character are health point increases after bosses, similar to what you would find in a Legend of Zelda title. What the game DOES have is an impressive array of hats that alter various aspects of your character (more damaging attacks, less damage taken, show treasure chests on the minimap, etc.), but Team Fortress 2 has that and I wouldn't classify that as an RPG either. I can't see ANY mention of the musical side of this game ANYWHERE on the Steam page which is very strange; I'd classify this game as a Musical Action game, if that's even a genre that exists.
The game places a fairly high priority in platforming, especially later in the game, and that is I think Gurumin's greatest weakness. Parin's jumps are a little hard to control, and her shadow is often not pronounced enough to tell exactly where she is located over sometimes excessively small platforms. The spastic camera, which refuses to stay put and constantly tries to center itself behind Parin, certainly doesn't help matters. Why am I given a button to immediately center the camera behind Parin if the game does this automatically every time I start to move? If I move the camera, I want it in that position until I say otherwise; several of the game's tricky jumps would be made vastly more simple if only I could set the camera at Parin's side and leave it there until after the platforming section, but if this option is available then I never found it. In the end I usually resigned myself to platforming relying entirely on the minimap; at least with the minimap there was no ambiguity as to whether I was over a platform or not.
Combat, however, is enjoyable, even if it is a bit easy (note that I have only beaten the game on Normal, and that higher difficulties might actually be...difficult). The next few sections are going to be talking about combat since it has some nuances. Parin has a standard neutral attack string and a variation if you hold in a direction while attacking, but you probably won't often be using those. Parin's dodge is extremely long and forgiving, and she gets three of them in a row; I never timed it but it has to be at least 3 full seconds of invincibility which is pretty insane in a game like this. Beyond that, one of the first special attacks you get is an attack after the dodge, and you're ALSO invincible during that attack animation, which at higher ranks adds another second and a half or so. There's little reason not to simply spam this one special technique over and over until everything in the room is dead considering that the attack itself is extremely damaging and reaches over a very wide area. Certain enemies have shields or armor on and are impervious to attack, so the armor needs to be removed by utilizing Parin's charged drill attack (this seems to be its only purpose, as the damage the charged drill attack does is pathetic even compared to normal attacks), but after that you're free to attack in whatever way you wish. The game does add in elemental effects (fire, lightning, and ice) that can be changed at a whim. Fire burns enemies and causes damage (a fairly small amount) over time, lightning slows and paralyzes enemies, and ice freezes them in place. There is also a system in place where certain enemies take more or less damage from certain elements, but at least on Normal mode this is easily ignored and the damage reduction for using the wrong element is fairly insignificant. Elemental attacks are also used in several of the game's puzzles. The only non-special attack that I used often is her homing jump attack, which is not only very useful for attacking flying enemies but is also extremely accurate (fittingly enough) and does fairly high damage. It is also, coincidentally, absolutely vital for some minigames.
One thing to note is that all special attacks in this game are performed the exact same way; rotate the character either clockwise or counterclockwise and then attack.  Doing it without dodging/jumping performs a 360 spin, doing it during a dodge performs a projectile attack (this is the room cleaner I mentioned above), and doing it during a jump performs a slam. I used a PS2-type controller, and the game is very forgiving with its detection of turns. It is, in fact, TOO forgiving, and I can't count the number of times I was jumping during platforming to attack an enemy and found myself plummeting straight into an abyss.
The last thing I have to talk about concerning combat is the drill meter. Parin uses a drill as her weapon. The drill has 4 levels (the game only counts 3 but I'll explain why I say it has 4). The higher the level of the drill, the more damage it does (some special attacks also change animations depending on its level). When the bar is filled to max you get a projectile attack every time you swing the drill; the game counts this as part of the 3rd drill level but since it's only actually available with a FILLED 3rd level and not just IN the 3rd level I count it as its own level. Now, how do you increase the drill level? The standard way is to get critical hits, and this is where the music minigame comes into play. It's actually so important a consideration in the game that I'm surprised Gurumin isn't called a Music Action game. At the top of the screen is a bar that acts as a metronome for the current music; if you time your strikes with the metronome you get critical hits, and every 100 critical hits gives you a drill level. There are also items and certain areas within stages you can use to increase your drill level, but both of these are fairly rare and for the most part you'll be relying on critical hits. This is why I say its strange the musical side of the game is so underplayed on the Steam store page.
As for music and sound...music is good. I can't think of a single song I disliked and there were several I would actually nod my head to as they played. As fits the game most of them are fast-paced and quite a few are cheery (sometimes a little overly cheery) but they didn't grate on my nerves. The sound effects are fairly simplistic, but it isn't as though this is a complicated, deep game or story so it fits the tone well. What I WILL complain about is the voice acting. It's sub-par to downright awful all across the board. I'm running out of space but suffice it to say that I didn't like anyone.
The story is cookie-cutter and saccharine (it involves giving monsters furniture to make them happy so that their happiness drives away the darkness. No, I am not oversimplifying it), and though I rolled my eyes during much of it I never hated it. Characterization is rather sparse, but then I don't think anyone came into this game expecting Catcher in the Rye.
I spent a fair amount of time complaining during this review, but the main thing to take away from this is that while the combat was simple I enjoyed it. The VAST majority of the game focuses on the combat. I didn't like the platforming but in the end the platforming is little more than how you get from one combat arena to the other. Overall I really enjoyed the game, and I heartily recommend it. It's a good game.

I played RS: Siege in Alpha, then skipped the Beta until a little while after I realised the game had released. Since then I've bought both it's season passes and even some skins for my favourite operators. Is this because I'm a pawn in Ubisoft's money game? I like to think not. I got plenty of hours out of the game before the first season pass dropped, prompting me to buy it because I was enjoying the content so much. The same was true for the second season pass which even though some of its content was delayed for "Operation Health", I still enjoy and feel as if I got my money's worth.
I see alot of people complaining about Ubisoft servers or bugs, but I can't say I've encountered any in my 100 hours playtime. On the games release I had a NAT problem, but that has been fixed and since I've not been turned away by anything gamebreaking or even annoying. The game has worked fine for me and still entertains me.
To compare it to similar games; Siege is like the tactics of SWAT, the gamemodes of CSGO and the mechanics of Battlefield had a baby. It's graphics are nice, it's weapons are nice, it's tactical feel and drive are great and actually make for a good team-based game for once.
Overall I can't fault Ubisoft Montreal in any major way. Sure, maybe they could deliver on some DLC sooner, but the fact they release all Maps for free and give a way for new operators to be earned is much more generous than EA or other shooters. I enjoyed the game in my 100 hours and intend to continue enjoying it for seasons to come, therefore I recommend it.
