For a Star Wars fan playing this game again, is a luxury. Old memories came back and how I defeated enemies for the first time. I remember the first time when I played it and the emotion of being part of the Geroge Lucas universe. Feeling the Force with these characters, no matter the side you choose, light or dark.
Every member of your group,  every planet has a unique story and a continuity carefully created. The chance of gaining influence with your partners and unlock certain things you will discover during the game is being played is fantastic. One of the best ideas of Obsidian and Bioware could see in other games like Mass Effect for example.
Here you play the Exile, a former Jedi knight who followed Revan during the Mandalorian wars finishing at the disaster of Malachor V. There's a lot of story about Malachor V and almost a taboo among survivors. Only 5 years passed during that terrible war where the Republic suffered a great peril. You wake up in a station called "Peragus" and something is not there. Your powers. And the quest for recovering your connection with the Force starts there. What you do will have great repercussions in the galaxy.
There are a lot of history background at the missions, and there is a big plot in the whole game and the main character is the center of this plot, and maybe others, who knows?
You can play a male or female character and depend on what you'll have different partners and romantic options. Also, the dark or light side will affect some of the decisions you'll take. You even can change the perspective in the middle of the game, I tried and worked. If I'm not mistaken, I played this game like 8 times. Yes, I'm a big fan.
You don't do Star Wars? No problem at all. No matter the knowledge of the Old or new Republic, the Force and those issues, this is one of the best roleplaying games. And you'll have to try it if you like RPGs.
The player has to think very carefully the decisions, you don't even know when you can gain dark or light side points. That will allow you to gain certain powers or not. Also gaining influence with the onboard characters could jeopardize these points or even influence with opposing members of the group.
Comparing with the award winner, Knights of the Old Republic I think this second part is even more polished than the first but the previous one seems to have more choices in travel options.
The skills and powers are well established. What I don't understand why a light side could use dark side powers. Of course, Force Storm is the best attack power, and there are some light side powers who will protect you from attacks.
They never fixed some glitches and bugs, there are one in a cave of Korriban where you can get a lot of experience, also, there's a bug. You find Kreia and after the scene if you don't have a telepathic communication with her you'll be trapped there.
I have to mention something about music and graphics. comparing actual games graphics are not the coolest, but this is an AAA game, and had the best graphics in their time.
The soundtrack is one of the best I ever listened in my life. It's just precise and perfect for every moment. I'll make a special mention about the music in Malachor V, fantastic. Try to play that part in the dark and listen carefully. Amazing and a little bit creepy.
+ Star Wars, I mean it.

Hacker Evolution is a hacking simulation game which is played in terminal. You'll use several commands to do the "hacking" and some of them are real terminal commands.This game might look similar to
in the shell, although the execution is quite different.
There are some soothing musics played in the background. You can also change the music selection by pressing F4.
The game has a dominant dark yellow/brown color in it. There are 3 separate themes in the options which will change the UI design and color. Two of them are still using dark yellow/brown dominant color while the other is dark blue colored. The UI is okay for an old game.
The game shows an intro when you start the game and give you a background story before you start a level. You don't really have to understand the story in order to finish the game although you need to read the background story to find some clue in the level. If you don't really bothered to read the story at all, you can always brute forcing (trying all combinations) your way to find what you want.
Although the story looks promising at the start, the ending is quite dissapointing. The ending suddenly adds the "Time Dimensions" concept without even any hints beforehand.
The main story has 9 levels and 1 tutorial level in total. Although there is a tutorial, the tutorial will guide you in a wrong way. Every malicious thing you do (cracking, decrypting, even fail login attempt) will give you a penalty called trace % which will be raised by 50% if you fail to do it and that's what the tutorial will ask you to do. I understand that the game wants to teach you to be careful before doing anything, but this trace %, along with other things such as money and PC upgrades (will be explained later), will be carried over the levels and this will cause trouble later on.
If you let your trace % to reach 100%, you'll have a game over. You can reduce it by paying $500. This will make money to be a very important to save yourself. However, the money in this game is limited and you are basicallay screwed up if you don't use it properly. This limitation will be an obstacle for you to explore all servers and ports because one mistake can cause a game over and makes you to restart the level. If you messed up in the previous level, you have to restart the whole game since the game autosaves after you complete a level (there is no manual save). However, there is a cheat command and money glitch to get around it. You can also backup the save manually and replace the save whenever you screwed up.
Aside from the trace %, you can also spend your money for PC upgrades. You'll need to have a proper equipment in order to avoid being traced. If you have a low PC spec and you can't hack without being traced, you can also make a bounce to other server which will give you more time before being traced. However, you can only bounce to one server three times.
Having a low PC spec also means a long waiting time. Even if you somehow manage to bounce to a lot of servers to hack a server with a very strong defense, you have to wait for a very long time for it to finish, especially if you haven't upgrade your CPU. There is a time where i have to wait for around 1 minute without doing anything since there is no fast forward option.
There are a lot of commands that you can use in the terminal. If you are not familiar with the commands, you can type "help" to list all available commands. The list might be a bit overwhelming for people who are not used with this though. Most of the commands are self explanatory like "delete" which will delete a file, and "connect" which will connect you to a server. However, there are also some commands which might confuse people who never use a terminal before such as ls (list directory) or dir (directory) and cat (concatenate). Note that these commands are real terminal command. Although there are some duplicate commands which has the same function such as ls and dir, the game fails to add "rm" command which is supposed to delete file in linux although there is a "del" command (delete file in windows) in the game.
There is also an autocomplete which is triggered with tab button. However, the autocomplete doesn't behave exactly as how a terminal is supposed to be. If there are
and
, the text will autocomplete to
when you type x and then tab just because you register
first. Luckily, you can change the autocomplete suggestion by pressing tab although sometimes the autocomplete will fail to give what you want. In addition, there is also no copy paste option in the game.
The game may seem to be redundant since you just have to find a hidden clue to go to other server to advance. In later level (well, one level to be exact), this clue will turn into a puzzle where you have to solve a hint to find the next server. However, the puzzle might be too much (although solvable) to non programmers especially since the puzzle introduces an assembly language and configuration file (and there is also an equation that can only be recognized by programmers in it
. Luckily, there is an instruction to read the assembly and the hint in the configuration file is pretty obvious if you look it properly.
The game starts in full screen by default. You can change it to windowed although you can't change its resolution. The windowed game is too tall in my screen (1366 x 768) and i can't see what i type in the terminal if i don't clear the screen since i can't see the very bottom of the screen.
In addition to the main story, there are 2 Mod/DLCs (+1 "example mod") which has around the same length. The mods requires a different strategy from the main story although unlike the main story, the mod is only difficult in the first few levels. You can also make your own mod although you can't publish the mod since there is no steam workshop.
Pros:
- 9+1 levels
- 2 bonus mod/dlc
- Mods
- PC upgrade
- Autocomplete
Cons:
- Unforgiving penalties
- No copy paste
- Unable to adjust windowed screen
- No fast forward option
- No manual save (but you can save your backup manually)

One of my most beloved online games from the early 2000s. After the official Microsoft Gaming servers were shut down, FreeAllegiance surfaced and was still being updated by fans due to the source code being released as Shared Source in 2004. Sadly as of now, the game is still only available in English. So you should be able to at least understand English to get the most out of it. ;)
In 2017, Allegiance is back for free on Steam and with it a chance to thrive again. As Allegiance is a mix between space combat simulation and RTS I'd compare it to Natural Selection (Half-Life mod), Natural Selection 2 or Tremulous (Quake mod) as this games share the same base formular but as a space combat/RTS hybrid.
Playing Allegiance since the original release through the "FreeAllegiance" period I can say that the game has a steep learning curve, but rewards patient players with a unique gameplay experience, no other space combat simulator can provide up to date. The friendly and helpful community - established between 2004 and 2017 in FreeAllegiance - is still around, so give Allegiance a try if you like the genres of space combat simulators! But be sure to grab a flight stick, first and Ripchord! ;)

Firstly, I have mixed feeling about this game. It has flaws, yes but I can overlook it. Somehow. I'm going to compare this with Borderlands 2 (I played this on PS3, so I don't have it in my library) because they almost have the same elements.
Plot:
Borderlands 2 and Shadow Warrior 2 have a decent plot, not great but decent. Borderlands 2 have that charm on each characters, and my favourites are Handsome Jack and Tiny Tina. Even though the game is lacking in plot, every character feels contributing to the plot as a whole making you feel like a badass and care for the characters in the game (even though I only care for like 3 - 4 characters in the end). Shadow Warrior 2, at least to me, doesn't have any of those. There are only 2 types of characters in here, the first one being goody-two shoes that praise you a lot and the second one being that always a♥♥♥♥♥♥half of the time. Gameplay:
Both games have a little bit difference in terms of gameplay. While borderlands 2 has the click and shoot with 4 weapons that you set beforehand, Shadow Warrior 2 has the click, slash and shoot with 8 weapons that you set and upgraded beforehand. Shadow Warrior 2 has a faster pace and more frantic than borderlands 2 because the combat gives you the advantage of having upgrades but throw you lots of demons and bunny kings to kill.
Questlines:
This is where I'm kinda dissapointed, most of the questlines in Shadow Warrior 2 feels bland in comparison with Borderlands 2. I'm not going through any spoiler (even if there is one I still wouldn't), but the questlines feels repetitive and literally ask you to go somewhere, retrive an object/kill some demons, and you'll get paid. Jokes:

Conclusion:
Shadow Warrior 2 isn't a bad game, but I feel it could be much better. However if you like a frantic FPS and have friends, I would recommend this game for you. If you just want to have some good time playing alone and probably sip some tea while at it, Borderlands 2 is a great game to explore.

SUMMARY:
Back in the days when Microsoft Game Studios was a real and active presence that gave us games like this, Mechwarrior 3, Outwars, and Crimson Skies, Allegiance was one of the first multiplayer oriented space sims to come out. Designed to work with the now defunct Zone multiplayer service (God, I'm old. Hey, remember MPlayer? or Kali? Or Gamespy?), this game offers an RTS/FPS mixup like no other. Think less Natural Selection and more like X-wing versus Tie Fighter, but each side has evolving tech trees. Strongly recommended!
IN-DEPTH:
The two main methods of play are as a combat pilot, or as the commander of the team.
AS A PILOT:
Your job is to be one of the grunts you order around with Right Click in an RTS. The commander is supposedly in charge, but, uh... if you've been on the internet for any amount of time you know how the general public reacts to any kind of authority giving orders. The team's success now rests in your sweaty, possibly anti-social hands. God help us all.
This is a space combat game, taking place on a large map with several smaller zones connected by gates. There are semi-newtonian physics involved during normal flight. There are max speeds, but WASD lets you use lateral thrust, and afterburner slides are a recommended tactic.
Your piloting goals are to kill enemies (or just force them to eject, which is really inconvenient) and keep the team's economy going long enough to get stuff to kill bases with. To win, destroy all the enemy bases. Harder than it sounds. You can fly defense as an interceptor, or deploy proximity mines to ward off assaults, but winning requires that you take the offensive in bombers or escorting capships.
Similar to C&C Renegade, another FPS/RTS, there are AI miners who try and mine resources for money. If you manage to keep them from being annihilated, they eventually return home and give everyone a cash payday. If they take too much damage, they get cold feet and run for home with empty cargo bays, so keep a close watch!
In true classic RTS form, there are powerups and cash drops, so your awareness and pilot skills do make a difference, even in the economy! Even if you think you suck, you can still contribute just by spotting enemies and harassing miners.
AS A COMMANDER:
Congratulations! As the only person with some semblance of authority, you are now the first person to be blamed for everything.
Assuming you haven't been scared off, being a commander is not really so difficult. Your job is to be the omnipotent RTS commander, with the caveat that you can only order Miners, Constructors, and automated non-player objects. You may not be able to control a player directly, but you can give them orders, make suggestions, call out sectors, and are directly commanding how the game goes for your team. You tell the miners where to go to mine Helium 3 (Money) and other special resources to build new bases. You also control what to build, where and when.
To win, you need to expand into other sectors and get down your tech tree as fast as possible in order to take down enemy bases. You can build several different types of bases, which sometimes requires special asteroids. This means that you are always feeling some kind of pressure to expand and attack certain sectors - money alone won't win it for you!
You automatically get money when the miners return home from harvesting. The tech tree is quite involved and actually varies depending on the faction you're in. Iron Coalition has better fighters, BIOS have faster scouts and stealth, just to give a couple examples.
You're not chained to the command console, and can always go and lead the charge. You can access the command console mid-flight, but be warned you will make a highly tempting target for any combat pilots.
IN CONCLUSION:
A fine space action game desperately in need of an official sequel, featuring involved RTS mechanics, great skill-based combat, and a varied game experience with different factions and maps. Strongly recommended. Especially if you still have your Microsoft Force Feedback 2 joystick.

Honestely, this game is overlooked. And it's a crime.
So what IS Nihilumbra? Without Spoiling anything, its about a little blob-thing (named Born, apparently) who tries to escape from the Void and make himself exist in the world. Does he suceed? Play the game. You'll find out.
Gameplay-wise, it's a simple 2D Platformer/Puzzle game, implementing the use of different elements to continue your journey. This is definitely a game that you want to take your time on, not because its difficult, but just to take it all in.

Originally a Japanese PC game released in 2004 later ported, and translated for the PSP in 2007.
Gurumin: A Monstrous Adventure can be looked at as a "Kids" version of a Ys game (another great ARPG series from Nihon Falcom).
This game is an Action RPG Platformer, with a unique addition that allows you to attack to the beat of the music playing for critical strikes.
---
The game has a great clean and colorful look (but doesn't bleed out colors unnecessarily like other Japanese games), that still holds up well even today but now in 1080p, 60 frames.
***I'd really recommend turning off DoF as well as the Blur effect & BackBuffer (flickering in the title/main menu may occur with this one), to get rid of the "fuzzy" look many players are experiencing. Forcing AA & 16x AF on your control panel is also recommended.
The controls are responsive, and simple to use.
You simply go around Hack 'n' Slashing your enemies to the beat of the music with combos, while going through simple platforming and puzzles. Please bare in mind that when this game first came out, there was no xinput. Although gamepad support was added by Mastiff, you might need to configure your controller with the game config.
***But I can confirm that with a 360 controller or wrapper, you shouldn't need to do anything besides changing [Show Forward] & [Show Enemy] to the Stick Buttons.
The music was created by the Falcom Sound Team jdk internal band, which also made the original soundtracks for most of their releases (Ys series, The Legend of Heroes series, et cetera). So you can expect a great listen all throughout the game.
A must have for any ARPG lover, or Falcom fan.

It's a top down MMO space shooter with a bit of depth to it. 150 level cap and lots of resource gathering for upgrades. Flux is this game's currency used to buy ships and other nice non-essential things. You can either buy flux with real money or you will have to grind missions/daily logins for it in-game.
*Plenty of different ships, some have unique weapons pre-installed on them
*Plenty of weapons, over 100 of them and they are all quite fun to play around with
*Artifacts are this game's form of loot to help improve your ship's stats in general, they are randomly generated too
*PvP matches although it needs some improvements to keep things more balanced
*Open world PvP where you could of course take on higher/lower level players
*Boss battles that are quite tough, especially if you haven't got a good setup or a strategy for taking them on
*Storyline quests, gives you something to work toward as it takes you through all the systems
*Timed missions, these are randomly generated quests that give you some decent rewards
*Daily login and missions give you some cool rewards for minimal effort
*Playerbase isn't very large and not sure whether it will increase by much
*Lag spikes and desync seem to happen a bit of the time, especially when picking up lots of loot
*Boring for players that constantly want something new and fresh every time they play it as it's very grindy
*Crew feature which is used to upgrade your artifacts needs serious improvement (Takes too long to train them up)
*Co-op survival while fun, needs to be improved so that exp loss on death isn't something that puts people off of it
*Grindy, as mentioned before. If you want new ships, upgrades or levels, you will need to grind quite a bit for them
*Devs, apparently they are not interested in changing or adding much to the game (From what people say)
*Bugs, quite a lot of them and I'm not talking about the ones in-game that you shoot at
*Upgrading, requires too much resources after you've made previous upgrades to things on your ship. Prevents you from investing and experimenting with other weapons which ruins the weapon variety
Overall, this game has a lot of potential to be something amazing. It has loads of variety in weapons, ships, artifacts and strategies to go with them but it gets boring fast if you don't like grinding out levels and missions. Personally, I enjoy it very much and can see myself being part of this game for a good while. I do hope that the devs put in some more effort to make this game the best it possibly can be as well as add in some more co-op related stuff but for now, the game is good for what it is.
I would recommend trying it at least.

I feel that a forewarning before you begin playing is required..
When it comes down to it, due to how the game is laid out, it makes it like the narrator through the game is speaking to you, portrayed as your cute blobby character within the game. It's quite harsh and for anyone with a low self esteem, it can really be deterring to play, it was for me at quite a few points, too. Something of which I don't believe was thought through very thoroughly. It however evolves as your character does within each stage of the game. With that been said, let us continue!
The only thing I can draw a comparison to is perhaps Limbo, Portal, Oddworld: Abe’s Oddysee, Abyss Odyssey and partially Contrast.
Now, starting with a basic breakdown, you are part of the void (basically your replacement to being in a womb) a place of darkness and decay, and are born to be a little shapeless voidling.. You want to explore and be part of something bigger than yourself. Typically you let that take over and begin a journey that pulls you away from the void, however, this does not please the void as one does not simply leave it.
You begin by taking a human like shape, to feel as though you fit in the human world easier, while the voice continues to tell you that you are stupidly deluding yourself for trying to think that you could do such a thing. You ignore it and continue on through little puzzles along the way, and the further you go through, the more you learn about yourself and the world around you. The first ability you get is a blue goop, basically an icy slide (hence the little comparison to Portal I was half expecting the next one to be orange), anywho, this aids you to get through the next few levels of puzzles and annoying timing levels however the puzzles themselves are well thought out for the most part, and give you a decent sense of satisfaction and relief when you figure them out. You continue on to discover 5 other colors, all of which provides you something new to help you through each of the changing environments tailored to each color, (blue-ice, green-forest, brown-desert, red-volcanic, yellow-electricity, purple-void).
However, the fact that the void is closely following to recapture you means everything in it's path is destroyed. The world your voidling blob has come to love is being destroyed due to them being frivolous, leaving your character feeling responsible.
Final summation; in all, it's a really well put together puzzle/platformer. The scenery is gorgeous but can sometimes be a little repetitive. Music fits in amazingly with the atmosphere being slightly abrasive yet quite immersive, puzzles are escalated in difficulty slightly too quickly with it going from casual to incredibly complicated and requiring a need to have mastered all the colors you've been given, and lastly the initially discouraging narrator. All in all though, it's a worthwhile experience to play through and on completion, it gives you even more reply value, having to fix what you've destroyed.

This is Star Wars Noir - difficult to digest and somewhat bitter.
Like the previous game, it is slow in parts, but this is one of the deepest and profound stories I've experienced. Heck, it's even somewhat meta. The first game is bombastic and grand - quintessential Star Wars. This one is subdued and brooding and it shows in the colour palate, the music, and the mood of your companions.
May the Force be with you? Must it? Is the Force even worth it if it just seems to cause suffering to ripple outwards from well-meaning Jedi?

Arma 3 is a realistic military simulator set in the near future (2030's), now you may already know this but what you probably don't know is the extent that this game can extend beyond that!
Now, while it is true that this game can be a military simulator, and a damn good one at that as battles can be frightening, patrols can go from peaceful to deadly in seconds, and large scale battles on the games base maps Altis, Stratis and as of recently Malden can break out between the major factions, mods can change everything!
This games community is outstanding for turning an already fun and realistic military simulator into zombie survival, wars between more factions than what the base game already offers, weapons and vehicles of all kinds, roleplaying mods and so much more. This game is WHAT YOU MAKE IT TO BE! Mods can greatly enhance your experience!
That being said, the vanilla game is still absolutely great in itself. It provides a range of weapons and vehicles and customizable loadouts. The game comes with its own training and boot camp to help you get set with the games controls and strategies because if you know anything about Arma, it is a difficult game. If you come from Call of Duty or other fast-paced shooters, do not expect Arma to be of the same pace as it is far slower paced. The game is simply not forgiving.
The game delivers a dynamic feel by allowing the player to make their own missions in the Eden editor, with tons of scripts to help customize almost every aspect of your mission. Also the game comes with a real time editor called Zeus, making dynamic campaigns to give the players in the game a truly unique experience!
As for cons, this game might be a bit taxing on your computer. While out of battle you may run at 60 fps or above, your frames will drop once you start getting into larger and larger battles. Low fps is something you'll have to get used to, and another problem with this is it makes cqb combat a bit sluggish when compared to games like Squad.
Also, since you can play with and against AI, they can be quite stupid at times, especially your team AI, but the enemy AI consists of professional special operations marksman who can snipe you from 300m away with a pistol (I wish I was lying).
However, despite these cons, the game can still be enjoyable for those seeking a realistic military experience, and to those who use mods to seek other experiences. I highly suggest you find people to play with as this game can become much better with team effort and just playing with friends in general.
I highly recommend this game, though it isn't without problems. I hope this review has helped you out in buying or not buying this game, and I apologize if this review seems all over the place or if any of it doesn't make sense. It truly is a game you have to experience before you completely judge it. Thanks for considering my review, and I wish you the best of luck in your decision to purchase this game or not!

It is a beautiful thing in a way.
It's a far more ambitious game than its predecessor. Its failings are far bigger than in KOTOR 1, but its successes are also far sweeter. As a darker and more complex game than its predecessor, it sets the perfect tone for a sequel.
The production schedule of this game was insane. Obsidian had to make the game in a fraction of the time they should have had. As a result, much content in the game was cut. An entire planet was removed form the game to cut down on development time. Once the cut content is modded back in, one can truly see the opus that Obsidian had planned to craft, and it is breathtaking.
To make the most of the experience I would recommend the following.
Play KOTOR 1 first.
Install the Sith Lords Restored Content Mod
Install the M4-78 Restoration Project Mod
Be patient. The first 2.5 hours or so of the game take place in Peragus, a dreadfully boring place. After that section of the game is over, it becomes far better.
If you can do that, then I can unequivocally recommend the game for Star Wars and RPG fans alike.

Not only did they do all this, but they updated the windows version of the game to receive the benefits of this too. Aspyr went above and beyond for this port. They deserve no less than the highest praise.

This Mount & Blade was poorly done.  It just doesn't compare to its predecessors.
To start off, I'd like to say that Fire & Sword has an incredible problem with experience points and leveling, and on top of that, if you want to level up, you've got to kill countless people with firearms- It doesn't matter what armor you wear, damage taken can be as low as 16 points in heavy armor to a full 60 with none.  You get shot in this game, your fun is over.  The big problem there is that firearms are actually quite common to everyone except you...  Want a good one?  Be prepared to spend $2000 or more.  In addition to that, when you're actually trying to "aim", be prepared for ridiculous misses, while the enemy seems to have no trouble hitting you from halfway across the map.
Aside from the experience points problem and the stacked cards against you in the gun-crazed Eastern European atmosphere, the balance for the game feels a bit off, and nothing is as "pretty" here as Warband.  The map is overall darker, the bandits seem less regional as they are in Warband, and the game feels less alive than Warband.  My biggest problem with it?  It just isn't worth it when an infuriating mistake occurs.  Ride by a reloading musketman, put the reticle over him, miss about 2 paces from him, and get shot in the back as you're riding away...  When you finally *DO* kill him, you get 30 experience points.  Yay you.  23 more to go before you'll level up!
Mistakes like these show how little thought and reception was given to community concerns.  It's a dumbed down model, and I've been pushed away by the ridiculous level-up problems.
In addition to these slated issues, another problem is in regard to armor.  Armor is completely unbalanced, and much of the decent equipment is ridiculously overpriced.  There seems to have been no thought put into balancing the economy in that regard, which makes it nigh-impossible to outfit yourself to survive a few bullets.  So how do you deal with these gun crazy fools when your armor- and that which you manage to buy- barely protects you?  Spend about 20 minutes circling 13 Brigands until they run out of ammo, and you'll see my point.
This M&B is a definite Thumbs Down.  It just wasn't well-thought-out, and I don't think development was very receptive to the community on its issues, and there are many.

Being "cheesed" by certain classes and abilities can be frustrating to new players and people with a decent amount of playtime it the game. Biggest issue for me was the fact that they give you an option for a $40 season pass, but if you never read up on any articles online about this "pass" then you wouldn't know that everyone gets the DLC that comes out anyway. The only incentive for the season pass is if you want visuals and certain gearscore items/heroes before everyone else. No sense in buying it if you want a DLC bundle, you'll get them anyway.
Even with these issues, I would recommend For Honor to anyone that enjoys medieval melee combat, likes a challenge, and wants something new and different from the influx of rushed FPS's and the like.

SOMA is a game exploring through virtual interactivity what it means to be alive. Is it about freedom or is it about restriction ? No matter what you believe the game will twist those long lived dilemas with a convincing sci fi plot full of details about robotics, AI and the human brain. The game plays like a video game version of a Philip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥short novels, where the feeling of existential despair mixed with some cynical humour bends what your concept of reality is. The voice acting is especially great, and fleshes the character interactions out in a very convincing and pleasing way, especially considering how terrifying the game can be, you will appreciate every little word told.
But the game isn't only about interacting with a narrative inside a confined environment. This game is about mustering your courage to go on despite weird creatures lurking just around the corner. You can't just sit there and wait until the monsters disappear, because they won't, you have to get out and find a way around them. There are times I wanted to quit the game, uninstall it and never think about it ever again because of the terror I felt wandering through the dark, damp, twisted underwater corridors with unspeakable horrors at my heels. But the game is well designed, it makes you terrified but it doesn't frustrate you: death or being stuck is a rare occurence. The game manage to make you feel lost and desperate, yet you will always end up finding your way and reaching some "safer" haven to recollect your wits and breath.
Nothing beats the feeling of finishing a particularly terrifying section of the game. You always get rewarded for your courage by involved conversations, tidbits of informations, some interactions with machineries or computers and new goals that will give you back all the strength you used up. The plot and overall design of the game are so tight and well made, you will want to both flee and go on forward in equal measure. I can safely say this is my favorite horror game.

I rarely play horror games. I'm not the type of guy that enjoys getting scared. But I gotta say, Amnesia: the dark descent is a damn good game.
The atmosphere is absolutely fantastic. You always feel like something or someone is constantly keeping an eye on you, waiting to snap you at any second. This paranoid feeling made me traverse the game in extreme caution, although there were few times I actually encountered anything. The monsters are well-designed, scary and dangerous. They may not be as smart as you, but don't underestimate them. They will break you.
The story is pretty good. I'm always eager to find the next note, revealing more and more about Daniel's dark past. The way that the game slowly uncoveres the backstory as you progress is very well done, although I wonder why Daniel had to scatter all the notes over the entire castle.
Also, there are no cheap jumpscares. That's a win in my book.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent is a survival horror video game by Frictional Games, released for Microsoft Windows, Mac OS X, and Linux platforms. The game features a protagonist named Daniel exploring a dark and foreboding castle, while avoiding monsters and other obstructions as well as solving puzzles. The game was critically well received, earning two awards from the Independent Games Festival and numerous positive reviews.
Originally released independently via online distribution, the game has since been published in retail by 1C Company in Russia and Eastern Europe, as well as THQ in North America. A collection of five short stories set in the world of Amnesia, written by Mikael Hedberg and illustrated by the game's concept artists, was also made available. In addition, the game's soundtrack is available for purchase and a free content expansion Justine has been released as well as many fan-made expansions and stories for its unique "Custom Story" gamemode.

My entire previous review was not actually true because there was a critical flaw in the game where the sky and sun were not working.  So I had to redo my video now that we could see, and it completely changes the game.  Sight is an amazing thing!
So now I can see even fewer flaws in this game.  Now I will only complain about the game's performance.  I have built a new computer and I haven't tried a whole lot of games out yet but this one is one of 5 I have tried and it performs very poorly.  New system is a 24 core Xeon E5-2685 (12 core dual socket) with 32GB DDR4, Radeon R9 290.  When I play GTA5 or Witcher 3, I get activity in maybe 5-6 cores and overall it's like 1% CPU usage.  With this game for whatever reason it uses ALL of the cores.  When I'm not recording, it was like 40% split across them all and when I was recording it was 80% (across 24 cores!!!).  Not exactly sure what is going on, it could be just a unity thing, I will try out some more unity games today.  But I figured it was worth mentioning that there is something unusual in how this game is threaded.
Oh, 5:13pm edit: I was also getting like 20 FPS in GTA5 just now somehow randomly and was getting 60FPS yesterday.  Turned out that the new AMD Crimson driver was cooking my video card by locking the fan at like 10%.  So the card was at 100 degrees the whole time and if it caused bad FPS in GTA it probably caused bad FPS in Resilience.  So keep that in mind, I need to make a third video now... *sigh*, but at least in this 2nd video you can at least see what it's all about.  Stay tuned.  But I have not known of an overheating video card to give 80% CPU usage on its own so I still think the game has a threading issue.
That's about it.  So far it looks like a fun game.  I'll add to this more later I just wanted to remove my complaints about the pitch black world, it doesn't make sense once you play the updated version!

A truly horrifying game.
When I started this game I had no idea what I was in for. I knew, from simply browsing youtube gaming channels, that this was a popular game, but I had no idea as to why. I watch clips of videos where people would scream while playing the game, so I simply assumed it was a jump scare game that sought to exploit the trend that was going on during the time, similar to Slenderman and so on.
I can tell you though, after completing the game, that this is not the case. Does this game scare the crap out of you and make you whimper like a cancer ridden puppy?
Yeah, it does that.
But it does so much more. The story is amazing and enticing. Few games are able to get me to read all of the back story that they have laying around. Bioshock is another example of this, I spent considerable time to seek out the recordings in that game to get the entire story, that s how much I loved it. I experienced that same feeling in this game.
This game also presents many puzzles, an element I did not know was part of this game. The puzzles, though mostly simple, are fun and rewarding.
The game's level and sound design are also marvelous I should mention. The terror of the beast lurking around the corner would be nothing if the beast had the sound of a rubber duck, and the corner had the appearance of a bus stop. No, this game seeks to draw out every sense of fear in you. The only moments of relief you get are in those brief moments of narration, savour those I tell you. (A very similar feeling to F.E.A.R.)
I won't drag on here. It's a terrifically terrifying game.
Though if you're a homosexual and open about it, I don't recommend buying this game, it'll put you right back in the closet.

I should mention first that RTS games are the games I dislike the most. I really don't like the whole idea behind going down a memorized checklist for the best builds as quickly as possible. I just don't have the time or patience for that. That said, this game isn't bad so far. I've only played offline because of the above reasons and I don't think this game will change my mind on RTS as a genre. But, there is something about this game that is keeping me hooked where other major titles haven't (Starcraft, Warcraft, CoH, etc). Maybe it's the complete lack of combat or the unique focus on economics. Or that the skirmishes themselves are very short.
It probably helps to have some background knowledge of economics going in, but it's not required. The tutorials do a good job of explaining the basics. And, while I do find myself pausing a lot (and kinda wish there was a turn-based mode as a result), I haven't felt overwhelmed yet. And I appreciate the developers giving options for turning off the black market. If it does end up turning into the typical RTS “build order checklist”, that will be disappointing and I'll update my review accordingly. But, for now, I'd say it's worth the $13.59 price tag. The AI has been competent and the individual games, and approaches as a player, have been fairly unique.

This is a nice update of the Falcom classic. It is much more playable than it's PSP counterpart which Mastiff first brought overseas. The camera in that version was pushed in much too close to the player character, severely limiting your field of view. This update fixes that by not only going back to the PC original FOV, but also adds widescreen to the mix.

Theres an issue where the right-stick camera controls can't be mapped on directinput pads, but can be worked around by setting shoulder buttons to rotate the camera.  Another thing I noticed is the AA options either don't work at all or crash the game (@ 4x). I hardly noticed edge aliasing in-game anyway.
Since posting this review, someone in the forums discovered that disabling certain options, like DOF, might allow AA to work. I haven't tested this.

First of all don't let the negative reviews sway you from playing this game and even if you decide to play a different version of this, PLAY THIS GAME AND SEE FOR YOURSELF.
For me I played the old school/SNES version as well as this one and I find this one to be better/just as good for several reasons.
1.  One of my favorite character has been buffed and you don't have to wait for his skill to charge up which is mighty awkward if your playing active mode and this is due to the new ui layout.
2.  The battle UI has been improved in my opinion and frees up with alot of space and if you perfer the old style then you can switch to it anyway.
3.  The spirites look smooth and I didn't notice a thing picking this up infact when I looked at the older graphics I couldn't stand it of course this is a matter of opinion.
4.  Content that is exclusively avaliable to this version and the GBA version which are basically end-game dungeons.
5.  Exclusive to the IOS/mobile version is that you can auto-battle doubling the battle speed and making each character do it's previous move.  As a lazy person I tend to pace through final fantasies and just auto-ATTACK everything that is not a boss.  With this system I'm able to better utilise and enjoy the powerful and diverse magic and summons.  For me this is game changing and makes the game so much more interesting.
Keep in mind alot of the upsets of this new part is about lazy work on the visuals which I'm not very observant off but you might be so consider that seperately from my judgement of this port.
Now onto the part why Final Fantasy 6 is a great game.
It seems theres a theory that the first final fantasy sets the standard for most and as majority seem to believe ff7 is the best game and I started on final fantasy 7 BUT this did not stop me from rating ff6 as one of the best final fantasys.
1.  Character development and the large cast of characters you can play is insane, 14 characters! Most characters also has a large diversity of personality/backstory and it's entertaining the trials they face and how they react to it.
2.  The main antagonists of this game can be rage-inducing and it makes you wanna beat them even more whilst one of the smaller antagonist is very comical.
3.  Battle system is pretty decent and stand out from the other rpgs of it's age.    Each character has it's own playstyle but we also find the ability to cross-over skills/weapons as the game progresses.
4.  End-game content is decent and personally my favorite part of any final fantasy is near the end where you start to build the best arsenal of weapons ready to kick the final bosses butt.  This has a relatively large amount of enjoyable stuff to do to prepare for that.
5.  By the time I has finished all the side quest the transition to the end game was smooth as, there was minimal grinding for me as oppose to alot of final fantasies (5/10) where the final boss is somewhat awkwardly forcing u to grind unless you copy a speedrun perfectly.

Edit: Most of this stuff is fixed now, so it's pretty good. I'll just leave the original review below for posterity.
The game might be good, but I'm not sure if it actually is, because this port is abysmal.
First, control mapping. You can't map anything to a gamepad's triggers, the right stick doesn't work in-game, and there's no D-pad support. Movement with a stick is awkward, as 99% of the stick's range is for walking while only fully pressed out is for running. For the keyboard, you can only pick from a small selection of keys made available to you, for some bizarre reason. You can't even properly play the game with just a gamepad, as the opening menus require you to hit enter on the keyboard, as the gamepad won't work for them.
The AA option simply doesn't work. Even forcing AA through video card settings hasn't worked for some people.
There are very few resolution options.
It's currently dub-only (though easy enough to mod).
Tutorials all display mouse & keyboard controls, even if you're using a gamepad.
Hell, just look at the forums, there's plenty more issues listed, and there's no need for me to copy paste what other people have already pointed out.
I've heard plenty of good things about Gurumin, and as a Falcom game I expect it to be quite good, but I can't possibly recommend it until the port is fixed.

Other issues include the fact that upgrades gets much, much more expensive as you upgrade anything else. So this game gets grindy fast. To get the amount of resource you need to upgrade, you need to collect raw materials. As mentioned earlier, expect lots of your raw materials to be lost because either a sudden death or after a long skirmish. Progression on this game gets crawlingly slow, fast. Especially if you died with loads of resource with you(there's also no stash/bank to deposite these raw resources).
The most often arguments that people defend this game isn't pay to win because you can get flux for free. Well, true, but you also don't get much for free, and everything important in this game cost flux:
-Every ship cost flux (good ones cost several thousand, and you only get a few dozen per day depending on the day and amount you grinded)
-upgrade reset cost flux (first one is free, but those after cost 200 flux)
-protection from raw resource loss via death cost flux(for a duration, not perm)
-bigger pickup radius cost flux(for a duration, not perm)
This game could have been fun, but the extreme grind, and heavy penalty for those who don't pay is just too much. Avoid this game for its cheap cash grab.

is one of my favourite games of all time - in that way, it very much lives up to my love for its predecessor. The two tie for the #1 spot on my all-time favourite single-player game, and are cumulatively my favourite story ever, as far as I can say off the top of my head.
(NOTE: TL;DR at bottom.)
KotOR II is a third-person RPG game, with largely turn-based combat.
Whilst I certainly have a few problems with it, I truly believe that this game (as well as KotOR) is a game that any die-hard Star Wars
RPG enthusiast need to experience.
I'll break this review up into a few short segments based around the story in particular
, and will be reviewing this from a largely biased position, as I've been a fan of this franchise for over a decade. I'm new to the whole reviewing thing too, so forgive any mistakes on my part. For those of you who are just looking for a
, here are the pros and cons:
-Carefully crafted story, one that manages to touch the heart of most die-hard SW fans in a very powerful way. It’s absolutely great in just about every aspect, and it does something no other game does – it paints in grey strokes about the nature of the Force, not just ‘good’ and ‘bad’.
-Aesthetic and visuals hold up in the majority of places, considering its age. Just don’t look at the back of the Ebon Hawk, whatever you do. It’s certainly no stunner, however – if you’re cool with a lot of somewhat muddy textures you’ll be fine.
-Fans of the first game won’t have their love for the first game cast into the dirt like a dead corpse. KotOR II respects the first game and doesn’t undermine it. On an unrelated note, the same isn’t the case with the MMO.
-There’re some goddamn hilarious and exceptional characters. HK-47 kicks♥♥♥♥♥
-Combat is pretty damn neat, and becomes more satisfying as you progress through the game. Not everyone will love it, though.
Throughout a lot of the game, you may find yourself doing busywork that takes far too long based almost always on where you have to go. A certain mission sends you back and forth through an entire city twice, which is infuriatingly needless. Additionally, any who were a fan of the “RETURN TO EBON HAWK” feature will have to do without this time around.
There are times when your goal is not clear. The mission overview page could rely a little less on my memory, as it often lists only what I’ve done and what *will* happen, but not what I need to do.
Not all will be a fan of the UI, or the aesthetic – though personally, I like them both. There are places where textures go beyond horrific, but thankfully the majority of the game is free from that.
Thanks to Disney, the game technically isn’t canon. The most we’ve gotten in terms of that is a reference to a planet in the original game, as far as I know. I don’t know why playing non-canon stuff would be an issue, but I imagine someone out there will have a problem with it in one way or another. “Ugh, I’ve tainted myself with “extended universe” filth!”
Music can bug out and become repetitive.
Audio can fluctuate at times, forcing you to rip off your headset and smash your ‘lower volume’ key with a clenched fist.
Voice acting noticeably varies in quality. At times certain characters will suddenly sound as though they’re a different person (because it *is* a different person behind the voice). It ruins my immersion, I tell you!
Some characters could use a little love.
---
(Don't worry, I'm not going to spoil anything.)
This is the jewel of the game - again, much like its predecessor. KotOR II has a story that tugs at my heart, in no small part due to KotOR. If you want to delve into a world that’s chock full of lore surrounding the Force as well as the Star Wars universe at large, then KotOR II is the world for you.
Now, as a recommendation before I go any further, the story of KotOR II is hugely complemented by the first game. Whilst it isn’t necessarily crucial to play KotOR first and KotOR II is perfectly capable of standing on its own legs, there are quite a few references to characters and the plot that won’t quite make sense, which would be a travesty in my eyes. KotOR itself, though, certainly has a story that stands better by itself than KotOR II could, as KotOR II makes references that without the existence of KotOR would make far less sense and have barely any impact.
If you’re someone that takes a great interest in the Force, paying attention to key details in both games will go a long way.
*Sorry for spamming “KotOR” there.
The intertwined stories of the two games intimidate me, as a wishfully aspiring author.
Now, whilst this opinion is subjective, I genuinely believe that the story (including the first game) lives up to the movie saga itself – an opinion I’m sure I’m to receive a lot of flak for.
However, there is absolutely no doubt that the lore of KotOR II is immense, and if coupled with lore from KotOR, they far surpass the lore in the saga – I suspect that nearly all who’ve taken their time with this game(s) will agree with me.
There is little I can say about the story without spoiling it, so I can really only recommend that you experience it for yourself. The ‘protagonist’ of the full story is to this day my favourite character in anything. Yes, I even like them more than the likes of Vader, Master Chief and Solid Snake. (to be fair I’ve only played a bit of Metal Gear.)
Perhaps that’s because I was a lot younger when I first played KotOR, but I stand by my love for the protagonist.

The plot of KotOR II keeps the pace going and cuts off loose ends from KotOR, resulting in a very tidy story, with a small few exceptions – important questions that the more curious players may have asked themselves in the first game have been answered in a very satisfying way. It doesn’t need to stand on KotOR’s plot - the story of the Exile is just as enthralling as that of the former game.

There are noticeable improvements on character development in this game. The characters that surround you on your journey are very in-depth, and less predictable than the previous game’s characters were.
A few welcome faces from KotOR also join the mix, something that strummed my nostalgia-guitar to a mellow tune – if you were a fan of say, T3-M4 and HK-47, you’ll be pleased to know they’re back.
The only issue I can say I have with this is that you may not get a chance to interact fully with all the characters in one playthrough, especially if it’s your first time. Then again, that’s what replays are for, right?
This comes down to the player, for the most part. The sooner you get into high gear, the sooner you can blitz through the story if you want that. Given that it’s a game full of stuff to loot, chances are the pacing will be right for you – whether you want to get it over and done with – running past loot – or if you want to take your time and soak in the world.

Now that the hype is gone and the bugs slightly fixed, let's have a proper review.
Before reading this, please note that I absolutely hate the practice of microtransactions. However, that doesn't entirelly kill For Honor's status as a great game.
So what is For Honor in the first place?
Simply put, it's a game where you pick up a sword, start swinging it wildy, then curse and swear as your character misses and goes all over the place. Then you realize you need to understand the entire concept of this game.
But first, IF YOU DO NOT OWN A CONTROLLER, I'd advise that you stay away from this game in the event that you rage and smash your keyboard.
Although not exactly a fan of controllers, I found it way easier to use the controller when playing For Honor. Perhaps it's just the design of the game, perhaps it's just the layout and how buttons work. Another game which I might compare this problem to would be Dark Souls--you need a controller, mouse and keyboard won't quite cut it.
Gameplay wise, it's typical Rock, Scissors, Paper.
Opponent comes at you with a stance (1 out of 3 possible stances).
You come at your opponent with a stance as well(1 out of the 3 possible too).
He hits, you hit, blocks, counters, parries, throws are all thrown into the mix.
It's honestly pretty fun.
Although there exists a campaign in the game, I found myself unable to finish it after a few hours--I'm pretty sure the campaign is there just to show you the ropes, before throwing you into multiplayer where the real raging and laughing can begin.
You pick 4 x 3 classes, 4 classes per faction (Knights, Samurai, Vikings). Each class is pretty much unique and it's really up to you decide which is best for you.
Oh wait, here comes the part of the game where everyone hates.
Typical Ubisoft. MICROTRANSACTIONS.
In a paid game.
I swear this nonsense started in AC:Unity, and it's apparently here to stay.
Paid $70 for this game? Cool! Now we've blocked 9 of the 12 possible characters to play at launch. Want to unlock them? Progress deeper into the game, or you know...pay $30 to unlock them on the spot.
Clap. Clap. Clap.
Apart from that, comes the P2P connection issues.
No dedicated servers, you're going to have to pray that your host doesn't rage quit, or doesn't have a rubbish Internet connection.
In some games, it was pretty fun and smooth, in others however, I literally had a disconnect midfight.
Let's get back to more positive stuff.
The voice acting in this game is pretty great, apart from the female viking, which just wants to make me laugh for some strange reason. Soundtrack is good, but not memorable. Graphics are incredibly incredible for a game of this scale. However, there are some notable renders which have been made simple, probably for process-saving purposes.
Overall, your eyes and ears will be pretty much in for a treat (provided your system can run this game on max) as you play this game.
All in all, For Honor is a really great game.
I would recommend it for anyone that wants a nice hack and slash action.
But do take into consideration that you'll have to use a controller, get lucky with P2P connections, and most importantly, stand the shady practices of a paywall behind an AAA game.
Take into account the difference between developers and publishers. They made a great game, just that the publishers decide to be greedy and load microtransactions into it.

Shadow Warrior 2 is a great game, it's a different game from Shadow Warrior 2013 which is the reason why some people can find SW2 disappointing, however I think SW2 is still a fun and proper Shadow Warrior game if you can set aside some questionable gameplay features that should be changed/improved if a sequel is to be made.
Pros:
- One of the best fast paced FPS combat system out there, espectially swordplay, hugely improved from SW2013 which was already decent.
- Excellent visual design, enemy and environment design are simply one of the best.
- Great music.
- Co-op. It's not actually implemented perfectly, but it gets the job done. It's also optional because playing solo can be better.
- Rich enemy variety.
- Great skill system with a large variety of weapons to build your own playstyle.
- Good replayability value.
- Fortune cookie.
Neutral:
- The plot is actually decent and well-written enough, but it's not well executed (incohesive) and a tad too over the top compared to SW2013. Personally I'm fine with the story and the humors but I think not many people like it and it's really not as good as SW2013.
- Procedural generation maps, it's a love-hate feature for me, I prefer the good old linear, hand placed, proper designed maps. But as mentioned, the environment are beautifully designed and it helps the game become more replayable, it also plays well with the plot and the playtime. But after awhile you will realize it's just the same 3 maps (forest, city, town) over and over with slight difference, I hope this is something the dev will change or improve in the sequel.
Cons:
- Gem and loot system aka quantity over quality game design, probably my most hated feature of this game, it's not a bad idea but it was badly implemented. There are just too many gems to choose and they are all over the place in term of design as well. They are also a big distraction, every now and then you have to stop shooting things and spend a HEFTY time to pick and choose proper gems for a bunch of weapons you have if you want to keep up with the difficult. I think the reason why games like Shadow Warrior 2013 or DOOM 2016 stand out because it's not trying to be a Borderlands or a COD game, but in this case the dev tried to make it a Borderlands game which is something I think they shouldn't go with for the sequel.
- Long loading time, it's literally Witcher 3 loading time.
- Vague ending, I don't hate cliffhanger endings that much but SW2's ending is too abruptly and vague.

I loved the first game, but I'm not impressed with this second iteration, even though it is much prettier. I'll try to explain why.
The first Shadow Warrior game was an arcade style shooter with fancy sword fights, cool magical powers, and a pretty cliche, yet funny story, which developed logically. The main characters had some pretty good back and forth going most of the time, and Wang's one liners were usually lame, but funny.
Shadow Warrior 2 just ...
.
First of all, the game feels like a Borderlands clone, with strong influences from the MMO genre. You teleport to different areas willy nilly, fight constantly respawning monsters, and generally manage your inventory trying to find the best gear possible (weapons and upgrades). Also gone are most of your previous magical powers, which is BS to say the least. Sword fighting is now much more one-dimensional, and less refined. You hack away at enemies rather than suspending a bunch of them in the air with your abilities, and sending a single energy wave through them, killing them all.
There's also a main "town" that you always return to, where you pick up new quests, which are marked with an exclamation mark on your minimap. Totally in the spirit of Shadow Warrior, and not, say, WoW, right? Oh, wait.
But I could almost live with all this if it weren't for the fact that the heart and soul of the game are just ... dead. Wang was always straddling the line between bad-a$$ one liners, and lame comments. But now? He's always trying to be super cocky, usually to the detriment of the character.
Following the second mission, Wang becomes host to a second soul through a very contrived reason. The story feels so forced and weird that it manages - in only the first couple of hours - to make the first game seem a masterpiece by comparison. And this is where things really go down hill.
The soul you are burdened with belongs to the daughter of the Yakuza boss. She is some sort of genius who had infiltrated Zilla's corporation, and became his protege, but is caught spying, and punished by being injected with a poison which opens her up to demonic possession or something. And she is a grade-A, entitled, queen-bee, mean-girls-villain type b!tch.
Literally every other word out of her mough is a patronizing line about Wang being a brain-dead, over-muscled, insert-expletive-here loser, usually uttered in a hysterial, near scream. For example:
Do you have my item?
Give him the item!
Your contact was dead.
That's a shame. So the item is lost?
Just give him the f***ing item, you !d!ot!
The trail was not completely dead.
Give him the item!!! GAHHHH! *insert incoherent screams of rage and frustration here as the conversation continues*
The Yakuza second in command is also a raging b!tch who calls Wang a
-among other terms of endearment - for no discernable reason except to emphasize that she's in charge, and he's the scum she gets to walk all over. For example, she'll send Wang after some drug manufacturing competitors in order to "send a message". Seems pretty clear that she wants them dead. He kills them, then she chews him out for having followed her vague, shadowy instructions:
. It goes on for a while.
I simply do not understand what the developers though this kind of cr@p would add to the game, other than a compelling reason to stop playing it. Is this their twisted idea of what strong female characters should be like? Jesus.
In the first game
, what the heck happened here? The assassin twins showed him a certain measure of respect, and even Zilla acknowledged that Wang is supremely competent. Now we have to endure these sort of insulting diatribes all the f***ing time, and I, for one, just can't stomach it.
Wang, the man who took sh!t from
in the first game, simply let's these chicks walk all over him as if it were cool. This, more than anything, kills any connection I might have felt for the game.

Descent Freespace meets Starcraft in this ambitious 3D space shooter RTS.
Allegiance is perhaps one of the most addictive competitive online games ever made, evidenced by a community so dedicated that it convinced Microsoft to open source (including the art) the code and kept the game running for a decade after being shutdown along with other MSN Gaming Zone assets (Asheron's Call finally died this year as well).  The learning curve is steep, the code is being continuously developed by volunteers, the game "mods" (faction differences) are being tweaked by dedicated members of the community, this game is not for everyone, but it is possibly one of the best online space combat games ever made.
The good:
Intense space combat, multiple roles and play styles are all viable, though you will have to switch what you're doing constantly.  This is not just a game about getting the most kills, to win requires both tactical skills and a strategic mind.
The bad:
Commanding is HARD and you'll need to learn a lot before good players will fly for you.  The commander's job is to keep the resources and expansion aspects of the game running smoothly while directing players towards the overall strategic goal.  Fly a scout and learn to lead bombing runs, enemy miner assaults, base constructor escorts, and defensive formations before trying your hand at commanding.
The ugly:
The new default key map (as of October 1, 2017) is horrendous and not the same as the key map in the outdated tutorial.  You will have to get used to the new "WASD" key map or customize your own (use the Esc-G-C menu to access the keys and controls settings).
If you wanted a competitive online 3D space sim game with addictive combat and strategy elements, Microsoft Allegiance is still one of the best games ever made.

Amnesia? It doesn't have screamers. Well, not too many. Instead, it makes sure you get the feeling of dread just by walking through levels. The atmosphere of desolation and doom, the sounds that you make while walking across the creaky rotten floor, the creatures that make you feel disgust just by looking at them, not to mention the sounds they make... All of it is mixed together into a beautifully tragic and horrifying horror game, with a twisted story and a character to remember. Amnesia became a classic nowadays. There are better games, of course. I won't name them. But Amnesia is one thing you shouldn't miss out. Even if you're afraid of the year gap between now and when it's been created.

Probably the best and most rewarding survival/crafting game out right now. However, its not conducive to singleplayer/or two player co-op. You need a group of 3, but preferably, more to enjoy this game.
Here are some pieces of advice for anyone who decides to buy this:
- Find a popular server (a popular server most likely has good settings/mods that will make the game more enjoyable)
- Join an experienced player or group (shouldn't need to explain this)
- When building a base: find an area relatively far from neighbors, and that is wooded heavily. I would recommend putting up palisade walls as fast as possible and then focus on the monument. Don't worry about the size of the original area inside, you can expand and delete the walls as time goes on. (this is better suited for "full-loot-on-claim" otherwise the walls aren't immediately necessary, however most servers have KOS at night, so its nice having walls)
- Try to keep good relations between your neighbors (politics are a huge part of the servers on here, large claims will have wars, and the small claims will be caught in the middle; its best to have allies you can call upon when a raiding party decides to make a detour)
- Spar with your friends! (eventually you'll have to fight people, its inevitable, so its best to have a little experience beyond beating up the training dummy)
- Make trade deals (if you set up on an iron mine, and can make some quality gear, don't be afraid to offer your services in return for another's; trading, even in one or two instances, is a huge advantage and it also bolsters your relationship with the other party)
- Be prepared to roleplay (almost every server either requires or strongly advises RPing, most times its required before entering battle of any kind, so get ready to have some awkward conversations)
- Get an auto-clicker (even with increased skill gain, you're going to spend a lot of time clicking around and repeating tasks to raise stats)
Good luck, and remember: Its slow in the beginning, but once you're established, the game really opens up.

Allegiance is an awesome game, but a complex one. It is a mix of space combat simulation and real-time strategy in which you fly a variety of spaceships along with a team of other players, while trying to crush the enemy team's economy and capture or destroy their bases.
Both the space combat aspect and the strategy aspect of the game are pretty well developed; neither is "tacked on" to the other. As a pilot, you will have to decide which ship you should fly to achieve your goal, how to equip this ship, which devices to mount and which to carry in cargo for possible later use, how to minimize your ship's radar signature, etc. You will need situational awareness to know where to fly, and by what route.
The actual flying is a bit different from games like the X-Wing series in that inertia can be important; your ship doesn't handle like a plane. To some extent you can fly in one direction and fire in another, and if you cut engines, your ship will drift to a stop slowly, but will not halt immediately. Using your side-thrusters to try to dodge enemy fire is very important. It *will* take time to get good at all of this, and it will take time to get used to the control scheme (you can also change the controls any way you like, and taking a glance through the keymap menu will make it clear just how many options you have).
You can use a mouse or a joystick as you prefer; there is no consensus in the game's community as to which is better for flying.
The strategy aspect of the game involves sending (AI-controlled) constructor ships to the asteroids that you'll find scattered across the game's maps. These ships can build different kinds of space stations on these asteroids -- some just give your team another place to dock and launch from, some let your ships teleport across the map, some help your team generate income, and some, crucially, open up different branches of the tech tree. Said tech tree is fairly complex, and if your team is successful a wide range of ships, weapons, and other devices will become available to you. The RTS aspect of the game is handled by your team's commander, who will generally be an experienced player, and who will both guide the AI ships around, and give instructions to you and the other pilots as to what needs to be defended, attacked, scouted, mined, probed, etc. The commander can also jump into the action at any time; and if you and your team-mates don't like your commander, you can even mutiny and select a new one.
All this is just barely scratching the surface -- I haven't mentioned miners, escape pods, the stealth system... Allegiance is complex, and there are lots of details that can become important during gameplay. The upshot is that if you like space combat, if you like multiplayer games with an emphasis on teamwork, and if you like games that actually, genuinely reward good strategy and tactics, Allegiance is absolutely something you should try. It is complex, but it's a true, honest kind of complexity, rather than confusion for confusion's sake. There's a lot to dig into, and if you stick around and get deeper into the game, it will reward you. It's a unique game, and I have never seen any other quite like it.

I've played Allegiance for ten years.  I've seen it's highest highs and some of it's lowest lows.  It's a flawed Epic similar to Dark Souls or Metroid Prime.  It's a challenging game from a technical perspective, a knowledge perspective, and a social perspective a la Tribes, DOTA, League, Quake, Starcraft, Street FIghter, or SSBM.
This review is certainly biased, but I'm not going to convince you to download a game that I know won't appeal to you.  That's a waste of your valuable time.  I understand that not everyone wants what I want out of a game.
For those who want quick bullet points to summarize the pros and cons, here they are:
Pros:
-Deep, rich game
-Free to Play
-Community-run
-Player-run classes to show you how to not suck and have fun doing it
-Combat is fun and skill matters
-You don't have to be a good dogfighter to be a good pilot
-Supports mods
-Flexible game sizes
-A lot of playstyles available to players and teams (Team factions, maps, and game settings)
-Player-created content.  Most factions are player-made
-We've got some spicey memes (Ban Dome please)
-Unique stealth system
-The game is extrememly well balanced
-Competitive clan matches on Sundays (Squad Games)
-Faction lore, a loose storyline
-We actually ban people for violating our Code of Conduct unlike (insert competitive game that you play here)
-Your senile elderly family member's computer from 1996 can run it
-Downloadable high res textures for your high end rig to get 300fps on
Cons:
-Bad graphics. Not immersive.
-Teams aren't auto balanced
-Quality of Life issues
-Some incompatibility issues with certain systems
-The learning curve is more like a learning wall of spikes and explodey mines a la CS:GO, LOL, DOTA, or Street Fighter.  So to learn, you've gotta get blown up and make some mistakes.  The learning curve smoothes over after a week of playing.
-This game takes patience and isn't a "15 minute time-killer".  You're usually having to invest at least a half hour to get enjoyment out of playing
-You need other people to play with.  Game quality is reduced until team sizes reach around 7 versus 7.
-Involvement in the community is important
-Joining a competitive Squad takes some time and experience

This is a keeper if you enjoy competitively-oriented games and you want a familiar community to play it with.  If you don't mind spending a few days learning to fly and get to know the basics with help from the rest of us.  If you want to have long, hour long (or longer) space campaigns and stories to share with your fellow pilots.  If you like socializing over quick matches, and if you're looking for something with depth and variety.
For those who want an idea of what you'll get out of this game after you learn to play and meet our resident circle flyers, read below:
This is an old game.  Old games don't appeal to everyone.  Some call it Quake in space.  Others call it an RTS where your units tell you to go $#@! yourself and do something completely different.  Some of you will play this game for a few matches and move on to something that has put time into newbie accessibility.  Some of you will play this game and never get involved with our community.  Some of you will play this game and spend the rest of your Allegiance career learning game by game with the rest of us.  Ten years and there's still a bunch of things that I suck at.
This is not a pretty game when you look at it with an inexperienced eye.  It's ugly and the default textures aren't refined.   Why can't I see my cockpit?  Why is there no music?  What is going on around me?
This game has also been alive for 17 years for a reason.  A very good reason.
We, the community, have kept this game alive since 2003 because there is a lot that this game carries with it that can't be found in other games.  Whether it's the mix of RTS and FPS, the five hour slugfest games that grace the main lobby once the stars align and Spidey and Aarmstrong will it, or the fact that people with either horrible internet bandwidth, physical disabilities, or both, can be pivotal in a competitive environment.  I've flown with people from Israel to Brazil, to the U.K. and India, to Croatia and Serbia.  I've flown with a senile Vietnamese man from Texas, a man who speaks more than eight languages, a hoard of Brazillians who didn't speak a word of English and never stopped being team players, A wheelchair driving Italian man who manages to remain a close friend despite having opposite sleep schedules, a homophobic nazi who managed to both be an excellent pilot and get permanently banned twice (Good riddance, hi Metz).  Half the people I knew when I started in '07 now have families and children.
Allegiance has lived through a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥  We've lived through a company that tried to kill us, a Shared Source license that prevented a release to Steam for years, a high point of regular 30 v 30's, and a low point of getting together on a Saturday or Sunday to scrape together a 10 v 10.  We've gone so far as to bring back the game devs 15 years later to fly alongside them and show them that their labour of love is still alive.  Read the history of our game on our Wiki.  When you play this game, you'll see the regular vets.  You'll fly with them and against them.  You'll see how they react to wins and losses, how good they can shoot and what kind of a leader they are.  This is a game that takes from your ability to retain game knowledge (scan ranges, how many missiles to kill bases, how many nans you need repairing your bomber on a long range run, where to drop probes, etc) your technical skill (pew pew shooties, dodge the bullets Neo) and leadership skills (Hitting all caps and convincing people to do something - Command position not necessary).
This is what I mean when I say that anyone can play this game.  Games aren't won solely on a team's ability to do good pew pew shooties.  A seasoned scout can save an idiot team by keeping eyes in place you didn't know existed.  A solid commander can co-ordinate a team of mindless noobs to victory versus an unorganized assortment of experienced pilots.  A good dogfighter can build up damage bonus from kills, grab a bomber, and have just enough damage output to blow up that hardened techbase and send the other team into the Stone Age.  Your own natural abilities will shine in this game.
The community is mostly built up of competitive players.  The FreeAllegiance forums are where pilots durdle around, discuss Squad Games, game balance, rant about other people in the community, post recaps (usually drunk) of games that we just played that were pretty damn epic, and provide learning material for people who want to learn (Cadet Instructors are optional).
Final comments:
As someone who enjoys a wide variety of games.  From speedrunning Super Metroid, playing World of Tanks, relaxing with some RTS games, loading my save again in XCOM, sucking at CS:GO, uninstalling all of my MOBAs for the eighteenth time, or grinding tech skill in Super Smash Brothers Melee for two hours, Allegiance appeals to all sides of me in that respect.  I still remember my first days of flying in circles, not understanding what's going on, and having to ask for help from other people on how to even deploy a probe or look at my inventory.
The variation in playstyles and flexibility in what happens during a game have kept things fresh for many players such as myself.  Started playing when I was 13.  I've gone from circle flyer, to exclusive mindless lone wolf dogfighter who thought "that's all this game is about", to Squad pilot, to Team Player, to Squad Leader and assistant Cadet Instructor.  I'm 23 now.
Allegiance made me who I am today.
Allegiance is both a community and a game.  One wouldn't be here without the other.
Ten years and I'm still learning.
