I did this review in two ways. Here's a link to the video review, followed by the text if you prefer reading it.
SOMA is a follow up to the incredible success that was Amnesia: The Dark Descent.  It’s a first person sci-fi horror game in which the player has no weapons and must use their wits to avoid the dangers of the deep. 
The title was developed and published by Frictional Games.  It released on Steam, GOG and the Humble Store for Windows, Mac and Linux on September 21st and digitally on the PS4 on September 22nd with a stock standard price of $30 US.
You play as Simon, just a guy going in for a medical scan who wakes up in a weird place, trying to make sense of his surroundings and as it turns out, himself.
I got a review copy of SOMA and decided that for the first time, I’d give a horror game a try.  I’m not a horror genre fan and don’t particularly like horror movies either, so take that into account while watching this.
 
SOMA plays like just about every first person shooter that has ever been released.  WASD for movement, mouse to look, space for jumping and a few interactable items.  It does have a Skyrim style item pick up system in that you can move a lot of random objects around the world including some interactivity with the world but in general, this feels a bit gimmicky.  For example, early in the game you get to throw an object at a window to break it.  Don’t expect that mechanic to be useful again for a while.  Several mechanics are similarly used very infrequently.
I was expecting a horror game though, not a psychological thriller.  And while I don’t want that to count against it, the altered design from what I expected also had a fairly negative piece as well.
SOMA is very good at telling the story of a derelict settlement of sorts, but it does it with large expanses of walking.  Walking and walking.  More walking.  Enough so, that I honestly believe that I spent at least half my time playing the game, walking from one place to the next.  Sure, some of it is slow, very heavily atmospheric walking with terror lurking behind every shadow, but its’ still long expanses of uneventful walking nonetheless.
Where it comes to the actual horror part, you go for long enough in between creatures that there is still surprise when it happens, but that fear goes away fairly quickly watching them, or not watching as the situation dictates.  I found the primary source of nerve wracking to be the world design, location and what was once there, rather than what is there now.
 
This is a beautiful game.  Without spoiling too much of anything, the scenery is gorgeous, with plenty of nuanced item placements and creative designs.  Further to that, there are a significant number of underwater portions which, given the nice lighting will awaken -thalassophobia in any player.
The atmosphere of the game is enhanced by the graphical fidelity and the performance is very good as well.  There were some issues recording with DXTory though, with the framerate dropping to a fixed 30FPS, but outside of that, it was a solid 60.  It has all of the graphical options you would expect and yay for being able to turn off bloom.
I felt like this review would be a bit longer than it is, but that’s a function of a significant portion of SOMA being good, but not great or bad.  For me it was a bug free experience.  The graphics are gorgeous and the setting terrifying but when it comes to actual game inhabitants, and the patterns they follow, the game fell short for me.  The gameplay is not revolutionary or even evolutionary in any way.  The storyline is brilliantly told, for the most part with intricate and easily missed objects in the world that add to the overall presentation, but it has so much walking simulator filler that I frequently found myself wishing I could just skip to the next piece of story.
 
It’s a good solid game, but not exceptional.  And I found myself expecting more from a developer with such a critically acclaimed success as Amnesia.

Good Game, But It Needs Improvement
This is a great game; it captures a lot of depth into how long range bullet ballistics and historical facets of WWII. But it desperately needs to be reworked to fit. There will be many times within the game where you will be forced to think not as a sniper, but a Rambo style killing machine. The beginnings, half-way points, and endings will decently fit the bill as using precision skill and timing with your rifle. As in, scripted parts of the game. But in-between those key points it asks you to do things in another fashion. Such as level's two and three. In 2 you're in many tight corridors, so you have lots of straight shots. But you have zero visibility, enemies running up to you and killing you because you're on the ground, and enemies that will actually spawn before your eyes in the same tunnel. This means that your rifle is practically useless and your best choice is using your machine gun and running. Next we have level 3. Again, lots of tight corridors, low visibility, and more enemies that spawn only when you come within a certain close distance. Your only choice on any difficulty higher than the average is machine guns and running. It's a great game and I love it for its sniping parts, but it needs to be that at least most of the time, not a Call of Duty esc rampage. And I am sorry for using that comparison, but the Duty series appers to be the benchmark that the developers making this went for.

Hamlet or the last game without MMORPG features, shaders and product placement aka the worst game name I have ever heard in my entire life is a point and click game, where you play as little time traveler who disrupts the tale of Hamlet.
As stated you play as a time traveler who accidentally disrupts the tale of Hamlet and now has to save Ophelia Hamlets bride to save time.
In the game you don't actually don't control the small man, but you actually control the environment around you. Solving puzzles and stuff like that.
The game has a somewhat decent art style and that's about all the good I actually have to say about the game. This game otherwise is rather boring and not even worth purchasing and let me explain you why.
Now I absolutely love adventure games. It's my absolute favorite genre of games and the staple of this genre is cryptic puzzles, but in most adventure games there are only a few puzzles that are cryptic, but Hamlet and the rest of the name I won't even retype the entire game is cryptic.
You won't be able to solve all of the puzzles without resorting to a guide. Now let me explain a bit why some of the puzzles are just way too hard. In one puzzle the little alien guy is knocked out and to wake him up you have to make him think 2x2=4 which is not explained anywhere and you only think of it logically and imagine now that the entire game is full of puzzles like that and you have yourself this game.
The game is also incredibly short. With a guide (which you will definitely use by the end of act 1) will take you around an hour finish the entire game and after that there is next to no replay value what so ever.
This game also sets up a sequel and since this game came out in 2012 and there's no sign of the sequel I highly doubt it will see the light of day. The developer of this game is also working on Franz Kafka The Game which is supposed to release in 2017 so hopefully his mistakes on Hamlet are fixed in that game.
In the end this game is bad. It's only saving grace is the rather cute art style. Apart from that there's literally no reason to play this game as it's too cryptic. I suggest skipping this and picking something else.
Final Rating:
4/10
Pros:
+ The Art Style
Cons:
- Puzzles are way too cryptic
- Short

I imagine if you were to see this as a simple game for kids or something it may be quite appropriate for that. As a point and click game, the kind that adults might enjoy, it’s not very engaging at all.
A few of the puzzles are clever but there are an odd few that are a little harder to see what you’re supposed to be doing. Especially nearer to the end.
It took around an hour to finish and really it’s nothing all that special. A childish re-hash of Shakespeare’s Hamlet.
It’s alright but I’m in no hurry to convince you to try it.

Lovely older game. You've got to use teamwork to win.
Things can get really crazy when you've organized an assault and you all show up at the enemy's base at once:
There you are, poised and ready to go at the Aleph (Wormhole) to the enemy sector. You are in the bomber with two others. One pilot & bombardier, two gunners, one of them you. Four of your team are in scouting ships, carrying repair guns to make sure your team's bomber stays in one piece. The rest of your team are strapped into interceptors, bristling with guns and fueled up with powerful afterburners.
The commander uses the quick voice command shortcut [`cg], the prerecorded message echoes over everyone's comms at the same time: "Go, go, go!"
In go the interceptors, blazing the trail. All at once they dive into the Aleph and disappear into the enemies' sector. Resistance is heavy, the first small pings notifying you of fallen teammates are starting to be heard in the background.
Then your pilot takes you into the aleph as well, scouts fast on your heels.
You're in the enemy sector, gunfire is all around. Slowly but surely, your team's interceptors are cleaning up the area immediately near the Aleph. The way is clear. Your pilot puts the pedal to the metal, and your supporting scouts start ramming the bomber from behind, transferring their momentum to you. The bomber picks up speed, hurtling in a mad dash towards the enemy base.
The enemy mounts a panicked defense, their initial camp has been broken, and the ejected escape pods don't all make it home in time to relaunch in another fighter. They try to go for the bomber, but the scouts keep the bomber's hull in fine shape, and so the enemy fighters switch their attention to them. You fire your turret gun at them, but one by one they manage to kill off your support.
In that moment, when things look their darkest, a massive explosion occurs and a chorus of pre-recorded 'Yeee-haw's sounds. Your pilot has fired off the final anti-base missile in his rack, and it's hit home. The enemy base is destroyed.
Now you just need to pull that off 3 more times to win this game.

Microsoft Allegiance is a game I got into late, sometime in 2007.
I played it hard, long, and eventually well for years.
It's an extremely difficult game to pick up, you'll need to adjust your resolution to 19020x1080 because it defaults to 800x600 (you need to set it in the lobby AND in the game.) You'll need to dedicate some time to setting your keybinds. You'll need to do the tutorials and spend your first two or three games absolutely clueless as to what's happening.
Once you do all that, you're going to experience the best game you've never heard of.
It's a classic space fighter combined with RTS, much like Natural Selection 2 combines a simple FPS and RTS elements.
Allegiance, however, has depth for miles. There are more factions, more tech trees, capital ships with multiple pilots, bases can only be destroyed by escorted special anti-base weaponry, specialized faction specific ships, a deep economy that varies between factions, and more.
This is a game worth playing and exploring, if you have the time and the will to overcome the initial lack of user friendly interface.

Medal of Honor is a reboot of the classic WWII franchise and is set within the modern day conflict in the middle east. The story campaign tries to focus on the epic yet somewhat cliche'd story of a group of special forces soldiers doing super secret missions and the like, we've heard that all before. But what makes Medal of Honor different from other games in the genre is it tries to maintain a realistic, gritty war atmosphere with its authentic and fantastic sounds, real-world weapons and most controversially the taliban. While some may pass on the single player due to its "been there done that" feeling thanks to call of duty, it isnt half bad, and is recommended for anyone looking for a good time. But where the game really shines is in its multiplayer, taking the authentic sound and feel of the game into the online battlefield. The modes feature capture point, attack and defend, and elimination among a few others. The graphics and sound are great and while multiplayer is fun to play, it does suffer a bit from little customization of weapons and characters, set classes, and frustrating hitbox detection. Even so the game does manage to be fun and is something different if you're looking for something other than call of duty or battlefield. Just stay away from its sequel.
> PROS
Great graphics and phenominal sound
Decent single player campaign
Variety of online modes
Authentic feel
> CONS
Bullet sponge enemies and annoying hitboxes
Few maps to choose from
Small amount of online players
Hackers online can ruin matches
Cliche'd story
BOTTOM LINE: Pretty Good
Medal of Honor is what you'd get if you merged Battlefield and Call of Duty together, and its pretty good. The multiplayer is a refreshing and authentic alternative to call of duty but not quite big enough to be its big brother battlefield.

I first went into the game adoring the feel and wishing for it to be a longer classical tycoon style game.
I'm so glad it isn't.
This game is an incredibly intelligent and unique strategy game that requires players to manage a company and successfully out-play their competitors in short to intermediate matches, where the objective is to buy out the oppoisition. With limited claims, a♥♥♥♥♥♥of resource types and locations players will have to adapt their strategy to what they can get their hands on, and if a competitor is getting a bit too powerful, players can use a series of corporate espionage actions in order to temporarily cripple parts of their competitors, to get that slight edge.
Everything about this gamem requires you to think ahead and plan out what you want to do, while being able to adapt said plan to the ever evolving playing field that competitors provide. Your stocks might suddenly be bought or maybe someone decided to shut down your production, and it's through this that you have to carefully adapt and react to these situations. The interactions between players is done incredibly, with fast-paced gameplay that'll keep you on the edge of your seat the whole time.
Accompanying this is of course beautiful and stylized graphics combined with incredible sounds and music to create the perfect mood, depending on where you're at in the game. They successfully managed to make Mars up close beautiful, and after the release of recent DLC, they did the same with Ceres.
While the lack of players is definitely a problem, the AI is honestly one of the best I've seen in any game. The devs have spent so much time and money on making an extremely intelligent AI that can adapt and plot just as well as the player, and will create many intense moments where you and the competing AI are racing to buy the other's last stock, with the most satisfying feeling when you finally manage to beat them.
Ultimately this game is incredible and definitely deserves a try, though it may not be for most casual strategy players. You'll find hours of entertainment, whether it's through the AI or other players that by some magical chance you manage to find. GG Mohawk, GG.

I realize this port of the mobile version of Final Fantasy VI gets a lot of hate, and for obvious reasons, including that the sprites with bilinear filtering don't look too great and the combat UI doesn't work well. While this is true, many issues in this port can be fixed using mods. It's gotten to the point where the mods make me prefer this version over the SNES. This port also includes the original music, along with proper translations. For example, in one part of the game, after the boss fight with Vargas and meeting with Sabin, the SNES text is as follows: "Terra: For a second, I thought you were one of Vargas' bears. Sabin: You thought I was a... bodybuilder...?" While the port is correctly translated, making it into: "Terra: For a second, I thought you were one of Vargas' bears. Sabin: You thought I was a... bear...?" And you can also revert the sprites back to original with a certain mod, that's still under development. And if beta mods aren't for you, you can still remove the bilinear filtering and add sharper sprites, as well as numerous other optional improvements, like making Terra blond/Super Sayan, or removing Celes' bandanna.

Basically, Squenix should be ashamed of this port. It's quite possibly the laziest crap I've seen. To me, this is near-unplayable.
So: go buy this on any other device. The PSN version's nice from what I hear, I also like the PSP version, the gameboy advance version, the wii virtual console version... Life is Feudal: Your Own has some real pros and cons.
They also just recently made the game 64-bit and fixed a whole bunch of crashing issues! The game now runs smooth and crashing is rare.
Pros:
Entertaining realistic medieval combat with archers, lancers, knights, pikemen, etc. based heavily on footwork and precise attacks
Realistic castle builds
Occasional realistic battles and sieges
Large open world map
Lots of crafting and opportunities to collect resources
Will be releasing an MMO version of this game
Guild system + grind = need for cooperation which results in game politics and strong communities
Cons:
Combat breaking "exploits" such as the drag-stab used by top-tier combatants
A combat style that does not favor defensive players who like to parry or block and armor that can be cut through like butter
Obnoxious, extremely time-consuming grind that feels endless
Leveling up on default settings takes ages
Combat is extremely difficult to improve at because of lack of information available on web and not many combat practice servers available to public
Non-Issues:
-Complaints of hit and run combat. You have a lot of projectile weapons available, throwing axes, bows, crossbows, etc. so players who complain that they can't chase someone down to slice them are not thinking outside the box.
-In the MMO they will have instanced battles and people are claiming this will ruin the "realistic" combat and the option to pick armies off in guerrilla warfare and no need for logistics and armies marching and that it won't be like real-war at all. Wrong. An instanced battle lets you knock down the claim protection, but you still have to march over to someone's base if you want to steal their stuff, cause some havoc and damage their economy. What I foresee is win an instanced battle, then march as quickly as possible to their base and steal the stuff on the outer ring of their base, where players will be fighting to save their stuff and bring it back to the center of the base.
I would recommend this game, but I forewarn you, it will suck you in and frustrate you and make you wonder why you aren't spending your time more productively in the real world.

Fun can be had but it's few and far between...
The networking is a real issue, its full of errors and drops. Most matches you will ending up "synching" multiples times a round, disconnecting and not getting any rewards, or joining midway through a match (usually on the losing side), assuming you can even get a match to start at all...
Hero balance and the current "turtle meta" is the other big issue. You can attack and you can defend, but defending is superior because you don't risk opening yourself up to one of the many guaranteed (uncounterable) forms of damage (GB's into heavy attacks mainly, from dodges or parries). Then the top heroes have some ability or feature to penetrate the defensive game, either through speed and spam (peacekeeper), a kit full of a bunch of hard to counter stuff like health, hyperarmor, fast attacks, undodgables, etc. (warlord), or a simulated version of RPS where you have to guess what action to take in order to not take damage (warden).
On the rare occasion you don't have a network issue and you have a fair match, between two heroes that aren't just cheesemasters or exploiting bugs, it's a pretty fun game...assuming you aren't both trying too hard, then it becomes a staring contest to see who attacks first (which will open them up to punishment) or leaves first.

Let's get the negatives out of the way first:
1) Steep price tag to pay for a game loaded with 'micro'transactions (Some of which are pretty expensive.)
2) Season Pass.
3) Peer 2 Peer matchmaking.
Now, is the game fun? Yes. Yes it is.
It's got a fairly (not too) deep combat system and still remains accessible for all players. Someone with immensely more skill than you may have the upper hand, but with some mind games and a quick push they'll be falling off the ledge giving you a victory whether they find it honorable or not.
In my games I haven't found too many salty players. The community seems to be fairly solid. Everyone pushes the objectives and runs to revive you if you die so long as you do the same. No team-chatting needed outside the quick-chat buttons. Of course grouping up with a friend and planning things out does help a lot too.
If you go into eliminations and pair with a bunch of people who'll wait around and 1v1 each other it feels a little like Dark Souls' PvP as well.
The game performs well and also features plenty of practice modes to ease the way into online. Single player exists but it appears to be kind of like an extended, tacked on tutorial. Maybe the harder difficulties will make it more enjoyable. The real meat is definitely online.
If you like Chivalry or Dark Souls PvP this game is a good timesink.

For those who would like to see gameplay -
Bridge Constructor Stunts is actually a pretty fun game, though it’s not as satisfying as it could be. The game is plagued with a very slow tutorial, mediocre bridge construction, basic stunt car controls and has a UI and input options that don’t feel natural on the Mouse & Keyboard.
The levels are broken up into two stages, a build phase and a stunt phase. You see the level, have a limited amount of resources, maybe restrictions in where you can build, and your goal is to get your vehicle to the other side. You can do some pretty wacky things and you have a lot of options when it comes to how you can form shapes, but it just isn’t up to the quality of something like Poly Bridge.
On the other end we have the stunt portion, the bit where you get in your car and drive. Simple controls, back, forward and rotate, nothing special. It’s nice having a little bit control of these segments but they aren’t that interesting, I felt having an automatic system would have been just as enjoyable as I got more frustrating moments out of this phase than pleasure. Also there are some weird game mechanics, to pass some levels you need to collect stars on a level, or reach a certain score (by doing tricks and collecting stuff), I feel these should be optional as they aren’t that engaging and force you into certain structure builds and movements within the stunt car.
Overall it’s pretty unique and fun, but at the same time it’s nothing stellar. I have not finished the game yet, but from the looks of things there are 33 stages, not sure what you’re supposed to do after that. There’s a replay system but that’s about it when it comes to bonus features. Unless you really want to be able to build a bridge and ride it to I’d pass the game for now, but for $6 it’s pretty subjective.

-- During the "match setup" you can not customize your classes/heroes
(and that is not all, just the thing that annoying)

-- While the matches itself are peer-to-peer, this is synchronized with ubisoft servers for rewards and faction map... 50% of the time there is an "network error" and you get no rewards, nothing
-- Though there are 60.000 players playing and the load for a specific mode is "very high", it still takes an eternity to find matches... I do not know why, maybe because the "match up" criteria are very strict and loosened after every minute of searching for a match.
-- once a match is setup and starts, a host is determined for peer-to-peer play. And do not let others fool you with commets the For Honor p2p is better then half life, it is not. Ubisoft may be explaining it otherwise and in theroy and their wishful thnking it is so, but the reality is something different. The host machine decides everthing... I have seen matches that took 20+ minutes to start because the players could not be "synchronized" (usualy 90% of players leave the match like that and when it finaly starts, there are not enough players and the match cancels). I'd happily wait 5 mins to be matched if it meant I wasn't playing with people on the itnernational space station. There is no way to filter out regions, or select to play with low pingers. Of Guards and Thieves is a competitive multiplayer stealth game, and you don't really see a lot of those around. Plenty of cooperative stealth but rarely does a game put you against other players. In fact, the best comparison is the “Spies vs Mercs” mode on Splinter Cell: Blacklist. Basically, if you liked that mode but found it to be too severe on the Call of Duty spectrum of gaming, then I have news for you!
OGAT is the same idea but in a more indie/flash game type style. Makes sense, as many people who play it through Kongregate and aren’t even aware it’s on Steam.
The core mechanics are simple; The Guards tend to be better equipped with more health and assault weapons. The thieves have crossbows and silenced weapons, less health, but one major advantage; Night vision. They must navigate all the maps and turn off the lights while they steal a specific item that only they know about. The guards can find and patrol the multiple items but are not aware of which one it is, giving the less-equipped thieves a tactical advantage. Distraction is a major gameplay element here.
There are also other modes to mix this up, including a Team Deathmatch, Capture the Flag, Bomb Defusal, and more.
If I had to find a criticism, well... There’s two. They both overlap slightly.
The first is that the playerbase is incredibly small, usually peaking at 200 people and going down to 40-60 in off hours. While this is a fine core for the main game mode, I have found it very difficult to explore other game modes such as CTF, or that extra large map where you explore and loot (and what ever happened to Slender?!) I pretty much see 0/10 on all servers unless it’s private or just on a different gametype.
Due to the small base of players, there’s no matchmaking and games don’t always autoshuffle so sometimes it can feel like a team is outclassing another. If it does shuffle, there may be a couple of particularly experienced players crushing everyone who just downloaded and are giving it a try. I'm not the worst player but I have on a few occasions found myself in an endless loop of failure because one enemy was just crushing it. I have some friends who can barely play it for more than twenty minutes at a time and it’s a shame.
The flip side of this; There's no equipment or pay2win system here. If you play enough you can eventually learn the maps, figure out decent hiding patterns, and perform better yourself.
(Protip: Guards can turn off their flashlights and hide in bushes themselves, which is hard to see even with night vision). That kind of thing.
Regardless, It’s a great, small game with a fair amount of replayability. The matches are quick and bite-sized, and you can usually get several games in just twenty minutes or so.

The game casts you as a nameless astronaut who gets the Planet of the Apes treatment and then some, getting sucked into a wormhole and spat back out to an Earth so far in the future that the entire surface has been consumed by water and ice and humanity appears to be extinct. You descend beneath the frozen waves in a submersible to explore the sunken remains of millennia past, blow up giant sea monsters for upgrades and piece together the final fate of mankind.
I only played with M+KB but the controls are easy and responsive, the difficulty curve is robust but not unfair, and the game's combination of aquatic-industrial graphics and chill electronic soundtrack make for an engaging, easygoing experience. It autosaves before every boss battle and offers periodic manual save station/teleport bases at major zone hubs to keep backtracking to a minimum, which I appreciated because I'm pretty bad at Metroid-style boss fights and usually have to repeat them at least half a dozen times to lock down the pattern. Definitely worth a look if you like Metroids, ocean adventure or a post-apocalypse that isn't a bleak and desolate desert hellscape for a change.

This game is a perfect example of a dark, serious storyline, while still knowing how to tell a joke. Final Fantasy first-timers are probably scrolling through reviews on every game wondering, "Where do I start?" Well, if you're worried about chronology in these games, have no fear. As 90% of these games aren't chronologically linked to any of them. You can pick the series up at any game with no regard to the others. (save for FFIV- The After Years, FFVII- Crisis Core, X-2, XIII-2, and Lightning Returns) With that said... if you're truly willing to listen to a seventeen year old... Y'see, every character's job and abilities are pre-determined, thus making YOUR job only to learn how each character works at your own pace, and work around what you learn. I play the game with the window size at 800x600, and it works like a dream. With that said, I can't speak for first-party controllers such as XBOne and PS4 pads, as I own neither of them. Yeah.... strict Nintendo fanboy here; you'll have to forgive me...

I grew up in the 80's, with the Nintendo and Super Nintendo, so I am no stranger to classic role playing games. The Super Nintendo is what got me into role playing games to begin with. I've played a majority of RPGs that have come out then and now, Final Fantasy 3 (Final Fantasy VI) being one that I've played through many, many times.
It's a classic RPG with great elements, that may not seem that amazing now, but were a breath of fresh air when it first came out. The characters, story, game mechanics, they were all just perfect; a shining example of Square's faded glory.
I orginally played the remake of Final Fantasy VI when it came out on IOS and Android. I enjoyed it immensely and took up a better part of a week at work. The game was well designed, did not deviate from the classic enough to be an issue, had newer graphics, which were attractive to me and the controls designed for a touch screen device were pretty much spot on.
So how does the PC port compare to this? One of the first things I noticed were that they took care of a tiling problem that was present in the IOS and Android versions. If you looked close enough, there would be tiles that didn't match up properly in the game and caused some slight staggers. Now for me, this wasn't a big deal, but people were♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and moaning about this when the mobile port came out. I am happy to announce that so far, it appears Square took care of this issue and it is no longer present.
The graphics appear to be very much the same to the mobile versions and that's fine with me. I played the classic games so much, just a change of appearance was already wonderful for me. The PC version looks great, I have no complaints about that. I know there has been some complaints that Square could have done better, but I think it's fine as is. I would have prefered a 3D remake, but this will suffice.
I noticed on Steam, there has been some complaints about the controls. I play most of my PC games with a Xbox gamepad and to be honest, I haven't had too many issues. When I first started playing, it was a little confusing, but the developers did a good job at the layout of the on-screen buttons, after playing a little bit I had no issue. If a button is present on the right hand of the screen, chances are a button on the right hand of the controller will trigger it. It is a non-issue and if you take a couple of minutes to adjust to it, you'll be fine.
There has been add-ons to the game, the combat mechanic has been adjusted, you can also crank up the speed on fights and a wonderful "auto" option will use your last moves and speed fights up even faster. This can be a major boon for "Blitz" techniques, as you no longer have to put in the correct code every time. The layout of the game's combat windows and choices have been change around, but it was never an issue for me. The only thing that bothers me, even a little is the fact in the mobile versions, you just selected a Blitz technique, in this version they went back to the stupid code input, which I have always hated.
Besides that, the only thing that has been even remotely bothering me is the change of dialog scripts. For the most part, dialog remains the same, but every so often, you'll come across dialog you KNOW isn't correct. I don't know why they decided to change some of the dialog, maybe it was to make the translation more accurate? Whatever the case, it bothers me on some minor scale.
There's been some complaints about censorship in the game, but considering this is one of the least censored versions in the entire game's life, it's a invalid complaint based on misinformation and a lack of understanding of the game's history.
All in all, it's a fairly decent game, if you've played the original to death like me, there's enough of a change to justify the price. Some folks have been ♥♥♥♥♥ing that the classic graphics are the best and I suppose Sqaure could have added an option for "retro" graphics, but frankly, if that's what's stopping you from playing the game, you need to reevaluate your priorities.
I highly recommend this game and during a sale there's no good excuse not to pick this game up.

Hamlet or [insert words here] certainly lives up to its satire laden title. The game lampoons not only its Shakespearean source material, but also the expected conventions of adventure gaming. Reading scraps of paper will only provide false leads. Multiple interactable objects... sometimes whole areas of the screen... are useless in these lateral thinking-esque exercises. There are some "normal" puzzles, sure, appearing just frequently enough to lull you into believing that the zaniness has stopped, right before you run smack into the next inane situation. But, unfortunately, none of that is actually enjoyable.
For most, the appeal of puzzle games is in solving puzzles. Here, however, there is no sense of accomplishment when the screen temporarily goes black, signifying the move to the next level. Oh, you might recognize the cleverness of the developer in constructing such an abstract solution, but you didn't actually solve anything. You just clicked on the part of the screen that was clickable... for one "level", you clicked on the exact same spot a few dozen times, just waiting for something wacky to happen.
Hamlet or [etc] would make for an entertaining animated short. The character designs are cute, the movement is fluid, the sound effects surprisingly catchy. Most importantly, the surreal sense of humor would work perfectly in that medium, fitting into the mold of Chuck Jones cartoons. Take the existing assets, drop the forced clicking, and you've got something here. As a game, however, it's not worth playing at any price.

The Aquatic Adventure of the Last Human is an indie Metroidvania from a two-person design team that takes place entirely underwater, ruminates on the nature of humanity and our destiny, features a ton of creative boss battles that sometimes make you feel horrible for fighting them, and a high but very rewarding level of difficulty, all to a soundtrack that I don't think is quite Genesis chiptune but definitely has echoes of that feel to me.
In short, it scratches a heck of a lot of my gaming itches. It scratches them gooooooooood.
The basic premise is that you, the last human, went into space thousands of years ago and, due to relativity shenanigans, are finally returning from your journey to find a changed Earth, one flooded by the ice caps melting and none of your species in sight. And so you go exploring to find out just what happened...
The basic gameplay is wandering around in your submarine, viewing gorgeous pixel vistas and strange wildlife, in environments that start out quite peaceful but slowly become very unsettling, especially in the deep ocean. It's the usual Metroidvania thing: areas gated off until you get certain weapons, minor upgrades for your health bar, attack power, and so on. In contrast to the wandering are the boss fights. So many boss fights, and they're arguably the main draw. The bosses are varied, difficult, and amazing to fight. My two favourite bosses are the two that, to me, best encompass the game's strengths. I'll try to explain with minimum spoilers.
The first I'll talk about is an encounter with one enormous, slow moving enemy and a giant mob of fast-moving, small enemies. At first, it seems completely chaotic and impossible. How to damage the big boss? How to deal with the horde? It's so dark, and there's so much going on! But, as I played, I fell into this... this dance, almost, getting a feel for how the different types of enemies moved, and by the time I finally beat the encounter I was almost in a trance. It was absolutely fantastic and I felt amazing afterwards.
My other favourite boss, on the other hand, I felt... bad, when I won. Again, with minimal spoilers, it's probably the largest creature you encounter in the game, so huge in fact that the only way to fight it is by slowly, agonisingly dismembering it. There's no way to get a quick kill on something that big when you're that small.
It doesn't even initially attack you.
It's just in your way.
I think that particular encounter says at least part of what the game was trying to say about the destructive side of humanity better than any of the later story crumbs. At times, some of the ways the game expresses its messages were a little on the nose for my tastes, but overall I think the tale of what brought humanity to its end is told well.
Content warnings for the game include quite a bit of blood and some gory and occasionally very disturbing enemy designs and sequences, as well as the usual attendant warnings about stories set underwater. There's no air meter or anything, but the deep ocean is weird, dark, and scary.
I only noticed one minor gameplay-impacting glitch: the late-game item that helps you find upgrades sometimes didn't save that I'd found an upgrade it was pointing out until I died. Other than that, it's a question of mastering the controls and boss patterns; anytime the player dies it's the player's mistake and not the game breaking its own rules.
It's way too easy and reductive to say a game feels like X meets Y, but as an overall verdict: do you like Ecco the Dolphin, Metroid, and/or Shadow of the Colossus? Then have I got a game for you! Recommended if the difficulty, subject matter, and aforementioned gore isn't a dealbreaker.

NOTE: Comments in this review will focus on the quality of the port. Story, characters, gameplay and music are virtually unaltered (from the GBA version, with the exception of the music which is borrowed from the SNES version). Personally, this is my all time favorite game, and I've 100% each version, so it is with great hesitation that I do recommend this port.
While the most convenient method of obtaining this classic, it is hard to recommend this version of Final Fantasy VI. By far, the best version is the GBA version and this version carries a lot of the positives that the GBA port had, but it is nearly destroyed by poor support and a misguided art direction (the art itself is not bad, but the filtering of the sprite work creates a shinier and overly smooth overlay that makes the sprite work and background contrast with one another).
However, I feel it should be said that many convenience features were added in this version and the game is fully playable and not incredibly buggy. You WILL get what you pay for; I just wish more effort was put into this port. However, I do feel that SqueEnix has learned a great deal from the previous PC ports, as the one major positive I can say about this port is that it has not yet crashed on me.
On a final note: This is NOT the worst port of Final Fantasy VI. Personally, due to the worse translation and load times on the playstation version, this version just barely wins out. Still, if you truly want the ultimate FF6 experience, please find a GBA and the GBA port.
Thank you for reading my review.

ARMA 3 is considered a simulator by most players, I can see why. Unlike most FPS shooters, ARMA 3 has a much slower pace. You deploy, arm up, await transport, land on LZ, march across enemy lines, encounter threats, hopefully not die, await extraction, get back to base, and repeat. And that is just on the co-op mission servers, it would well take around an hour before you encounter threats. Take note that this simulator aims express as much realism as it can, you will encounter fatigue, hunger and thirst in wasteland servers, and possibly die in one shot.
I reccomend this game to players that want a hard core fps expirence, and a bit of role play, perhaps some disipline and patience when interacting with veteran players. ARMA 3 wants to showcase military warfare with deep (somewhat confusing) mechanics and control to try and make a game as realistic as it can.
The first enemy you encounter is a boss with a one hit kill, good luck

As others have mentioned, This game is a HORRIBLE port/rendition of the classic from the SNES. First off, I won't list the graphics as being bad since this is an updated version with new sprites. Even though I missed the old sprites from the main map screen, it was kind of refreshing to see something a little newer.
The sound however. Why did they even bother to change it? it sounded fine on the SNES, PSone, GBA advance after the sound patch and roms. The sound is so terrible that I asked for a refund. My atari 2600 has better sound quality than this port has. we're talking over 30 years worth of technology in which apparently sound has been improved in our gaming systems and computers. Why would this game sound like complete crap? A commodor 64 has better sound effects than this.
The game itself however is my personal favorite in the series. Even though I requested a refund, I will continue playing the rom since my SNES bit the dust a few years back. Hope this helps anyone looking into buying this. Get the ROM rather than this game if you can help it. Save your money.

I played on hard.
Look, the game can be both fun and frustrating. It's enjoyable sniping and sneaking, but the levels are not very balanced.
Its one of those game where you get frustrated enough to just quit, but enjoy it enough to try again (to a point). Enemy AI is inhuman, challenging because it basically cheats to know where you are etc.
Those elements of sniping, the firing and moving to a new location, the covering of fire through various techniques just aren't there. So you end up in a quasi-fps military shooter that is very difficult because every weapon besides the sniper rifle is basically worthless, but a vast majority of the situations penalize you for using your rifle at all.
On the flip side, the game can be fun when those sniper moments arise, the multiplayer is also fun and pretty fair, and I think the future titles could improve a lot on those design issues, so I do support it.

Today is Friday the 13th of October. A great day especially for the franchise. The physical copies for this game arrive. And it's also a good day to rework my review of this game I wrote on the release day.
This review should pretty much sum up everything of the game as well as the circumstances. And Yes, this review will become REALLY long so keep that in mind before continuing.
Here we have the review of May the 26th on which I'll comment afterwards:
------------------
Thank god, it's friday. Will chill out with some of my old friends.
Or kill them but this are just details ...
F13 the game is one of my highest anticipated games this year and it's like I've wished it. It is similar to DbD, but has some major differences. And it's great.
Here are a few main pros, most times compared with DbD:
+ As a counselor more challenging (could also be a negative point, depends on own opinion of challenge)
+ More ways to escape as a survivor (more options)
+ Executions, often look very sadistic and awesome :D
+ Graphic does not look that good, but compared to the soundtracks it creates a great atmosphere
+ Much love for details: Original voice actors of the movies, OSTs of the movies, references to the movies ...
The only problem is that currently there are major server issues, but the developer are on the way to fix them and I hardly had some of these issues.
And if youre not familiar with asymetric multiplayer games or if youre not a fanatic of the movie franchise you should wait for a sale.
Ki Ki Ki Ma Ma Ma ...
---------------------------
First things first, I still love the game. I cannot tell if it is because Im a Friday fanatic or because I like how the game work or whatever. However, there were really big problems with this game which also exist today. So where to start ...
First and most important, dont do the mistake like I did and compare it with DbD. These games are entirely different. Such comments in the forums like "F13 will beat DbD" ... are such stupid. You can only compare them in a few aspects. So keep that in mind especially if you're a high DbD player cuz you might complain afterwards that Jason is "OP" and not like the anti-overnatural DbD-killers ...
The price is compared with the content still an issue for not-hardcore F13 fans, even after the latest update. However, the devs announced that you only have to pay for cosmetic stuff like clothing packs etc when the new content arrives what is a fair model. And they published a really full road map a few weeks ago, so you can be excited for new content in the future ... what the game unfortunately needs.
The servers are mainly fixed while this review gets written. However it took ages till this got finished especially on XBOX 1 but the devs rewarded the playerbase with new stuff and a double XP weekend.
Now I go to mainly negative aspects about the circumstances of the game. I mainly sum them up so you can try to make a clear picture of the game's circumstances which may help you to decide to purchase the game.
The very old debate which is also discussed today is the Savini-Jason-Problem. To keep it short: The devs implented a special Jason for people who backed the game. The problem is that this is not a skin - as they still advertise it - but a full new character with own playstyle and own kills - and not bad one - . The community, however, really destroyed itself with this topic and the devs still dont want to find a solution for this and delete every post in the forums mentioning it. They argue that this is an exclusive "skin" but it lost its exclutivity by two "ACCIDENTLY" re-releases on PS-Store and for XBOX 1, the last one mentioned being for FREE and open for nearby half a day.
But let's switch the topic. The community itself. Trolls and Jason-Teamers (Counselors teaming up with Jason to kill the others) are highly present and in the forums they often "harass" each other. I have to admit that I cant tell much about this topic because Im no full time gamer and I wasn't confronted with them too often in matches, but others surely were like e. g. you're a german and you're getting called a Nazi because of your nationality and you're getting teamkilled.
Teamkilling was also a widely common "issue" until the devs patched it out. But now, more or less, blocking objectives and similar stupid things are still used by these trolls. Another issue, just to mention it here, are people leaving when they dont become Jason or during kill scenes. The problem is that the choice of who is Jason is random in public matches and the leave-during-kill problem is ... eh ... because of trolls.
To stay in the section Jason-Teamers and so forth the devs at some way started to ban people for teaming, harassment and other such stuff. However this tends to get out of control when people got banned "randomly", the most famous example was the ban of Krimmy Krumble who got innocently banned for "sexual harassment" of people who teamed up against Jason. His review stating the story, however, got deleted because it "didn't suit to the SSA".
Surely I forgot anything important but I wanna end my review here. It may look like a game with a "dirty community" and "mad devs", but the game is fun even if it is difficult. My warmest recommendation if you choose to purchase this game: Go get friends playing this game and play Private Matches! You can also lvl up there and there you can avoid the trolls and the scum.
In order to not put the devs in a too bad light: I really love they job they generally have done with this game. There were many mistakes they have done, especially at the very beginning, but I can do nothing more than thank them for this game Im personally really enjoying.
To be honest I would give this kind of "neutral", but because this is not available, this review will remain positive ...

The polish winged Hussar's taking the russian lands that they seek to reclaim in this game are taken in that film and when making my character I looked into a wiki page called "Women at War" I found a russian woman who led 600 men in a rebelion who worked with a character in the game called Stephan Razin who you can start a rebellion with. It made me feel very immersed in my character and the history of the time. This game is excellent really, and maybe I will enjoy the earlier titles more but I don't regret choosing this game as my first play of M&B. I loved the first Shadow Warrior because it used to be an "oldschool" shooter.
You just experienced a nice little story, found new and better weapons on your way
and solved a few puzzles here and there. Much like Half Life or Max Payne. Just a "normal" shooter.
They replaced their former story shooter with an "open world" shooter.
Basically you are just in the main hub all the time, where you can buy new items and get new quests.
Once you have decided which quest to do, you enter the map and select the location you want to go to.
The game loads the new map and now it wants you to explore and have fun on your own.
However, what I ended up doing was just to run in the direction the minimap showed me because I, as someone who is interested mostly in story, just wanted to complete my quest.
Of course you could ignore it all and just play the main story. But that doesn't change the fact that the game forces you to port from one big detailed map to another big detailed map all the time. It makes you feel like you are in a big open map just for the sake of it, because there is no real reason in exploring and discovering.
Especially not, if you just want to move forward storywise.
Actually it even made it feel difficult to follow the main story because you are playing random missions in a random order. Often you won't even really notice whether you are playing
a mainquest or just some random sidequest right now.
1. the funny story
2. the awesome 1st person sword fights.
Now don't get me wrong on this. Shadow warrior 2 still has the same smooth fighting system the first one had, but they decided to add "new" swords to the game.
Shadow warrior 1 lets you play with one sword which eventually became stronger. The sword was always your main weapon, no matter how far you had already played. They did an awesome job in balancing the game and all the ranged weapons around it.
Shadow Warrior 2 gives you a ton of weapons (and swords!) so suddenly, it doesn't feel special anymore. Your "Lil'wang" which has been your best friend during Shadow Warrior 1, is just one of many swords now.
Additionally you have to exchange and upgrade your weapons constantly to stay strong. This whole feature feels just like they want you to spent time finding new weapons and upgrades rather than playing a story.
Another outcome of this is that you are not automatically collecting everything like you did in Shadow Warrior 1.
It really felt strange when I played Shadow Warrior 1 for the first time and every singel loot would fly towards you.
But in the end it was a very important feature because you had no time to care for the loot and even less, when you were fighting against some strong enemies. Why doesn't Shadow Warrior 2 do the same thing?
You still auto loot money but you have to collect upgrades on your own. I understand that the reason for this is that they want you to realise you found a new upgrade or weapon but in the end it just slows down the gameflow.
Nevertheless there are some good changes. For example there are enemies with weaknesses like fire or ice. It is fun to use different weapons depending on the enemies you are facing.
BUT you have to apply those modifiers on your own.
Unfortunately it just feels like another way to keep you upgrading your weapons. There is nothing wrong with upgrades - Shadow warrior 1 let you upgrade your character, too. But having to upgrade
your weapons
by yourself with different damage types is just too much for the simple story shooter Shadow Warrior used to be.


If you enjoyed Shadow Warrior 1, because you liked to kill a bunch of enemies with awesome swordmoves and you liked the "wang" jokes, you won't regret buying Shadow Warrior 2 at all. They really did a good job with that.
However, if you enjoyed Shadow Warrior 1, because it used to be a simple shooter without
unnecessary features, or you like to play games mainly for their story, Shadow Warrior 2 is not for you.

I have seen matches that took 20+ minutes to start because the players could not be "synchronized" (usualy 90% of players leave the match like that and when it finaly starts, there are not enough players and the match cancels). PvP games with 500+ ms lag are extermely funny... you press a button, it takes half (and more) second to execute the action (and truth be told, 80% of all games are laggy). But this lag is not just about action commands... a player with no lag is something like having a 5m weapon... hitting you (exxageration) half acrosss the map.
All in all: the combat itself is fun, but the story mode too short and actualy only there to let you learn a bit about the game. First off, this isn't a bad game but it's an extremely disappointing sequel to the 2013 Shadow Warrior.   It's more geared towards fans of the borderlands series or looter shooter players.  So if you like borderlands, you're going to like this and would be the only reason why I'd recommend it.  The game is such a large change compared to the first, it's rather jarring.
I'll list some pro and cons comparing it to the 2013 Shadow Warrior:
Pros:
-  Movement is greatly improved (no more fall damage, unlimited dash)
-  Frame rate is better
-  Guns are actually useful
-  Looks graphically better
-  Lowang still funny
Cons:
-  Level design is a huge step back.  Revisiting areas multiple times isn't fun.  The first game the levels were crafted beautifully with every area having a purpose, pushing the narrative forward. SW2 is pretty much arena like areas filled with cool looking stuff to give you the illusion of an open world
-  Story is complete sh*t compared to the first game.  I have to stop drugs and get shouted at by an annoying c*nt.  wtf?
-  Instead of Hoji, you get annoying a*shole in your head for the entire game.  Horribly written and looks like a beginner player mesh.
-  No flow with the story as levels were designed for you to go back to them, breaking the amazing flow the first game had.
- Characters are one dimensional and predictable.  In the first game, you wanted to learn about the characters.  They are dumbed down here, making you not give a sh*t.
-Music is forgetable, with the exception to the title screen and last boss music.  Not sure what happened here.  The music in the first game is above and beyond Shadow Warrior 2s
-  Crafting and inventory management is extremely sloppy.
There's nothing really mechanically wrong with this game, so I can't fault it here. Just disappointing.
Overall in my eyes, this is not a sequel worthy of what came out in 2013.  Shadow Warrior 2 has no soul.

The first time I saw the name of this game, “Spartan vs Zombie defense,” I got excited as I love defense style games thanks to custom defenses in Warcraft. But I digress, the game itself has many good and bad points and I’ll explain them soon.
Firstly before I do get into the points, I want to point out that after you’ve played a few rounds or even look at the pictures advertising the game on Steam... That the game is named wrongly. They call it Spartans VS Zombies... When in fact the game actually uses Skeleton sprites and not Zombies... Like they could be Zombies but to me well, no, just no.
Now onto the Positives and Negatives.
Positives:
♦ Unlockable Modes,
♦ Unlockable Spells,Units, Items and Upgrades etc
♦ Easy but time consuming Achievements
♦ Easy Concept
♦ Great UI
♦ Awesome Range of Units to Verse
♦ Awesome Character, Army, Castle and Item Skill upgrade menu
♦ Micro-transactions are optional and doesn't force you to buy anything
♦ Spells can level up (Casting them without purchasing upgrades for them)
♦ Fast loading between rounds
♦ Endless Modes are a good concept (However, implemented wrongly)
Negatives:
♦ Graphics (Most of the graphics and sounds are copyright from 300 or the likes)
♦ Can be pay to win (This would be a once off Micro transaction of $25, Really expensive for a Micro transaction)
♦ Minimal Options (Only music and sound check boxes with no control setup, resolution, graphics etc)
♦ Poor Mobile Device Port (Says, touchscreen to move, tap to summon etc)
♦ Alt+Tab doesn't take you to desktop (It pauses the game on screen)
♦ Pressing ESC in game gives you the option to quit only (No way back to main menu, you have to click a pause icon and then hit quit to get to main menu again)
♦ Point & Click but not advertised as a Point & Click
♦ Micro-transactions (Makes the already simple and pointless game pay to win)
♦ No way to map controls to A and D or Left and Right arrows to move (Must use Mouse whole game)
♦ No way to keybind units or spells (Again really annoying as you have to click everything)
♦ Hardly get any coins per game, compared to buying them through micro-transaction option
♦ Game seems really slow paced
♦ No Steam Trading Cards (Could have easily included some)

TL;DR: One of my favorite games ever.
KotOR II takes all mechanics that KotOR had and makes them better, plus it adds a ton of new stuff.
The companion influence system is one of the most interesting, deep and rewarding to be found in all of gaming history. You get different companions based on your force alignment and sex, and interacting with your companions will not only give you access to lots of personal background and general lore, but also lots of special unlocks - force powers, abilities, and new classes for your followers. The only downside to its vastness is probably that you never will be able to experience all of it in one go - you'll even need at least 2 runs to merely recruit all possible followers, and then probably some to reach maximum influence with all of them (or, use some of the various influence guides on the web).
The characters never fail to attract my interest, and draw me into their stories - almost everyone has more to them than meets the eye at first. There are also lots of scenes of banter between you companions aboard the player ship, some of which are hilarious while others are dark and sinister, which lets you experience many different facets of their personalities, and many of them are also based upon your influence with the different companions.
There are new force powers, as well as different fighting stances and 'force forms' which let you customize your style of play even more. For example: your a Jedi Master with nearly unlimited force use but a little squishy in hand to hand combat? Use a force form which makes your force attacks more powerful, at the cost of greater drain of your force points - of which you have more than enough anyway. Or you're a Sith Marauder who slays his enemies solely with his lightsaber? Adapt to every situation by employing stances which give you higher blaster deflection, increased defense against multiple melee fighters, or greater attack and defense against a single lightsaber-wielding opponent.
Crafting is expanded and more useful, too. For example, lightsabers can be upgraded with 5 different components (2 crystals, energy cell, emitter, and focusing lens) instead of the 2 crystals only, as in KotOR. There are a lot more robes for Force users, with various boni to them, and they also look a lot better than those in KotOR.
The story is a bit of a divisive point - some feel its attempt at analyzing the eternal light side vs dark side struggle and putting some moral ambiguity into it strays too far from the star wars formula. Yet, like many people, I think it's the most interesting thing that has been done in a star wars story ever. Overall the story is quite dark and at times melancholy in its tone, which is also aided by the game's fantastic soundtrack. I still don't tire of the atmosphere and the stories of the game, even 10 years after I originally played this game (and countlessly replayed it since).
The 2015 update which brings support for widescreens and high definitions is the perfect excuse to finally play this game (again), and with steam workshop support it's easier than ever to experience what the game was meant to be, thanks to the incredibly great TSL restored content mod and the M4-78 enhancement project, which even adds a planet that missed completely in the original release of the game. I definitely recommend to get those mods, but I also loved the original, admittedly unfinished version. If you can't stand open endings, TSLRCM is an absolute MUST.

In general everyone seems to think KoTOR is better than TSL. I am not among the general.
That said, TSL has some buggy stuff where suddenly you and all your people are Sith aligned. CTDs. The script language does not always make sense, and the paths forward are not always clear. The said, the scope here is almost as impressive as the philosophy.
You are again a mysterious stranger. You don't wait as long to find out who you are. Mentored by an old Jedi, once again you assemble a team and make choices. Some of these forward your relationship to gain character backstory. Some of these increase your leanings. Again, you decide how you want to play: Kill 'em all and let the force sort them out, be at peace with anything that doesn't aggro you, or meh.
The depth of the story, though, is impressive. There is betrayal, Jedi gone rogue, some dude who is literally falling apart after trying to kill his master, and a boss that consumes the force for sustenance. They all tie-in to the greater story explored in the novels of who is Revan, was he good or bad (or she, again, the canon is overthrown), and what force exists beyond what can be seen by the Jedi council that threatens all of Republic space? You can also help "rebuild" the Mandalorians, train your own Jedi/Sith team, and destroy a planet. It's really cool. Toss in the restored content and other mods (just like KoTOR), and you've got serious replayability.

Final Fantasy VI is my favorite game in the series, but this really is a terrible port. Maybe this interface worked on mobile or tablets, but absolutely no thought was put into making it serviceable on PC. Barebones option menus, ridiculous key bindings that you can't change from within the game itself, awful sprite art, spotty controller support. A big strategy in the original game was using curative items on undead enemies to damage them. With this incredibly awkward setup I can't even figure out how to do that. Then there are the smaller touches that take away from the impact, like the opera scene's onscreen lyrics being completely de-synced from the music. And the fact that if you set your "Confirm" button to a letter key, it appends that letter to the end of your character names when you enter them in, so you end up with "Cyana" and "Celesz." It's so, so amateurish and sloppy.
It's really painful to witness Square Enix taking a dump on its own history like this. The SNES version (Final Fantasy III), even with its more rudimentary translation, was much better than this. Download that, save your money, and be happy.

Shadow Warrior 2 is a game developed by Flying Wild Hog and published by Devolver Digital and is the sequel to the reimagining reboot of 3D Realms classic of the same name
I played the first game starring everyone's favourite anti-hero; Lo Wang- and was happy to see this sequel. However it feels like such a chore despite the massive improvements that Flying Wild Hog improved from the first game
The previous game has the edge with story as I was engaged and interested in the journey of Wang and Hoji. The blend of fantasy with realism worked quite well and when it ended I had many questions. The sequel sort of answers these but not to it's greatest achievement. Much of it is extremely obvious but I feel like we've lost a connection to characters and so much happens in between that I seemed to have missed
What it does get right is very good, though is combat has improved, building your character is slightly easier and a better array of weapons. Not to mention graphically its very lovely. Combat in particular is a massive improvement as you can choose a blended style of guns/melee or just one
The first game had me focusing on swordplay, but now the free flowing nature of combat is a big plus for me. Especially as you can upgrade weapons with bonuses
Aside from a very clumsy story, at times, there is a huge amount of repetition. A lot of areas are re-used over and over to fill countless side missions. So if you're grinding for something repeating areas can be a bore. Enemies are re-used also as they become 'upgraded' to match you with buffs and so on
Generally speaking this is a fun game but the repetition gets boring extremly quickly. Shadow Warrior 2 is definitely not my favourite and if I had to choose between the first one and the sequel, I would definitely pick the first game but definitely not terrible. I suggest getting it on sale and I don't think you'll be dissapointed

I will start by saying I was a big fan of the original 1997 Shadow Warrior. So much so that I have used Lo Wang as my nickname when gaming for years since 1997, on both PC and Playstation. With that said I was hoping this installment would live up to expectation.
This game is kind of a new direction. It feels almost like an open map, with areas randomly generated. Each time you go back to roam an area it can be slightly different. And evidently I read that they had a few Borderland team members who worked on this game, and it shows. But in my opinion they took some of the best of this, with loot drops and weapon upgrades galore. The jokes and commentary from Lo Wang were always hilarious to me. After a very long time they still did not get old, which was contrary to my initial thought. Lo Wangs crude jokes and comments often came at perfect moments and added to the fun and carnage. Graphically I am running it at max setting and it looks great, especially when raining. And there are plenty of weapons to find and upgrades. You can really tweak your character into what you want it to be, but mostly a choice of melee, guns, or jack of all trade with some variance in between. There is crafting which is nice, but besides elemental upgrades I cannot find a way to craft others in a reliable fashion. I feel this may be more useful higher levels in possibly new game plus.
Another negative I had were the inventory screen. After looting for a while, these screens would fill up and it was really hard to determine which upgrades would be an improvement and trying to sort through them. There were one or two times where levels did not generate correctly. Once this prevented me from completing a side mission and I had to start it over. Another thing is that as I'm writing this, there are not too many people to play with online in multiplayer. I have played it several times, but many times I will check and there was no one in multiplayer.
Besides the few flaws, this is an amazingly fun fast paced game. It is definetely worth the buy when on sale and I highly recommend getting this game. Many cutscenes had me laughing out loud, and I always wanted to get back into the game on a daily basis.

It feels like you're driving on ice. Stopping distance is infuriatingly long for even high-end vehicles, attempting to drift is next to hopeless, the shallowest turns and the slightest taps of the handbrake will send you spinning out and tumbling off the road and into the void.
But MAN, if it isn't a beauty to look at. Vehicles warp, dent, rip, and break with startlingly realistic detail. There's no "damage meter" like in other driving games: you just go until you can't go any more.
All in all, I can recommend BeamNG.drive if you can get it on sale; $25 is a bit steep for a racing game in which racing doesn't seem to be possible. Buy it for the destruction physics and at least attempting to get somewhere in one piece, and you've bought yourself a fun few evenings with it.

Offworld Trading Company is easily one of my favourite real-time strategy games, and it picks up right where M.U.L.E. left off back in 1983, even making a few very sweet references along the way.
I'm an economics dunce and a total sloth at real-time strategy but Offworld Trading Company grabbed me by the cahonies right from the moment Christopher 'Baba Yetu' Tin's Red Planet Nocturne pattered out of my speakers to the words 'Earth may be dying'. It's a wonderfully evocative set-up and one perfectly scored by Tin.
Here's a war game that's fought on a different front: the Martian stock market. It's Corporate Combat. There's no diplomacy, and there are no weapons in the literal sense either; your weapon is cold hard capitalism and your trusty steed supply and demand. Ride it well.
It seems some people go into OTC expecting some sort of longform, perhaps story-driven campaign, that plays like a laid back empire builder. It isn't like that. At all. This is a trading game and it's cutthroat. Quick and sharp. Dog eat dog. "Screw with us, and we'll screw with you."
Single rounds can be over in as little as 15 minutes or drawn out towards an hour depending on how well (or badly) you play, but the game goes to great lengths to ease you in with a fine set of tutorials, a 'full fat' tutorial skirmish, toggle-able auto-pausing when you're doing certain tasks, speed settings, and it also comes bundled with a comprehensive and in-depth almanac. Oh, and the tooltips are superb.
There is a campaign mode but it's not a linear single playthrough affair. It's dynamic, replayable, meaty and as such something you can really sink your teeth into. Think Invisible Inc. or Infested Planet's new Planetary Campaign DLC where each skirmish is linked together by a strategic layer, rich with tough but exciting decisions that may have far reaching ramifications as you progress.
The Daily Challenges too are worth a pop just to hone your real-time skills with no pausing and see how you fare against other players. The competitive multiplayer is demanding but there's also co-op against the AI which knows how to play and can be a formidable challenge in itself. My friend and I have yet to beat it on the recommended Manager difficulty!
All in all, if you like your strategy to be focused and deep then Offworld Trading Company might just be for you. It's such a smart game and one I foresee myself coming back to again and again. I'm yet to pick up the DLC but it sounds fantastic.

November 2017:
The first thing to take into account with regards to this game is that it is still an Early Access game so, for now, this is just giving us a basic working model and I am already pleased with it.  They are also releasing patches fairly regularly with the last one on 8 November 2017 and an active community group helping find and report bugs.  These are all important to help confirm that this game isn't an Early Access Sleeper and hopefully should finish the product.
As I know little about FPS Esports, I have only played the MOBA side of this, so my thoughts and recommendations are solely around this.
What I like:
- Team creation; yes more could be added, but being able to create a logo and set colours is pretty cool.  You can also upload and edit team and player information if you wanted to put in real m.  How is stated in  community forums.
- UI; they updated the UI for this in some recent patches and it is pretty easy follow.
- Management features; like traditional sports managing games you can recruit staff and players, set their training and relationship building exercises.  It even has their  transfer windows - very similar to Football/Soccer Manager games
- Side cups; you sign up to also take part in other cups between season matches which gives a nice little boost in earnings.
- Champ select; they actually have example champs in game. These give the feel of helping players during the champ select phase or putting together planned drafts.  This can be vital in helping you compete against stronger teams.
What could be improved:
- Tutorial; there doesn't seem to really be one and whilst  game mostly intuiative, a tutorial would help, particularly in understanding different epic monsters.
- Tactics; whilst a good starting point (I can still do a lot through this), there is room to add some more unique commands whilst could impact how to approach a fight.  Some of this is also unclear without experimenting and players can randomly die under tower when your tactics say to push passively.
- Team in Cups; Some cups I have come across have had a team that is far and beyond better than the rest.  This could do with tweeking so the teams match the stated difficulty of the tournament when signing up.
- Easier ways to add/amend teams, champs and players
I know there is more to improve, but this is a very good start to a game I am still really enjoying.  I completely lose track of time when playing this.  If you want a Football/Soccer Manager Esports game, this is a wonderful start and the team is working hard on further improvements.  I have asked questions previously and they have been pretty quick to help me.
Help this game develop and give it a try; I knew it was a risk but couldn't be happier.

This had huge potential.
Let me tell you why you shouldn't buy this game if you want a good survival game.
1. They said they had a huge community input system, where they decide what to put in from the community. In theory this should create a good game, but it made it extremely bad when they were just adding new content instead of fixing the previous content that was horribly broken.
2. If you like pvp in a game that requires you to be stealthy and think your actions before you do them, this isn't the game for you. This game is Walk around => See someone => Shoot before they get away => Spend about 15 bullets killing nether => loot => get killed 10m down the road.
3. The loot system was good, but there is no goal in mind. You get to level 31, then what? Get the best guns, then what? Get the max amount of nether kills, then what? Get the max amount of human kills, then what? If you like to walk around doing ♥♥♥♥ all, whilst you follow a loot route you're not going to have a good time.
Oh and items don't spawn outside the loot routes.
4. They tried to make the Nether this scary enemy instead of zombies, this was a good concept but just some simple basic kiting can get you up to level 31 with three hours at most. Most guns kill the Nether in one hit and ammo is abundant if you follow the loot routes. Not difficult.
5. The sound location is horrible, I have a good headset which in most games I can roughly pinpoint where I'm getting shot from or where people are. In this you get shot from 200m away, it feels like it is all around you like 10 people shooting you from 5m away.
6. Collision issues are the hardest part of the game. That said added with 10 second dc time that makes you a sitting duck no matter what you do.
Final rating:
6.5/10

In Hamlet you play the part of a time traveler who inadvertently squelches the real Hamlet with his time machine and thus decides to take his place as the hero of the story: you'll be solving puzzles in five different chapters made up of five levels each.
While sporting some nice art and a quirky humour Hamlet can sadly quickly turn into an exercise in frustration due to its obtuse puzzles and somewhat useless hint system.
-nice art style
-quirky sense of humour permeates the whole game
-some puzzles are interesting and offer a fair challenge
-apart from the title and characters the Hamlet theme is basically never touched upon
-most puzzles have an obtuse design and are very vague in how they function. Sometimes you have to click more than once, sometimes the clicking is timed, other times you have to memorize a quite lengthy sequence or just try and make sense of very vague ambiental clues...I honestly managed to solve a couple puzzles simply by randomly clicking all elements once I was frustrated enough
-no way to know what you can actually interact with in each screen, leading to random clicking all over in every scene
-the hint system is fairly bad, not only you have to wait five full minutes before you can get said single hint but its quality ranges from feeding you the solution to a drawing as vague as the puzzle itself
-not much in the way of a story and the characters offer very little apart from their name
-quite short, unless you get stuck on a puzzle you'd be done in 1,5/2 hours
I really appreciated Hamlet's tongue in cheek take on the genre, its quirky humour, nicely drawn art and first few puzzles: but things soon got frustrating when logic got thrown out of the window and I started facing puzzles that required me to decipher a few extremely vague hints and hopefully understand what I was supposed to do. A few puzzles also require you to very quickly click certain items before they disappear and the split second timing involved can get aggravating aswell. There's a fine line between a challenging puzzle and an obtuse, frustrating one and I often felt as if Hamlet crossed said line way too many times to stay enjoyable.
All this is made worse by the hint system, waiting five minutes for the hint if you're already stuck on a puzzle is not fun and, once opened, the hint was sometimes as bad as the puzzle it was supposed to help with thus leaving me bashing my head on the problem or just trying to find an external guide.
