Is the game good / is it worth playing? Yes. Very much, yes.
With that out of the way, here is my rather long diatribe regarding what I consider to be the greatest JRPG of all time.
The history - and ups and downs - of the
series are an extremely convoluted matter and would require quite a lot longer than I have in this review to completely discuss. That being said, I've generally found that four games in the series are routinely listed as people's favorites: IV, VI, VII, and X. There is an argument to be made for each of those as being the "best in the series" but it usually comes down to which one has the greatest nostalgic value for whomever is making said argument.
I've been playing videogame RPGs since
on the Mattel Intellivision in around 1984, so I have nostalia for virtually the entire catalogue of Squaresoft's flagship series. Why, then, do I gravitate so strongly toward
..?
Many of today's more modern-era gamers might find this difficult to understand but back in the days of 8-or-16-bit consoles, graphics were rarely more than "functional" and only served to let you have something to follow with your eyes. RPGs in particular often suffered from a lack of high-end graphics and - seeing as they tend to be very story heavy - the telling of the tale largely had to be left up to the dialogue translator and the musical composer.
Feel free to Google the name "Ted Woolsey" some time if you want to find out what problems tended to befall game translation during those dark times. Mercifully, the more recent versions of the game have been retranslated, but the issue I wish to discuss is the game's soundtrack.
has what is unquestionably the single greatest score ever composed for a videogame; whatever opinion you have to the contrary is meaningless. Nobuo Uematsu wrote an opera for a Super Nintendo game. I cannot stress enough how important and unusual that is. Taken out of context every track is a masterpiece, but combined with the game itself, they become an epic poem that builds the tapestry surrounding one of the greatest casts of characters in gaming history.
The gameplay itself is nothing particularly remarkable as JRPGs go and the plot is essentially the one you find in
but with a steam-punk flavor added to it. No. The most wholy amazing facet of the game is undoubtedly the cast of characters that you set out on the journey with.
If you do not genuinely feel doubt, sadness, anger, regret, exultation, and pity over the course of the travails of the game, then I would be very much surprised. Each character has a heartwrenching event, memory, or doubt to overcome and while not everything ends happily - and in any great story it shouldn't - they all break the shackles that are holding them back by the time you face off against Kefka at the end of the world.
The long-and-the-short of it is that
is absolutely brilliant and if the "enhanced" sprites are what's holding you back from playing the game, then you're not the sort of person that deserves to play it in the first place.

Nihilumbra is a short, mild puzzle game with above-average storytelling for a platformer.
Normal Mode is fun, though not challenging, and there are many worlds, enemies, powers, and ideas to encounter on your journey to escape the nothingness.
Void Mode (unlocked after completing the game) is completely unforgiving, which I suppose can still be fun if you like dying instantly after every screen transition.
The combination of a mostly dark color scheme with the protagonist's colorful "flower-powers" is a good contrast visually, but it also serves to effectively set the protagonist apart from their origin. They grow in many ways as they travel, or rather, run for their existence.
The deep, velvetly voiceover suits the air of the game well, while the music and sound design are light and fitting, but ultimately forgettable.
Overall, it's pretty fun, and it's nice to see this kind of existential theme discussed in a type of game that usually doesn't.

Offworld Trading Company is a rather interesting take on Real time strategy games. Instead of blowing up enemies with machine guns or explosives #Offworldtradingcompany takes a new look at things by using Economics!
The game actually has a lot of content as well. My video is based on all of the DLC and honestly Im not sure where one DLC starts and another stops so Ill be talking as if you have all the DLC.
The tutorial for offworld trading company shows you the basics then walks you through a set of scenarios with increasingly challenging computers. By the time you complete these challenges you should easily be able to jumpy right into the multiplayer side of things if thats your cup of tea.
If not there is plenty to do vs the AI which is NO slouch! Skirmishes like any other RTS allow you to just jump in vs a certain number of opponents where your job is to out perform them financially with the end goal of buying out their business.
There are a variety of resource gathering options, factorys that produce different luxury goods, devious blackmarket sabotage moves, and if all else fails access to an offworld market that you can launch missiles to exploit.
Campaigns bring an interesting twist to the game. You get the core game with a twist in the rules the restricts who can do what. This forced specialization completely changes your focus. Also instead of straight buying out your opponents you must support a colony. The person who does the best on any given week gets a bonus for the following week. Make a few mistakes and your opponents can snowball. Once a certain week has passed you again have the ability to buy out your opponents like normal.
There is also Daily scenarios very similar to binding of isaacs dailies. You are given a set scenario blindly, forced to adapt, and you are scored with eveyone else for that day. Quite a bit of blind competition the person who adapts quickly gets a better score and the leader board ensures bragging rights vs your friends or the world.
Finally if playing against an AI bores you there is a rnaked multiplayer option.
I ran out of time in my review but ranked and custom matches were both available.
If you'd like a more indepth review here is my first impressions video!

Weapons sound cool and monsters can make you jump from time to time with their screams.
All and all this is a great game and you should try it and support!

Gameplay wise, there were a lot of small things that were improvements upon the first game (e.g. when you find a datapad it pops up right then so you can read it instead of having to search through all your belongings for it; your health points heal slowly when you're not in battle even without having to use a medpac, footlocked/corpse say whether they are empty if you've already looted them, no more really difficult to beat turret battles that you have to get through to continue the game!!!)
The storyline and characters are wonderful.  There are so many well-nuanced, non-traditional-trope-following characters.  Kreia and the Exile are awesome.  Darth Nihilus is one of the best-designed scariest-looking Sith from the Star Wars Universe ever.
The storyline (to me at least) felt rich and complete up until the final planet/boss showdown.  Even with the Restored Content Mod (which is essential, by the way), the last level did feel rushed, empty, and incomplete-ish.  However, to me it still was a fairly-satisfying conclusion to the game.
I had a few small problems with bugs (namely on Nar Shaddaa and one at the beginning of Telos, so I recommend saving often and having save files available).
All-in-all, I really enjoyed this game and overall found it just as good if not better than the first KOTOR game.

TLDR: The game is Great. Give it a shot, but only if it's the type of game you really want to be playing, do some research, and don't expect something it's not.
Life is Feudal is a fantastic game, if you understand what you are going to be playing.
You can tell from the reviews that many people enter this world expecting a survival experience or something they can play solo.  That's just not the case, and don't buy this if that is what you are looking for.  Unless you have a large group (6-10 active people is awesome) progress is slooow
.. and you can play it with less, but you have to exhibit some patience and find some people to enjoy the grind with.
The game is mostly about building and being a part of the community, whether that means being a bandit, farmer, knight, or peasant.  This game is going to bore the ever-loving-hell out of most people if you can't find a way to socialize at least a bit.  Get to know your neighbors, do some trading and a bit of role-play, and work your way into a bit of conflict while you build yourself up, and you'll find the true LiF experience.
PvP is prevalent, and is the main focus for some.  This can be quite frustrating for those that want to enjoy a peaceful life in-game, and are not used to dying in the games they play.  However, what you'll need to learn is that dying is nothing to fear.  Just be smart and don't keep your best gear on you while laboring, and the times you may die now and again shouldn't bother you in the least.
Combat is fun, but takes some getting used to.  Similar to the Mount and Blade series, and War of the Roses for those that know those, but quite a bit less fluid at times.  Nonetheless, once you get the hang of it, a good scrap will always be interesting.
City/castle building is where this game shines in my opinion.  You can make some pretty impressive and cool looking stuff if you have the mind to do it, and patience to complete it.  If you are just starting out, remember to start small, if you get too ambitious with your builds, you will quickly find that you will never finish and most likely burn yourself out.
The UI is bad, but gets better/easier to use as you grow accustomed to it.
Basically, LiF has been in and out of my life for a great deal of time during the period that I have owned it, and I woudn't trade my many hours in it for anything.  I've met a good deal of great people who I have continued to game with until this day.

After finishing The Aquatic Adventure of the Last Human, I must say that is one of those small jewels that faintly glitter in the dark.
First of all, all be advised: This game is not fair until the very end. You will be facing a lot of Overpowered bosses with different mechanics that will (probably) drive you insane. Your ship will always be underequipped to handle these fights, and you will find yourself inside a bullet hell most of the time. That, combined with the ship's desperately slow maneuvering speed and the Harpoon's low damage, will make each victory a titanical feat for newbies to this genre.
The art direction, level design and soundtrack are purely awesome. Every inch of the environment is worth looking, and wandering around the sunken human cities alongside whales and very big fishes is a feeling you will not forget anytime soon. I love Pixel Art games, but this little jewel is one of the best examples on how to have an awesome ambience with such a simplistic art style.
The plot, when understood in its totality, is better than most of the games I have played, but not better than many of them. I think that, if explained properly, it would have enhanced the player experience, but sometimes wandering around collecting the Holo-Diaries that contain the information about what happened to Earth tends to be tedious.
Finally, if you finish the game you also have a New Game + option, a Boss Rush mode (with leaderboards!) and a Hardcore Mode (which has to be unlocked), so it has a nice replayability in the short term.
If you like Metroidvanias and Souls-esque games, get it! If not, wait for a sale and grab it, because it is worth a buck!

Date: 2/1/16
Review Number: 7
Game: Hacker Evolution
From (Creator Publisher): exosyphen studios
Played On: Laptop
Steam Price as of Review: $9.99
Total Time played: 40 minutes
Review:
Yes, technically this is being released on the second, however I have yet to go to bed, so I’m still calling this as day 7.  Though really, the biggest reason why this was delayed was because I actually took some extra time to play the game that came up on the I’m-a-die-die today, Hacker Evolution by exosyphen studios, a mostly console oriented hacking game.  Now, at first glance you would think a game like this would be a somewhat boring little text based adventure game, and really that is what this, a simple concept that at its core is no different than trying to fix a busted DOS prompt before your mother finds out you’ve been messing with the autoexec files again so you can play your games with the proper soundblaster IRQ settings and accidentally the whole drive system.  However to some of us, that throwback is half the fun.  Being able to sit down with nothing but text descriptions and a little blinking cursor you find you have to use your imagination to tell half the story, while the game does a very thorough job of guiding your imagination through a rather ingeneous story, and makes the CSI-level ‘hacking’ both enjoyable and engaging, if not addicting.  This is one of those games I would like the play the whole way through, I honestly think.
Game’s Fate: Kept, surprisingly.  This game is deceptively addictive.
Buy/No Buy:  Honestly a good buy, even with as little as I’ve seen, it’s a unique concept I can sink my teeth into.

The points Aquatic Adventure of the Last Human gains for style, detail, and intrigue, it loses threefold for a lack of coherence and even playability.
I will preface by saying I have not been able to finish this game for a critical reason I will discuss further in this review.
I bought this game during the 2016 Winter Sale and was thrilled to immerse myself in a "MetroidVania" styled deep sea exploration game. While I usually roll my eyes at pixel games I was impressed at the level of detail put into the general atmosphere of this game. Watching scores of monstrous fish swim through the ruins of immense undersea cities was a sight to behold within the first five minutes of gameplay, and I smiled a bit when I saw electronic signs and lights on buildings briefly flicker to life. There was clearly care put into level design, and the pixel aesthetic wasn't just a cynical cash-in of nostalgic retro appeal.
As an exploration game, it goes without saying that the game is non-linear and the player has a degree of autonomy in deciding where they want to go and when. However I felt truly lost in this game, wondering if I had unknowingly stumbled into a boss fight I was simply not well-equipped enough to win due to not having scouring the depths for upgrades to my submarine. Adding to my confusion was the holo-notes I occasionally discovered. As they are not found in any sort of coherent sequential order and are the only real plot source, the fate of the Earth is something the player must frustratingly piece together themselves.
I have come to an insurmountable roadblock during the fight against
.  Whenever I destroy the rocks blocking the path to my escape, I encounter one of two errors that crash my game. One is due to the game's inability to render all of the crumbling rock debris. I am unable to progress any further past this point. Other players have experienced a similar problem and have brought it up on the discussions page, where the developer has attributed it to a problem with the game's engine and has claimed to fix it. Evidently something was overlooked.
The most frustrating aspect of my experience was not being able to enjoy a game I wanted very much to like. I was tempted to offer this game my forgiveness after yet another ruined attempt at the boss fight.
The screen then turned black, and an error message popped up, informing me of a shortage of memory.
I closed the game.

Great game, well polished and solid story.

NOTE: If you are reading this
buying the game, buy M&B Warband first. The learning curve for new players is almost vertical if you haven't spent a fair amount of time in M&B Warband first.
Mount and Blade: With Fire and Sword is game set in 1600's Europe. It is completely historically accurate, and has new weapons different from it's big brother Warband. These weapons include: Muskets, Carbines, Pistols, and Bombs. This also means that all types of weapons from Warband are in this game as well. The game starts out and asks you to make some chocies. Of course, no matter which choices you choose, you will always be put in the tutorial at the beginning of every new game. You start fighting bandits to learn the swordfighting mechanics. After that you find a man named
who helps you fight the bandits. Then, you all get on horses and fight some more bandits in order to learn the horse mechanics. But after that, you talk to
a little more and are left to your own devices. This is why the learning curve is vertical for new players. There are more bandits/looters/brigands for every area than there are in Warband, and i learned that the hard way. You'll be getting killed a lot and will have no idea what to do for a while. Now, on to my opinions on the game. I think that this game is the best game for swordfighting and primitive guns usage in any game ever. There. I just do. The mechanics feel nice, look nice, and when you get a bunch of perfect blocks against a Winged Hussar with a Lance and you only have a saber, it feels so good. The battles are fun and engaging, and when you have a decent party and engage in a battle, you'll ususally be looking forward to it. Of course, there is also the ruler part. For a long time you'll be independent, but when you kill the subject of a king or ruler, any nations that are warring with that king you can now join to be a subject. After that, when you lead a seige you can capture enemy strongholds and forts for them to be your own. I don't think you can become the leader of a nation or create a new nation in this one like you can in Warband.
Now the flaws. First, it doesn't look too good. I think it looks okay, but most people don't and will be driven away by this fact. It also is buggy. Every once and a while certain bugs will happen that will make you SO MAD.
All in all, i rate

Addressing most people's concerns:
P2P connection is a bad idea for a multiplayer focused game, HOWEVER it really isn't as bad as people like to make it out to be. I have open NAT Type, (DMZ'd my PC and custom-setup my firewall) so I rarely get DC'd from games. Like, maybe 1/30 games.

You can buy "Champion Status" with in-game currency (2000 for 3 days, 4000 for 7 days, etc.) and you get a 25% bonus to XP gain, extra salvage when you destroy loot, more loot after games, etc. I don't understand the pissy attitude towards this,  because you can make 2000 currency in 2 days if you do the Orders. Anything concerning graphics, this game is a f*****g masterpiece. Like, "Witcher 3 on ultra with 7 TitanX's stapled to your face" masterpiece. The charcter models are absoluetly f*****g beautiful, the maps are gorgeous, the realistic flesh and blood is incredible.

Let me preface this game with a simple sentence, Ubisoft is probably the worst company on the planet, and it is incredible that once again I've been suckered into buying a game that was good in the beta. I've bought too many of their terrible games, all typically based around medeival combat.
To start off, we'll go with the fact that the idea of this game is brilliant, however, Ubisoft has already proven it's gross incompetence with this game, and I'll explain how.
We start off with the Closed Beta, to which I was a participant. The Valkyrie, the Shugoki, and the Lawbringer were all locked during this session, and made unavailable to play. From the beginning, it was clear there were bugs to be worked out, the bleed and poison effects of assassins being too potent, the AI's being set to permanently too easy, and other glitches, such as weapons warping through people who slid back. At this point in time, most classes could fight one another on equal terms, I mained Warden, and was fairly good at it, able to participate in team fights or duals with a win ratio of over 80%.
I hoped to see the game grow at that point in time, but when it came to the Open Beta, it became clear that the developers had little to no idea what they were doing. Phantom hits became more prominent, and shields became able to take on entire teams. I still thought this would be my game, and pre-ordered it ahead of time.
Upon release, I actually had quite some fun. I switched to the Lawbringer, as the Warden became less armored, more dodgey. For a week I was able to participate in all styles of combat, duel or otherwise. Then, the meta became quite clear. Lawbringers are underpowered due to their inability to enact stuns, or move quick enough to parry fast attacks from assassins. Moreso, the fact that all classes were having difficulty with the Peacekeeper, the Beserker (who is unplayable at later prestiges), and especially the Orochi. The Orochi, on no stamina, can swing an overhead hit, and beat an opponent who has swung a similar heavy attack, first. The Peacekeeper's poison is spammed, as is most left-click tactics. All heavy attacks are impossible to use, as they are parried infinitely, resulting in the loss of stamina, and the inability to stand up, as most of those classes have ready to use knockdowns. Add this to the fact that on release, the Shugoki can swing an unbreakable that is quite literally, unbreakable, as there is no parry indicator or ability, and the pile of bugs and "balance" notes keeps piling up!
Seriously, this game is a mess, don't buy it. Ubisoft just f*cked us all over again for another piece of crap that could've been good. Funny thing is, even though the Peacekeeper's poison is fixed currently, they're going to patch it, to make sure that you can lose three bars of health to her.
I may keep playing it, but it's only stress, I may as well play against AIs, at least those you can fight without getting spammed.

Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Siege, despite the constant support/updates post launch, has been a mixed bag in my experience.  One moment, you can be rockin flawless victories with your team in multiplayer and in another, getting destroyed 0:3 for reasons that are outside of your control. It's widely known that Siege has been having tons of feedback regarding hit registration, rubber-banding, and sometimes sluggish performance. Ubisoft have been attempting to address these issues through many updates, including an update dedicated solely to the issues mentioned (Operation Health). However, many of these bugs and glitches still persist if not worsened. There are even game-breaking map exploits and matchmaking hiccups that still haven't been completley fixed yet (Bank for example). Much of my frustration while playing highlight the questionable hit registration though.
If you can look past the glaring issues, there definately is the potential for lots of fun and tense moments that can get more addicting with each consecutive match. The gunplay and movement feel solid most of the time and the simplicity of the game objectives make it more approachable (pvp hostage, bomb defuse, secure area). There is also a huge variety of operators to choose from on both attack and defense, with Ubisoft promising even more in the future. A decent number of maps exist but its been said that possibly two or more maps may be removed from public matchmaking (yacht was already removed for bug fixing apparently). Make of that what you will.
For $20, I say its a worthwhile purchase. Any more though, I suggest looking elsewhere.

Spartans Vs Zombies Defense is a free casual defense game with microtransactions.
Sparta is under attack from zombies and it is the task of King Leonidas and his soldiers to stop them.
The gameplay is very simple. It consists of a series of waves, which goes up until wave 60, with enemies attacking from the right side of the screen. The enemies are moving to the left side and trying to overrun your castle. The player moves Leonidas left and right with his mouse and when Leonidas and an enemy meet they start fighting. The aim is to defeat all enemies before they destroy the castle or kill Leonidas. The player accumulates silver over time which can be used to hire units to help defend the castle. They will move forward automatically to fight. Besides of the regular mode you can also play some endless mode (you have to unlock them by completing wave 60), it is the same like the regular mode but instead of waves you will have a timer.
The game is really boring, each wave plays like the wave before. After the first few waves everything the game has to offer has already been seen. There are microtransactions which let the player purchase coins with real money.
The game has the name Spartans Vs "Zombies" Defense but the enemies are all skeletons and not zombies.
Another poor aspect is that every complete sentence in the game is grammatically incorrect.
It could be possible that Spartans Vs Zombies Defense could be removed very soon from the store due to copyright infringement. Besides of the look of Leonidas from the movie 300, you can also hear music along with some sound effects right from the movie. Also the game has a very similar look to the mobile game Army of Darkness Defense.
The game is a complete waste of time. Hands away!

For me, the year of 1995 was also the year of Final Fantasy 6. It was, next to Secret of Mana, one of the only SNES games I ever owned, so I put a lot of time into that classic RPG. At one point I even had a 100% complete game. Everyone was at level 99, I found all of the items, collected every last one of those stupid rages, and even idled long enough for the game-save to read "99:99" on the clock. Not even a week later I discovered the "Relm-sketch" bug, received thousands of items, and accidentally wiped that 100+ hour save from the cart.
But I'm not here to wax nostalgic, I'm here to figure out why this game can only garner a
review average on Steam. FF6 is one of the most-beloved entries in the franchise, and it would take a total dummkopf to botch a port of a 20 year-old game, but here we are. I would have preferred to discuss FF6, its successes and its faults, and offer up a thorough analysis. However, everything takes a backseat to Square-enix's incompetence.
The presentation in FF6 Steam/IOS is a huge step backwards from the SNES game. The new sprites aren't just ugly, they clash with the scenery, and create visuals that are shoddy and inconsistent. The special-effects also look worse, and some spells (like "Ultima") lose all of their splendor. The music is fine, but the sound-effects are truly awful. I can't understand it. One of the most effective sounds in FF6 is the sound of wind-blowing. This version screws that up. The wind never sounds right, and takes away from the mood of every scene. There's some other stuff in here that I won't even qualify with the word "sound", they're just noises.
FF6 is a landmark entry in the franchise, due to its many inspired set-pieces. However, when the presentation is botched, many of these scenes lose their impact. For example, I've noticed a number of cuts in the Opera sequence. The music will stop at the wrong time, or the transitions don't quite gel. Even if you never played FF6 before, you'll notice when these things happen, because it's just that jarring.
To its credit, this version of FF6 includes a couple improvements and additions to the design of the game. For one, the entire battle-party is no longer required to sit and wait, while Cyan charges for his sword-skills. Unfortunately, Cyan is still a bum and a failure to his wife and son. The auto-battle is pretty nice, especially if you have Sabin in the party, since it also auto-performs his last blitz. Not much was done with the underlying mechanics of the game though, which is nice I suppose. Magic still dominates, and it's a little too easy to craft practically invincible god-characters, but that's part of what I like about FF6.
The one major issue of this port, the one that crawls under my skin and chews away at the bone, are all of the hitches. Every time I enter a place in FF6, whether it's a house, the next floor of a dungeon, or any other location, there is an ever-so-brief pause. Locke, Celes, or whoever will stop for a fraction of a second, and then resume walking. This happens no matter what direction I'm holding the control pad in, and it's so minor but also completely absurd. Somebody at Square-enix signed off on this, and it drives me up the wall.
Several years ago I had to get a new transmission for my old car. The repairs were over $2,000. Yeah, I got taken for a ride that day. While it was nice having a car again, whenever I moved the gear-selector from park to drive, the car would make this loud "THUNK" noise, like it was about to crap its metallic innards all over my drive-way. Despite this alarming noise, I was able to drive the car for another four or so years without incident. Still, every single time I heard that noise I thought "I paid $2,000 for this...."
While I only paid $8 for this version of FF6, I get that all too painful "I paid $8 for this..." feeling, every single godforsaken time Sabin or Edgar stops for an impossibly brief moment.
What else can I say that hasn't already been covered in other reviews?
- Lack of decent resolution support.
- The interface is junk.
- Bugs (I haven't finished the Cultist's Tower yet because I keep getting stuck at the top)
I often wonder why Squre-Enix has never considered developing a serious revamp of FF6. While this game is a classic, it could stand to benefit from some fresh game ideas or a few new twists. FF4 recieved a pretty significant overhaul for its DS/IOS/Steam versions and it was really cool. Then again, wouldn't revamping the game require effort? That sounds like way too much work for S-E.
Actually, I take that back. S-E puts a lot of effort into their ports, they're just terribly misguided as to what makes for an enjoyable experience. I'd rather see S-E provide an emulator and just charge people for roms. Heck, they could even be like Sega and offer workshop support, so gamers can use rom-hacks. Granted, as you've probably heard, this has opened a Pandora's box. Some of the stuff uploaded to the Sega Genesis Collection workshop has been pretty dire, and even illegal (masking unsupported games as "rom-hacks" for supported games). But that's the deal with Pandora's box, it contains all of the evils of the world, but it also contains hope.
There's no hope to be found in this edition of FF6.

This game can be a serious challenge. But unlike other difficult games, this one will not turn you off.
PROS:
You got to place structures. That's fun, right? I'm not being sarcastic. I mean this. You can choose where to place them (with certain rules of course). Whether it's a combat RTS or an economic one like this, doesn't matter; how often do you get to do that these days? There's a very subtle Sim City feel beneath the surface, which someone of my age appreciates.
Smart play is rewarded.
It requires you to think. Yes, this is a PRO.
It was developed by a man who was an important piece of the Civ III and Civ IV team (say what you will about IV, but I'm one of the IV lovers, and III was fantastic).
CONS:
While billed as an economic simulator (and it is, that's not a fib) the Black Market mechanic I feel is a bit overused, and makes it seem like a low-key combat type RTS as a secondary. I wouldn't mind doing without it.
Learning curve. But don't let that scare you away.
If you like to use the Steam discussions forum, there's very little response going on from players, and the few who are regulars can get a little... bothersome sometimes. (But as a PRO, the man behind the game itself responds in the forums!)
In general, I am very pleased with this game. It might seem boring and too casual on the surface, but believe me, once you play it, you will see how exciting and tense things can get. Watch as you lose shares in your business! That's a big deal! Better secure your shares! Buy in to the competitors! But how? What can you produce for a profit? What can you ship? What can you take the hit on for having to purchase? You better decide what you can produce and what you have to buy, because if you try to do it all, you WILL FAIL.
I give it a 7/10. 8s with me are rare, 9s rarer still and the day I give a game a 10 that's been produced after the golden age of PC gaming is the day Hell freezes over, so my 7 means a lot more than you think.
My number 1 tip: Do not give up. Do not get frustrated. Accept when you screw up. There's always something to learn.

Economic strategy game? More like Business Wars!!
Offworld Trading Company does a good job capturing the essence of managing a corporation and trying to push out your competition by buying them out.
Simplistic yet detailed.  Though there is a lot going on, everything can easily be learned.  For example: Iron needs to be mined for your refineries to create steel.  Steel is then required for a lot of other buildings and reduces the overall cost to build more if you have a bunch in stock.  Or you can sell it on the market and make a tidy profit.
Smooth gameplay. Short on supplies?  The game automatically purchases what you need and increases your debt thus making the gameplay flow smooth.  Indicators also let you know when your facilities are not working and also lets you know what materials you do not have.
Corporate espionage.  Though you cannot directly attack the other corporations, you can cackle to yourself twisting your long mustache as you sabatoge your opponent's greatest money maker.
Ranked Multiplayer.  The AI is more than enough challenge, however there is a ranked multiplayer you can jump in challenge other individuals to see who is the master of economic warfare.
There really isn't much negative things to say about this game.  Except that maybe this game may not appeal to those who wants to bring out their troops and order them to attack.

I had never eard of this game until I saw it on a weekend sale.
Looked interesting so I checked a few videos and reviews and decided to buy since it was so cheap.
I'm really glad I did it.
It's a strategy game unlike any other I know off.
Feals a bit like a sci fi 4X strategy game but with minimal eXploration and no eXtermination, at least not in the way we are used to, but played like an RTS without the insane APM requirement.
Unlike typical 4X games a game of Offworld Trading Company can be as short as 30 minutes but that doesn't meen it's shallow.
There's a lot of depth and tecniques to master with 4 very different companies to choose from, 13 resources and a decent amount of advanced structures that have the potential to turn arround the result if used well.
Every game plays different because the map is randomly generated since we need to adjust to the resources available. That influences the company we choose with it's very distinct playstyle and overall all 4 feel balanced on most scenarios.
Some people may dislike the quick nature skirmishes but for those the game offers the campaign mode where you choose a CEO from 8 available and try to be the dominating company over the course of several skirmishes.
Each CEO starts with different setups of structures that force us to very different strategies.
Between skirmishes we have an extra strategic layer that provides a sense of progression and increasing difficulty. That's not just a gimmic, that's a fully developed feature that adds a new level of importance to some of the game's mechanics such as the acumulated debt, but also adds new ones like purchasing colony modules.
The only gripe I have with the campaign mode are the scientific CEOs because they do feel handicaped because they miss some key structures.
Overall I really enjoyed my experience with Offworld so far.
It's pure game design genious, simple yet deep. You can play a quick skirmish on a short 30 min break, or do a campaign for a day long without getting boring or repetitive.
If what you read fealt interesting even for a slight bit then go ahead and pick this game, you won't regret it.
TL, DR:
I have plenty of 4X strategy games and plenty RTS games. Offworld Trading Company fills the void between those 2 categories and at least to me it felt really refreshing and super fun.
I my opinion it's even worth the full price.

My first touch for LiF was from the MMO closed beta. Despite the crashes and occasional bugs, I enjoyed the game very much because everything is time consuming, hard and can sometimes feel like work but the feeling of accomplishement is way beyond explanation. Life truly is feudal.
During my MMO closed beta period, I joined this guild X and after the Beta MMO went down for maintenance, we still decided to play together and my guild leader gave me free copy of LiF: YO so that I can join them.
Life is Feudal: Your Own is very similar to LiF: MMO but since the servers in "Your Own" are hosted by other players, the rules can get messy and the leveling rating of skills can be adjusted so high that this game becomes way easier and this is a relief for those who do not like to work really hard to get nails or rope just to build a chicken coop or a well. Also the map of Your Own is a lot smaller and it's always the same island unlike the MMO that is one big world.
Despite the fact that the world in "Your Own" is just boring and small, everything else in this game is nearly perfect. You can and have to do everything from scratch. It took me nearly 3 hours just to even out the ground so that I can build my first shack and basic stuff like Kiln so that I can make charcoal from billets that I saw out of the wood that I cut down myself with the axe that I made myself from the rocks, sticks and plant fiber I gathered with my bare hands. This game is very deep and like everything in this game, even explaining it is very time consuming.
The thing about this game is that it's hard and complicated and it can be frustrating to start build a camp, a town or a fort when you realize that you really need to do so much work to be able to do the simpliest stuff. The thing here is that every player should find other players to play with and divide the jobs between players and actually play as a feudal community.  This game also has PvP and you can attack who ever you want where ever you want but if you die, you lose everything.
Personally I enjoy this game vastly, I hope that the developers just make the MMO version for this game stable enough since it's pretty much perfect in all the other ways when it comes to open world sandbox game but I will wait for the MMO to come out and take it more seriously and use "Your Own" as an learning tool for incoming challenges.

Decided to write a new updated review, this time its more or less the same. But still a negitive review. Going to rate this game on factors based on game design, playability, and longevity.
Game Design 7/10- The only thing really holding this game back is Moba styled classes. Everything about it a breath of fresh air except classes... You have Assassins or so called heavy hitters, Tanks, and harassers/disablers. It could be a balanced issue, but Tanks are took defensive, impossible to kill unless you use a class that counters them. This applies to every class, what does not make sense is you have 'dueling' game mode, that really when two skilled players no matter who is better match up, whoever counters who wins. Tanks generally dominate because they have a massive health/pool severely disable more offensive characters while lacking in damage (only slightly) all characters do for the most part the equal damage, its the health pool that differs.
Playability 4/10- You CAN NOT buttom smash this game, combos timing and some can be slow, some moves require you to actually wait for the opponent, such as parrying and most dodges. Some players are good enough, too good in fact that these moves don't work on them elimiating half and creating a 'Meta' saftey net. If you are seriously interested in buying this game, do your research play what is considered 'good' Currently the Centurion and Shunobi are by far the best designed characters in-game, too bad they are locked behind a pay wall or some serious game-time. 15000 Steelm each class unless you feel like shelling out 40$ so you don't feel like you wasted your money (yet)
Longevity- 3/10 How long the game will last? Well, honestly, we can all agree this was the best selling game in march on console. However, steam charts have seen a over 50% decrease in player activity since launch...But it picked back up again since the DLC drop. I wouldn't give it hope, its fun, its competitive and the fighting is something you really can't get from anything else. However I am going to wait for all the DLC to drop, as well for some balancing patches.
Personally, in order for this game to survive. Just like any Moba, they need an actual team dedicated to solving balancing issues and technical ones as well. This is a gem but its a very rough one that could easily be sorted with all the coal that has been coming out recently..

Amnesia: The Dark Descent is my favorite game ever, and when SOMA got announced, I was so hyped for it. I knew that it was going to be really good, and I was not disappointed. Unlike Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs, but we don't talk about that game.
I actually enjoyed the game's futuristic, underwater, post-apocalyptic setting more than I thought I would because I wasn't much of a fan of the first two Bioshocks. But this game really made me think of Bioshock and even Portal 2 at some points.
Pros:
-Holy crap, the sounds are amazing and so unique for everything.
-Very errie, dark, and creepy locations kept me on edge.
-The story is pretty interesting, may seem a bit like an overused scenario, but it's still good.
-The visuals are just awesome to look at.
-It really feels like an open world with the lack of immersion-breaking loading screens.
-Use of lighting, both light and dark, were very good in not only as far as setting, but as to showing where your objectives were.
-It's just really fun to play.
Cons:
-Limited FPS. There's a nice little guide in the forums that walk you through on how to uncap the FPS limit which I HIGHLY recommend doing. Choppy frames are not nice.
-Confusion and lack of direction at certain points. I spent 20 minutes looking for one little thing that I couldn't move on without and it was very frustrating.
-Lack of fear for most monsters. I don't know if it's just me being jaded from other horror games, but most of the monsters didn't scare me because of how easily I could juke them and just book it. There were some really good ones though, ones that really made me scared, but most were so easy to just run around.
-Important dialouge only played once that includes information on how to advance. There were a few times I didn't know what to do because I didn't remember or wasn't fully listening to the conversations happening and I missed information on what exactly I needed to do. A reminder line of dialouge here and there probably would have helped me a lot.
Overall, I really liked this game. I'll probably play through it a few more times, but Amnesia: TDD still tops the chart for me as the best horror game I've ever played.
This game is definitely worth buying and playing.

My take on it after the first few games, for those who are looking at it now and thinking of buying it.
In comparision to other games of the ilk, this is a game more favored towards Jason, as he really has a lot going for him and escape routes for survivors can take a great deal of exploration around the map and some luck in that you get items that you need. And, if you are a DbD fan, don't bother juking; Jason has throwing knives that will just slow you down to a crawl and there are hardly any places around the map that are good for that style of play.
However, that is not to say the game isn't fun when being a survivor. There are some genuinely tense moments, like hiding in a closet while Jason chases someone else and you hope he doesn't know you are there. The question is this: is the tension of the match going to be enough for your entertainment? Couple this with the fact that xp gain is relatively slow, and if you get unlucky during the match and are one of the first to die you will get hardly any xp, meaning it's a slower amount of progress towards character unlocks that may fit your style perfectly. At start, you get the basic, no good no bad guy, the bait girl who runs a lot and fast, and the girl who barely touches being a stealth character but is more for being composed. They are good entrance characters, but I already get the feeling they will be migrated from.
There isn't much to say about Jason; he's fun and you get to chop people up. While DbD killers focus more on tracking and hunting prey who know how to escape, Jason is there to impede progress and stop players from completing objectives, whether by scaring people away or by outright killing them. If you manage to be picked for Jason, you'll have fun; it's a fair power trip.
The last thing to note is to not go into the game expecting to main Jason. In full lobbies you have a 1 in 8 chance of being picked. You will be playing a lot of counsulor before getting Jason.
For a day 1 purchase, I'd give it a try if you can afford it. The price is steep, though, for the content that it has. For me, I enjoy it for what I paid, for now.

Fantastic game. If you are into FPS, but also like a bit of strategy, thinking and skill, rather than just running into a room with a shotgun and laying havoc, this game is spot on.
Instead of a regular FPS where all you need is accuracy and a good gun, this game relies heavily on you having good senses of hearing and sight, good map knowledge, and your thinking skills need to be able to adapt to any situation. Every game is random, as the same window a sniper flew threw last round, could be untouched the next.
If you are the type to sprint around a map with a shotgun, this isn't for you, as this game punishes you heavily if you make too much noise or if you are not ready for what may be waiting around the corner. From a launcher that fires a breaching round to destroy walls, to a cluster charge capable of clearing whole rooms out, to a mounted DP-28 able to mow down an entire enemy force, to a knife and some silent boots; the arsenal options in this game are endless.
But again, don't go gung-ho, because you could end up dropping to the floor with a knife to your throat, threatening your life for your teammates' locations. One person's death can mean everything to the match.
FPS - 8/10
Suspense - 9/10
Brain Usage - 10/10 (excluding having yours blown off by a Desert Eagle)
Explosions and Map Destruction 14/10

Wow! I haven't played that long yet, but let me tell you I would recommend anyone get this game! I personally don't care about the 40 dollar price tag because - suprise! Games cost money :O I think it's well worth forty dollars, and I'm sure the devs will continue to grow the game in the future.
As of now, the gameplay feels pretty good. I'm absolutely terrified as the counselor, and feeling god-like as Jason. I think that is a good thing, a real horror, ASYMETRICAL experience. I also play Dead By Daylight, and while the games are similar in some ways, I feel they satisfy two different niches entirely. I couldn't really compare them, as many people seem to be doing.
As of now, I played as Jason only once, so the rest of my review will be more counselor-oriented. (Which I love tbh. I've seen some people not like being them, only having fun at Jason. But I love being counselors.)
As a counselor, I love the scavenging part of the game, along with the unlock system. I like how they did not give you every counselor at once - giving you something to aspire to. I'm neutral on the perk system - random chance, which could swing either way. It's fun to have that gambling aspect though, because you'll never know what you get. What I really like about this game, that differs from the survs in DBD, is each one of them has their own strengths and weaknesses, allowing you to pick and choose based on how you want to play.
Ex:
Chad is super lucky, but has super low composure and will freak out a lot more - allowing Jason the opportunity to track him better
Vanessa has great speed and stamina, but absolutely no stealth. (if I play as a stealthy character like AJ, I try to avoid all running Vanessas as much as possible. Has led to my discovery and death before).
I really love the indiviudal feeling that it provides and allows for choice of gameplay. Do you want to hide out and scavenge? Protect other players with strength? Use hit and run tactics? Repair things? It's up to you!
For a little of Jason from my experience, it was super fun to hunt down the teens and slaughter them for Mommy Voorhees. You can kill any way you want to, as well. You can go for fancy, cinematic kills, or simply throw knives, set traps, or bludgeon them to death with your weapon.
I would say the game only has a few cons. One of them is defintely the fact that you have to wait until the end of the match to get full XP. Which could be a pain if you die in the first five minutes, or escape early on. Another thing that I personally didn't like was the lack of push-to-speak on a controller (if there was one, I didn't see it). I prefer to play on controller if possible, and it was mildly annoying that with controller, speech was automatic. For me, with two barking dogs at home, and a busy house, I didn't like it too much, especially since it would be loud for other players and kinda immersion-breaking.
Besides that, nothing wrong with what I see!!! Do yourself a favor and get this game! Super fun and you won't regret it!

I had never eard of this game until I saw it on a weekend sale.
Looked interesting so I checked a few videos and reviews and decided to buy since it was so cheap.
I'm really glad I did it.
It's a strategy game unlike any other I know off.
Feals a bit like a sci fi 4X strategy game but with minimal eXploration and no eXtermination, at least not in the way we are used to, but played like an RTS without the insane APM requirement.
Unlike typical 4X games a game of Offworld Trading Company can be as short as 30 minutes but that doesn't meen it's shallow.
There's a lot of depth and tecniques to master with 4 very different companies to choose from, 13 resources and a decent amount of advanced structures that have the potential to turn arround the result if used well.
Every game plays different because the map is randomly generated since we need to adjust to the resources available. That influences the company we choose with it's very distinct playstyle and overall all 4 feel balanced on most scenarios.
Some people may dislike the quick nature skirmishes but for those the game offers the campaign mode where you choose a CEO from 8 available and try to be the dominating company over the course of several skirmishes.
Each CEO starts with different setups of structures that force us to very different strategies.
Between skirmishes we have an extra strategic layer that provides a sense of progression and increasing difficulty. That's not just a gimmic, that's a fully developed feature that adds a new level of importance to some of the game's mechanics such as the acumulated debt, but also adds new ones like purchasing colony modules.
The only gripe I have with the campaign mode are the scientific CEOs because they do feel handicaped because they miss some key structures.
Overall I really enjoyed my experience with Offworld so far.
It's pure game design genious, simple yet deep. You can play a quick skirmish on a short 30 min break, or do a campaign for a day long without getting boring or repetitive.
If what you read fealt interesting even for a slight bit then go ahead and pick this game, you won't regret it.
TL, DR:
I have plenty of 4X strategy games and plenty RTS games. Offworld Trading Company fills the void between those 2 categories and at least to me it felt really refreshing and super fun.
I my opinion it's even worth the full price.

I can only write for a brief while since I am an adult with a baby to take care of. But it needs to be said - this is one of the Rainbow Six greats, right up there with Rogue Spear and the like. Destructible environments really make this game - the closest thing there is, the Battlefield series, doesn't compare. Here you can poke a small hole in a wall so you can ambush hapless enemies, or blow them wide open with explosives. Floors, ceilings, objects, windows - there is a constant metagame in each match where opponents breach and seal against each other.
There's a lot of complaints about R6, I know. But they break down into these few categories, and I'll just briefly refute them here.
1. People are toxic! - That's the internet. For ever 9 people who are great sports, there's always going to be a jerk with a big mouth. Learn to deal with these people. It's part of growing up in the internet age.
2. Hitreg is bad! - No, it isn't. Thin operators like the skinny fast females (Ash , Caviera, etc) are indeed harder to hit than the big fat guys like Tachanka (balanced out by armor differences). If you have a problem with this, you have a problem with reality.
3.  Game is glitched! - Every game has exploits. The exploits in R6 are seldom used in actual play, rather ranked or casual (for example, the glitch to fall through the map by using deployable cover). That is because their usefulness is low, and it's really hard to "activate" them. Furthermore, Ubi does actively work to resolve them. There are also some other "glitches" that really aren't - they are just creative ways to use the enviroment. Whiners will insist that these are glitches, but they are fools and their comments should be ignored.
4. It's too expensive / too hard to buy new ops / too P2W - No, it's not. It's expensive if you want to get instant access to operators instead of earning them, it's not too hard to buy new ops at all even if you have the starter version, and its certainly not p2w as even the most basic recruit can hold their own against any operator, regardless of what gear they have.
In short, it's a good game and well worth the money.

Amendment regarding the negative reviews: Most who do not recommend this game have probably played barely past a chapter which is mostly a tutorial. No time to get immersed into the story, find out how you use your abilities or explore the harder puzzles later on.
Incidentally the music is among the best fitting soundtracks I have come across.

.

Don't get me wrong, Final Fantasy VI is my absolute favorite of all of the Final Fantasy series, but I and pretty much everyone I have talked to have had various issues with this port.  My particular issue is a bug that is not fixable at present in which the Font shows up only as funky shaped blocks.  It is COMPLETELY unreadable.  In a game where reading is critical, that means the game is not even remotely playable.  I have tried multiple solutions, including various font replacement mods, reinstalls, verifying game cache... you name it, I've tried it.  What it boils down to for me is: I wasted my money on this port, and then spent too long trying to troubleshoot the issue and it is no longer refundable.  I cant play it, its just taking up space on my pc.  If you want to know what problems other people are dealing with, just read the other reviews - its all there!  Unfortunately, I was never able to play it enough to verify if any of these other issues are even that severe, or if its just people being dramatic about not liking the sprites.
In summary, if you have another way to play FFVI than this port - DO IT, 999999/10 I recommend playing the game.
However, if this port is your attempt to try the game for the first time, do yourself a favor and find a GBA emulator instead.  Experiencing an amazing game through a broken port is just going to ruin it for you.

GAMEPLAY:
Great gameplay requires skill, the depth is massive and it plays like a easy to learn, hard to master, there are bushs that can be hid in by both teams (get to teams later) areas that only the thieves (vents, broken windows, etc.) can enter but guards can look inside and shoot inside/outside. now there are 2 unique teams and has the name of the game says The guards and The thieves each with balenced out diffrences The thieves can see in the dark (night vision) and mostly have silenced weapons except the juggernaut which has a AK-47, and the thieves have diffrent goals depending on the gamemode like bomb defuseal or plain out steal a precious item in the main gamemode that the guards dont know what to protect out of a whole bunch of items laid around the map (you can tell what they are by a orange circle around them and 2 for the objective) you do get bonus points for extra items taken as well just as a quick hint. I got this game, thinking it'd be great to finally be able to do DayZ since that was all I knew about Arma 3 at the time.
I never spent more than about 15 hours in DayZ. Haven't even finished the campaign.
Now, before I begin on this amazing game, beware that if you go to school, or have any other kinds of commitments (like to a GIRLFRIEND MAYBE) those risk being sacrificed in this game.
I think the most I've binged this game for in one sitting is around 14 hours. You might think that's a lot, but that's probably not even coming close to the record.
Most of my gameplay has been spent in the Eden editor, a masterpiece of game engineering that permits me to create almost any scenario I can envision with the aid of completely customizable events that can be scripted from the ground right up to heaven.
I spent about 100 hours making scenarios for myself, we're talking singleplayer CQC breaching situations, hostage extraction/elimination/defense, and HALO drops behind enemy lines. This stuff is so engaging, and is awesome beyond words. After that, I met some other dudes who were in a clan called the 313th that host all sorts of events for small groups in the clan.With them, I went from my little dim vision of Arma to learning how to be a decent combat medic (I never took to it), learning how to crash-land a helicopter (The fate of the helo is that of the pilot!), and going right into some really intense battles with insurgents, where my half-decency with medical equipment saved a few lives on the battlefield. I even overdosed my squad's light support gunner on morphine!
From therein, I initiated my girlfriend to the tactical cult that is the ArmA 3 community, and now she's into it too. I've got 400 hours and I've not got a doubt that that's going to drastically increase this christmas break, as unfortunate as that'll be for my average at school.
Anyways, the ArmA can be whatever you want it to be, though the game is pretty demanding when it comes to resources. However, for a game of its scale, it's nicely optimized. For about 300 of my ingame hours, these were my specs and what they gave me in terms of FPS and graphics quality:
I ran an i5 3470 along with a GT730 2GB (Not a GTX!) and 16GB of DDR3, with which, on lowest settings, in optimal conditions, I could get up to high 30s in FPS. Usually I was in the mid 20s, which, for a game like Arma, can actually be pretty fine in most combat conditions (Avoid close quarters against players, and piloting helicopters unless you're able to compensate for the low FPS with some pretty impressive maneuvers).
What more do I need to say? You might thnk 400 hours in this game is a ton, but it's really a tiny portion of what a real dedicated veteran will play. I've seen up to
hours of ingame time. It's not a joke.
If you can get it cheap, go for it. It has pretty much no replay value, but the gameplay in that first run is quite great.

Of Guards and Thieves - a third person stealth shooter with a heart for details.
OGAT offers plenty of different modes, like TDM, Bomb Defusal, or the classic Guards vs Thief mode. The game plan is simply but great: The "guards" are heavily armed and have to defend one of the official or usermade maps against the "thieves", who are much weaker, but able to see in the dark. The graphics are not photorealistic, but wellmade with an eye for details. The community is small but friendly and new players usually find a helping hand, if they ask for one. The developers themself are very close to the community and actually consider suggestions of the community.
The players can either play on one of the huge dedicated servers or host smaller servers themselves, to play with their friends. The game is free to play and the classes are available by level-up. The money from the premium accounts is only used to develop the game and to pay for the work of the developers.
To sum up:
If you are a friend of Indee games and if you love the idea of a stealth shooter, Of Guards and Thieves is the right game for you.

I am the biggest fan of all kinds of shooter games. But this one.. This one is extremely frustratig and annoying. I always like a challenge, especially if the enemies are realistic and stuff.. But this game is ridiculously hard on Medium difficulty. And also, the checkpoints (from which you can start if you die in a current mission) are very few. So you end up memorizing every enemy's position, and suddenly you press a wrong key and you get killed. And of course, the last checkpoint was a billion light-years away; so you have to go on stealth again (because otherwise the enemies are OP) and try to silently kill the tons of soldiers again. I've been playing for 5 hours continuously and I barely made it to the end of the third mission.
Surely, it has it's neat features, like the bullet camera, and the x-ray vision on bullet penetration; but it really doesn't matter anymore when you end up restarting from checkpoints over and over, just wishing that you will get this done with already, so you can save your progress. Otherwise, if you made it to a checkpoint, then you quit, next time you'll have to start the mission from the beginning.
So overall, you can still go and try it, but I do NOT recommend it. Go play Sniper in TF2; it'll be much more fulfilling. And free.

Man oh man, I wish Steam reviews had an option to put an 'it's okay' rating.
Hacker Evolution is one of those games that I bought as a bundle because it was on sale (Hacker Evolution bundle for around £2.20 haha). But is the first instalment one I can recommend? Before we go into that, let's cover all the points.
The story seems a little bit convoluted but in simple terms, a lot of crazy stuff happened in the world and it's up to Brian Spencer to find out who did it by taking the back door in, hacking computers and following leads.
The graphics are decent and also rather fitting for a hacking type game. The controls are entered into the console and you type them out, just like a real hacker. You can even upgrade your hardware and the like, which becomes very important later on in the game. The music is catchy the first time you hear it but I'm not sure if it fits in with the aesthetic. It does sound cool though.
However, the objectives are very vague and there is very little direction on what to do next (except in the tutorial level but that doesn't really count). It's erring very dangerously on that line of frustration. Some brief guidance would help a little but just like a real hacker, that guidance isn't given. Is this a good or a bad thing? That's a bit difficult to say.
What about the difficulty curve? More like difficulty leap. After you finish the tutorial the difficulty skyrockets. You'll definitely need a pen and paper to take notes of all the commands as well as any other important details. Plus, any 'trace' you've acquired will be carried over to the next level so one has to watch that.
Does it feel like hacking? Yes, in quite a few aspects.
Does it give you that slightly badass feel while playing? In a sense.
Should you definitely buy the game? Not at full price. £6.99 is a VERY steep asking price for a game like this. On sale, buy it if you want. But full price? No.
All in all, I can just about recommend this game. But it is a very fine line. If you like a big challenge and feeling like a hacker, then go for it. If you don't have the patience or can't handle frustration, steer well clear.

SOMA is an ambitious work of science fiction which grapples with questions of consciousness and what it truly means to be human.Things never get boring in SOMA, thanks to an engaging story.
The developer, Frictional Games, are masters of the survival horror genre, and it shows, as some areas invoke fear before you even see a monstrous robotic being. I expected nothing less from the developer behind Amnesia: The Dark Descent and I have to say, they've out done themselves this time.
While some scares are unquestionably intense and terrifying, other monsters like the one you meet in Lambda are more annoying than scary.  The other half of the game consists of puzzle-solving and exploration making this game feel more open than the previous Penumbra or Amnesia games. However, at times and particularly in under water sections, the freedom creates unfortunate pacing problems.  I found the lack of maps / "you are here" signs in the under water section hindered my progression. I was irritated that I spent almost 2 hours at one particular station looking for a zepplin control panel to take me to the next area.  There is no marking to indicate where your next objective lies, and a great deal of time can be spent trying to find things.
Like the very best horror stories, SOMA maintains an unsettling level of ambiguity and dread, which has you doubting everyone and everything around you. The main character, Simon, wakes up aboard a dilapidated, abandoned research facility at the bottom of the ocean shortly after having his brain scanned by a doctor.
The prequel story of PATHOS 2 can be pieced together by frequently encountered (but often unreliable) black-boxes. It’s genuinely disconcerting, and few games play with ambiguity so well while telling a story that players can follow.
Simon’s awakening is prefaced by a famous quote from Philip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥ “Reality is that which, when you stop believing in it, doesn’t go away.” The quote alludes to the particular type of uncertainty at play; as you soon meet a variety of malfunctioning robots who talk and behave like they are real humans.
You soon realise these robots don’t perceive themselves to be machines at all, since they’re running digital and identical copies of a person’s mind scanned for the A.R.K Project.  This plot point opens your mind to philosophical questions to be tackled. At first, Simon thinks these machines are being remote-controlled, functioning as avatars for people located elsewhere.
These robots aren’t sleek, fleshy androids like the "Working Joes" in Alien Isolation.
Although slightly bipedal, they’re rusty, broken-down heaps of metal, spewing oil, yet this only intensifies the tragedy of the situation. They believe themselves to be human, and can’t understand why you can’t see them as such.
It’s simultaneously intriguing and tragic, and when you’re given the choice to unplug these machines or "save them", SOMA throws up some fascinating dilemmas which I’ve thought more and more about since finishing it.
Did I do the right thing by killing Amy? Or could I have saved her? Should I have saved Carl instead of electrocuting him?
These were questions I asked myself upon dealing with their consequences.
SOMA is fascinating on multiple levels. It has fewer original ideas than amnesia did, but ultimately it’s built upon the framework of Amnesia with the ‘hide in a corner crying as the monster slowly approaches’ feel to the gameplay.
Gameplay involves cowering in corners or behind doors waiting for the big bad thing to lose interest and wander out of the area you happen to be in. The robots infected by a rogue, self-replicating AI are intimidating and scary, but after a while they become frustrating since there’s no discernible way to avoid them.
For instance, Amnesia had a mechanic at your disposal that gave the player the ability to pick up objects and throw them to lure a creature away to investigate a noise. Sadly, the mechanic has been removed from SOMA.
Exploration and puzzle-solving fill in the rest of SOMA’s gameplay. While some of its research stations are dimly-lit and streaked with blood, there’s a surprising amount of variety to be discovered. Horrible, claustrophobic places where cables wrap around objects like sinew on bone. In fact, one of SOMA’s most consistently terrifying sequences takes place in the Mariana trench and there’s a rather hungry sea creature after you.
Puzzles are more infuriating, however. There are a couple of decent ones, with some of the best puzzles being linked to SOMA’s premise.
It entails booting up a ‘person’s’ consciousness and manipulating their reality via an operating system, in order to extract valuable information. It made me think about how people torture Sims and I found that it wasnt so different...

Highly recommend this game if your the type of person who loves the thrill of nerve racking FPS scenes with freaky enemies!!! But the story to this game is amazing. It had me thinking the whole time and made me wonder if maybe one day, putting your mind in another body could be real. The game play of this is absolutely gorgeous. Might not be crysis like but the scenery, especially underwater, is so full of colors and beautiful marine life. The mechanics were very pleasing as almost everything is interactable an can be manipulated which is very useful when solving puzzles and getting to the next part. I enjoy the fact that there are parts of the game where the player is relaxed or solving a puzzle, then there are nerve racking moments that your on the edge of your chair with your cornea .02 mm away from your screen. Not to mention that the generally placed scares are very well scripted although the unscripted ones are just as good. Few jumpscares but i guess the five night at freddy players will enjoy those. Wow! I haven't played that long yet, but let me tell you I would recommend anyone get this game! I personally don't care about the 40 dollar price tag because - suprise! Games cost money :O I think it's well worth forty dollars, and I'm sure the devs will continue to grow the game in the future.
As of now, the gameplay feels pretty good. I'm absolutely terrified as the counselor, and feeling god-like as Jason. I think that is a good thing, a real horror, ASYMETRICAL experience. I also play Dead By Daylight, and while the games are similar in some ways, I feel they satisfy two different niches entirely. I couldn't really compare them, as many people seem to be doing.
As of now, I played as Jason only once, so the rest of my review will be more counselor-oriented. (Which I love tbh. I've seen some people not like being them, only having fun at Jason. But I love being counselors.)
As a counselor, I love the scavenging part of the game, along with the unlock system. I like how they did not give you every counselor at once - giving you something to aspire to. I'm neutral on the perk system - random chance, which could swing either way. It's fun to have that gambling aspect though, because you'll never know what you get. What I really like about this game, that differs from the survs in DBD, is each one of them has their own strengths and weaknesses, allowing you to pick and choose based on how you want to play.
Ex:
Chad is super lucky, but has super low composure and will freak out a lot more - allowing Jason the opportunity to track him better
Vanessa has great speed and stamina, but absolutely no stealth. (if I play as a stealthy character like AJ, I try to avoid all running Vanessas as much as possible. Has led to my discovery and death before).
I really love the indiviudal feeling that it provides and allows for choice of gameplay. Do you want to hide out and scavenge? Protect other players with strength? Use hit and run tactics? Repair things? It's up to you!
For a little of Jason from my experience, it was super fun to hunt down the teens and slaughter them for Mommy Voorhees. You can kill any way you want to, as well. You can go for fancy, cinematic kills, or simply throw knives, set traps, or bludgeon them to death with your weapon.
I would say the game only has a few cons. One of them is defintely the fact that you have to wait until the end of the match to get full XP. Which could be a pain if you die in the first five minutes, or escape early on. Another thing that I personally didn't like was the lack of push-to-speak on a controller (if there was one, I didn't see it). I prefer to play on controller if possible, and it was mildly annoying that with controller, speech was automatic. For me, with two barking dogs at home, and a busy house, I didn't like it too much, especially since it would be loud for other players and kinda immersion-breaking.
Besides that, nothing wrong with what I see!!! Do yourself a favor and get this game! Super fun and you won't regret it!

As much as I can enjoy myself with the core gameplay, the frame work holding it together is a complete mess and inexcuseable for a company as large as Ubisoft - Peer to peer is simply so mindnumbingly annoying to deal with, it outright ruins the game experience.
Be it random disconnects, and there are a lot.
Or maybe desync between players, allowing bogus hits or moves; that guy you just executed while you were on a single sliver of health? Turns out he got the bias and finished you with a light attack to the face.

Now, while the framework is trash, make no mistake - the game itself is fun, smashing friends and randoms alike is a pure joy when the game does work, and when it does, I almost never stop grinning, the only other game to provide such entertainment came from the likes of Chivalry, another medieval title. /When it works/
Because once your right at the climax of a Domination match, nearly about to win and you get cut off by a disconnect or multiple members of your team are dropped and you're left with AI? It simply kills any of the aformentioned fun.
Now then.. Do I suggest the game? If steam had a Maybe or a Neutral option, I'd pick that.
But as of now, you try it yourself if you feel like it's worth investing the time, if you suffer connection problems as frequently as me, refunds are there for a reason.

I love short games, and I love cheap games. I love short, cheap games that tell touching stories with impossibly deep characters. Conversely, I don't love short, cheap games that are unfortunately lacking in quality—games like the obnoxiously titled Hamlet (or the last game without MMORPG features, shaders and product placement). Although it does have an attractive, cute art style, Hamlet is rife with non-intuitive, often frustrating puzzles and a plot that is ridiculous in a way that far surpasses the tasteful.
Hamlet starts out with the plot of Shakespeare's famous play, but within a couple panels of the first cutscene, it's transformed into a grotesque attempt at a modernly witty version of a classic. The main character, Hamlet, is quickly replaced by a time-traveling scientist from the future who, after crashing into Hamlet and incapacitating him, is required to rescue Ophelia from Cladius in Hamlet's place. This scientist is forced to follow a line of plot that is loosely based on Hamlet to return Ophelia to her proper place at Hamlet's side. While an intriguing idea for a storyline, the delivery of the oddly sci-fi events is done in such a way that the game goes from quirky to downright deplorably ludicrous.
The gameplay of Hamlet is not a standard point and click adventure. The player is missing the typical inventory system and dialogue of such a game. Hamlet is instead played in silence, with the main character only communicating in brief, uninteresting thought bubbles. The short puzzles that the player is presented with are often incredibly nonlinear, to the point where I often found myself simply clicking all around the screen to see if I could simply stumble upon the answer to some of the more farfetched puzzles. The illogical solutions to the puzzles are made more frustrating by an interface that in no way highlights which objects on the screen allow for interaction.
Hamlet's frustration-inspiring, nonsensical puzzles do very little favors for its equally nonsensical plot, and not even its somewhat attractive atmosphere can pull this game back from its failings. At only an hour or two of teeth-gritting, boredom-inspiring gameplay, this tiny indie game isn't worth a misplaced dose of hopeful curiosity or the irritation that comes with its small price tag—even if it's picked up in the middle of a Steam sale. I suppose, in this case, the old adage holds true: you get what you pay for.

Sadly, after the first couple of tutorials they start introducing mechanics that make the game less fun. Once you really get into the game, you're no longer focused on colonizing, because you get an extremely limited amount of buildings. Once they're built, you need to watch a little stock ticker and sell off your spare resources. You can't do it all at once though, because selling dips the price, so you need to pause the game every 30 seconds or so to do it. It gets really tedious.
There's a goofy stock mechanic where you dump all of your extra money into your own stock (which doesn't seem to do much because people can and will still buy you out) and other people's stock, where you buy them out. If you get bought out (which can happen with no warning if you're not paying attention) it's instant game over.
This is a well made game and I'm sure lots of people will find it's what they're interested in playing, but a 30 minute game of micromanaging silicon prices isn't what I want to play. Maybe that's my fault for not looking into what this was more thoroughly, but I can't think of anyone I would recommend this to.

Outside of matches you can upgrade your building and individual rooms which all give different benefits. You can set up individual training plans for your players, which do cost quiet a bit money. Hire or fire players. Read email, sponsor offers etc. and check your schedule and ranking. Currently there isn't a whole lot to do in the game, but since the early access just released I'm sure it will change.

For anyone who isn't a die-hard tycoon/manager fan you might want to wait a little longer before purchasing the game. Anyone who is really into tycoons and MOBA's or competitive FPS like CSGO can already enjoy the game to some extent.
