The Earth is dead, well at least above sea level, and as the humans move to the sea and use up the resources there as well they are put into a desperate situation. They must send submarine like ships into a wormhole in the sky to see if they can find a new habitable place to live. That's where you come in. You are one of the brave pilots to go through the wormhole, but something strange happens. You return to Earth but a million years into the future. There appears to be no one left alive, and it is up to you to explore and discover what happened under the sea.
This is a challenging game, The Aquatic Adventure of the Last Human, that will have you pulling your hair out one minute, and then getting lost in the music and the retro-graphics the next minute. The reason why I say you'll be pulling your hair out is because you are going to be set with a certain amount of limitations that you'll have to unlock, or solve in order to advance the game. The thing is that in order to truly advance you will have to take on the bosses, and none of them are push-overs. Hell the first boss might take you a couple of tries to beat, and it only gets tougher from there.
As I mentioned before this game has retro-graphics. You are not going to be blown away by any photo-realistic graphics, but you will feel like you are playing a polished game from the past. There are several different locations, all with their own look that will have you wondering what exactly happened. You will travel through ruined underwater cities, through a sea of pipes, a warehouse, and more. There is definitely plenty to see, not to mention the fact that all the bosses have their own look which might haunt you in your dreams if you can't defeat them in combat.
To be honest the difficulty in this game REALLY only centers around the bosses, outside of that its just a matter of dodging some projectiles, avoiding corrosive gas, and keeping very far away from snapping clams. That's not to say that you can't die while just exploring the underwater world, believe me I learned that if you go straight at a floating mine you will die on impact.
The game is broken up by the power ups you gain as you play. You'll get a harpoon gun, which shoots from the bottom of the craft, and doesn't aim further up than parallel to the bottom of the ship, you'll also get a saw that will power through shining vines, and that's just the tip of the iceberg. The one thing I recommend doing is finding out where the second boss on is and then exploring every nook and cranny to see if there are power ups for your hull recovery or the hull strength. You will need ever single one of those power ups if you are going to survive.
Alright so here's the one issue with the game, and to be honest with you it's not a deal breaker, but its very annoying, and it has to do with the checkpoint system. You have to consciously interact with each checkpoint, while not fighting a boss, in order to respawn there. If you don't you will respawn somewhere far from where you last started and so you are left backtracking a ton, sometimes losing where and what you were previously doing.
There's also the area maps. I would have loved to uncover the map as I'm moving through the area so I know where I've searched on the screen, but instead as soon as you hit a new screen the entire map is displayed leaving you to wonder if you've been to that screen before, and if so have you searched EVERY inch of it. You never know what could be hiding in that section.
This game is not going to be for everyone. It is challenging enough that its going to scare away some of the people who don't like on the fly strategy and some luck when it comes to bosses, but that being said this is a game that you're going to keep coming back to because either you want the challenge, or maybe you just want to shoot the poor defenseless fish that can't actually hurt you, but you sure as hell can massacre each and everyone on the screen, over and over again. This game gets an 8.6 out of 10.

The game tries to be a bit of a metroidvania -sort of affair, with new paths of exploration opening up as you gain new abilities. However, the game is surprisingly limited in it's offerings. The game also lies: it says it can be played with a gamepad. I did, but I would not recommend it. Especially towards the end you need to be able to aim fairly precisely and switch firing directions very quickly, so a gamepad simply could not provide the required level of accuracy, which led to even more frustration.

After beating the game, even if I have to admit I like the premise, I didn't enjoy the experience enough to recommend.

In short, yes I would recommend the game.  It is not a perfect port but I still feel it's the definitive version of the game to me.
I think the world environments, battle backgrounds, spell effects, and static enemy sprites are absolutely gorgeous.  The character sprites overshadow that to many people, but for me the beauty of the other quite faithfully remade tiles and sprites makes up for that.  On the topic of those character sprites, people have a great many terrible things to say about them. I was among them, but I admit I got used to them. The graphics revamp was definitely not "lazy" though, even if those sprites stick out like a sore thumb.  It would have been far easier for them to use the old art assets than remake everything (and most of the remade assets are faithful enhancements of the original art in higher resolution).
On the topic of the UI there are postives and negatives, but I feel the positives outweigh the negatives.  When it comes to the main menu, overall the information is presented in a much more efficient format than the original SNES game.  For example the equipment and relics menus are one menu now, which makes much more sense.  Overall I feel it has saved me more time than not, and I feel the main menus are definitely superior.  I wish the controller input mirrored the SNES version, but the controls work fine for what they are.  I can't figure out how to scroll through pages quickly or manually sort items, which are the only two annoyances I have with the main menu system.
For the battle menu, originally I slammed the rising portrait mode.  There is an alternate mode too, but I find I like the default better.  In the end it turns out to control very much like Chrono Trigger's battle menu, in which you can easily move between each character's commands on screen.  The down side is the menu entries are large enough you must scroll unless you choose one of the other menu formats (which do not show all four characters' menus at once).  I would have liked the option for ATB bars on the side, but overall I feel the battle menu system allows choosing which character to use much smoother than the original system.  The character Cyan's special ability has been made a little more useful than the original and now lets him charge his move on his own after you select it, rather than forcing you to sit idle with the other characters while waiting.  Auto-battle is more accurately "repeat the last commands used." This includes the character Sabin's Blitz command, for example.  It is the built in enhanced equivalent of the "hold down the button to keep pressing what you did last" that worked in the SNES version, and can be toggled on and off with a button.
I like the redone script.  There are many scenes that feel like they go on longer than they did in the SNES version, showing how much had to be cut to fit on the limited cartridge space.  Some more classic lines from the first English translation are still retained though, which was a nice touch in my opinion.  Some of the more puzzling lines also make more sense now as well.
In rare very specific instances the music does have issues.  In one particular scene in which the music should keep pace with the rest of the scene, it loses syncrhonization.
In one portion of the game train sound effects are missing from the original version.  I have read that smooth transitions are missing in another portion:
I could swear that one of the cinematic scenes was much shorter than in the original:
Strangely, the opening music doesn't sound quite right, but everything else in the game does sound just like the SNES version including the sound effects.
I used a mod to remove the bilinear filtering, but if I could not it would not have ruined the experience.  I just think it's better without it.
The game was modified to drop the always-online DRM, instead using Steam's normal protection.  I think that was a very smart decision on Square Enix's part, and I applaud the fact the feedback criticizing that was taken seriously.  While for Final Fantasy V the game seems to have been completely unsupported after release, including for critical bugs and others easily reproduced, this game seems to have been treated better.  The overall experience seems smooth to me and I like most of the graphical changes.  It includes the GBA's added bonus featuers without the horrible GBA music.
This is not perfect, but that is not what I am gauging this recommendation on.  This is overall the definitive version of the game in my opinion and I recommend it to both fans of the original and others curious to try it.
(A note on Final Fantasy V, the game is still great and works fine for most, but I could not excuse SE's complete ignoring of its critical bugs.  It doesn't have a single patch. This game was treated much better.)

I figured there should be some more explanation why i do not recommend this game. The thing some of you have in mind are the so called pros and cons. There are many pros but they work against themselves so in the end the pros become cons.
How?
Graphichs: With the new models and textures + effects the game looks really good. There is a skill in the game called Herbalism where you gather herbs for making preparations like antidotes for snake bites or flux for making of mortar and steel. However the grass meshes are taller than the herbs. You need to turn the grass off in order to gather herbs. So why have good looking grass if it's not functional?
The trees in the early access stage of the game were thinner than the ones that came with an update at games release. What they didnt change was the activation box which remained small. So now instead of just walking up to a tree and selecting it you need to find a spot where you can actually access the activation box to be able to select it.
Mechanics: Starting from horses beeing stuck, wildlife able to walk through trees, fighting system wich ends up to be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥because the hitboxes are a mess and you cant hit anyone if you arent aiming for the nuts. On the other side you have animal husbandry where you can tame few animals and domesticate them. Once you place them in barns or stables these become just listings. In the index you can see the age and quality of an animal but its just a list, the are no actual animals (meshes+textures+animations) in these stables. So why build a freaking stable? It could as well been a rock called "the stable/barn", you can activate it put the animals inside, feed em, clear the dung, slaughter and so on....I mean...if i need to build a massive stable I want to see the animals in the freaking stable.
The Content: There are lots of things you can do. Crafting is one of them. From primitive tools basic object to more advanced ones. Every item has its quality. The better the quality of resources used and the higher your crafting skill the better the results you get - which translates into better quality tools and objects and longer durability of tools. Let's say you get into forestry like i did...increase your skill to 100 (and it takes forever to do so depending on server settins), get some sprouts and plant them. Friday the 13th passed away peacefully on the development floor after being cannibalized by its own "F13 Army," early 2017. Friday the 13th is survived by several sycophants who passionately insist that the game is still alive. "It's unreal," said one commenter, somewhat weepy and staring disillusioned into the newly occupied cemetery plot. "I can't believe it's dead. They were just releasing a whole bunch of new content. AI bots, Shelly, other... stuff..."
Coroners remarked that a release of half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥content is typical of games that die, and games often spastically release content sometimes well after death. Close neighbor Dead by Daylight added that Friday the 13th had always been "quiet."
"F13 never won any awards, and it never even really left its store page," said DbD. "We knew F13 was diagnosed with Chronic Bug Syndrome, and we knew F13 was struggling to get by after that banning incident in the summer of 2017 and suffered a blow from a ton of bad media... But we never knew it was this bad."
Friends and family had noticed F13 had become more reclusive after the summer. "But we just figured that F13 needed some time," said another fan, who preferred to remain anonymous. "If I knew it was this bad, I would have bought more emote packs and virtual cabins to help it get back on its feet."
The local shelter insisted the fans are not to blame.
"Fans aren't born to attack the developer. It's how the developer treats them that ultimately makes them turn. Blame the game." Still, others argue that some fans are born bad and will inevitably hurt a game if given the opportunity.
Friday the 13th's family asks that all gifts and donations be sent to the charity of their choice: Jimmy John's.

I'll admit, despite my amount of playtime with this game, I didn't think much of it. I would just play it because I thought I either had nothing better to do or just wanted something to do while watching or listening to something else. But after all of my playtime, I eventually realized why I kept coming back to this particular game and why it's one of my most-played games on Steam. That reason: It's legitimately one of the best third-person shooters out there.
Which doesn't seem to be the case on the surface, as the environments, though randomized for each playthrough, are mundane and generally constant. That can deceive the average viewer into thinking the gameplay itself is just as mundane as the environment, and it's anything but. Through my time playing in very Early Access to now (still in Early Access, but after many updates), I've witnessed a variety of both major and minor changes, and each update has generally improved the gameplay, and even if more problems are introduced they're typically solved fairly quickly, and some aren't really problems anyway. I've seen even people who otherwise really like the game harp on the most minor, nothing bull crap, and though there were times I've disagreed, it has led to the game only improving as time goes on anyway since the developer does actually listen to players.
To be exact, it's not just the randomized map layouts and bosses which provide the fun, nor is it the variety of weapons and add-ons you can apply, all of which actually perform vastly different functions and thus provide to each player's tastes (and new items have been added every so often to boot). It's the balance this game has with its leveling system compared to the enemies and rooms you encounter. It's how you encounter so many enemies in a room without feeling overwhelmed by everything at once, and even when you're overwhelmed it feels challenging rather than frustrating or ridiculous. It's the satisfaction you get when you slowly discover more items and what you can do with them along the way, as it's rare you get much of anything at once. There's even a level of strategy with how and what you want to level up and when as often you can only do one thing or the other. Should one buy a health upgrade before the boss, or buy the probe sensor so your probe weapons can fire on it as well? Or at least that's something you can contemplate if you happen to have purchased the map and know where the boss is, which means you can seek out the other rooms available beforehand and find more chances at obtaining items or experience points. Otherwise, you'd have to rely on your instinct and sometimes just pick something to upgrade or purchase before moving to the next room, boss or no boss (but especially for just in case there is a boss), and it's easy enough to do considering you can teleport from anywhere you are to anywhere you've been already.
Essentially, there's a serious polish to this game to the point where a lot of what many players can take for granted nowadays is thoroughly exemplified here. It's not big, it's not extravagant, it's not epic, it doesn't need to be any of those things. Even if other games within this same mold have more customization options or better graphics or even better level degisn or aesthetic touches, they have those merits but they don't have all of the solid fundamentals this game has. A game like Tetris is extremely popular and well-loved by virtue of just being simple and well-made, and that's what this is, and thus shows that sometimes that's all you need. I'm not saying this game should be considered an all-time great game like Tetris, but I still wouldn't have any qualms about saying it's the best isometric third-person roguelike shooter out there, and it's only getting better.

TL;DR: a fun twin-stick shooter with major bullet hell tendencies.  Still shows shortcomings from being an early access title.
EDIT: below has been updated to be more accurate.
You are a robot who, for some reason, must fight the other robots.  You have a weapon, and the other robots know they don't like you.  You destroy the other robots, and some of the standing structures around you to collect some things that act like XP, and some like money.   Some robots teleport in.  Sometimes alternate weapons and slot or collectible items appear.  Some structures are activated by battery cores and a fee of the "money" items.  Higher-level robots have upgraded bullet technology (see the videos) that disperse in more dangerous patterns.
You fight in arenas, that are all adjacent; like most room-level games, you are locked into the current arena until all the robotz r ded.  There is a quick transportation system, where you can teleport to any visited room instantly, as long as there are no enemies.  "Keycards" raise your access level to new arenas, where the robots are a higher level.  There are occasional boss arenas, who have multiple shield levels that must be destroyed before you start "hurting" them.  Items are persistent in rooms, so you can go back to a previous room to get that health/armor you didn't use.  You continue to fight robots in the expanding arena map until you die.
There is no persistence or upgrade between games (yet), other than revealed blueprints.  But there is a game end, if you defeat all five bosses.
In general this is a fun game, except for the shortcomings; you can tell this is still an early access title:
* No storyline, though this is not a big deal.
* Save game/restore feature is a bit clunky.
* A good number of crashes-- sorry, your game is gone.
* Occasional glitch where you get stuck on something and can't move.  Too bad you're in the line of fire!
* No explanation about how the items fit into your loadout.  Is this a passive item, or a slot item?  Did I spend money on something I don't want, because it takes up a slot that is already filled with something I'd rather keep?
However, I expect these will be overcome, if they ever finish the title-- it's nearly a year since the release.

Rush Rover is a simple but awesome game where you play as a robot fighting waves of evil robots. You find weapons and upgrades that help you battle the increasingly tough enemies. You can even find a little probe buddy that shoots enemies, too!
- Arcade mode that boasts up to 40 minute runs through 6 areas of increasing difficulty.
- Tons of powerful weapons and helpful plugins to be discovered, along with an upgrade system that makes you feel like you are truly getting stronger as you progress.
- Probes are small, flying bots that can be found randomly and they follow you around, shoot enemies on their own, and they can be upgraded too.

- Lots of different types of enemies, each with their own unique abilities. Each area has a boss that is selected randomly from a difficulty pool that scales up as you progress.
- Cores and Ultra Chips will upgrade your weapons, probes and plugins to make them more powerful and effective.
- Buildings that create weapons, give upgrade cores, reveal the map, and more can be found randomly and sent to home base, allowing you to use them any time.
- Along with the normal Arcade mode, there is a Hard mode that makes the game much more challenging without flooding the screen with enemies.
- Dodge mode that allows the player to practice dodging whenever they want. Dodge rooms can be found in the Arcade mode too, and rewards players who have practiced dodging well by surviving long enough.
- Great chiptune soundtrack that fits very well into the game's setting makes exploring and fighting even more exciting. Not a huge variety of songs, but they'll get you humming along.
- Well made sprites and environments that fit the game's atmosphere.
- Amazing price for such a well made game. I mean, 6 dollars? What a great deal!

I remember disliking this game the first time I played it.
Compared to the first Knights of the Old Republic game, it was a major tone shift and didn't evolve gameplay enough to justify it as a proper sequal.  It doesn't have a plot twist like KOTOR 1, and I was quick to deem it a wasted oppertunity.
Now after replaying it a few years later, I've completely changed my mind.
This game is darker, more mature than KOTOR 1.  The characters have all suffered at the hands of the Force in one way or another, and the Jedi aren't just the good guys.  There's moral complexity in the plot.  Sadly this muddled morality doesn't really factor into gameplay, but the story is great.
It is carried almost completely through characters and their dialogue.  Everyone is flawed in some way, and it makes things a lot more interesting.
In terms of gameplay, it just uses KOTOR's system with a few more upgrades and weapons.  Force powers make things more interesting.
Where KOTOR 2 really shines is with the graphic upgrades and score.  The game has aged really well, thanks in big part to the fantastic modding community now available with the Steam Workshop.
That being said, the game feels unfinished unless you install the Restored Content mod.  It's critical to letting this game pack the biggest punch.  It makes an incomplete game feel whole, and the extra battles are fantastic and a delight to returning players who felt short changed.
Overall, I recommend KOTOR 2 to people who liked KOTOR 1, because things aren't so simply good and evil.  Everyone is in the middle to some degree.  It's just a shame that the moral choice system doesn't really factor that, as the influence system can make every character 100% good or evil while they're really not.

A lovely bit of retro pixelgraphic melancholia for people who like their exploration interrupted by boss fights.  Which I don't.  And based on my limited play time, it seems like a lot of boss fights per square inch.  More than the average Metroidvania, at any rate.
Interestingly enough, based on the achievements as of this posting, 33% of the people who bought The Aquatic Adventures of the Last Human either gave up before reaching the first boss or haven't even started the game yet.  Considering the first boss shows up within mere minutes, I'm guessing most of those 33% haven't started the game yet.  But of those who have started, 85% have made it past the first boss.  I am in this group.  The other 15% got to the first boss and bailed before beating it.  Among those of us who made it past the first boss, it seems only 60% of us have made it past the second boss, which you should reach in no more than twenty minutes.  I am not in that group.
So assuming my math is right -- not always a safe assumption, by the way -- about half of the people who started The Last Adventures of the Aquatic Human bailed before beating the second boss.  Maybe they just took a break and they'll be back later.  Maybe they only play twenty minutes at a time.  Or maybe, like me, they were hoping to explore a little longer between bouts of figuring out patterns.  I've had enough Capcom games for one lifetime.

From the haunting melodies by Karl Flodin, to the wonderous seascapes of post-apocalyptic Earth,
is an audiovisual treat. I'm not much of an art-critic, but to me, this is a game that feels...significant. I'm overcome with this feeling of inspiration. At any moment, I could sit down at my desk, turn on the PC, and write something really powerful. Anyone who read it would also become inspired, and the cycle would continue until the entire world became just a little bit grander.
Well, maybe I'll do that tomorrow. For now, let's focus on the game itself. Some of the first videogames I ever reviewed originated in the arcades, so I tend to pay more attention to basic qualities like controls and design. My approach to reviewing this game is to strip away all of the extraneous elements. The visuals are lovely, and the soundtrack is excellent, but right now I'm tuning all of that out. All I see are lines, dots, and rectangles. If I open my ears enough, I'm sure I'll hear some bleeps and bloops. With this scenario in mind, do I still consider
* a good game? Yes!
Aside from light exploration elements, this is a game that revolves entirely around boss-fights. As a
fan, I've always been a sucker for oceanic-themed adversaries. While that series operates under the basic trappings of a 2D shooter,
goes in another direction. Each of the 12 bosses are approached differently. Aside from each boss having a unique look, they also have their own patterns, weaknesses, attacks, and environment. Not only do you have to pay attention to the projectiles the boss might fire, but also your immediate area, and the following action the boss is liable to take.
This is not a game to approach lightly. You're going to die, possibly a large number of times. In my view, all of these deaths will be fair. The sub, even at its default speed, is fast enough to avoid every attack, it's just a matter of understanding movement. Yes, it will seem slow at first, but there will be cases where you can avoid attacks entirely with a little fore-thought. The first boss (a giant worm) has an attack where it spits several smaller worms at the player. The player can attempt to hang back and dodge every single worm, or they can work their way around the giant one. By doing this, the player avoids the entire attack, and gets a nice opportunity to do a lot of damage to the boss. Unless you're after a specific achievement, the sub can also take quite a bit of damage through the acquisition of hull and auto-repair upgrades.
The most important weapon you'll have for the boss-fights is your harpoon. In order to get the most out of this tool, you have to grasp the basics of risk vs reward. The harpoon can be charged to hit distant targets, or the button can be mashed repeatedly if an enemy is close. Naturally, the closer you get to the boss, the more dangerous they become, but they can be destroyed more quickly. As you develop strategies to defeat these bosses quickly, you'll discover the real depth found in this game. It's almost entirely boss-fights, but it does them justice.
Since the game delivers in terms of the more important qualities, I feel more comfortable talking about its artistic side. Videogames that take place in or around large bodies of water have always intrigued me. When most other games have the obligatory water stage, I can't stand them. I think it's because nobody really appreciates the ocean, they just want to have some harebrained swimming mechanics, in order to pad things out. Videogames that embrace the ocean and the life that inhabits it, such as the
series, are just incredible.
really captures those immersive moments, where you're blown away by all that's happening around you. The world's surface (and humanity) is long dead, but the seas are as lively as ever. The minor visual details like the remnants of human architecture and various types of marine life bring everything together.
The soundtrack can not be praised enough. This is a short game, so it's welcome to have a unique track for every part of it. I've always said that good music can elevate any game, and this is as appropriate an example as any. The boss themes in particular are superb. You're the last human in existence, fighting off an abomination, for reasons you can't quite grasp. The music in these tense and disturbing situations really preys upon the game's sense of hopelessness.
While
isn't lacking in quality art and sound, it also holds up well purely as a videogame. There is some entertainment in poking around a small yet visually dense world for upgrades and other secrets. However, most of the fun and challenge is in learning, defeating, and then mastering the myriad of bosses. Overall, this is a unique experience that's definitely worth checking out.

A good game. Though it isn't as good as Mount and Blade: Warband, it is still awesome in its own way.
Pros:
Guns - guns are OP. Sure, they take a long time to reload, but they have power and can wipe out whole armies.
Actual trading - assessing local prices actually means something and you can make lots of money by doing it. Also, you get to form your own caravans, which is awsome and makes you very rich if you do it right.
Banks and Guilds -you get to deposit money in banks and gain interest on that. You can also take loans as well. There are special guilds which can sell you special armor and weapons. Though expensive, they are very cool and can provide you with some cool stuff.
Useful Castles - sounds weird, I know, but now every fortress or castle has a tavern and a marketplace. Unlike the Warband castles, which were basically just strongholds, the WF&S castles allow you to sell stuff, access the tavern, and talk to a mayor for quests.
Interesting story-based quests  - there are special series of story-based quests for the Poles, the Russians, and the Cossacks. These stories are well-done and are quite interesting, giving you some history lessons while at the same time letting you campaign and battle Mount and Blade style.
Grenades  - sure, they're almost always inefficient and usually not worth the steep price, but they are freaking GRENADES. IN MOUNT AND BLADE!!!!
Cons -
Bugs and Glitches - the developers moved on before the game was fully fixed, which is a huge shame. Though the game is mostly smooth and most problems have been dealt with, you may experience some graphical glitches here and there. At the worst, you will have a bug that wiill ruin your game. For example, a faction leader will be defeated in battle and never reappear, or the story-based quests will break and you'll be forever stuck on one part. Hopefully, you won't have these, but you've been warned.
Lack of variety - in Warband, all the factions were truly unique, with obvious strengths and weaknesses. In WF&S, all the factions seem the same. Aside from appearances and some strengths (Poles= cavalry. Swedes = infantry), the factions don't have enough variety to make they feel truly unique in battle. At the end of the day, they are all essentially the same.
No Story for Crimeans and Swedes - while the Russians, Poles, and Cossacks have story-based quests, the Crimeans and Swedes have none, which is a shame
Map is Bland - in Warband, you have a desert, a steppe, a tundra, a mountain range, and a plains region. These added variety to the game and made the different areas unique. In WF&S, the entire map is flat, with just rivers and a few patches of forest. Woop-ee.
Overall, don't let the cons prevent you from buying the game. It is a very fun and exciting experience which all Mount and Blade fans should have.

I'm not experiencing any real technical or network issues that some other people are facing. Game is running amazingly well for me. I did experience a
d**k punch when I first launched the game. It got attached to the wrong Uplay account, which really f**ked me over. However, Ubisoft's support fixed my mistake for me no problem and it didn't waste any of my season pass premium time, which was totally rad.
I love how seamless the whole game is. For instance, the ability to chat with other players while the game is loading. That's a really cool feature and there's a lot of really seamless intergrations in the game that make it a really pleasant experience. Being able to peruse the game's many interfaces without being locked into one screen while loading is an incredibly underrated feature. The UI in-game is really well done too. Very clean, easy to read, and understand just what the f**k exactly is going on. Big points for a visually pleasing interface, imho.
The combat mechanics are really quite amazing. I was a
disappointed when I found out that feats had to be earned in-game every single match. After reaching reputation 2 (kind of like a prestige system of sorts) with the Samurai's Orochi, I came to realize that's the right decision on Ubisoft's part. Feats are incredibly strong and you can slightly tailor them with different ones if you want, which is really nice.
Speaking of customization, holy Batman is there a lot of it. Helmets, armguards, chestplates, sword blades, hilts, etc. You can even choose what gender you want for most classes. Some of them are naturally gender locked, like the Valkyrie, for obvious reasons. But, the amount of customization is insane.
I'm proud of Ubisoft's offerings in this department this day. You have no idea how much character customization means to not only myself, but a lot of other people too. Really helps you feel attached to your character (I get sad to see my Orochi get skewered by that big Lawbringer a*sh*le and his massive pollaxe.)
A big, big part of the game is the focus on the 'war' aspect of it. At the beginning, you choose which faction you want to represent on the fields of honor. Then, as you play the game, you accrue war assets every match, which goes towards your faction's war effort. Every 6 hours, the map then updates with cool little animations and you can see how your contributions are helping. Plus, depending on how much you contribute, you get special rewards at the end of a 'round' during that specific season. Really cool. Good job, Ubi.
All-in-all, I
love this game. Sure, the P2P sh*t is kind of a♥♥♥♥♥♥off, but hey, at least the gameplay makes up for it. You can tell that the developers really put a lot of effort into this game. It's Ubisoft's 'upper level' that chose not to give us dedicated server support. So, with that being said, I'm judging the game on it's own merits alone. Therefore, without a doubt, this game is hands down f*cking amazing.
10/10

The Aquatic Adventure of the Last Human:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Life on earth is not what it used to be. Due to climate change, the surface of the earth has frozen up and the human race has been forced to live underneath the water! A great expedition has been planned to send a sub-aquatic spaceship (of which you are in command) to the nearest wormhole. The idea is to look for a new habitable planet. However, after entering the wormhole, a small hiccup occurred . . . Nothing too drastic, you just find yourself back on earth a thousand years after the extinction of the human race . . . You are the last human! That’s a bugger, wouldn’t you say?
The aquatic adventure of the last human is an action/adventure game where you take control of the sub-aquatic spaceship, Argo 9. After piercing through the thick layer of ice, you will start your underwater adventure with not a defensive or offensive mechanism to your vessel. You will explore the very colourful underwater scenery. Despite all of this, you will encounter obstacles the likes of underwater mines, sewerage pipes and more. Within the map, you will find upgrades for your ship – a harpoon, a saw and more. You will upgrade the hull of you vessel by finding crates here and there.
As you explore the map, your will come across “Holo Tapes” which will give you some tips and information about the underwater world. As soon as you see a station, make sure you reach it; it is a checkpoint so if you die for some reasons, you will respawn from there.
In term of the enemies, within the map (as far as I have seen so far), the giant clams are pretty much the ones you will need to be careful of. In regards to the bosses, you will find them quite challenging to beat. As this game is more exploring than anything else, you will find bosses in different places without a specific order.
The pixel graphics are beautiful and the underwater surrounding atmosphere is well portrayed. The soundtrack is good too. For the controls, you will use the gamepad.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good pixel art graphics
-	Well designed bosses
-	Good soundtrack
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Very challenging bosses
-	Few enemies beside the bosses
The Aquatic Adventure of the Last Human has beautiful pixel art and portrays a very good underwater atmosphere.
7/10

calculating each attack and dodging them just so you can get a hit or two in, which generally lands you at ten-minute unvaried battles, only lengthy becuase of how much time you have to spend swimming away and not fighting. Your primary weapon, the harpoon, was probobaly my least favorite part of combat. It requires a really long charge-up period to actually get some good distance, which even FURTHER adds to how lengthy and tedious the battles are. Even then the range is poor and you'll probobaly end up just barely falling short on most of your shots. My final problem witht he game stems from the bosses themselves. Most have them have balls to the wall massive health bars, and though they're all varied in terms of gameplay strategies, they're generally all a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ By far the top culprit for me was The Tranquil, which sucks. I love octopuses. The Tranquil kinda just sits there as it flails four massive tentacles at you, that slowly move back and forth across the screen. Even touching them wille eliminate roughly a third of your health and if you get caught against two or one smashes you against the wall? Game over. Back to the beginning of the fight. (By the way, this doesn't just apply to the tranquil. You die? Back to square one.) You have to slooowly take down the segments of the tentacles, chop them off, and only then can you shoot it's eyes and mouth to take down it's health. At about a third it will suddenly regrow all three tentacles and start it all over again, but with an extra flail attack that is practically unpredictable. It's tentacles extened waaay farther then their normal length and if you haven't already gotten out of the way, you're doomed. This really brings it all down to luck. Wrong place wrong time? Start over for you. You have to repeat the tentacle chop eye process a couple times and then its dead. Eeeeeeh....
I'm sure there are some people out there who cleared it all on their first try and look at this thinking (Lol$ n00b.) But for me, I found it way more frusterating than challenging. The bosses wern't difficult becuase they made you put your skill to work, they were difficult becuase beating them meant a whole ton of long and tedious trial and error, and boring camping technuiqes that drew the fight out way longer than it should have.
I really respect the game's art and I think they did an absolutley amazing job in the department, but the gameplay is just really under par.

Good horror is difficult to come by. So often, when I'm looking for horror films or games, "not awful" is the criteria for success. Amnesia: the Dark Descent was a rare jewel that rose to the ranks of "actually good" and quickly became one of my favorites. So when I discovered Frictional Games' new release, I was eager to see if they could do it again.
But calling SOMA "good" would be doing it a disservice. This game is a masterpiece, a stunning example of what horror should be. Every element of this game adds to your sense of unease and dread, from the grim environment to the scattered records of a past tragedy that you slowly piece together, to the lighthearted dialogue attempting to mask the characters' internal existential crises. The monsters out to kill you might even be the least frightening aspect of the game - but by no fault of their own.
SOMA is beautifully written, both in what is said and what is shown without needing to be said. It foreshadows upcoming events well, and when the twists come, it doesn't play them with a heavy hand, because the game knows that the best part of the twist was discovering it for yourself and the reveal comes more as an affirmation of what everyone already knows. And believe me, knowing what comes next only makes it even more disturbing.
And disturbing is a very good description of this game. Because between the heart-pounding-out-your-chest moments of terror as you flee from the denizens of this nightmare world, you get to reflect on the nature of what this world has become, what you have become, what death means, what life means, and whether it is worth it to go on living when there's nothing left to live for. And you'll keep on thinking about it for long after you've reached the end credits.
Now, this game isn't perfect. Many times there seemed to be puzzles stuck in just to have puzzles, which detracted form the immersion, and there were some minor typos and plot holes here and there. But these were small infractions, and it still did better than Amnesia at working more of the puzzles into the story to make them feel like real tasks. It's nitpicking, but enough to keep the game from being completely perfect.
All in all, SOMA is the best horror game I've ever played (by a HUGE margin,) the best single-player game I've ever played, the best horror story I've ever heard, and possibly the best science fiction story, too. If you don't buy this game, I would recommend at least watching a walkthrough, because everyone should see this work of art.

Fresh from completing Sniper Elive V2, I thought I'd give a brief couple of points on the game.
Positives:
+WWII setting.  Differentiates itself from the current 'modern' trend.  Appreciate WWII was the big thing 5-10 years ago.
+Graphics.  Decent graphics, some nice effects like fire and explosions that look good without too much scrutiny.
+Physics.  Completed on Sniper Elite difficulty so got to experience some decent bullet drop balistics etc.  Shots are definitely missable if you're not careful.
+X-Ray Kill Cam.  This just never gets old.  Ever.  There's something immensely satisfying seeing the skeleton of your enemy shatter into little bits.
+Campaign length.  Though it could be completed quicker (I'm sure), I got a good 10+ hours out of the single player.
Negatives:
-A.I.  Far too easy.  The game can effectively be progressed by simply giving your position away, letting the A.I. run around in the open as they try to hit you.  Makes sniping actually a little too easy.
-Opernplatz.  There's a progression bug on this map. I hit it, couldn't get past and ended up shelving the game for 6-12 months.  Thankfully, a fresh download seemed to let me move on when I finally returned.  Very disappointing.
-Story.  Generic America saves the world (well, America saves London in this instance).  Not very exciting and a little too Hollywood.
-Linearity.  Maps can be moved across using various routes but it's essentially a point A to point B fare.  Shame really.
-Kit too situational.  I had mines, trip mines, dynamite, grenades and a rock (no, NOT  Dwayne Johnson) but using them was VERY situational.  Had the game given me better A.I. (i.e. supressing and flanking etc.) then maybe I'd have used a more tactical approach such as trip mining doorways and the like - but the game just doesn't need it.  You can treat it like any other shooter and progress just fine.  A massively missed opportunity.
Overall, I'd definitely say I had fun with Sniper Elite V2 (taking aside Opernplatz) and would recommend it as being 'worth playing'.  Arguably one of the better sniping games in recent years.
Lastly, it's really cheeky of Rebellion to peddle DLC and the next game on the exit screen.  Bad form, folks.

Summary: A good looking side-scrolling platform puzzler which offers little challenge and presents its story in a very overbearing fashion. Severe pacing problems left me bored and unwilling to complete it.
First impression: I won’t say review, because I will not be finishing the game. I made it to the third area (Ash desert) and it still feels like I’m in the tutorial. The game holds your hand despite not offering anything resembling a challenge. I assume that it becomes more interesting later in the game when you have more abilities that can interact. Moreover, I do not question the benefits of letting the player get used to the basics first and gradually increase the difficulty, but why let the game go on so long before doing so? While many games are able to present interesting challenges with a single mechanic, this one had not presented anything interesting even by my third ability.
The game looks good and the narrator is competent. Unfortunately the narration, which otherwise would be the game’s strong point, feels like it is trying to force me to feel something rather than letting me feel it. Rather than explaining what Born is feeling or thinking, it is saying that I am Born and “You are sad, you feel guilty, you will not escape.” In contrast to, for example, Thomas Was Alone, I felt completely disconnected to the story.
The combination of severe pacing problems and an overbearing narration makes me not recommend Nihilumbra. Sure, it is a cheap game and it looks good, but it is also boring.

As far as first-person shooters go, I'm not world-class, but I can hold my own. The intro cutscene for the story campaign got me really interested into what was about to happen.
After going through a quick tutorial on controls, setting mines and sneaking, the actual gameplay started. But while the shooting was fine, the parkour and graphics seemed off. I hate to make the comparison, but Call of Duty and Battlefield have much better graphics than this. It's not about being an older game; it's that it hurt to see.
On top of that, this was the very first game to introduce me to the concept of "input lag". It took at least one or two seconds for the game to recognize that I had moved one of the analog sticks. (For reference, yes, I do use a PS3 controller, but I have used this same controller on dozens of other games and, like, I said, this is the first time I've ever seen input lag.) That kind of difference was really annoying when it happens every time I do anything.
What really clinched this negative review was the fact that "Exit Game" from the pause menu didn't exit the game. It just brought me to the desktop but kept the game playing. I tried returning to the game, and, in fact, it was still running. I tried clicking "Exit Game" again and it still didn't work. I had to use the taskbar to close it.
All-in-all, not an enjoyable experience for me. But if you can get over the problems I mentioned above, it is still a pretty good shooter game. The mechanics are all there, and they've got some smart AI from what I can tell. I didn't bother with multiplayer (since input lag would have really irked me in there), but from what I hear it's incredibly fun. So if this is your cup of tea, don't let my negative review deter you. Just let it be a word of caution.

As a die hard fan of classic survival horror this little guy stands out among the best. Its not a perfect game by any means but it delivers in all the ways that count. The first thing that stood out to me was the performance when compared to so called "AAA" games. It portrays a perfect lovecraftian atmosphere laden with detailed textures, beautifuly sculpted architecture,  all while keeping a steady 60 fps the entire time. This is truly where the game shines and gives you plenty of opportunities in between the scares to immerse yourself and enjoy the enviroments. While there are lots of genuine scares and well thought out survival mechanics with an engrossing story, sadly the game play trails behind. So many aspects of this game were very clearly well thought out which makes it a real shame when you encounter a situation that doesnt follow all the way through. My biggest gripe is the scaling AI. This game has cheap one hit deaths which will trigger while you are in a corner with no exit and If you die 3 or so times you will spawn away from them or they dissapear entirely. I understand they wanted to maintain the flow of the game and prevent getting stuck but it makes me wonder if the addition of maybe a couple more hiding spots, alternate exits or defensive actions could have enhanced the experience without diminishing difficulty.
Pros
+amazing graphics/performance
+engrossing story
+actually scary
+controller support
+scratches that survival horror itch
+puzzles are inventive and amusing
Cons
-visual cues lack polish in some places which leads to lots of backtracking if you miss something
-puzzle solutions can be cryptic in a bad way (you WILL need to visit a walkthrough at least once)
-scaling difficulty
-crude in game menu

Offword Trading company is a base building game...that's pretty much it. But that's amazingly NOT it. There is something really EXCITING about this game, and that taps into a real world scenario were a company attempts to become a monopoly and take out competition through the white and black markets. Buying out a competitor and turning them into a subsidy feels really good. Oddly good, actually. There is this odd feeling of power involved that i've never felt before from a game.
To kind of put this into perspective I finished a match and had to sit back and stop for a while. My heart was racing and my palms were a little twitchy. I don't know how a game about building a base and mining resources got me to that state but.. somehow it did.
Actually.. i know how. You know monopoly? This game reminds me of a particularily brutal Monopoly win. You know the kind.. where you own most of the board but start to auction off your chores to the highest bidder. When you don't just win, but emotionally crush your friends/family who are playing with you. Yea.. somehow this game taps into that exceptionally powerful and dark corner of our minds. Obliterating someone financially feels so much more powerful than just hsooting them with a gun like every other game. It's intense.

I. Love. This. Game.
I am one of those people that really loves the narration.  It reminds me of Portal mixed with this cool flash animation I once played.  The artwork is awesome, and I love the color scheme.  It was a lot of fun to play.
Now for a more in-depth review:
Main Story: This is a really nice indie puzzle game, and the feel is similar to Portal.  The concept of the colors is nice, but it does get repetitive the further you get into the game.  Accept that you'll die a few times on some of the levels because you won't be prepared for what's coming.  The puzzles are simple, though.  If anything, play through the entire main story.  It's short and worth trying.
Void Mode: Void mode is hard!  I'll give them that.  It's a nice challenge, but at times, it seems to be a little too difficult.  You have to have the timing just right to get through the levels.  As void mode goes on, you'll notice that some levels are super difficult and some are super easy.  It feels like the developers might have been running out of ideas as it goes on (or just gave up - the cave levels on void mode are super easy).  I got through the entire thing without help, so it's doable.  Just accept that you'll die many, many, many times to get through it.
Secret Language: If you get to this point, it is worth playing through the main storyline in the secret language.  It appears just to be the developer's rant mode.  Some of it is really stupid, but some of it is really funny...especially the end.  The one thing I didn't like is that they assumed that you are most likely a guy playing.  Ummmm...no.  I find that slightly offensive since I'm a girl and a gamer.
Achievements: They are super reasonable and at just the right difficulty.  I'll admit I did look up which level the Easter egg was hidden (though I didn't look up where in the level).  I would have eventually found it if I replayed the entire game again to look for it.  I saved that achievement for last (after already having played the game through three times), and I was being lazy.
Overall, I would highly recommend this game.  I don't think it's for everyone, but it is a fun way to pass the time.  Yes, it's worth the cost with or without a sale.  :)

It's shocking to me how hyped this game was, and how terrible it is. This game is generic to the max. It's like they looked at Battlefield and Call of Duty, distilled the basic features out of them, and stripped out any unique or iconic gameplay. It really feels like CoD with less recoil and no soul.
I've tried both multiplayer and the campaign, but I'll be mostly reviewing the campaign. One thing I'll say about multiplayer - unless they've changed this, snipers start with no scopes, and you have to spend two hours getting spawn-killed and shooting one enemy per life to earn a crappy scope.
Again, the campaign is uber-generic. You are a soldier in a special ops unit. You get briefed on objectives you don't care about, and are thrown into some fighting. Your guns have no recoil. Occasionally you get a slow-motion event.
The missions aren't even put together well. There is a sniping mission where you work alongside a veteran sniper, an obvious attempt to copy the flashback mission in Modern Warfare, but executed so badly you'll be failing repeatedly while trying to figure out what he wants you to do. Everything has an extremely linear layout, but there are couple of places where it's still easy to get lost because the level doesn't flow well.
Several missions are extremely frustrating or repetitive, or both. One mission has you sniping enemy soldiers on a hill. They're pretty far away, in some trees, and you can't see jack♥♥♥♥♥♥ You sit there and wait for your spotter to call out someone, try in vain to figure out where the target is, and then lose. But in the end you'll get it down because they keep spawning at a handful of locations.
The most memorable moment for me was a mission where I was halfway through the level, and a scripted event had us pinned down by enemy MGs. An ally ordered me to provide covering fire with my own light MG so they could move up. But... I dropped my MG at the beginning of the level for a different weapon. So I tried to provide covering fire with my AK. Over and over. Time after time, I wasted entire magazines, but my allies didn't do anything. I tried shooting the enemy gunners, which should have been easy because they weren't very far away, but they were invulnerable. I looked all around the area but there was no LMG available. Finally I realized I could try to pop a grenade in the MG nest. That took a few tries to do without dying, but when I finally got a grenade in there, I was rewarded with... nothing.
They seriously made a scripted event halfway through the level where you have to have an LMG to continue, but don't force you to keep the LMG from the beginning of the level and don't give you one when you need it. I had to replay the entire level with the LMG just to be able to pass that part.

TL;DR Break cars, break trucks, break the physics engine, break logic. Development is alive. Modding scene is alive.
Some people aren't happy with the 30$ price tag... I say don't buy the game then... don't buy any game if you aren't willing to shell out 30$ for a game, but you can some how afford the 900$ rig to run it on.
====
Cons
====
*Cars handle like they are buttered up
*Acceleration acts like you are a lead foot (unless using keyboard controls)
*Advanced controls (like slowmotion and free cam) are tucked away behind a *show advanced controls* button in the controls menu
====
Pros
====
*The cars can wad up like a ball of paper
*There are some pretty cool mods
*Seems to run fine on some potatoes (big lag if using multiple cars or big mods)
*If the physics engine wigs out and crashes, the game does not crash, it will simply reset the vehicle it was simulating at the time. This is a godsend.
*You'll get better used to the "buttery cars" I mentioned above after a few hours of play.
*The UI is clunky but becomes easier to understand after just an hour or so of play
*The hud is completely customizable with many gadgets you can place, remove, move around, and resize to your hearts content! (You can also select wether they show in the "driver cam")
If you were looking for a serious driving experience you won't find it here. This is a sandbox smash 'em up at the moment. They do have a campaign and the likes in the works right now though. So maybe check back later.

(Word of Warning: The game requires a fairly recent graphics card. Check the specs.)
Not as scary as Amnesia, Soma is all the better for it; focusing on a more coherent and unsettling story in a far more plausible world.
Graphically, while not necessarily full of mind-blowing special effects, the design and ambience of every environment is spot on and the lighting is perfect. There is some truly beautiful, and truly creepy scenery in this game. Acoustically, the game must be heard to be believed; everything ticks and whirs and breathes and gurgles and wails and hisses and creaks, and trying to quietly open a desk drawer has never been so tense.
The story is very impressive. While you may expect the identity of your character to be a major plot twist... that twist turns out to be less important than its wider implications. In other words, if you've seen Cargo, if you've seen The Thirteenth Floor, The Matrix etc, and you think you've figured it all out - it doesn't matter. Soma will still punch you in the gut, because there's something horrible you didn't consider.
Literally the only things I can criticize are:
* Long initial loads. Once in the game, the whole thing unfolds fairly seamlessly (no overt loading screens, though the occasional stutter when you transfer to a major new area), but when you first click "load", you'll be sitting there for a while.
* Graphical anomalies, mainly underwater; flashing lights, disappearing scenery. That's on an AMD R9 380. They're not really obtrusive, especially since visual distortions are part of the game, but there it is.
* At times, the monsters become annoying; every now and then, their AI breaks and they stand still, blocking your path. Other times, their presence simply impedes your exploration and there's no way to kill them, trap them, or otherwise cause them to despawn - every monster encounter must be resolved via scripted sequence or game progression.
Oh, and people have been saying that it's not that long. I'm sure it's *possible* to complete the game in one solid session, but that's if you're rushing. According to Steam, I've been playing 15 hours, and I haven't completed it. I haven't died repeatedly. I've just been playing carefully, exploring everything and paying attention to the narrative.
EDIT: Completed it. Truly brilliant. Frustratingly, I can't really say anything much *about* the story because that would spoil it... but this is a game that will make you think. It'll make you think about humanity, and your own mortality, and even the nature of the parent-child relationship.

I initially gave this game an unfavorable view, but felt this was unfair because I was 'stuck' at a certain point in the game. I was finally able to overcome my obstacle, and stick with the game until the end (or one of the endings, rather).
This game certainly has its appeal, but not without some drawbacks:
~The game is dated: and I'm not just referring to the graphics. I'll be honest, the biggest headache with this title (and similarly with its prequel) was compatibility issues with Windows 10. I had to wait a few months until another update fixed what the last update broke.
~There's still a few bugs: or at least my copy had em. I was pretty into the story up until the ending, which felt very anticlimactic because it would skip over all of the dialog that was between my choices; it left me with only a very fuzzy idea of how the story ends.
~It has many RPG features that were pretty advanced for its time like item upgrades and breakdown/creation; however the combat style was very clunky, and turn-based feeling, almost like FFX was. It can also get pretty repetitive with the game pausing with every new enemy that enters your line of sight.
~The quest info from your journal entries were sometimes pretty vague, which took me much longer to find out where I needed to go, or objectives I needed to accomplish. Nothing the Internet couldn't fix with no shortage of walkthrough guides, but nonetheless made the game more tedious than fun
~The added achievements are really the only thing that gave the game any replay value. The story was good, but even going back and finishing with the alternate ending seems pretty empty, knowing all the twists and turns that ultimately lie ahead
If you're a Star Wars fan, I would definitely pick this one up for a bargain price, or in a bundle. It's no Skyrim, so exercise patience while playing. 5/10

Aquatic Adventure is clearly an art project, and a labor of love at that. The beautifully crafted pixel art environments are very impressive, and the atmosphere of a hopeless, long-ruined civilization behind a lively undersea environment is well realized. All in all, it's avery nice-looking piece of work.
So, what about the gameplay? AALH is probably best defined as having metroidvania-style game progression. You must pilot your submarine throughout the game world, exploring the map until you find bosses to fight and upgrades that allow you to explore further. The gameplay serves its purpose adequately, but it's not without several caveats.
1: You move EXTREMELY slowly. It's ignorable at first, when you are admiring the scenery of a new area, but as nice as the environments look, once you've seen them, you've seen them. It quickly becomes very tedious to slowly drift through already-explored maps looking for missed upgrades or paths. Granted, there are a few fast-travel stations(although they're few and far between), and there's an engine upgrade that helps a little, but not enough.
2: Once you realize how slow you're moving, you'll notice that the game map in its entirety is actually pretty small. The slow movement speed and the occasional one-way path make it seem like the game is much larger than it is, and it's a disappointing realization to come to.
3: It's up to the individual to decide if this is a pro or a con, but aside from a couple areas with mines and several stationary projectile shooters, there really aren't any enemies except the bosses. This means that you don't have anything to do while you trek from area to area other than look at the scenery again or take pot shots at the occasional nonagressive fish.
4: Your weapons and tools seem pretty weak for the entire game, and the optional upgrade crates you can find don't seem to help much. However, keeping in mind that basically the only things you fight are bosses, there really isn't a good metric for judging this.
There's not really any story present in the game, either. The opening cutscene shows your ship leaving earth in the near future and promptly landing in a wormhole, then being spit back out an indeterminate yet incredibly vast number of years in the future. Your ship crashes back to earth to find it covered by ice and water; all humans, and their civilization, appear to have long since died. This is all that is given to you in terms of your own story. As of this writing, I have not yet finished the game, but I can't see it ending positively.
There are 'holotapes' sprinkled around the world map. Ideally, they should give some sort of backstory about the end of humanity. However, they never have more than a single dialog box worth of text in them, and there's definitely not enough information to cobble together any sort of cohesive narrative. They're mostly filled with a bunch of vague political and environmental alarmism, which, while applicable in a game about post-humanity, seemed heavy-handed and unnecessary to me.
The quibbles I've listed above might sound a little harsh, but they didn't stop me from sinking(har) a couple hours into this game, and I suppose they might even contribute to the game's overall aesthetic. If you enjoy atmospheric experiences, I can definitely recommend this at its current price. If you're not so hot on atmosphere and just want to play a game, well... it's still pretty fun, so you could pick it up on sale and give it a shot.

Despite short length of one playthrough, the action / pace of the game seems just right.
Rush Rover is a top-down 2d action/roguelite game. In the game, you control a robot that fights the other, “converted” AI bots. Each playthrough consists of multiple randomly generated rooms, and you must defeat 5 bosses to win the game. As you kill enemies, you level up and get to upgrade various abilities.
•	Content: enemies are very different, their movement paths and attacks require different type of maneuvering and dodging from you. Some rush towards you and you have to dodge, others shoot in circular patterns so you have to keep moving in-between bullets. In any case: standing in one place means certain death. The guns are also really interesting: some charge up before firing, the homing missiles lock on targets before flying towards them, the “wave” gun tries to fry the enemies in a cone pattern.
•	Skill-Based Gameplay: the drops are random, but damage is not. You have to dodge lots of bullets and fire accurately, otherwise you get obliterated. If you die – it totally feels like your fault, which is a great game design.
•	The game handles roguelite randomness really well: your initial weapon does not suck. It’s not terribly powerful, but you can upgrade it as you level up, so even if you don’t find a new one, you can still complete the game. In fact, I’ve completed my first run without actually changing the weapon.
•	One playthrough is extremely short: it took me about 40 minutes to finish one game. It’s not easy so you won’t be able to do it on the first playthrough (probably), but it took me a bit more than 2 hours to finish the game for the first time.
•	The graphics are not that great: the animations are well-detailed, but the backgrounds do get repetitive after some time. The UI is also a bit clumsy, i.e. you can’t pause the game by pressing ESC, you have to open inventory and click “menu” there before the actual game menu opens.
Rush Rover seriously made me think about what makes the top-down shooter games good. Frankly, I have not felt this excited about top-down games since Enter The Gungeon. However, the game does some things much better than the former: namely, the room balancing. First, you can teleport from every room after you kill all enemies. Second, the room is always equally full of enemies. They won’t rush towards you. You need to start approach them, and then they attack you. This contributes to a feeling that every room is literally filled with enemies, but still leaves you space to maneuver.
At the time of this review, the game costs 5.99 EUR (or your regional equivalent) and I definitely recommended it, as it’s a great price for the entertainment that you are getting.

When I first played this in high school on my Super Nintendo, it was mind-blowing, and every few years I go back and play it for the nostalgia factor. It still stands up as a great JRPG, although it's a bit dated compared to modern games - you know your gameplay needs some work when there's a fast-forward button. The negative reviews on Steam almost scared me off from checking out this long overdue Steam release, which mostly seem to gripe about the graphical changes and some bugginess, but I'm glad I got it, and experienced no bugs whatsoever in a full play-through.
On the graphics: The sprites look fine to me - character sprites are blurred, but I don't think the quality is anything worse than various emulator filters. Environmental sprites look just fine to me, including the "3D" shaded overworld ones. The redrawn character dialogue portraits are a huge improvement and look great, apart from Emperor Gestahl who got hit by an airship which prematurely aged him several centuries. The new 3D models for towns and castles on the overworld map do look wonky, but whatever. There is all new background imagery for battles, and spell animations, which all look pretty good. Anti-aliased text and an overhauled interface are a big step up over playing this on an emulator. It's clearly an iOS port, the battle menus have touchscreen-friendly largeness, forcing one to scroll when they could easily fit on any PC monitor.
This release is the same content as the Game Boy Advance version from 2007, which I never played and was my main reason for picking this up on Steam. It fixes a large number of bugs from the original SNES version, and has vastly improved text translation, truer to the original Japanese, such as for Cyan's arsenal, and truer to the intent, as in the spell "Meltdown" instead of "Merton". Added after the final Kefka fight are the multi-party Dragon's Den dungeon, the Soul Shrine, and a new final boss: Omega Weapon. Dragon's Den was fun for a while, but overstayed its welcome. The Soul Shrine and Omega Weapon feel tacked-on. So I'm a little underwhelmed by the bonus content, but it was still a good time. Outdated gameplay, but fun characters, fun story, and nostalgic appeal.

Ok let's start positive. This at it's core, despite any changes cosmetically, is still FFVI. There are issues and I will get into that, but this is still FFVI. And FFVI is arguably the greatest video game ever made. The story, the charecters, the battle system, all of it is just fantastic. This is by far and away my personal favorite video game ever. But of course, my love with the game came from the SNES days. This version of the game, is not the SNES version.
It's not even the GBA or PS1 version. This is a port of the mobile version of the game. As such, it comes with some baggage. The most obvious, is the sprites. A lot of people have talked about them, and yes they are ugle and terrible. Though not as bad as some make them out to be. The main issue in fact with them is the emotes. The SNES version with the 16 bit sprites has some charm when the charecter freaks out, or wags their finger, because it was 16 bit, and looked great for it's time. And it was just funny. These new sprites when they do emotes, it just looks weird. Difficult to describe it any other way than that. Perhaps worse than the sprites is the text. Yes I know, I am complaining about font, but seriously, the font just looks terrible here.
There is also issues with the port. Controllers do not work, at least not for me. Some have had no problems, many others have. There are work arounds to get them to work and various things, but still. In my game if I just press a button on my controller, the game crashes. There have been other crashes and errors killing the game. Square continues a track record with bad PC ports (certainly not all are bad, but many are).
But once again I return to the beginning. It is still, despite the flaws, FFVI. Thus I have to still recomend this game. Are there better versions you can get your hands on? Absolutely. But this is one of the best video games ever created and not playing this game would be worse than playing it in this version. Thus I have to still recommend this, even if the port is terrible and the sprites and fonts ugly.

So Offworld Trading Company and me have had this "thing" for a very long time. I love RTS, always have since the mid 90's. I also love innovative games, well since games have existed. So when this game was announced, I watched and followed it like a hawk. Except I kept and maintained my distance. OTC was like a woman I'd see in a bar every week, it seemed love at first sight. She was beautiful, intriguing, like no-one I'd ever seen before.. But alas I was always drunk when I saw her and I had no courage to approach her, buy her a drink, get her number, maybe take her home.
It was like this for months. The more I found out about her, the more character that she seemed to divulge, the more personality she put on display, the more I wanted her. Moving up the ranks in my little black book known as a wishlist. The more I came to the bar, the more she'd flash (sale), the more of her clothing (Price tag) she'd remove. It was at this point, I knew she was flirting with me, and it became apparent she's was now bundled in gold. So a weekend in mid-October she returned to the bar wearing 65% off... This time I was not drunk, I was no longer on the fence... I saw her for what she was, so after flashing my credit card, I finally took her home.
After a 6 hour session with her... I have to say, she's rather intense. She showed me the ropes, showed me the many facets of her personality and showed me step by step what made her tick. Then she untied me and let me get to work on her...
At first she was easy. I kept winning her charms, satisfying her needs... Things were going smoothly, she allowed me to tackle a single element of her, and then she ramped things up, adding more and more, asking for more and more. Things began to get more and more intense... Then she showed her true colours. The more you play her, the more she dares to push you. She becomes a shady, manipulative, dirty scheming devil woman who will push you into a corner, pin you there, and drain you economically for all you're worth.
The thing is. You will not learn to back down. She leaves you wanting more, she wants to be dominated. Taken control of, but she isn't going to let you have it without a fight. In my case on a couple of occassions, she's kept up with me with everything I throw at her, and just when I'm about to get the upper hand, she will kick me down and laugh in my face... I should be humiliated. But I cannot get enough of her. I will keep going for the long-term until our relationship is exhausted. Until she has no more to give and finally submits to my own superior evil ways.. Just like she taught me...
Offworld Trading Company... The game is indeed like a woman who wears the trousers, makes all the rules, is controlling of you... But wow, what a woman she is... My only regret is that I didn't take her home sooner.

Not for everyone, but good frantic RTS fun.
Off the bat, one thing needs to be made clear, this is an RTS, not a 4X game. Matches are fast paced, hectic affairs, rarely lasting more than 30 minutes, even with a bunch of players. This isn't Sins of a Solar Empire, where games can stretch 4 hours, but Starcraft, with rapid strategy shifts in response to opponent actions culminating in a chaotic every man for himself finish.
From the very first second of the game, when you're choosing where to found your HQ (and which HQ to choose, you don't have to make that selection before the game starts), you're shoved into direct competion with other players. I've purposefully built my HQ over some High Carbon deposits when playing against a couple Scavengers. It's a♥♥♥♥♥♥move, but it drives up the price of Carbon, and the market is an unforgiving battlefield. You need to be prepared to seize advantages and exploit weaknesses.
Even playing on Slow speed, there's not a lot of time to think things through. You make decisions on the fly, relying on intuition as much as anything. There is no optimal strategy in OTC, as what works in one game might backfire in another. There are certainly things to learn, strategies to master, but there's no top to bottom plan that will lead to victory. You'll learn when it's worth expanding your HQ, what buildings synergize well, when to research and how to exploit the various Patents, etc. Most importantly, though, is learning how to "feel" the market. That Water surplus, is one of your opponents attempting to stockpile before researching Water Engines or Cold Fusion? Are they attempting to reduce their life support bill? Are they trying to reduce the value of another player who has a large stockpile of Water so they can buy them out? Or was it really just a random event? Whatever it is, react fast, and you might just be able to take advantage of it.
There are people who play online in the Ranked Multiplayer, and OTC certainly has what it takes to be considered a competitive game. However, personally I have had the most fun playing with people I know, so, if you can, find some friends to get this game with. The Deluxe edition comes with some DLC and an extra copy, if you split the cost with someone it's cheaper than buying it outright. Unfortunately, the cost is a major sticking point with this game. As much as I like it, it's not worth $40, or even the $30/copy with the Deluxe edition. I picked it up for a little over half off, and I'm happy with that.
TL;DR: Wait for a sale, but definitely pick this up if you enjoy fast paced RTS games.

It's fun with literally any number of players except 3.
It's in the same vein as other economic hostile-takeover games like TTD but it's much faster-paced, so instead of a game taking days to complete, it's over in 20-30 minutes. This is a good thing. The time between "It's obvious who the winner is" and "The winner is declared" is very short. Games don't last very long after the first buyout, so if you're playing multiple rounds with friends, you won't have to sit out long.
The basic premise is to acquire resources and sell them to get money to repeat the process. Resource prices change accordingly every time something is bought or sold, and there are various market manipulations that can be done. There's plenty of ways to mess with your opponent there, and you can buy usable-once-only sabotages for further shenanigans.
It has its problems - the first buyout practically doubles your stock price, so in a 3-player game the first buyout determines the winner; the remaining player has a 0% chance of catching up and should just concede immediately. The Offworld Market is a necessary evil on Mars (as otherwise all resource prices drop to 1, but whoever has them is basically guaranteed to win) and utterly useless on Ceres (as all resource prices eventually become 1000). The AI is WAY too good at the game, as it makes no attempts to hide that it can and will react instantly to situations, inputting commands faster than any human possibly could.
Overall though, it's an excellent strategy game that doesn't take nearly as long to play a round of compared to others in the genre. A good game to grab if you like economic games or quick strategies.
