Shadow Warrior 2 is a great sequel to an already fantastic game. It offers most of what the first game had, and then multiplies everything in terms of scale by loads.
This game goes a slightly different path compared to the first however. Some would say it sort of has similarities to RPG games. The reason for that is the new skill and weapon system. You can now craft specific stats to your weapons, which can be anything ranging from more fire damage, ice damage, more bullets and fire rate from guns, and so forth. This has been under heavy debate for a while because of how the game seems to be more in favour of melee weapons, but I did not see an issue with it personally. The game has received many free updates since I first started playing this around release date, so some balance changes may have been introduced.
The game also offers quests and a randomly generated level system, offering more replayability compared to the first game. As in matter of fact the game wants you to beat it multiple times so you're able to increase the difficulty even higher for a more challenging experience. By doing so, you will also become stronger.
All in all this is a fantastic hack'n'slash, RPG, arcadey game, whatever you wanna call it. I can definitely recommend this game if you're looking for some intense first person action.

They decided to try some new things with this new iteration of shadow warrior. The initiative is great but unfortunately the outcome isn't great. I found SW2 to be bloated and incohesive.
The levels are the first strange aspect I found about this game. My first impression playing the first mission was positive. The level is HUGE. So much exploring to do, I thought I would get lost in there. My second impression was less positive, because now these levels are starting to look like multiplayer maps re-purposed as single player levels. It's a different kind of 'big level', if you know what I mean, because I noticed I gain nothing by exploring the level. Everything looks the same and plays the same, there are no new experiences to be had going any other direction. And this is where my final impression of these levels parked, more or less, they are so big that one can excuse the repetitiveness of the assets, but it makes the levels look and feel like a procedurally generated roguelike, without the perks of an actual procedural generation.
Add to that a map that tells you the way to the next objective and these huge and repetitive maps become small, linear, repetitive maps. Instead of invisible walls you get an abstract wall of boringness. If you cross this wall you won't see anything different, but you'll be further away from your goal.
This is a FPS, however, and one needs to ask how that minute to minute gameplay feels like during the action parts. It's ok. There is a good variety of enemy types requiring different strategies, however, I was getting by without knowing what I was doing and that's not a good sign. Lack of visual clarity is the thing. Everything looks gorgeous, but when bullets are flying and I'm dashing everything blends together and I end up just mashing buttons and hoping for the best.
There is an overwhelming amount of customization. So far I have unlocked dozens and dozens of different weapons. I have hundreds of different upgrades. Each weapon can hold 3 upgrades and can be switched at any time. You can combine upgrades and create new ones. There are also upgrades for your character, of course. And I don't think that helps the game at all.
Yes, I know, every gamer wants more and more customization and there is no such thing as too much customization, according to most gamers. Well, I disagree. Sometimes it works against what the game is trying to achieve.
What is shadow warrior 2 trying to be? The fact that I don't know after playing for 12 hours is a huge problem. It's not a good linear fps game, I know that. I suspect the reason I don't know is because I haven't played multiplayer yet, and everything about this game screams multiplayer. The maps seem like they belong in arena matches, the amount of customization and weapon variety would be adequate for a game that wants to foster individuality among its interacting user base. So, yeah, I believe that's what I've been playing so far:

SOMA shouldn't be compared to Amnesia or even Penumbra. It's not really scary, but that's not the point either. Story is its strong point here, and it's definitely better than what Bioshock 1 or Infinite had. It has its weak points, like WAU just seems out of place and is defeated without even trying. It's also not like System Shock because WAU isn't exactly enemy here and this storyline is barely even developed.
As for gameplay, yes, that's this game's weakness. It largely consists of walking, running, jumping and interacting with things, and those parts are the ones you want to be over and done with as quickly as possible. Enemy AI is rudimentary and seems to always know player's location. I also suspect enemies teleport around, like Alien in Isolation did.
Even with all that said, this game is definitely my GOTY candidate. Why? Because you're bound to lose in this game, yet you still win. Everyone dies, yet still lives. Have patience to sit through credits and you'll see what I mean. This is truly a masterpiece!

I didn't hear about this game until about a week before launch, but I'm glad it did get pointed out to me. It's short, but sweet. My first run through took me a bit over 4 hours, with some getting lost but not finding every upgrade.
The Metroidvania style exploring is fun, although a better map would be nice. Toward the end of the game you get an upgrade which lets you see more details on your mini-map, but it would have been nice to have something like that from the start. Or at least let it apply once you've explored each area of the map.
For the most part, the boss battles hit a perfect level of challenge for me. A couple of them were pretty easy, but most of them required a number of tries, sometimes dying very quickly, but generally learning a bit more about their patterns each time. Some of them have definitely got some bullet hell going on, so hopefully you're into that kind of thing.
I found the music generally pretty suitable. The pixel art on some of the non-hostile fish was a bit blurry, but everything else looked quite good. I think a good job was done on the sound design, too. Especially the squelching noises.
If you're easily frustrated this might not be for you, but if you're up to throwing yourself into a grinder to get a little bit better at a fight each time, there's fun to be had here. Just try not to curse too much when you get trapped between an enemy and a wall and torn apart in a second.

All in all this is an excellent game with a LOT of potentiel. If they can fix server issues and balance their "Steel" currency this game is going places.

This game seems to be a lot less fun in the early game than Mount & Blade: Warband because it's harder to get started. For instance, you can't simply recruit men from villages and level them up anymore. Also, firearms aren't really that fun to play with, given their inaccuracy and very long reload times. They're interesting, but not fun, at least as far as I could see.
I wanted to play more to see if it got better later on, but the performance of this game is terrible. I can run Mount & Blade: Warband with maximum settings and hundreds of men on the field at 200 FPS, but this game on low settings and 20 men on the field gets only 20-50 FPS. (It seems to be more related to terrain than battle size.) It might be okay if the frame rate was at least constant, but it stutters quite a bit, causing the gameplay to speed up and slow down frequently, which messes up the timing in combat. There are numerous forum posts from other people with the same problem, but no good solutions, so I found this game to be essentially unplayable.

Why are there negative reviews, you say? Connectivity issues, purely. Match-making queues are fine. However there are issues that merit a full game restart such as the 40000004 error. Unstable peer-to-peer handshakes (frequest disconnects). NAT issues which can be fixed by setting your NAT to open (user-driven).
Red connection players teleporting all over the place. For a highly-reactive game, that spells bad news. Sometimes you'll just receive attacks or guard breaks to the face, instantly.
Aside from the abovementioned, the battle system is avant garde and awesome. Steep learning curve, highly reactive. Perfect for very competetive gamers who find fun in meauring their capabilities against other players in pure pvp combat. One mistake can mean your doom.
Will still recommend the game based on pure potential. Ubi has never had a good launch for soooo long- which is sad. I trust that the company will do right by the players eventually. Don't get me wrong though, I am supremely disappointed with them- these issues are preventing me to enjoy what could have been a great game.
Also, all updates are free, there are microtransactions for cosmetic items/steel. All of which can be farmed in game. Not an issue for me.
I wish I could give this a neutral review, because, for what it is, it's not fair to call it bad. It's not good either though.

I am not sure why this game gets so much hate. It is, as others have said, a clone of Army of Darkness Defence (which isn't available on PC), and is a mobile port. The main complaint people have is that It may use assets from other games/movies, but that's for the owner's of those assets to decide. I actually liked the game quite a bit, though it is repetitive, and not very deep. I liked Army of Darkness Defense, and this is basically the same game. And it is free.
The game is basically a side scrolling action/strategy game. Your hero character has to defend your castle against waves of enemies. In each level you have to balance buying upgrades for your tower (just increased gold production) with buying units to help you defend against the enemy waves. Between levels you can spend earnee gold on upgrades to your hero, units, castle, or spells. The upgrades have a huge effect on how tough you are, until they cap out at level 10. If you die during a level, you keep the gold you earned during that level, but don't get the win bonus. If the levels are too hard, a few tries is usually enough to earn the gold needed to upgrade something and make the level easier. I made it to level 40 with just a couple deaths, but then the game got quite tough. The startegy in the game is in deciding which units to upgrade, and which units to buy (and when to buy them) during each level. It's not real deep, but I quite enjoyed it.
The game is free to play. You can buy gold in the game with real money, but I can't imagine why you would want or need to. I earned gold plenty fast enough to make it to level 40 without much trouble, though the game started getting pretty tough after that, mainly because I maxed out the stats on my favorite units. I'll have to start diversiying my unit unage more, and play a bit smarter, if I am going to actually beat the game. I plan to play it more and try to beat it. I think there are 60 levels in the game (the top achievement is for beating 60 levels). and at some point you unlock some endless modes, but I haven't unlocked them yet.
My conclusion: It's a mobile port with repetitive gameplay, but also quite a lot of fun.
One small grumble - there is no control for sound volume. I could turn the music off, but turning the sound off didn't work.

Those who complain about the audio must have computer issues or hearing issues. As for the sprites, they're an adjustment, but hey, they're designed by the creator of the original sprites, and it's hard to argue with that.
The soundtrack is wonderfully done—normally, with adaptations of 16-bit games such as these, you get a lame-sounding MIDI sountrack with instrumentation that's all wrong. I'm not sure what kind of audio engine they're using for this adaptataion, but it faithfully captures the spirit of the S-SMP chip, for which this soundtrack was originally composed. Very happy with that. The iconic opening scene with Tina's Theme gave me some nostalgic tingles, which wouldn't have happened if the music just weren't right.
I'm not very far into the game yet, so I can imagine I'll find some things to gripe about along the way, but so far, most of the negative reviews seem unmerited. I'm happy to show my support for classic titles via Steam.

Sandbox games are my genre of choice and LiF:YO is one of my favorites.  While I do recommend this game understand that I do so with this advice:
1)  Worth it if $20 USD or less.  It is still being developed.  The MMO is still in beta.  There is not enough content for most people that I would recommend the game if it was more expensive.
2)  This is a slow, involved game.  By slow I mean that it will take several RL days to build most structures and some you will almost have to have help if you want to complete it.  And it is very involved.  Down to crops you grow, animals you raise, what industry you want to focus on (mining, carpentry, building, weaving, farming, etc), what weapon(s) you like to fight with - the game has depth.  At times, especially if you are playing solo, many of these things can become tedious tasks to take care of (such as cleaning the coop so animals don't die in their own feces) before you move on to things you want to do.
3)  Watch youtube gameplay videos (look for more current ones).  I can talk about the gameplay, slowness, combat, and other aspects but the videos will do a far better job showing.
I have had this game for a long time now and it is one of the better early access investments I've made.  The dev team is still plugging away at it, working on the MMO portion, supporting the player community, and trying changes to improve the game.  While the game will continue being tweaked and worked for months (years?) to come, it is very playable and can be quite enjoyable.
It's like having a morphine addiction in space. You. Can't. Stop. Playing.

Worth Every Penny..
The map maker has made this game my go to for a shooter, its simple yet deep and thats hard to find. If you are on the wall just hop on over to my side and make the purchase.
The only Negative thing I can say is that the game has low playerbase, but it does not hinder the experience. Once you are in a match it can go for hours non stop.

Highs

It had smooth, enjoyable, and varied gameplay, comparable to Doom, although the enemies could get stacked too densely in tight areas. Pathfinding was improved over the original with the inclusion of a mini-map. Also, all the explodey things you could ever want every 20 feet.

Lows

If only there was a "sweet spot" difficulty setting between Normal and Hard. As it was, Normal bordered on being boring and Hard was limited by too few ammo drops.

Powers and weapon upgrades were excessive and required too much micro-management for every single weapon. The game could have used a fraction of the available pickups, especially if they had been more significant.

A straight up linear game without a hub would have been preferable rather than revisiting similar locations. Plus, the story was too convoluted, too hard to follow, and unnecessary for this type of game. It needed Serious Sam's simplicity, not Deus Ex's complexity.
Highly recommended game.

Greetings fellow gamers! This is Gamer Guy (In a Suit) from the Echo Army YouTube channel! Today I am bringing you a review of the new Indie Pixel-Art Adventure, The Aquatic Adventure of the Last Human. The Aquatic Adventure of the Last Human was released onto Steam by Developer/Publisher YCJY on January 19, 2016.
(NOTE: This game was reviewed using a key provided by the Developer and/or Publisher)
The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
Pretty, Mellow & Fun. Good Boss Battles. 4/5
The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
If you like a game that's essentially explorable art, with some good boss battles thrown in, then this may be the perfect game for you! The majority of this game is simply spent exploring the story slowly through the art (and little messages spread about). There is enough to keep you engaged (toxic spillage to avoid, etc) but nothing too stressing. Just an enjoyable ride through some great pixel-art and mellow sounds. Occasionally, you'l stumble your way into some very interesting boss battles. These will get intense, quickly. At one point, I am pretty sure a seahorse was spewing forth his, um, seed as an attack. Two of them were, actually. So, it's definitely got the "Interesting Boss Battle" category covered. All in all, it's a pretty solid game at it's price point ($10). The art alone may be worth that, especially if you like Pixel-Art. This is Pixel-Art done right. If you seek more action from your metroidvania-types, then this may not be to your liking. The action sequences are essentially confined to the boss battles. However, if you're all for some exploration and relaxation between bouts of action, this is perfect for you. 4/5 and worth $10 for sure.
Happy Gaming!

You are basically just plunked into a series of half-baked boss battles and then told that the game is now over, thanks for playing. And unlike the excellent KOTOR1, the major plot developments were so obvious that it was almost insulting when the characters acted surprised by them. There are fan mods that restore some cut content to the game, but even then the story feels incomplete.
It certainly wasn't a terrible game, by any stretch. It was fun to play and started strong, but the ending was so disappointing and badly done that I don't think I will ever play it again. I guess if it is cheap and you just want to play some more KOTOR but with a few fun new mechanics, I might recommend it. But don't expect the story to really pay off. I'll just play KOTOR1 again.

There are customization items which can be purchased using real cash which remain with your character even after death, but for the most part are not a requirement to enjoy the game. The only criticisms would be levelled at a lack of cohesive story and introduction for newcomers, some generic looking enemies and perhaps the absence of varied solo objectives other than courier missions, surviving and levelling up the character. For the asking price, this is well worth a punt if you like  survival type games, and with its impressive recreation of a fallen city, proves to be a game you can get lost in for quite some time. The game is still early access at present and hopefully will have more content added as time goes by, but for now in its current state, it’s definitely worth checking out as it continually evolves for the better.

After the success of Amnesia: The Dark Descend, Frictional has released SOMA. A game that delves deep into the psychological aspects of consciousness and what it means to exist as a human being. What are we? And are we really what we think we are?
The concept is one that would seem very hard to handle for a game, but is expertly crafted and manifested in SOMA. It is very conscious about how it tells you the story. It is also very well implemented directly into the gameplay. There are no cutscenes. Everything happens from your own point of view, which helps to magnify what Frictional is trying to make you think about.
This game gets under your skin. There are no jumpscares, but it is still easily one of the scariest games I've played. Its eerie atmosphere, great visuals (especially when underwater) and stunning soundscapes all comes together to form a game that just won't let you go, even after finishing a play session. You'll think about it when you go to sleep. You'll find yourself holding your hands up in front of you and wondering what those hands really are. They are you, right? Sure they are...

Short review:
Pros:
- Graphics are beautiful, scenery and character models. Animations are very well made as well
- Fun fighting game, when it works as intended
- Variety of game modes to play and a fun way to fight with the campagn map showing where the front lines are.
Cons:
- Per to per servers just don't work in a game that requires reaction time fighting, where a split second determines whether you win a fight or not, lag basically kills you and will kill this game unless ubisoft fix the lag issues
- Hard to find and play a game due to countless server errors
- Guard break is broken, almost impossible to counter and once hit, you lose instantly
- Parry is too easy and determines fight outcome
- Some classes are not played because they are not viable against skilled players
- Attacks from ledge one shot you no matter your health
- Unresponsive control inputs, sometimes when you try to perform a move, it does nothing and you die
- People leave games with no penalty, which causes more lag and syncing issues
Overall I cannot recommend this game because in it's current state, it's almost unplayable. The foundation for a great game is there but with server issues and lag it makes the game impossible to enjoy. Do not buy until they fix their lag and imbalances.
Detailed review:
For Honor has a lot of great things, graphics and animations that make it fun. The fighting is fun, although a bit unresponsive.
The lag that's caused by people constantly leaving and joining kills you often. Sync issues occure very often and sometimes cause a game to drop entirely. Also there are countless connection errors that prevent you from joining a game. The lag is one of the main reasons I don't recommend the game.
The second major reason For Honor is not fun is the imbalance. Every fighting game has balance issues, I do understand this but this game has some glaring problems that seem to have been overlooked. Guard break and parry are the biggest imbalances in For Honor at the moment. Guard break basically stuns you and allows our enemy to do whatever they want to you, this wouldn't be an issues if guard break counter actally worked, but it doesn't. You can counter the guard break but you have a split second window in which to do it. This means that you will miss the guard break counter and when you do you will lose the fight. Guard break is usually followed by a throw, which is usally followed by you dying by falling off a ledge, which is followed by unmeasurable amount of salt because you hit guard break counter but it didn't work. Also guard break only works some of the time, such as if a person is guarding or just finishing an attack, this means if you guard break at the wrong time you are exposed and will be guard broken and unable to counter, this means timimg is everything. Since timing is everything the lag spikes are what kill you most of the time, or the control inputs not responding.
My last point on why this game is not worth purchasing is control input issues. For Honor requires amazing reaction time in order to win fights, so any control input that doesn't work means you will lose fights. When plaing Orochi or Peace Keeper you are encouraged to dodge roll in order to counter and attack and get a free light attack in. The problem is dodge roll doesn't resond sometimes, meaning you press left or right and space and you don't dodge and attack. Basically it means the enemy can get free attacks because the control inputs aren't being registered, when this happens two or three times in a fight you are almost guaranteed to lose the fight. When no dodge roll works for an entire game you lose every fight and the game. This happened to me where none of my control inputs were going through and I couldn't dodge roll any attacks. This is completely unacceptable for a fighting game. Also if you dodge roll a guard break, it still hits you because guard break range is larger than dodge roll and if you get hit by a guard break after a dodge roll you can't counter the guard break because your control inputs are still busy processing the dodge roll. If you can't do esential things that your character is designed to do then you can't play that character at all and the game just isn't as fun because you have to play the few classes that are imbalanced at the moment, Warden, Warlord and Peace Keeper (in spite of the dodge roll problems) are two of the most imbalanced right now.
For Honor is fun and an amazing concept but Ubisoft has a lot of work to do in order to make this game enjoyable to play for any measurable amount of time. Lag and control input issues are the biggest fun killers and have killed this game for me.

Not for the faint of heart. All hacking games inevitably involve an element of 'hollywood', and this game is no exception. Superficially, Hacker Evolution appears pretty authentic; you type unix-like commands into a plain looking terminal and search through server config files for clues on your next target. You might even feel cool doing it. Of course, after playing for a short time you will get a feel for what the core game mechanics are really about. At it's heart, Hacker Evolution is a game about balancing resources: money, open servers, hardware configuration, etc. It's this careful balancing act of resources that makes the game challenging, and unforgiving. A single missed opportunity could lock you into an unwinnable game from which the only recovery is to start again from scratch at the tutorial level. Still, for those who are determined enough to see it through, Hacker Evolution can be a rewarding experience.

I played the first game starring everyone's favourite anti-hero and purveyor of crotch jokes- Lo Wang- and was happy to see this sequel. However it feels like such a chore despite massive improvements.
The previous game has the edge with story as I was engaged and interested in the journey of Wang and Hoji. The blend of fantasy with realism worked quite well at times and when it ended I had many questions. The sequel sort of answers these but indirectly. Much of it is very obvious but I feel like we've lost a connection to characters and so much happens in between that I seemed to have missed.
What it does get right is very good, though, as combat has improved, building your character is slightly easier (if much simpler), a better array of weapons and that 'Wang' humour. Not to mention visually its very lovely. Combat in particular is a massive improvement as you can choose a blended style of guns/melee or just one. The first game had me focusing on swordplay, but now the free flowing nature of combat is a big plus for me. Especially as you can upgrade weapons with bonuses. Sadly there is no long range rifles, like sniper rifles, though the bow kinda makes up for it.
Aside from a very clumsy story, at times, there is a huge amount of repetition. A lot of areas are re-used over and over to fill countless side missions. So if you're grinding for something repeating areas can be a bore. Enemies are re-used also as they become 'upgraded' to match you with buffs and etc.
Generally speaking this is a fun game but the repetition gets boring quickly. I also draw some parallels with Dark Souls as you sometimes need to dig for the story.
Get it on sale and I don't think you'll be dissapointed.

I'm surprised this isn't more popular. Yes, it's short, but it's super fun and something you'll enjoy replaying. It's the perfect thing for those times when you just want to relax with a casual, cute game.
As for the gameplay itself, the trailer does a pretty good job of showing you what the game's all about. Each object that you can build your fort out of has varying amounts of hp, which determines how many hits it can take, although some cats hit harder than others. Some items have additional effects which can be quite humorous, and each costs time points to place. You can gain a larger pool of time to place objects with by successfully completing rounds, clearing rooms, etc.
There was no penalty that I noticed for losing a round. It just starts you back at the beginning of that round with your fort exactly the way you built it so you can make adjustments to improve your defense. The controls were intuitive and I didn't run into any bugs or crashes. So no cons for me.
If you're looking for a challenging game that's going to frustrate you and have you beating your head against a wall, you're going to be disappointed here. But if you're just looking for some casual fun and the trailer and screenshots look good to you, then buy it. You won't regret it.

Okay, so I'm going to put the important bit first. If you're a fan of the RTS genre, but you dislike the intensity of the micro required to perform in the genre at a high level competitively,
Don't even read the rest of the reviews; just buy it and prepare for a fantastic experience.
Offworld Trading Company is a
game. A very deep game. What you need to succeed is an ability to accurately assess a given situation, and make good decisions based on other players' actions. That's pretty much it. The difficulty comes with how many variables there are: buildings, resources, money, debt, the black market, and other players. These variables interact in many ways, but never through direct conflict.
It's pretty clear that the inspiration behind OTC was board gaming, and there are ways in which it feels like a board game at times. But computers are capable of more calculations than humans which, coupled with the fact that so much thought has gone into the intricacies of the economic system, makes building an economic empire both very rewarding and enormously fun.
Multiplayer is balanced extremely well. All of the game-breaking exploits have been quashed by this point, and watching streams of the very best players makes it apparent that it's careful consideration of options, and not raw APM, that's rewarded in this game. This fact alone makes it almost unique within the genre, and as a result I can't recommend this game highly enough. There are enough active players in the ranked queues at the time of writing that you'll pretty much always get a game, and that will be improved further when you (yes,
!) buy it and start playing. So off you go.
Oh, and the guy who made it is the guy who made Civilization IV, which is the best Civ game to date by a long way. He knows how to make games.

So I've owned KOTOR 2 for many years now. I got it for Christmas the year it came out, same as the original. Since then, I've owned 2 more copies of the game, one on the original xBox, and then this version on Steam.
First off, this game is amazing. Comparing it to the original, it keeps a lot of the good, and makes most of it better. Don't come into this game expecting an amazing story based on your character, however, because rather than that, it gives you an amazing (and in my opinion, better) story based on how your character's actions affect your companions and the galaxy as a whole.
While this game's combat and mechanics are basically the same as the original KOTOR, several mechanics are much deeper than before. Upgrading is greatly expanded, giving many options for creating your ultimate weapons. Creating and Breaking Down items has been added, forcing you to decide on what to sell and what to break down into components, in order to create another weapon or item. And since this game focuses on companions, an influence mechanic has been implemented into your interactions with them. Now, what you say and do can change how your companions look at you and change their light and dark side orientation.
Now, for the bad. This game is packed full of amazing content, but due to some issues, the game is left… unfinished. The final few areas are lacking. The developers were rushed for the end of the game, and it feels lacking. Luckily, there is a fix for this. The Restored Content Mod is available here on Steam, and helps to fill in the gaps and slightly clear up the problems the developers left behind.
As for the quality of this version, it is superior to the other two I owned. The others were riddled with bugs, and frequently crashed. This version hasn't crashed once in the hundred hours or so that I've played it. On top of that, it is extremely easy to get mods for the game, some of which are very important (such as the Restored Content Mod), for creating a better experience for your game.

I used to love this game. Now it's trash. The game sucked upon release in May, got slightly better throughout June, was incredible in July, a bit boring but still fun in August, okay in September, picked up in October, and now, in November, it sucks just as much as it did upon release.
Friday The 13th: The Game is super fun and probably one of the most fun things I've ever found myself playing, and this game has incredible potential for many years to come, but at the moment I just cannot recommend it. Why? For multiple reasons.
First off, the development team cares jack about fixing bugs and lag. They're all caught up in adding new maps and effects, and clothes for the counselors to wear. Frankly, I couldn't care less if we never had another content update. I'd much rather play with everything we have now and no bugs. The development team only cares about adding new content. They barely ever fix their bugs and lag. And, with all the new content they bring in comes new bugs. The game just keeps getting more unplayable.
Second off, Jason is an absolute joke now. Jason became a mockery with the release of the Party Emote Pack, where they added taunts and dances to mock Jason with. That was fine, not a problem. But the problem came with the patch that followed. This patch gave counselors the ability to see dropped objective parts on their map. Even that isn't too big of a deal, but also in the patch came the update where Jason could no longer stack traps. That was Jason's key thing that always caused him to be on top of the counselors. Now they can avoid most of your traps while only taking one out, which can be done easily and silently with a pocket knife, and then just like that. The police are called and you're barely likely to get all of the counselors anymore. Jason was never too overpowered in this game, and neither were the counselors. But now they are, and Jason has become an absolute joke.
Let's say the emote pack or the most recent patch never happened. The counselors still had several opportunities and ways to mock Jason, but at least they weren't harsh and over the top. They could chain stun when he tries to take out a group in the car, and honk the horn when they're about to escape. That's pretty much it. Annoying, but just minor annoyances. But what we have now is just no.
If you're not somebody who gets frustrated easily, and you want a fun game to play, I would recommend this game. But if you want a perfect game, go play something else, because this game is FAR from perfect, and will never EVER be perfect. This game is full of bugs and more bugs come with every update.
TL;DR: The development team only cares about content, the community is cancer, and Jason is a joke.

Amnesia the dark descent is a true masterpiece in the forgotten art of survival horror. this terrifying game is i feel the benchmark for which other survival horror games should be measured.
STORY: You play as daniel who sufferes from amnesia and needs to kill the baron of castle brenennburg for reasons i will not divulge here. the story is told primarily through flashblacks and notes scattered across the castle. as you come to grips with just what is going on, you will find yourself horrified and intrigued at the same time making more of it a genuinely unnerving and interesting story reminiscent of Hp Lovecraftian horror.
GRAPHICS: considering the limited budget and small development team, i think they have done a phenomenal job at creating a detailed and horrific environment. blood cascades the wall, shadows and candles reflect off of surfaces and the architecture is done well.
GAMEPLAY AND SOUND: gameplay consists of exploring the environments, solving puzzles and avoiding monsters. the exploration is self explanatory and the puzzles are challenging but fair. as for the monsters, you have no weapons so you must run and hide before they kill you. this creates a feeling of helplessness and terror unlike any other, hiding in the corner while the monster effortlessly tears down the door searching for you is unlike anything i have ever experienced in a horror game. while other survival horror games such as silent hill, resident evil and dead space have their own unique style that makes them scary, you cant help but feel this game is scarier just because you are unarmed. another unique feature in this game is sanity in which looking at monsters or otherwise disturbing things alters your vision and makes the environment that much more terrifying. you start hallucinating, falling to the ground and generally feel helpless. your only salvation in the game is light which is granted to you by a lantern which is your only companion thoughout the whole game. the lantern runs on oil and you need to constanly find oil to refill it which adds a layer of tension to the game. you can also find tinderboxes to light candles and such in the areas to conserve oil and generally brighten things up a bit. as far as sound design goes, they have nailed it. the effects are superb whether its the haunting growls of the monsters, auditory ambiance like screams from the environment or the moody soundtrack, it all comes together to create the perfect audio setup. this is why it is paramount to play the game in the dark with headphones to immerse the player as much as possible.
REPLAY VALUE: The game features 3 endings but the real star of the show is custom stories which keep this alive for nearly forever. the community is constantly creating new stories that you can download for free and play to get more out of the game than you can ever imagine. some of the custom stories are so well done, you will swear it was part of development. there are even custom stories that are total conversion mods which completely change the game making it an entirely different experience. excellent replay value.
OVERALL: Amnesia the dark descent proves that survival horror is alive and well. the fantastic sound design, engrossing and disturbing story, and the constant tension and nail biting induced gameplay all come seamlessly together to provide a survival horror experience unlike anything you have ever played.

Sure, I could have used any number of free software out there. I've certainly done so in the past. None of them were as convenient as this.
That's really what you are paying for here: convenience. You certainly can do up a ram drive yourself and get the same performance out of it, but by god is it cumbersome. So much so that I dropped the idea for a long while and just bought a SSD.
The SSD absolutely helped fix a number of issues I was having with another Bethesda game: Skyrim. Unfortunately, that's the only game it helps with, since Skyrim + all of the mods I use take up most of the drive. I don't regret it one bit, but that's a bit of an expensive fix just for one game.
I decided to try dimmdrive for Fallout 4 after a number of suggested ini edits did absolutely nothing to help my 2 minute load times between areas and 30 second long weapon switches mid shootout. Long load times are annoying but being stuck
is showstopping.
What finally gave me 10 second load times and instant gun swapping was a combination of a
and dimmdrive here. I set dimmdrive to load the textures folder into ram and nothing else. About 6 GB worth of ramdisk textures fixed all the loading troubles I'd been having.
Admittedly I ran into load problems again near the end of my play session, but I suspect that's due to the fact I just entered into DLC territory and didn't have the DLC textures loaded in memory, just the base game's. After ticking that box, it bumped up to a 7 GB ramdisk. After seeing what it did for the base game, I expect the issues to just disappear.

I'll be honest: after finishing Nihilumbra, I quite disliked it.  It tries to establish a mood with a constant narration, in the style of Bastion.  But the writing is mediocre and the voice acting is boring, so the entire thing comes off as trite and cliche.
I was just about to uninstall the game and never think about it again, when I decided on a whim to quickly try out 'Void Mode'.  Void Mode, unlocked once you complete the main game, is a new game + of sorts.  You start over with all powers unlocked, and are tasked with going through the game again.  However, things are much harder.  There are entirely new setpieces, enemies, and mechanics that really force you to think about things.  All voice acting and story elements are removed.  Void Mode is when the game really comes into itself as a puzzle platformer, and I found completing it genuinely satisfying and enjoyable.
I'm recommending the game for Void Mode alone.  If you're looking for a good puzzle platformer, rush through the main game and enjoy Void Mode.  If you're looking for a story-driven experience, I suggest you give this one a miss.

I'm going to go through both the positives and negatives as in depth as possible.

POSITIVES-

1. Combat- Combat is very fun and incredibly satisfying There's a lot of depth here from things like countering, parrying, feinting and alot more.  I guarantee you'll find even more elements to play around with even after spending countless hours on a particular character.

That's it for the positives, here are the negatives now

NEGATIVES-

1. Peer 2 peer networks- essentially this means the game relies on connecting to each other via your broadband rather than Ubisoft having dedicated servers for the game. Considering they're a huge company it's unacceptable. It opens up a bunch of problems. Ghost npc's in games, random disconnecting from games half way through, painfully long loading times and game freezing which literally requires you to close the game for it to respond again. All these things happen very frequently.

2. Game mechanics- This one just bugs the hell outta me. With a game which is so heavily  combat focused' why have they implemented a way in which you can  insta kill someone by knocking them off the map or into a geyser? It literally requires no skill or thought. simply press 2 buttons and voila! dead. it's absolutely ridiculous.
-If someone from the opposite team is climbing down a ladder it can one shot kill you for some reason.
-Revenge mode. This is essentially a bar which gradually builds up during a game and quickly fills up if you're outnumbered in a fight. When activated it gives you a stat boost to help you fight. it's a good idea, however there are many cases where I'm standing next to a player who activates it and it makes you fall over so they can just go ham on you and you can't defend yourself, so you die.

3. Balancing- The game currently has 12 playable heroes, however there are clear distinctions between who's good and who's not. Some heroes are tremendously overpowered and some underpowered. This wouldn't be as bad if people didn't abuse certain moves and attacks. For example 'The warden' has a move called 'The vortex' which not only hits hard but it can literally be spammed and it's so difficult to block or dodge. Similarly the Shugoki can just rek you by running into you and breaking your back. It's stupid and should have been tested before release.

4.Microtransactions- Okay here me out. The game is $40, season pass is $30. So we're at & $70 now. The game has many cosmetic items which can be bought for 'Steel' (in game currency) you can get steel from playing games, doing contracts and etc. Here's the stupid part. The better skins cost alot of steel. To the point where if I wanted to save up enough steel legitimately. it would take me atleast 8 months of playtime to get it and it's ridiculously expensive to buy. (One mythical skin is around $14). The worst thing however is something called 'loot' it's essentially bits of armor and upgrades for your weapon you can get by playing games. Having better gear means your character stand a better chance at winning. However you can buy loot boxes with Steel! meaning while you're busting your♥♥♥♥♥trying to grind for loot. Someone can easily just buy them and get better gear than you. BROKEN!

5. Map Design- This just triggers me, again a game focused on movement and combat is given maps and spawn locations which are just idiotic. if you play either 'Elimination or duels' Instead of having a big area to fight in, most of the time you're given a narrow corridor you can't even move side to side on and it's usually a race to see who can guard break who first.

6. Bugs and glitches- Not many that I've encountered but there are some. For example, if there aren't enough people in the game the rest of the team is filled with bots, which is fine, but it's when you kill the bot you were facing and then a real person replaces that bot, spawns behind you with full health and one shots you.

I will update this review as time goes on, as despite my negative points, it's still a game I like playing with my friends from time to time.

Hope this helped :)

A truly epic game re-released with a classy update.  I mean this too.  I first played Final Fantasy '3' on SNES when I was 14 years old, and have re-played the game every few years since.  It is like a favourite book that one returns to again and again.  I realise that some folks wanted this game to have been completely redone in 3D and voice acted, but frankly that would simply have destroyed it.  This game got exactly what it needed.  A touch-up.  It's rough graphics, sound, and translation are smoothed out.  A few handy features have been added to make it more accessable.  And that's it.  All they did was wax a classic car, which is what they should have done.  You don't put modern mag-wheels and jam a spoiler on a '55 corvette no matter how much you think it will add to the ride.  Same thing.  So whatever all the nay-sayers are throwing out about this, it is a faithful reproduction of an exceptional game.
Thoughts as follows:
The graphics were gorgeous in their original 16-bit, and they have been carefully touched up to look even better in this version.   This is not a simple video filter, as anyone who has ever played this on an emulator like zsnes should pick up instantly.
The Character sprites do not look out of place, they just look different than they used to and they do look better.
The addition of the original art profiles to the dialogue is actually very nice and adds character without spoiling ones own visualization of the characters as a 3D rendering could have.
The Score is enhanced and cleaned up from the old SNES midis and sounds much closer to the original instrumental score, released  on cd in 1994.
The translation is touched up and some of the more ridiculous and confusing moments in the original release make more sense.  No change to substance whatever.
The only two gameplay tweaks, auto-battle and quick-save, ease the playability by taking away some of the pain of grinding and eliminating classic frustration with the great old glitch/power outage, 'holy xxxx, i haven't saved in an hour' moment. All without changing the gameplay in any substantiveway.
only complaints:
Naming fail.  stupid error that I trust will be rectified with a patch, but you can't use 'wasd' for arrow keys without adding 'd' to the end when naming character.  Hardly a game-breaker though as all you have to do is use your arrow keys for 'abxy' and use backspace to eliminate the addition before accepting.
A few glitches - game has stopped a couple of times in about 8 hours of play, as expected in any new release.  happily though, every time I was able to start where it froze by virtue of the game auto-quicksaving with each room change. So you just hit continue when you reload and start where it froze.
All in all the game is more beautiful, more enjoyable, and gently tweaked rather than sullied by 'upgrades' that would have cheapend this fine game like coca-cola in a glass of Bowmore's 15 year old 'Darkest'.
Happy to spend the price of a mediocre bottle of wine on this well-cellared gem.

After spending 152 hours in this game, I feel it is time to share my experiences with you guys.
Life is Feudal is a little difficult to describe.
In it's core, it is a survival RPG, set in a medieval timeframe, on an unknown island.
The game mechanics are relatively complex, the graphics quite demanding and you will have to invest some time into it as there is very little in the game to help you.
I wasn't convinced, when a friend introduced me to the game. I found myself on the shore of an island, equipped with nothing but a cookie and a piece of bread from a former life left behind
I was able to collect flintstones and grass from the ground, a branch from a tree to build my first simple tool.
Then I made a little basket, a fireplace and a bed and I tried placing the items on the ground. I cursed at the overly complex mechanics to place items, I cursed at my friend for making me play this game.
And then our characters met and we started to work together and build shelter on the outskirts of a small forest.
We started to dig into the ground to find iron and copper, stones and soil, lots of soil.
Now, I wanted to be a blacksmith. A grumpy one.
My simple pickaxe kept breaking every ten minutes, forcing me to make a new one.
Finding ore wasn't an easy task either, as the only indicator is your own common sense and your skill in game.
After two days of cursing and giving my friend his first grey hair, we made a forge and an anvil.
We build our first barrel and a little roof because it started snowing and we were so content with our progress, our new home. I was able to make better tools, allowing us to build more things.
We convinced more friends to join us.
One collected herbs, the other was making food.
So far we had survived on moldy apples and fish we occasionally caught.
Soon we had a stew, made of whatever we could find on the ground. It was delicious!
Everone had their job, everyone was depending on the other to survive.
We sent people to hunt deer or bore, while others cleared a field to construct a house, with the shovels, nails and metal plates I had skillfully forged.
We grew into a small village, with a little shed, fields to grow vegetables and lots of enthusiasm.
Soon, we met other people from other parts of the island, some were friendly, some were real turds.
We knew we had to be prepared, so we began training with weapons and more than once we spilled our own blood, trying to become fierce warriors.
Life is Feudal, while it is far from being perfect, offers a truly unique game experience in terms of atmosphere, teamplay and role playing. The game inspires you to create your own story, play the game the way you want it to.
You can not really play this game by yourself.
You are depending on other people, just as much as they depend on you.
The game is still in development, updates appear regularly, all heading towards turning LiF into an MMO.
-- EDIT: --
Now, almost a year later, I feel it is time to edit my review. After having spent more than 1000 hours in this game, I have to tell you: forget about Feudal.
The last update I can recall was from June and it broke more than it fixed. Ever since, LiF has slowly been dying. The competitors are many and they have been on the market only for a few months and are already better than Feudal will ever be.

Okay, so I'm going to put the important bit first. If you're a fan of the RTS genre, but you dislike the intensity of the micro required to perform in the genre at a high level competitively,
Don't even read the rest of the reviews; just buy it and prepare for a fantastic experience.
Offworld Trading Company is a
game. A very deep game. What you need to succeed is an ability to accurately assess a given situation, and make good decisions based on other players' actions. That's pretty much it. The difficulty comes with how many variables there are: buildings, resources, money, debt, the black market, and other players. These variables interact in many ways, but never through direct conflict.
It's pretty clear that the inspiration behind OTC was board gaming, and there are ways in which it feels like a board game at times. But computers are capable of more calculations than humans which, coupled with the fact that so much thought has gone into the intricacies of the economic system, makes building an economic empire both very rewarding and enormously fun.
Multiplayer is balanced extremely well. All of the game-breaking exploits have been quashed by this point, and watching streams of the very best players makes it apparent that it's careful consideration of options, and not raw APM, that's rewarded in this game. This fact alone makes it almost unique within the genre, and as a result I can't recommend this game highly enough. There are enough active players in the ranked queues at the time of writing that you'll pretty much always get a game, and that will be improved further when you (yes,
!) buy it and start playing. So off you go.
Oh, and the guy who made it is the guy who made Civilization IV, which is the best Civ game to date by a long way. He knows how to make games.

I really can't describe how much I enjoyed playing SOMA. Every element is near perfect, from the stunningly realised world of Pathos 2 and the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean, to the
sound design that physically wrenches you out of your seat and transports you into protagonist Simon's nightmare world, not to mention the flawless pacing that expertly intertwines periods of calm exploration and philosophical musing with breathless sequences of heart-stopping terror, building inexorably towards a magnificent crescendo.
To reveal anything of the story would be to spoil it but suffice it to say I was utterly engrossed from start to finish and went to great pains to track down every last audio recording, email, call log and journal entry. I even tracked down all the hastily-written notes hidden away in drawers or pinned to notice boards in order to absorb every detail I could. And what exceptional detail there is to be found - by the end of the game I'd built up a mental timeline of everything that had happened at Pathos 2 over approximately an 18 month period, pieced together from the various snippets of information I'd found. Everything is consistent and believable and cements in place the feeling that this is a real facility and was only recently populated by dozens of people before something went very, very wrong.
SOMA isn't as terrifying a proposition as developer Frictional's previous game, Amnesia, but that certainly isn't to say it's not frightening. The atmosphere is thick and foreboding, the clangs, creaks and groans of the facility around you menacing and, on more than one occasion, I became so spooked out I simply couldn’t continue. At these moments I would stare at the corridor or ladder I had to navigate next for full minutes, the deeply unsettling ambient sounds around me only serving to further increase the tension, before eventually admitting defeat and leaving the game altogether. Despite this, it’s clear a deliberate decision has been made to turn the horror down a notch, presumably to make the game accessible to a wider audience. This is a bold choice, given Frictional’s pedigree, but one that I applaud as it allows SOMA’s story to take centre stage and gives it room to breathe.
With SOMA, Frictional have proved beyond doubt that they are masters of the horror genre and have demonstrated that they’re pretty well-versed in science fiction and story-telling as well. It’s not often that the many disparate parts of a computer game coalesce this coherently but somehow they’ve managed the impossible and have crafted the finest horror experience since Amnesia.

Full disclosure: review copy provided by developer/publisher!
The Aquatic Adventure of the Last Human, in addition to having the least marketable video game name since GOLF Magazine Presents 36 Great Holes Starring Fred Couples, also tells you everything you need to know about it: you are, in fact, the last human... having an aquatic adventure.
Unlike GOLF Magazine Presents 36 Great Holes Starring Fred Couples, which had maybe 20 great holes total.
It is the very distant future and humanity has royally screwed the pooch – as it is wont to do. At some point in the past we sought a future amongst the stars and that, presumably, did not work out... so you've returned to an Earth reclaimed by the sea to discover, adventure, and generally faff about in your little submersible until you die from toxic fart buildup.
It won't be long into your faffing before you learn that, in the absence of hungry, hungry humans, some underwater creatures have grown to enormous, Captain's Platter™ proportions – with tempers to match. Fortunately, because this is a Metroidvania-y kind of title, you'll also find various upgrades with which to kill all the  giant oceanic critters that give you trouble. You'll pick most of these upgrades up, ironically enough, after killing one of the dozen-or-so bosses – though there are more passive upgrades (improved hull, speed, etc.) to find while exploring. Besides helping you better kill enemies, in true Metroidvania fashion some upgrades will help open the world up to explore.
The boss fights are great, generally. There were one or two I could have done without but they were for the most part fun. Every enemy has their own range of attacks and patterns and you'll seldom “nail it” on the first encounter. With each kill you'll fill out a bestiary for the respective boss to learn a little bit about it, and when you complete the main game there's a boss rush mode and a hardcore mode.
While there are a few hazards here and there (and boss battles, of course), this is a very laid back, lonely, peaceful kind of title – very akin to Shadow of the Colossus... not because of the titanic boss battles per se, but because of the soft ambaince, the wandering, and the unavoidable feeling of being an incredible ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for murdering unsuspecting giants. The Aquatic Adventure of the Last Human has a world I got lost in for hours. The backgrounds are some of the most beautiful and haunting I've seen in this pixel art style – and the music definitely does its part.
That's not to say this one is perfect! There are hologram messages in every hub with bits of exposition and... at its BEST it was uninteresting, at its worst it was preachy. “The forest offered us plentiful bounty, and we wiped our asses with it.” Well what did you want me to do devs, use a bidet like some kind of European or something?  Also, the dinosaurs didn't live for 65 millions years, they died 65 million years ago... they actually lasted closer to 200 million years! Just a minor nitpick. Oh, and there's no map function, really. You have a mini map you can refer to while traveling but it's just for the immediate area you're in. There are save points in each section that have a world map you can refer to but I found myself backtracking and getting lost to the point of frustration near the very end.
I still really enjoyed this one in spite of those minor quibbles. It's peaceful and pretty, like a walking sim but with boss fights sprinkled in to keep it interesting. Every environment is unique and lovingly crafted, every boss fight is singular and special (and the names for each one... excellent), the music accents the loneliness perfectly – it's a great little experience overall, and a wonderful way to start off your 2016 Gaming Year.
Plus. it's just better down where it's wetter – take it from me.

I used to love this game. Now it's trash. The game sucked upon release in May, got slightly better throughout June, was incredible in July, a bit boring but still fun in August, okay in September, picked up in October, and now, in November, it sucks just as much as it did upon release.
Friday The 13th: The Game is super fun and probably one of the most fun things I've ever found myself playing, and this game has incredible potential for many years to come, but at the moment I just cannot recommend it. Why? For multiple reasons.
First off, the development team cares jack about fixing bugs and lag. They're all caught up in adding new maps and effects, and clothes for the counselors to wear. Frankly, I couldn't care less if we never had another content update. I'd much rather play with everything we have now and no bugs. The development team only cares about adding new content. They barely ever fix their bugs and lag. And, with all the new content they bring in comes new bugs. The game just keeps getting more unplayable.
Second off, Jason is an absolute joke now. Jason became a mockery with the release of the Party Emote Pack, where they added taunts and dances to mock Jason with. That was fine, not a problem. But the problem came with the patch that followed. This patch gave counselors the ability to see dropped objective parts on their map. Even that isn't too big of a deal, but also in the patch came the update where Jason could no longer stack traps. That was Jason's key thing that always caused him to be on top of the counselors. Now they can avoid most of your traps while only taking one out, which can be done easily and silently with a pocket knife, and then just like that. The police are called and you're barely likely to get all of the counselors anymore. Jason was never too overpowered in this game, and neither were the counselors. But now they are, and Jason has become an absolute joke.
Let's say the emote pack or the most recent patch never happened. The counselors still had several opportunities and ways to mock Jason, but at least they weren't harsh and over the top. They could chain stun when he tries to take out a group in the car, and honk the horn when they're about to escape. That's pretty much it. Annoying, but just minor annoyances. But what we have now is just no.
If you're not somebody who gets frustrated easily, and you want a fun game to play, I would recommend this game. But if you want a perfect game, go play something else, because this game is FAR from perfect, and will never EVER be perfect. This game is full of bugs and more bugs come with every update.
TL;DR: The development team only cares about content, the community is cancer, and Jason is a joke.

Nihilumbra seems to be automatically compared to LIMBO by those who have played both, and rightly so as they are quite similar. However, where LIMBO is dark, eerie and gorgeously gothic, Nihilumbra revels in the atmospheric use of colour and an inventive, immersive style of puzzle-based challenges. The idea is to find and use "colours" to change your environment to allow you to move through it in different ways, overcome obstacles and defeat enemies. The visuals are stunning, with an oil-painting feel and beautiful rendering. The captions and voice-over in story mode are beautifully done and almost reminiscent of being read a story from a picture book, but with deep meaning-of-life type of stuff going on. I almost felt the need to take constant screen shots to capture the beauty of the "pages"!
Moreover, for those looking for a real challenge, the Void Mode that comes after the main story line will make you weep blood - the puzzles require a serious amount of thought (one of the achievements is to die 10 times in a row on Void Mode, which I achieved with depressing ease and totally unintentionally on my first attempt at the first level!) but that just makes it all the more rewarding when you finally find the solution. I bought this game on a bit of a whim and I'm so glad I did, I love it.  I think the metascore is a little on the low side; this is a wonderful, beautiful and challenging little platform game that I recommend to everyone.

Weapons and damage model in MP are also horrible. Hit detection, is most notably, the worst I've seen in any game. Would not recommend MP.

So, rather than copy the files to the RAMDISC, which on some drives may take slightly longer, it completely moves them. The downside to this, is that if the computer crashes when a game is loaded into the RAMDISC, it's gone, completely. You have to re-download the title. There's also virtually no configuration settings to speak of. Pick a drive letter, change the drive loaded alert, drag and drop non-steam games (or software otherwise not recognised), pick which ones you want to load, then turn it on.
On the plus side, this will use "up to" any available ram. This is based on  which games you choose to load. The load times compared to my SSD are noticably faster, but not by any large margin. This is probably due to the fact that I'm running 1866mhz ram, and the SSD is also holding my entire OS. Only have 32G of the stuff, and it will only allocate up to 23.9G, so my larger games simply can't afford to sit in ramdisc (like Dark Souls). That being said, the performance I get from smaller games makes this software really handy. I can install anything < 16G on my HDD and quick-load them to RAM whenever I want to play something for a few hours.

Exactly what is shown, is exactly what you will get. A top-down shooter that requires solid team-mates for it to be rather enjoyable.
Of Guards and Thieves comes in many game modes. There is the original and most enjoyable game mode (IMO), guards and thieves where the thieves attempt to steal documents from the guards. It's somewhat comparable to what Splinter Cell Double Agent had as it's multiplayer minus the 3D aspect. Team deathmatch is also featured (pretty self explanatory). Bomb Defusal where terrorists must place a bomb in one of two spots. Zombie rush which emulates zombies versus survivors. VIP extraction mode where guards have to protect the VIP while he rushes towards an extraction point. IG mode where you have to get a set amount of kills (usually 40) to win the game. Capture the flag mode (which is also self explanatory). There are also "fun" features to the game such as a soccer mode, Mad Ball where like TDM there is a set limit but explosive like balloons are on the map, and a slender mode (slenderman game?) where players only have torches and have to search for the slenders. I have yet to play soccer as it's been difficult trying to get a game going but for the most part (and especially with a good tactical/thoughtful/mindful team), GaT (guards and thieves) mode is the best.
Controls are quite simple where the mouse will direct your player, can fire your weapon and turn on your light with the right mouse button. Different classes are capable of having different weaponry and moving and different speeds. You cannot equip a gun and throw a grenade at the same time though, either one or the other has to be done. Thieves have night vision and can see in the dark while guards can't. They can also enter or walk through certain parts of the map (like vents) to gain better access to rooms. One of the greatest feature in game is the ability to turn lights on and off. Having them on can deter thieves while having them off invites them. Adding features that enable one to bend the environment are extremely limited at the moment. You can move an automobile (by driving it) and you can turn the lights on/off for cover or exposure of enemies. This is about as far as it goes.

The file sychronisation for changes made to the ramdrive-held files will be written back to the existing storage media, but on deactivating the ramdrive and re-activating it again, those changes will be deleted, as they are not written back to th original locations, and the sync directory gets deleted when the ramdrive is re-started.
The file/folder listing to choose a subset of game files will continue to show obsolete and deleted files.  For example, you exclude a folder that contains game crash logs from being added to the ramdrive.  Sometime later, you delete some of the old logs and want to make a small change to the subset of files you have added to the ramdrive for that game.  The deleted  files/folders will still haunt the selection list.
TL:DR;
A pair of SSD drives in Raid 0 will be as effective and more reliable than this program!

First off, a lot of people seem to be confusing P2P with server-client hosting.. In P2P, the information is basically passed around between everyone and not through a single host, which ultimately puts everyone on the same playing field so to say. In server-client, a single host is picked and all information is handled entirely by them, which definitely would not be good in a game like this. It's a good thing that For Honor uses the former and not the latter... There's lots of information about this available online, so make the prudent decision and go learn for yourself :)
With that out of the way, For Honor is actually a really decent game with great fighting mechanics once you get used to the "Hero" you're using. There's a steep learning curve in the beginning, but that just adds to the fun of getting those combos mastered.
There's a bit of pay to win going on for sure, but a skilled player with a fresh char can easily beat a noob in godlike gear. Even there, you can earn enough "Iron" (the ingame currency) through doing the 2 tutorials (4500 total) and completing the campaign (i believe 8000) to get some pretty incredible stuff going on. That said, don't buy gear until prestige 3!!!!!
The community is extremely "meh", it's potentially more toxic than the Chivalry community, which is saying something. Every match is filled with bickering, whining, crying, accusations, and everything you don't want to see when you're trying to chill and play some GAMES - key word GAMES. Some lobbies are okay, but for the most part nah.
The game modes are about as diverse as they can be, with 1v1 duels, 2v2 brawls, and a few 4v4 options. In the 1v1 and 2v2 modes your gear level doesn't count for anything, which is great for those who are salty about the "pay to win" people (who they could beat if they were actually good).
Try it for yourself, if you don't like it then get a refund!

Tactical team shooter of up to 5 players with many different multiplayer and co-op / vs. AI game modes. Plant the bomb, defuse the bomb, protect hostage while other team try to eliminate you, terrorist attack where you and your team clear map from AI enemies. As well as some PVE missions to hone your combat skills.
There's a healthy selection of characters both in defense team and attack team. Men and women from different countries with different skills and weapons, attachments and utility gear to use in missions. Some have higher armor, others are more agile, pick the one that is more suitable for the mission.
You can customize characters not only with different weapons and weapon attachments like scopes, laser sight, barrel attachments but also uniforms and helmets, different camo options, weapon accessory charms that dangle on the weapon while you move around.
Game has a lot of different, detailed maps with some destructible environments, a lot of ways to the objective. Be it rushing head on through the front door or grapple onto roof for a sneaky breach through window or ceiling window.
There are micro-transactions in the game but I haven't noticed any P2W elements in this. All the weapons are unlocked and you just change visual appearance of your character. Skins and shop items can either be bought with in game credits or money, but not all of them. For example loot packs you buy only with in game credits, and few uniforms and weapons are bough with real money only. You don't need any additional items, unless you like customizing your character.
I recommend buying standard edition if you want normal game experience, and only buy starter edition if you want to check the game out and not spend a lot, because there are few limitations that will make the credit grind for items a lot more tiresome.
Also for those who have R6 on uPlay, but want to have it on Steam as well. You can buy starter edition on Steam, thus when you install and run it, game will sync your info with uPlay game. Stuff you had unlocked will be available, but all attachments unequipped, and Situation progress reset. You will retain your level, credits and currency, items, unlocks, characters, etc.
Personally I play it only in Terrorist Hunt mode vs. AI as I'm terrible in PVP.
Game runs great with recent updates, 60 fps on very high. The HD textures might give you a few FPS spikes if you don't have 6GB VRAM. Always match settings to your hardware for best results. Have fun! ;)

I loved this game for the SNES.
I loved this game for the GBA (though I played it on the DS with a GBA cartridge).
I saw that they were putting this game on Steam and my Nostalgia Goggles slipped down from the brim of my hat and landed firmly on my face.
I bought the game as soon as it was made available and played it with high hopes... for an hour.
I couldn't play past an hour because my overworld sprite had vanished, making it nearly impossible to tell where I was at.
Beyond that, the change they have made to the sprites completely dumbs down the over-all tone of the game.
Final Fantasy VI was one of the more dark games that I'd played in the series, and to be able to do that with such limited resources was a tremendous accomplishment.
One thing which lent to this tone was the appearance of the game - the sprites, and what they did with the sprites dealt a blow to the theme of the game; a relatively small group of individuals who, against all odds, fight for the future of the planet against a massive military power. The game saw the deaths of several main characters (or their families/love interests), and each character had their moment to be "THE main character".
They didn't ruin the game for me, they just did a really bad job with this rendition of it.
My advice to anyone considering buying this game from Steam :
Go buy a GBA and find this game in a local game shop instead.

If this had been nothing more than an improvement on the first game it would have been fantastic. Instead it feels like it was trying to be more like Borderlands and not really succeeding. The linear progression of the first game has been replaced with a "safe hub" and a map where you can travel to each mission. Enemies now drop loot you can use to upgrade your weapons, but the overwhelming majority of stuff that drops is useless and it's a massive pain to sort through your inventory to find the hidden gems.
My big complaints about the first game were that the guns felt like they were pea shooters and the gameplay could often get repetitive. Not only were those things not addressed in this game, they are actually worse now. There are more guns to choose from in this game but the katana is still by far the most effective weapon you'll use. It's not that the katana is too powerful or isn't fun, but the guns all just suck. Even after being upgraded the guns don't feel very useful for killing things and you'll find yourself running out of ammo even trying to kill just a few bad guys.
The environments are pretty but they start feeling repetitive very quickly. Almost all the missions take place in levels with a randomized layout. There's only about 3 types of environments in the game: forest/village, town, and futuristic city. While the layouts of each level are randomized, nothing about them is distinct enough to make them feel very different from one another, so every futuristic city level looks the same, every town level looks the same, etc. Even different sections within the same level feel the same. After a while you start to feel like you're playing the same missions over and over again. While each level is labyrinthine, there's also no incentive to explore because there's nothing to do except kill things, so you might as well get to your objective as quickly as possible. With that said, there are a few story missions that do take place in linear levels that aren't randomized.
It's hard to recommend this game because I feel like they made too much of a departure from what made the first game a lot of fun. If you did like the first you might like this one, but I personally feel like it's too different. I hope the third game goes back to its roots.

I'm a huge fan of the older Final Fantasy games and Final Fantasy 6 is by far my favorite for its diverse, fleshed out characters and rich story. I've owned and played through the SNES cartridge a few times, played it on the Playstation's Final Fantasy Anthology and I've played the GBA version as well.
If the changes to the artwork and sprites are too jarring for you then I wouldn't recommend this game.
If that doesn't bother you, I
recommend this game on its own merit of functionality (I have had absolutely zero bugs or problems with it) and content.  I don't consider myself a purist and the odd choice of character sprites that seem to clash with the other artwork of the game do not bother me that much. Fundamental changes aren't made to the gameplay with exception to the UI but it's easy to get used to on the default setting (tab settings are made for touch screens) and the auto fight feature more than makes up for that. It also keeps the original SNES music but it's been tweaked to give it a higher quality sound (this is a good thing).
People have reported problems with controllers not working and the game not supporting some HD resolutions. I've had no problems using my rock candy xbox 360 controller and since I use an old 19 inch CRT monitor, HD resolutions are lost on me anyway.
As a gamer who grew up with the original I'm not going to say this game is better but I can understand where people who hate on it are coming from. This game, in its own right, is solid and IMHO a welcomed experience for fans who want more of this entry in the franchise. Far from perfect and far from my idea of a definitive version, for what it is I do recommend it.

Overall, this is a fascinating experience! The Hacker Evolution series is a serious treat for the geekiest gamers. What makes it unique and positively special is that it's essentially played by in-game console commands! There are no other games I can name that utilize this as a core game mechanic. In fact, I wish Watch_Dogs played less like Grand Theft Auto and more like this.
My only complaint is that there are a number of points within levels that feel like "Guide Dang It!" Either my brain is not up to snuff, or the levels barely give a clue (if at all) on how to complete the objectives (such as figuring out the names of all the servers for each level). Fortunately, it is ridiculously easy to add content and your own levels with provided mod tools. This gets even better, because the main game levels are treated the same way, meaning they can be opened up and used as an answer key or even changed to the players' liking.
