If you've never played this game, it's probably not for you. I have had it since it's release in 2005ish - so I will admit to a great deal of sentiment clouding my objectivity. That being said, here's another couple of reasons why I would not reccomend it: the campaign mode tries to take elements from the Total War franchise, but does this poorly and the end result is a very distilled game in terms of control features and options. If you're playing in total domination mode (you win by conquering the map) - all other nations are HELL-BENT on your destruction, you'll be lucky to have 2-3 allied countries at any time, the AI of any other nation other than yourself is much too aggressive. In terms of politics, any offer that is made to you by the AI (doesn't matter what the issues is - resources, alliance, coalition, ect.) that you turn down, decreases your sympathy standing. In order for your own offer to land a deal - you more often than not have to spend more resources than you gain. Moving on to the battle mode, I'll say that naval battles are absolte trash, if you're trying to manage more than two ships at a time, you simply can't move around the battle area fast enough and track all the activities (I've always hated the sea battles and left them to be settled by the AI, it considers numeric superiority anyway, so it doesn't really matter how you fight). Land battles have always been my favourite, as they are very simple to manage, in this part of the review, however, that is a bad aspect and in no way a compliment to the game. Unless you're using explosive ordinance (Congreve rockets (only available to England) or howitzers) artilery is utterly useless, simply doesn't have the range and/or time to do significant damage, and since there is no morale standing as in the Total War franchise they won't scare anyone either. I've seen somewhere in the reviews here, someone compared the battle scenes to an android/iOS arcade type battle mechanic - and I have to say that is very accurate. Realism? Forget about it. I can have 360 men armed with sticks be obliterated, with no casualties whatsoever, by a regiment of 60 men (or less, for as long as they can actually form a square formation). The battle mechanics are also very... paper-rock-scissor'ey, cavalry reigns supreme, an infantry regiment, while having a lot of firepower, can realistically (in the sense of the game), be used for two-five battles at the most (since you can only restore your casualties starting with the third era, which is at the very end of the game, when you can build military hospitals, up until then - if your regiment has one man left - that's what you get in your next battle - one man). As I said before, artillery has no real use other than ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles. On the defense the game expects you to come to it, sending a cavalry regiment ahead of your line will trigger an all out attack by any melee unit, and you can simply lure them in to your men standing in square formation, since the game never leaves artilery unescorted, and it is superbly slow, by the time it gets in range, you've already dealt with any melee/cavalry unit - and the infantry escorting their artilery on the enemy side simply can't do anything from that point onwards. Quite often the game will glitch, and the enemy artilery will simply stand there looking at your troops.
All these shortcomings aside - here's why I like this game, and in the end would recommend it: it's simple, it's light - even on hard it is a walk in the park, and that's what it has over the Total War franchise, which requires commitment and thought (not necessarily bad traits, just that sometimes, it's not what you're after). Here you can have battles every other move, advancements are super simple and relatively fast. For times when you want to feel like a Generalissimo, grab yourself cheat engine, ramp up your starting resources and have at it (or not, whatever floats your boat). Imperial Glory is to the strategy gaming world, what "Hot Shots: Part Deux" is to the movie world - it's a dumb movie, but whenever you're bored, and you just want to watch something - it's a very nice, easy view, and as such I recommend this game, not only out of sentiment, but also for it's simplicity. Try and score it on a discount, it's deffinitely not worth the 5 quid it's going for.

It's a shame to see a game like Final Fantasy VI handled so poorly.  What could have been a great addition to the Steam library is nothing more than a lazy version of a mobile port with zero effort put into it.
This version features a new art style, that completely disrespects the original. This new art style is soft and saturated, stripping out the soul of the game.  From the first scene of the game, things are far too bright, losing any sense of atmosphere.  The characters are soft and bland where once they had texture and contrast, and they clash with backgrounds.  If that wasn't bad enough, the sprites have been put through a nasty blur filter that makes them look smeared with vaseline.  Now, many environments are smooth to the point they look molded from cheap plastic.
As for gameplay, the entire menu interface has been replaced with giant buttons designed for touch screen.  The standard battle option sees each character have a tab that rises out of the bottom of the screen instead of the ATB bar of the original.  There is a tabbed option that isn't much better.  There is no option to play with the menu style of the original game.  You can get used to it over time, but it's clunky and awkard.
There are a couple of improvements to the way a couple characters abilities work, and it includes the redone translation and extras of the GBA version, but that doesn't make up for the rest.  I would only recommend this version if there is literally no other option available to you to play FFVI.

This is one of the scariest games in recent memory. The loading screen recommends you turn the lights off and play with headphones, something I'll strongly echo. Amnesia: The Dark Descent's puzzles aren't especially impressive and the voice acting can range from convincing to goofy, but the atmosphere Frictional has infused into the experience is as powerful as they come. It's a tale of terror that's menacing and disturbing from the very first moments, and only amplifies the further you progress. Any fan of horror, every Lovecraft fan, and any with even a hint of curiosity should give Amnesia a shot!!
In Frictional Games' Amnesia: The Dark Descent, you get no gun. When a gruesome shambling creature rounds a corner on wobbly knees and its yawning rictus comes into focus, you can only succumb to its onslaught or flee in terror, hoping the shadows will provide safe haven. It plays more like a first-person adventure game than anything else, and borrows many of the environmental manipulation mechanics of Frictional's previous Penumbra series. It's a fairly short game, but one that's near impossible to forget.
What follows is a tale told mostly in flashback as you' re beset by ghostly visions and uncover journal entries on dimly lit desks that tell of scientific expeditions that lead to the discovery of ancient terrors. By itself the story is strong enough, and told effectively assuming you take the time to explore and pick up a majority of the notes. Yet what really adds a quality of unsettling authenticity to the tale is the unshakeable feeling of pursuit and inevitability of some kind of horrific climax.

As a kid, I've spent four years living at the seaside. I've always respected sea as the strongest of all the forces of nature and trembled under the attacks of my imagination. What kind of horrors these dark depths hide from puny humans? Years later, Frictional Games delivers the answer - unimaginable horrors and philosophical questions about humanity's own existence.
You're playing the role of Simon, your average, twenty something guy that goes for a brain scan and wakes up... somewhere? That somewhere is PATHOS 2, science station hidden in the vast universe on our planet - below the waves of Atlantic Ocean. You'll take Simon on 8-12 hours journey to depths of watery hell, in an epic struggle to survive and find answers to loads of questions.
If you've played Frictional Games titles before, you know very well what to expect. First person movement, no HUD and you use mouse to interact with objects. It can get clunky from time to time, but it's never dull. Your enemies are strong and there's no way to fight them, so you'll need to crouch and get past them - if you don't like stealth, this game is not for you. The nicest thing about enemies in SOMA is that they are difficult, yet not frustrating and even if you die, you will gladly reload and get back on track.
In my not so humble opinion, SOMA reigns over other FG titles because a) story; b) design and atmosphere; c) sound.
Story may appear to be well known (at least some of its elements) to sci-fi enthusiasts, but it still manages to create a perfect combo with design and atmosphere. I don't want to spoil anything for anyone, therefore, I'll just say SOMA is story-driven experience and it progresses as a fine piece of art, an interactive movie that makes you come back for more once your gaming session is over. The end of the game is emotional and well directed and the emotions you will experience from witnessing the end game are directly influenced by your own opinions about life, achievements and goals.
Design and atmosphere, hands down, game of the year. I'm not sure what kind of games will be launched until the end of 2015 to beat SOMA in this fight. Everything about this game is terrific - sense of loneliness, desperation, isolation. When you first exit dry and enter wet and start walking the ocean floor, you'll experience such a tremendous impact, a fusion of beauty and horror not seen so often in the games like this. When you go even deeper and end up in a violent ocean current, you'll feel nauseated, lost and alone.
Sound. Man, oh man... SOUND. Samuel Justice and his team. I had to google the name of the guy who was in charge of SOMA's sound. Horror games usually let sound engineers play with sounds. Justice and his team did not do that - they've literally ruled the sounds and used them to terify the players. Dry sounds, underwater sounds, mechanical sounds, enemy sounds, voices. Everything is so perfect and binaural, YOU NEED TO PLAY THIS ONE WITH GOOD HEADPHONES. Fantastic sound design, a lot to be learned from these guys. SOMA could prove to be revolutionary in the field of horror games audio design.
Personally, I feel SOMA's the pinnacle of Frictional Games work and they've set up the new standards with this one. The next thing they deliver will be judged heavily by standard known as SOMA.
Buy. Play. Get Scared.

This game should NOT exist!  To justify my statement I'll point out a few issues I've noticed in the time I played.  I played for just short of an hour but it was all I could stomach and in that time I noticed a few glaring problems.
Aesthetic: The first thing that occured to me was that the enemies for the first 10 "waves" had NO Zombies in.  I see TWO total in the advertising screen-shots.  ALL the enemies are differently armoured versions of Skeletons.  The Game also uses the exact same background in every single wave which made me realise that Spartans didn't live in Castles!  But that's enough of the aesthetic gripes.
The mechanics: NO KEYBOARD CONTROLS!  Everything in this game requires the mouse to click and all the appropriate buttons are at the extreme corners of the screen making moving "Leonidas" around AND using his abilities AND buying your army a complete hastle.  There's also the little problem that you can actually walk THROUGH the enemies but Leonidas can't attack the other way, so there's an irritating moment where you run one way to pick up resources and then you have to run to catch up so you can attack again.
The Options: Virtually non-existant.  You can turn off Music and Sounds but there are no graphics options (As if you'd need them, this game would probably run on a toaster!).  There's no option for Windowed, it's always in full screen and there are no resolution options AT ALL.  There's also a little thing that happens, if you press "Esc" to get to the "Exit" menu and press "Esc" again, it'll bring up ANOTHER "Exit" menu every time you press it, so if you frantically tap "Esc" to try and skip something it'll bring up a half-dozen menus for you to close.
The Elephant in the Room: COPYRIGHT!  These developers have NEVER heard of it.  Virtually every aspect of this game has been stolen from somewhere else.  The game itself is a blatant reskin of the Army of Darkness: Defence by Backflip Studios, I recognise most of the skeleton growls and noises from Terraria and the advertising poster is a complete copy of the "300" movie poster and various audio clips from the "300" have been used, obviously without permission from Warner Bros.
Whatever you do, do NOT give these people your money!  DO NOT go for their micro-transactions!  All it will do is fund their enevitable lawsuit when they get slapped (soon, I hope).

I went into this game not really expecting much, just an average adaptation of a Steam game from an app, but I was pretty surprised with how well this game translated, and I would even say that the PC version was better! Basically, you take control of a being created by "The Void", who is searching through the world, trying to discover what he is and where he belongs. Along this journey, he takes control of many different elemental powers, which makes up the basic gameplay. This may sound like an overused story with a basic platformer, but the game is extremely charming and a load of fun. Top it off with the low price of $9.99, a good soundtrack, and an overall great atmosphere, and you have a game that I can't help but recommend. The only downside that I can see with this game is the brutally punishing difficulty curve, via Void Mode. You basically go from a game that even young kids could play with relative ease, to a game that I doubt the developers themselves could beat with ease, but that's not necesarrily a bad thing, especially to anybody who wants a good challenge and added replay value. Just be prepared to be left floored by some of the especially challenging levels. Overall, this is a game that I really enjoyed playing through, and I recommend it to any platforming fans that are looking for a good side-project.

Fantastic game. If you are into FPS, but also like a bit of strategy, thinking and skill, rather than just running into a room with a shotgun and laying havoc, this game is spot on.
Instead of a regular FPS where all you need is accuracy and a good gun, this game relies heavily on you having good senses of hearing and sight, good map knowledge, and your thinking skills need to be able to adapt to any situation. Every game is random, as the same window a sniper flew threw last round, could be untouched the next.
If you are the type to sprint around a map with a shotgun, this isn't for you, as this game punishes you heavily if you make too much noise or if you are not ready for what may be waiting around the corner. From a launcher that fires a breaching round to destroy walls, to a cluster charge capable of clearing whole rooms out, to a mounted DP-28 able to mow down an entire enemy force, to a knife and some silent boots; the arsenal options in this game are endless.
But again, don't go gung-ho, because you could end up dropping to the floor with a knife to your throat, threatening your life for your teammates' locations. One person's death can mean everything to the match.
FPS - 8/10
Suspense - 9/10
Brain Usage - 10/10 (excluding having yours blown off by a Desert Eagle)
Explosions and Map Destruction 14/10

Cute cats in a very interesting and one of a kind physics based defense game.
This game is wonderful, for the short time that you're playing it.
It has stylized graphics that make up it's own uncommon art style.  It's very pretty but at the same time slightly unusual (in a good way) and you can recognize that it's not just generically pretty but it's got a unique look to it.  If you saw characters from the game elsewhere, you'd recognize their art style.  I find that refreshing in a world full of pretty but very generic graphics that we see in so many other games.
There is a short but interesting story to follow.  I gobbled up every bit and read every little note.  Some people will probably just want to skip through that and play the defense part of the game, but the story here adds to the atmostphere and lets you see what is going on.  I would have very much have liked to see the story go in a different direction, but at least it wasn't super predictable I guess.
Speaking of the defense part of the game, it's absolutely wonderful.  Being a physics game, sometimes you will win by accident because of something falling over into a certain place.  But sometimes you will also lose when that happens, so it does balance out.  Each item has it's own shape and behavior and way it affects the cats and reacts to other items and movements.  During the short time you play, you will really get to know most of the items pretty intimately, which helps during one single frantic time of the game.
While the game says you have "time" to set up, that's actually just your "currency" for placing objects.  You can spend as much time as you want setting stuff up for 95% of the game.  There is one time where you don't get to, which completely changes the mechanics and feels as if it should have been a different game mode, but it's not super hard and I got through it in a single try anyway.
The cats are incredibly cute and all have their own unique behaviors as well.  You will get to know each and every cat too and need to keep careful watch of what types of cats are incoming for each wave.
While I love this game and definitely recommend it, I feel it's a tad short and probably should have been priced at about $5.  I was completely done in under 3 hours and that's with taking my time and going afk a few times.  While the experience is great and *is* worth buying at $7.99, I just feel that $5 would have been a more reasonable price point for how short it is.  Once it's over, it's over, there are no additional modes and not much reason to play any more again sadly.
I missed playing after it was over and was thinking of it all night.  Usually I feel a sense of accomplishment when a game is finished, for this one I just felt longing and wished I still had more levels to play.  This isn't a complaint about the length again, but it's a compliment about the gameplay and world.  I miss playing.  I want to keep playing and it's in my mind thinking how great and fun it was.  I'd love to see an expansion or sequel.  I'll be waiting and hoping one comes out.

I can only write for a brief while since I am an adult with a baby to take care of. But it needs to be said - this is one of the Rainbow Six greats, right up there with Rogue Spear and the like. Destructible environments really make this game - the closest thing there is, the Battlefield series, doesn't compare. Here you can poke a small hole in a wall so you can ambush hapless enemies, or blow them wide open with explosives. Floors, ceilings, objects, windows - there is a constant metagame in each match where opponents breach and seal against each other.
There's a lot of complaints about R6, I know. But they break down into these few categories, and I'll just briefly refute them here.
1. People are toxic! - That's the internet. For ever 9 people who are great sports, there's always going to be a jerk with a big mouth. Learn to deal with these people. It's part of growing up in the internet age.
2. Hitreg is bad! - No, it isn't. Thin operators like the skinny fast females (Ash , Caviera, etc) are indeed harder to hit than the big fat guys like Tachanka (balanced out by armor differences). If you have a problem with this, you have a problem with reality.
3.  Game is glitched! - Every game has exploits. The exploits in R6 are seldom used in actual play, rather ranked or casual (for example, the glitch to fall through the map by using deployable cover). That is because their usefulness is low, and it's really hard to "activate" them. Furthermore, Ubi does actively work to resolve them. There are also some other "glitches" that really aren't - they are just creative ways to use the enviroment. Whiners will insist that these are glitches, but they are fools and their comments should be ignored.
4. It's too expensive / too hard to buy new ops / too P2W - No, it's not. It's expensive if you want to get instant access to operators instead of earning them, it's not too hard to buy new ops at all even if you have the starter version, and its certainly not p2w as even the most basic recruit can hold their own against any operator, regardless of what gear they have.
In short, it's a good game and well worth the money.

I really enjoyed playing through this game.  If I wasn't going for the achievements (which I did end up having to do a second play-through to get) my playtime would have been much shorter.  If you're looking to throw away a couple hours on a fun game, I would definitely say that this game is worth the money.
Essentially, you are a girl who has come to spend some time with your grandparents.  Upon your arrival, you find that neither your grandfather, nor your grandmother are around.  Searching for something to do until they arrive, you find your grandfather's journal and become enthralled with his detailed account of what he's been working on lately.  However, there is one minor flaw with reading the journal...your grandparents have some VERY needy cats who crave your attention.  To keep them at bay, you must build a fort and read the information that they may not want you to know...
While this review might show a conlist that outweighs the pros, the game itself is fun and the cosmetic issues are things that can be overlooked in the longrun.  I would give this game a rating of 9/10, as it is a unique idea and was generally fun to play through.
Pros:
- This game is entertaining.  The storyline itself was interesting and the side quests were entertaining.  I was not bored the entire time I played through Fort Meow.
- The game continually builds upon itself.  You are tasked with collecting side items to strengthen your fort, as well as clues to chip away at the mystery of these overly affectionate felines.
- Both the music and the art style add to the gameplay.  The music isn't grating upon one's ears and it's lovely to look at.
- The random drops from the packages were a nice touch, giving the player a chance to hoard the items and use them when a level was too hard to conquer without the use of something else.
- The creators were thoughtful enough to include Steam achievements and trading cards.
Cons:
- You cannot skip scenes.  I do not like being forced to read the entire dialogue.  For 1 playing, this might have been an irritating quirk.  However, only having the ability to click quickly to speed along the dialogue would not be nearly as useful as a skip button for entire scenes.
- It's short.  You can knock this game out entirely in one sitting.  Some people might like this, but it would be nice to give this game some more replayable content, like the last level.
- The only challenging part of the game was the last level, where you must rebuild your fort multiple times while the battery is recharging.  While the later levels do try to increase the challenge of cats, I felt that the outcome was entirely luck based.  You had to have a little more strategy in how you built your fort to keep its stability.
- It's a bit repetitive and is almost entirely luck-based.  I've found that by using the same shoddy builds up to 10 times, you will eventually get a success.
- There was a lack of introductions of the new cat introductions.  I felt as if I was having various new cats thrown at me constantly and noticed that the description of the cats in my journal did not always pop up upon their introductions.  Sometimes I would have to wait until after the level had finished to read about them.  Having a notice popup upon each cat's arrival might have been more useful.
- The inability to return to the certain areas in the last level(s).  Do not head past the Dark Room or you will have to replay the entire game to get the achievements.

The short: reverse Angry Birds. I found the gameplay to be quite fun.
The long: a charming and entertaining little game. You construct a physics-based pillow fort out of varrious house-hold items to defend yourself against waves of relentless cats. There is a wide varriety of construction matterials, all of which varry in shape, size, and armor/health, and many of which have added bonuses or abilities, such as the Lamp, which reduces damage done to materials next to it, or the Pot of Catnip, which magneticly draws cats to it, redirecting them from more fragile targets.
The cats attacking you are likewise varried, which adds to the strategy. When you have limited resourses, do you fortify the sides against the bull-rushing melon cats, or do you invest in bubble machines to defend against the incoming tiny cat swarm? How do you organize your fort when you want to reserve your beanbag chair to nullify the Fat Cat, when there's a wave of Regular cats thinning your defenses before it will arrive?
The story is short, nothing amazing, but cute.
The price is right for this short but clever and quirky little game.

There are very few video games that can be called "Art" and much less deserving to be recognized as masterpiece. SOMA is clearly one of them.

I will not spoil your experience, but this thought-provoking sci-fi drama will walk you through the deepest corners of consciousness making you questioning the nature of your own Self and reality.
If you are looking for a dark meditative experience stimulating self-exploration and philosophizing - this game is 100% for you. In contrast, avoid it if you are looking for an action-focused horror like DeadSpace. For me, that was the first time when playing a video game felt like reading Dostoevsky..

The game seems to be trying to show the realism of war, the bleakness- as the colour palette shows. But the game mechanics prevent it from doing this. Lack of health packs means lack of tension, ammo can be gotten from team mates so the fact that you have limited ammo in your weapons is a bit of an illusion. At many points during the game the music will just stop. One example is during a mission as a character you’ve never played before, you and your three (every level is you and 3 invulnerable team-mates) holding off against waves of insurgents. There’s no music to provide realism and tension! Except there is no tension, the enemies come at you from the same paths again and again, I’ve been playing this character for about 20 minutes, why should I care if he lives or dies. MAKE ME CARE GAME. If the game is relying on the fact that it’s based on real-life events to make me care about the characters then it’s sorely mistaken. The game’s mechanics of what is essentially unlimited ammo, team-mates that absorb whole clips of both enemy and friendly fire, incredibly stupid AI, bullet spongy enemies, extreme linearity and oh much more mean that it cannot in all fairness successfully convey real-life situations and make me feel the horrors of war. Either you go the ARMA route where one bullet can kill you, where the realism of warfare is far more apparent than MoH or you go the CoD route of arcade mayhem while conveying emotions through storytelling. Medal of honour is an absolute mess.
The game is disjointed, horribly disjointed. The story is only carried by the cinematics which bookend levels, if your players need the cinematics to follow the story/care about what is going on then you’ve failed at FPS storytelling. Every few levels you change character, moving from special forces to simply infantry. That’s fine in and of itself, but I actually became slightly disorientated, if you skip the cinematic it can take a few minutes to work out who you are playing as based on your location and team members. Not that you can give any orders to your team mates, even medal of honour European assault let you do that. They just follow scripted events and bark orders at you. The game has predictable scripted sequences that even Activision would laugh at. You see all the Call of duty references? That’s because it’s so ♥♥♥♥ing clear that MoH is EA’ response to call of duty. Now in 2013 it’s obvious that they’ve focused on Battlefield as their counter to CoD, even though the games are very different (multiplayer wise) single player wise they’re both a boring as one another.  But of course, it’s the multiplayer component that sells both games.
Medal of Honor lacks colour, which is part of this aim at ‘realism’- though in the sense of feeling not in gameplay. Its so boring and depressing, which sums up MoH. Not depressing because of its focus on real-life events or questioning the legality and morality of what the soldiers are actually fighting for (which would actually make an interesting twist to modern military shooters) but because it shows complete and utter disregard for originality and the medal of honour franchise. The lack of a HUD reiterates part of this  ‘realistic approach’, yet in a game where you cans till take a handful of bullets before dying it seems like a bit of useless attempt at getting across whatever message about war Danger close are trying to convey.
Forget about the series being set in ww2, even if MoH were set in the second world war, itd still be ♥♥♥♥ing boring. The guns feel boring, and the enemies are not interesting in the slightest. They’re just Nazis in middle-eastern garb. By that I mean they have no character outside of them being EVIL. We don’t see anything that makes us question why we are killing hundreds of these guys, it’s like the game just paints the word TERRORIST in great big letters on their heads. That’s all the motivation we need apparently. Maybe that’s a joke at how soldiers have to remove those thoughts from their heads in order to do their job properly. Or it’s just lazy storytelling, you pick.
Graphically this game looks about 3 years older than it should. 2011 was only a year away which would herald the use of the frostbite 2 engine. Even battlefield bad company 2 looked far superior to Medal of honour and that came out the same bloody year. The only decent textures are on people’s faces, everything else oozes muddy brown pixels. I’d argue that this is due to an attempt at making a console beating CoD killer, but EA must have been utterly delusional to think that. If CoD gets complaints for being stale then MoH is a loaf of bread left behind two biscuit tins for 4 years, dusted off and then put in shiny packaging to sell to people who only want call of duty clones. Not that it can even be called a clone; the changes it does make (aside from the MoH ability to lean around cover) make the game into a boring mess. Oh and the bugs, these mainly revolve around the AI and the ragdoll/physics effects, at least they make me laugh I guess, something in this game has to.
The studio behind this game have an interesting history, as EA Los Angeles they created the battle for middle earth games, all MoH games from Frontline and created both red alert 3 and the terrible ending to Command & Conquer, tiberian twilight. A history of some great and some terrible games. Rebranded as ‘Danger Close’ the studio made the two modern Medal of Honour games, the last of which has been classed as a franchise killer. Now EA have rebranded the studio yet again as DICE Los Angeles, and set them to work on the extremely anticipated game, Battlefront 3. I really hope danger close rethink their fps game design. Clearly modern military shooters were not a genre the studio was good at, taking tons of tropes and clichés, covering it in cardboard and serving it on a grey plate in a grey room for grey people to sit and eat while they laugh at re-runs of Miranda.
That all said, Battlefront 3 is being designed by the DICE team behind Battlefield, so hopefully Danger Close, I mean DICE LA, won’t be able to suck the life out of this one.

SOMA is Frictional Games newest fear fest. Being the developer who created Amnesia, which essentially defined the “hide and seek” gameplay, they have some pretty big shoes to fill. Especially after the second Amnesia, A Machine for Pigs, was not received as well.
SOMA takes place in an underwater science facility called PATHOS-2, and man, it’s f*&$ing gorgeous! The atmosphere has a perfect mixture of both horror and wonder. Wondering the dark underwater tunnels was extremely immersive for me and although I was pretty on edge for the duration of my play, I was still compelled to explore the environment around me. Putting aside the fact that you have to look around anyway to solve most puzzles. Which is another reason I liked it, SOMA does not hold your hand unless you ask for it.  Although, the puzzles themselves were a bit easy, you still have to figure your way around. Often resulting in some frantic chase sequences when the monster appears! The sound alone when this thing is around you is terrifying in its own right. The guys at Frictional put a tremendous effort in the quality of sound in this game. Playing without a good headset would be a crime, missing all the little creeks and bumps going on everywhere around you. Although, the voice acting could use a bit of work honestly but the story and what’s being conveyed more than makes up for it. The story is the best part of the game yet. It’s refreshing finding a game with such amazing and thought provoking story. I honestly would’ve called this a perfect game if not for the voice acting and some issues with the A.I. There’s nothing worse in a horror game that can happen other than when the monster is no longer a threating. As we learned in Slender (whomp whomp), this can happen when the monster’s A.I. gets STUCK. This happened to me twice and the weird thing was it was in the strangest places. There wasn’t a box in front of them or some kind of tricky object, sometimes it just looked like they were stuck on some clipping from walls! I was confused at first, even to the point where I was throwing objects at them, hoping they would snap out of it or something, but nope…I could just move on without impediment.
TL;DR All in all, the game is awesome. I think it’s safe to say that Frictional Games was able to meet the huge standard from their previous games. Although there were some minor complaints, some may not even experience the same issues. It’s seriously not too often a game has so little downside. With a 30 USD price tag, this game is definitely worth buying. Out of 10, I’d give this an easy 9.

Let me be clear - I preordered this game at Babbages in 2001 (unlike the famous Slash000 example, GameStop did not honor my preorder reciept).  So I did start the game with a bit of a bad taste in my mouth.
Yes, you can point to the original 2-weapons limite (later patched to 4), the confused design, the odd linearity, the dated graphics, the vehicle sections, and objectively you have what could be called a bad game, or mediocre at best.
However, within that mediocre game, there are still gasps of greatness.  The shrunk-down levels, particularly at Duke Burger, and unique and incredibly fun.  The vehicle sections, while not the most engaging, are sill playable.  And the first one, again shrunk down and driving an R/C car, is downright creative.  The shooting is solid, with the feel of the original Duke3D weapons maintained well throughout.  The nods to the history of the series are executed in the perfect tongue-in-cheek style.  And the Ego health system, while evocative of the Halo shield system, is still a stroke of genius.
And the there's Duke.  While some may take issue with Duke getting out of breath after short sprints, or the fact that he clearly has laid off the roids since he can no longer carry the entire National Guard armory with him, it doesn't matter.  Duke Talk is still voiced by the incredible Jon St. John, and while many of the references are dated, they are dated to a time period that the target audience for the game will remember.  While the line "I'm your huckleberry." won't be a reference many millenials will get, it still made me laugh out loud (possibly becuase I had watched Tombstone a scant few weeks before I played DNF).
It isn't a masterpiece, but in my opinion, neither was Duke3D.  Duke3D had the virtue of being the first mainstream shooter with a real protagonist, and with adult content.  The subsequent Build Engine games were better shooters (Blood and Shadow Warrior come to mind), the concurrent id titles were both mechanically better, and once Quake came out, graphically lightyears better, but Duke was the first of a new genre.  He made a strong protagonist in shooters a "thing", for better or for worse.
For me, it was worth paying for the game twice - once as a preorder, and again on Steam, just for the positives I've mentioned, and for nostalgia.
If you didn't play classic Duke3D at an impressionable age, it isn't likely going to be for you.  If you are expecting purely classic shooter gunplay, it isn't for you (the concessions to modernity are to pervasive).
But, if you are looking for a healthy does of 'memberberries bringing you back to the mid-90s, pick it up on sale.

Let me get this straight ahead and confirm that the wait for SOMA was, 100%, well-worth it. Frictional delivers yet another masterpiece. I even dare say they followed the saying: ''There's always room for more.'', after their fantastic Amnesia series.
What we got from them here is one of those existential questioning games... combine that with horror, well-suited atmosphere,
sound effects and you get a memorable gem.
SOMA has less enemy encounters than Amnesia, but I say it's for a good cause. What it lacks in terms of monsters, it completely delivers with the story. I'd say they got the perfect balance between hiding and actual advancing through the events. More encounters would have made me forget about the plot and it would have gotten unimmersive.
But when there is a monster showing around, expect it to be a challenging part. No more hiding in a corner and waiting for it to leave as in previous games, as SOMA's creatures are not just randomly going away after a while. They'll stay in your path and you have to carefully progress through the chambers and remember the map, in order to get away safe and sound.
I did mention this is more of an existentional questioning game. I can't dig deeper into details on this one as it would all lead to story-breaking spoilers. Heck, even the premise of it is a spoiler. All I can say is that it successfully made me question what it is to be a human and what distinguishes us from artificial intelligences --robots-- .
What I also loved about it was its length. 13 hours to finish an indie game is nothing short of amazing and I didn't even stay to read all notes and journals. I'll definitely give this game a second playthrough.
The inventory has been massively simplified since Amnesia and the sanity/health system is also changed. Looking at some monsters for too long will give away your position and health can be restored at healing places throughout the journey.
Technically speaking, the game suffers from a poor optimization. I was getting massive frame drops in some places. Visually it does not excel either. But I can get past these issues coming from a small company. On the other side, I haven't encountered many bugs nor grammatical errors and kudos to the developers for taking their time and patching up their game!
*End-game debate incoming (definitely spoilers ahead); please skip to next paragraph for general personal rating if you haven't completed the game yet.*
The feeling that was following me up to the very end was one of déjà vu. There is another game out there that raised the exact same questioning:
+ Excellent plot and an overall amazing storyline. The journey that the player takes from the beginning to the end never ceased to amaze me.
+ Incredible sound effects. Not just one time have I thought some environment sounds are actually coming from my room.
+ Perfect mix of horror and story telling.
+ Impressively long while still maintaining to not get boring.
+ Great puzzles that add to the core, just like in the Amnesia series.
+ The atmosphere perfectly blends in.
+ The voice acting is also well-crafted.
+ More types of monsters with different behaviors. They also have some great sound effects implemented, you will hear them if they're wandering on a nearby corridor or if they have detected you.
+ Overall balanced difficulty. Does not make the player replay the same area countless of times due to dying, but is also thought as to not be rushed through with ease.
+ Does continue Frictional's unique horror style.
+/- Different system of health and sanity, like shortly described above. Some players may welcome the changes with open arms, while others may dislike it compared to the old one from Amnesia: The Dark Descent.
+/- Depending on everyone's tastes, I suppose the game suffers from a lack of replayability.
+/- Enemy AI. They're not brainless, but nothing amazing about their thinking either.
- Poor optimization... may encounter frame drops, stutter and even freezes in some areas, even while lowering the settings.
- Infinite battery flashlight. A similar system to the one from older Frictional titles would also suit SOMA better in my opinion and would add to the difficulty.
- Uhm... where's the enemy robots? I was disappointed to only encounter the big machines with flashlights 2 or 3 times and only in the first quarter of the game... They were some great enemies in my opinion and would have surely also suited some other areas.
- Can get extremely frustrating to cope with the visual screen tearing while the monster is chasing you. Later on in the game, you're almost always getting caught by it if he sees you, anyway.
SOMA is a must for anyone that loved Frictional's other games. For the others, this is a great decision if you're looking for a thrilling story with scary elements and atmosphere. I definitely not regret pre-ordering this one and I want to thank the developers for bringing in another masterpiece to Steam.

This is a fun platformer game with an incredible gameplay idea. You gain powers, each power being a different colour. Blue for example can make things slide/go faster, like ice. There are many colours, and the combinations provide for interesting answers to how you must progress throughout stages. There are enemies that are quite tricky to avoid, plus the void from which the protagonist was born will chase after you at the last level of every stage.
Apart from the gameplay, the narration is great, and many of the music tracks are wonderful as well. The enemy design is high quality as well, though some of the background art could be better.
The main story is just challenging enough to keep you interested, but after you're done, the Void Mode unlocks and it's.... so tough! I'll probably spend the next two years trying to finish it.
All in all, this is a really interesting game, though if you don't think you're going to bother with the Void Mode, it might be better to wait for a sale since the main game is about 3 hours long.

Nihilumbra is a sidescrolling puzzle game like many.
The game has beautiful scenery for its own, and the gameplay is good.
At first the main story of Nihilumbra tricks you into thinking the game is easy, as the main story is basically a tutorial.
Once you finish the story, you have the option to replay every level from the start, only with new challenges, and these challenges are actually quite difficult compared to the plain story.
I recommend the game, as the narration is great, and the gameplay is fun, and surprisingly challenging once you get to a certain point.

The graphics are excellent and the gameplay is great (so long as you like frantic and short), and replayability is the whole point. The soundtrack is neither bad nor inspiring.
So why the "Not Recommended"?
What there is of this game is good, but I can't help but to think that other developers must be looking at it and thinking, "Wait, people will review a game this well even though it's basically one scenario, without a campaign, over and over again, as long as that one scenario is *really* well polished?"
There just isn't enough game here to warrant a recommendation, especially not for $40. I think I paid $20 for it. It would be a good game a $9.99.
The game is not even very deep, contrary to what others have said. You get whatever your specific group needs to grow, and then you get whatever is rare, and you win. That's every single playthrough, each of which takes maybe 20 minutes. There is no story, no campaign, no reason to play any more than a few matches as each faction, which I have already done in a whopping 17 hours (according to Steam). This is technically a strategy game, but, since each playthrough starts from nothing, plays frantically, and ends quickly, it plays almost more like a board game with good graphics. It feels more like a mini-game from a AAA title than a game in and of itself.
On the plus side, I swear that's Jeffrey Combs (Weyoun from Star Trek Deep Space Nine, among other things) doing the various announcements, so there is that.

The colony provides us everything except for violence.
The game’s tagline is a fitting one, since this title provides nothing but violence in wholesome abundance. To put in summary, Ubermosh is a fast pace, bullet hell game, in which you must survive for as long as possible and compete for a high score.
A typical session of play would last between 10 to 90 seconds, though more likely than not, you will experience a short life of less than 30. This is by no means bad, since you are pump and psyched to abort, retry and fail; over and over again. The mechanics is simple, as a rookie gladiator you must utilise your sword to slice bullets that are fired your way, that or dodge to avoid your demise.
Any creatures you kill in the Mosh Pit will drop their gun, with which there are 4 variants to pick from. While they might function in similar ways, the firing rate and spread pattern are different, so you must learn and adapt according to different situations. Turtling can be a good tactic, but you also unwittingly minimised your encounters with foes, thus limiting your end score. Run and Gun might work better score wise, but you run the chance of dying early. The game rewards you well in weighting the risks and taking the gambit accordingly.
Music was another aspect of the game done well, sporting a soundtrack over 30 minutes long, it accentuates the chaotic action to a new height. You will be motivated to survive longer, for each subsequent round, just so you can hear the track go further beyond. While I don’t normally buy game soundtracks on Steam, this is one of the rare occasions which I did, with no regrets.
The weakest department of this title, arguably, would be the story. Let’s be honest, the lore is practically nonexistent here, though for an arcade game, it didn’t need an extensive one. In another way, the lack thereof plays to the favour of this game by remaining vague. As each sequel in the series contain a tag line with which the plot advances slightly, while revealing little in the progress.
For conclusion, if you are new to the series and don’t mind spending a few dollars, I would say get it all in chronological order (or in a bundle). Though if you are really strapped for cash, just get the latest release of the series instead, since you aren’t missing much besides minor changes in mechanics and game modes.

If you like being a knight and fight vikings and samurais, or the other way around, this might be the game for you.
The combat system is intense, where fast reflexes are needed at times. The simple idea of attacking and defending three different directions is quite a thriller. Add guard breaking, parrying, dodging and feinting, and we now have ourselves a hand sweating gladiator match. However simple reflexes are not the only way to reign supreme over your foes. Learning each character's capabilities and weakness ca give you the upper hand, as you exploit your opponent's weaknesses while figuring out ways to cover up your own.
The Online, unfortunately has some clear cons for a fighting game that requires good reflexes. First of all I had to go through multiple sequences such as port forwarding and firewall tweaking just to be able to join a game, which can leave a pretty bad impression for those who just bought the game for 60 dollars. Hopefully this is changed soon in an upcoming patch.
Story Mode is pretty ordinary for a game where PVP is the main content. Its not exactly a tutorial for all of the characters, and each mission doesn't offer too much variety, although the big duels you sometimes have are definitely atmospheric. Not much wows or boos, other than knowing that your character can one day become fancy as the characters you meet in the story mode.
The online multiplay system itself is one of my favorite parts of this game. A pretty nice character customization screen, plenty of quests to gain ingame currency and exp to level up your favorite character, an interesting reward system where winning doesn't directly give you more ingame currency or exp, but by playing the factions of war mini game you gain better loot by the end of the season. More wins mean you participate in your faction's victory, which equals better end season rewards. Lastly, it is not pay to win. This is a personal thing, but I had a lot of times where I just couldn't continue playing because you had to keep up by paying real money. You don't have to pour cash just to be viable or dress up your character in the perfect look. However you do have the option to buy ingame currency to make your character sparkle. It is your choice.
Overall, this game does have flaws, and pretty big ones too. However I myself am having a lot of fun, and I hadn't had a lot of games where I felt like I would continue on in a while. If the 60 dollar price seems a bit high, well maybe you can wait for a sale later on. Maybe first try it out if your friend bought it. There is very little to lose for not being a first day gamer, other than some color schemes for your character. However there seems to be a lot more promising content coming in the future updates.

I have very mixed feelings about the game. On one side, its atmosphere is great, on the other side, it's a giant piece of junk.
Let's sum this objectively up:
Another game that jumps upon the high popular
-bandwagon with a name that makes me think of Minecraft. My first thoughts when I filtered the informations I had about this game together were rather negative.
After quite a long time since the game was available on steam (In the also very currently very popular early-access-model) I wanted to try it out so I bought it to see for myself if this was just another ridiculous excuse for a video game like former WarZ (which is now found under a name like Infestation - Survivor stories, but is still the same old garbage) or actually something decent.
Here I want to add that I had some problems even getting the game to run properly. I saw other people complaining about the problem on the forums before, but I just thought that they were too dumb to simply install the game or were simply a bunch of whiny kids who bought the game with a credit card stolen from daddy and tried installing it on the very sames computer. Long story short - If you buy the game over steam, calculate some hours or maybe even a Day into your plan of when you can play the game. Once someone of the mods or devs took care about the login problem (took
some hours) I managed to get into the game.
Nether features a rather big map, PVP and PVE like you would know it from the other Apocalypse-Zombie-Mutant bandwagon games. The graphics are good when your system can run the game on full specs. This along with the good sound and ambient effects creates a unique atmosphere.
Everything is a horrible chaos. Now I know that the
counter arguement for this is always the same sentence, no matter on which game.
But the fact that many stuff is still work in progress doesn't even bug me. The city consists of tons of cloned towers or gas stations that all look the same on every level? Doesn't bug me much. The northern wasteland or swamp islands are buggy as hell? Doesn't bug me either, theres tons of good loot out there.
But the
of the game gives me negative feelings. The important "base frames" of the game, the mechanisms and implemented things.
Let me be more specific about this.
The safezones all look like some impatient and stressed out modder created them as a fan mod for the game Killing Floor. Botchy NPC models placed into some patched up buildings surrounded with walls and with some colourful advertising signs.
I enter "Vlads weaponsmith-store" and see some careless made up player model with an eyepatch on which I can open up some even more uncompassionate created trading dialoge.
" 1 PISTOL GRIP + 1 9MM FRAME = 1x9mm PISTOL"
No♥♥♥♥♥♥ sherlock. I know games that are more than 10 years old that have better trading dialogs than this one. And making those run smooth and look sizeable isn't more work than implementing ridiuclous weapons in the game.
Which is where I'm going to complain about next, the weapons and items.
The role model for all the weapons in game is probably Call of Duty and Counter Strike. You find Desert Eagles, Spas 12 Shotguns, silenced UMP 45's or military machineguns with red dot sights basically around every corner. Of course all of them are in perfect condition and some even have funny smileys or colourful camouflage on them.
Now call me an Elitist ♥♥♥♥♥♥, but this kinda stuff pisses me off. Well, then please write "Open World Zombie Death Match" into the games description and don't tell me stories and show me rendered trailers about some Apocalypse and world ending scenario.

The developers (Pyro Studios) certainly won't be accused of producing a AAA title here, but if you can dismiss the limited aesthetics, it will reward your time with a lot of historical flavor and enjoyment.
Get it on sale for $10.00 or less, and it's worth adding "just one more game" to your library, and you may just find yourself playing "just one more turn".

Fort Meow is a somewhat short physics based pillowfort simulator. In this game you follow Nia as she unravels the secrets of her grandparents sudden disappearance and why there are so many cats around...And why they're so clingy!
You begin the game building a basic fortress from chairs and brooms, and eventually you have an entire house worth of furniture in there, all ready to ward off the cats who keep trying to interupt your quest to figure out what Nia's grandpa wrote in his journal the days shortly before this all.
Once you have lasted a few waves, you will be able to go through the house and take more items with you to build. Some may be more your playstyle than others, and some may appear to be amazing but in effect are less so, and you can be surprised by the usefulness of an item you thought you would probably never use more than once to see it in action.
The game has a gradual learning curve that feels neither too fast nor too slow, and allows you plenty of freedom in designing and building your fortress. The story is well made(Don't expect a grand literary masterpiece though),  and the art style consistent.
Of course, no game is without downsides, but Fort Meow is a well-rounded game with the obvious downside of its length. It's a short game, as you can likely see from the time played in both this review and other reviews, and one thing that could be both good and bad was the physics in use. You can not perfectly stack up everything and count incoming cats. For some this may feel random, but personally I found it nice to see that you could not just turn it into a math equation and solve it before playing. For your fort to be succesfull, you need more than just theory. You need to have it made in a way that it still works if things -don't- go as planned.
In the end, Fort Meow is a good, if somewhat short game that offers you a few hours which are entertaining, easy to play, and rewarding to finish.

The campaign is a strange beast, torn between an earnest attempt to render the tedium and dispassionate remove that color modern warfare, and the Hollywood bombast that colors Modern Warfare a la Call of Duty.
Arma III uses the full keyboard for its array of possible actions, split between personal affairs like toggling flashlights and binoculars, and issuing orders to your squad. Much of the heavy lifting is foisted on the mousewheel, of all things, which scrolls through contextual actions for almost anything that's to be done in the game. The controls alternate between instrumental and overly finicky, but they never cease to be an aspect of Arma III that requires constant attention. The unwieldiness does lend combat a certain gravitas, however. Most modern shooters grant an athletic flourish to the act of killing; here, the satisfaction of downing an enemy comes from the knowledge that he won't be shooting at you anymore, not in how adroitly you head-shotted him.
So, keep update Bohemia!

This review covers Hacker Evolution and its expansion, Hacker Evolution: Reinsertion, which is included with the base game. From the very beginning, as you start the tutorial, you realize that Hacker Evolution is all about the command-line interface. This has its pros and cons, but fortunately, it all comes together quite well. Scrolling up and down in order to read through information that has since gone off the small window can be a little problematic and sometimes confusing, as you will be fishing for short lines of detailed text in order to perform various text commands. The music is constantly of the techno genre, but it is overall enjoyable after you get used to it. Being that this is the developer's first (as far as I know) effort in the hacking simulation genre, it is much more polished, much more user friendly, less cumbersome, and with far less flaws than Uplink in every way. This still means that the game play will be slow at times, and you will need to appreciate this type of game in order to enjoy it. The missions are interesting, challenging, and with personality. You actually believe that you are part of the short story in meaningful ways, and after completing each goal, there is a feeling of accomplishment and significance. The story progression makes sense and manages to remain interesting, as each level provides new challenges. Also, if you do not have enough funds at the end of each level, in conjunction with a high trace count, you will need to start the game over from the beginning, which is a very serious problem, in my opinion. If you are not careful from the very beginning, the game simply tells you "your fault, start over". Which I suppose means that it is an attempt to go along with the simulation aspect of the experience. It is trying to be as realistic as possible. All missions are exceptionally designed, and it is clear that the developer took great care and attention to detail to prepare all of them, in conjunction with the storyline. It is also valuable to point out that even though the amount of commands is limited, all missions have a different feel to them, and must be approached from different angles in order to succeed. It is amazing how much excitement is offered in this game as everything on screen is mostly text based, with the exception of the background graphic and mission briefings. It is the most engrossing and captivating hacking simulation game I have ever played, despite the fact that it does not have many competitors. The overall experience is fresh, fun, and with an absorbingly interesting atmosphere. It is a game that should be used as the prime example and inspiration for what all future hacking simulation games should be and must be.

Let me get this straight ahead and confirm that the wait for SOMA was, 100%, well-worth it. Frictional delivers yet another masterpiece. I even dare say they followed the saying: ''There's always room for more.'', after their fantastic Amnesia series.
What we got from them here is one of those existential questioning games... combine that with horror, well-suited atmosphere,
sound effects and you get a memorable gem.
SOMA has less enemy encounters than Amnesia, but I say it's for a good cause. What it lacks in terms of monsters, it completely delivers with the story. I'd say they got the perfect balance between hiding and actual advancing through the events. More encounters would have made me forget about the plot and it would have gotten unimmersive.
But when there is a monster showing around, expect it to be a challenging part. No more hiding in a corner and waiting for it to leave as in previous games, as SOMA's creatures are not just randomly going away after a while. They'll stay in your path and you have to carefully progress through the chambers and remember the map, in order to get away safe and sound.
I did mention this is more of an existentional questioning game. I can't dig deeper into details on this one as it would all lead to story-breaking spoilers. Heck, even the premise of it is a spoiler. All I can say is that it successfully made me question what it is to be a human and what distinguishes us from artificial intelligences --robots-- .
What I also loved about it was its length. 13 hours to finish an indie game is nothing short of amazing and I didn't even stay to read all notes and journals. I'll definitely give this game a second playthrough.
The inventory has been massively simplified since Amnesia and the sanity/health system is also changed. Looking at some monsters for too long will give away your position and health can be restored at healing places throughout the journey.
Technically speaking, the game suffers from a poor optimization. I was getting massive frame drops in some places. Visually it does not excel either. But I can get past these issues coming from a small company. On the other side, I haven't encountered many bugs nor grammatical errors and kudos to the developers for taking their time and patching up their game!
*End-game debate incoming (definitely spoilers ahead); please skip to next paragraph for general personal rating if you haven't completed the game yet.*
The feeling that was following me up to the very end was one of déjà vu. There is another game out there that raised the exact same questioning:
+ Excellent plot and an overall amazing storyline. The journey that the player takes from the beginning to the end never ceased to amaze me.
+ Incredible sound effects. Not just one time have I thought some environment sounds are actually coming from my room.
+ Perfect mix of horror and story telling.
+ Impressively long while still maintaining to not get boring.
+ Great puzzles that add to the core, just like in the Amnesia series.
+ The atmosphere perfectly blends in.
+ The voice acting is also well-crafted.
+ More types of monsters with different behaviors. They also have some great sound effects implemented, you will hear them if they're wandering on a nearby corridor or if they have detected you.
+ Overall balanced difficulty. Does not make the player replay the same area countless of times due to dying, but is also thought as to not be rushed through with ease.
+ Does continue Frictional's unique horror style.
+/- Different system of health and sanity, like shortly described above. Some players may welcome the changes with open arms, while others may dislike it compared to the old one from Amnesia: The Dark Descent.
+/- Depending on everyone's tastes, I suppose the game suffers from a lack of replayability.
+/- Enemy AI. They're not brainless, but nothing amazing about their thinking either.
- Poor optimization... may encounter frame drops, stutter and even freezes in some areas, even while lowering the settings.
- Infinite battery flashlight. A similar system to the one from older Frictional titles would also suit SOMA better in my opinion and would add to the difficulty.
- Uhm... where's the enemy robots? I was disappointed to only encounter the big machines with flashlights 2 or 3 times and only in the first quarter of the game... They were some great enemies in my opinion and would have surely also suited some other areas.
- Can get extremely frustrating to cope with the visual screen tearing while the monster is chasing you. Later on in the game, you're almost always getting caught by it if he sees you, anyway.
SOMA is a must for anyone that loved Frictional's other games. For the others, this is a great decision if you're looking for a thrilling story with scary elements and atmosphere. I definitely not regret pre-ordering this one and I want to thank the developers for bringing in another masterpiece to Steam.

Since the MoH-series is sort of a big brand, I was expecting a somewhat decent shooter and started out playing it with an open mind. The game is 3 years old when I got it via the Humble Bundle. I was SOOO wrong. In fact I will rate this game as the perfect example of how a company can screw up when they release a single player game on steam.
It starts out even before you get to play.
First you need to sign in to an EA-account to play... and then you need to enter the serial code for the game.
Entering the serial is a pain in the unmentionable because the game only lets you type, no cut'n'paste from the clipboard. AND to view the code you need to ALT-TAB between the game and Steam.
So what do you get for doing this? Nothing. It's not like the game saves your progress online or anything. The only reason for doing this is that EA now ties the game to your EA account as a form of DRM. This means that you can't sell the game to someone else.
Sell it? Wait? That was already impossible in the first place, since this is a Steam, right?
Yes, all the pain you just went through to find your EA account details, enter the key was for nothing.
It does not end here though.
In case you want to reformat your pc or delete the game, you must remember to deauthorize the game. If you don't you'll some day end up having spent all "your installations" and the game will simply sit in your Steam library as a game you can install, but never get to play.
This is again EA's stupid extra DRM. They should have removed this for the Steam version but probably didn't bother because it would cost them a few hours of programmer wages.
Then finally you get to the game.
I remember back in 2010 when I didn't buy the game. There was something fishy about it. The SP was being developed by another team on another platform... Surely this was being done because "every game needs a single player campaign" and the result clearly shows. You don't need to play for more than a few minutes to realize that this game was made to make a quick buck, not to become the best game ever... or anything.
The first impression is... hmmm...were graphics that bad back in 2010?
Overall things look fine, but you'll find: repeated textures, flat looking tekstures mashed in between fine bumpmapped textured... and every single hut in the game looks exactly the same. If it wasn't for the high detail in textures this game could belong in 2003.
Level design is extremely bad, even for it's time:
Blind pathways that block you off with invisible walls are all over.
Some objects "have physics" while the same looking object, just next to it, does not.
The entire map is clearly small, but twisted paths are supposed to make you feel like the area is huge. This joke is obvious in one of the first levels where you ride a quad bike. The quad is there because you have to go far, and the tutorial text tells you that you can powerslide and everything. But there is nothing to do at all. The "fun freeroaming desert ride" that this is supposed to look like, is just as much fun as a kiddie train going in circles. You can't drive off the road, and there is no reason what so ever to use the powerslide. You simply drive behind some other dude who is magically driving just as fast as you all the time.
I have difficulty in comparing this to any other game or time. MoH is simply the prime example of a shooter on rails. I have never seen a game with such a little possibility of choice.(And I've played FPS's since they showed up the mid 90'es. )
Bugs and design errors:
You don't need to play for more than a few minutes to realize that this game was never properly tested.
The game was properly designed to give sort of "the real soldier expericence". And it sort of does that. The HUD is not really doing anything, and you need to listen to what your teammates say. They tend to talk a lot of army lingo and between all this you can somehow figure out what to do. If you miss any of it you're in big trouble.
Some times the HUD will help you, but at other times you will spend some time jumping around the completely empty enemy base, back to your teammates etc. just to find that magic spot that will spawn the next bit of script and bring life to the base.
Your mates do not help. It's not like you can go to them and they will tell you what to do, again. They will just stand completely still in a catatonic state, and wait for you to do the right thing. For me this usually meant ending their miserable lives and in this way restarting the mission at the last checkpoint due to friendly fire.
Conclusion:
I can see why some people might like the game. There is some sort of dark theme over it, that probably makes is more real than many other shooters... however it's simply so badly executed that it's impossible to play the game without becoming mad at it. I've played it for 3 hours, and this is the first game ever that I'm going to CHOSE not to play to the end, simply because it's not worth it.

Somewhere between all the YouTube wecams and mindless fans blindly praising Amnesia, is a game that I don't think quite lives up to the hype as the "scariest game of all time," but is still pretty damn good.
As we all know, the game takes place in a deserted castle and you play as Daniel, a man who awakes with amnesia. As you wander around the castle for the next few hours, you'll learn about the history of both the castle and it's caretaker, and Daniel's intentions for being there. The game is excellent at building tension and atmosphere, you will hold your breath many times while walking the halls of the castle.
The gameplay is where some of the problems begin to arise. I just found the game to be a little too forgiving. The tinderbox system is pretty much broken; I had a ridiculous number of them at the end of the game, somewhere in the 20s. The sanity meter is interesting enough, but I never really felt threatened if it got to a high level. If the meter gets too high, Daniel will pass out and awake after a few seconds. This happened once or twice during my playthrough, but nothing seemed to change afterwards. However, the absolute worst aspect is the enemy AI; Once you figure out the secret of their pathfinding and realize that they only stick to certain areas, the game becomes a breeze, and all feelings of horror and fear are lost. The puzzles aren't very tricky, but I did have to look up where to go once (I had to stack boxes because there was a hatch on a cieling... go figure).
So while Amnesia does capture a constant feeling of dread, you can only be as scared from the game as you want to be. It makes no attempt to hide that it is in fact, just a game.
Do I recommend Amnesia: The Dark Descent? Yes, to every horror fan. Old school horror fanatics will be pleased by this treat, and younger fans will scream at their Twitch followers.

Amnesia made us afraid of water.
SOMA put us under the sea.
Thanks Frictional.
-SPOILERS-
First things first, this was an amazing game. A round of applause for the crew at Frictional. They made this game worth waiting for and it was everything I hoped and so much more.
I approached this game as if it were Amnesia, I tried to play this as if it were Amnesia. We might be lacking a sanity meter and inventory but that does not take away from the game. Do not let yourself think this is AAMFP either. You can't play this game like Amnesia, the enemies are different, more intelligent, and do not despawn. There is so much to say about this game it's even hard for myself to put it into words.
Simon is a treasure. That's put simply. As much as it hurts me to admit it, Simon is now my newest favorite Frictional protag. He is the only being who can come off as an actual human compared to the rest of the cast. So out of place and confused, much like the player themself playing for the first time. Simon thinks about the things others do not want to. Where does he belong? He cannot go back to being that man who lived a simple life in Toronto a rough hundred years ago. By the time we reach our destination, Simon wants to feel that belonging, that heaven, the ARK. Somewhere he can rest easy and be who he is. Sadly only a copy of him can feel that.
I did not expect such a diverse cast of enemies, all of which have unique features and abilities that makes them all different. It's difficult to even choose which enemy was the best. All were placed in enviroments they could best showcase their talents. Now I expected no mercy from these enemies such as the ones from Penumbra and Amnesia who would attack until we safely hid/killed them/died. I was quite shocked upon blacking out the first time from the robot at Upsilon. This blacking out feature added a few method to the game when moving around the enemies.
Now as for downsides, I loved the game but I feel like we could have benefited more from interaction with the WAU and Simon's girlfriend. The WAU was everywhere we went but I wanted more interaction with it, that might just be because I was playing the game for the campaign and not the backstory. As for Simon's girlfriend, she was viewed in game twice and I thought the would play a bigger part in the campaign or have some lurking presence. However that does not take away from the atmosphere the game already gives off.
Frictonal redeemed themselves from AAMFP (even though they might not have developed it), SOMA revived their trademark scares with a whole new way. This game deserves so much more attention and less hesitation from gamers who played previous games. Frictional spent the last five years on this and it was very well worth the wait.
Thank you, Frictional. You guys made another memorable game which will stay with me for years to come much like Prenumbra and Amnesia have done before. You guys know not only how to scare me but to break my heart and make me think about life itself. Very much like Simon himself. This game will make you think much like how they want you to. Are you really alone in this world?

Whether KOTOR II is better than KOTOR I is a matter of preference. Personally, I prefer KOTOR I due to better story and companions.
KOTOR II added a few new features such as creating and breaking down item, more force powers and better use of cinematic cutscene. However, these new features could've been done better as most of the times, they are practically useless.
Remember how easy and fast players got their lightsabers in KOTOR I? Players had to wait for a longer time in KOTOR II to actually get a lightsaber.
Some of my complaints in KOTOR I remained in KOTOR II. Kreia tried to balance things out with the light and dark side but ultimately, you are either benevolent as f*ck or evil as sh*t. There's a few new force powers but still not enough useful powers. Items and equipment are still disappointing, even with more upgrade.
My main complaint is the difficulty spike and the main bosses. Most parts of the game is easy and the two main bosses are complete pushovers, while in some parts of the game, it's very hard due to the game separates players from it's companion. I had to rely on a bug to defeat the twin Twi'leks using Atton. And the last boss? Unfair is the word I'll use.
Speaking of companions, KOTOR II's companion are easily inferior to KOTOR I. Their characters aren't well fleshed out and it's hard for me to get attached to them. I loved HK-47 in KOTOR I but in KOTOR II, he's just... well, there. The only other character I had some attachment is Handmaiden but not enough for me to care for her.
Like I said, whether KOTOR II is better than KOTOR I is a matter of preference. I prefer KOTOR I. But it's still an enjoyable 2005 game.
RECOMMENDED       : KOTOR I fans
NOT RECOMMENDED: KOTOR I fans who wanted better story, companions and improved gameplay.

Ever Managed a company?
If the answer is yes, then this will seem familiar.
Dont get me wrong, its cartoonified and simplified, but its every bit as involved, with the management systems impeccably balanced between your own needs, your competitors needs and your balance sheet (as in real life).
This is not particularly easy, and the game means what it says for its difficulty levels. Most games I see recently have it set so that easy means brain-dead, medium means easy peesy, hard means youll need to think etc, not so OTC. Of the 5 levels to choose from the 3rd (Apprentice, i think)  is recommended for anyone who wants to graduate to online, and the game will truly try to win and challenge you. I lost my first 2-3 games on apprentice, but after you have picked up all the tricks (underground nuking their minable resources is my personal favourite) youll always have a fighting chance if you stay focused and flexible.
