What an absolutely fantastic game!
The premise is very simple: you are on Mars, you have a company, and you can mine/produce various resources as well as buy and sell them. Your goal is to buy all  of your competitiors (like a real world market aquisiton, you need 51% of their shares to control them).
And here is what makes this game so brilliant:
1) You have complete freedom over what you do - there are no compulsory buildings or anything of that sort, you can choose any strategy and even change it on the fly (glass is becoming too cheap? Then destroy all your glass production faciliteis and build electronics factories instead), so there is never a set path and you are always engaged
2) The free market that makes the game superdynamic. Let's say you've decided to produce chemicals and sell them on the market. But if everyone starts producing chemicals, then obviously there will be a surplus of them, the prices will go down and no one will be making any money! This makes you constantly think about what do you want to produce, what the competition are producing, what will be required in 5 minutes (if everyone will be upgrading and will need glass for it, but no one is producing it, then maybe you can do it right now - or simply buy it cheap now and sell at a much higher price later), and seek the most profitable endeavor on the market.
3) The factions - there are four of them, and they all play very differently. For example, the Scavengers use no steel, but carbon instead for their buildings. So, if there is just a little bit of carbon on the map, then you can easily organize a carbon monopoly! Or, let's say you believe steel is going to be very expensive in the game - than you can take the Scavengers, and avoid the much higher costs of building that everyone else will have.
All of them have their disctinct advantages and disadvantages, and you get to choose any of the four every game!
4) The abilities - you can buy them of the black market, and oh boy can they mess up the production!
The energy prices are high? EMP your opponent's solar panels, and he will have an insane debt from having to buy all the expenisve electricity
The Scavengers are doing very well? Underground nuke their carbon deposits, so that their productions falls almost two to three times and slow themm down
There are tons of abilities, and you can buy them as well as protection from them, and using them at the right moment can win you or lose the game
5)And, of course, the tension - it lasts till the absolute end and always keeps you on the toes, and makes each game very fun and engaging.
There are tons of other nuances and depth to the game, but you can find out most of it during your games, as this review would be way too long for it :)
Overall, it a an extremely dynamic and fun strategy game, and I would definitely recommend it to anyone!

"A DAYZ Killer" they said in the banner... well as much as I love DAYZ, I had to go research. A survival game the research showed! In a sprawling urban environment with tribes working to capture and hold parts of the city. Ok, so it looked like a more robust end game style, perfect! The videos and screens were of some sort of monsters that I could only guess were mutated zombies of some sort. Well... that'll teach me to do dive too quickly and not read further...
So I bought the game. First load in showed the city to be beautiful. A stark setting under a dark sky with strange sounds all around. I hestitantly walked forward 30 feet... bam... dead. Oh it looks like another survivor in this sprawling expanse found me and wanted my butter knife. Ok no prob... respawn... get two blocks and find an axe!! Perfect that wil... bam... dead from behind. Oh... ok. Respawn in the world... 1 minute later... bam... They sure do want their butter knives in this city. Ok so I will respawn in a "safezone". Spawn in... bam bam bam! Oh good, a tribe is camping the safezone during an event where the safezones are not...safezones. Ooookay.... So began the frustration. I did like the character leveling tree, but it's gone as soon as you get killed. Items seem cheesy when you run into them. If you have ever played DAYZ or few of the mods you'll see what I mean. Let me stand perfectly still while I hold the "E" button down to spend four seconds of actual time to pickup a... soda. That doesn't expose me at all in this "survival game".
And now the creatures... horrifying... kind of. Relatable? No... Sci-fi-ish? Yes... And that is how this game should have been marketed. They should have never mentioned DAYZ except for purely the money grab to get people all excited to buy it. The creatures are fairly decent models and have great sounds. They also teleport... yup that is right. Flashy light, poof, they are behind you, to your side, etc etc. In a first person game, that makes them a pretty decent threat. Ok... so I am new spawn with a butter knife, I know I can't take on some of these things. I'll run! The game does have a cool stamina bar that as you level your character (don't get killed!), can be beefed up. Problem... the creatures don't need to run. They watch you run like a fool, teleport to you and swing. Ouch... you keep running, they teleport again, poof, swing aaaaand your dead. And I tested it... it doesn't matter if you jump over things, try to lose them in a building, etc. They WILL find you. So that means no running. Ok I will swing with them with my butter knife! Boom health points start to drop on you rapidly. One or two confrontations and you are smoked. Creature mechanics... ='s bad.... especially when players are taking you out with a few swings of their melee weapons.
In game stores... this is kind of neat. An end of the world shop area where people trade you for things you find. Cigarettes etc. This makes it so you can get currency that allows you to buy a little better gear. Just don't get caught here when the safezone nether devices fail. Tribes camp people here... not creatures... why? Darned if I know...
In short folks, if you are COD/Battlefielder where you shoot everything on site, this may be a slight distraction.
So 6 hours later... here is the first impression
So for the scales: 1 worst, 10 best
Character Control: 7 (I liked the jumping, was fairly smooth, but dropped it a point due to not being able to side step when sprinting)
Weapons: 7 (when you can get them, they are fairly cool)
Graphics: 7 (dropped this due to the item graphics and flashing, makes for no real searching like in other games. Just run around looking for the flashes/glowing to find things to search)
Creature/NPC: 6 (superbad mechanics for newbies - other players are bad enough to deal with)
Leveling: 7 (I liked the idea of the tree leveling - but it lost it's flair when I realized how fast you lose it)
Crafting: 5 (interestingly enough you find pieces of things to piece together back at the safe zone. But holy heck... give me a weapon I can actually use seeing as a person can get killed every minute by creatures or players. Pick a low pop server at first folks if you want even a chance of trying this out!)
UI: 5 (rudimentary UI, with a decent map waypoint system. Horrible settings/config. It doesn't even show all the key bindings but will holler at you if you try to remap something that is already bound)
Ingame Chat/Voice: 4 (I never found a way to have a local/area chat so anything you say goes straight to global/largescale area. Better not plan a tribe take over in that! The voice chat was fairly horrible the few seconds I heard someone try it.)
Community: 1 (yup a 1... better bring some friends if you are serious about trying this)
Clan/Tribe Activity: 4 (you can take over area's of the city. I went to area's that said they were unclaimed and was told that I had to stand in a certain area for five minutes. Supposedly a bar would come up that showed my progress. Again, with no basic level info, I went out to forums to find out just this information. No one would say in global or chat. I never did get to claim any area's. Perhaps you have to be a clan, but I never really got to talk to anyone in an attempt to join one. Pretty much anyone that I saw coming, was filling me and my butter knife full of lead...)
Grouping/In game event: 6  (I saw some people talking in global chat, and they went and secured some type of objective. It reminded me a little of Defiance and Rift in that aspect. The problem comes from people also going there to shoot you as you try to complete said objectives.)
PvP: 8 (If you like the COD/Battlefield style play with a little sci-fi-ish NPC's thrown in, you might like this)
Survival Aspect: 4 (The emphasis on this game is killing creatures and players. It feels like the food meter is an after-thought, that adds one more thing in the game that can kill you. Trust me, unless you bring a posse', this will never be a real problem for you. If you come into this game expecting the feel of DAYZ SA, you will not find that here. This survival is based against other players and the creatures which makes it feel just like another CoD/BF4ish game. It's a run and gun... or butter knife...)
Storyline: 5 (rudimentary tutorial missions when you first start - IF you can finish them. No over all arching story missions or quests. You have no idea why you are running around trying to kill people other than to just take their stuff)
Overall rating: 4.93  (I may try to play it another hour so that I feel I haven't completely wasted my 14.99... but I am not sure if I can bring myself too)

Date: 2/23/16
Review Number: 25
Game: Rush Bros
From (Creator Publisher): XYLA Entertainment/Digital Drive
Played On: Steambox/Controller/Keyboard/Nothin
Steam Price as of Review: $9.99
Total Time played: 15 Minutes
Review:
So, only two bits into our reviews here and I have already come up with a game that I couldn't finish.  And I don't mean entirely, I mean I couldn't finish the thirty minute minimum review time for the game I have set for these reviews.  Ostensibly, Rush Bros is supposed to be  a sort of rhythm based platform racing game where two people run through a track bouncing off of walls and jumping over obstacles in a somewhat custom designed course with a backing track of music as accompaniment.  Or at least, that was what it said on the tin, which is in some ways the making of a fairly decent time waster.  But that really wasn't what I got.  Instead I got into the game, only having to get back out of the game and figure out how to properly remap the controls (this being another one of those games that just doesn't like the Steam Controller) and then start another game round.  Instead of timed platforming, I got mediocre sprites over graphics of somewhat pretty backdrops, jerkily moving about in a odd monochrome environment.  I also got sloppy controls, regardless of what controller I inevitably used.  I got music that sometimes fit the mood of the levels, but never really played well as a background track.  And I also got a dead steam instance after the game crashed fifteen minutes in and killed steam in the process.   To add insult to injury, after relaunching the game, the control scheme was completely useless, and no amount of controller remapping could fix it, so I had to simply walk away.
Now, I like being generous in these reviews.  I know game developers take a lot of time and put a lot of their energy and often times souls into the things they create, so I don't like to disparage people beyond attempting honest critique.  However, with this game,  I just can’t bring myself to be anything other than disappointed.  I feel like the value for the cost on the storefront is terrible, the game itself is lacking in so many characteristics, regardless of the somewhat interesting premise, and the technical side of the game was in many cases non functional.  All in all this is certainly not the sort of game I would be spending time with.  Pass.
Game’s Fate: Gone.  Just gone.  If I want to play rhythm games, I'll whip out stepmania, or beat my head against the wall in time to Another One Bites the Dust.  Either way would be better.
Buy/No Buy: Nope.

I started off as Great Britan. The people needed a good, strong leader, and because of reasons, they thought that I would fit the bill.
I started doing what any person would do, spending all the money on a military, opening up trade routes, and scamming other countries into buying my "quality" materials that I was only to happy to get rid of. (we were a bit overstocked on them)
In attempts to increase government/military quality, I decided it might be best to forget about educations and hospitals to focus on more important things. Trading and Diplomacy.
As my diplomacy skills went up, I wanted to be better friends with the surrounding nations, so I gave France ten bucks to strengthen our relationship. They were not amused, and it backfired on me.
With that out of the way I decided that the best move from here was to wipe Denmark of the face of the map, for the sole reason being that it was there. I put my troops on a ship, and once I could convince them to swim to shore, I had to make a bunch of allies so I could march across other peoples land on my way to Denmark.
I attack. It was a hard fight in the mountains, and we sustained heavy casulties, but we drove them back. VICTORY......until they brought in a bigger, meaner army for reinforcments and then gave me a whoopin.
With my army crippled, and thus my country, I threw in the towl. Well played Denmark, well played.
In all seriousness, I bought the game on sale for 49 cents. I don't think it's quite as big,  detailed or complex as some of the newer Total War games, but it seems easier, which is good for RTS newbs like me. With that in mind, and you don't mind outdated graphics, then you might consider giving this a try. You could go on adventures like the one above.... :)

TLDR:  For Skyrim with a lot of mods I see about a 30% increase in load speed using DimmDrive instead of my Raid 0 of SSDs.  If you use a HDD and have a lot of RAM, get DimmDrive.  If you have a TB of SSD space that runs at 1 GB/s, like mine, DimmDrive is less of a necessity.
Skyrim with RealVision ENB and the highest resolution version of all recommended mods for RealVision.
I added my data folder to Dimmdrive.
For the tests below, I opened Skyrim loaded a save to an outdoor cell and timed the load then closed skyrim and repeated two more times.  The first numbers are the three load times, the second numbers are the disc access times according to Windows Process Monitor.  Note:  the "disk" I'm using is a raid 0 of two SSDs, it benchmarks at about a GB/s sequential read.
I did this multiple times in different areas.  The below data is indicative of the results I'm not showing.  I don't include them, so that I can keep this short.
With DimmDrive: 15.90 s , 14.02 s , 13.99 s
Process Monitor: 12.01 s for 13.4 GB total disk access
5.68 s disk access for 3.83 GB on the first run
W/o  DimmDrive: 22.83 s , 12.95 s , 13.03 s
Process Monitor:  23.83 s for 11.3 GB total disk access
23.8 s disk access for 5.2GB on the first run
Explanation:
For the first access of a cell (a room or outdoor area) DimmDrive is far superior for large disk accesses.  Once the data has been cached in memory DimmDrive has a small amount of overhead that makes it slightly slower than straight ram access.
For general play I see about a 30% improvement in performance when disk access is a question.

*Edited Mar30/2015* I have done some timed tests, see bottom of review.
The difference between DD and the SSD is negligible. Put the 30$ to a new SSD!
This review is mainly for anyone who plays a modded Skyrim (such as ENBoost, SKSE, Unnofficial Patches, SFO/SRO/CoT, etc.) and is looking to speed up load times. Instead of DD, I would suggest purchasing an SSD. I've used Dimmdrive for a couple hours testing out different variations on which files to load onto the dimmdrive (I have a 8 GB dimmdrive) since all of skyrim is too big. I initially tried the ones he reccomended in the video but it did not speed up my loading times at all. I've run procmon to find the files most read and tried those. Nothing so far has sped up any loading times. Eventually I figured that since my skyrim is heavily modded (Skyrim STEP Project), I would look through the mods and try to find the largest ones that are loaded the most. I tried combinations with large mods, core files, texture packs, everything that made sense and nothing worked. My skyrim has no problems running or anything like that but the dimmdrive simply just didnt change anything for me. (See the below for specific test information.)
It should be noted that Tim (the developer) has reached out to me twice to try to help my situation. He really cares about his product and wants everyone to have a good experience so in terms of customer service and troubleshooting this gets an A.
*Edited march 30th 2015* So I did a couple tests. also note i have a little less than 200 mods:
When I first reviewed this product I had an HDD, those older tests can be found in the comment section. After purchasing a new SSD, I had done tests and I have stated that the SSD is a better purchase than DD. Tim has reached out to me to try some more tests as DD has been updated recently so here are my results:
I used procmon for 5 minutes of regular play and here are the files most read for me (sorted by Bytes) and these are the files I put on my 8 GB DD:
HighResTexturePack01.bsa
HighResTexturePack02.bsa
Textures.bsa
Meshes.bsa
Unofficial Skyrim Patch.bsa (this is common for heavily modded Skyrims)
Dragonborn.bsa
Time to load files ONTO the DD: 26.37 seconds
Here are some load time tests (i did a couple and took an average):
*also note that each test was seperated with a full shut down and no other programs other than Steam, Skyrim, and DD were launched*
NO DD:
initial skyrim load into Dragonbridge area (Large cell to load):
31.11 seconds
initial skyrim load into Understone keep (smaller cell to load):
20.51 seconds
WITH DD:
initial skyrim load into Dragonbridge area (Large cell to load):
30.02 seconds
initial skyrim load into Understone keep (smaller cell to load):
20.6 seconds
As you can see the times are, unfortunatley, still the same when comparing my SSD to DD times. If you are wanting faster load times, pick up a SSD. If you already have a lot of RAM that isn't being used and you are seeing terrible load times then this purchase may be justifiable. However, for me with my SSD (and at 30$) it is not. (Again please remember that I am only talking to the people who play Skyrim a lot, and have a lot of mods.)
If you have any questions on my system specs, the install/update process of DD, my mod list, or any of the test data feel free to message me.

I got this game just before they released SOMA, when they were offering it for free. I downloaded it, but it sat in my library untouched until tonight. I was looking for something that I could play for just a short period of time, because I didn't want to be up late. I  gave Amnesia a try, figuring that I wouldn't play that long because I've never really played a game like this. Boy, was I wrong! At first, I thought the game was weird. The environment was strange, the unusual events happening were disturbing, and I didn't quite understand what was going on. It drew me in, though, because I wanted to understand what the heck was going on. I ended up playing for almost an hour and a half, immensly enjoying the simplicity of the gameplay and the effectiveness of the atmosphere Frictional created. The game is CREEPY! I was constantly wondering when something was going to jump out at me... but (at least at this point into the game) nothing has. I DID catch a glimpse of an enemy, but he/she/it has its back turned to me.
The atmoshpere of the game is exceptionally well done- you move from rooms that look almost normal to rooms that look like they've been torn apart. The overall feel of the place is ramshackle and haunted. Sound effects are superbly used- voices heard not-so-distantly, footsteps on the floorboards above you, creaks, rattles, shakes, groans, and very appropriate music! The soundtrack is haunting right when it needs to be, and quiet when it should be.
Considering this game is almost 6 years old, the grapic quality is astounding! The details in the various paintins are excellent, the use of light vs dark lends to the excellent atmosphere, and colors and textures look convincing.
If you're at all squeamish, this game is not for you. If you like pulse-pounding action and fast game-play, again, this game is not for you. If you just like to frag everything around you, bypass this one. If you enjoy games that keep you on the edge of your seat in suspense, wondering what's going to happen next, you've come to the right place, because this game WILL make you jump.
I'm looking forward to playing it again soon... I wonder how long I will last before I die the first time???

This game is a mixed bag from first glance. Honestly, the first half of the game is very dry and has copious amounts of needless narration. The narration is so rampant that you have to sit still each screen just to hear it, and honestly little is being said. To borrow from Shakespeare: the narrator speaks an infinite deal of nothing. It left a bad taste in my mouth as I felt the world could speak for itself in most cases. Less narration is more in this sense; the only reason why
got away with gobs of narration is because there were interesting things to say, which were said in colorful ways. Do yourself a favor and drag the narration volume slider all the way to the left. The text alone, ironically, is more immersive since the narrator ends up getting cut off mid-sentence during normal play.
That said, the second half of the game is good. Don't get me wrong: the story is interesting, but the color mechanic is the real star of this game. The initial game is mostly a tutorial, while the void stages allow you to get creative with solving the problems ahead of you using the five colors you acquire during the main game. Many puzzles can be solved in multiple ways, some of them probably in ways not intended by the developer. However, I ran in to two major problems.
First off, there's some collision issues in the game, and often they can break puzzles entirely. In some cases, they are surmountable obstacles, such as the player's character getting snagged by the terrain. Those same snags, though, can send the player bouncing in different directions when using the green color. It's frustrating to be punished by the game for using the powers as intended.
Second, bullet collision is absolutely broken when vsync is on. It took me a while to figure this out, but my experience was tarnished by it. Several puzzles required bouncing bullets using the green color, and often those bullets would inexplicably implode before hitting a target. Some of the collision is off in the game, such as metal boxes, but turning off vsync at least allows the player to finish the game.
I definitely enjoyed the second half of the game way more than the first half, so take that with a grain of salt (and maybe wait for a sale), but I can still say this game is decent enough for someone looking for an interesting puzzle/platformer hybrid.

The game is also evolving towards a full-fledged MMO (its currently 64 players max per server) on a gigantic map, which is currently in closed Alpha. It will eventually open to all owners of the game. So there's very active development and huge future.

This game drew me from its approach. I find the game world and environments suitable foreboding and tense. The controls are decent and for the most part exploration is easy. The visuals are good and look nice for something that is essentially an MMO. I like the weapon options and the safezone hubs that dot the world. I understand this is early access and is still being tweaked to its final format. With that in mind I have kept an open mind on everything that has befell my numerous nameless characters. However, after spending a solid 4-5 hours with one character feeling very confident in his abilities and weapons, it was tragically cut short when I picked up an escort box that I suddenly found that I could not set down and made an irritating beeping noise that essentially made me a big noisy target. Realizing my plight I ran for six blocks towards the safezone where I would find safety and shelter. Unfortunately a block away from my salvation, another "survivor" happened to be waiting in ambush for unsuspecting people fresh out of the safezone and chased me down and killed me. I lost my weapons, (more importantly) my time, and the reward I would've received for carrying this big stupid box to the safezone. Did I mention I couldn't put this thing down and that since it was occupying my hands, unlike the courier boxes you find in safezones which go in your inventory, I could not hold a weapon? Defeated, irritated, and tired I started again sunk another one and a half hours into another "survivor" and met my demise at the hands of two people I shot repeatedly, only to be gunned down and all of my possesions taken as well as the glider I spent two account "gold" on.
This game needs a means of separating those who are PVE and PVP. I appreciate the idea of trying to get these two concepts working so that players will band together, but the king of the hill focus and player confrontation are ruining this game for me. I appreciate the idea of losing everything upon death and think that its a good core gameplay mechanism. Buy constantly getting shot by every ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I see is frustrating to the point where I just don't feel like playing. It's good to see a solid group mechanism implemented. There needs to be a chat window or a means to communicate other than voice. This game has a lot of potential to be something excellent, but I worry that those of us who want a cooperative environment without getting shot by some lazy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who can't scrounge for himself is going to drowned the bright points of this game.

Nihilumbra raises questions about life and existence during its (3 hour or so) story. It's an unique game. One that I really enjoyed. It's a puzzle platformer game that's light on the puzzles; you have to use one or more of 5 colors to paint the landscapes and that way solve these puzzles. Paint the landscape green to jump, paint it brown to stick to the ground or use stealth, paint it yellow to generate electricity etc. At the beginning you'll use only one color, but after a few levels you'll be combining two or more colors in order to advance. The puzzles are never hard and even the most casual gamer will know how to solve these.
The voice acting is ok-ish. The narrator has a boring, uninteresting voice. I think no voice acting would've worked better in this case.
The graphics look okay for the most part. The environments are just perfectly fine, but the character you control as well as the enemies around you seem to lack animation frames. It all looks really basic and wooden in motion. A terrible shame. A few more frames would've definitely benefited this game. I didn't get immersed into the game and I think it's because of this. It's just too obvious. Anyway, enough about the animations.
Nihilumbra is a clever game that all gamers can and probably will enjoy. If not for the gameplay, then most likely for the story it's trying to tell. Recommended.

Hacker Evolution is a brilliant game. A 'Hacker Detective Mystery', which blends both puzzle and sim genres into the gameplay. The gameplay is objective based, and involves hacking other systems looking through files, finding clues, downloading/uploading/deleting important files, and locating new IPs to hack to complete your objectives. Meanwhile managing the balance in your bank account, which is used not only to upgrade your computers specs, but to reduce your current trace level. If your trace level reaches 100% or you are caught decrypting or cracking a server, you lose. You can find money by locating IPs for ATM Machines, also some servers occasionally have money in them to transfer. While hacking in the game is simplified, it still does take time to learn the commands. There is a tutorial, also typing HELP will bring up a list of commands when needed. Hacker Evolution provides a great experience for those who invest the time and patience to learn the ropes.
Fun, better than the rest of the survival games out there.

Offworld Trading Company is a very refreshing take on the RTS genre. Once ruled by the likes of Starcraft, Warcraft, Age of Empires and Command and Conquer, the genre's popularity has currently taken a turn for the worst. Many attribute its downfall to the success of League of Legends: by distilling the genre to it's very core and simplifying the gameplay, it has become the most played multiplayer game. Offworld Trading Company does this to an even greater level: while League eased the burden on the player by allowing control of just your hero, OTC did away with controlling units entirely.
This game innovates in so many aspects that it's difficult for me to list them all. There is no combat, but the multiplayer still feels vicious and fierce. Instead of fighting with guns and swords, your tools of conquer are liquid assets, market manipulation and sometimes Filthy Pirates. No two maps are ever alike: sometimes silicon is lacking, and whoever can secure a monopoly on it will certainly profit later on. Other times, there is little aluminium and by keeping the price high you can prevent your opponents from upgrading. Every game starts with you settling down on Mars as one of four corporations, each as different from each other as Starcraft's factions. The purpose of this is twofold: you are assisting the local colony by producing whatever goods they need, while also looking to become filthy, filthy rich.
The early game consists of rushing to upgrade as fast as possible by securing control of your primary resources. Once your HQ reaches level 3, the focus becomes sabotaging your opponents as well as (ab)using the market and other players to make money as fast as possible. Is one of your opponents shipping resources from far away, without producing any fuel? Put down some reactors and make bank on the high fuel price. Does he start producing his own? Sabotage his factories and turn his debt into your money! These kinds of decisions pop up constantly, and you need to be vigilant to seize the opportunity. But when you do, it pays off fast and hard! The game usually ends (after around 20 minutes) in a frantic race to make enough money to buy out your opponents, while preventing them from doing the same. While there may be a clear leader at times, he can be toppled if two or more players gang up on him.
This game is fantastic. I wholeheartedly recommend it to fans of the RTS genre, as well as anyone looking for an unique, intelligently designed game. While there is a learning curve, the in-game tutorials do a great job of explaining the interface and the basics of gameplay. I also recommend
to anyone looking for a more in-depth guide.
is one of the best resources for this game, you can get specific advice and guidance, or just chit-chat, with players that have hundreds, if not thousands of hours played.

This is my first review on any game and my English is not very good, so I apologise in advance for any mistakes.
Knights of the Old Republic 2 was developed by Obsidian Entertainment and was released in 2005 on pc.
It got an update in July 2015 and now it supports resolution up to 5k and it has controller support.
I will split this review in the following sections: Gameplay, Performance and Story. There will be no spoilers.
Gameplay:
-Kotor 2 is an RPG. Which means that you can progress your character by leveling up and adding points
to attributes (such as strength and dexterity) and skills (such as Persuade and Awareness).
The game does a good job explaining each attribute and skill in the level-up menu.
-The combat and movement in this game work with point and click. As a result the game doesn't use the players
own skill in aiming and swinging. But uses a mechanic of chance to determing whether you actually hit the target.
It is really for you to decide if you like it or not. Personally I find it frustating that the only thing I
do in combat is choosing attacks and not execute them myself.
-Quests: Like in the movies, the force comes in two versions: The Light side and the Dark side. This is also an
important feature in the game. Any quest you do, any character you talk with. You can decide to take actions like
a jedi (helping people), or a sith (robbing, than killing the people asking for help). Because of this the player
can achieve each quest in multiple ways and with different outcomes. This adds a lot of depth and makes the quests
much more fun and interesting to do.
Performance:
-Kotor 2 came out in 2005, so the graphics are as you would expect. But lets be honest, you're not going to buy
this game for the purpose of being impressed by a bunch of nice shadows. So lets look at the frame rate. I only
played this game on one pc, and my frame rate stayed between 40-60fps. I don't know what caused this but it doesn't
impact the gameplay much because you don't control the fighting yourself.
Story:
You don't have to play Kotor 1 before Kotor 2. There is not alot of reference between the two games. The only thing you
need to know is this: 5 years ago the republic was attackted by the mandalorians. The Jedi, whom don't really like war didn't pay much attention to it. So 2 jedis, Revan and Malak decided is was time to do things differently.
They became evil and after defeating the mandalorians they started to rage war against the republic itself.
Your character fought in this war and now the galaxy needs you again.
The game follows the same kind of progress path as Kotor 1.
On your way to accomplish the main quest you meet multiple individuals whom join your team.
Some of them are very interesting while others can be incredibly annoying, for example Kreia:
An old hag whom can't stop talking about random force-related crap each time you make an decision.
The player will travel across multiple planets. Some planets have more content than others.
Nar Shaddaa is in my opinion the most fun planet to visit, it has alot of exciting quests and an intriguing storyline.
However Kotor 2 was not finished at release, many cutscenes/events were not included in the game and although the TSLRCM mod restores most of this lost content. A lot of things seem to be missing. Especially the villains are not "fleshed out" enough. They only appear 2 or 3 times and it is dissapointing that their part in the overall story was so small. Especially the last few hours of the game are not so good. There are alot of plot-holes and at the end I didn't feel like I got a good conclusion.
I just think it could have been much better if the developers had a couple more months to finish the game.
My verdict:

I honestly don't know how it happened, but I got hooked onto this game.  At first, learning the commands and how to use the interface is very confusing.  The game does not have a very comprehensive tutorial and the beginning can be muddling.  DON'T BE SURPRISED IF YOU'RE RE-DOING LEVELS OVER AND OVER. There's a lot of strategy involved with completing the levels; who to hack first, how to hack, how to gain funds to upgrade your computer, whether you should trade information with other groups, etc.  It's like a game of chess. Although it's not an action game, it's definitely engrossing if you enjoy something that can make you work your brain.

You're a renowned IT specialist that retired as an ermit on an isolated island following your family's death. However, you're asked to investigate on 4 different problems, that seemed tied. What will you discover?
Hacker Evolution is perhaps a writing simulator, as you need to type the command but you need your brains to avoid to be traced and to have a game over. You're going to read files, find passwords, find exploit files that will make your life easier, crack, decrypt, use your brains to know how many hosts you need, upgrade your hardware (should I add a faster modem or a better firewall or more CPU Ram?).
Now, the product is stable, there was a time where exosyphen messed up with keyboards (mainly AZERTY) but they're really listening to their customers.

Hacker Evolution came with Reinsertion Pack, since then replaced by a nice mod called Operation Electrosphere.

I had never played
up until recently. I played
multiple times in the past, loving its story and gameplay, but never its sequel. And now having played it, I feel that the game tragically never realizes its full potential, even with the restored cut content. Yet, I also feel that it surpasses its predecessor in several ways.
employs the Odyssey engine and d20 system from the first game, effectively translating
concepts to the setting of blasters and lightsabers. Combat is real time with pause and although there are a few oddities and annoyances, I always felt that the combat worked mostly well. The game's item crafting and upgrade system is decent, and thankfully so, as almost all the items you will find are randomly generated, including merchant stocks, and you will need to upgrade your gear to remain competitive.
Special note needs to be given to the influence system. Depending on your actions, you can gain influence with your companions and thereby earn their respect, change their alignments, learn more about them, and even train some of them in the Force. The system has significant flaws, as it tends to encourage gamey tactics in order to maximize your influence points. It is also undermined by the fact that you cannot have more than two companions with you at a time, making it nearly impossible to influence everyone in any singular playthrough and restricting access to some parts of the story. However, watching your companions follow you to the Light Side or to the Dark Side is very cool.
The background story of the
is far more ominous than its predecessor. Darth Revan has left the known galaxy for mysterious reasons. Civil war has crippled the Republic. And the Jedi, relentlessly hunted by a new wave of Sith assassins, are nearing extinction. Yet, your character, despite being a Jedi, has been divorced from these events right up until the game's beginning.
You are an exile from the Jedi Order, who condemned your actions in the Mandalorian Wars and ordered you to give up your lightsaber. You also somehow lost your connection to the Force. But suddenly, it begins to return.
Thus you embark on not just a physical journey, but a spiritual and philosophical journey. Delightfully, you are given the opportunity to opine on the nature of the Force and are encouraged to decide for yourself whose teachings are right, whose are wrong, and if the Force has a destiny for everyone or if your fate is one of your own choosing. In many ways, this game is a successor to
and it all but explicitly asks "What can change the nature of a man?"
It is not your typical
story. And here, that is fantastic.
The game has excellent dialogue and many times gives you a plethora of dialogue options. Overall strong voice acting and writing permeates this title and nearly every character has depth far surpassing their counterparts from the first game. Admittedly, the writing does have its share of inconsistencies and the story has its issues, including a series of somewhat unsatisfying retcons regarding Darth Revan's motivations and the "True Sith," which cheapens the value of
as a continuation of
.  But when the story and writing are at their best, it is wonderful and makes up for nearly every weakness this game has.
I was very charmed by the fact that you can play a character that adheres strongly to the Light Side, the Dark Side, or one that rejects both the Jedi and Sith orthodoxies and still arguably be justified in your choice. It is so much more interesting to have genuine motivations for your actions rather than a superficial veneer of rationalizations and this game succeeds at providing such motivations. The character I played prior to this review generally showed charity, courtesy, and hospitality to those around me, but I also decided to exterminate the remaining Jedi masters and constantly criticize the Jedi Order for its many hypocrisies. It was deliciously heretical.
Although I love that this game readily permits, and sometimes encourages, toeing the line between Light and Dark, I was a bit disappointed at how it can lock you out of some content. While I could forsake the alignment specific prestige classes, I was far more annoyed that there was a level on Korriban that required a strong alignment commitment, thus prohibiting my only mildly Dark Side-aligned character's entry, and that the ending of the game is merely dependent on how devoted you are to the Light Side or Dark Side rather than on any given choice. I'll also note that I was stopped short of completely and utterly denouncing the usual conception of the Force as having specific Light and Dark natures rather than emphasizing the value of an individual's choices and actions, perhaps because there was still an expectation one would ultimately pick a side. Nevertheless, I enjoyed this run and the game is very replayable.
Although almost any game will have its weakness, this game's are pretty prominent. One of the most noticeable was some wildly varying level design quality alongside a relative lack of content in some areas. For instance, Onderon had many sidequests, many locations, and an interesting plotline with many remarkable characters. But Nar Shaddaa and especially Malachor V have some lifeless and rather poorly designed environments. And Korriban was almost pathetically short. The ending of the game's story can also be disappointing, as it refocuses on the aforementioned retcons and takes away choice from you regarding what your character does next. While it was supposed provide a sequel hook, it feels cheap. In a way, it feels like some parts of this game were never fully finished.
I also encountered some bugs, including graphical glitches on some of the player character models and some pathfinding oddities. There was also a bug where dialogue would start constantly skipping if I didn't close and reopen the program around every two hours. Massive praise must be given to the people behind the Restored Content Modification for crushing so many other bugs, but the presence of the ones I found still speaks of an abridged quality control effort due to the rush to get to market back in 2004.
For all its problems and unrealized potential, I really liked this game. I liked it for its story, its characters, its willingness to confront some of the normally sacred concepts of the
setting, and most of all, its fantastic writing. So long as one enjoys RPGs, is cognizant of this game's flaws, and can appreciate its complexity and subtleties, I strongly recommend this game.

Shadow Warrior was my favorite FPS shooter of 2013. It was fast, beautiful, challenging and just so much damn fun. The sequel builds upon that success by adding co-op, loot, crafting, challenges, more weapons and a reason to keep playing even after the credits roll. It's fantastic but in some ways too much and broken. A weak story, some underwhelming boss fights (outside the 1st) ,limited locations, useless weapons and some terrible online connections keeps the sequel feeling more of a side step than a step forward. Its still better than most and if you are a fan of loot games SW2 is a must own.
Shadow warrior 2 is set five years after the events of SW1(not required to enjoy the sequel). You play as the smart mouthed, funny Ninja warrior Lo Wang who is again hired to battle hordes of hell demons that have been released onto Earth by his nemesis Zilla. The main mission is to close the portal that has let the demons escape while also retrieving the body of young lady Kamiko whose soul has been placed in your body as a portal. The interaction between Kamiko and Lo Wang are the best parts of the story while the rest is just not very good. The dialogue with a lot of characters is cringe worthy and while the first SW nailed Lo Wang's attitude and humor this one is trying way too hard and  it's noticeable. What's weird, for you lore fans, there is a books worth, not kidding, of lore that you will collect while playing. Enjoy.
What Shadow Warrior 2 lacks in story can easily be ignored due to the amazing game play. As in the first SW game play is fast, furious, rewarding, and challenging  as you slice,dice, shoot, and explode your way through hordes of enemies with sword(s) or guns. Game play is simple get a mission, go to location and battle hordes of enemies to retrieve, open, close or kill. There is a solid roster of  aggressive enemies(a lot more than SW1) and all are procedurally generated with different stats(more on this later) and they will spawn in different areas of a map during replay. Some of the enemies include ninjas who bicycle kick grenades(fckers),  some wield swords, guns or throw deadly uchiwas and some like the serpent snakes throw or stab you with their tridents(also fckers). There are also mechs, robot soldiers, and flying orbs and all will be buffed with(or shielded) with effects such as fire, ice, toxic, or electricity.
To battle the demons of hell you will be given an arsenal of 70 different types of weapons to choose. They range from the usual handguns, shotguns, machine guns, rpgs, and bow to the weird medusa head that spits toxic poison or the saw blade that, like it sounds, is a sword that's like a chain saw. All the weapons come with random stats of damage, critical, etc and most will also include effects like listed above. Each weapon also has 3 slots to place gems which are the main loot item in the game. As in any loot game, upon killing an enemy they will drop gems, money, ammo or health and its glorious. Gems carry numerous stats that can increase your weapons damage, armor defense and as they become more powerful, they will also carry negatives. Gems can also be used to change weapons by making them turrets, allow you to dual wield, and use explosive ammo to name just a few options. There are also special orbs used to permanently upgrade any weapon with more damage, larger clip for ammo, less reload, etc. You can also craft gems which is a dice roll of lesser gems + $$$ for a higher level gem.
Skill points for your character can be added to a series of cards with multiple slots to move faster, increase health, carry more ammo, more fire damage, etc. There is a good deal here for your character(very familiar) but I would have liked some more uniqueness to the cards and the ability to do loadouts. This should have been a loot item as I only had an enemy drop a card once(already had it). Its the weakest part of the loot system as it just feels basic.
Graphically SW2 is no slouch. Running again on their own engine SW2 looks beautiful. The use of color in the outdoor environments is more natural while neon highlights the city scapes. I would like to have seen a larger template of environments but what is here looks amazing. Almost everything is destructible(except buildings) and cutting, shooting, , burning, exploding particle effects makes the 4th of July fireworks look minor. It can get easily hectic especially with multiple players and its easy to lose yourself in the chaos but damn, it's fun. My system ran the game at a solid 50-60 frames at 2560x1080P ultrawide with every setting ultra and never had any serious drops. The main issue came online where no matter what the game would hard crash or lose connection all the time and probably a good reason why player count online is low.
Shadow Warrior is easily one of my favorite franchises and FWH is a one of my favorite developers today. Its combination of fast game play, awesome melee/gunplay combat and Lo Wang himself is unique to an ever crowded and growing market. Its a good game but because of some online issues, basic character development and weak story it doesn't outshine the first SW but damn its still better than most.
Note: I would still be playing today if it wasn't for online performance. This could be attributed to most players being in eastern Europe region as US/US server connection seems to work fine. I play a lot of games online and this is by far been the worst from a connection pov.
Positives
Amazing Fast and Furious game play
Good variety of enemies and weapons
Graphics and Performance is really good(all Max/ultra settings 50-60 fps)
Satisfying Loot and crafting
Tons of replayability with multiple difficulty tiers and challenges
DLC and still being supported by FWH
Negatives
Not a lot of location variety
No loadouts
Comparing weapons/armor UI
Constant online crashing
Weak story
Player hit box seems to be big
Difficulty spikes

"Of Guards and Thieves" is a multiplayer stealth shooter, and it's the first game by Subvert Games.
The game plays from a top-down perspective and pits a team of Guards against a team of Thieves. The Thieves must steal an item and the guards must prevent that. Only thing is, the Guards don't know which item the Thieves are stealing, so you must always be careful: you might be guarding the wrong item.
The game looks really pretty, and has amazing lighting effects: the shadows are the best friends of Thieves, and hiding in them can save your life (and end the one of the unlucky Guard).
The game does lack in music, but it makes sense since you must listen carefully to lights going off and people getting killed.
Other game modes include Zombie Rush and Soccer, and more modes, skins, characters and maps are being added constantly by the developers.
Overall, it's a fun multiplayer game, full of stealth, action and references to other indie games. A fantastic indie game to support.

I have mostly positive, but still mixed feelings about this game mostly because of it's Early Access status. It's not that the game is buggy or unplayable. It's the contrary, this game is fairly polished and without glaring technical issues. The problem with this game comes down to the underpopulation, which is usually a problem with multiplayer only Early Access games.
OGAT is a fast paced game despite being a rather technical, strategic team game. Round timer is 5 minutes and games can be over quicker than that if the offensive team completes whatever their objective is. Each class has a set primary weapon, secondary weapon and varying numbers of equipment items. There is no way to switch out of your default class set and you have a finite amount of magazines for each of your weapons. It is important to note that I said magazines. In this game, if you reload prior to emptying your current clip, you lose all of the remaining ammo. So don't go shooting a couple of times for a kill then reload. You'll end up running out of ammo and will have to go on a literal suicide mission to get some more.
The maps are asymmetrically designed to suit the strengths of each side. Maps start out lit in favor of the Guards. Lights can be switched off or on to give each side an environmental sight advantage. There are vents that can be used only by the Thieves but Guards can still shoot into them if they see a thief run into one but vice versa also applies. The other movement limitation that applies to the Guards seems silly to me. Guards cannot pass through a broken window. I would undertand if it was a size issue, but there is a Juggernaut class for the Thieves and he's larger than the majority of Guards and has more health and weaponry too. The Juggernaut should abide by the same movement restrictions that the Guards have.
The balance of the classes will take some time to figure out because of the many factors involved. Each class has a different movement speed, different weapon set, different max health value. That's keeping it simple because you have to analyze each weapon's balance too. Each weapon has max damage, reload, rate of fire, ammo(capacity) and magazine count stats. I noticed, like other tactical shooters, your shots will spread to the left or right of your crosshair if you repeatedly fire a weapon for longer than 3-4 shots. I like that it's a factor in the game because despite being a top down shooter it adds to the tactical element and technique needed to successfully aim your shots. The equipment covers your usual tactical pieces of equipment: flares, grenades (frag, glue, incendiary, smoke), healing syringe, molotovs and stones. They are planning to add a few more, so don't worry about the lack of flashbangs, because they are planned for the future. The currently provided equipment does a good job of controlling space. Can't see around the corner because of darkness? Throw a flare over there and spot that sneaky thief. Guard watching the exit of the vent shaft you plan to pop out of in the light? Smoke grenade has you covered. Need to slow down that thief approaching an escape? Glue grenade will slow that thief down to a crawl.
There are multiple game modes besides the eponymous Guards and Thieves mode. Soccer, Zombie Rush, Team Deathmatch, Instagib Team Deathmatch, Bomb Defusal, VIP Escort, Capture the Flag, Instagib Capture the Flag, and Mad Ball. There is work currently going on for a few additional modes as well. Hosting games is easy enough and the admin tools are fair. You can choose the combination of game mode and map that you wish to host, friendly fire (on or off), team swap, auto-balance, player kick.
Now the one downside of this game is its current popularity or rather a lack of it. I haven't seen more than 150-200 global players logged into this game at once, even during primetime western hemisphere gaming hours. Even when it has reached over a 100 players, usually between 50%-66% are in game. For as easy as it is to host in this game, that is inexcusable. You'll even see host in the world chat room asking for players to join up to populate their game.
Overall, I'm mostly positive on this game because of all that it has to offer. If the community grows for this game it could be a hit. Otherwise, this game is not going to last for too long without the support of a good community. I'd like to see this game do well and it would be a blast to see this game streamed among friends.

Imperial Glory is not at all what i expected.  A friend got this game for me, while it was on sale for 59p. For it's age, Imperial  Glory can still compete with other, more modern games of its type. Though the graphics are not the best, the game mechanics are in many respects better than the likes of Empire and Napoleon Total War. If you have played either of these, you will be well aware than when two units clash in melee, it is not uncommon for several men from each unit to be doing nothing while a few others fight and the rest get in the way looking for an opponent. Well Imperial Glory, now 10 years old, actually doesn't do that. It was really good to watch the intense melee with everyone taking part. Though indeed the kill moves, and graphics cannot compete with the likes of Empire and Napoleon Total War, it was a nice part of the game that i really enjoyed.
The sound effects and general playstyle is very similar to that of Napoleon and Empire too, but from my short playtime, it is a lot faster and seems a lot less buggy. I like how the lines all fire pretty much at the same time, but the reloads are a bit too fast. I found the interface a bit tricky to work out, but i soon got the hang of that and everything was fine. Formations cannot be changed merely by right click and dragging the unit across the map, as you can in Empire and Napoleon, at least i couldn't get it to work like that.
Unit sizes are pretty small which realy is the bggest downside to the game, and it kinda kills the realism, but really its fast paced and relatively easy playstyle really does make it a game still worthy of some respect, in many ways better than most games from the Total War series.

Ok, so after a few weeks of using this thing I've come back with a more insightful look of what this program did for me.
First of all, I'll elaborate what kind of setup I have:
8 GB of RAM to work with
4 GB of RAM dedicated to DD whenever I run the program.
A majority of my games are installed onto my 2TB Seagate Barracuda ST2000DM001 7200 RPM
I also have Windows installed on my Intel 335 Series 240GB SSD
i5-3570k
Why didn't I post my GPU? GPU doesn't do anything in regards to the performance of this program at all. We're looking at faster load times.
So like I said, the majority of my games are loaded onto my HDD, while I only have one or two games installed on my SSD (and a majority of my intensive programs such as video and video editing sits there too).
Now that being said, I do have limited RAM. And a bit of INITIAL TWEAKING is needed properly configure DimmDrive to what I need. Thus, I have to use the LESS RAM FEATURE in order to get what I want with this. I do realize this isn't the pancaea for my performance problems; my hardware is old by a few generations and probably needs an upgrade in two years or so.
So after tweaking DimmDrive for games like Killing Floor and Team Fortress 2, both on my HDD. My map loading times for these games have been so much faster. HOWEVER, when I tried to tweak this for Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn, I see little to no difference. This is because this game was on my SSD.
Do I expect a huge difference for my games on my SSD? Not so much, an SSD is already fast enough as is. On my Hard Drive? Oh gods yes. I was able to get into the game faster, and in the case of Skyrim, experience a more seamless adventure because of the little to no loading times this has provided me.
Now onto crashes. I experienced crashes while using this. I'm not going to lie, the Less RAM feature is a feature not for those who have no idea what they're doing with their computer. I messed up several times and had my games crash on me randomly or not even start at all when using this. It was not until I started monitoring which processes/files that were used/accessed the majority of the time when running the program is when I was able to configure DimmDrive with the correct files. This program isn't perfect; Tim said he's going to implement an "auto-learning" that will make the program allow to "learn" which files are accessed multiple times and save that as info for its use. That's a feature I am looking forward to.
That being said, why did I buy this program when it's not perfect or doesn't work as "advertised"? I could've gone with a free alternative. Yes, I could've gone with a free alternative, but I did not want to bother spending much more time figuring out which files I need to designate for the RAMDrive. Plus, it provides a soft link to most of my installed Steam library. That's a plus in my book. And while I can't say that I'm currently happy with the lack of Steam saying I'm actually playing the proper game while using this, I still think this program has a lot of potential and right now it has made me happy for what it is capable of doing considering my hardware.
In conclusion, I should point out that the program isn't perfect. DimmDrive isn't a one click solution to your performance troubles. You are required to do some tweaking on your own which may result in a few failures but once you get it to work properly, it does its job.
Right now I can't exactly recommend DimmDrive in its current state; I want something more out of it or perhaps a way to make it "dummy proof" for your more average user who simply looked at this and say "HEY THIS IS PERFECT FOR ME!" and avoid disappointment.

FF6 is by far my favorite game of all time, but let's get these bad things out of the way
first. No 1080p resolution, I haven't the slightest idea why they didnt format it for this resolution considering like most of the  monitors or tvs people use are this resolution,
second complaint. Saw some graphical glitches as soon as i started the game just small things like pallates randomly flashing on npcs
But it's FF6 imp the greatest game ever made so these small issues can be completely overlooked!

+ Graphics to some extent, lighting/shadow effects are good.
+ Sniping mechanics are good.
+ Kill cam is very cool looking but almost a bit too accurate with its gore. It also gets quite boring quickly when it activates with even very mediocre shots.
- The level design is lacking as most of the game is just one route you can take without any actual freedom of choice.
- The AI is quite irritating as when you are spotted everyone in the area knows exactly where you are and can hit you accurately with an smg from hundred meters away. When they discover a corpse they seem to do predetermined search patterns covering only small sections and rarely finding you. There are also some locations the enemy just dont walk into no matter how you try to lure them.
- Third person view, which I personally dislike in shooter games.
The biggest reason I do not recommend this game is the level design and "console mechanics". There are invisible walls, collision detection is a bit stupid (you cant crawl over a single brick lying on the ground!), you can climb only certain preselected locations whichs means you can only use the locations to your advantage when the level designers wanted you to. This very much takes the feel of a sniping game meaning you cant effectly be creative finding the best spots to snipe. Most of the levels rarely give you the possibility of true sniping as distances are small. The game still forces you to use the sniper rifle as all the smg's are bad even at close range (5 shot burst to the torso dont kill quite often).
Why did I get the game then? Because it was free.

Server problems aren't as bad as people make it seem. I have a smooth and good game 7 times out of 10. And if there are connection problems you can always jump into practice and get a little better while you wait.

The fighting is fun. It's challenging, and requires patience, but it's a blast. Pick a hero you think you'll do well with, look over their moveset, play a couple practice rounds, go fight some AI online, and then once you feel comfortable fight people. (Fighting people is actually easier than AI, assuming you're just starting off, so don't be scared)
All in all it's a solid game, albeit a little over-priced. If you've got money and you're interested, get it. If not, wait for a sale.

An interesting economic simulation. It really puts you in the shoes of a business CEO. You have to choose which resources to buy and which to produce, as making everything slows you down to the point you can be overtaken rather quickly. The basic idea is that of a resource management game, one where the costs of every item are in flux, just like in the real commodities market, and you have to decide the best course of action. there are power-ups to help you control this, and four factions each with their own abilities. You can pause the game in single player, and while i haven't tried multiplayer yet, i believe it would be an interesting change of pace to play against humans. While this is an interesting game, bear in mind that you will do better if you have a basic understanding of supply and demand, at least at the start. (ie. flooding the market with one good will kill the price of it, destroying your revenue.)

This is a really charming game.  It has a very present sense of identity.  Contols are generally pretty good, graphics are vibrant and stylish, the music is very relaxing and well-done.  The story is a nice change of pace from the hack'n'slash or shoot-everything-that-moves tropes, and goes a long way to set a serene atmosphere.
I've noticed some use the term metroidvania to descsribe this title... I'm not sure I agree with that.  It does have pregression to new areas by backtracking through older areas but the progression is through found keys and flipped switches rather than new abilities/mechanics not previously avaiable.  Maybe nit-picky on my part, and I don't mean it as a mark against the game.  The exploration is rather fun and the levels are interestingly designed.  The primary means of progression is through finding and collecting crystals, and it may take several re-visits to a given area to find them all... some areas have hidden entrances from later parts of the game and others are simply well hidden.
I noticed some reviewers have complained about the worm sections.  The worm controls like the supersheep in worms.  It is constantly moving forward and the player turns it left or right.  But it moves through the ground and assumes a parabolic trajectory out of the ground.  Some of the objectives while controlling the worm are out of the ground and require somewhat precise arcs.  I actually enjoyed these parts, as it was an interesting change of pace, and occasionally rather challenging.
I didn't particularly like the last boss fight.  I found myself dying a lot due to the a rubber-band kind of effect with how the player moves in the fight sequence and unclear boundaries to the arena, and found it difficult to time my attacks due to the how the player's weapon functions.  However, in the end (and after probably 30+ deaths), I did make it through.
In the end, I rather enjoyed the game and would love to see more from this developer.  This is exactly the kind of game I think of when I think of indies.  It is designed with a lot of love and heart, and this shows through when playing the game.

The game is a platformer with some clever mechanics, divided into two modes. The initial story mode is effectively an extended tutorial with little actual challenge. New mechanics are introduced very slowly, while the plot presented at this point is about what you'd expect from a casual indie game; very forgettable and completely predictable. The atmosphere is pretty nice though, and the voice is pleasant to listen to.
Once you finish the story you get access to the extended challenge mode; think Super Meat Boy dark world. The mechanics are much the same, but the game tries to add extra challenge by presenting a lot more complex scenarios. Unfortunately for the most part these extended challenges end up being nothing more than timing puzzles or trial and error memorization of where the enemies spawn.
Get this full price if you really like precise timing puzzles. Wait for a sale if you like platformers and artsy games. Skip it if you're looking for deep or thought evoking challenges.

People shouldn't praise this game just because it's functionally better than DBD. The game still has many problems which were knowingly present in the beta. Inconsistent camera angles, the usual post-launch balance issues, (seemingly for us Aussies) US only servers, gameplay issues, lobby problems, the inability to re-bind control options (I mean come on, seriously?) and more things that add up to make it a pretty underwhelming experience. While it's more fluid, plays better and arguably is a better overall game than DBD by comparison, it suffers from that same "lack of things to do differently each game" downside. It doesn't matter if the map is different every game, it's still the same choice of 3 ways to escape for the councillors and the same 'kill them all before they escape by x means' for any of the Jasons. There just isn't enough there overall, and not enough has changed since the beta, for it to really be a lasting experience; at least for me anyway.
Many people will have given DBD a solid shot when it was released because they had hope that it'd turn into something better; because it was a catalyst for the genre. But if this game didn't have a F13 skin over it all, I don't feel like many people would/will stick with it.
Visually, at least, it's great. It's decently optimized for what it is, audibly most things come together to give you the atmosphere the game's going for.
But at the end of the day, I'm playing a game. And there's not enough game there for me to recommend it to anyone, at least in its current state. I won't refund it, but they've got 2 weeks to change my mind.

This game is simply brilliant.  I'll leave it to other reviews to extol the value of the gameplay on offer here, but this is easily the best strategy game released in the last year.
Several negative reviews criticize the game for being too easy or too simple.  Difficulty options easily address the first point, as the AI is perfectly competent and can challenge even the best players.  If you think the game is easy, you need to step up the difficulty level or try your hand at a human opponent.  They don't bite.
Anyone who says this game is simple has no grasp whatsoever of the nuances of the design.  Under the hood, the game's primary system is a simulated free market economy.  On the surface, you can influence prices by buying and selling goods, but the ability of the player to influence both supply and demand through interaction with the colony and other players is really what the game is all about, and those possibilities are limited only by your capacity for foresight.  That's the way a strategy game is supposed to be.  The player who wins is the most clever one who can exploit whatever situations present themselves, not the one who can click the fastest or can memorize a hundred opening builds.
Of the short list of critiques you can level at Offworld Trading Company, lack of depth is absolutely not one of them, and the mere thought of it is preposterous.  This remains true even at the end of 2017.

Contrary to this game's description, it is not a hacking sim.  Rather, it is essentially a text adventure/puzzle game wrapped in a hacker facade.  The game is divided in to 10 chapters where you will scan websites, decrypt keys, and crack passwords in order to complete level objectives.  Puzzling out how to complete your objectives without getting traced can be quite fulfilling.  However, you will find yourself frustrated by a number of things.  Firstly, the game's tutorial and help menus are mostly useless.  They don't enumerate all of the syntax at your command, and the descriptions that do exist are unhelpful.  Once you do figure out how to actually play the game, you may find that you have played yourself in to a corner and have to restart the whole game from scratch.  This is essentially just a couple of poor design choices and overall shouldn't impede your enjoyment of the game.  If you were fascinated by mid 90s cyberpunk hacker culture, then you'll dig this game. 7/10

Of Guard and Thieves is a team based top down shooter. It is currently in early access and honestly there aren't many problems. Let's get the negatives out the way: there seems to be some issues with networking and not being able to join other players games at times, although I personally never encountered this in the free demo. The other team are the Thieves who have to steal an object which isn't revealed to the other team. There are a multitude of classes each with their own pros/cons in certain situations. The developers have added a BUNCH of different gamemodes such as Soccer, Zombie Run, Capture the Flag, Instagib and more. Each gamemode brings a new style of gameplay to the table that make the game refreshing & fun.
I can 100% recommend OGAT if you are ok with playing the game in EA and if you have some friends you can get to tag along for the ride.

A very fun game that takes capture the flag to another level in it's classic gamemode (the one this review will talk about). The guards are tasked with keeping the thieves from stealing one of the various marked items throughout the map. Here's the catch- only the thieves know what that object is. This opens up oppportunities for strategic play, such as pretending one object is the one by continually trying (and failing) to steal it. This will bring the guard team's focus to that item, and leave the actual target less defended. As a thief you have night vision goggles, allowing you to see the guards from much farther away than they can see you. The guard team relies on flashlights and lights that can be turned on and off allowing for strategic advancement or better area control. While the thieves have less firepower than the guards one of their classes, the cobra, features a metal gear solid-esque knife pistol loadout that is a one shot kill from the knife (sacrificing range and encouraging sneakier play). Best of all, this game is free. Free? Yes, free! If you think it's a game you'll enjoy but you don't want to invest in it or you are considering supporting it you can download it from the website at

Rainbow Six Siege is a fast paced and slow FPS depending on how you play but slow is where the roots of the game start.
You'll be put in a 5v5 lobby where Attackers must breach objectives where they either can- Secure an Area, Disarm a Bomb or Extract a Hostage.
You first need to pick an operator. Each operator has unique abilities and weapons from Grenade Launchers to Cloaked Poison Mines. The operators own ability means that each time you change an operator it means you play differently.
Each of the detailed and easily recognizable maps have walls, floors and doorways that are completely destructable so you're able to punch a murder hole to pick off an enemy. Destruction and versitility is a large part of Siege. You need to play smart or you will die very quickly.
Pros- Great Maps, Unique Gameplay, Constantly Updated and Intense Gameplay
Cons- Crappy Servers (sometimes), Friendly Fire is always on in Multiplayer, Some Players are Toxic, Bugs and Glitches and Hit registration is broken
Despite its flaws Rainbow Six Siege is a great shooter, very different from Call of Duty or Battlefield. Its tactical and based on real life special force CTUs. With a new type of gameplay it brings new life to the FPS table. Great to play and communicate over microphones and it gets your heart pumping at times.
Ubisoft, definitely not the best games developer but this is still a great game that is going in the right direction in my opinion.
By the way. For your first operator get this guy called Tachanka, he has a LMG turrent that's really useful ;)

So I have put in an hour into the FF6 remake.
First impressions:
The graphics are cute. There are lovely battle effects for Terra's magic and I think the sprites are growing on me. The music is the same classic soundtrack, which is always lovely, and I LOVE THE PORTRAITS.
The meat of any RPG is the battle system, so let me tell you about it. There are these windows that represent a character on the bottom and when the window reaches all the way up, then that character can have an action from their list. You guys know that every character in the game has their own unique commands, right? At first it was just weird, but once I got the hang of it, I found it very fast to navigate! I am playing with a keyboard until I get a Xbox controller, which I am not used to, but once I learned all the commands, I was happy with it.
It does not go full screen. I don't care about that, most of the time I play in window mode to easily navigate what else I might need on the computer. There is no start up thing like in other Steam FF games, either, and I don't mind. I had to figure out all the commands until I reached the Adventurer's school, but at that point everything was explained.
The text is almost the same. Some parts are translated better, but some parts are word for word what we had on the SNES and PSX Anthology versions. I love this story a lot and I'm looking forward to collecting all the achievements!
Buy? ♥♥♥♥ YES BUY. I'm glad I got it.

Dimmdrive won't necessarily make your game run faster. It may not make load screens significantly shorter (though it probably will).
In my current, recent build, I invested in more RAM - 32gb - in order to use Dimmdrive effectively. Manually swapping games I wanted to play from a conventional hard drive to an SSD for a reasonable performance boost seemed so
, and Dimmdrive seemed effortless in comparison.
RAMdisk technology has existed for quite a while and, yes, free implementations do exist, but Dimmdrive has been designed with Steam integration in mind, and it handles it fairly well. Certainly better than other solutions which generally require much more work just to
them work, and can only offer the additional 'benefit' (or curse, if someone happens to read your impassioned comments) of
Of the things that bug me about this software, my major issues are that:- when set to launch on startup, it automatically opens with Steam despite Steam itself being configured NOT to launch on startup. In addition to this, when set to minimize to tray while launching on startup, the app reveals itself by showing an 'about' window, suggesting I visit the store page to review/ rate. It asks me to do this every time Dimmdrive launches, and I can't opt out of this annoyance.
Dimmdrive's Steam version annoyingly depends upon Steam to launch, and I would prefer to be able to use it without starting Steam. I held off purchasing the app elsewhere at a discounted price because I thought a Steam version would enable additional ease of use. I'm not yet sure if this was a mistake, but I hope future updates can validate the choice I made.
While I don't think this software is reasonably priced (£22.99 as of writing), it does seem to be priced in line with other two-trick software solutions available elsewhere. It's easy to question the cost of an application like this when I've bought entire game franchises for less in the Steam sales.
The sum of my input:
Despite suffering from a few tedious issues, this software works well - provided your hardware can properly utilise it. So far it's reduced (perhaps eliminated) I/O-related slowdown and ugly texture/ model pop-in within the few games I've tried it on.
I'm also confident that the above mentioned issues can be ironed out by the dev over time.
It's up to you to decide whether or not you need, would benefit from using, or can justify purchasing Dimmdrive. Do a bit of research on the relevant technologies (RAMdisks, benefits of faster hard drive speeds in gaming, etc) before you purchase.
Avoid purchasing, confusing yourself, and posting an incensed comment amounting to libel, by taking the above precaution.
