WF&S is basicly a mod for M&B: Warband, sacrificing some of Warband features for actual historical background.
If you played Warband, you know what to expect. If you haven't - M&B is a sandbox game. You are being thrown into a pretty big map, full of villages and cities belonging to one of five factions. And then... well, you tell me. You want to become a bandit, rob caravans and burn villages? Why not? Want to be a vigilante, taking down bandits and doing small jobs for the lords? Why wait? How about joining the faction, gaining fiefs, and taking over hostile factions? Go on. Or maybe... create your own faction, and become a king? Your call. Or you can always be a merchant. Still a good idea if you enjoy it. This applies both for warband and With fire and Sword.
Factions in WF&S are Polish Commonweatlh (with their extraordinary cavalery), Kingdoms of Sweden and Russia, Cossacs and Tatars. Each faction has it's strong and weak sides, as well as it's unique units. Speaking of units, i have to say that I'm  disappointed. not by the numbers - there are plenty of them, but upgrades.... most of the units can only be upgraded to veteran/elite status. Even village recruits can be upgraded maximally to Mercenary status. Which means - obtaining unique faction units is really hard.
A word about equipment. Crossbows were removed, instead, you get muskets and pistols. Pretty good and deadly weapons, if you know how to use them. Of course, they need bullets. Luckily, they refill after each battle. Weird enough, granades (yep, there are explosives. Quite powerfull, yet, quite pricy) don't refill. So if you buy pack of 3, use one - next battle you'll have 2. Quite annoying, isn't it?
To sum up, if you enjoyed Warband, but got a bit bored with Swandians and other Nords, and want to try something new, but not THAT new, try WF&S.
P.S: Just realised that it's just like Napoleonic wars, if it were abit more to the east, and contained single-player

So lets get this out of the way first.
One of the other reviews on here complains that this game cannot be played in full screen.
ALT+Enter is full screen mode.
Also, the graphics suck. The new sprites are really blurry and the environments lack the character of the original.
Everything about the game is simplified/streamlined just like its IOS iteration (since this is a direct port of that version).
The music isn't spot on with the SNES original but it is very good nonetheless.
The writing is pretty strong in this version compared to the original. The original translation (woolsey) is the version we all loved growing up but this new translation is really great. Things are worded/described in a more eloquent way and the naming conventions fit in better with the overall Final Fantasy mythos.
This IS Final Fantasy 6. If you love this game for its beautiful story, fantasic music, and intriguing gameplay you'll find most of that here (the only thing that is weird is the new battle interface).
Emulation of the original has been a viable option for years but has never really been an option for people wanting to own a legit copy of the game on PC.
I recommend this version of the game as it holds true to the amazing story that made the original so good. If you can look past the really stupid graphics you'll be fairly happy with the purchase.

This is the most terrifying, thought provoking, epically gorgeous game I have ever played. Big kudos to Frictional, they have truly outdone themselves this time.
The story speaks for itself - you WILL be thinking about this game and the twisted moral questions it asks long after playing.
The graphics are STUNNING! They stay true to Frictional’s moody and haunting style while bringing a level of polish unrivaled by any other survival horror game to date.
The sound – OMG YOU GUYS THE SOUND – is truly what separates this game from anything else on the market; the creaking moans of the abyss will keep you up at night, play with headphones if you dare!
Enemies are unique, varied, and just as haunting as Pathos-II itself.
The puzzles are where this title takes a bit of a departure from the other Frictional titles, which, in my opinion, was a breath of fresh air as a fan of the developer. There is no inventory, no notebook (I know!), and the find-these-pieces-to-complete-this-puzzle puzzles are limited. Instead, the puzzles are much more subtle, making them not feel like puzzles at all, pulling you even deeper into SOMA.
This is truly the first triple-A, pure survival horror game I have played. The bar has been set for every other developer in this genre. Can’t wait to see what these guys roll out next!
P.S. to anyone with good headphones – take a leap into the abyss, it is a treat.

Ugh, I hate this. I wouldn't say this game is recommendable, but at the same time, I can see why people like it. So, just read this review instead of simply looking at the thumbs up-icon to the right.
Pros:
1. It has a nice soundtrack. It can get repetitive after a while, but it still manages to create the right atmosphere.
2. Enjoyable artwork. Of course, that's debatable, but I enjoyed it.
3. The general idea of manipulating your environment. It's nothing new, but the abilities themselves are rather cool.
Cons:
1. The dialogues. Seriously, can't the voice actor just shut up? The acting actually isn't the problem, that's well done. But the dialogue itself is so atrocious and annoying and pretentious. I don't need a comment on everything there's happening. The game would have been _much_ better without any dialogue at all.
2. Which brings me to the next point: Too easy. The puzzles are so easy to solve because most of the time you just have to use the one ability you just acquired. Combining abilities happened very seldom and if for some reason you are stuck, the game literally forces the solution upon you through the narrator and the hints. It's a puzzle game, I want to find the solution myself.
3. The length. I don't have anything against short games, but the game can be completed within less than two hours. Then of course you can beat in the hardcore mode again, but that's not the solution. They could've added more content, really.
4. The controls. The character is... "wobbly". It's really difficult to land accurate jumps and even more so, when I have to do the same section all over again, because the last checkpoint was two miles away.
5. The tutorials. Okay, seriously. Why do I need those? Not only do you get to know the different abilities, before you can use them, but there's plenty of opportunities to test them out in the actual levels. I don't need a tutorial that basically teaches stuff I already know.
So, do I recommend the game? For a discount, yeah, why not? At full price? Rather not, no. I don't know, the game feels a bit too pretentious, like it's trying to jump on the "platformes with a deep background"-bandwagon we already know from Thomas Was Alone (which was excellent) and LIMBO (which was excellent as well).

This is probably the best survival apocolypse games out there. This game basically entails you starting out with a butter knife, and collecting loot to better equip yourself. You have to manage your food and water so that you can survive. There is an XP system which allows you to level up your character and aquire perks to make your survival easier, or easier to hunt and kill the "zombie" in this game known as nether, or easier to hunt and kill other players. The main types of loot you'll find are sellable items, health recovery items, food/water, ammo, and guns or gun parts to craft your own weapon.
That is the main goal of the game, to survive and thrive. Now the thing that wards players off from these types of games is permadeath. I wasn't a fan of this game for the longest time until I noticed that they added something pretty neat. Along with your character level, there is an account level. This level will not be lost on death, and when it is leveled up, you will get perks that accumulate and are there everytime you play, even if you die. The perks can be very useful, like more cash everytime you spawn, more health, more carry weight, and I'm not very far in the levels yet. I really think this is a great feature, because even when I die I don't feel like I've wasted all those hours on that character just to get shot.
Just a few more features that I would like to add which I appreciate are taunts, from flipping off the world, to dancing on corpses. Character customizations, with different outfits and hats and masks (There's a Deadpool mask too) which all can be bought with real or ingame currency, and stay with you no matter how many times you die. A balanced loot system in which loot isn't impossible, and it isn't around every corner.
This game is updated more often and with more significant updates than any other Early Access game I've seen. If you're interested in this genre of game then I recommend you pick it up.

Really cool idea with a terrible execution. I love rhythm games and I grew up playing platformers. The game doesn't play as much to the beat but rather tries its best to simulate one. Some of the later levels are Super Meat Boy level difficult, but with all these terrible obstacles sort of matched to the rhythm it makes the game frustrating.
The game has 47 levels and the difficulty ramps up quite quickly. Eventually, spikes start to move so quickly that prediction is necessary to avoid death, but the game is extremely checkpoint heavy to its benefit. There are some spikes that move backwards, and at this point the game devolved into masocore (eg I wanna Be The Guy) levels of nonsense.
Early on the most painful levels are ones that make you repeat the stage repeatedly, unlocking the next door only to be forced to drop down to start the level over again to get the next key for the next door. The worst levels are those that are heavily layered and filled with traps so if you fall you can lose a lot of time. After that are the "boss" levels, which get rid of the generous checkpointing you rely on. The thing I found to be most helpful was to find the song with the quietest beginning that wouldn't trigger most obstacles and spam LB to replay it over and over again. It took away from the musical aspect of the game, but the musical aspect is a suggestion at best.
The game doesn't react very well to your music and there are only a few obstacles that do: spikes, table saws, rising platforms, repulsor bumpers (think Super Meat Boy) and zombies. There are a handful of others that are static like buzz saws and spikes. The repulsors are the worst obstacle in this game because on any given song it seemed to be random when they would activate, which led to a lot of long falling and time lost.
The zombies are probably annoying too but I couldn't see them because there was a bug(?) where they stopped spawning after I restarted my game to fix another bug where the game wouldn't checkpoint me at all. I considered the former a beneficial bug so I didn't restart the game again.

TL; DR: KotOR II is excellent, but unfinished. A must play for Star Wars and/or RPG fans. Play through it once without the Restored Content Mod and play through it again with the mod installed.
I have owned this game for a very long time. I originally played this game countless times on a disc, so my Steam hours do not accurately reflect the time I have spent with this game. I am one of those people that say that this game is better than the original (although the original is extremely good too).
Let's get this out of the way first. Knights of the Old Republic II is an unfinished game. It was rushed to release to meet a Holiday release date. As a result of this, many sections of the game were cut out entirely, including an entire planet, along with vital story dialogue with characters and an ending that actually makes some sense. I am aware that there is a mod that restores a good chunk of the cut content called The Sith Lord Restored Content Mod (which is very good by the way), but I will bring that up into more detail later.
Take the Star Wars formula that you know (Jedi = Good, Sith = Bad) and completely flip it on its head. It doesn't do a complete turn around, but you start thinking of the Jedi and the Sith more in shades of grey than in one being absolutely good and the other absolutely evil. You get more of a nuanced education in the Force from one of the best Star Wars characters ever, Kreia. Let's be honest here, Kreia is absolutely the best character in this game and is probably one of the best Star Wars characters ever, yes you heard that right.
In KotOR II, you play as the Jedi Exile, a former Jedi Knight that was kicked out of the order due to his/her involvement in the Mandalorian Wars. You were one of the Jedi that followed Revan and Malak off to war, and you were also the only Jedi that returned to face judgment. Ten years have passed since then and you return to find a threat facing the galaxy that hides in the shadows. What follows is a galaxy spanning quest in the same ship as the first game collecting companions to aid you in this threat while rediscovering your connection to the Force. It is one of the most unique takes on the Star Wars license.
But, as was said earlier, it was rushed to meet a deadline. A lot of vital content was cut from the final release, but the files were still in the game. A team of modders took it upon themselves to restore this content (what they could, anyway), and it is a crime that Obisidian was not given enough time to finish this game properly. However, I do recommend that new players do not play through the game first with the Restored Content Mod and save it for a second playthrough. Playing through it first unfinished and then switching to the mod gives you a much better idea of exactly how much stuff was cut, and how important the cut content really is.
If you are a fan of Star Wars, or of RPGs in general, then there is no question, KotOR II is a must buy.

I love this game.
The concept is great: heavy armed guards are protecting some items from stealthy thieves. You have few cool classes:
Guards= the scout (run fast and throws flares and glue grenades to slow thieves), assault (the guys with a the best rifle, throws frag grenades), riot (the though dude with a riot shield, a gun and throws smoke grenades), carrier (the versatile one who throws incendiary grenades to defend), medic (he heals from distance with a TF2 seringe gun, attack with a pistol and his melee weapon heals too).
Thieves= the shadow (uses a crossbow to take down guards from afar, throws smoke grenades to lure), the cobra (like solid snake, he uses a knife, a pistol and throws rocks to make noise), saboteur (same as the guards carrier but weaker), medic (same as the guards but....), juggernaut (the thought guy with a rifle, a gun and frag grenades).
You see the game from above so you can anticipate enemy's movements and set strategies. Plus you can see nice lighting effects.
Many guys are ranting because they want first person view...
But it's out of the subject of the game.
Maps are nice but some are difficults to master, like the cemetery or the millitary camp.
Usually you will play on the offices or the mansion...
Some modes to play (you got some others but there is a full list on the wiki):
The Guards and Thieves or Gat (thieves must steal a specific item and reach the exit, there are some other items so they can lure the guards...)
Zombie rush (zombies must eat a brain the guards are protecting. Zombies are weak but fast and deadly in close combat. They have 5 classes, from the zombie runner to the bloiter, everything you saw on other zombie games is here except the one with a retractable tongue).
Vip (a player is the target of the thieves/assassins, and must reach the exit without dying)
Bomb defusal (few locations are marked and the thieves must plant a bomb and let it explode, guards must stop them)
Capture the flag (everything as been said).
Team deathmatch (same !)
Soccer (well the most annoying one, you hit the ball to throw it... in the goal).
But again the problem is, like a guy said on an other game, balance.
This game is too much unbalanced. Some games modes are incredibly unfair, like zombie rush.
So you will see all the time players taking the same classes and will rush mindlessly.
Very few of them are working together. Only thieves are forced to work as a team because they are very weak.
Actualy teams are composed of the assault class vs cobras.
And like other indie multiplayer games, the community is sometimes bad.
Players are not the only problem. In fact it's servers admins.
Games are hosted by players. So quite oftent you have conection problems. But this is not the most enerving...
Admins are often completely not responsible.
They can do what they want and it's usually for the worst.
Many players thinks the game is unbalanced so they punish if someone take a specific class.
And the most annoying, they do not "clean" their hosting.
Few times i was insulted by players and the admin just do nothing about that.
So i don't recommand this game until they bring dedicated servers and do more stable hosting because actually you lag and are often disconected.
If you buy this game, please..
Be fair play !

This is surprisingly good.  I'm pretty skeptical of Early Access games, and I generally don't like them because they are usually unpolished, barely playable (like DayZ) and just messy.  So, after wasting money on other early access games, I was hesitant to shell out $15 for another one.  However, I was really amazed at how well the game played.  It feels like a "finished" game, rather than a placeholder until they eventually make the game you bought, which you might hate in the end.
The concept is good and it is executed well.  It's a 3D top-down shooter and light plays a huge part of it.  You play as one of two factions,  As a guard, you get guns, a flashlight and must fight off the sneaking thieves in a dark location; the Theives slink around turning off lights and climbing through vents and windows to reach their objective.  They are much weaker and use the dark to engage up close.  It's actually pretty scary as a guard as the lights off on the corridor you're in, meaning there's an enemy behind you.  It's actually fairly tough, but not overly unfair.
There's also a zombie mode which plays basically the same, except with a zombie enemy team.  That needs the most work, I think.  There's some parts of the game that really need to be refined, like the aiming and hitbox system.  If your crosshair/character isn't at just the right spot/angle, you'll miss - which, as a thief, is very bad when you have one chance to not die.
All in all, in spite of all these petty issues that need to be addressed in the future, I am very satisfied with this game.  If The company that made this skipped town with all of our money and the game never got updated beyond this, I wouldn't feel like I didn't get a full game.  If the devs stick around, there looks like a lot of promising content coming down the road.  I wait impatiently for the level editor!
So, in short, yeah - it's pretty good.  It's not for everyone, but I think you'll know if you're the kind of person who would like a multiplayer stealth shooter.

In order to use a ramdrive efficiently, you need to do some basic math.
16 GB system ram - (1 to 4) GB for the OS = X GB left for the game + ram drive.
Find out how much peak memory usage a game has by playing and checking task manager (Details view, select columns peak data set).
Pay close attention to the amount of memory available during play.
If you notice lag, open task manager, if memory is full then you should load a smaller ramdrive or get more ram.
Even if you only select textures or audio files, it would result in a noticeable decrease in loading time.
Loading times are reduced significantly, even when you play games from an SSD.
Some loading time remains, as not all loading time is used just to load textures, there are almost always some decompression and setup steps.
You can also use the ramdrive to increase speed of temporary folders (my favorite io hogs are my browser, unity3d GI cache and photo/video editing scratch disk)
Dimm Drive is easy to use, but does so at the price of making it a little too easy, if you get bad performance check your memory.
If it is full, windows will resort to the swap file on your storage drive, which is slow even if it is on your SSD.
Contact the dev with bugs, be reasonable and respectful, any steam launch is bound to have some minor hickups.

Final Fantasy 6 on PC!!!! (Need I say more?)
Yes, actually it seems I do need to so here's a few things review-wise:
(please keep in mind that I am comparing legitimate versions of the game, not emulated versions)
1. This game has one of the most memorable and engrossing stories in all of gaming history, so much so that it makes the story of Final Fantasy 7 seem mediocre by comparison.
As a side note, the translation has been tweaked and improved from the GBA version which is always nice to see.
2. The GBA version, has terrible sound quality, this preserves the original SNES sound quality with some modernized improvement tweaks, very pleasent to listen to overall in this steam version. As someone who started playing this when it was still called Final Fantasy III in NA, the only sound that seemed out of place so far were the organs on the intro screen. Whether or not the new organs are good or bad is again, subjective.
3. This modernized version of the game runs smoothly in a comfortable windowed mode, much like emulators would be used to run the older version, there is no real need to full screen it since the art assests are not meant to be blown up that large anyway...
For those of you that DEMAND full screen here's a trick: alt+enter (I know, magic)
On that note it should also be mentioned that the text is very crisp and easy on the eyes in this release compared to  the GBA version or the even older versions.
The updated sprites, in my opinion, fit cleanly into the updated background textures of the world they are in. Also, these new assests add fresh life and color to an old world. Considering they are products of the original sprite designer, they function quite well and do not feel out of place at all within the moving world of the game.
To add to those points, this version is visually a large improvement over the old versions that were made for a SD display. It seems important to remind some people that the original game, being a game made for SD display, will look very distorted and blocky at any resolution higher than 640x480 while this game can reach higher resolutions.
4. The game has full controller support in my experience with no lag and responsive input. Navigating the updated menus works quite well with an analog stick.
Speaking of menus, everything from the battle menu to the inventory menus seem to fit nicely after a few minutes of adjustment seem quite sensible for the functions they are meant to perform.
Ignore the haters, dont pay attention to the nostalgia whiners, this game is worth having and it is a story that will stick with you for a long time to come.
Just remember that it is easier to complain and nitpick than it is to actually make one of these games yourself, but as someone who has played this game since it's original NA release, this is a version worth having considering it does not look like blocks of color at resolutions higher than SD.

Is it a high price? Maybe. It's tough to say at this stage, it's a AAA title so $60 is the norm these days. If you liked games like Dark Souls, Chivalry, Mortal Kombat then you will enjoy this and find it quite gripping.
Community is pretty unpleasant already, the typical "git gud" or "ez" happens in larger matches, where as 1v1 and 2v2 tend to actually have more honor and less cheese style of play, plus friendlier people.
Overall I'd give For Honor a 7.5/10. It has a lot of replay value, but Ubisoft needs to make some changes and additions going forward or the game may suffer holding it's playerbase long term.

This is the most terrifying, thought provoking, epically gorgeous game I have ever played. Big kudos to Frictional, they have truly outdone themselves this time.
The story speaks for itself - you WILL be thinking about this game and the twisted moral questions it asks long after playing.
The graphics are STUNNING! They stay true to Frictional’s moody and haunting style while bringing a level of polish unrivaled by any other survival horror game to date.
The sound – OMG YOU GUYS THE SOUND – is truly what separates this game from anything else on the market; the creaking moans of the abyss will keep you up at night, play with headphones if you dare!
Enemies are unique, varied, and just as haunting as Pathos-II itself.
The puzzles are where this title takes a bit of a departure from the other Frictional titles, which, in my opinion, was a breath of fresh air as a fan of the developer. There is no inventory, no notebook (I know!), and the find-these-pieces-to-complete-this-puzzle puzzles are limited. Instead, the puzzles are much more subtle, making them not feel like puzzles at all, pulling you even deeper into SOMA.
This is truly the first triple-A, pure survival horror game I have played. The bar has been set for every other developer in this genre. Can’t wait to see what these guys roll out next!
P.S. to anyone with good headphones – take a leap into the abyss, it is a treat.

Summary:
Shadow Warrior 2 is an FPS with RPG elements. Some of my favorite parts of the game are the leveling/customization aspects and the weapon variety. Parts I didn't like include grindiness when trying to collect all the weapons/skills, a lack of area variety, and gameplay that encourages spamming overpowered abilities.
Pros:
-The skill upgrade system felt great. Planning how I was going to invest my next few skill points was one of my favorite parts of the game.
-Weapon customization is fun, with several gems (weapon upgrades) that unlock unusual gun abilities, such as piercing bullets for assault rifles and grenade launcher remote detonation. Also, weapons continue to be useful for a long time; endgame weapons are only modestly better than those from the beginning of the game, and some midgame weapons were still my favorites at the end of the game.
-There's a nice variety of weapon types. Only a few weapon types felt like worthless additions, and some of those may only feel that way because of my playstyle.
-Combat is mostly fun, and while there's not an overwhelming amount of enemy variety, it's sufficient.
Neutral:
-The difficulty is a little low. I usually play FPS games on normal difficulty, but I should have played this one on hard. I was expecting the difficulty to ramp up, but it never did - or maybe I just did a good job with my skill choices/weapon upgrades. Of course, you can always test one difficutly and change as necessary. There's a difficulty higher than hard, for those who want more of a challenge.
-There's a New Game Plus mode, where you keep your weapons/skills/upgrades and gain access to additional mission rewards. I didn't play much of it, but it seems like a pretty normal replay of the game, making it a worthwhile addition, but nothing special. Note that you can use this mode to keep your old equipment but play at a higher difficulty.
-The storyline is passable, but far from exceptional.
Cons:
-Abilities are easy to abuse, and the grindy nature of most sidequests encourages this abuse. Most enemies with ability immunity can be made susceptible by a combination of the right skill upgrades and the right equippable item. After a Chi (ability energy) regeneration skill is maxed out - which can be done early - you can repeatedly disable groups of all but the strongest enemies. This could have been mitigated easily by adding ability cooldowns. While you can obviously choose not to abuse these abilities, it's much faster to pin down a group of enemies with an ability and kill them with melee than fight them in other ways; when you're just trying to clear out an area, sometimes you just want to do it the fastest way possible - especially when fighting the most annoying enemies (e.g., enemies that run away to shoot and enemies with knockback/bullet-blocking abilties).
-I ran into several graphics/saving glitches. For example, I noticed unintended invisible walls, a floor that didn't load, rock walls and parts of roofs that unintendedly loaded inside houses, and two crashes during quicksaves. Quicksaves also frequently stalled the game, especially if I was moving quickly. (Note that while I have plenty of RAM and an Nvidia 1080 graphics card, I don't have an SSD; some of these issues may be less severe or absent if playing the game on an SSD.)
-Areas are overused. If I remember correctly, there are only four or five main mission areas. This is mitigated by the fact that certain parts of these areas only unlock during a few missions, but I was hoping for a lot more variety. (To be fair, the areas are very large, so it doesn't feel like you're constantly traversing the same ground.) Also, a lot of assets were overused within each area. If you enjoy feeling like you're in a fleshed-out world during your gameplay, you'll be disappointed here. (If you're not a "collector" type of gamer, this may be less significant for you, as you won't feel like you need to play all the side missions to get all the unique weapons/skills.)
-Characters mostly didn't do it for me. The secondary protagonist seems to be intended as a comic foil to the main protagonist during most conversations, but the conflict between them is more annoying than endearing. The main protagonist's relationship with the tertiary protagonist is more interesting, however.
-The protagonist's voice lines were played too often for me. If they had been reduced in frequency, they would have been fine. A few of the repeated lines are funny the first few times, but hearing the same mid-combat quip over and over gets old quickly. (I once had the same line play three times in a row within a span of 10 seconds.)
In conclusion, I felt like this game was a decent experience, but wasn't anything amazing. I recommend purchasing it on sale if you like RPG elements in your FPS games and don't mind things getting a little grindy.

Some games are just fun, some tell a good story, and others can only be called works of art. Nihilumbra manages to be all three at once. The gameplay is satisfying as it blends tricky yet manageable platforming with puzzles involving physics-altering pigments. The story is charming at first, since you can not help but cheer for the little blob of life who has just been Born of nothingness, then slowly becomes more tragic as he is forced to bring death into the world around him simply by the act of surviving. Nihilumbra is also a beatiful artistic piece, sporting deep, ponderous themes and striking visuals both in the background and in the foreground. All these factors grip you and hold you so that you do not want to stop playing until it's done. I can't say for sure whether this game changed me as a person, but it certainly made a powerful impression on me. This is a wholehearted recommendation from one very impressed player.

This is still a review in progress, but after 12 hours, initial impression is a thumbs up.
The game is, essentially imbalanced. You have to understand that going in. Jason is dangerous, but he's not infallible. For example, he gets radar pings when using his (short-cooldown) sense ability, when players make noise. If you run around a lot and carry out a bunch of actions, you make noise, and Jason can just teleport up near to you and attack. Seems OP except you can just try to avoid making noise, duh. You have to make *some* noise, searching for items, otherwise Jason would never be able to find anyone, and being silent takes longer to get things done, which is the trade-off. As a counsellor, time is the biggest resource you have to manage. Over the course of the 20 minute game, Jason's "rage" builds which gives him far quicker cooldowns and the ability to smash through doors easily. So you're in a race against time to get one of the escape methods ready and get out. Suddenly, taking your time stealthing around becomes a matter of judging whether Jason's likely to notice.
If you do get caught out, it's *very* hard to lose Jason. Barricading yourself in a house and trying to slip out a window seems the most viable tactic, but an attentive Jason will soon be on your tail. So that's where other items come in, such as a pocket knife (instantly escape his grab attack), a single-shot rifle, a flairgun, or various poor melee weapons. None of that will kill Jason, but it can stun him for long enough that you can run and try to lose him.
As Jason, you're essentially hunting the map for anything to give away counsellor locations. Audio clues, doors or windows left open, etc. It pays to play defensively in a way, focusing on cutting off their potential escape routes early in the game until your rage builds enough to make kills easy.
Is it unbalanced? Yes, in a way. But it's 8 vs 1. I can't imagine a round where everyone escapes, but if 5 or 6 do, that's a victory of sorts. Jason can kill relatively easily but you can make it a big pain in the♥♥♥♥♥for him to do it, and there's enough of you that he can't afford to spend 5 minutes chasing a single player down as everyone else will be readying to escape. Heck, the game's pretty generous with XP and the credits used to unlock perks and kills, so dying doesn't even dampen the fun for me despite me usually being super salty.
There is, in my opinion, one particular sore point that probably need addressing. One is that Jason can essentially turn invisible and move really fast once in a while... and insta-grab someone coming out of his invisibility. It's an instant game over if you don't have a Pocket Knife item to escape his grab. It's an absolute zero-fun move you can't avoid if you don't know it's coming, and should probably have a slight delay before he can grab, because it's so frustrating to die to.
There's undeniable jank. Glitches galore, many animation issues, there's a lot of work to be done patching this thing up which obviously should have been done before release (delay it till October, polish it like crazy, and release it on Friday the 13th October just in time for Halloween season, c'mon marketing guys!), so those who need a game to be polished will not enjoy it, but the actual gameplay is crazyfun.
Oh, and it's a treat for fans of the movies. There's a huge attention to detail here. From there being 6 (7 including backers kit) Jasons to choose from, each modeled uniquely down to their faces if their masks get knocked off (Jason part 2 even has his long hair, and Jason 8 looks every bit as ridiculous as in the movie), to Jason part 6's "spear" being the same accurately-modelled fence railing Tommy used to impale him at the start of the movie, to female counsellors being able to stun Jason by using his mother's sweater and telling Jason to stop, it's nonstop loving attention to the little details.
Couple of final notes. It's a well optimized game. It isn't a beautiful game but it runs super smooth even on my potato machine. Also there are some day 1 problems with the servers. The devs aren't doing themselves any favours, posting memes on social media while their servers are down leaving no-one able to play, and giving timeframes like the guy cooking sausages in the movie Snatch. It's a small and passionate indie team but their informal nature isn't very professional and doesn't really assure you that this game will be well looked after.
Bottom line? This game requires some forgiveness of its many janks and glitches, and an understanding of what it's trying to achieve (counsellors, you are part of a zerg rush, not each unique mighty heroes deserving of survival), but so far it's been nothing but a riot to actually play. Just please, please patch this game like crazy and fix your servers. Oh, and one specific piece of content already please: Who wouldn't pay for a Jason X model and a space station map?

I've put in quiet a decent amount of time into this game at this point and figured it was about time to write my own honest review of the game...
As a tl;dr for anyone not looking to read through this entire review before buying:
I give the game a 6/10, I'll give it a thumbs up because it's enjoyable enough, but I don't necessarily recommend it. The game itself isn't for anyone and if you're planning on buying it, wait until its $5 or less as the $10 price tag is too much for this game.
The game itself is exactly as it claims it is when it states that it's "a music reactive Platform Racing Game". The game itself is centered around competing against other players online (or against your own times) while avoiding obstacles that are
reactive to the music. But this "reactive" element is where part of the problem I have with this game arises. Depending on the song currently playing, certain elements of levels can be virtually impossible to complete. As songs get more and more upbeat obstacles seem more aggressive and unpredictable. Be it those strange "bass" obstacles that send you flying away from them, the pulsing buzz saws, or those obnoxious cannon like things, certain songs will make these obstacles about a million times more difficult. I myself would often find myself waiting for the brief moments of peace at the end of one song while another was preparing to start before trying to quickly rush through an obstacle I'd been stuck at for what seems like ages.
Next up, level design. While all the stages themselves are unique and different, there's a few major problems I've noticed in levels that just makes the game itself incredibly frustrating to play sometimes. On some levels you'll get a checkpoint nearly every 20 feet, so a death is meaningless and can cost you only a few seconds, while on other levels I felt like I'd spend a minute at a time avoiding obstacles only to die and be sent right back... And that without mentioning some horrible level layouts where I could miss a jump, fall down for about 15 seconds and land on a platform near the beginning of the level, forcing me to start almost the entire race over again.
Multiplayer itself seems to work well enough, however I haven't been able to play much online. Half the time I can't find a server with anyone to play against, and whenever I can, they'll often leave before we can even pick a level or make it any significant distance into a race. However racing against a friend while chatting over skype can be a blast.
Overall the game itself isn't bad... but I wouldn't by any means call it great or even necessarily good. It's a basic platformer, with controls that can be a little bit slippery, beautiful background images, and a diverse and enjoyable soundtrack. While I wouldn't necessarily recommend the game at full price unless you're really really itching to get your hands on it, I would recommend it if it drops to $5 or below. And at that point you may want to grab a 2-pack so you could send a copy to a friend if you ever wanna play a quick game to pass some time.

If you like cars, if you like crashing cars, if you like customizing cars, and you like offroading, this is the game for you. Because it has lots of cars (with many more from mods), has a somewhat detailed customization system that's continually getting better, has really good physics and tire models for offroading (I don't think their is a better game for rock crawler and trail driving as of writing this review). FYI, I only have 40 hours on steam, but I bought it when it was on their website and had a few maps and 5-10 cars in total. I've seen it grow and really like the devs.
Ratings:
Physics overall - 10/10
Handling Physics - 8/10 (only for sporty cars imo. Offroad cars like prerunners and rock crawlers are spot on. Hell I'd give rally cars a 9/10)
Graphics - 8/10 (Graphics get better as time goes on.)
Customizaton - 9.5/10 (A vinyl system would make it literally perfect.)
Optimization - 9/10
Content - 10/10
Crash Physics
Now the Crashing. OOOHHHH THE CRASHING. No not the game, THE CARS!!!!! No game has ever had better crash physics. It's probably the maximum realism we can get with todays hardware realtime. Hell, even big crashes can cause really good PCs to slow down some (which you can't blame the game for. The physics simulations going on here are nuts).
Handling
The only negative in my opinion is the handling of sporty vehicles. It's not bad, it's just slightly lacking. Some cars seem a little less stiff than they should be. It's still really fun to carve through mountain roads though. As far as general driving though it's great. I haven't used my wheel in about a year in this game, but last time I used it it was so so. It could be far better, so I won't rate that as of now.
Offroading
Offroading is amazing. No game does it better overall IMO. Spintires only has the lead in mud physics, which are still decent in this game. Rock crawling and trail driving are amazing, and you can customize ride height and suspension stiffness rebound etc so you can make a trail truck or a trophy truck. Rally is really amazing too, especially with some of the mod maps.
Content
If you like having objectives, you might get bored, but if you enjoy exploring and making your own fun, you'll never run out of things to do. It has some basic scenarios in built in, but I prefer exploring myslef. The game has great vanilla content, and with mods you have tons of awesome stuff. The only annoying thing is telling if mods are up to date. The devs seem to be working on better mod sorting systems on their website. The only thing it doesn't have is multiplayer, which would be nice, but imo isn't needed.
Customization
Amazing. You can change the wheels, steering wheels, suspension, car panels and exterior parts, sometimes interiors. You can customize suspension, engine, transmissions, and even diffs on many of the cars. You can literally remove everything but the chassis and engine if you want( and even strip those down, although you won't be going anywhere lol). The only thing it's lacking is a NFS vinyl type system. You can download skins for cars, but being able to do it in game would be icing on the cake.
Optimization
This game take some horsepower. It just comes with what the game itself is. Over time, it has gotten better and better, but I would recommend a Sandy Bridge i5 equivalent or better. Graphics aren't very demanding unless you crank them up high. It runs fine for me with an R9 290 and a i5 4670k overclocked to 4ghz. I bet it will play fine with a worse CPU, but you might lag a little.
AI is also really cool in this game, which allows for some fun custom or premade scenarios. It's cool, but not something I use all the time, so I'll just say it worked good in the scenarios I played.
Tl;dr - Buy this game if you like sandbox games, cars, and smashing stuff. It offers decent customization with endless replay value due to the awesome mod community. Not to mention the devs are awesome, support the community, and release well spaced updates with significant progress made each one. Tons of great mods to go through on the forum. If I had to give this game any negatives, it would be no multiplayer. The game stands well on it's own, and it's definitely not a reason to skip out on this game. It could happen in the future. but it's not on the top of the list as far as I know. Also, make sure you have a decent computer. You don't need lots of graphics horsepower, but have a fairly recent i5 or AMD FX 8 core CPU to get the best experience. You can still play it ok with lower CPUs, but you might lag when you crash and stuff. Pretty much what it says on the store page.

CAMPAIGN MAP
Imperial Glory takes aspects from the early Total War game Shogun, using the exact same troop movement and province control on the campaign map. The unique feature of moving your troops anywhere in a province as long as you only move to one province per turn. Moving a unit stack to a new province will simulate your men gathering supplies and getting ready to move out, thus you cannot interact with that unit again until next turn. That includes the transferring of units from barracks to armies, or armies to armies. In order to take over provinces you must move your army which consists of 3 units to the target area to immediately take it over. If an enemy army is stationed in that province you will begin a battle at the beginning of the next turn. If the targeted province is the capital of the country that you are at war with, you will begin seiging that province for however many turns depending on the quality of units you have.
RESEARCH TREE
The research tree is mandatory to advance in the campaign, without any technologies you will only be able to recruit Militia, which is the most basic melee based infantry unit. Advancing in the research tree allows you to build barracks, cavalry stables, cannon depots, and other economic/cultural buildings. In order to gain a constant flow of incom you must research the trade technology to unlock trade routes to friendly countries. It is a pretty standard research tree compared to any other TW game.
DIPLOMACY
Diplomacy is kinda limited to the research tree as well as everything else at the beginning. You only start with 4-5 options for diplomacy until you advance further into the campaign. I'm not a big dimplomatic player anway, so I won't go further into detail.
OPTIONS
The options have some variety to the graphics and sounds, the only thing I really consider not up to my standards is that the resolution doesnt go up to 1920x1080.
BATTLE MAP
The battle map is very similar to a Total War game, you play as the commander using a birds eye view of the battle field to direct your troops. The troop deployment is more similar to Shogun and the actually troop manuevering is more alike Real Warfare. The combat is a very simple representation of early 19th century warfare. The front rank of line infranty are the only sprites to actually fire their weapons, while the rear two ranks sit in reserve. Obviously this would not really be the case but due to game limitations its understandable. Militia units are the most basic units that are recruitable from the very start of the game. They are only limited to melee and are sometimes very over powered, because they have more melee strength than line infantry, probably to simulate the larger numbers. The UI in the combat map makes it so you do not have to use any hotkeys if you do not want to and that is fine with me. The AI is pretty... not good to be honest. The Infantry would rather engage in melee than engage in ranged combat which can make things a little iffy strategy wise.
More will come when I continue to play the game.

One of the most complex resource management games I've ever played.
What I found charming about the game is how it simulated not just the basics of economics but it had elements of consumers, terrain (including weather effects), sourcing and patents. Players are also able to manipulate some of these factors through the 'black market' basically debuffs or buffs you can buy on a periodic basis.
Not counting for daily challenge or multiplayer, there are essentially 2 game modes.
Skirmishes are 1 off rounds where all buildings are available and your goal is to buy off the shares of your competitors to win.
If you like progression then campaign mode is pretty nice. Instead of buying your oponents, you buy buildings for the settlers on the colony to win which would also help you tamper with supply and demand (Personally I built more houses so I could drive the price of food and oxygen up lulz). it adds a little more depth to the game as you do not own every building and would have to choose which buildings you'd like to acquire or upgrade though the downside is that this mode lasts for only 7 rounds.
TL:DR
Fairly complex with a variety of strategies to win and ♥♥♥♥ over your oponent that doesn't make you rage quit.
Realistic resource manager cause it adheres to a lot of basic business and economics principles.

If you're system has the extra RAM it makes sense to cache an entire program into memory - in theory it should be faster. However target-audence systems are already so over built that gains brought by this software are negligible. If you're system is sub-optimal in RAM then chances are trying to fit a AAA game, or partially, into RAM will only cost you performance in missing ram for system (other reviews have touched this thought).
Bought this in response to Developer's give-away on Reddit, the video made for a decent sell, so I broke down and bought it -- I wish I had held onto my money. My first experience was Dimmdrive crashing on me trying to run Diablo 3; the sync system fowled up and had to manually rename three steam games (which I marked for ram drive) back to orginal names, remove hidden attribute, and propogate attribute allowing me to run the games normally and remove a persistant error trying to enable Dimmdrive. On positive note I haven't had any errors since.
As for system performance enhancement,  enpirically I've seen little to no performance enhancement running with Dimmdrive. As for real data best I could do was run Valley Benchmark for numbers; producing one more FPS for minium, and two for max FPS. Ran using Direct3D11 render, 1920x1080 fullscreen, extreme HD preset. The game is so good, I literaly bought it again on Steam, only so I can give it a positive review.
With Fire and Sword is a standalone thrid party created Expansion to the Mount & Blade.
It put's the game into the real 17th century Europe, and does provide player with an optional story mode, and tons and tons of new features and usage eases. After you get used to playing with Fire and Sword, the Warband itself will just feel empty, and limited.
The game however requires a bit of mindset changing if you are a Warband fan already, since 17th century armies were marginally different from the villager raised armies of Calradia.
The multiplayer game also provides players with slightly altered combat system (Difference can be felt only by the very dedicated players), that is the matter of taste. I persoanlly like the way combat works in Wfas more than WB, but I do understand that some people my like the feel of WB more than Wfas.
Generally the game is worth your money, especially now that it is on sale. I have spent more than  1000 hours in the game over the last 4 years I have it.
(Some of the features that were added to this game :
- Optional Story lines
- More siege possibilites
- Better siege AI navigation
- Training soldiers in castles and towns
- A LOT of new buildings to build in your towns
- Buildings now also require hiring people to operate them
- Being able to choose equipment for some of your troops
- Ability to talk with Guild master / Village chief without finding them in city
- Building provisoric defenses to help you on field batte (wagon fort)
and many, many other minor changes like loaning money, sending NPC's to academies, tavern brawls, sending merchant caravans etc.)
The game however does not feature :
- Marriages
- Tournaments
- Training camps (They serve different purpose now)

Mount & Blade: With Fire and Sword takes place in 17th century Eastern Europe. There are five factions to choose from, the Polish Commonwealth, Muscovite Tsardom, Cossack Hetmanate, Kingdom of Sweden, and Crimean Khanate. Each faction has unique troops each with its pros and cons. There is a leveling system in this game so you can upgrade your character throughout the game. You can play in first person or third person. Throughout the game, you will recruit soldiers to join your troop. They can be upgraded once they have a certain amount of experience. You can also hire mercenaries too. In combat, you can command your troops to form a certain formation. The game is very similar to Mount & Blade: Warband. There is some addition in Mount & Blade: With Fire and Sword, there are new weapons such as muskets, pistols, and grenades. There are some UI improvements as well.
Mount & Blade: With Fire and Sword is quite similar to its predecessor, Warband. The buildings and troop uniform look accurate. The towns and villages look nice. I really like the UI improvements, it's really neat. There are many mods for this game as well.
However, there are some bugs and glitches in the campaign. The animation when someone died because of getting shot looks weird. There isn't much ragdoll from the grenades as well. Some aspects of the game, such as the loading screen, aren't optimized for widescreen resolution. There is no Steam Cloud support for this game too.
To conclude, despite some of its flaws, Mount & Blade: With Fire and Sword is still a very fun and addicting game. I really enjoy the hours I played it.

Nihilumbra, by Beautifun Games, is one of those games; when stumbled upon and given time, you really get to see all the heart it holds, and the care it had been given. When you are introduced to its world, you can't help but marvel at its art, deep in the frigid mountains to the ruins of a city long abandoned, and you're drawn further in by the awesome music that it emits. It truly tells an interesting tale.
You are Born. A being that escaped from the Void to see and live a life for yourself. As you traverse Nihilumbra's world, you come across various 'colors', which act as both your tools and your weapons. For instance, Blue is Ice, allowing your character to either move quicker and jump further or to allow your enemies to slip and slide off a ledge to be trapped or to their untimely doom. Each color that you get are often used in conjunction with one another to help solve the game's many puzzles. Puzzles that I found very appealing, and interesting, some of them simple, some of them more complex. It's all about how you analyze the situation and how you yourself are going to utilize what has been given. With a solid control scheme and responsiveness, the game didn't feel it was trying to work against the player, which is crucial for a puzzle platformer.
When you start, it gives you a 'Story-esque' tutorial, here is where you learn how to play, what to expect, and how Born and everything around you reacts to your actions. It was interesting actually, and didn't feel as if the game was holding my hand, but rather an introduction. It was a nice touch by developers. After the 'story' as been completed, you are far from being finished. Now, you must right the wrongs that you have done, and this is where the real fun begins. It was a lot of fun figuring out the puzzles, and after completing each one, the accomplishment was indeed satisfying.
Overall, it's a game that is well worth its price. With an overall great infrastructure, and charm, Nihilumbra has easily become one of my favorites. I highly recommend it to those who enjoys puzzle platformers, or to any gamer in general. It's that easy to pick up and play, and easily be drawn into its fantastical world.

It's really awesome, one of the most fun games I've played in a while.
It is by no means perfect.
For those who won't bother reading, I would give it a 8/10.
I'll explain later why, keep reading.
I've played the open beta, wasn't that much impressed to be honest. I thought the combat system was very limited.
I have never been more wrong.
The combat is all about precision, timing, knowing when to strike, how and from which direction.
Each of the 12 heroes (so far) have unique movesets, combos, counter-attacks and so on.
What I really, REALLY love is how much you can customize your heroes visuals.
My god, the options are huge, you can really make the hero your own and special.
Single-player is enjoyable, narrative kinda cheesy but still good.
Multiplayer is where this game shines.
Particularly Dominion mode! You know the drill, you've played it in countless games before.
But the setting, to see 100 AI soldiers in each team fighting over the central control point, and you come in and OBLITERATE 5 of them in one blow.
But then, a enemy hero is in your sights. You two are surrounded by soldiers from both side fighting as you measure one another.. Until one of you strikes, and then it's ON!
Feels like a movie sometimes, and it's gets your adrenaline going.
Duels are also pretty cool, 1 vs 1, and really, no class has an advantage over the other.
BUT, each hero requires a different approach. If you try to spam light attack, you're gonna have a bad time.
Deathmatch/Elimination often gets very chaotic and unfair as you will often find yourself in a 1 vs 3 scenario.
In that case, you can run to find your teammates if they're alive or die.
PROS:
-Highly enjoyable combat
-Great gameplay
-Various aproaches to combat
-12 UNIQUE heroes with their own moveset
-Graphics are quite good, could be a BIT more detailed, but the heroes look amazing
-Customization of EVERYTHING
-Dominion Mode is so much fun and you'll often find yourself yelling out your warrior cry!
CONS:
-Seems like a long-grinding kind of game, some of you will mind that. If I didn't have a job, I wouldn't care TBH.
-Rewards are somewhat "poor".
-Connectivity is a b*tch. Until I fixed my NAT type I could only play with my buddy in DUEL. That's a big no-no Ubisoft.
-Graphics could be a bit more next gen, especially terrain, but this is just me nitpicking.
-Very often it gets unfair, 3 vs 1 and you don't have a chance
-Getting pushed of the edge and dying
Overall, I'm loving it, will continue to play it for a long time to Git Gud.

For Honor is the latest game that's published by Ubisoft and it is as addicting as it is nerve-racking. Let's list the pros and cons shall we;
Pros
+ Gameplay is amazing, and the game really shines in multiplayer
+ Graphics are amazing, even in the lowest settings that I use, so I can play it on my toaster of a PC
+ Characters: Each character that you use on multiplayer is unique with his own kit that you have to master
+ The Faction War aspect of the game: It's a really cool concept and I want to see how they will add to it in the future
Cons
- Peer to peer connection hell: What you can see from every other negative reviews, trying to play multiplayer is a disaster. Kicked from lobbies, matchmaking stops on its own, game is losing connection while you are playing, and you can sometimes suffer rollbacks in the middle of the fight.
- Story mode is nothing to write home about. It's as basic as it gets, but it really is not that important since this game is clearly focused on its multiplayer aspect ( for those who can suffer through the bugs ).
- Upgrading: Upgrading your equipment is bad. When you upgrade your equipment all the debuffs grow as well as your buffs. For example; if a piece of equipment has an attack buff and a defense debuff, you will get more attack, but your defense debuff will grow as well. Since you are using materials that you have to grind for in order for you to do it it just seems to not worth it.
All in all this game is amazing. I have had it for 3 days, and I have already played 22 hours(at the time of this review). Despite the fact that I am gonna give this game a positive review, I will suggest to everyone that is thinking of purchasing it to wait for a price drop. Otherwise you will weep about your decision. Multiplayer is the main aspect of this game and since its not working properly right now you should either wait for the problems to be resolved or the price tag to be lowered. If you have the patience of a saint and don't care about the price tag, then by all means, buy the game you'll have a blast. But just know that you will also be helping Ubisoft, and other similar companies, continue with the behaviour of releasing unfinished buggy games.

Before I begin, I'd like to note that I have the original as well. I'll try to judge Portfolio Edition as it's own, and then compare it with the original in two categories.
Game Character Hub Portfolio Edition is an upgraded version of Game Character Hub. The main differences between them are a few additions, along with PE supporting MV. While the GUI is the same, the Portfolio format is a welcome edition to an excellent tool. The new format can now store multiple sheets (this depends on which kit of chracter parts you'll use), making easier to manage multiple characters. The app practically runs like butter, even on underpowered systems. Adding character parts to the sheets is a breeze as well, since a part will be applied in all of the sheets.
Unfortunatelly, there are some dissapointing parts as well. Unlike on VX Ace, there aren't any additions or modifications on the MV parts, so unless you need an easier way to move and edit parts around, there isn't anything that would be better than the default generator. Exporting is a mixed bag. You have to restart the program a lot of times, just so you can make multiple expressions for one character (or more, if you have multiple files open). And importing img files is just as confusing as the previous version. You can import them, but you can't map them properly, so you can't tell the program which exact color you want.
While I do reccomend the program in the end (barely, mind you), this heavilly depends on you. If you need something better than the generator and/or you are on a Mac or a Linux computer, then I do reccomend it. If you already own the old version, it's a pretty difficult descision to make, since most of the additions don't make it easier to sell. I bought due to the improved workflow and MV support, but I do feel that it should have been released as an update.

For those of us who aren't exactly experts at pixel art, or just want to make edits, or need help with frame mapping and so on, this is an excellent piece of software. It might not diminish what other image editing software like GIMP,
, or *shudder* PhotoShop can do (and if you're looking for extra features such as bloating/shrinking and such, I'd reccomend those in place of this), but it does a great job at creating character/face assets really quickly, and even more for those with more advanced skills! (literally, the possibilities are endless with this software)
There are complaints that this is a cash grab, scammy, not enough resources, and so on.
Yes, these complaints are, for the most part, valid in some form. However, I do believe that while this is great to use for existing resources, I do believe that custom resource creation is the main selling point, which does include making your own resource parts as well. (FTR, I create custom makeup and hair parts and there are no resources for this short of three of the facial marks that are provided with the MV parts)
I too, have some of my own issues (but have worked around most of them).
-GCH Character Types are unsupported (only .json files can be used)
-GCH Workshop is broken (it does appear but your subscriptions will not show up)
-GCH backwards compatibility is non-existent (can only save as .gpf files rather than the .gch types)
What I do like is that it comes with XP, VX/Ace, Looseleaf, and MV resources already.
One more thing I'd like to mention before conclusion is that I had been looking for a way to create angled faces easily, because as much as I do like the VX Ace generator faces, they do seem out of place when paired with VX/Ace's angled faces from the RTP. With the MV parts at my disposal, I can create angled faces rather easily.
For the Record, I did receive this as a gift, but it was gifted by someone who did have to pay for it.
The developer/s had no involvement with me receiving this lovely software for free.

It seemed great at first, a economy / builder game. But then you see what it really is. A weak RTS that you play in twenty minutes flat. And a boring one at that. Pick a resource, hog it and hope others need it more than you need other resources.
The only difference is some basic mechanics between the factions, and the black market.
The black market gets more expensive the more you use it, and the only thing it does is delay or destroy things, or stop other from doing the same. A simple binary PVP system with exponential cost. BORING.
The AI? Boring, the moment you look anywhere close to winning, the AI will nuke you into orbit with the black market, something you can hardly do anything against, and it just delays the inevitable. If you're not winning you still get annoyed by those black market shennanigans but it means that the AI will beat you anyway.
Simply put, flat, boring gameplay, the only spikes are annoyance. Might be mildly fun VS human players, but then I'd go for a real RTS instead of this binary system where the richest wins ANYWAY.

Medal of Honor is one of the♥♥♥♥♥est games I've ever played in my entire life in almost every single way.
First off, yeah, this is a big-budget military first-person shooter. I am not a fan of these at all. However, that doesn't mean that I'm not willing to be enlightened by one. Like, maybe this one was going to be good?
However, it's Medal of Honor:
It has absolutely nothing new to add to the bland, tired genre of games it belongs to, besides the emotional story the blandness hides behind.
Cool. It's story is a little deep, and a little "Go America"-y, a trait that I find charming.
But that's where the compliments stop.
I don't have to explain how this game works, because you already know. Point your retical at dudes and click a button. Follow little icons using your WASD keys, repeat ad nauseum until you win.
And you know, I really thought that was a stereotype of the genre. No, really. It's reasonable for me to think that just because Call of Duty did it, it doesn't mean that Medal of Honor won't try to throw somethnig new at me.
This game reminded me, "oh yeah. Every modern-styled FPS is trying to BE Call of Duty."
All of it is redundant or boring, almost completely lacking any human input.
And it's easy.
Insultingly easy.
Even with starting on the hardest difficulty, this game is a Sunday morning skip through my front yard. I was literally sliding through doors, where upon my quick halt, I'd shoot one dumbfounded AI soldier in the face, and I stab a horrified terrorist on my right, busy reading something like Ulysses, translating from latin to balochi, taking his sweet time to respond to the death of his buddy.
Other times, the terrorists would just shoot at me while my avatar, invulnerable, stands out in the open, taking it all, alive as some very coordinated zombie.
And then other times, I just slowly walk towards my foes while they just stand and stare. Eventually, they start shooting. I realize I have an empty gauge, so I decided to reload my gun, being pumped in the heart with hundreds of dollars worth of bullets. I shoot. I kill the dude, still with half of my health left, which is instantly refilled, let's see, one second later.
I have only died about 5 times.
On hard mode.
That just speaks for itself.
My PC is very nice. It can definitley handle games with this much graphical calibur and then some, but it's so horribly ported from consoles, textures are constantly popping in and out. Tall grass looks like it's been taken straight out of Doom, facing the same direction no matter where you stand.
So no. I recommend that you don't buy Medal of Honor.
Unless you're a masochist, in which, yes, you should buy this.

I was a little lost at first, but the tutorial helped get started. This software is full of capabilities, it supplies a large library of generator parts, which you can pick from to assemble your character.
But I was more interested in using my own custom parts for my own game that do not use any RPG Maker engine. I was glad to see that this program can adapt to any sprite format you need:
- You can create a new blank document with as many views as you want (for instance, walk, run, fight, etc...), and where each view has its own frame layout.
- You can define animations for your custom character format that can be played in the animation player. Animations are played
you are editing your character, which greatly helps get a preview of your work.
- Most importantly, you can import your own generator parts in it. You can proceed in two ways: either by the user interface (which I did), either through some external tool.
- Once your generator parts are added, they appear in the program item library along with the items that are supplied by default. You can then use your generator parts to create your characters. The program also provides some post-processing tools: you can recolor, resize, draw some parts of your character (like its hair, eyes, cloth). The pixel selection tool allows to be really precise.
- And last but not least: you can define your own random character generator! You start by defining parameters, and then you define which of your generator parts should be spawn and assembled into a character depending on the previously defined parameters. It may seem confusing but it's not. Once the generator is configured, I can randomly generate dozens of female, male, or soldier characters in a single click! I simply set the right values to the parameters that I defined, and click on Generate and voilà!
Conclusion: This program is a very nice character generator. If you take time to learn how to use it, it can be easily used with custom graphic assets, and not only for RPG Maker engine games.

The game is alright. It is pretty addicting and gets frustrating in some levels but has some nice music and looks good.
---Gameplay---
It is a game that is a bit like Super Meat Boy where you have to go from point A to B as fast as you can while dodging obstacles and doing a bit of puzzling. If you die you go back to a checkpoint and continue, but you lose time and for some achievements you have to try not dying at all which can be hard. You can move left and right, slide and jump. Along the way in some levels there are also powerups like dubble jump or speed boost which can be used. If you fail within the time for the achievement there is a ghost 'you" that you can race against.
---Visual & Music---
The game looks good, it uses bright colors with good looking backgrounds. The environment changes a bit with the music like some of the moving elements will adapt to the beat, but you almost do not notice it. This is a shame, I like the concept but the execution is not good enough to really make a difference. The music is a dubstepp/dance kind of music which is really good, but sometimes also distracting. And you can use your own music like in Audiosurf.
---Score---

Thumbs up for this program. It's a good character generator:
- It is faster than RPG Maker MV character generator because it offers an option to any amount of characters in one click (for instance, you can ask the program to generate 200 random white elf female MV characters, and it will generate each sprite for the 200 characters in the folder you want).
- It is also more flexible than MV generator: you can build your character manually part by part, by picking character parts from the "library". Each part is added as a layer which can edit as you please (recolor, resize, rotate, draw over it, add noise, change opacity, blending options, etc...). It adds more versitality to the characters we can make!
Once the work is done, it's easy to import the character to MV: the program exports each sprite into its own PNG file. It's then easy to move them into your MV project folder.

I come from the area of stealth lovers. As a stealth lover I often play games like Metal Gear and Splinter Cell. So it is no surprise that I have found this game! I have a need a need… to be unheard and unseen, like a phantom in the night.
This game reminds me of the multiplayer on the Splinter Cell series. Spies versus Merks is a game where one team with heavy weaponry and little vision. With only their flashlights for site in the dark. The other team the ability to see in the dark and escape in shadow.
Of Guards and Thieves filled the whole Ubisoft left when they took my beloved Spies versus Merks out into the backyard and beat it over the head with sticks and stupidity. After that incident I couldn't find the game that was as good as what Spies versus Merks was. And this is it, Of Guards and Thieves has given me what I've been looking for.
Not only that but there are other game modes besides the asymmetric game mode of stealth action. A variety of games and more to come. Such as Zombie Rush, Mad Ball, Soccer (Football), and Instagib (A game type taken from the classic game Quake). Even a level editor currently not released but will be. Soon I hope!
PROS:
An easy game to learn and play. There are not many game breaking glitches and the ones that are there are not easy to come by. Like I stated above it filled my need for stealth. You can lose yourself for hours in this game. The art style is perfect!
CONS:
Players on the game are rare to find when it comes to someone that knows what they're doing. Some classes on the thief side are unbalanced such as the medic, more of a personal opinion but I feel the medic on the thief side is pointless. As well as the juggernaut, a heavy weaponry class given to the thieves that is pretty powerful. I have given a suggestion to the developers in terms of balance in this class. However no response has been given. On that topic the developers are not clear whether or not your opinion and suggestions are noted. The developers haven't given a clear direction for this game. Whether or not it's going to be Free to Pay or one time pay model. If the idea of an almost purely economical RTS "battle" appeals to you, then this is a game you definitely should own. However I feel like the 40 dollar price tag is too steep for what it is.
First off, where this game really shines is multiplayer. Small battles, even just 1v1 with a friend, are really fun. Everything is about speed. The game is different from most traditional city builders. There's not a whole lot of "city building" going on. That is to say, the way that you decide to lay out your "town" is not overly important to the game. You can get certain bonuses for having some buildings next to others. For instance, placing any building next to another of the same type gives you a production bonus that is stackable, and buildings touching your HQ don't need fuel for transporting goods. Other than that, city design isn't a prominent aspect. Instead, the gameplay is all about speed. Claim territory, make money, and claim more territory as fast as possible.
More often than not, the person who manages to claim the best territory the fastest will end up winning. Because of this, games can often be decided in the first 5-10 minutes. They also usually don't last more than 20-30 minutes. That is part of what makes the game so cool. If you're looking for a quick multiplayer session with a friend, it can become a natural choice if you're both good at it. Skirmishes are very fast paced and don't last long so you can squeeze games in whenever you feel like it. However it's also one of the game's hindrances.
I think it could do with a good deal more content. Games almost feel
fast. You rush to figure out what the key resources on the map are and acquire them, rush to build some factories, rush to research some technology to give you advantages, always keeping an eye on the fluctuating prices of various commodities and having to deal with your opponents sabotaging your production through various "black market" means. There's so much to keep track of that games can flip around on you in an instant. One second you can be on top, well ahead of the game, next thing you know WHAM game over you just got bought. It can often leave you going "what the hell just happened?"
This is part of what makes it so fun and deadly, but at times it can feel somewhat lacking. So much of the game is just looking at numbers on the sidebar, constantly guaging prices, resources, buying, and selling. The actual graphics are very nice, but the funny thing is you don't actually spend a lot of time looking at the graphics, because winning is all about crunching numbers quickly. In my opinion the game would be better if there were some more layers of strategy that involved the actual graphical, planet of mars, city building related stuff. That would make this game a 9/10 for me at least. Alas, it does not, but if the devs keep developing it as they are it will get better.
If you get it on sale, it's definitely worth it.
