As many of the other reviews have pointed out here, this game is not at all like Dead Island. It is an action stealth game, with a strong focus on story, and a lot of the complaints about it seem to be from people who did not read the description or any reviews and wanted just more of the same DI. I also liked DI, but please, judge this game for what it is actually trying to do here.
Pros
-Amazing story. One of the best stories involving zombies period. It's not the standard "bunch of survivors who don't get along," it tries to do something new and really succeeds.
-Good graphics. Cell shaded comic book stuff, but occasionally uses that look to do some really cool, surprising things.
-Fine combat/stealth. This isn't the reason to buy this game, but it works fine. Hits feel weighty, like they should, stealth isn't overly complicated, and you can usually handle the stand-up fight if stealth fails. Takes a little thought to get dodging and timing right, but once you get it, it's fun and not particularly frustrating.
Cons
-A little clunky. EDI was developed by a small team, and it kinda shows. Nothing is particularly fluid, but not in a way to really take you out of it. Some invisible walls and getting stuck on terrain, but it's better than quite a few AAA titles out there.
-Unskippable cutscenes. Some are skippable, but most are not, and they replay if you die after one. Annoying, and they waste a few seconds each time.
-Weapon switching. It takes about a second after selecting a weapon, for Cliff to start switching, which is frustrating when the zombies you were shooting jump at you, and you want a melee weapon quick. This killed me most of the times I died, and you really need to do some planning for when you will need something.
A final note: when I started this game, I was not very into it. Cliff begins as an incredibly insufferable character, the tutorial has you going back and forth though the same areas, and I hadn't really got a handle of the combat. But, having played trough the whole thing, there is a good reason for those things. It is important that Cliff is a jerk, and the game is better for it, same with the backtracking. So keep with it, and play it for what it is, a truly great story in a good action-stealth game.

I bought this game awhile back when it was on sale and it's been sitting in my library collecting dust. Finally I got around to give it a try and I'm really glad that I did. I'm a huge fan of the Dead Island series but this one is definetly not the same as the rest. This game isn't made by the same people who did the Dead Island series, Techland. It's made by Fatshark. So with that being said, most ppl should know it's not going to be the same exact anything from the others. Clearly if you watch the trailer or gameplays, you can see that for yourself.
This is a third person action adventure game. It can be approached with a stealth style or pure hack n slash with it's variety of melee weapons you encounter through the game. You also can choose to use gunplay as well, also just about finding the different kinds of weapons throughout the game. t's a cel shaded graphics style game which I happen to be a fan of. None of the weapons are customizable as in the other DI series and I didn't mind that much, no skill trees for your character either which was fine. The plot is basically how the zombie outbreak in Banoi Islands took place, the who and the why.
I know that this game has a lot of negative comments and reviews just like some of the other DI franchise did. I tend to not really believe much of the hype and find out for myself.  Sure everygame has a few glitches here and there but to be honest I only came across 1 in my whole gameplay. I had died and when I was respawning, I kept falling through the game model into a cloud of nothing, over and over. So a simple fix was to quit the game and join back in. It worked and I was in the exact same spot but this time no falling :) So the melee combat isn't superb and I found to be a tad bit clunky but a lot of that has to do with timing and knowing when to dodge and swing. Which is why I think why most ppl gave it bad reviews in this area. Which is cuz most ppl want to just go in and slaughter, fast and easy. Where in some cases especially on the special zombies, you have to know their moves and how to handle them properly. So it takes a bit of skill, smarts and ofc good hand and eye coordination (timing) So if you're one to be a bit lazy in those departments, this game may not be for you. One thing I did find extremely annoying was there were certain scenes you could skip. If you died though, the short cut scenes couldn't be skipped. And I won't lie, I died quite a few times especially in the area leading up to the final boss scene. Hearing the same short lines over and over can make you go a bit postal if you let it lol. But other than that, it's a small gripe that can be overlooked in my opinion. If you still are unsure if this game is for you, my best recommendation is to do your research. Check out gameplay videos and see for yourself, hearing other ppls opinions will only take you so far. At the end of the day, we aren't all alike so you know best & what's good for you. But I definetaly recommend this game, grab it when it's on sale and get to killing! =)

I saw many videos and trailers of this gmae and thought "hell yeah, that looks like fun. I'll buy it together with my friend and then we'll play and fun bla bla...".
But when it was released the hype was away and we waited for a sale....we got it. We paid 1€ each....and we want it back. A cup of ice cream would have been a lot more fun for the money.
Now to the real review (I've been even using the Co-Op Mode): The game is fast and dynamic, in the first few seconds it's awesome, but soon the first flaws appear:
- Why do they have a running animation, when you can spam the slide and are a lot faster? Keep that away, it looks like you're glitching, but if you're not doing it, you know that you should do it or you'll lose.
- The game and level design is awful. Flash games look better and are for free. And you can't really tell if an obsticle is just there or if it is deadly. Maybe it is the color, but everything is glowing and so I didn't care and got kinda frustrated. And if you play coop and "kill" your friend....oh god the animations look so horrible.
- There's no aim. You have all songs and all levels (or am I wrong? But starting with over 30 levels doesn't seem too unlockable) and therefore I don't know for what I'm playing. Me and my friend were battling and the winner got...nothing. We started the next level, had a bit fun, but it got boring soooo fast. Now you're asking "but there are achievements which save us!" Wrong. "Beat XX in YY seconds." that's it. For every level. Yay.
- The level design isn't fun. In games like VVVVVV or Super Meat Boy (which I have both beaten with a sh*tload of fun) everything was hard, but fair or fun. In RB you run, fly or fall into something and ask "WHY? WOW IS THIS SUPPOSED TO BE FUN". My friend isn't a noob either and had the same questions.
- The music is meh. I'm totally into EDM and it's the most common thing I hear, but in the game I liked about 2 songs (one was the main theme). After using my songs (which took an eternity to load, my friend dealt with the same issue) the levels didn't change that much, so no "wow" in this either.
After all, this game is so disappointing, even for paying only 1€.

More than a year ago, the developer of this program went to Gamefaqs to get some opinions on the software. I had been planning on building a new system with lots of extra RAM and this was the perfect excuse to have that extra RAM so I bought it way back then.
Now I see it's on steam which is excellent.  I've used the program off and on for more than a year and I'm very impressed with the progress Tim has made.  The interface is more polished and I think everything in general seems to work a bit more smoothly.
Games may appear to take longer to launch, but that's because it's putting everything into RAM for use later.  One delay and then lightning fast access times.
Now I just need to buy another 16GB of RAM
EDIT:  So having 16GB of RAM only realistically leaves me with 8 or 9 GB to use as a RAMdisk, but thankfully you don't need to store the entire thing in RAM.  You store the most commonly used files in the RAMdisk and leave the rest on the hard drive and you're fine.
I've been using it with Elite Dangerous and also combining it with the USB 3.0 thing and it really doesn't take much extra time at all to get started... I see it start loading the most used files into memory for about 20-30 seconds and then after that I'm done.
I start up the game and anything that would normally take time to load is down to nothing.  I still have to wait if the game decides to lag on me (like going into supercruise) but that's a network issue, not a drive issue.
They've also fixed the problem of this showing up as the game you're playing 24/7.  Now you start it up, it runs for a minute or so and then steam stops showing it as active so you can play something else.
The Instructional videos Tim has put up are a big help if you're not sure how to get a certain game working right.

I loved the original, but lets face it, there comes a point when there is no more challenge or suprise to obliterating your opponents on the field of battle. That game was drying up for me, it was finished.
Then this little gem appeared, and the love was reborn!
The game is the same concept; pick a faction, crush the opposition.
What makes this game so great? They give you freaking muskets, pistols, and grenades!
The reload spead is faster than reality, but who wants to stand around reloading all the time?
But the powder weapons, even at their worst stats are devastating.
The grenades are a lot of fun, but leave a bit to be desired. You can choose from three different sizes: Small medium and large. (Sounds like a freaking fast food menu, right?) The problem with each of them is they do not replenish after each battle as bullets and arrows do. But hey, they're already OP, so theres gotta be a drawback somewhere, right? Now here's where I have an issue with the game: Some unknown set of circumstances casues them to explode but do no damage. (Believe me, Im not missing. When you are taking the walls and you are the first one up, get to the top of the ladder and look down at the horde waiting for you [units set at 150]. You cant miss a target like that if you tried. So after the first two grenades, the rest seem to stop working.) But with any of the three types of grenades, you can expect 3-4 kills with one throw. Oh! There is nothing more satisfying than watching a surge of blood-thirsty warriors coming at you with every ounce of confidence that you are going to be splattered across the walls. Then with a single throw, 7 of them just drop dead. And the rest? Well, there seems to be a large impact on morale with these explosions. Sometimes you dont even have to hit anyone. They hear these beasts go off nearby, and that's all for them! FT! Im done!!
Another drawback to this game: They took out a lot of the weapons you could get in the original. My favorite was the heavy axe (Or something it was a one-hamded axe, dealing 40c) and they also took out the lucern (Fudge spealling, the pole-hammer) both gone. Replaced now by generic fencing swords and eastern equivalents. The game is still entirely playable, but you just yearn for your tried and true steel buddies of old.
Other features of note: You can upgrade and armor recruits at mercenary camps. Each camp has their own nationality and their upgrades only affect that nationality. (Rascist, I know)
In cities and Castles/fortresses: You can visit Weapon, Armor, and Horse masters to order "custom" associated gear. There is also a WONDERFUL new adition of the Merchant Guild!! Leave a couple thousand Thaler (money) at the "bank" and let it accrue interest.
Theres even more to mention, but if you even managed to get this far in my review, I salute you! If you liked Warband, just stop reading and get Fire and Sword already! You wont regret it!

I've used tons of RAM drives and while they all obviously run at the same speeds (as that is hardware based), Dimmdrive has the best UI, is the easiest to use, and offers more features than any other one I've ever used. Dimmdrive is the ONLY RAM drive that is offered on Steam and is the only one ever made that automatically syncs with Steam.
Unlike the non-Steam version of Dimmdrive, this version is usable offline, which is a pretty big deal to people with laptops with a good amount of RAM and/or people who have bad internet connections.
All currently downloaded Steam games automatically appear in Dimmdrive without any need for user input, and non-Steam programs (like EA games, Ubisoft games, LoL, WoW, etc.) are super easy to put into Dimmdrive.
Dimmdrive is the only RAM disk that I have ever seen that allows for you to select specific files from a game, letting you play larger games (say 20GB) on computers with less RAM (say 16GB). This is a pretty big deal, especially considering that a lot of newer games have been ridiculously large.
While SSDs are really fast, they come nowhere close to the speed of even the crappiest quality RAM. To match the speeds offered by Dimmdrive with SSDs you would need to spend thousands of dollars and put dozens of SSDs in RAID together.
I recommend Dimmdrive to anybody with at least 8GB of RAM and I recommend it as a MUST HAVE program for anybody with 16GB or more.
I will not play any game on my PC with slower than instantaneous load times without using Dimmdrive.

Admittedly I was hesitant about purchasing For Honor for a few reasons but the main ones being:
1) it's a Ubisoft game, notoriously horrible issues on PC versions of their games
2) No dedicated servers, in a game that's making a name for itself through it's multiplayer component
That being said, it has arguably some of the best and most realistic graphics I have ever seen in a PC game. Not only are the graphics amazing it runs incredibly smooth maxed out (i5, GTX970, 16GB RAM). It does not feel like a clunky console port, but rather a well progammed PC game.
As for the multiplayer, I have had barely any issues. No more than what I would otherwise get in games that do have dedicated servers. I have had no issues with lag or packet loss, and if the host does drop out, a suitable replacement is put forth to take over the connection without issue.
Overall, very glad that For Honor is as good as I had hoped and the potential negatives have not come forth. 10/10 good game!

TL DR: The game has a few technical issues right now, but nothing critical. It's still one of the best games I've played in the last years (30 hours in 3 days tells something about being hooked). I would expect a game of such gameplay quality from Blizzard, not from Ubisoft.
PROS
- Easy to get into, hard to master (particularly on some characters)
- Dark Souls-like combat, MK-like combinations and cancels, Chivalry-like setting (what can be better?)
- Deep metagame (numerous ways to surprise your opponent, victory heavily depends on being able to adapt to your opponent playstyle and counter it)
- Almost endless customization (don't even get me started here)
- Enough characters with different playstyles to fit any kind of player
- Great and extensive progression that will take a couple hundred hours at least to fully beat
- Kills are extremely satisfying, deaths are infurating as hell (the game is really good at provoking true, primal emotions in you)
- Bots in this game decimate and BM you (I swear it's hilarious)
- Beautiful, seamless and fluid animations (on par with Witcher 3)
- Atmospheric and well-designed maps (except for a few oversights here and there)
- Amazing visuals
CONS
- Random disconnects. Sometimes the game will drop you from battles and kick you from matchmaking queue. You can simply requeue though, so nothing too bad here. Doesn't happen too often to be very noticeable and is probably going to be addressed soon.
- Language lock. Some regions are language-locked (including mine). However, you don't really see any text in this game and all the audio is English, so not a big deal unlike singleplayer titles.
SUBJECTIVE
- Connection type. A lot of people claim it's P2P while it's not, however the only fact that it doesn't have dedicated servers is enough to turn many away from this game. Firstly, the game is P2M (peer-to-master) which means it chooses the best machine (best connection, best hardware) to host a game on and validate player actions with additional cheater protection unlike peer-to-peer when everyone is connected to everyone else. Secondly, if you have a good connection and just ignore the p2p cancer for a moment to actually try this game, you'll probably find it's absolutely fine. I haven't had a single lag or ping issue with it. The game attempts to recognize your NAT type and assigns a color to you — if it's green, you're golden. If it's not green, you can try different tweaks that are usually done in your router settings or with the help of your ISP (UPNP, port forwarding, static IP) and get it to be recognized as open (green).
- Microtransactions. Yes, there are microtransactions in the game, and yes, some of them even directly influence your effective power in battles (I say effective because it's only up to you if you can benefit from it). However, since players are matched by their relative skill and performance, it doesn't really matter. If you spend a lot on buying equipment but you're not a top player, you will still have a lot of fun because the game will match you against an opponent with similar performance, not simply by gear. Besides, there's no content hidden behind paywalls - you can achieve anything simply by playing. And there are separate modes in the game where gear is disabled (like duel and brawl). All in all, I haven't noticed microtransactions being an issue in the game.
- No harsh leaver penalty. Actually, if you leave you don't get anything for the battle which already is a penalty since people mostly play for XP/steel and victories. Besides, you probably get an automatic defeat which screws your winrate. How is that not a penalty? A leaver instantly gets replaced by a bot player, and trust me - bots in this game are brutal, level 3 bots are better than 90% of players.

The game; 'Friday the 13th' revolves around a group of counselors attempting to escape the masked killer: 'Jason Voorhees'. But you all already knew that. So, here's my opinion on this game and you can draw your own conclusions from it. Lets begin with the Pros and Cons.
Pros:
- Fun with groups of people
- Multiple ways of escape means the game is less repetitive
- Range of stats for each counselor that suits to different styles of gameplay
- Has aspects that are just like the movie, giving it a nice feel to those who watched them.
- Graphically looks nice
Now for the Cons:
- Glitchy at times
- Animations somewhat clunky
- Limited content at this time
- Combat is questionable
Now for an 'explanation'. The game itself is really fun to play, but definitely more so with friends. You will have games where you are alive for 5 seconds and believe me they suck. But you will also have games where Jason nearly gets you and you just manage to escape, which feels amazing. One issue people have with the game is its price, which, currently is understandable. If the game would not have any more added to it besides counselors or maps etc I would completely agree. The reason for me not agreeing with this and instead saying that it is indeed worth the price boils down to one specific, that being Singleplayer. Once singleplayer is released (being released this summer in the US) I personally believe it will be well worth the current pricing.
So, to wrap things up, this game is very fun and worth it. Would recommend to play with friends, however, by yourself is still fun.
Edit: They removed Oceania servers so now I can't play without lagging everywhere. Fun.

KoTOR 2 is one of the best Star Wars stories ever told in any medium. For that reason alone, this game is a must-have for Star Wars lovers and casual gamers of all stripes. It has also aged well - I've played both Kotor games off and on since they came out over 10 years ago, and most recently binged on Kotor 2 for like 60 hours over winter break 2015. Not too shabby at all for a winter 2004 rush release, eh?
The game engine is, of course, exactly the same as the first Kotor's, with most play remaining the same. However, just enough updates were made (cooler powers, no more level cap, more Jedi classes, better crafting, actual use of "skills", "influence" with party) to make the gameplay experience of the sequel a lot more fun than the original. Replayability is quite high as well, as certain important plot points can diverge greatly depending upon your dialogue choices and overall play style. I was still discovering the occasional new cutscene as late as this year.
That said, DO NOT PLAY the vanilla version of this game. Remember: it was a rush release, and parts of it were broken as♥♥♥♥♥♥before some saintly modders got to it and made it the gem we all knew it could be. Before you even start a game, download the Restored Content Mod off of Steam, which puts back in all the best of the mechanics that didn't quite make it into the original release, as well as some great content that was inexplicably cut. If, after the first playthrough with the mod, you still want more, you can also download the other part of TSLRCM (not included in the regular Steam package, for good reason), which puts in a whole other planet that didn't make it to market. The quality of this planet is not always wonderful, mostly because there was no original voice acting, but it does allow you to tie up a questline or two more neatly than in the basic version and build up some more levels, which is always nice.
TL;DR: 10/10 will still be playing this game in 2024, as long as it's modded. Also, it's way better than The Force Awakens.

This is quite a special game that does not fit into any conventional category. It's an RTS-like game but there are no combat units to manage. You win by out thinking your opponents (AI, in my case) by outplaying them in the commodity market. The game's premise is that you and a few other AIs are setting up shop in Mars. You race against each other to see who make the most money out of mining minerals in the planet. The more of certain minerals you sell, the price of the minerals will go down in the stock market. This manipulation of the stock market will enable you to influence the net worth of your company as well as your opponent's. You win buy buying the company shares, having a corporate take over. The action is pretty intense and yet, you can always auto pause to take a breather and think of your next strategy. Having high reflex and able to execute many actions per minutes does not matter here, this is not your usual RTS. And yet, the amount of excitement from creating espionage to influece the stock markets, causing the shares of your competitors to drop is very real. Each game is short, maybe an hour for each sitting, very useful for a quick fix before bed. Highly recommended!

As a big fan of 2D sidescrolling puzzle platformers, Nihilumbra gave me exactly what I wanted while also bringing in a fresh perspective.
You play as Born, a creature that was created in the Void, and you are trying to outrun your fate while discovering the new world you are in. You learn to use elements of the world to your advantage, by finding colors and 'painting' (or erasing) those elements onto the world around you. You can make yourself slide, bounce, etc. You can also use those elements to make OTHER things in the world slide, bounce, and so on. This becomes fun pretty fast, and satisfying as well. The satisfaction I used to feel after making something blow up in Oddworld is the same satisfaction I feel when I make a monster slide off a platform or I successfully rebound a bullet off of a few walls to thwart my enemy.
Most of the levels can be taken at your own pace, and offer fair, regularly placed checkpoints to assistant you in advancing. There are a few, but still fair, timed levels, where the Void chases you. There are checkpoints during these levels as well, and though I normally hate timed levels in platformers, these are made to be player-friendly.
Though there is a lot of dialog from the narrator, it's spoken as you move, so you don't have to stop for it. So far the levels have been increasing slowly in difficulty, allowing the player to adjust as they continue.
I think this is a great game for any for any fans of puzzle platformers. It has the feeling of being detailed, unique, and well thought out, though it's easy to toggle through your colors/elements with a click of the mouse, so it's also nice that it's far easier to control than some other games I've come across.

If I had to describe what Offworld Trading Company is like, the closest games to it in terms of feel and gameplay are those from the Starcraft franchise, minus all the combat units. That sounded like a good sales pitch to me- I've played a bunch of Starcraft and Starcraft 2 and enjoyed them thoroughly.
The problem with this is that if you analyze a Starcraft game, the first few minutes are always the most boring ones- you (usually) just execute some well-rehearsed build order before you get to the more interesting and exciting parts where your units interact with your opponents'- and Offworld Trading Company never gets to that part, by design. There are no units, no army compositions, no micro-management. The entire game is like those boring first few minutes of every Starcraft match, but there's no payoff afterwards.
The Free-for-All nature of the game's standard game mode is problematic. The optimal move is to invest in raising your income and buying as much stock for your own company as possible and not waste any money buying your opponents' stock until endgame where the Offworld Market gives you (or your opponents) enough money to win the game. The extremely passive gameplay that the game rewards makes getting to the lategame feel like a chore, and victory does not feel very exciting. You can mess with your foes via industrial sabotage, but it doesn't feel very satisfying when you use it (whereas it does feel annoying when it gets used against you).
There is a frustrating lack of clarity as to the game's systems. Last game I played, I had bought out 2 of my 3 opponents, had the most improvements to my production buildings and the most patents, plus the most total land claims... and yet my remaining opponent's stock value was somehow 50% higher than mine. Why was it higher? I have no idea. But his higher stock value meant that he managed to buy me out first, so I lost- and I have no idea what it was that I did wrong, or how to do better next game.
I'll end my review by saying that Offworld Trading Company is a very innovative game. I haven't seen another game quite like it and I'm glad to see new concepts like this one take form. That said, for all its innovation, Offworld Trading Company is not a good game. I never really enjoyed any of it, and I would not recommend it to anyone.

Alright, I am very conflicted with this one.
I got this game in a bundle and thought I might use it to get into the Dead Island franchise, since I had heard of it but never actually played it. Didn't need to go far into the game to realize this isn't really what I expected Dead Island to be...I could tell without ever having played Dead Island in the first place. From the beginning to the end, I really couldn't tell whether I enjoyed playing it or hated it. The story bounced back and forth between being interesting and cliche, the characters between likable and completely forgettable, even the combat was a mixed bag. Let me elaborate:
Story:
The story revolves around the main guy, Cliff. He is an okay dude. He sets off with his friends to investigate the quarantine of some island to write a huge story about it and get approved by his father, who recently disowned him for being a f*ckup. He is accompanied by a nerdy girl and some black dude, who really doesn't add anything o the story. The chick, Linda, however, does. At least more than the other dude does.
You can pretty much guess the rest from there. They get to the island, get stranded, then try to escape. This part of the story is actually pretty stale because it is pretty linear and on the level of "fetch me three keycards from around the island to get the master key to unlock the secret dungeon"-kind of storytelling. It felt like a chore more than anything, despite being so easy, due to all the pointless backtracking.
The interesting stuff, however, happens in between all the backtracking in form of Cliff's growing lunacy.  It's the only unpredictable part of the story and is what keeps it fresh and interesting, even just because it feels so random and weird. It's also very entertaining because the voice actress for Linda who voices his mad side actually does a very good job for it, sounding so delighted, teasing and mocking whenever it is needed. I enjoyed those passages.
Sadly however, and this is a spoiler, it never actually gets explained what causes this madness. The best bet I have is that hitting his head upon trying to save the boat caused Cliff to lose it, but that's really stretching it. It also never got explained why the boat's engine suddenly exploded in the first place. Feels like a plothole to me.
Characters:
Well, Cliff is an alright dude. He starts as a cocky jock and while his cockiness never changes, he does undergo a certain growth in my opinion. My main gripe with him as a character is less due to how he is written and more due to how it never gets explained what actually happens to him. The player's curiosity about his mental health gets piked to the max only to never get an answer to it in the end.
Linda starts off as a character you would normally disregard as someone who would die first for shock value, never to be important again. Turns out she stuck around until the end, after all. And in a way I would have never expected her to. In hindsight, I would actually have to say she was probably even the most entertaining character in this whole story.
Davan, the token black dude, felt like he was...just there. Sure, at one point it all began revolving around him when it came to actually escaping, but for the majority of the game he just exists as a name in the back of your head. You don't see him, you don't hear him and over all you don't really care about him anyway because you expect nothing from him. Sadly, I was right about him from the start. He seems to be a nice guy, but he adds nothing meaningful to the story.
The other characters in this game are...sort of a mystery to me. They exist, but I don't really get why. Could be that they are cameos of the Dead Island franchise I don't recognize, but I somehow doubt that.
There is a Chinese chick who crash lands on the island only to ever be cryptic about her goals and intentions. All she ever does is provide Cliff with weapons she just drops at his feet as if she didn't have a need for them in the first place. If I didn't know better, I would say she was a plot device to give Cliff new weapons as well as his quest to search for the key cards.
Aaron the mutant and the chick that was with him...I don't get what their deal was at all. They weren't antagonists despite sometimes trying to look like ones. At least they didn't feel like ones.
Well, in the end, it just boils down to Cliff and Linda who are interesting and everyone else who, sadly, isn't.
Gameplay:
This is where people will most likely get disappointed, for the combat itself isn't very deep. It just boils down to hitting zombies with a melee attack until they die. Aiming feels wonky and redundant when almost all enemies in this game a close combat oriented and rush you like maniacs. There is never enough time to reload, so why bother?
Yet, despite this simplicity, you will likely still get the impression this game might be "hard", but that's not due to complex combat mechanics, but rather due to the games unforgiving checkpoints. You will find yourself getting put back to placed you had been MINUTES ago, even several fights prior to the one you died in. In the first place, you likely died because you accidentally missed one of your three combo hits on a zombie, causing him to recover and hit you back. That's actually the only reason to ever die. To mess up a combo and be out of stamina to dodge away. Needless to say, it adds to your frustration to have this annoyingly long death and revive animation upon death. While it is cool and fits the theme, I just wish it would be cancel-able.
The enemy's AI is generally potato level. They just rush blindly at you and perform their single scripted attack.  Once you learn how that attack loops, you will never have trouble with them at all. You only die if your dodge gets body blocked by the environment or enemies or when a combo of your axe doesn't connect. Wouldn't be a problem if it wouldn't send your character 10 minutes back in time upon respawn...
The combat CAN be fun sometimes, when there are new things to test out, such as new weapons or environmental damage like electricity or pushing enemies into rapidly moving fans. However, it gets stale really fast and you will find yourself running past most enemies if possible (most enemies will be too stupid to notice you unless it's a scripted battle)
Sound:
The overall quality of the VA and music is pretty good. Never found a reason to complain. There were even a few cases where I thought the Voice over was especially well done.
Overall:
Well, I would be lying if I said I didn't get SOME enjoyment out of this game, but most of it was experienced only during the endgame and mainly the last level. Sh*t really hits the fan then and the game becomes a madness simulator, which I enjoyed at least as much as it confused me.
Unfortunately, this leaves the rest of the game, namely the beginning and middle part, to be very boring. The DLC that adds another underground level also feels very weak. While it certainly was the longest level in the game, its design was very underwhelming, consisting only of tunnels upon tunnels of grey and dark concrete or steel. There was little to see and many enemies to grind through (which, remember, is boring since the combat is stale) only to reward the player with no cutscene whatsoever. You beat the level, faint and start at the entrance of the level again as if nothing ever happened. What a huge waste of time :/
Given how the most enjoyable thing about this game was Cliff's madness and Linda's role in it, you could probably do yourself the favor and save yourself the money by watching a Let's play instead. If there were an option to give neutral feedback, I would have chosen that, but since there isn't, I will have to go with a negative one, since there are less good things about this game than bad things.

This is essentially a classic adventure game set in Dead Island's "Banoi Archepelago". It touches a bit heavy on stealth, spookiness, and wiredness than the original games do. There are no rpg elements, its straight adventure, exploration, and upgrade collecting.
If you're squeamish about horror games (I handle horror like a ♥♥♥♥♥) but still want a bit of a scare this is absolutely perfect. It doesn't go full bore "Gonna♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants" horror, but retains a fantastic thrill element.
Combat is simple, very different from DI's combat, but they did keep the stamina system and I feel it is implemented very well. Weapon swapping and reloading is a ♥♥♥♥♥ and will often break, forcing you to try again. This is onlly seemed to be an issue while cornered or surrounded. (Could just be me panicking)
Cutscenes and story are done very nicely, including almost MGS-esque artwork on some cutscenes. There were a few times where the voice lines or models bugged during a cutscene, and the character would awkwardly stand still while things were going on shouting randomly.
A fair warning on the story. Hide the ♥♥♥♥ing peanut butter, because♥♥♥♥♥♥is about to get weird.

Summary: fastpaced, action game, it was a steal on release price.
Let me get the bad out of the way first:
- Story is not at all interesting nor compelling.
- Doesn't stand up to its predecessor's level of comedy.
The good far outweighs the bad IMO:
- Open level design: procedually generated blocks, but has enough variaty to keep all map and encounters interesting.
- Combat variability: Ranged & Melee are both fun to use. Mix that with Ninja abilities, you get a frantic, fastpaced, gore glory action going from encounter to encounter. Not to mention elemental damage.
- Enemy variaty: making a player [forcing on higher difficulties) plot out a strategy before going in. Some kick you away and rain bullets, others hook you in and try to surround you and some explode. With higher levels, you'll see high ranking enemies with immunities to certain abilities and elemental damage types.
- Lots of upgrades for lots of skills, loot for weapons and a crafting system for useless loot. With the updates they added Orbs, which can be used to upgrade weapons further.
- The support for the game: I've hit level 112 on insane difficulty 51+ then i faced enemies i couldnt take down. By then there wasn't much i can do. With current free content, Bounty Hunts award skill points the first time and orbs in the second. The awards increase with difficulty increase. I'm hoping i can exceed the level i was at, though now i'm certain i can.
- Graphical fidelity beyond belief from an indie studio: that said, indies have been looking more and more like AAA titles. This one is special because the PC port is highly optimized and supports technologies that aren't mainstream yet. I'm not ashamed to say i played this game with a controller for one playthrough just to see the HDR everyone is speaking of on my TV that supports it.
Always out numbered, never outguned.
P.S. I get why fans of the original didn't like this one as much. This isn't a sequel, even though it builds on the original plot, its a return to a pure action game. The story/script came last and it shows. The combat system has to be my favorite of all time.

A game i highly recommend, with a warning.
This game is a fantastic amount of fun for a first playthrough. Simple to learn and hard to master combat, great melee combat, fun guns. The first time you play this you will have a ball, especially with friends.
HOWEVER
That comes with a slight set of conditions you need to be aware of.
First off, on difficulties above easy, the game is not a matter of you killing baddies together, its about you and your friends ALL having to focus ALL of their bullets on ALL bad guys to kill them, in a similar vein to borderlands bosses, theres no "duuuuude I killed the bad guy" theres just you and your friends fighting over who got the last shot of 1000 shots in on a baddie. I dislike this myself, but not everyone does. I just tend to prefer difficult enemies or more of the enemies rather than just making the same enemies into bullet sponges.
Speaking of that, theres very few bosses that arent just massive versions of the normal enemies, which is another big red mark for me. I hate that mentality with a passion.
Next is the replayability. This game was touted as a randomized mission generator where you could replay missions over and over and have a new experience every time. The issue is, you can't do that at all. You can revisit "Locales" and just roam around aimlessely killing things, but no redoing missions, no random mission generator (even though that would be stupid easy to implement) You play through the story, then restart, and do it again, no replaying missions or generating new ones.
Last on the red marks list is the RPG system coupled with the guns. In a game with so much firepower diversity, seeing weapons that are statistically total upgrades of other guns is a red mark. All the melee weapons feeling essentially the same (Save for a few that have ranged abilities and such) is another red mark. The RPG system is at both times cool and infuriating. Grinding and desperately trying to get the upgrades you need so your gun doesnt totally suck can take an immense amount of effort and time and its likely it will be a FEW PLAYTHROUGHS before your gun or sword is as badass as you wanted it to be. The bright side to this system is that some upgrades actually drastically alter the guns behaviors (Akimbo, for instance) and are animated and fun and not just stat changes.
So there you have it, I said you should get it then listed problems, how typical of me. Shadow warrior 2 IS fun and it does satisfy that niche where doom meets random generation and has some snuff film aspects thrown in with a peppering of poorly written♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes. You will enjoy this! but the lesson I want to convey is I bought a random generation coop game with tons of guns in it, and only played it for 15 hours, which is just 1 playthrough with all side missions and main missions done to their fullest with LOTS of exploring. A game that offers all this game is supposed to should be a 100+ hour game, easy. Thankfully its price is fair in the face of this, and you will still likely feel you got your moneys worth.

Shadow Warrior is what would happen if Warframe and Borderlands 2 had a child. You slash things, dice things, run around and blast enemies in viceral fast paced combat. You also customize your many kinds of weapons in interesting ways, from adding elemental damage to making your gun blow through your entire ammo supply and kill everything in a ten block radius in like two pulls of the trigger. The weapons are varied enough that most of them feel completely different from one another and the upgrades make it to where you can use one weapon you really like through most, if not all, of the game.
Wang loves combat and also makes phallic jokes constantly. This normally is annoying and not executed well in most games, but in Shadow Warrior 2 Wang seems to somehow stride the line between funny and immature. He constantly makes jokes and doesn't take much seriously, but he does care about WHY he is killing things. I won't spoil much, but there is a mission where he has to save some demon girls and for once he stops being funny and starts being serious, even calling out other allies for not caring enough to save them themselves. So the game doesn't hit the level of humor that gets campy, nor does it take itself too seriously.
The game is also surprisingly deep. There's a lot of world building and lore scattered around the map and it isn't silly tidbits, it is actually well written material and there is a lot of references to japanese and norse mythologies everywhere. Wang himself seems to be a Susano expy, trying to balance his love for combat with doing the right thing.
Overall, Shadow Warrior 2 is just fun. It doesn't really try anything new or groundbreaking. Its a mish mash of a bunch of genres and does all of them pretty well but not expertly. But the combination of all the things just makes for a good time. The co-op makes it even better. The game knows what it is. Its a hack and slash with an interesting story and doesn't try for anything different. It just delivers on those two things perfectly.

I absolutely love survival games.  That said, I played this game for 4.8 hours the first week I had it back in 2014 and I never touched the game again.  That should be all the review you need.  If you want more, read on.
-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-
Back in 2014 I was really on the fence about buying this game in it's Alpha status and had it sitting in my "wish list" on Steam for a few months.  Unable to bare it any longer I did some searching and found a bundle site that had this game available for around $25, which included 7 other games, so I picked it up.  I'm not going to post a link to that bundle, as it's long expired.  Now, on to my first impressions (original review), and then I'll get into updated stuff...
I had a pretty rough time getting started with Life is Feudal, and when I say that I'm not just talking about the lack of any real tutorial.  I mean I actually had to try 5 times to get a game started.  I believe it has to do with the fact that when you play single player you're not actually playing single player.  You're starting up a local multiplayer server and blocking everyone else from joining it.  That, to me, is a serious waste of resources in a game that's already a huge resource hog.  When you run single player it should just run the game, not have to start up it's own private multiplayer server.  It's signs of lazy development, and it didn't stop there.
Once I was in the game I literally had no clue what I was doing.  Pressing F1 got me some basic knowledge of the keys to use but everything else was as confusing as hell.  5 minute tutorial, or tooltip popups when you first open a window, would have been a godsend but sadly the developers didn't bother to program that into the game.  That may have changed by now, I haven't the interest to reinstall this game.
The music in the game was absolutely wonderful, how be it a little repetative after a few hours of playing.  There didn't seem to be enough musical tracks to keep you from noticing the eventual loop.  After a while I simply muted it and fired up Media player with my own music.  Not unheard of with other games, so I'll let it slide with a simple "nothing special" comment.
Sound, on the other hand, was completely nuts.  While I enjoied the occasional sound of wind blowing through the trees, or a bird chirping in the distance, the actual action sounds were apauling.  Eating was, by far, the worse.  Sounded like they put the microphone up to a cow's mouth while it was chewing on straw.  Gathering used the same 5-second audio clip and looped it.  Normally using 1 gathering sound wouldn't be much of a problem, if it didn't loop during the gathering cycle.  But no, every time you gather something in this game it took about 12 seconds, so with a 5 second audio clip you got to hear it almost 2 and a half times.  And trust me, it's noticable.  That's partly because it too is one of the most annoying sounds they could have possibly found for gathering.
The graphics in this game were kind of a mixed bag.  Up close everything was nice and crisp, looked great.  The farther things got away from you, however, the worse they looked.  There was a clear visual line of where the "detail" shut off and left you with just basic forms.  Then, to try to cover it up, it looks like the developer blurred things the farther they got from you.  It looks really sloppy.  I'm not going to harp much more than that about it.  One graphical thing that really bothered me was the fact that when you ripped bark from a tree the tree had no visible appearance change.  Even when you got to a point where it said there was no more bark to strip, the tree looked the same!  After stripping 20 chunks of bark off a tree it shouldn't look the same.  That's just lazy.
Animations in the game weren't much better.  "Praying" was the same animation played over and over again until the progress bar finished.  When you put on ANY equipment it looked like you were patting yourself down.  Gathering plant fiber (grass) resulted in you physically punching the ground.  Gathering rock, bark, or sticks used the same animation which was nothing more than bending down a bit and twiddling your fingers in the air.  Examining an object had virtually no animation, you just stood there while the bar filled up.  Seriously, it's lazy work AGAIN!
Crafting in this game was the highpoint, and why this game got so much attention.  Yes, you can build an entire medieval city from scratch including walls, buildings, houses, keeps, etc...  That said, don't expect to do it quickly.  Unlike other crafting games, in this game you have to grind skills to unlock higher skills.  Hell, I had to click on a tree 190 times and then punch the ground another 78 times before I could craft a log into a nicer log.  Crafting skills take FOREVER to train, although you CAN adjust the learning speed if you like.  That was a smart move on the developers part, because after all that training (at default speeds) I have to admit I was getting REALLY bored.
Speaking of the skill trees, they're quite a mess as well.  I can understand having to practice tilling soil before being able to successfully plant crops.  That makes sense.  What I don't get is why when you learn how to chop down a tree, you can't just do it to any tree.  You start out by only being able to cut down 2 types of trees, and then you have to grind those in order to learn how to chop down another 2 types of trees.  We're not talking about crazy differences here.  I'm pretty sure if you can swing an axe skillfully at a pine tree you can swing an axe with the same skill at an oak tree.  But noooo, not in this game!
All of that aside, the biggest problem with Life is Feudal: Your Own is the developers behind it.  It's almost like they got bored of this game and decided to move on.  Their small indie company has branched off and begun working on two more Life is Feudal franchise games, before finishing with this one, including an MMO.  Speaking of the MMO, it's highly unlikely that this game will ever be finished due to the development shift to take this game into an MMO world.
Because of all of this, I can't recommend this game.  It has way to much grind and way to little of anything else to be an enjoyable survival game.  On top of that, it'll likely never be completed.  The developers are dreaming if they think this game is worth over $40.  I wouldn't value this game much over $25, and even that seems high.  As mentioned, I happened to get this game as part of a bundle for $25, so I'm not too bitter.  While I may not have played this game much, I certainly got my money's worth out of the other games I received along with it.

I was deciding between 3 similar themed games, DayZ, Rust and Nether. Read several reviews and videos of the gameplay, and finally decided to pay for Nether because i was told this is the most "matured" release among the 3 alphas. Logged into the game and first thing is the character creation. At this very point, players are asked to customize their character. Even before getting into the game, i'm instantly disappointed by the approach the developers are taking for Nether. You are only allowed a total of 2 choices, and both are Males. Being a girl, I'm forced to play a male with soldier cut hair. You can further choose a total of 3 type of faces, but all of them looked the same except for their tan colour. The clothes are similarly disappointing, all of which are same except for 3 choice of colours. So there you go, that was as far as you can customize your character. Any other customization at this point of the game involves real-world money. It is a poor approach as we have paid 14.99 for a game that further asks for more money just to gain access to basics like costumes. Imagine that!
Next, in-game. While I fully understand the meaning of Alpha releases, the gameplay is seriously lacking. The servers I joined usually has an average of 20 players. But somehow you almost never see anyone except in the SafeZones (camps where you can purchase things and again spend real world money if you want to buy almost anything that is actually interesting in this game). Sure there are lots and lots of buildings in this game, which one might wish to explore, but you'll soon find out that all the buildings are bare and totally empty and void of any purpose except for players jumping to death from high grounds suicide (so to respawn randomly at better locations)
Game objective - this is another very sore point about Nether. This game is NOT about survival in a deserted city. Do not buy this game thinking of this! I did, and was sorely disappointed. There isnt much to do in-game except running around trying to find "parts of weapons" so you can craft a weapon and actually start to play the game. But again, you'll be very disappointed to find out that once you die, you restart the game again from ZERO. all your earned skills and items are totally gone. Some may argue that this game is about PvP. Well I loved PvP shooters, but this game does not give you any satisfaction from killing other players. The rewards? Probably some canned drinks and chocolate bars - of which is already so easily found in-game that they do not worth anything. The bullets of your gun is probably worth more than what you gain from killing other players.
Perhaps, in the end, people will argue about this game being Alpha, but that doesnt change the fact that everything in-game asks players to spend lots of real-world money. I would forgive this if the game was free to play, but having paid 14.99 for the game and kept being asked for more money to enjoy the game? heck no. Unforgivable.
So summary, to anyone planning to purchase this game? I'm willing to give it away if I can. It is horrible. And the last update to the game was a month ago to date. So, expect slow updates.

I think Nihilumbra kinda went under the radar for pretty much anyone or maybe I wasn't paying enough attention to the news. Nihilumbra is a puzzle platformer with a very unique looking to it, you start the game being born in The Void and after you escape you end up on a strange world where The Void sends his creatures and it's coming to get you. The plot of this game along with a mindblowing soundtrack is what make them one of the best puzzle platformers of this year. According to the narrator, which identity remains a secret, The Void is one and you can't simply escape the void, he needs you in order to become one and that's why he's after you.
[MIGHT CONTAIN SPOILERS FROM NOW ON]
Your journey is divided in various environments ,you'll  travel to cold montains, a desert, a forest, volcanic fields and a city. Each of this places will great you an unique power which comes into place in the form of a colour and you can use them by clicking and dragging the mouse cursor on any surface, the montains grant you the blue colour which when used on any surface will make that surface slippery which will alow you to run or slide faster, the forest will grant you the green colour which if you jump on it it grants you a huge jump boost and sometimes is used for changing enemy projectiles course, in the desert you'll gain access to the brown colour which will grant you the power to slow things down or making you walk stealthly and even get enemies trapped in corners, the volcanic fields of course will grant you the red colour which when an enemy steps on it (including yourself) it will start burning and this is the first time you can actually kill an enemy by yourself and last but by no means least, the city which takes a huge role on the story grants you the colour yellow which represents electricity. During your journey you'll not only use the last power you've earned but you'll also need to remember what you've learned before. When you step into the Cold Montains you feel that you're in a different place from the void, it's cold. When you go into the forest you'll start to notice that everything in it is alive, the trees, the plants, and that starts to make you feel alive in some way, because before you were nothing, you were void. When you go to the Desert you immediately notice it's warmer there than the previous two locations and you start to wonder if you're actually starting to have "something" inside of you. After that comes the volcanic fields in which you feel it's even hotter than the desert and you realize your journey started cold, then warm and now hot and that someone makes you think that you're actually becoming "something". And last, the city, which was once inhabited by someone, there you'll start wondering if those people were actually the ones that doomed this world and not yourself, since the void has been consuming everything while it's after you, the forest, the montains, the volcanos, the desert, everything. And so you realize that youre death is inevitable, it wouldn't matter if you kept running, even though you wanted to be alive, there's no life without death and so you let yourself be consumed by the void but... the void rejects you because throughtout your journey you've consumed the colours and each one of the elements and you've become alive, "the void is nothing and there's nothing in you". And so you become free... but the game doesn't end here. After this end you'll unlock "The Void Mode" which is basicly you fighting off the void that has consumed the world in order to clean your conscience.
Nihilumbra is certainly not a game for everyone, but if you enjoy a great story, very emotional and meaningful then my friend, this game is certainly for you. One of the best indie puzzler platformers I've ever played. I recommend it 100%, please buy it because I don't think it got the attention it deserved.

TL; DR; : Yes, I enjoyed the game somewhat, I liked the story and the sound design(excellent) but I was frustrated by the "stealth"(non-existent) mechanic and poor visuals(see below). Also it was short and all the "puzzles" are laughably easy(no brain needed here). I would recommend it but at about ~20E or less and to somebody who expects more of a "walking simulator" than a stealth game.
To elaborate like I said the story is decent, maybe it would have felt more real if the other aspects of the game were more polished.
STEALTH:
The biggest beef I have is that this is not a stealth game, you basically just find the nearest corner to hide and listen for the "monster" to go away(you can't look at it for long). The AI on the monsters(if it can be called that) is basically just have the monster roam its patrol route. If you get too close it will close in on you but if you find a corner that is out of the way of the patrol path and don't look at it you have a 95% chance to be ignored by it even if it is really close to you(seriously I only got caught about 9  times during the whole game(counting the scripted sequences as well)). Also the monsters seem to be triggerd by your running and this is the only way you can have them run after you(apart from the 2 - 3 scripted sequences, as throwing objects or any other noises do not enter the equation, which again is sad).
So the gameplay around the "creatures" is as follows, avoid patrol route, wait minutes at a time in a corner watching ther ceiling or walls for it to leave the area. Or if you get bored and think you can make it to the elevator/exit/ladder you can run. This is tedious to say the least and the worst part of the game.
GRAPHICS:
Yes I did not expect state of the art graphics. But the garphics are there for immersion and some of the textures are so low res that you have to think they were lazy(the only explanation I can come up with). I mean on "Ultra", the "bulbs" or "nuggets" from the growth on the wall seem awfull pixelated(just an example, there are many more instances where the textures are lacking).
What really bothered me more is the models. They feel so "artificial". The corpses seem plasticky which is a shame because I want to feel disgusted or frightened but the only thing I feel is regret that I couldn't get better looking models in what could have been a really great game.
I'm really not looking for pixels in a game like this but things like this really take away from the experience, like I said this is 2010-graphics they really didn't make an effort.
LENGTH:
Like I said it's very short, I backtracked a lot through the open ocean segments and explored almost everything and I took only 10 hours to do so. Expect about 8 hours on a normal playthrough or if you're really impatient and want to get to the bottom of thinngs expect 6. Pretty short.
PUZZLES:
Like I said no brain required. Why would you include such simple puzzles in a game already intended for mature audiences? There is nothing more to say they are truly so trivial that I feel they were added just to prolong the already short gameplay instead of adding something to the experience.
I focused on criticizing the aspects that I hated, I have nothing agains the story(good) and that sound design will massagge your ears(If you do get it(though you should wait for a cheaper bargain) play it with some high quality speakers or better audiophile headphones).
Fun interesting story. But it feels as if its aimed towards more newer people of the card game.

Overall, I neither hated nor loved Nihilumbra.  If there was a "Meh" recommendation option, I'd pick that.
The first half of the game is enjoyable, which I think most of the reviewers agree on, based on their play times.  The story is interesting and the mechanics are fun and easy to grasp.  8 fairly short levels in each of 5 areas, with a new color/ability found in each area.  There's nothing terribly unique or groundbreaking in the game, but it's 5-10 hours of fun if you just play through the storyline.
On the other hand, the void mode -- which is unlocked after completing the storyline -- is aggravating.  I understand that it's meant to be challenging, but most of the challenge comes not from the puzzles or mechanics, but from the interface.  My main complaint with this part of the game is with the "window" effect -- instead of a smooth side-scroller, we get a series of screens which are mostly independent of each other, puzzle-wise.  Not a big deal until your screen/window resolution actually impacts where this transition occurs.  Too high a resolution, and critters from the next screen react to your presence.  Too low and you may not see a trap before it's too late.  Not to mention there are a few places where you'll want to sit near the edge of that transition area for at least a few seconds to size-up the next screen (I found 1600x1024 to be fairly good for most levels).
With that said, the difficulty also varies wildly, and doesn't present a smooth ramp-up as you progress.  Some late-game levels are easily completable in a few minutes or less, while some mid-game levels requirie multiple retries due to timing/strategy (I'm looking at you, volcano area).
If you can pick this up for under $5 and like a side-scrolling platformer, then definitely get it.  Otherwise, there are probably better games that deserve your time.

This game is brilliant.
An RTS merged with a euro-board game, OTC takes many great things from both camps.  The frantic nature of the traditional RTS doesn't manifest via physical twitchiness like APM based like Starcraft, but rather primarily takes the form of difficult mental calculations in a confined time period.  Speed poker or speed chess comes to mind.  From the euro-game side, OTC takes cutthroat trading, manipulation, and grand economic scheming.  OTC also does something that almost every competitive designer in either of the previously mentioned genres strives for:  It's easy to learn, and extremely difficult to master.
A game of OTC will start with either map exploring, or the players analyzing an already revealed map.  Depending on the resource formations and georgraphy of the map, they decide on a faction and a placement for their main base.  They place a few buildings on resources, and start gathering those resources.  They may place some buildings which refine those resources into something else.  Only 3 or 4 tiles are available at start, though, so decision making is crucial.  From this point forward,  get a few tiles to claim for each 'level' of their homebase, which will increase over time at the cost of resources.
Resources don't have to be mined however:  They can be bought on the open market, in real-time, via a UI on the left corner of the screen.  And this is what makes the game deep and challenging.  Manipulating the markets, observing your opponents, suffocating them when they need a certain resource, faking one strategy and going something else.  There is no fog of war once the game starts, but there is fog of resources, and that can be even more important in this game.
Other than resource collection and creation buildings, there are buildings for upgrades, new scientific patents which of course your company alone will hold if researched, an offworld rocket that allows you to exploit an entirely different market for goods, and a hacker array which allows you to cheat and manipulate the market outside of the usual supply and demand.  Finally, on top of all of this is the black market, a mechanism which gives you some potentially game winning attacks against your opponents.  Crippling a key structure at a key moment, or EMPing someone's solar panels when the sun comes up, right after you've built a few of your own.
The only problems I have with the game are the following:  Not enough people are playing multiplayer, the multiplayer matching and netcode is mediocre at best, and the ladder system doesn't give you much information.  I'd love to see more statistics (factions used, game time, etc), and be able to browse the entire ladder at will.  The campaign, while fun, is just too damn short!  Mohawk added plenty of cool features, like deciding what kind of bonuses to shoot for, and what specialists to buy to customize your company the way you want.  Problem is, the campaign is over once you have a few of them.  Other than these quibbles, OTC is a triumph of game design.  Elegant and polished, fairly simple to get into, but extremely deep in competitive play.   If you like euro-board games, or if you like the mental aspect of competitive play more than the physical aspect (and are ok with economic competition), I'd highly recommend it.

Nihilumbra is a poetic 2D platform game.
In my opinion, it's very similar to Limbo, but the game  also made me think about Another World and Heart Of Darkness for the design, the level-design and the gameplay.
The poetic side of the game is reinforced by the off-voice of the narrator in almost every screen of the story mode.
The story mode is not very difficult, and its main purpose is to tell a poetic story, the birth of the protagonist from the void, and his discovery of our world through different and various landscapes.
The gameplay is based on the mastering of colours, which have different properties, such as the possibility to slide, or to bounce, etc...
Once you've finished the story mode, you unlock the void mode.
Here, forget about the story, the poetism and the narration, it's all about thinking, skill and timing.
The void mode visits all levels of the story mode once again and modifies them into much harder puzzle levels.
It's somehow like the dark world in Super Meat Boy, but in a more easier way though.
I had a good time with this game, and I recommend it to every Limbo-like lovers.
Nihilumbra has just one big problem : its length.
It'll take you about 3 hours (maximum) to finish the story mode, and maybe the double to beat the void mode, depending on your skills.

What a great game! It's definitely unconventional as RTSes go, but what's wrong with that? We're all looking for something new and exciting to try, right? If you are reading this you probably know basically how this game works, so I'll spare you that.
The game is challenging. And to do well even against the non-cheating AI you have to think and react fast. After a while you get to understand the "personality" of the AI and you can get to a point of being able to beat the Manger AI (standard) regularly. At 45 hours I'm not there yet. Once you can do that you can bump up the AI so that it cheats (or maybe you're just handicaped...or both...I actually don't know yet). Better yet, hop into multiplayer and play against people who really know what they're doing. There is ranked 1v1, ranked 4-player free-for-all, and custom games up to 8 players, in free-for-all, teams, and comp stomp.
I've watched some live multiplayer on the MohawkGames twitch channel where they are essentially game casting as they play. Soren (the creator) is pretty good at this, but Zultar is amazing! I have learned from watching them, but the biggest lesson is that there is a huge skill curve to this game. I cannot say whether that skill curve is steep, shallow, or moderate, but there is so much depth to this game that even though I understand all the mechanics I'm not even close to understanding more than 10% of why the top players do what they do. The game has observer and replays, and is pretty well balanced it seems. I've watched some youtube videos of the OTC Tournaments during beta and release, and I personally think this game could make it into the competitive scene, if other top players pick up on this gem.
Now if your major draw to games is graphics, you'll want to pass for now. The graphics don't suck but this game isn't about eye candy. All the factions use the same buildings and "ships", except their starting base. They have some good animations and there is some life to the maps, which is pretty nifty given this is taking place on Mars (cloud shadows, flares, dust storms). I don't spend much time looking at the art...I enjoy the gameplay.
If your major draw to games is character and story, you'll want to pass for now. The tutorial brings a little bit of life and humor to characters that you'll encounter in the campaign. Incidentally the campaign is designed to be played after you've played through the tutorials and have some experience with skirmishes, not before. The campaign is largely a string of skirmishes where you take the role of one of the characters and try to be the best corporation over the course of seven rounds. "Only seven" you ask? The campaign is designed to be more of a single-player mini tournament that is replayable. You play one of the four factions through the rounds, starting with diminished capability but building up toward the final round. Each round you have the chance to gain some new abilities and after each round you "tech up". The maps available to play during each round are selected randomly, so each play-through is different. There is also some progression between runs of the campaign where you get to unlock other campaign characters to play. A neat system, but again not for one who relies upon story.
If your major draw to games is replayability, both singleplayer and multiplayer, this is your game. Skirmish, the campaign, and I think multiplayer have a really neat system to enhance replayability. While there are some preset maps that have standard terrain, I think most games are played on procedurally generated maps, made fair by allowing players to plop down wherever they want. Not only is the map terrain procedurally generated, the resource locations are too. In the game there are some random events, like dust storms and solar flares, plus a colony that affects the economy through granting random bonuses and creating random (though predictable and exploitable) demand. In short, no two games will ever be the same. UNLESS...you input a random seed, which will produce the exact same map if you happen to want to. That's a great idea, which I can see it being used in tournaments.
Lastly there is the "Daily Challenge". This appears to be a skirmish seed that everyone can play to compete for top spot on the day's leaderboard. So far it seems the top spot is whoever can win the game the fastest. And right there next to their time is an icon which you can click to watch the replay! A great way to see how the top players play.
Does this game have what it takes to catch the RTS world's eye? I think so. I hope so. It's the most fun RTS I've played in years. I can envision a future of DLC with more factions, resources, buildings, and gameplay mechanics that will make this game's replayability and multiplayer even richer. But first, you have to buy and play this game. What are you waiting for?
Pro tip: Don't be afraid to bulldoze buildings and put down more profitable ones. The good players are refocusing constantly based upon the market.

The game looks neat... but that's about it. Don't get me wrong it has a unique game style, and it is pretty fun for a few to a couple of hours, but not more than that.
GAME INFO-
Unlike other RTS games, where the player builds and gather resources to buy armies. Offworld Trading Company is mostly about economic RTS. The player has to claim certain lands, which consist of natural resources, and manage those resources by buying and selling on the market. Each player has a share in the stock market and the prices for the stocks will range on how well the players are doing (The better income the higher the stock price will be). There are special abilities that the players can buy from the Black Market and interfere the progress of other players (I will not give the details but players need to buy this abilities to help win the game). Whoever buys all the stocks wins the game.. and that's, that is how to win the game.
It Sounds complicated but it is not. You get the hang of it when playing the game for a couple of hour, but that's the problem. When you start to understand the mechanics of the game it gets boring because the game itself feels very... linear unlike other RTS games. Most RTS you have to strategize your moves and attacks to win the game, and there are so many ways and routes to plan and play which makes you hooked to it for days, months, even years. However, Offworld trading company has limited strategic gameplay... you just manage your resources in the best way to make you profit.
MY OPINION-
+Fun game :D for couple of hours.
-After that not fun :(
+If you are into this type of game go for it.
-If you are not into this game don't buy it because you will regret it when the game is sitting in your library for years and realize that you had only 20 hrs+ or less of in-game.
+Why did I buy the game? Because of Quill18.
+Why did I thumbs up? I had fun even though it was for a couple of hours, and I recommend this game for those who are into Economic RTS.
-But it is too expensive... So
+I recommend this game when the price is low and those who are into this game:p

Honestly, I'm probably a bit biased in saying this because SSD and good internet, but the connection problems that other people seem to be having don't really bother me all that much because I can consistently play a bit before seeing a minor hiccup that doesn't last for more than a few seconds.
That being said, I fooken love this game.
The gameplay is astoundingly complex (when you fight somebody who knows how to play and is experienced). The amount of different heroes adds to the fact that you can adapt to your own playstyle. The amount of different combo strings you can execute are inumerable and its satisfying finding something new you can do with your favorite hero. There are limited game types but that doesn't detract from the main meat of the gameplay.
The faction system isn't that interesting but it can be like rooting for a team in whatever sportsball game you enjoy watching, so its mainly just not for me. You can choose from three factions (I chose samurai by accident) and can deploy war assets when you complete games. There are seasons and rounds and junk that I don't really care for. I'm just in it for the meaty goodness that is fighting.
The graphics look really nice when playing on a decent rig! I haven't had any experience on a lesser machine (I'm running a 1080 and 6700k) so I can't really speak for that. But the characters are well designed, the animations are super crisp, and the particle effects look amazing. Other than a few ragdoll flyers here and there, this game looks super nice.
With how much I love this game and how much fun I've had and probably will have, I can't in good conscience give this game a good review looking at how many people are having  problems with connection. I wish people could experience this game for how much fun it is but right now Ubisoft needs to implement a solution.
SO, in conclusion, do I reccommend this game? Yes if you have a good internet connection but sadly if you live in the US that might be hard to come by so for the vast majority of people, I would have to give a no until Ubi implements something like dedicated servers.

For Honor is something that Ubisoft made that generally surprised me. Like Siege, I thought it'd be a competitive fighter with a high skill ceiling. And for the most part that's true. The game however.... suffers from a few things that most people won't notice or particularly care about.
1. Forget being offensive. Going balls out and being unrelenting is something that works for a while, but eventually gets you stone-walled. What I mean by that is the game is geared towards being defensive. With half the cast labeled as "Counter-Attackers" or "Disabler", and none of them being called Offensive or Attacker; this implies that being the first to attack is looked down upon. This is a theory about the game, and for the most part you can take this paragraph with a grain of salt.
2. Heroes are thankfully different in combat style. That being said, there is something for everyone. However, certain heroes are bonefide "noob-stompers" or otherwise geared to deal with mechanics most people new to the game aren't aware of. Case in point, the Peacekeeper punishes people who are over-aggressive and aren't familiar with counter-guard breaking. People who play her kill the fun in most games, but that's just my opinion.
3. Now, in a game where guarding is IMPORTANT. I capitalized that for your benefit, you'd think the system would be rock solid, ja? (That's German for yes.) But behold! There are.... problems with this system. Things like a normal attack ignoring your guard, you dodging an attack yet you rubberbanding back for the upcoming blow, or a parry animation actually starting yet the attack goes ahead and kills you. Stuff like that is unheard of if you go to the forums, yet I'm running into it more and more frequently. Could be that I usually play when I'm exhausted, and my tolerance for nonsense is thinner than a human hair.
4. There is no dedicated servers to ensure the highest quality of gameplay possible. It's peer to peer since Ubisoft is being Ubisoft. So this Peer to Peer system is responsible for segment 3. Even if the scoreboard shows everyone with green connections, you'll get shafted from time to time.
