A lot of things in this game are straight from the first of Flying Wild Hog's Shadow Warrior series. Like the quick-witted protagonist and his comedic relief sidekick. Many other things in this game are very new, despite taking inspiration from other games.
The weapon upgrade system is definitely a little empty but with a charm that I see in Borderlands 2, without the extreme dependence on RNG. It allows you to take a basic weapon and craft it into a much more powerful version, crafted from your imagination. That may be an overexaggeration though, as it is still very lacking. Taking the fun of the elementals of Borderlands and simply making them a damage booster. Sure you can use them strategically against enemies but not the unique bosses.
Many of the bosses are very boring and requiring you to do the monotonous task of constantly laying in damage as they're typically only bullet sponges. Not only that but they rarely utilize the interesting idea of having you use specific weapons from your arsenal to either increase damage or prevent damage reduction. This is most prevalent in the last few bosses, where one who would be very exciting and highly anticipated for any fan of the last installment of the series is so poorly thought out. The boss' aesthetic design is somewhat nice, if you forget the other smaller versions with slightly different detail. Although it might makes sense that the CEO of a company has similar battle equipment as his employees, giving him the same sort of attacks just shows the developers only wanted to make larger versions of common enemies. Hammering in the idea of a lack in creativity in the designs of bosses. And the most interesting boss, fought three different times throughout the game, gets boring by the second and ruined by the third.
A fun fight the first time as it has its own interesting design with an appropriate combat style. It gives you an expectation of a constantly evolving enemy which you have to chase down, only to contradict itself with a second fight of the same exact thing with no significant change in the dynamic. Your objective has not changed and neither has the boss. Now giving you the expectation of the exact same thing for the final showdown with the last boss, only to contradict itself once again. And not even in a good way. The boss is different but much more restricted. Instead of being quick and agile, it has become bloated, filling two-thirds of the arena. Doing more uninteresting attacks with absolute silence. Which is odd considering it has a decent soundtrack. Boasting good music and supplying none during what is supposed to be the most intense moment of the game. Well, there is a soundtrack. All you have to do is die. Then as you respawn it will begin to play. Making the final boss the most disappointing and confusing of all. And not even the two protagonists can fix it.
The main protagonist never wants to be serious, giving a comedic value to the game but taking away from any moments that would be considered dramatic or realistic. The sidekick doesn't help this problem either. Supposed to be a clone of the very similar sidekick from the first installment but with a very significant flaw. Instead of delivering puns it forces complaints. Most of her dialogue consists of being sassy until the near end when the writers must've realized that being sassy is not the equivalent of being funny, and decided to change their methods accordingly. But instead of rewriting the script they just kept going. Giving the character an abrupt change in personality.
Something else which was unexpected was the difference in level design from what was shown at E3 long before its release, to what was actually given to the consumer. Giving the impression that there would be more thought and foresight put into the world, like subtle indicators for a boss' difficulty. Rather than a bunch of information floating over its head. Removing you from the actual game to compare stats and determine your survivability. Another error that would've been promising.
But it's only my fault for having faith in such an empty promise. And still, I enjoyed this game. It is fun and has a lot of variety despite its many flaws. It is very fun for a first playthrough, as you don't really know what to expect, but I wouldn't recommend playing it more than that. It has very little replayability.
It has its quirks but it's still very enjoyable. 7/10
Also the ending was weird as ♥♥♥♥ and came out of nowhere.

This game is fun, I like it, but I also hate a lot of things about it.
The AI is complete garbage. It doesn't matter that much because of how fast paced the combat is but its comparable to most gamecube games. If the enemy is aggro you will get hit as soon as you come around a corner, even melee units with ranged attacks/charge attacks will often just snipe you. It can be frustrating and just really annoying because it doesn't feel like you should be getting hit.
On the other hand, the AI also sucks. Sometimes the AI will get stuck on simple thigs like corners of buildings, so you can easily pick them off.
Oh and the challenges on harder difficulties are just broken. Since the enemies always know where you are you just get swarmed and then eventually get stuck becuase you are in a tiny♥♥♥♥♥maze  getting body blocked by all the enemies. That's when the AI just get's frustrating as hell. You try to run away so you don't get blocked in. Then you just keep running into enemies who instantly hit you when you turn a corner. Eventually you can herd them so they can't block you in, but you have to run in circles picking them off really slowly. It's just not any fun. I don't know who thought that was a good idea but it's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ time.
The game is also buggy, I have had times where I would climb a ledge into a pole and get stuck.  then have to restart the level. The AI, like I said, is♥♥♥♥♥♥and sometimes will get stuck on simple thnigs like corners, so you can easily pick them off.
I wish they had focused more on the level design then the world design. The game being kind of open worlld is not really good for it. It doesn't feel like a shadow warrior game in that sense. Theres no levels, its missions that you complete objectives in parts of the world for.
Enough of the negatives. The game has great combat, its just very fluid and extremely customizable due to the RPG elements of the game. If you just like gunning down and slashing up monsters and mobsters its a lot of fun. It's the core of the game and it is done well.
The humor is pretty good all around. It's great because the story is serious but wang is wang. It's a good balance and it keeps me interested while I'm off murdering thousands. I find the dialogue for the weapons to be extremely repetitivly annoying though.
If you like borderlands, you will probably like this game. It's more customizable and just a better fps. The AI is much worse though, but because of the nature of the game it's not the biggest deal most of the time.

While SOMA does try to incorporate a lot of themes from all over, it fails at following any of them consistently. There's a distinct lack of even theoretical explanation for anything either. Certain mechanics and plot devices are just thrown at the player and neither the player nor the NPCs bother to question them. Sure, hand holding would be bad it is still never clear what rules SOMA's world lives by. SOMA raises a lot of questions but does not bother answering them or at least showing any kind of author's viewpoint.
Another big disappointment comes from the fact that gameplay directly counteracts the story. Attempting to listen to audio logs gets you killed by enemies with 200/20 hearing, for example. At the same time the enemies are hardly interactive and, being also invincible, become more of an immovable object than something you can outsmart. Most of the time the best course of action is to sit until you can no longer hear the enemy and then make a break for the next door hoping it actually allows you to progress, since it's impossible to have a plan.
The pacing is also heavily damaged by lack of clear objectives or feedback. While it is realistic in the setting of the game, more often than not it feels like the game simply wants the player to guess what he's supposed to achieve at any given moment.
All in all I find it really hard to compliment SOMA on anything in particular. The graphics and sound are okay, it does not crash to desktop... ...anymore, there are no loading screens. Itsa ok, no more.

Additionally, this version is missing a lot of content. There are no challenges and there is no two-headed giant or revenge modes. I would estimate that this game has less than half the content of the previous versions. The "expansion", Garruk's Revenge, is a complete joke. Turns out that there is no co-op campaign and it's basically just multiplayer skirmishing against AIs or other humans that can be considered cooperative.  I wish games would stop being labeled as co-op if they only have it in the multiplayer mode - that should be called multiplayer co-op or something to differentiate the two.
The ugly:  The single player mode is well designed and has some very interesting mechanics but it's damn short.  It hardly feels like the mechanics of planning your company and investing your personnel while managing your cash flows have a chance to amount to anything over the few chances you get to make choices.  It feels like they cut the single player down to the shortest allowable length, which is too bad as it has potential.
I recommend this game but be aware of the above.

Short version, I liked this game.
Longer version;
At 5 hours of play I loved this game.
At 10 hours of play I thought this game rocked all out.
At 15 hours of play I was wanting more.
At 20 hours of play I probably wont play this game very much anymore.
Offworld Trading Company is an excellently balanced economic/base building/strategy game.  But in some ways it is too well balanced in that while there are 4 different styles of play based on the base you choose, those 4 different styles of play have very little opportunity for variation within themselves.
Even on the mid-range difficulty levels I found that you had to play a particular way determined by your base type and too much variation was usually a quick way to lose.
On the upper difficulty levels forget about trying something new, either you play a flawless game with a very specific and particular build order (and hope you don't get disproportionally screwed over by the black market) or you might as well not have bothered starting the level.
Now none of the above makes it a bad game, but unless you are the sort who has a hard-on for the multiplayer experience or grinding out every "Do X 100 times" achievements OTC has limited replayability.   I enjoyed my 20 hours of play and have no regrets on the purchase but probably will never reach 25 hours of play.

I can really recommend this game.  First, I would like to say something about the negative criticism about the "simple rules"  of this game. Indeed, the rules of the game are clear and not that difficult to learn. However, "simple rules"  do not imply a simple game.
I think this is not a simple game at all. You really have to think strategically about each choice you make, because you only have a certain amount of money to spent, a certain amount of building locations, a certain amount of resources... etc. You all have to balance that out and watch your opponent carefully.
Besides playing a skirmish game against AI or playing a game in multiplayer, there is also a single player campaign. This campaign is not really story driven, but gives a twist on the standard skirmish game. After 11 hours of play, I barely touched it, because I am still trying to beat the AI  in skirmish on a higher difficulty level.
This brings me to the next positive side and that is that there is a wide range of AI difficulty levels. On the lowest level, I find the game pretty easy. On "standard" AI (in which you and the AI do not get any bonuses, and so is the most fair game) I am still not able to win.
The variety between the different skirmish matches comes from different resource availability, different resource locations, and also different factions. There are four different factions in the game, each play a bit differently.
Even if you only want to play singleplayer I think this game has a lot variety and replayability to offer. I did not play in multiplayer at all yet.
People that like strategy games will probably like this great game. So buy it!

Offworld Trading Company is a frustratingly fun game! I have only played vs. the AI and it feels rewarding and fair when you outplay it or when it outright buys you out. Furthermore, I found it interesting that setting up the difficulty level (whether for the AI or you) means that you are setting up a handycap. The AI with the same handycap as the player still beats the player if s/he does not play "correctly." This means that you should pay attention to what your HQ needs and what other HQ use as resources. You should use your AI games to figure out which strategy you like (or as in my case keep you alive) best. The random resource allocation and the map designs increase the complexities of this game. Say you want to grab the water, fuel, and food markets. If the map only has 3 water tiles and they are located in a very narrow ridge between craters, you may have a problem. Why? Well, if you are rushing stocking early fuel expecting the prices to go up (because everyone will have to grab resources in weird locations and far from their HQs), you may not want to spend fuel to get fuel transported to your HQ. Furthermore, if you place the HQ near the water tile, you may not have the space to properly place the fuel refineries. You see, how you place buildings affect what bonuses you get from the production of the resource!
As you can see, the game is complex enough that I don't dare venture into the multiplayer ladder without having a clue of what I should do under different conditions to maximize my early game profits (also, I have an unreliable connection sometimes). The mechanics feel solid and balanced. You usually lose because you of some badly managed resource or market or because you failed to ship resources offworld before the competition.
Overall, I love the game! The animation quality is great! I like the voice over and sounds, although the early access text-to-speech (placeholder?) voice over assets had their own personality. Heck, even the menu surprised me. This is the first game I have seen that differentiates and supports three types of color-blindness.
Please, do not ignore this game and grab it as soon as it becomes affordable to you. Then, play it and join the ranked ladder so we can buy each other's companies some day!

As a long time RTS and stragegy fan, as well as an extreme Civilazation fan, I have to say I was a bit disappointed with Offworld TC.  As a whole, this game feels more like a fantastic foundatation for a spectacularly complex trading sim versus what it actually offers.  Do not be fooled, you will devour this game in its entirety in a matter of hours.  It does not hold a candle to the complexity and depth that the Civ titles (and other leading titles) have to offer.
I purchased the deluxe edition of this game (on sale) for 39.59.  Within a matter of 2 days had not only beaten the campaign, but had exhausted (unless I missed something) every aspect of playability and replay value that the game has to offer.  A more reasonable price for what this game actually has to offer, at least in single player mode, is more like $10-15.
I found that I had lost the desire to keep playing after a very small amount of time.  I even stuck with it for a bit longer just to see if there was more that I perhaps had missed...turns out I found no reason to keep playing beyond the couple days I devoted to mastering it.  As a fan of the genre, I had high hopes of progress, strategy, and replay value that the best RTS/stragegy/sim/farming/economic games have to offer.
This review is not meant to ONLY bash the game.  With more content, resources, campaign options, and other things of this nature, this game could be epic.  In reality it's nothing more than a foundation for what could be an absolutely fantastic game of depth and strategy.  I would recommend this game only when the price is reduced to something more befitting of a game that lacks everything that was mentioned above.
In summary, this game is great and certainly worth playing, but only if the price is right for what the consumer can get out of it.  As of right now however, it feels incomplete and very limited as far as play choices, resources, strategy, economy, variability, and overall complexity,  Kind of sad that its almost over before it begins...
I am recommending this game because of its uniqueness and potential but on a scale of 1-10 this game is a 4, at least for the price.

I can't bring myself to recommend this game, even though parts of it were enjoyable. KOTOR 1 by Bioware far, far outshines this game and credit for the enjoyable bits has to go (mostly) to Bioware. It's been many years since I've played the first game, but it's one of the most memorable RPG experiences I've had.
The only reason I picked up a copy was because it was on sale. I'm glad I never bought the original at full price, for after my first playthrough, I'm pretty sure I'm just going to delete this game.
First of all, everyone should know that this is a turn-based game-although screenshots might lead you to believe otherwise. The gameplay, game mechanics and combat is as  deep and rich as you'd expect to be from a turn-based RPG.
My problem though is that Obsidian seems to have done very little in terms of improving or updating KOTOR 1, whether that's the game mechanics, characters, story, or even graphics.Somehow it always feels like an expansion pack to the first game, and one that has been poorly put-together at that. Yeah, it runs fine and the quests and story progression are fine, but it somehow lacks the savoriness of the first game.
While I can't say that the story's 'bad', it didn't exactly enthrall me like the first game did.
I did like the characters and their individual back-stories, and the voice acting is top-notch. But on several occasions there'd be a cutscene and I'd be like "WTF is going on!? Who the hell is that, the hell are they on about?"
Personally, I thought several cutscenes were either unnecessary or left me with a "Whatever" kind of feeling. I found some to be downright irritating.
The villains and antagonists also leave much to be desired. One of them is described as this huge bad♥♥♥♥♥by every game character, and he literally features twice in the game. Then you easily dispatch him and it's on to the next bit of the story. What gives?
The worst bit, I thought, was the end. I mean there's this big fight as expected, but then the moment you're done  it just cuts away to you flying off into the sunset. Like, BAM end of story, thanks for playing. Roll credits. Ugh.
Anyway, I don't know if I'm being excessively harsh. If this were an independent game that had nothing to do with a much better predecessor, I might have recommended it. But as it stands, save some money and get KOTOR 1 instead.
Skip this one and pick up Mass Effect.
Pros:
1. Good voice acting
2. LIght Sabres. Whee!
3. Deep and rich turn-based RPG
Cons:
1. Poorly written script. Nowhere close to the "Whoa!" moments that Bioware makes you experience.
2. Really abrupt ending.
3. The cutscenes are downright WEIRD. Poorly directed, and often jarring.
4. The story really leaves a lot to be desired. It was hard to be emotionally invested in my character.
5. More like KOTOR 1: expansion pack by new developer! than KOTOR 2.

KotOR 2 is without a doubt a half baked piece of garbage compared to the first game.  The story is highly intriguing, but man, this game is eternally buggy and incomplete.  Character conversations are out of pace with the progession of the plot.  Action sequences (such as when you fight Visas Marr) can be awkwardly left and returned to later (I was able to walk around the Ebon Hawk like it was business as usual despite there being a Sith on the ship).  Voice acting is sloppier and of generally of lower quality than the first game (aside from Kriea, who is the only reason that I might consider still playing this game).  The first level, Peragus, is one of the most boring maps I've ever played and lasts way too long.  Side quests are uninspired (feel more like chores than adventures of importance) and are obviously used as filler rather than a way to embellish the planets you visit (especially Nar Shaadda); some are actually unfinishable.  Cut material is still apparent in this "final product" (e.g. in the Old Military Base on Telos, the Sub Basement area is never accessible).  Level design is lazy and unremarkable, with the same hallway patterns (grids) used across levels.  I could go on.
I know that this game was released on a tight deadline but this is unacceptible, especially with the amount of praise this game receives.  I've read reviews comparing KotOR 2 and KotOR 1 to The Empire Strikes Back and A New Hope respectively in terms of complexity and quality.  They could not be further from the truth. KotOR 2 had promise and ultimately could have been a superior game to the first KotOR.  LucasArts and Obsidian squandered this opportunity years ago, however.  No amount of apologism can change the fact that this game is a crappy, unfinished mess.

Overall, this RTS game is a refreshing take on a familiar concept: Corporate Warfare as Alien Colonization RTS.  I've been playing it now for three days, and overall - I really like this game.  My only issue is that it seems the devs really took a few shortcuts that seem to show, the sort that you might not see in a release from one of the more established publishers.
First, typos - you'll see them in the game and referred to in discussions.  Seriously, guys - if you can develop a game you can spell check.  Just lazy IMO.
Second, balance - the game does not seem balanced between the difffering factions nor with the AI.  So far it seems to be either very easy to win, or impossible to win.  There are a lot of "moving parts" in this game - i.e. a lot of resources, upgrades, and attack options via the "black market" and hacker array to contend with, and no matter what you do the AI will make all the necessary calculations much faster than a human to determine the best strategy to win.  Devs have said this isn't true in discussion, but with respect they understand the game differently than a new user and they should listen to the criticisms.
Third, font/resource icon size - there are many instances when the fonts are honestly nearly too small to read.  Anyone who might need reading glasses (not just middle-aged gamers like me) will find it hard to read numbers, which is pretty important given this is a game of corporate warfare and espionage.  Seriously, make the fonts/resource icons like 10-15% bigger and it's much more playable.
Fourth - there seem to be issues with multi-player, but I cannot speak to that specific complaint because I've not yet attempted to get into a MP game, but read the discussions if you want to learn more on MP bugs.
That said, I'm confident that future relases and patches will address these issues, and one of the best features in my opinion is the lean and effective use of code.  I was THRILLED to see that it only took up a little over 2G on my MacBook AIR.  I'd strongly consider this title if you're a fan of any of the Civ games, as well as C&C or other RTS titles.

I put this game on my wishlist based on the Pedigree of the developers. It seemed an interesting and different take on an RTS and it looked like a harsh business trading simulator. I bought it on sale at 35% off and that came with a free key for a buddy. Called my go to buddy to give it to him and he said "Oh man, I already have it and you are not going to like it. It's fun for a couple of hours but that's it. It's too simplistic to enjoy much longer".
Sadly, he was dead on. The game is extremely simplistic. So if you are looking for the varied and intersting types of games you could get from Civ, you won't find it here.
I literally enjoyed it for about 4 hours and that was pretty much it. You have four factions who are largely identical. They all make a variation of mines and factories which make exactly the same core components. You take those core components and build one or more of 5 different buildings that can give you an edge like help you produce resource X a bit faster, or get a monopoly on a tech like teleportation, which eleminates the need to transport your goods to your home base.
You can then begin to sell your goods to try and make money to buy out your competitor faster than they can buy you out.
In the meantime there are a handful of repetitive, boring, dirty tricks you can use to slow them down or speed you up in your pursuit of the one goal, which is buy your competitors out.
That's it. That's the whole game. Their variety pitch is that there is an infinite number of ways to play each match because you won't always use the same dirty tricks, but there are only a handful of dirty tricks.
If you are interested in a repetitive experience of skirmish matches which last 15 - 60 minutes, and you like fine tuning your ability to deliver the same strategy over and over, then this game is for you.
If you are looking for a deep, strategic, intereting RTS with a variety of playstyle and paths to victory, then absolutely not.
As polished as the game is, one can see that there is very little depth or substance. My go to gaming friend nailed it when he called it "simplistic". Wish I had called him before I bought the game. I'm going to have to bust it out once a month or so to get in some skirmishes and still have it feel fresh and get my money's worth out of it.

Do you love run & gun FPS shooter action, where you can live out your wildest dreams of being a nigh-on invincible Super Soldier on the battlefield?
Then this game is NOT for you!
On the other hand, if you find you get a thrill from setting up that perfect shot, finding just the right firing position, just the right angle to take off a helmet, maybe get two targets with one shot, look no further.
Follow your instincts as you sneak past sentries, lay trip mines and bundles of dynamite as traps, seeking your perfect sniper hide to take out that high value target, reap as much chaos and collateral damage as possible, and get away untouched, possibly even unseen!
I love this game.
The third person perspective takes some getting used to if you're a FPS veteran, but the bullet time and x-ray ballistic cam are great rewards for setting up good shots, and the AI are smart enough and good enough shots that you will very quickly learn you cannot run & gun in this game.
Hide, take a couple breaths, then put a round through the enemy sniper's scope!

Honestly, at this point, it's hard to not recommend because the game COULD turn into a game I've ALWAYS wanted - a medieval RPG with a player run economy, politics, and world. That appears to be the vision, but it stumbles in execution. It's just so... bland. I have two underlining problems with the game.
1. the amount of time it takes to make things. Don't get me wrong, I understand where the devs are coming from. I think they're taking a similar approach to EVE Online, where acquiring new licenses for certain ships took literal YEARS to do. And that's fine. But it's pretty dull to sit there and watch my character take 3 minutes to cook a fish. That's literally half the time it takes me to cook a fish IRL. As the game stands, I feel like I need a book to entertain me while whatever is going on in the game takes its time to finish. It sounds like part of what they're going to do in the MMO is create mini games for everything to fill the time in, and that might help, but I still think taking 10 minutes to do anything meaningful is too long. The purpose of the game should be survival and construction, and you don't need to create mechanics that cause you to spend every moment of your free time to accomplish the most base tasks. The time spent should be spent on making things truly epic.
2. The game seems pretty empty. You walk into any town, and it is empty. Empty homes, empthy trading posts, empty "schools" - all the building are there only for aesthetics, with no real reason to exist. At the very least, being able to fill them with furniture would be nice. At the most, the furniture you fill it with should all serve some function. And all of this compounds problem 1. What point is there in spending 10 real life hours to build my first humble shack when there's no real purpose to it? I guess if you're into things like legos, and you enjoy building things because it's fun to accomplish something, than this might suit you. But I play games because they're interactive and allow me to do things I wouldn't normally be able to do IRL.
So we'll see, maybe the promised MMO will fix those two issues. But as it stands, I didn't really have fun in this game and don't recommend it.
EDIT: When I wrote this review, I intended it to be just my two cents on the game. Instead, it has become the "most helpful" review of this game. I only noticed because I get comments every other day from some very passionate fans. Still, I thought it would be a good idea to follow up with a few comments (and fix a grammar mistake or two in the original review).
First of all, people getting worked up on whether it actually takes 3 minutes to make a fish IRL are missing the point. One of my favorite game series of all time is the Sims. In that game, your sims do such mundane tasks as poo, eat, laundry, and dishes. But you're empowered to tell a story. It gave you a canvas to tell a story that could spread over generations. It made every in-game day special as you worked towards whatever goal you had established for your virtual family to achieve. Of course, it didn't hurt that Maxis' (and eventually The Sims Studios) signature humor was sprinkled throughout.
LIF is missing all of that charm. It takes so damn long to do anything, every task is a chore instead of an exciting step towards a greater adventure. There is no charm, just a generic medieval world with even less character. Obviously I've already mentioned how everything felt empty. The game just needs something, anything, that's fun. As it stands, all you have to hope for is finding a decently populated server where some good samaritan will donate a basic set of arms and armor to you, allowing you to participate in fights sooner. Oh, and you die fairly quickly. If everything else is useless and the only point is fighting, why not make a pure fighting game?
Finally, yes, I only played the game for 1.1 hours. I don't have a problem with that. It isn't
responsibility to figure out how to like a game, it's the developers responsibility to sell me on their game. They failed to win me over in the alotted time and I feel other, like minded gamers should know about it. I agree with others, it's a little disappointing that the review from the guy who played for 1.1 hours is currently "the most helpful", but my intention was just to throw in my thoughts. That being said, those who've played for a few dozen hours have walked away with similar impressions. Regardless, I had watched a few hours of Let's Plays, but because it takes so long to do anything in the game and the videos tended to be heavily edited, I thought it would be worth trying the game out.
My dream game is where I can live in a medieval world. Be a tavern owner making ale and attracting all the adventurers in town as we discuss the latest war and get buffs from my ale. Be a farmer and cower as I run from the most recent raid by a neighboring fiefdom. Be a merchant and sell goods from city to city. Be a guard-for-hire and assist caravans as they travel the sands. Be a part of a political movement as we overthrow the current government. Be a rogue group of hedge knights that fights for the freedom of
all folk, giving each new soul a fair shot in the harsh world.
This game is not that game. That's all I'm saying.

Okay so heres my review after reading some of the reviews.
i agree on some opinions such as name tag shouldn't appear unless close as that would give away positions but some of the opinions i just disagree with. i can understand why you feel the way you do but people who say leveling isn't worth anything is wrong in a way as leveling in a game like this makes it much more fun and gives just a little something extra as what you could call a prize or gift for surviving that long while fighting your way through those levels to survive. also the safe zones being camped isn't that bad, well as far as i've played but i haven't played since december due to it being early access and i want a proper and full game experience when it fully releases but me and my brother always snuck away from safe zones without any trouble. There are many ways in and out of a safe zone and any route could be taken, althought some safe zones are limited to 2 entrance/exits such as the camp in the north. thats what sprinting away really fast is for and also you must make sure you are aware of your surroundings and not just running into a bunch of nether creatures haha xD imo most of the stuff such as pvp, trying to sneak away from safe zones etc is what makes this game intense and adds to the environment and fun of the game. leveling just adds to the tension as it makes you not want to die so you can keep all the perks but it only helps a bit and doesn't make you invincible. you need to try and enjoy the game without triyng to take out all the fun, try and get someone to play with. it's even better when you get a full inventory full of stuff you just found and ending up in a gun fight in the middle of no where with another group of survivors LOL. everyone wants to survive and tensions are high which makes people trust others less as they are scared of dying and losing their levels and equipment.
But when me and my brother played, it didn't have the group system or the other updates which i've seen in the updates, but there still was a negative to killing just anyone as if you killed a lot of people, you would end up attracting a ton of nether which would just literally tear you apart no matter how geared up you are. unless of course u had lots of stamina and one of those nether bombs to throw in a different direction or one of those machines that make nether creatures flee for a little while.
Really they should add more stuff like a roaming boss as i don't currently like that reaper thing that sits in the middle of no where in a random park in the north. they should have a large slow roaming creature which would add so much tension and excitment into the game. and it could also create a small area of fog around it so it cannot be seen very well from a distance. oh how that would be amazing! and also it could grant a decent peice of equipment or something for the people who helped slay the beast but ofc that shouldn't be easy. so much things could make this game better.
I have nothing against other peoples opinions as this is just my own opinion of some and i respect your opinions.
But i find this to be an excellent game which could be so so much better
But anyway this game is really not friendly to those who honestly play alone. you should definitely grab a friend or someone trust worthy to play with and atleast have voice communication with. When getting into game, you should always expect some sort of pvp encounter unless you are lucky to avoid such things but they are always quite fun if it ends up as a group war,
Item spawning is terrible as some have said, needing food and health and not getting any while still loosing it in a safe zone is just rediculous but then again force you to go out and look for items to survive on. there should be something such as go out and kill some nether and depending on how much nether you kill, you get a reward for going back into a safezone or even just going back into the main safe zone as there is a large shortage of supplies for people just getting into the game. maybe even some supplies for a first time visit into the main safe zone just to help someone who has nothing, but won't give to those who have obviously stored food and health supplies into their bank.
There can be so much going for this game yet. maybe in the future this game would show its true colours and what it can do and hopfully a great game like this doesn't go to waste.

ALOT shorter than i expected. Also, as i exposed myself to the original trailer and not much else to avoid spoilers, the plot and setting were alot different than i expected. That being said, i thoroughly enjoyed this game though cant help but feel slightly disappointed.
Once i truly look past my expectations this game shines, a real gem. the plot is intense and rather well paced in my opinion. The characters are all well voiced and well written with special mention to the actual player character which i found uncommonly refreshing. The monsters only seemed a bit monotonous at one single point and then they always seemed to mix it up and hit you with something different and terrifying.
The main theme is built around the idea of consciousness and what it is that makes you "human". They do a wonderful and truly daunting job of expanding on those ideas. IMHO, and here comes my expectations again so this is merely my personal bias, while they did expand upon the main theme rather well it fell slightly short compared to the way a few other games did the same topic.
But the harshly moral choices you are confronted with come down to a spectacularly metaphysical dialogue with yourself about identity and the act of being, which i think really makes this a terrifying game.
All things considered this game gets a solid 8/10 from me and i definitely recommend this one for its amazing atmosphere, story and harshly characterizing choices.

This game is a very good representation of horror, one that i would definitely recommend to any who like horror games.
I would describe it as containing fear of the environment (dark and foreboding, with really good sound placement that constantly kept my nerves on high), fear of the things that go bump in the dark (these sections are really tense and made me yelp quite a few times) and fear of myself, which is the point of the game as the choices given to me, the things I had to do to finish the game made me question who i am and what i was willing or unwilling to do to progress the story.
Long after the credits finished i'm still pondering and thinking about the game, it really is well written and thought provoking!
Graphics are really impressive, the underwater sections are a beauty to walk through and the interior environments incredibly detailed.
Sound is brilliant in this as I already mentioned, i do recommend having surround sound of some sort on during this.
It plays almost identically to the Amnesia games (no surprise there) and is pretty solid. My only quib with controls is for a game based on stealth and hiding/running from enemies in those sections, you are pretty limited in what you can do, something that i would love to see enhanced for future Frictional games :-)
Highly recommended game, i loved every minute and do not regret dropping all games to play this on release :-)

Nihilumbra is about destruction. Basically the main character Is born in the void. He then leaves the void to live and see the world. However, the void follows him, creating monsters to slow/end his journey. He moves from location to location, damning each one by passing through it.
Nihilumbra is a platformer/puzzle game. You spend most of the first campaign running and jumping with no combat ability. You never get a direct face to face combat option but you get a way to kill enemies. I think this adds to the appeal. Nihilumbra has some great platforming and some seriously challenging puzzles. Sometimes both are required.
The gameplay involves color which you use to change the surfaces around you by clicking the mouse. During the main campaign the narrator will speak about what you're doing and question the nature of it.
I loved the nihilistic tones and questions of meaning. Existing only to stay alive. Destroying things by your existance. It's a fun idea to explore.

I think this game is great, but at the same time theres a pacing problem. The difficulty curve is breakneck and the gameplay is great in itself. The main problem is the disconnect when you die is pretty obnoxious. When you die, which will happen a lot, you have to wait around 1.5 seconds for it to say you're 'being extracted' and then you're at the start screen, then you can hit play again then you wait another 5 seconds for stuff to start showing up on screen. The problem is that 6.5 seconds is seriously jarring for me personally because it's like you're ready for the bullet hell and you died instantly but now you have to wait another 6.5 seconds for the game to wind up to a speed that feels instense and fun.
Hotline miami did it well at times. Here's it's sort of like that but a time survival thing. The big difference here is that hotline miami  never took away your control of the pacing. Which would often time leads to massive frustration that you died for the 20th time  on a level and you just throw yourself at it and do everything as fast as possible with the most and sometimes you could smash out a part on just sheer frustration because the second you died you were back in the fight again. That 6.5 seconds is seriously jarring here. One second im cutting waves of bullets and sending them back the sheering sound effect is really great, and then suddenly it says being extracted since i died to a massive light show that...snuck up on me. and im like ♥♥♥♥ and then in the next 6.5 seconds my adrenaline high is gone because it has to crawl up to speed again. It's a fun game and really if it's on sale it's completely worth it. Even might be if it's not on sale. But the fact that it takes so long to move from attempt to attempt really kills the adrenaline fast pacing that this type of game has going for it.

I'm honestly not sure why this game has gotten so many mixed to negative reviews. Perhaps they've updated the game since then to address some of the complaints it received. As a person who has played all of the PC MtG offerings from Steam, I think this one is BY FAR the most polished. The deckbuilding screen is fantastic with easy to use filters in a simple but aesthetically appealing layout that makes the system extremely user-friendly and satisfying.
I read many complaints about menu speed but I don't have have any qualms with the menu at all. It's easy to navigate and it doesn't take long to load or jump from place to place once you know where everything is. And I don't have a fancy gaming PC, just a 5 year old desktop. I'm not really sure what people were complaining about there.
I also read some complaints about how the game was overly difficult with starter decks. In fact, I read it so often in the reviews that I started out playing on the easiest difficulty because I was concerned about getting wrecked. However, this wasn't my experience either. I've played through all of Innistrad with the cards I got buying the basic game (as well as the boosters you earn as you beat the planeswalkers) and I'd say I have over a 75% winrate for games I actually played through (sometimes I'll just restart a challenge if the manascrew is too steep). For the sake of reference, I only have a moderate amount of experience with MtG but I do have some experience with other ccg's- most notably Hearthstone.
So with about eight hours of playtime, I am quite satisfied with the purchase and I'm glad I didn't let the negative reviews scare me off. In my opinion, I've already gotten my money's worth (GoGo Holiday Sale!) and I've still got probably 80% more game to play.
tl;dr
Pros:
- Aestetically appealing and highly functional deckbuilding screen. I can't overstate how much this is improved from previous installments.
Neutrals:
- Basically an updated version of the same format from previous installments. There doesn't seem to be anything new and exciting (beyond the deckbuiding being vastly improved). This isn't bad or good, it just is what it is.
Cons:
- The full screen mode does this weird thing where it messes up the second monitor I have for my desktop (it pushes whatever is displayed there halfway off the screen. Previous versions did too). When I play in windowed mode, it doesn't appear to have a size that is close to my full monitor size. It's not awful, but it's not ideal either.
- I guess some people were complaining about the lack of puzzle challenges in this one as compared to previous installments; Unless that's somewhere in this version and I haven't gotten to it yet. I guess that would be a con too, although for me personally, I don't really care much about that feature.
So, my initial impression is that Magic 2015 is definitely worth the money. If you enjoyed the previous installments, you'll like this one as well. It satisfies the MtG itch without having to spend assloads of money on an actual card collection. If I run in to anything else that seems off-putting, I will come back and edit the review, but based on my expectations from having played the previous iterations of the game, this one has pleasantly exceeded my expectations.

Escaping from the void, trying to become more than you are and risking the world you seek in order to do so. This is the story of Nihilumbra, a puzzle based 2D platformer from Beautifun Games.
The game follows a vey narrative series of events travelling from the cold Icy hills through the forest, the desert, the volcano and finally to the city. Each location brings with it new challenges and a new skill to brave them. These skills come in the forms of colours, paints that can be spread around the environment at will. The first colour you obtain is blue, allowing the creation of ice. Then comes the green followed by the brown, creating bouncy and sticky surfaces respectively. From the volcano comes red, the ability to burn some things and  supercharge others. Finally there is yellow, the ability to create conductive lines to transfer power from energy sources to unpowered machines. It's the combination of all of these that will let you progress and aid in your escape from the void.
The gameplay is well established as you play, with a "tutorial" for each new colour. The levels are relatively easy on the first play through but after finishing once there is a new "Void" version of the levels, being more difficult and involved. The controlling of the colours is intuitive and easy to do, and if you make a mistake it's just as easy to undo your moves.
The visual style is fantastic with detailed painted backgrounds and foreground objects that have a parallax effect. When applying colours it is always easy to distinguish. The soundtrack is one that is extremely well fitting and only adds to the atmosphere. The voice over is a crucial part of the game and it wouldn't be the same without it. The tone of voice is one that makes the player feel safe while traveling and discovering.
Overall the game is solid and everything seems to work as intended, some sections seem to be reliant on trial and error. There is a large difficulty curve between finishing the first playthrough and starting the second, it could have eased into it more.
It's has a good bang for your buck and the only thing I would like to see is a level editor with steam workshop integration. Other than that it's a great game.

I put this game on my wishlist based on the Pedigree of the developers. It seemed an interesting and different take on an RTS and it looked like a harsh business trading simulator. I bought it on sale at 35% off and that came with a free key for a buddy. Called my go to buddy to give it to him and he said "Oh man, I already have it and you are not going to like it. It's fun for a couple of hours but that's it. It's too simplistic to enjoy much longer".
Sadly, he was dead on. The game is extremely simplistic. So if you are looking for the varied and intersting types of games you could get from Civ, you won't find it here.
I literally enjoyed it for about 4 hours and that was pretty much it. You have four factions who are largely identical. They all make a variation of mines and factories which make exactly the same core components. You take those core components and build one or more of 5 different buildings that can give you an edge like help you produce resource X a bit faster, or get a monopoly on a tech like teleportation, which eleminates the need to transport your goods to your home base.
You can then begin to sell your goods to try and make money to buy out your competitor faster than they can buy you out.
In the meantime there are a handful of repetitive, boring, dirty tricks you can use to slow them down or speed you up in your pursuit of the one goal, which is buy your competitors out.
That's it. That's the whole game. Their variety pitch is that there is an infinite number of ways to play each match because you won't always use the same dirty tricks, but there are only a handful of dirty tricks.
If you are interested in a repetitive experience of skirmish matches which last 15 - 60 minutes, and you like fine tuning your ability to deliver the same strategy over and over, then this game is for you.
If you are looking for a deep, strategic, intereting RTS with a variety of playstyle and paths to victory, then absolutely not.
As polished as the game is, one can see that there is very little depth or substance. My go to gaming friend nailed it when he called it "simplistic". Wish I had called him before I bought the game. I'm going to have to bust it out once a month or so to get in some skirmishes and still have it feel fresh and get my money's worth out of it.

This is a brilliant, polished game. It has everything that should make it an addictive experience for me... pausable real-time, many divergent strategies for victory, brutally smart AI opponents, some nice tongue-in-cheek atmospherics, different factions with totally differing playstyles, and more.
So why the thumbs down? Why aren't I playing the game right now?
What it comes down to is this: to keep ahead of the game, you need to keep track not only of your own company's development, but ideally that of all your competitors as well. Your AI opponents will try to sabotoge you using dirty black-market tricks, and you have to do the same to them to win. That means you have to know what's really going to hurt them, and what's not. That means you have to understand their strategy. Which means you have to look over their operations on the map, count their buildings, try to work our what they're up to.
I could pause the game and do all that, but even if I did for each of the 3-7 opponents, I'd have to do it all over again a few minutes later, because that's how quickly the game moves.
Info about your opponents is not easy to find. There's no summary screen of how many building of each type each opponent has, which might allow you to piece together their strengths and weaknesses at a glance. Instead you have to maually count buildings if you want that info. I hate situations where a game makes information available, but very hard to access!
Another turn-off for me is the difficulty of assessing what investments will generate the best return. I end up making most of my investment choices using a sort of intuition, but I have the feeling that on higher difficulty levels you really need to flawlessly min-max to win. Again, I could pause the game and do a bunch of calculations by hand to min-max... but that's not much fun. Too much like my real job.
So despite being very drawn to the game in concept, I find in practice it just leaves me feeling frustrated at being unable to keep up with the constant min-max calculating that the AIs are able to do in real time.
I could pause the game every 30 seconds and try to keep up, in my feeble human way, but why bother?

Offworld is a unique RTS game that captures the best and worst parts of capitalism, in space! I've been following this game for some time, and I am not disappointed by the results of the hard work of the development team.
The overall objective of the game is to become the most profitable off-world trading company by becoming the most profitable and efficient corporation around. You'll achieve this by building supply chains of goods, selling them to a local colony, shipping them off the planet, and using your gains to buyout your competitors while avoiding being bought out yourself.
Positives:
+Amazing soundtrack by Christopher Tin (composer of Baba Yetu, of Civ 4 fame)
+Quick cutthroat gameplay; the decisions on where to land, and what to start producing are the beginnign of a race to quickly provide goods that meet the demands of a local colony.
+The gameplay is unique: there isn't any 'militay' component to this game; instead you will be competing with other corporations in the marketplace to become the most efficient and profitable offworld-trading company.
+Interesting hostile actions - while you can play it straight and just compete on the 'free market', there are a variety of options to sabatoge your competitors through illicit means.
+Unique factions  - each faction has their own set of strengths, and weaknesses; playing one versus another feels very interesting and different.
+Great writing (in the tutorial and opening missions, at any rate).
Negatives:
-It seems like there's not really a comeback mechanic once you start to fall behind; if you make a few mistakes early, you're probably going to have a bad time. I could be wrong, but once I start to lose, I continue to lose.
-The factions aren't visually all that different.
-This game is probably overpriced for the content that you're getting; I recommend purchasing this game on at least a 25% sale, probably closer to 50%.
-I'm unsure about the replayability of the game; so far, the experience has been novel; outside of multiplayer, I don't think the game will provide more than 20 horus of gameplay.
Overall, I highly recommend this game for RTS players who want a different experience - namely one that focuses on competitive supply chains and economic efficiency. The game has a lot of character, and has been very enjoyable to explore.

Apart from these, anything else is really just nitpicks on a brilliant experience, I wholeheartedly reccomend this game to any Star wars fan, and any RPG fan period. 9/10 and 10/10 with the Restored Content Mod.

At first, Imperial Glory may seem like a dumbed-down version of Empire: Total War. And for the most part, that is sadly true. There isn't as wide a selection of tactical options, the units of different nations are all reskinned and renamed versions of each other, and the graphics are not nearly as good. Artillery shoots through your own ranks if you can't get it on high ground, which is usually impossible, and you can't even group your units. Despite these many and serious flaws, Imperial Glory does have a few redeeming qualities. It's low graphic requirements mean it can run on old or non-gaming systems. Empire is so poorly optimized that even new rigs often can't run it well. Imperial Glory is also cheaper. The campaign map, which uses figurines to represent armies on a paper map that looks like it is from the time period and sitting on the desk of you, the general, is a great touch. Battle can be grand in appearance and tense, if you don't mind the lack of ability to use artillery. Overall, I would only recommend this game to someone with particular imterest in late 18th to early 19th century warfare, and who can't run Empire: Total War.

I recommend For Honor.
Well, let's see. What's good?
First of all, the game looks fantastic. Graphics-wise, it is a knockout, even on low settings. When you are in a match on one of the "wilder" maps you really get a sense of the jungle or snowy mountainside surrounding you. The environments are very well done and unlike most games of a similar type, For Honor utilizes the environment in many different ways. It creates hazards and vantage points, even places to set up ambushes and choke-points for funneling enemies. And through all of it, the environment actually pretains to the world and makes sense.
On to the gameplay. From all outward appearances, I should hate the combat system of this game. I've never liked a rock-paper-scissors style combat system but the way they do it here really works. In the heat of battle I become one with the controls. I find myself parrying and blocking, attacking and counterattacking without even realising I'm doing it. Even as a noob, I never once felt completely helpless when faced with one or even two opponents. Sure, I got my butt kicked plenty of times, but at least I felt like I had some kind of a chance.
The only downside to this is getting ganged up on, but that happens in just about any multiplayer game ever. Few games I've played actually have a system like this, and here it kinda works. Okay, scratch that. It definitely works.
Now on to the characters and classes themselves. All of them are unique in their own ways, which right off the bat is something that gets brownie-points with me.
There are three factions and each faction has four heroes each. A powerhouse-style class, a swift assasin-style class, a defensive class, and a hybrid class which contains aspects of all three. I'll admit I don't like some of the classes, but the ones I like I find myself really enjoying. Just like any game with multiple classes, there are a couple of classes in For Honor that are well, crappy.
However it seems that the opinion of which classes are actually the crappy ones tends to vary among the community greatly, and everyone can generally hold their own against anyone if they know what they're doing.
Hell, even the single-player campaign isn't that bad. It's not amazing, but then again it probably never was meant to be. It's certainly done better than in some other games that have tried to do the same thing.
The biggest problem I think I have with the game has to be the P2P connections. Yeah yeah, every review mentions it and I suppose I can't just overlook it, but I'll be honest I haven't run into enough issues with P2P for it to really bother me that much. It can be annoying every now and then, but 9 times out of 10 I can play through an entire match without issue.
Secondly I suppose I have to talk about the microtransactions as well, and I've never really been big on them myself, but I like that whatever you can buy with real money(minus some minor cosmetics) you can eventually unlock or obtain ingame yourself. Buying feats early seems wasteful and it doesn't really give that much of an advantage in combat as one might think. A lot of people I've talked to tell me they often even forget that the feats are even there until it's too late to use them. And to add on to that, in the online modes I really don't run into as many trolls and jerks as many people seem to.
The customization is very well done in my opinion. The game has a nice way of letting you design your character despite never seeing their face. You can create your own custom emblems and crests, color your armors and even customize your weapons.
If I had to have one problem with the customization, it'd be that colors generally don't matter when you're playing online as you're usually plastered with blue or orange depending on what team you're on for that round. But even that is understandable and I can easily get around that.
TLDR:
To sum it up, I think For Honor is a great game despite all the flaws. It's absolutely addicting and I can't stop playing it.
If you like games with fast-paced and fun combat and are willing to work around some flaws, you should give this game a try. I'll very tentatively say that it is worth the money.
Feel free to comment and give me your opinion or tell me if there's anything else I should cover in this review!

(Originally written 6/11/2011 - my effusive praise being representative of how much I liked the game at the time, not being aware in years to come how I'd regard it pretty much like the rest of the community. Decent, not as great as all that. Still will represent here what I wrote back then.)
The King is back; does he still reign? Spouting one-liners, kicking alien rear and wooing all the hot babes like he always has, I’d say he does.
The story picks up around fifteen years after Duke’s last adventure, just like in real life. Duke is living high off of the fame and worship of his adoring public; the world simply loves Duke Nukem, and why not? He singlehandedly saved Earth with an impressive arsenal of weapons, secured the safety of the beloved women of the planet, and undertook many grand feats all over the world! After all that, he lapsed into semi-retirement in Las Vegas; he bought a casino, surrounded himself by beautiful women as is his wont, and parlayed his fame and marketability into media enterprises, fast food chains and more!
When the aliens come back under a pretence of truce, however, he is warned to keep out of their way by the President himself, saying he’s in talks with the Cycloid Emperor himself, whom Duke defeated in his last encounter. His General friend and handler grudgingly agrees, that maybe the aliens are here to make peace, but all that quickly becomes moot; his secret hideaway, the Duke Cave, as well as Vegas itself, is under attack! Just like before, the aliens made the first move, and now it’s up to Duke to make the last.
Gameplay is definitely a throwback to classic FPS’s, and seems like a tribute to the real fans of Duke from years past. It works really well, but has, unfortunately, also worked to turn off fans of “new-school” gameplay, who have blasted the game for lack of originality as well as its use of several modern gameplay mechanics mixed in with the old, including regenerating health, and limitation to two weapons carried at one time [This was patched soon after release; now we can hold four weapons].
That doesn’t, however, mean a thing to me. Things have to change, and I think Duke Nukem Forever brings just the right amount of change to keep things fresh, and the new turret and vehicle sequences, as well as fully interactive minigames including pool, pinball, video poker and others, mean you’ll be playing the game for a very long time.
Multiplayer, again, samples from the new-school without being in it. The persistent leveling system and challenges of many other recent FPS’s make appearances here, with the reward system relating not merely to gameplay enhancements, but additions to Duke’s personal penthouse! That’s right, when you’re not bashing the aliens’ heads in during the campaign, or those of your buddies in multiplayer, you can walk around a multi-room museum of Duke’s accomplishments and conquests, which are unlocked as you level up in multiplayer. The replay value is definitely there!
So, as Duke says, COME GET SOME! Five out of five!

Come for the sniping, stay for the X-Ray kill cams. Everything else is perfunctory.
The Reich is having one of its worst weeks ever, the Allies are pushing East and the Russians are marching west, leaving Hitler's desired empire an almost continent-wide shambles. Berlin is in tatters, but the Nazis aren't bowing out of the fight gracefully - not without using their planned game-changer. Their V2 program's already laid waste to Antwerp, Paris and London, and the Allies would very much like to avoid repeat performances.
Enter Karl Fairburne, an American OSS who so happens to be a crack shot with a Springfield rifle and with fairly incredible Lung-Fu capabilities. Your job as Fairburne is to prevent the V2 scientists from falling into Russian hands while ideally preventing the Germans from firing extra payloads in Winston or Charles' backyards. You'll do that by making Team Fortress 2's Sniper proud. Very, very proud. Masochistically proud, I'd say.
Expect a lot of internal "Boom. Headshot." moments, preferrably with your inner voice momentarily sounding like John Patrick Lowrie.
The entire game is centered around your rifle of choice, whether it's a Springfield, a Mosin Nagant or a Gehwehr. You'll typically end up casing an arena with your binoculars, only to make your way to a designated perch point or roost (I like to think of snipers as really lethal flightless birds, so sue me) and do what you can with what you have in order to set up a temporary Area Denial setup. Landmines, tripwires, grenades both American and German, dynamite, rocks... All of that's going to help you keep the Nazis and the meddling Russians off of your heinie.
Once your rear is covered, however, what's up front needs tending to. Out comes the rifle, as well as the game's comprehensive ballistics system. The more evolved you set the aiming difficulty to be prior to starting a playthrough, the more you'll have to compensate for gravity or bullet drift. The game can show you a little red icon that displays the next round's projected final point, but only if you use Focus mode. Focus works a lot like Bullet Time, except it depends on your sniping-dedicated lung's current saturation and your heart's overall beats per minute. Line up your scope after sprinting for half a map and your aim's going to go everywhere except where it needs to go. When that happens, Karl has to cool off. Lie prone, use the scope to keep track of your enemies - but don't shoot! Wait. Wait for the sweetest of moments, where the sniper's recovered his poise and his personal focus combines with the Gehwehr's quadruple zoom in order to allow you to land some truly insane shots.
Ever shot a target from five hundred meters away? I have. It's awesome.
The game rewards particularly ballsy shots with an X-Ray kill cam that liberally cribs from Mortal Kombat 9, showing you all the deliciously juicy bits your little metal slug's going to ruin as it goes through its Matrix-worthy sojourn. Skulls and their contained brain matter, lungs, hearts, teeth, fingers, livers, intestines or some poor Luftwaffe member's oesophagus; it's all fair game, and all rendered in the goriest of detail you could imagine. Even testicles can be reduced to mush, with the game being more than happy to paint out Fairburne as a truly sadistic mofo.
Then, there's what happens when you try and stick to the Thompson, or the Webley or the Welrod. The game just doesn't fare well outside of its sniping conceit, close-quarters combat being a general chore and stealth sections not being hard, so much as they feel unecessary.
You're a SNIPER, for God's sake; don't go around trying to throat-punch sleeping SS officers or lining up silenced pistol headshots if the hardware isn't fit to actually support that! Couple that with the fact that Fairburne is no modern action hero and can only take so much damage, and you earn close-quarters situations that are just plain infuriating. You'll frequently trigger them at normal distances and get your rear end handed to you, only to figure out when and how the Jerries spawn and stick to long-distance spawn camping from then on.
Narratively speaking, the game barely delivers. Then again, it doesn't really have to. You're playing a slice of made-up military history; I wouldn't have expected an involved and introspective journey inside Karl's mind, much less for the one non-evil German character to last more than a single mission. "Saving Private Ryan" this ain't, but it absolutely is a chronicle of how the Allies would have gone about mucking with the V2 program beyond just recruiting scientists. You won't care much for Fairburne and the few named NPCs are basically checkpoints on legs that are generally too busy spouting clichéd German or Russian phrases to bother interacting with you.
Unless you consider long-distance and rifle-enabled murder to be a form of interaction.
Similarly, the game is visually underwhelming. There's a ton of texture pop-in, and the overall quality of the design isn't all that special. You've seen one level with a ruined Berlin square? Then you've seen them all. There's a ton of focus thrown at the X-Ray cams, but most soldiers have one or two faces, max. You'll kill endless clones over and over and over. The mood is served by precisely two tracks that loop incessantly, plus a fairly bombastic and highly synthetic main theme.
Overall, Sniper Elite V2 is a sufficient game with its occasional moments of brilliance, especially when you're left to your devices with one solid perch and an unobstructed view on an entire courtyard's worth of mooks. You'llt occasionally feel like a walking god, once you'll have the honor of taking down tanks, of all things, with a single well-placed round.
When you're not allowed to spin a web of traps and vantage points, though, and when circumstances or the game's script both force you to get down and dirty on a more personal level, the package falters. Fairburne is a crack shot with his rifles but a horrible "spray-and-pray" type with anything that isn't scoped or pistol-sized. Here's hoping that Rebellion does its homework and improves on the close combat options for the upcoming third game.

This is basically a review for all three episodes:-
First of all i have to say that it is highly preferable and recommended that you watch the entire Wakfu first and second seasons (found on Netflix) as well as the Ogrest movie (here on Steam) to fully understand and truly appreciate what's going on in these there episodes.
Pros:
-We get a direct continuation of the series, all our fav characters are back as well as few new ones.
-It's central plot ties really well with previous events from the Wakfu mythos and it all comes together wonderfully at the end, not to mention a series of unexpected twists and as usual excellent villain who actually have real good reasons for doing what they do, Wakfu doesn't have any i'm-just-a-lunatic villains at all and i love it for that.
-Epic action scenes, did i say EPIC, yeah .. specially the third episode, as good and epic as the final big battles from the first and second seasons if not better (and it is hard to top the epic finale of season 2), great camera work, fluid beautiful animation and great sound effects make you feel like you are in the middle of it all.
-Character developments galore, relations evolve, some get broken, some are rekindled, all in all there are some excellent developments for all main characters and even some side ones.
Cons:
-I watched the two seasons with french voices and English subs so it took me some time to get used to the English dub, it's not BAD by any means but the french voice grew on me and they feel more passionate and involved in the acting than the English one, a minor problem really.
-The versions here are stream-only with no download option so if you have a slow internet it will be agonizing to watch even at the lowest quality, sad thing but it's the only problem i could think of, if this comes out on DVD or Bluray i'd buy it in a heartbeat .. along with the two main seasons (which sadly are only available on Netflix and on DVDs/Blurays for kickstarter backers which really is weird and doesn't make sense, so many people love the show and want to own it, why deny them that and limit them to the fickle streaming option.
Final verdict = 9.5/10 ... will watch again ;)
================================
Anyways, thanks Anakama for releasing this on Steam and i hope you guys reconsider releasing the entire show on Bluray with both versions (English/French versions subbed and dubbed) and all the extras for the whole world to enjoy it properly, it's a shame this amazing show is so hard to get, it's truly a wasted potential.

EA's attempt to resurrect the Medal of Honor series by tapping into the modern war such as the fight in Afghanistan is almost universally judged as an also-ran that failed to distinguish itself from its chief rival, the COD: Modern Warfare series. And after playing it I can see why. The SP portion was designed apart from the MP portion (by different teams, even) and never quite tightly integrated. The SP campaign went for authenticity by recording actual soldiers and model missions that they went on, albeit somewhat dramatised, but the result, while authentic, seem to lack the "punch" or the dramatic tension that MW seem to deliver. The authenticity also reduced the enemy into ragtag group of poorly armed peasants that relied on numbers that just got lucky by pure amount of lead flying in your direction. You play several different people with bare transition between them which adds a bit to the confusion. All in all, the SP campaign offered all sorts of challenges, from standard cover shooter with flanking to rail-shooter sequence (the gunship sequence), to sniper alley (aka Whack-a-mole) to stealth escape, and turret defense (shoot anything that comes down that mountain). But it is primarily a shooter, albeit a rather... derivative one that broke no grounds.

Introduction:
My only prior familiarity with Magic: The Gathering was via my oldest son, who gravitated towards the card game.  Such games follow an effective business model, encouraging individuals to invest large quantities of money into cards to ensure probability is in their favor.  Though the game seemed somewhat interesting from what I had seen, I simply did not want to go down that investment path.
After looking at the Magic: The Gathering - Duels of the PLaneswalkers series, my interest grew as not only did each new version add additional layers, but was also a finite investment, regardless if one purchased all the DLC.  From the standpoint of true Magic: The Gathering fans, I can understand how this would be a complete affront, given it is a trading card game.  Looking through the reviews, I gathered as much.
Summary:
After assessing all the Duels of the Planeswalkers series, I can say without a doubt that my favorites are 2013 and 2015.  Personally, I think 2013 is a great way to get started with the game, moving towards 2015 once one truly is ready to truly get into deck building.  Having stated that, if you are tride and true CTG fan, perhaps something like HEX might be of more interest.  Nevertheless, given Magic Duels is shutting down for good, I caution anyone considering that route as such games can quickly become a money sink.

If you enjoy the boardgames Risk and Battleship and ever wanted something like both combined or are a fan of Shogun Total War and the rest of the Total War genre of games - well then, Imperial Glory was made and put here for you. Try as hard as you can by land and sea to take the world for yourself using modern wit and Industrial Age military hardware in an effort to survive and re-write history one invasion at a time. You'll find a vast research-tree and diverse array of units from basic people/militia to advanced warriors that cost an arm and a leg and take a few turns and fortunes to make... but there are something like 12 turns in a year so your biggest gear-grinder will be developing the income for those expansionist ambitions of yours. You are not the only one with big dreams on the map by far though. The AI will generally do its best to rip you a new one, which maximizes replayability from the very beginning.
GLITCH WARNING:
I did experience one glitch. I call it the post-battle crash glitch. You can resolve this by selecting "run in compatibility mode" in a setting screen pertaining to the game file either in "C" drive or in the "properties" menu. After selecting Compatibilty Mode I've had zero crashes and can actually enjoy the game now.

Very deep and cerebral RPG. Explores the moral ramifcations of having the force in a way that no other Star Wars medium has. Worth playing for the story alone.
Gameplay is enjoyable if you can really figure it out, it's based on D+D and the combat is turn based, but it still feels pretty visceral. Being able to properly level your character and knowing where to properly spend points to get the character build you want is very important and very rewarding.
The recent update is great, it runs at modern resolutions excellently and the controller support is actually quite pleasant to use. It could be better though, there's no dedicated inventory, stealth or weapon switch buttons despite how important those features are and combat can be a bit finnicky, as the left and right d-pad buttons control both the usable items menu and the combat menu. It would probably benefit from a seperate, controller focused UI, but the controller support is otherwise rather good - there's nothing you can't do with the controller.
Due to the nature of the game, there is no benefit to using keyboard and mouse over a controller, or vice versa. It's all personal preference, and since I've played through this game about 10 times using keyboard and mouse, I found it quite nice to be able to relax and play with controller.
Performance is a bit dodgy, I'd recommend turning off Frame Buffer Effects to maintain a solid 60fps. This removes some of the effects though, like the stealth effect, so bear that in mind. I found that I got about 25-30fps with the buffer effects on and 200fps+ with them off, so it's quite a difference. This is with an I5-3570k and two GTX 780s as well, so it's a bit ridiculous that I have to turn off any effects.
The game is a bit buggy, but far less buggy than it was prior to the recent update. The bugs I had before the update included suddenly being unable to move, which required quicksaving and then re-loading, and dialogue randomly skipping. The random dialogue skipping pretty much ruined the ending of the game for me, as it just skipped all the important dialogue and I didn't realise what was happening. This was prior to the update though, so I'm keen to know if that bug has been fixed. I'll update the review if I experience that bug again.
So yeah, if you enjoy Star Wars, enjoy RPG games and enjoy being immersed in lore and thinking about things, this game is worth picking up. Try and play the original game first though, this game is a direct sequel to the original KoTOR.
